->*To the Most Honorable Lord,*<-

# Lord JOHN ROOS
## Son of the Most Illustrious JOHN,
## Earl of *Rutland*,
### WILLIAM SPENCER.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial 'G' containing a figure, likely a saint or scholar, seated in a pastoral landscape with architectural ruins in the background. The letter is surrounded by intricate floral and vine scrollwork.</image-desc>This book is eager (*Most Honorable Lord*) to display your name at its front no less than that of *Ambrose* <note>Ambrose was the wealthy patron of the early Christian scholar Origen; Spencer is drawing a parallel between Lord Roos and this historical figure</note>; relying on the very argument it treats: the defense of the *Catholic* <note>original: "Catholicæ"; here referring to the universal or orthodox Christian faith rather than specifically the Roman Catholic Church</note> faith and the *Christian* Religion. This cause alone is your love and delight, and it has stirred such great and wonderful passions in you—as if the face of virtue were somehow made more beautiful—that I would seem to be detracting from the honors due to you, and from the most upright patron of a most honorable cause, were I not to commend this volume of *Origen* to a stronger protection and to a most Illustrious name, insofar as it is yours. It is plainly worthy of your piety, and worthy of that rank in which God, the Best and Greatest, has placed you, to look out for the Christian cause and to give solace to the ashes and bones of *Origen*; so that those who preferred that the brightest light of the Churches be hidden in mist and darkness may see him recalled into the light and graced by the splendor of your name. How pleasing and delightful it is to the *Christian* people when they seek bright examples of piety and of protecting Religion from the highest men! When a man of the purple <note>A reference to high nobility or aristocratic status</note> does not blush at the worn-out gowns of men of letters! When one descended from the most ancient lineage vindicates the truth—which is older than any family line—from the frauds of the *Innovators* <note>original: "Novatorum"; a common 17th-century term for those perceived as introducing heretical or unauthorized changes to religious doctrine</note> and from childish deceit! How beautiful it is in the first flower of youth to undertake these exercises of a good mind and these duties of genuine piety, which grown men avoid and old men scarcely learn! How glorious to despise the madness of the common folk, and to care more solicitously for heaven and the seats of the blessed than for broad fields and majestic palaces, in which most men are accustomed to glory! How blessed it is not to depart even a fingernail’s breadth <note>An idiom meaning "not in the slightest degree"</note> from integrity of life and innocence of character, and to be sustained by a noble conscience of deeds well done: so that when the time comes for you to depart from the earth, as the common lot of men dictates, a great hope may cherish you; and may a lighter headstone adorn your body, while a conscience unburdened by the weight of even the smallest sin adorns your soul. Indeed, relying on the best omens, we do not despair that all these things will come to pass according to your heart's desire. Truly, it is incredible what gladness we enjoy, what great pleasures we perceive, and with what great joys we exult, while we behold piety without deceit, di-

One may behold affections toward Religion that shrink from that tearful and womanly piety which puts the highest matters at risk; in short, a man fashioned from an ample abundance of virtues and ornaments. In this alone are we unhappy: that we are able to see such an illustrious example of virtue, but not imitate it. Since this crown (Most Honored Lord) encircles Your head, and since these consolations of a soul soon to depart tickle Your heart with solid pleasure, *that Day* shall come, more welcome to You than it is to be dreaded by the greedy, the sacrilegious, the tyrants,

# TO THE READER.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring a figure in classical attire within an architectural and foliate frame.</image-desc> Perhaps you wonder, and would most gladly hear, what reasons impelled us to take care in producing a new edition of Origen: since a great part of the learned world, and the more sound theologians who have at heart a right faith in God, would celebrate triumphs if Origen had met with total destruction, and if a silence more profound than that of the Pythagoreans <note>The Pythagoreans were famous for a five-year vow of absolute silence during their initiation.</note> were enjoined upon this strenuous defender of *metempsychosis* <note>The transmigration of souls, or reincarnation; a doctrine Origen was famously accused of holding.</note>. For it has not escaped them that the most ancient overseers of Christian truth—as soon as this infinite evil began to creep into the Church and spread wider day by day—used censorial severity to brand his writings with the mark of heresy and blasphemy. It is a wonder they did not, with brains overheated, reduce to ashes the six thousand books which Origen, according to Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his fierce opposition to Origen.</note>, composed. Every one of those critics, wonderfully delighted by the reading of the Fathers and having attained therefrom a most full knowledge of Ecclesiastical matters, is now able to flash lightning, thunder, and throw the Church into confusion (just as Pericles did to Greece), and to summon witnesses from the monuments of the Fathers who will prove Origen guilty of heresy. They will feed and distort the ears of all with the recitation of impure dogmas even unto nausea. Among these, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate, who was initially an admirer of Origen but later became one of his most bitter critics.</note> holds the first rank; he begs you to give credit to his pronouncements, asserting that you will depart from the true and Orthodox opinion if any other view occupies your mind. <margin>Jerome in the Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus regarding the errors of Origen.</margin> Believe one who has experience: I speak as a Christian to Christians: his dogmas are poisonous, foreign to the Holy Scriptures, and do violence to the Scriptures. The learned Father proceeds, chastising Origen’s levity with the sharp judgment he is accustomed to; nor will it be enough for him to have narrated Origen's dreams, unless he also refutes the follies of the "Origenists" and offers up the most crafty patrons of such a wicked dogmatist to the laughter and mockery of all. <margin>Jerome, ibid.</margin> Some say more firmly: "How," he asks, "shall we condemn those whom the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD, which defined the nature of Christ's divinity against Arianism.</note> did not touch? For the Council that condemned Arius would surely have condemned Origen also, if it had rejected his dogmas." As if one medicine ought to cure all diseases at once! And therefore the majesty of the Holy Spirit must be denied, because in that Council there was silence regarding His substance. At that time the question was about Arius, not Origen; about the Son, not the Holy Spirit. They confessed what was being denied; they remained silent on what no one was asking about. And yet, they secretly struck at Origen, the fountainhead of Arius. For by condemning those who deny that the Son is of the substance of the Father, they condemned him and Arius alike. When Jerome feels that these arguments are held in little esteem, he calls Kings to his aid, so that those whom arguments and gentler warnings did not correct, <margin>Jerome against Rufinus.</margin> the laws and arms of Emperors might restrain. The writings of the Emperors, which command that the Origenists be driven out of Alexandria and Egypt, were also dictated at my suggestion: so that the Roman...

The Bishop of the city of Rome detests them with a marvelous hatred; it was my counsel that the whole world, after your translation <note>Referring to the translation of Origen's works from Greek to Latin</note>, should catch fire with hatred against Origen. My pen has worked so that those who previously read him with simplicity now reject him. Nor is Jerome any wiser than the rest. Epiphanius—who either discovered or created infinite heresies in the Church—joined his side. When the situation seemed to demand severity, he admonished John, Bishop of Jerusalem (a supporter of that same heresy), with great leniency. For I see that all your indignation has been stirred up for this reason: because I said to you that you ought not to praise the father of Arius <note>Arius was the founder of Arianism; the author here claims Origen's theology led to that heresy</note>, namely Origen, the root and parent of other heresies. --- For who among Catholics could endure with a calm mind—even those who adorn their faith with good works—to hear the doctrine and counsel of Origen, and believe in that famous preaching of his: **The Son cannot see the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit see the Son, etc.** To these are added Methodius, Eustathius, Apollinarius, and Theophilus, whom Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, the 5th-century church historian</note>—I know not whether led by blind love or relying on the consciousness of his office—called in the Sixth Book of his *Ecclesiastical History* the "Sharpness of the superiors."

<margin>
Baronius, Volume 7, Year 538.
</margin>
To the later ones was added a thunderbolt. Even now the Emperor Justinian has flared up with anger and resentment against the heretics. He struck our Origen—whom God, having pitied human infirmity, had called to His kingdom and rest—with a terrible thunderbolt. Perhaps by this art he attempted to benefit the living rather than harm the dead. For if he proposed another goal for himself and intended harm to a dead man, it will be necessary for us to assign these counsels of His Imperial Majesty either to ignorance or to malice. But these are the lightest matters. The wrath of God is weightier than the fury of Justinian; nor do the thunderbolt and threats of an Emperor strike as much horror as the face of the Supreme Judge and the fires of hell.

<margin>
Baronius, Volume 7, Year 532.
</margin>
Moreover, around the ninth hour of the following day, Brother Theophanes, who was in a cave, saw someone standing near him, terrible in appearance, saying: **"Come, and see the truth."** And taking him, he led him into a dark place, exhaling a foul-smelling fire, and in those very fires he saw Nestorius, Eutyches, Apollinaris, Dioscorus, Severus, and Origen, and certain others. And he who had appeared said to him: "This place is prepared for heretics, and blasphemers, and those who follow their dogmas." I omit mentioning the older disputes that occurred, and the gathering of infinite arrows which now Fathers and Popes, now Synods and Emperors, have twisted against Origen. I shall come to more recent men, and from these I will cite a single religious witness to this matter to save time:

<margin>Fasen. ibid. book 1, chapter 5; book 2, On the Pelagian Heresy, chapters 5, 7; book 4, chapter 19; book 6, chapters 6, 13; book 7, chapter 4. Volume 3, Page 474.</margin>For when Origen—out of no necessity, but solely from a desire for disputation—wished to debate at length in those books <term>On First Principles</term> <note>Greek: "Peri Archon" - Origen's most controversial work on the foundations of Christian doctrine</note> regarding the mysteries revealed by God to His Church, using the principles of Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy in which he had been polished, he accurately prefigured almost all the errors by which the Church was afflicted for three hundred years and more: the Arians, Macedonians, Photinians, and Pelagians <note>These are various early Christian groups later declared heretical for their views on the Trinity or human nature</note>, with God pursuing his audacity. *Do not the ears of the "Man of Brazen Guts"* <note>Latin: "Chalcenterus" - a nickname for the tireless scholar Didymus of Alexandria, here applied to the reader or Origen</note> *ring upon hearing these things? Is this the son of the martyr Leonides? Is this the patron of the Christian religion? Is he worthy to thunder against Celsus the Epicurean?* Indeed, he is most worthy; and we shall prove this in our treatise **On Ecclesiastical Writers**, who flourished from the birth of Christ until the Council of Nicaea. This work, God willing, we shall publish when we have gained a little more age. In that work, we shall separate the genuine writings of each man from the forged ones, and also their lives and doctrines, about which the learned have stirred up no small controversies. Thus it can be better discerned to what extent they agree with or oppose the Papists, Socinians, Arminians, Calvinists, and other sects of the Christian religion. If we do not weave this together with the same ornament of learning and speech as others, we shall do so with greater integrity.

Indeed, these critics must be earnestly entreated to deal more kindly with us, and to voluntarily remit and pardon the animadversions and torments they use against those who have slipped. For I have been able to acquire none of those things which are usually a help to others, even though all my care was occupied in obtaining them. Hoeschelius had two manuscript codices which he had drawn from the Palatine, Bavarian, and Augustan libraries, and distinguished men provided Tarinus with an abundance of many more: I have used only these printed editions, and shall I call it my good fortune or misfortune? --- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the biographical account of Origen of Alexandria, likely from Jerome’s "On Illustrious Men." The catchword "Ori-" indicates the continuation of Origen's name.</meta>

He wrote Commentaries on Matthew, through which he also attempts to confirm his own doctrine. Furthermore, he discovered with wonderful labor the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions <note>original: "quintam, & sextam, & septimam editionem"; these refer to versions of the Old Testament used in his massive Hexapla project</note>, which we also obtained from his library, and compared them with the other editions. And because I have already placed an index of his works in the volumes of Letters which we wrote to Paula—comparing them in a certain letter against the works of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro was a prolific Roman scholar; Jerome often compared Origen’s vast output to his</note>—I will omit it now. I shall not remain silent regarding his immortal genius: he so thoroughly learned Dialectics, as well as Geometry, Arithmetic, Music, Grammar, and Rhetoric, and the sects of all the Philosophers, that he even had zealous followers of secular literature, to whom he gave interpretations daily. Great crowds flocked to him, whom he received for the purpose of instructing them in the faith of Christ under the pretext of secular learning. Concerning the cruelty of the persecution which rose up against the Christians under Decius (because he vented his rage against the religion of Philip, whom he had killed), it is superfluous to speak; since even Fabian, Bishop of the Roman Church, perished in it, and Alexander and Babylas, the Bishops of Jerusalem and Antioch, died in prison for their confession of faith. And if anyone wishes to know what happened regarding the status of Origen, he can learn it clearly first from Origen's own Letters, which were sent to various people after the persecution, and then from the sixth book of the *Ecclesiastical History* by Eusebius of Caesarea, and from the six volumes written in defense of the same Origen. He lived until the time of Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until the 69th year of his age; and he died in Tyre, in which city he was also buried.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek translation of the Latin text above, provided for scholars of the period.</note>

He wrote commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew, through which he hastens to confirm his own doctrine; likewise, having found with much labor the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, some of which we also have from his library, he compared them with other editions. And since I have set down the list of his compositions in the volume of letters written by us to Paula, comparing them in one letter to the works of Varro, it must now be passed over. I will not be silent about his immortal natural talent, for he so learned Dialectics, Geometry, Arithmetic, Music, Grammar, and Rhetoric, and the doctrines of all the philosophers, that he had students who were listeners of worldly letters, and he explained these to them at every opportunity. Many crowds gathered to him, whom he accepted for this reason: so that on the pretext of teaching, he might lead them all to the faith of Christ. Regarding the cruelty of the persecution moved against the Christians by Decius (for he was maddened against the piety of Philip, whom he also killed), I think it is unnecessary to speak; for in that very persecution, Fabian, the bishop of Rome, died, and Alexander and Babylas, the bishops of Jerusalem and Antioch, fell asleep in prison as confessors. If anyone wishes to learn about Origen, he will be able to learn clearly first from his letters sent to various people after the persecution, and then from the sixth book of the history of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and from the six books written on behalf of the same Origen. He lived until Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until the sixty-ninth year of his life; and he fell asleep in Tyre, in which he was also buried.

### ->PORPHYRY in the *Life of PLOTINUS*.<-

When Origen had once come into the Schools, Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher; this anecdote illustrates the high respect the pagan philosophical world had for Origen's intellect</note> immediately, his cheeks flushed with a blush, wished to stand up. But having been asked by Origen to continue his discourse, he replied that the desire for speaking ceases when the speaker perceives that he is about to address those who already know exactly what he is going to say; and so, having discussed a few things, he rose from there.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the Porphyry anecdote translated above.</note>

When Origen once attended the gathering, Plotinus, filled with a blush, wished to stand up; but being requested by Origen to speak, he said that the impulses to speak are reined in when the speaker knows that he will be speaking to those who already know what he is about to say. And having thus conversed briefly, he stood up.

<summary>This page concludes a biography of the early Christian scholar Origen, detailing his vast education, his efforts to convert pagans through secular teaching, and his death in Tyre. It also includes a famous anecdote from Porphyry regarding the philosopher Plotinus's deep respect for Origen's intellect.</summary>

<meta>This is the opening page of Origen's "Against Celsus." The text is presented in parallel columns: Latin on the left and the original Greek on the right. The Latin translation was provided by the scholar Sigismund Gelenius.</meta>

# ORIGEN
# AGAINST
# CELSUS
->BOOK 1.<-

# ORIGEN ADAMANTIUS
# AGAINST CELSUS,

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.

Pilate said: "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor wondered greatly. <note>Matthew 27:13-14</note> For it was truly worthy of wonder, even to those capable of only moderate reflection, that one being accused and faced with false witness—who was able to defend himself, demonstrate his innocence of any crime, and recount the praises of his own life and his powers as coming from God, so as to provide the judge a path to pronounce a more favorable sentence—did not do this, but instead looked down upon and loftily disregarded his accusers. That the judge would have released Jesus without hesitation if he had made a defense is clear from what is recorded about him, where it says:
<margin>Matthew 27:17</margin>
"Which of the two do you want me to release for you? Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" * and
<margin>* and also</margin>
<margin>Ibid. 27:18</margin>
by what the Scripture adds, saying: "For he knew that they had handed him over because of envy." Jesus, therefore, is always being falsely witnessed against, and there is no time, while wickedness exists among men, when he is not accused. Even now he remains silent toward these things and does not answer with a voice, but he defends himself through the lives of his genuine disciples, which cry out his excellence and are stronger than any false witness, thus refuting and overturning the false testimonies and accusations. I dare to say, then, that your <note>Referring to Ambrosius, Origen's patron who requested this work.</note> request for us to make a defense weakens the defense found in the facts themselves, and the power of Jesus which is manifest to those who are not senseless. Nevertheless, so that we do not seem to shrink from the task commanded by you, we will attempt to dictate, according to our present ability, a response to each of the points written by Celsus which appeared to you to be subversive—not that any of his words are capable of shaking a person's faith. For may it never be that anyone is found who has so embraced the love of God in Christ Jesus that he could be shaken from his purpose by the words of Celsus or any like him. Indeed, Paul, listing countless things that usually separate one from the love of Christ and the love of God in Christ Jesus—over all of which his love was superior—did not include "words" in the list of things that separate. For observe first that he says:
<margin>Romans 8:35</margin>
"Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or
<margin>Psalm 44:22</margin>
the sword? (As it is written: 'For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.') No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us." Second, setting forth another rank of things that tend to pull away those not firmly rooted in godliness,
<margin>Romans 8:38</margin>
he says: "For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to [separate] us..."

Pilate: "Do you not hear how many testimonies they speak against you?" And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor wondered greatly. For this was truly worthy of wonder to anyone even moderately prudent: that he, who was pressed by crimes and false testimonies, though he could defend himself and prove his innocence and recount the praises of his whole life and divine virtues—thereby showing the judge a way to a milder sentence—made nothing of this, but rather despised and boldly contemned his accusers. Moreover, that the judge would have acquitted Jesus without delay if a defense had been heard is clear from these words of Scripture: *"Which do you want me to release to you, Barabbas, or Jesus, who is called Christ?"* and from those which he soon adds: *"For he knew that they had handed him over because of envy."* Jesus is never not spoken of ill among men. He is silent indeed even now and does not answer with a voice; otherwise, he pleads his cause sufficiently while he cries out against his accusers through the lives of his true disciples, and refutes all the lies of the witnesses. I dare therefore to affirm that this defense which you require from us hinders that defense which consists of things and facts, and the power of Jesus which appears evidently to those who do not lack all sense. Nevertheless, lest we seem to reject your commands, we have endeavored to respond according to our strength to whatever writing of Celsus seems to you to be subversive; although his speeches are not able to move anyone from the faithful. For far be it that anyone should be found who has attained such charity of God in Christ Jesus that he is moved from his purpose by the words of Celsus or similar men. Certainly Paul, enumerating innumerable things which are accustomed to separate others from the love of Christ and from that charity of God which is in Christ—over all of which his own charity becomes superior—does not place "words" in this number. For attend first indeed to him speaking thus: *"Who shall separate us from the charity of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? (as it is written: 'Because for your sake we are handed over to death daily, we are accounted as sheep of the slaughter') but in all these things we overcome through him who loved us."* Secondly, indeed, listing another order of those things which are accustomed to tear away those little-strengthened from piety, he says: *"For I know that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from..."*

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book I

Those who established sects in Philosophy were endowed with no common genius in such matters. And just as no one would call a faulty diagram in Geometric speculations a "false writing" if someone were to draw it or even write it out for the sake of exercise; so too, books ought to report the opinions of some Philosophical sect, which might deservedly be called an empty deception and a tradition of men according to the elements of this world <note>original: "inanis deceptio, & hominum juxta hujus mundi elementa traditio" — a reference to Colossians 2:8</note>. It seemed good to us to place this preface before the beginning; hereafter we shall respond to everything in turn, up to those things which Celsus speaks against Jesus from the persona of a Jew. This is so that whoever reads our responses to Celsus first, upon encountering his work, may know that he did not write for the faithful, but either for those entirely ignorant of the Christian faith, or for those who are weak in the faith, as the <margin>Rom. 14. 1.</margin> Apostle names them when he says: *Accept the one who is weak in faith*. Let this also be added to the preface: that our purpose was one thing while we were responding to the beginning of Celsus’s writings, and another while responding to what followed. For at first, we attempted to touch upon individual chapters and reduce what I might say against them into a compendium; afterward, we aimed to gather the discourse as if into a single body. Later, however, the matter itself warned me to save time, and being content with those compendious responses, to strive in the following parts to the best of our ability against the crimes alleged. Therefore, we ask for indulgence regarding the first part of the work which follows the preface. But if even the following parts do not seem sufficiently effective to persuade you, and you seek further responses to Celsus’s words, I refer you to others more prudent and more capable, who are able through speeches and books to refute his accusations. Yet it would be better to need no responses at all, even if someone should happen upon Celsus’s commentaries, which any faithful person in Christ, through the spirit dwelling within them, would deservedly despise.

The first chapter of accusation for Celsus is that secret assemblies are held by Christians, which are forbidden by the laws. For he says some assemblies are celebrated openly and legally, while others are done in secret and are condemned by the laws. These points tend toward his slandering of what Christians call <term>Agape</term> <note>The "Love-feast" or communal meal of the early Christians</note>, claiming it was instituted because of common danger and as if it attempted to violate oaths. Therefore, since he boasts of public laws, saying that Christians hold their assemblies in contempt of them, it must be answered that just as—

# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## B 3.

Just as if a stranger among the Scythians <note>A nomadic people of Central Eurasia, often used in classical literature as the archetype of "barbaric" or lawless people.</note> who use wicked laws were unable to withdraw himself from there, and was compelled to live among them, and used true laws, he would seem to violate the rights of the Scythians and to conspire with those of a different opinion: so the laws of the nations judge against the truth, which introduce the worship of statues and of an impious multitude of Gods, and in this part they surpass Scythian cruelty. It is not, therefore, absurd to form associations against the laws in favor of the truth. For just as if some people were to conspire against a Tyrant who had seized a city in order to kill him, they would be doing this rightly; so if Christians, oppressed by the tyranny of the devil and of falsehood, conspire against his laws and against the devil himself: they take care to save as many as they can by their persuasion and withdraw them from him, as if from the law of tyrants and Scythians. Next, he says that this sect is of barbaric origin, clearly censuring Judaism, with which Christianity is joined. And rightly he does not blame the barbaric origin, since in the very beginning of his discourse he praises the barbarians as the inventors of doctrines. He adds to these that the Greeks excel in judging, confirming, and exercising toward virtue the inventions of the barbarians. This, therefore, we seize from the writings of the adversary himself in defense of Christianity: since it is true that a man trained in Greek disciplines, if he approaches it, would not only approve the truth, but confirm it by exercise, and if anything should seem to be lacking, he would supply it with Greek reasonings, to establish the truth of the Christian religion. To these things it must be added, that our discipline has a certain demonstration of its own, more divine than are the demonstrations of the Greeks, which the Apostle calls the *demonstration of the spirit and of power* <note>original: "demonstrationem spiritus & virtutis"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:4.</note>: inasmuch as the spirit establishes faith through prophecies in those things which are told of Christ, and power truly through wonders, which we believe were done both by other arguments, and because even now traces of them remain, at least among those who live according to His will. After this, when he had said that Christians do and teach whatever they please in secret, and that not without cause, namely so that they might drive away the capital punishment threatened against them, he compares this danger with the dangers of the professors of philosophy, such as Socrates—he could have added Pythagoras and other philosophers. It must be answered to this, that the Athenians immediately repented of the crime committed against Socrates, nor did they retain their hatred beyond his death:

<column-break/>

Just as if someone among the Scythians, who use lawless laws, being unable to withdraw or having no opportunity, were forced to live among them; this man would reasonably, through the law of truth (as opposed to the lawlessness of the Scythians), and having formed agreements with those of like mind against those laws, act contrary to their established customs. In this way, the laws of the nations, which concern statues and godless polytheism, judge <margin>* judge</margin> against the truth; they are the laws of Scythians, or if anything is more impious than Scythians. It is not unreasonable, then, to make agreements contrary to established customs for the sake of the truth. For just as if some people secretly <margin>* were making.</margin> made agreements to do away with a tyrant who had seized cities, they would be doing well; so indeed Christians, since the one called the devil and falsehood among them acts as a tyrant, make agreements <margin>* to judge.</margin> contrary to the established customs of the devil, against the devil, and for the salvation of those whom they are able to persuade to revolt from the law, as it were, of Scythians and tyrants. Next, he says the doctrine is barbaric from above <note>meaning from its ancient origin</note>, clearly meaning Judaism, upon which Christianity is hung. And he fairly does not reproach the word for its origin from barbarians, contending that barbarians are capable of discovering doctrines. But he says of these things, that the Greeks are better at judging and confirming for the practice of virtue the things discovered by barbarians. This, therefore, is available to us from the things said by him, for a defense concerning the things laid down in Christianity, which are true: that someone coming from Greek doctrines and exercises to the Word would not only <margin>1 Cor. 2.4.</margin> judge them to be true, but having practiced them would establish them, and would fill up what seems to be lacking in regard to Greek demonstration, establishing the truth of Christians. But it must be said to this, that there is a certain proper demonstration of the Word, more divine than the Greek demonstration from dialectics. This more divine one the Apostle calls the "demonstration of spirit and power." Of spirit, through the prophecies, which are sufficient to produce faith in the reader, especially in things concerning Christ; and of power, through the marvelous powers which must be established as having happened both from many other things, and from the fact that traces <margin>* remain.</margin> remain among those who live according to the will of the Word. After these things, having spoken about Christians doing and teaching in secret the things that please them, and that they do this not in vain, since they are pushing away the penalty of death hanging over them; he likens the danger to the dangers that happened in philosophy, as to Socrates—he could have said also as to Pythagoras and other philosophers. But it must be said to this, that the Athenians immediately repented toward Socrates, and remained in no [hatred]...

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 1.

...the same remained with them always as was fitting, and also in the case of Pythagoras. For the Pythagoreans established their schools for a long time in Italy, in the region called Greater Greece <note>original: *magna Græcia*</note>. But against the Christians, the Roman Senate, the Emperors of the time, the military, the common people, and even the relatives of believers rose up against the Word. It would have been hindered and defeated by the plots of so many, had it not, by divine power, emerged and ascended to conquer the entire world that was plotting against it. 

Now let us see how he <note>Celsus</note> thinks to disparage the ethical portion of our teaching by saying it is common to other philosophers and is not a venerable or new doctrine. To this it must be said: if those who introduce the righteous judgment of God were to exclude punishment for sins, it would be because not everyone possessed a healthy, proactive understanding of ethics according to common ideas. Therefore, it is not surprising that the same God has sown the seeds of those things which He taught through the prophets and the Savior into the souls of all men. This was done so that every man might be without excuse at the divine judgment, having <margin>Romans 2:15. * the work.</margin> * the will of the law written in his own heart. 

The Word hinted at this in what the Greeks consider a myth, depicting God as having written the commandments with His own finger and <margin>Exodus 31:18 & 32:20</margin> giving them to Moses—which the wickedness of those who made the golden calf shattered, as if to say the flood of sin washed them away. But God gave them a second time, written <margin>Ibid. chapter 34:1.</margin> again after Moses had hewn the stones; as if the prophetic word was preparing the soul, after the first sin, for the second set of God’s letters. 

Then, addressing the matter of idolatry as specifically relevant to the argument, he prepares his ground by saying: Christians do not consider these handmade objects to be Gods because it is not reasonable to believe that works produced by the lowest craftsmen of wicked character—often constructed by unjust men—are Gods. In the following section, wishing to make this a "common" idea and not something first discovered by us, he sets forth a saying of Heraclitus, which says something similar: that those who approach soulless things as Gods act as if someone were to hold a conversation with walls. Therefore, it must be said regarding this that, just like other ethical topics, these ideas were sown in men, from which Heraclitus and any other Greek or Barbarian drew this opinion. He also points out that the Persians hold this view, citing Herodotus as a witness. We, however, would also cite Zeno of Citium, who says in his *Republic*: "There will be no need to build temples, for nothing should be considered sacred or of great value and...

<column-break/>

...and the same was done regarding Pythagoras. Certainly, the Pythagoreans held schools for a long time in that part of Italy which was called Greater Greece. However, against the dogmas of the Christians, the Roman Senate, the Emperors, the armies, the people, and even the very kin of the faithful conspired; they would surely have been oppressed, infested as they were by so many enemies on all sides, had they not, sustained by divine virtue, emerged from so many pressures and conquered the whole world that had risen against them. 

Now let us see how he thinks he can calumniate that part which pertains to morals, saying: "This is common with the rest of the philosophers, and there is nothing great or new in our discipline." To this it must be answered: those introducing the just judgment of God would be rejected along with the punishments for sins themselves, unless the common sense of all people had a predisposition toward moral discipline implanted within them. Wherefore it is not to be wondered at that the same God has implanted the seeds of those things which He taught through the prophets and the Savior into the minds of all mortals, so that in the divine judgment every man is inexcusable, having the intent of the law written in his heart. 

This is what the fabulous story (as the Greeks think it) obscurely indicates when it introduces God delivering the precepts written with His own finger to Moses, and those being soon broken through the malice of those who had cast the calf; as if he were saying that by the overflowing of sins, they were abolished. But God gave them a second time, written on stone tablets hewn by Moses, surely the prophetic word preparing the soul after the first sin for the second letters of God. 

Next, making mention of idolatry as properly belonging to the present argument, he thus clears a path for himself, saying: Christians do not hold handmade gods as deities, since it is not consistent with reason to count the common works of worthless and often wicked craftsmen among the Gods. Therefore, as the discourse proceeds, wishing to show that this opinion is also common to us and others, and was not first devised by Christians, he brings forward the saying of Heraclitus: that those who approach lifeless gods act just as if... <note>The Latin text here appears to have a slight omission or compression compared to the Greek regarding the "talking to walls" metaphor.</note> regarding this matter it must be said that the sense of it is implanted in men, just like the remnants of moral discipline, from which source both Heraclitus and any other, whether Greek or Barbarian, drew this opinion. For he relates that the Persians also feel the same, bringing Herodotus as a witness. But we shall also allege Zeno of Citium, writing thus in his book *On the Republic*: "It will not be necessary to build shrines, for nothing is to be thought sacred, or holy, or of any value..."

Certainly, such great power is in the name of Jesus against demons, that sometimes it is effective even when named by wicked men; which Jesus taught when he said: <margin>Matthew 7:22.</margin> *Many will say to me in that day, in your name we have cast out demons and performed miracles.* I do not know whether Celsus maliciously concealed this or omitted it through ignorance. But on the contrary, although this argument about the manner in which Jesus did these things may seem insoluble; it is nevertheless certain that Christians practice no incantations, being content only with the name of Jesus and other words in which faith is placed according to the sacred scripture. Then, since he frequently calls the doctrine "secret": this also must be refuted, since the preaching of Christians is better known throughout the whole world than the decrees of philosophers. Who does not know of his resurrection believed by many, and the announcement of judgment, which will render punishment to sinners and rewards to the righteous according to their merit? Indeed, even the mystery of the future resurrection is common knowledge, even if it is laughed at by unbelievers. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book I.

->**[Column 1: Greek]**<-

...being taught in secret those things not worthy to reach profane and not yet purified ears. Indeed, all mysteries everywhere throughout Greece and barbarian lands, being hidden, are not slandered for that reason; therefore, Celsus slanders the secrecy of Christianity in vain, without even accurately understanding it. He seems, in a way, to speak with great skill in favor of the martyrs of Christianity who stand firm until death, saying: “And I say this: that one who holds to a good doctrine, even if he is likely to encounter danger from men because of it, ought not to abandon the doctrine, nor pretend to have abandoned it, nor deny it.” And he certainly condemns those who carry the name of Christianity but pretend not to carry it, or deny it, saying: “One must not pretend in his doctrine to have abandoned it, or become a denier of it.” 

Celsus must be refuted here as one who says things contrary to himself. For he is found from his other writings to be an **Epicurean** <note>A follower of Epicurus, who generally believed the gods did not intervene in human affairs—a view Origen uses to show Celsus's hypocrisy.</note>; yet here, so that his accusation of the Word <note>original: *logos*</note> might seem more plausible, he does not confess the teachings of Epicurus. Instead, he pretends that there is something in man better than his earthly nature which is kin to God, and says: “that in those for whom this is well—that is, the soul—it yearns in every way for its kin,” meaning God, “and they desire to always hear and remember something about Him.” 

Observe, then, his own "adulterated" soul. While pretending that one who holds a good doctrine, even if he is to face danger among men for it, should not depart from the doctrine, nor pretend to depart, nor deny it, he himself falls into all these contradictions. For he knew that if he confessed to being an Epicurean, he would have no credibility in accusing those who in any way introduce **Providence** <note>The belief in God's intervention and care for the world.</note> and set God over all things. It is handed down that there were two Epicurean Celsuses: the first during the time of **Nero**, and this one during the time of **Hadrian** and later. 

After this, he exhorts us to follow reason and a rational guide in accepting doctrines, as if deception entirely happens to those who do not assent in this way; and he likens those who believe without reason to begging priests of Cybele, soothsayers, and those of **Mithras** and **Sabbadius**, or whatever phantoms of **Hecate** or other demons one might encounter. For just as in those cases, wicked men often take advantage of the ignorance of the easily deceived and lead them wherever they wish, so he says it happens among the Christians. He says that some, not even wishing to give or receive a reason for what they believe, use the phrase: “Do not examine, but believe,” and “Your faith will save you.” And he says they say: “The wisdom in the world is an evil thing, but foolishness is a good thing.”

* and he says
</margin>

<column-break/>

->**[Column 2: Latin]**<-

...others learned in secret the reasons not to be published to the profane and those not yet purified. The other mysteries, too, which are performed everywhere through Greece and barbarian lands, no one slanders on the grounds that they are done in secret; therefore, he also thoughtlessly slanders the secret rites of the Christians. Moreover, he seems to vehemently patronize the martyrs of the Christians who are constant even unto death, with these words: "Nor do I say this because I think one should depart from a right opinion because of danger threatened by men, or that a departure should be feigned, or that which you feel should be denied in words." Here he condemns those who, while feeling as Christians, deny or dissimulate it, disapproving of all fiction or negation here. 

On this account, Celsus comes to be rebuked as one who, being inconsistent with himself, teaches contrary things. For he is caught in his other writings being an **Epicurean**; but here, so that his accusation may seem more probable, not professing the decrees of Epicurus, he puts forward as if he feels there is something in man more excellent than his earthly nature, which has a kinship with God. He says this is the soul, which in those in whom it is well-disposed, seeks in all ways the divine nature kindred to itself, and they themselves desire to always hear and remember something concerning God. 

Consider, therefore, his own "adulterous" soul: he who prefaced that one holding a right opinion, even if he is endangered among men because of it, must not fail, nor feign a failure, nor deny it in words—he himself falls into all the opposites. For he knew that if he acted as an Epicurean by profession, he would take away his own credibility when accusing any kind of assertors of **Providence** who contend that God carries the care of all things. It is handed down, however, that there were two Epicurean Celsuses: one older, in the age of **Nero**, but this one in the time of **Hadrian** and later times. 

Then he exhorts that by following the lead of reason we should receive doctrines, since from rash assent all deceit arises. And those who are credulous without reason, he says are like those who are delighted by traveling charlatans and jugglers, and those of **Mithras** and **Sabbadius**, or whatever sights of **Hecate** or other demons. For just as wicked men of that kind, mostly mocking the simple common people, lead them wherever they please, likewise he says it is accustomed to happen among Christians. He adds that some of them do not even wish to either give or receive a reason for their faith, and use that saying: "Do not examine, but believe," and "That faith of yours will save you." And they are accustomed to say: "Worldly wisdom is a bad thing..."

What I have said about the wise and the common folk of the Egyptians, the same might also be said of the Persians, among whom there are mystic rites which are observed with certain reasons by men of excellent learning; but by the common people only the external signs are handled, with no concern for the deeper knowledge of those things signified through them. The same is to be felt regarding the Syrians and Indians, and as many others as have scriptures together with fables. through all dangers and the ever-expected deaths, they abound in traveling everywhere in the inhabited world for the sake of the salvation of men. Then, since Celsus says in these very words: “If they will indeed be willing to answer me as to one not merely trying them—for I know all things—but as one caring for all equally, it would be well. It must be said regarding the phrase, “For I know all things,” that it is most boastfully dared by him; for if he had read especially the prophets, who are full of acknowledged enigmas and words unclear to the many; and if he had encountered the evangelical parables, and the rest of the writing of the Legal and Jewish history; and having read the voices concerning the apostles, had wished with a fair mind to enter into the sense of the words; he would not have been so bold, nor said, “For I know all things.” Just as we ourselves, who have spent our time in these things, would not say, “For I know all things.” For truth is dear. None of us will say, “I know all the things of Epicurus”; or will be confident that he knows all the things of Plato; there being so many disagreements even among those who explain them. For who is so bold as to say, “I know all the Stoic doctrines,” or “all the Peripatetic”? Unless perhaps he heard the “For I know all things” from some uneducated commoners who do not perceive their own ignorance, and thought that by using such teachers he had known everything. And what I said about the Egyptian wise and commoners, one can <margin>\* say.</margin> see also concerning the Persians; among whom there are rites, conducted rationally by the learned among them, but performed symbolically by the many and more superficial among them. And the same must be said about the Syrians, and Indians, and as many as have both myths and writings. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.

<margin>1 Cor. 3:18 * among you.</margin>
...the passage reads as follows: *If any among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may become wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.* Therefore, the Apostle does not say simply that "wisdom is foolishness with God," but specifically "the wisdom of this world." And again, he does not say "if anyone seems to be wise among you, let him become a fool" in an absolute sense, but "let him become a fool in this age, so that he may become wise." By "wisdom of this age," we mean all the philosophy of those with false opinions which is rendered useless according to the Scriptures. And we speak of a "good foolishness"—not in a general sense, but when someone becomes a "fool" to this age. It is as if we were to say that a Platonist, who believes in the immortality of the soul and the teachings regarding its transmigration <note>original: *metensomatosis* (reincarnation)</note>, has taken up "foolishness" in the eyes of the Stoics, who mock such assent; or in the eyes of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, who chatter about the "frivolities" of Plato; or in the eyes of the Epicureans, who charge those who introduce Providence and set God over the universe with "superstition." Furthermore, it is much better to give assent to doctrines with reason and wisdom than with mere faith; and that the Word <note>The *Logos*</note> willed this for some as a concession, so as not to leave humanity entirely without help, is shown by Jesus’s true disciple, Paul, when he says:

<margin>1 Cor. 1:21.</margin>
*For since, in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom did not know God, it pleased God through the foolishness of the message preached to save those who believe.* It is clearly shown through these words that God ought to have been known through the "wisdom of God." But since this did not happen, God secondly was pleased to save those who believe, not simply through "foolishness," but through a foolishness specifically regarding the *preaching*. For the immediate preaching of Jesus Christ crucified is the "foolishness of the message," just as the same Paul says: *But we preach Jesus Christ, and Him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Greeks <note>original: *Ethnesi* (Gentiles/Greeks)</note> foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.*

<margin>Ibid. v. 23. * Gentiles.</margin>
Celsus, thinking there is a kinship among many of the nations regarding his own argument, names all the nations as having originated such a doctrine. But I do not know why he slanders the Jews alone, not including them <margin>* he himself</margin> with the rest, as if they had either shared the same labors and opinions as the others, or had taught very similar things in many respects. It is worth asking him, then, why he believes the histories of the barbarians and the Greeks regarding their antiquities...

<column-break/>

...are read there in this manner: *If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise: for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.* Therefore the Apostle does not say simply, that wisdom is foolishness with God: but the wisdom of this world: and again, not if anyone seems to be wise among you, let him be simply a fool: but in this world let him become a fool, that he may turn out wise. We call the wisdom of this world, therefore, that which is rendered useless and superfluous by the holy scriptures, being a whole philosophy filled with false dogmas: likewise we say there is a "good foolishness" not absolutely, but whenever someone becomes senseless to this world. As if we were to say that even a Platonist believing in the immortality of the soul, and those things which are handed down concerning its transmigration from bodies into other bodies, has assumed a "foolishness" as far as the opinion of the Stoics is concerned, who drive out this credibility of theirs with quibbles; and as far as the Peripatetics who hold the ravings of Plato in mockery; then as far as the followers of Epicurus, who reproach the assertors of providence with superstition, and those who believe that God is over the universe of things and governs it. To these things it must be added as a consequence, that it is better to assent to decrees with reason and wisdom, than by mere credulity, and that in some circumstances of life this pleased the Word, lest men should do nothing at all: this the true disciple of Jesus, Paul, indicates saying: *For since in the wisdom of God the world through wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.* It is clear therefore from these things, that in the wisdom of God it was necessary for God to be known: and because this was not done, again it pleased God to save those who believe, not simply through foolishness, but as far as the preaching is concerned. For since the beginning of the preaching of Jesus Christ is from his cross, it is the foolishness of preaching; just as Paul, understanding this, says in these words: *But we preach Jesus Christ crucified, unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them that are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.* But since Celsus thinks that a kinship of the same opinion exists between most nations (for he calls upon them all) as if they gave the beginning to such a dogma; I know not how he calumniates the Jews alone, not numbering their nation with the rest, as if agreeing with them in studies and opinions: wherefore I would gladly have asked him, why he is so credulous of the histories of the barbarians and Greeks concerning antiquities.

# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...regarding the antiquity of those whom he has listed by name, why does he deny credit only to the histories of this one nation? For if the writers of each nation have truthfully set forth their own affairs, why do we not believe the Prophets of the Jews alone? But if Moses and the Prophets produced many accounts concerning their own people out of mere favor <note>original: "ad gratiam" / "κεχαρισμένως" — meaning to flatter or show bias toward one's own kin</note>, why should it not be permitted to say the same of the historians of the remaining nations? Do the Egyptians deserve credit in their annals when they speak ill of the Jews? And do the Jews likewise lie when they complain about the Egyptians, recording that they were unjustly oppressed by many grievances, and that for this reason the just vengeance of God followed? This is something that cannot be said of the Egyptians alone: for we find the conflict of the Assyrians with the Jews, and mention of it in the antiquities of the Assyrians; and in turn, the writers of the Jews—for I do not yet wish to call them Prophets—have recorded the wars waged against the Assyrians. See then even now the arrogance of the man, who trusts others as wise, but utterly condemns the ignorance of these people. For hear the words of Celsus: *“There is truly an ancient doctrine, which the wisest nations, and wise cities and men, have maintained from the beginning.”* Yet he did not wish to call the Jewish nation "most wise," lest he should equal them to the Egyptians, Assyrians, Indians, Persians, Odrysians, Samothracians, and Eleusinians. 

How much more excellent than Celsus is that most learned man, as appears from his own writings, who scrutinized many more dogmas and collected from many sources what seemed to be true: Numenius the Pythagorean. In his first book *On the Good* <note>original: "περὶ τἀγαθοῦ"</note>, where he enumerates the nations that believe God to be incorporeal, he includes the Jews among them; nor was he reluctant to insert the words of the Prophets into his commentaries and to interpret their figures of speech <note>original: "figuras" / "τροπολογῆσαι" — referring to allegorical or metaphorical interpretation</note>. It is also said that Hermippus, in his first book *On Lawgivers*, recorded that Pythagoras brought his philosophy from the Jews into Greece. There also exists a book by the historian Hecataeus concerning the Jews, in which he so approves of the wisdom of this nation that Herennius Philo, in his own commentaries on the Jews, first doubts whether that work belongs to this historian; then he adds that, if it is indeed his, he seems to have been captivated by the persuasions of the Jews and to have accepted their decrees. But I marvel how Celsus, while he ranks the Odrysians, Samothracians, Eleusinians, and Hyperboreans among the most ancient and wise nations, did not deign to receive the Jews even into the rank of the wise or the ancient, although many writings are circulated among the Egyp-

-tians <note>The text breaks mid-sentence across the column/page transition</note> surprisingly, because among the many ancient writings circulated among the Egyptians...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

It seems to me that Celsus is doing the same thing as that Platonic character Thrasymachus <note>A character in Plato's *Republic* known for his aggressive and cynical definition of justice</note>, who would not allow Socrates to answer concerning justice as he wished, but said: "Beware that you do not say that justice is what is useful, or what is necessary, or any such thing." For this man, having accused the Mosaic histories (as it seems to him) and having blamed those who apply allegories to them—yet mixing in some praise by saying that such people are more reasonable—attempts by his accusation to hinder those who are willing and able to give a rational account of the whole business. 

But we are able to call for a comparison of books and say: "Come now, good man, bring forth the poems of Linus, Musaeus, and Orpheus, and the history of Pherecydes <note>Legendary Greek poets and mythographers</note>; and for the sake of investigating this matter, compare them with the laws of Moses: their narrations with his histories, and their moral rules with the precepts of our lawgiver. Consider which are more effective at changing the souls of men for the better, or at moving the listener away from his former way of life." 

And consider that those writers whom you have listed had almost no regard for the common reader, but wrote only for the learned, who are able to extract <term>tropologies</term> <note>figurative or metaphorical interpretations</note> and allegories of their own particular philosophy from them. But Moses, in his five books, behaved no differently than a vigorous orator who, having planned a certain figure of speech, pronounces his words accurately so that they might incline toward either sense: so that he neither provided the Jewish multitude an occasion for moral sin through an excessive number of instructions, nor did he leave the more prudent readers (who are rare) without material for contemplation and scrutiny. 

Indeed, the books of your "wise" poets do not even seem to be preserved any longer—though they certainly would have been preserved if there were any utility in them. But the writings of Moses have moved many even among those foreign to Jewish rites to believe; surely because, as is contained in the letters themselves, the first lawgiver of these things was God, the founder of this world, who delivered them to Moses. For it was fitting that the Maker of the whole world, after imposing laws upon the whole world, should add a power to them that would prevail everywhere among the nations. 

And these things are said by me while not yet inquiring about Jesus, but still about Moses, who was far inferior to the Lord; whom I shall show (as the proceeding discourse will make clear) to be much more excellent than your wise poets and philosophers. For it was fitting for the Creator of the whole world, having established laws for the whole world, to manifest a power in the words that masters those who have power everywhere.

# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...the name *Moses* was obtained. <note>original: "num nomen Moses consecutus est"</note> To this it must also be answered, that even if it be granted to him that Moses had heard an older doctrine, which he then passed on to the Hebrews: if he, hearing something false and possessing neither wisdom nor dignity, commended it to his disciples, he would be deservedly blamed. But if, as you say, he assented to wise and true opinions and taught them to his own people, what has he done that is worthy of reproach? Would that Epicurus, and Aristotle—who was somewhat less impious toward providence—and the Stoics, who affirm that God is a body, had heard this doctrine! Then the world would not be filled with disputes denying providence, or tearing it apart, and introducing a corruptible and bodily first principle. According to these Stoics, God is a body and is mutable, capable of all alterations, so that nothing prevents him from being corrupted if he should meet a corrupter; and he is "happy" only by the single fact that he lacks one. On the other hand, the doctrine of the Jews and Christians, which preserves an immutable and unalterable God, is held to be impious, because it does not follow the impiety of the impious, saying in prayers to God, *But You are the same*. <note>Psalm 102:27 (Vulgate 101:28)</note> God is also believed to have spoken that word, *I do not change*. <note>Malachi 3:6</note> After this, Celsus, not finding fault with the circumcision of the private parts practiced by the Jews, says they *borrowed it from the Egyptians*, preferring to believe the Egyptians rather than Moses, who records that *Abraham* was the first of mortals to be circumcised. <note>Genesis 17:24</note> Indeed, the name of *Abraham* is not only read in the writings of Moses, where he is described as a friend of God, but many of those who cast out demons <note>Exorcists using "magical" papyri often invoked the God of Abraham regardless of their own faith.</note> insert into their spells the phrase, *the God of Abraham*, indicating by this name his familiarity with God. Therefore they employ this expression, *the God of Abraham*, even if they do not know who that Abraham was. The same must be said of Isaac, Jacob, and Israel; which, although they are admittedly Hebrew names, are frequently interspersed among the more "effective" rituals of the Egyptians. Furthermore, regarding the reason for circumcision—which began with Abraham and was forbidden by Jesus, who did not wish his disciples to use it—it is not my purpose to explain that here. For the present time does not require a lecture on these matters, but rather a contest with Celsus to refute his slanders against the Jews. He thinks his refutation of Christianity will be easier if he can show that its beginnings flowed from a false Jewish religion. Next, Celsus speaks thus: *“These people, following their leader Moses, goatherds and shepherds, rustic*

<column-break/>

*...follies.”* <note>The Greek text on the right column mirrors the Latin on the left, providing the original source for Origen's citations of Celsus.</note> <margin>Note the end.</margin> ...so that the world might not be filled with words rejecting providence, or cutting it off, or introducing a corruptible physical principle, according to which even God is a body to the Stoics; they do not say he is incorruptible, but changeable, and through all things alterable and shifting, and simply capable of being destroyed, if he had a destroyer; but he is fortunate in not being destroyed, because there is nothing to destroy him. But the account of the Jews and Christians, which maintains the unchangeable and unalterable nature of God, is considered impious, since it does not share the impiety of those who think impiously about God, saying in prayers to the Divine: *But You are the same*. <margin>Ps. 101. 28. Mal. 3. 6.</margin> And God is believed to have said, *I have not changed*. Therefore they take up the phrase, *God of Abraham*, not knowing who *Abraham* is. And the same things must be said about *Isaac*, and about *Jacob*, and about *Israel*; which names, being confessedly Hebrew, have been scattered in many places among the Egyptians who promise some power in their studies. But the reason for circumcision, beginning from *Abraham* and being stopped by *Jesus*, who did not want his own disciples to do the same, it is not the present purpose to interpret. For the present time is not for teaching about these things, but for a destructive struggle against the charges brought by Celsus against the Jewish accounts, he thinking that he will more quickly make Christianity appear a falsehood if its beginning in the Jewish accounts has a charge already existing against those as being false. Following these things Celsus says, “that following their leader Moses, goatherds and shepherds, with rustic deceits...”

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book I.

> "...being led astray, they believed in **one God**." <note>Origen is quoting Celsus's dismissive view of the Jews.</note> Let him show, then, how—while goat-herds and shepherds have (as he thinks) irrationally abandoned the worship of many gods—he himself can establish the reality of the multitude of Greek or other barbarian gods. Let him demonstrate the actual existence and essence of Mnemosyne <note>The personification of Memory</note> who bore the Muses to Zeus; or of Themis <note>Divine Law</note> who bore the Seasons; or let him prove that the Graces, always depicted naked, exist in their own right. But he will never be able to show that these Greek fictions, which seem to be personified, are actually gods based on the reality of things. For why are the Greek myths about the gods any truer than, say, those of the Egyptians? The Egyptians do not even know in their own dialect a Mnemosyne as the mother of nine Muses, nor a Themis of the Seasons, nor an Eurynome as one of the Graces, nor any of their other names. How much clearer, then, and better than all these fictions, is the conviction drawn from visible things: that because of the orderly arrangement of the universe, one should worship its Creator—He being one, and the universe being a single harmonious whole. For this reason, the world could not have been made by many creators, just as the whole heaven is not kept in motion by many souls.
<margin>the one who carries.</margin>
For one soul is sufficient—**the one who carries** the entire fixed sphere <note>original: "aplanē", referring to the sphere of fixed stars</note> from East to West, embracing within it everything the world needs that is not self-sufficient. For all things are parts of the world, but God is not a part of the whole. For God must not be imperfect, as a part is necessarily imperfect.
<margin>these things were.</margin>

After this, Celsus says: "Those goat-herds and shepherds believed in one God, whether they call him the **Most High**, or **Adonai**, or **Celestial**, or **Sabaoth**, or by whatever name they delight in calling this world; and they know nothing beyond it." And he goes on to say: "It makes no difference whether the God over all is called by the name common among the Greeks, **Zeus**, or by a certain name (for example) among the Indians, or another among the Egyptians." It must be said in response to this that a deep and secret discourse arises concerning the **nature of names**. Is it, as Aristotle thinks, that names are given by **convention**? Or, as the Stoics believe, are they by **nature**, with the first sounds imitating the things they name (which is why they introduce certain principles of etymology)? Or, as Epicurus teaches (differently than the Stoics think), are they by nature...

<column-break/>

...deceived by tricks *they believed there is one God*. Let him show the substance and essence of Mnemosyne who bore the Muses from Jove, or of Themis who bore the Seasons, or let him present to us the Graces, always naked, in their own essence. But he will never be able to prove from the facts themselves that the Greek fictions, which seem to be given bodies, are Gods. For why are the Greek fables about the Gods truer than (for example) those of the Egyptians, who in their own language know no Mnemosyne as mother of the nine Muses, nor Themis of the Seasons, nor Eurynome as one of the Graces, nor the names of the rest? How much more probable and better than all these fictions it is, that someone, content with those things we see, should acquiesce to such an excellent disposition of the world, and worship the one Creator of the one world which harmonizes with its parts: from which it is clear that it could not have been created by many founders, nor can this whole heaven be moved by many souls. For one is enough, which carries the **fixed** <note>original: "aplanē"</note> sphere (as they call it) from the East to the West, containing within itself all things which the world needs, which are not absolute through themselves. For all things are parts of the world, but God is not a part of the universe. For it is necessary that God be not imperfect, just as a part is imperfect. But perhaps a deeper reason will reveal how, just as God is strictly not a part, so He is not a whole, since that consists of parts: nor will reason admit that God, who is above all things, should be understood as if He consists of parts, of which each one is by no means as powerful as all the rest. After this he says, *Those shepherds of goats and sheep chose one God for themselves, whether it be the Most High, or Adonai, or Celestial, or Sabaoth, or by whatever name they finally rejoice to call this world, beyond which they know nothing more:* and thereafter he adds, *it does not matter, even if by this name common among the Greeks the God of all things is called Jupiter, or by some other name used, for example, by the Indians or Egyptians.* It must be answered also to this, that the present dispute concerning the nature of names is deeper and more hidden: whether, as it pleases Aristotle, names are imposed on things by **institution**; or, as the Stoics prefer, by **nature**, with the first words imitating the things themselves which are named, for which reason they also introduce certain elements of etymology and reason; or, as Epicurus teaches otherwise than the Stoics think, they are indeed by nature...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.

...are names, but rather that the first men uttered certain sounds haphazardly regarding the things themselves? If, therefore, we are able in this present discussion to set forth the nature of efficacious names <note>original: "nomina efficacia" — names believed to possess inherent power or energy</note>, some of which are used by the wise men of the Egyptians, or the more learned Magi of the Persians, or the Brahmans or Samanaeans <note>Buddhist monks or ascetics</note> among the Indian philosophers, and so on for each nation: and if we can show that even what is called magic is not—as Epicurus and Aristotle suppose—an inconsistent thing, but as those skilled in these matters demonstrate, is something consistent, though having principles known to very few: then finally we shall say that the names **Sabaoth** <note>Lord of Hosts</note> and **Adonai**, and others handed down among the Hebrews with great veneration, were not applied to ordinary and created things, but contain a certain hidden Theology <note>original: "occultam quandam Theologiam"</note> which pertains to the Creator of the universe. For this reason, these names are efficacious if they are pronounced in a certain way and order proper to them. Other names of demons uttered in the Egyptian language have their own particular power, and others again in the Persian language; and thus among individual nations, different names are employed for certain uses. And so it will be found that, just as the earthly spirits <note>original: "genii"</note> have been allotted diverse places, so they are called by the specific names of those nations throughout each region. Therefore, whoever bestows even a small amount of thought on these matters with a more noble mind will religiously take care not to apply foreign names to things, lest something happen to him like those who, by error, attribute the name of God to inanimate matter; or who transfer the title of "the Good," which is due to the First Cause and to virtue and honesty, unto blind riches, or the proper proportion of flesh, blood, and bones in health and fitness, or that which is considered nobility of birth. And perhaps there is no less danger in bringing down the name of God or of "the Good" to things where it is not appropriate, than in exchanging names in secret words, and applying the inferior to the superior, or the superior to the inferior. I do not say that at the mention of **Jupiter** one immediately understands the son of Saturn and Ops <note>The Latin translation uses "Ops" for the Greek "Rhea"</note>, the husband of Juno, the brother of Neptune, the father of Minerva and Diana, the ravisher of his own daughter Proserpina: or that by the name of **Apollo** is heard the son of Latona and Jupiter, the brother of Diana, the half-brother of Mercury born of the same father, and whatever else those wise fathers of Celsus's doctrines and the ancient Theologians of the Greeks put forth. For by what chance did it happen that Jupiter is so named, and not otherwise? And that his father is Saturn, and Ops his mother? The same must be thought of the others who—

...names, the first men having broken off certain sounds for things? He, therefore, who has grasped the concept of these things with a more magnificent nature, even slightly, <margin>* will be careful.</margin> will be careful to apply different names to different things, lest he suffer something similar to those who erroneously apply the name "God" to soulless matter; or who separate the title of "the Good" from the First Cause, or from virtue and the beautiful, and apply it to blind wealth, and to the symmetry of flesh and blood and bones in health and well-being, or to supposed noble birth. And I do not say that with "Zeus" <note>The Greek text uses "Zeus" where the Latin used "Jupiter"</note> there is immediately understood the son of Cronus and Rhea, and husband of Hera, and brother of Poseidon, and father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who mingled with his daughter Persephone; or with "Apollo" is understood the son of Leto and Zeus, and brother of Artemis, and the brother of Hermes by the same father; and whatever else the wise fathers of Celsus's dogmas and the ancient theologians of the Greeks bring forward. For what is the logic that Zeus is the proper name, and that his father is Cronus and his mother Rhea? The same must be done for the others...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book I

...called Gods. This accusation is most unjust; whether they use the name **Sabaoth** <note>Hebrew: "Lord of Hosts"</note> for God according to some secret reason, or **Adonai** <note>Hebrew: "Lord"</note>, or any of the other names. When someone is able to philosophize about the secret nature of names, he would find much also regarding the invocation of the angels of God; of whom one is called **Michael**, another **Gabriel**, and another **Raphael**, named according to the duties they minister by the will of the God of all things in the universe. Our **Jesus** also belongs to a similar philosophy of names, whose name has already been clearly seen to drive out countless demons from souls and bodies, acting upon those from whom they were expelled. Furthermore, regarding the topic of names, it must be said that those skilled in the use of incantations report that the same incantation, when spoken in its native dialect, is able to effect what the incantation promises; but if translated into any other language whatsoever, it can be seen to be weak and powerless. Thus, it is not the things signified by the words, but the qualities and properties of the sounds themselves that have some power within them for this or that purpose. In this way, we shall defend the fact that Christians struggle even unto death so that they do not declare **Zeus** <note>Latin: Jupiter</note> to be God, nor name Him by any other dialect. For they will either confess the common name, "God," indefinitely, or with the addition of "the Creator of all things," "the Maker of heaven and earth," who sent certain wise men to the human race; when the name of God is applied to their name, it performs a certain power among men. Many other things could be said on the topic of names to those who think it should be a matter of indifference how they are used. For if **Plato** is admired for saying in the *Philebus*: *“But my fear, O Protarchus, concerning the names of the Gods is no small thing”*—since Philebus called "Pleasure" a goddess while conversing with Socrates—how much more should we accept the piety of Christians who do not attach any of the names used in mythology to the Creator of the universe? But enough of these things for the present. Let us see in what way **Celsus**, who claims to know everything, slanders the Jews, saying "they worship angels and are addicted to sorcery, of which **Moses** was their interpreter." For where in the writings of Moses did he find the lawgiver handing down the worship of angels? Let him who claims to know the affairs of Christians and Jews say. And how is there sorcery among those who have accepted the law of Moses, having read also this: *“You shall not cleave to enchanters, to be defiled by them.”* <note>original: "Τοῖς ἐπαοιδοῖς οὐ προσκολληθήσεσθε, ἐκμιανθῆναι ἐν αὐτοῖς."</note>

To this kind of philosophy of names belongs also our **Jesus**, by the efficacy of whose name already innumerable demons have been seen clearly put to flight from the bodies and souls of those possessed.
