# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...be polluted? Next, he promises that he will show how the *Jews, deceived by ignorance, have gone astray*. If he had grasped that their ignorance in recognizing Jesus Christ was born from a neglect of the Prophecies, he might truly have been able to prove the error of that nation; but as it is, since no such thing even entered his mind, he considers things to be errors of the Jews which are not. And having promised that he would speak later about Jewish affairs, he speaks first of our Savior, as the leader of this generation by which we are made Christians, *whom he says was the author of this doctrine only a very few years ago, and was held by Christians to be the son of God*. Regarding this point, that *he says he arose a few years ago*, we shall respond: in these very years in which it pleased Jesus to spread his word, he achieved so much that in many regions of our world he wonderfully affected not a few Greeks and barbarians, the wise and the foolish, so that they struggled even unto death for Christian piety <note>original: "pietate Christiana"</note> rather than deny it—something which is recorded by writers to have happened in no other school of thought <note>original: "dogmate"</note>: for indeed, this could not have happened without the favor of the divine. Truly, I speak not to win favor, but taught by experience, I would dare to assert that not even the bodies of the sick are restored to their former health without divine help; how much more so if someone were to free souls from the filth of vices, from lusts, iniquities, and contempt for the divine, and gave proof of this work in (for example) a hundred men: surely no one could reasonably say that he had instilled in those hundred men such powerful reasons for deliverance from so many vices without divine aid. He who considers these things prudently will agree that nothing among men is restored for the better without God; how much more will he who has confidence in Christ demonstrate this, if, inquiring into the lives of those who have given themselves to the Word, he compares their former way of living with that which they have now established? Let him notice in what great impurities, in what great iniquities and desires each individual was, before they—deceived, as Celsus and his like babble—received this doctrine, which seems to them ruinous to human life. From the time they received the Word, how much more just have they become, more serious, more constant; so much so, that some of them, out of love for extraordinary purity <note>original: "puritatis"</note> and so that they might approach divine worship more chastely, do not even use the permitted and lawful pleasures of love. He who reflects on these things will understand that Jesus dared things greater than human strength, and accomplished what he undertook.

<column-break/>

And he promises to teach next, "how the Jews also were deceived and fell into error through ignorance." And if he had intended to address the ignorance concerning Jesus Christ among the Jews who did not listen to the prophecies about him, he would truly have taught how the Jews were deceived; but now, not even wishing to imagine these things, he assumes that things which are not errors of the Jews are errors. And Celsus, having promised to teach later about the Jews, first directs his discourse toward our Savior, as having become the leader of the swarm of our nature according to the Christians, and says, "He himself, only a very few years ago, led the way in this teaching, being considered by Christians to be the Son of God." And concerning this point, that he existed only a few years ago, we shall say this: was it without God that Jesus, wishing in these years to sow his own word and teaching, was able to do so much that in many parts of our inhabited world not a few Greeks and barbarians, both wise and foolish, were so disposed toward his word that they struggled even unto death for Christianity so as not to renounce it—which no one is recorded to have ever done for any other doctrine? I, for my part, not flattering the Word, but attempting to examine the facts with scrutiny, would say that not even those who heal many sick bodies achieve the result of health for the bodies without God. And if someone could also deliver souls from the flood of wickedness, and from acts of licentiousness and injustice, and from contempt for the divine, and could give a demonstration of such a work, having improved the number of a hundred (for let the argument be based on these)—no one could reasonably say that he had implanted a word capable of delivering from so many evils in those hundred without God. If a fair-minded person considers these things, he will agree that nothing better has happened among men without God; how much more will he declare this with confidence concerning Jesus, examining together the changes in the former lives of many who come to the Word, from whatever injustices and greed each has been separated? And let him consider in what great licentiousness and injustices—as Celsus <margin>\* even if.</margin> and those who think the same as he does say—they were deceived and received <margin>\* but.</margin> a word that ruins, as those men say, the life of men. But from the time they have received the Word, in what way they have become more equitable and solemn and stable, so that some of them, through a love of exceeding purity and for the sake of worshipping the divine more purely, do not even touch the sexual pleasures permitted by the law. Anyone examining the facts will see that Jesus dared something greater than human nature, and having dared it, he achieved it.

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 1.

For although from the very beginning all have resisted the sowing of his Word throughout the whole inhabited world—including the kings of various times, the generals and governors under them, and, so to speak, everyone entrusted with any power whatsoever, as well as the rulers in every city, the soldiers, and the common people—it has nevertheless conquered. Being the Word of God, it is not of a nature to be hindered; and having become stronger than so many antagonists, it has mastered all of Greece and even more of the barbarian world, transforming countless souls to the worship of God according to its teaching. Now, it is necessary to see that since a great multitude are mastered by the Word,

<margin>* many times over.</margin>

the unlearned and more rustic folk are many times more numerous than those trained in logic; <note>Origen is arguing that the sheer number of converts naturally means more common people are represented than elites, simply by ratio.</note> indeed, the unlearned and rustic are many times more frequent than the intelligent. Then he says that after being cast out by her husband and wandering about in disgrace, she secretly gave birth to Jesus.

<margin>* he withdrew.</margin>

> "And because he [Jesus], on account of his poverty, went to work for hire in Egypt, and having there tried his hand at certain powers in which the Egyptians pride themselves, he returned, greatly puffed up by these powers, and because of them declared himself a God."

Now, to me—who cannot leave anything said by unbelievers unexamined, but who searches into the very origin of things—all these points seem to coincide with the fact that Jesus was worthy of being the Son of God according to ancient prophecy. For among men, it contributes much to someone becoming distinguished and famous, and his name well-known, when his parents

<column-break/>

For although all have resisted from the very beginning, so that his word might not be scattered through the whole world—the kings of every age, and their military as well as civil magistrates, and finally all endowed with any power, and the presidents of the people in every town and the prefects of the garrisons—the Word of God has conquered, which by its own nature does not allow itself to be suppressed, and remains invincible. And so, having subdued so many adversaries, it has brought all of Greece under its sway, and the greater part of the barbarian lands, and has led countless souls to piety. It was necessary, however, since everywhere there are more unlearned people than literate ones, that in such a great multitude of those giving their hand to the Word, there would be far more illiterate and rustic people than those notable for their erudition. But Celsus, unwilling to consider the kindness of the divine Word, which does not withdraw itself from any soul under the Sun, thinks the matter is a vulgar thing for ignorant men, as if a raw and by no means refined doctrine had persuaded only the plebeians and the unrefined; although he himself says that not only the unlearned were led to religion by the word of Jesus: for he confesses that many among them are modest, temperate, prudent, and fit for understanding allegories. But when he fashions the persona of a Jew, imitating in a way some pupil of the Oratorical art introduced to speak, he introduces a Jew saying to Jesus certain childish things, unworthy of the grey hair of a Philosopher. Come, let us examine these with all our strength and prove that he did not even preserve the decorum of the persona in the Jew's speeches. For he now makes the Jew arguing and rebuking Jesus on many counts, as it seems to him, and above all, that he had feigned himself born of a virgin; he even reproaches him that he was sprung from a Jewish village, and from a poor native woman who prepared her living by manual labor, whom he says was cast out by her husband, a builder in wood <note>original: "fabro materiario" (carpenter)</note>, as if caught in adultery. Then he relates that, expelled by her husband and wandering ignominiously, she gave birth to Jesus in a secret delivery; and that he, forced by poverty to serve for hire in Egypt, and having there been taught certain effective arts in which the Egyptians please themselves, returned swollen with such great power, on account of which he demanded to be held as a God. To me, indeed, who can leave none of those things which are objected to by infidels undiscussed, searching the principles of things, all these seem to agree, so that Jesus was deservedly called the Son of God according to the oracles of the prophets. For to men, lineage contributes much to illustrious fame and clarity of name, when their parents are power—

### Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...eminent and excellent, endowed with ample means for cultivating the genius of a son, and born to a great and noble fatherland. But when someone possessing everything contrary to these advantages can emerge from so many obstacles to clarity, and move the minds of the multitude by the fame of his name, and become celebrated throughout the whole world amidst diverse rumors echoing about him—should you not deservedly marvel at a nature of this kind? It shows itself noble while engaged in arduous affairs, and, being equipped with a confidence in speaking, is by no means to be despised. If anyone should wish to inquire further into such a man, would he not ask how one educated frugally and in poverty, instructed in no liberal disciplines, nor a candidate for eloquence or the suitable arts for swaying the minds of the people in assemblies and soothing listeners, could have undertaken to profess himself a teacher of new doctrines? He introduced to the human race a teaching that destroys the decrees of the Jews—while nevertheless preserving the authority of the Prophets—and tears up the laws of the Greeks along with their rites and ceremonies. Furthermore, how could such a man, so educated, having learned nothing great from any human (as his detractors admit), discourse upon the judgment of God, the punishments of the wicked, and the rewards of the good with such great admiration? He captured not only the rustic and illiterate common folk, but also not a few of the wiser sort, who were able to look more deeply into the fact that, once the viler elements of what seemed to be announced were set aside, there was something secret hidden beneath—so to speak. In Plato, a certain man from Seriphos <note>Seriphos was a small, proverbially insignificant Greek island.</note> reproached the most famous general Themistocles for his renown, as if it were not won by his own virtue, but because his fatherland happened to be the most noble city in all of Greece. He heard from the grateful Themistocles, who acknowledged that his country had indeed contributed something to his glory: *“I would not have become so famous had I been a Seriphian, nor would you have been a Themistocles had Athens been your fatherland.”* But our Jesus, although his fatherland is mocked as a mere village—and that not even a Greek one, nor of any celebrated nation—and he himself is defamed as the son of a poor woman and a laborer, and then, on account of poverty, having left his home to serve for hire in Egypt; to use the present example, he was not only born a Seriphian from the smallest and most ignoble island, but even, so to speak, the least of the Seriphians. Yet he was able to shake the entire inhabited world, not only more than Themistocles the Athenian, but even more than Plato or Pythagoras...

And yet, among men, it is a great achievement to attain fame if one has been able to take up *more [honors] at once. For one is admired for wisdom, another for generalship, and some among the barbarians for the powers of their wondrous incantations, and others for other things; in many such ways have men been wondered at and become famous. But in him, besides all else, there is wondered at his wisdom, his power, and his leadership. For he did not, like a tyrant, cause some to revolt with him against the laws, nor like a robber arm his followers against men, nor like a wealthy man provide for those who approached him, nor as those who are admittedly blameworthy; but as a teacher of the doctrines concerning the God of the universe, and of worship toward Him, and of every moral way of life which is able to reconcile to the God over all the one who has lived according to his [Jesus's] word. And while to Themistocles <note>An Athenian politician and general</note>, or any of the famous, nothing occurred to oppose their glory; to this man, in addition to what has been said—which was sufficient to hide the soul of a man even if he were quite naturally gifted—even the death which is thought most dishonorable by crucifixion was enough to vanish both his previous glory and that which had already taken hold, and to make those who (as those who do not agree with his teaching think) were falsely deceived, to stand away from the deception and condemn the deceiver. In addition to these things, one might wonder from where it occurred to the disciples—as those who speak ill of Jesus say—who had not seen him risen from the dead, nor were persuaded that there was anything more divine about him, not to fear suffering the same things as their teacher, and to go forth to meet the danger, and to leave their homelands for the sake of teaching according to the will of Jesus and the word delivered to them by him. For I think that he who examines the facts fairly would not say that these men gave themselves up to a life of flight for the sake of Jesus's teaching without some great persuasion which he instilled in them, teaching them not only to be disposed according to his lessons, but also to dispose others. Although it has happened to few men to attain glory by many titles at once; for one by wisdom, another by the arts of command, and some barbarians by the power of incantations, and others by other things, have prepared for themselves admiration and glory in not many things: but this man, beyond the rest, is to be wondered at for his wisdom, for his power, and for his knowledge of commanding. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.

-> ...that they might act in a way pleasing to the Creator of all things, is it not paradoxical that he should not have had a miraculous birth, but rather the most lawless and shameful of all births? I will speak as if to Greeks, and especially to Celsus—whether he truly follows these views or not, he certainly cites the teachings of Plato. Would the one who sends souls down into human bodies <note>Origen refers to the Divine or the Providential order</note> have thrust a soul that was to dare so much, to teach so much, and to turn many away from the flood of wickedness, into the most shameful birth of all, not even introducing him into human life through a legitimate marriage? Or is it more reasonable—and I speak now according to Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles, whom Celsus often names—that each soul is entered into a body according to certain secret reasons <note>original: "aporrhētous logous," referring to mystical or hidden principles of providence</note> and according to its merit and previous character? It is likely, then, that a soul which was to visit human life for the benefit of many (not to say all, lest I seem to speak prematurely) would require a body that was not only different from ordinary human bodies, but superior to all others. For if some souls, according to certain secret reasons, are deemed unworthy to be placed in a purely irrational body, yet not purely in a rational one, and thus put on a monstrous body <note>referring to congenital deformities or "portents"</note> so that reason cannot be fully realized—having, for instance, a head disproportionate and much smaller than the rest of the body—while another soul receives a body that allows it to be slightly more rational than the former, and another still more so, depending on whether the nature of the body offers more or less resistance to the grasp of reason: why should there not also be a soul that assumes a body that is entirely miraculous? A body having something in common with humans so that it might be able to converse with them, but also having something exceptional so that the soul might remain untainted by vice? If the claims of the physiognomists <term>Physiognomy: the ancient "science" of judging a person's character from their physical features</term> hold true—whether those of Zopyrus, Loxus, Polemon, or whoever else has written on such matters and promised wonderful insights—then bodies are entirely suited to the characters of souls. For a soul that was to visit life in a miraculous way and perform great deeds, was it necessary, as Celsus thinks, that it come from a Panthera <note>Celsus alleged Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera</note> and a corrupted virgin? For from such unions there would necessarily arise someone foolish and harmful to men, a teacher of licentiousness, injustice, and other evils; not a teacher of temperance, justice, and the other virtues. But, as it was fitting to say, the promise of a sign was to come from a virgin for the one named Emmanuel <note>Hebrew: "God with us"</note>, signifying that at his birth, God would be with men. And it seems appropriate to me, in addressing the character of the Jew <note>Celsus wrote his critique in the voice of a Jewish character</note>, to put forward the prophecy of Isaiah...

<column-break/>

...to the Creator of the world, should have had not a wonderful birth, but the most iniquitous and foulest of all? I will ask the Greeks, and especially Celsus, whether he agrees with Plato or not, since he certainly brings up Platonic ideas: Did he who sends souls into human bodies thrust one who would dare so much, and who would instruct and recall so many from the filth of vice, into the foulest birth of all, not even introducing him into human life through legitimate marriage? Or is it much more probable (I speak now according to Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles, whom Celsus often names) that each soul is assigned to a body by secret reasons according to its merits, and assigned also according to its past character? It is credible, therefore, that this soul also, being more useful to the life of men than many (lest, if I say all, I seem to speak prematurely), coming here had need of an outstanding body, indeed the most excellent of all. For if other souls, by certain secret reasons, are held unworthy to be placed in an entirely brute body, yet not worthy of a rational one, and a portentous body is put on, so that the one so born does not enjoy perfect reason, having a head smaller in proportion to the rest of the body; while another receives such a body that it is a little wiser than that one; and again another more or less according to the measure of the body not obeying reason: what forbids there being some soul which takes up a body in a new and wonderful way, which has something in common with men so that it can live with them, but also has something extraordinary, so that the soul remains immune from all vice? If the science of the physiognomists is true, whether of Zopyrus, Loxus, Polemon, or any of those who profess these things, what wonder if all souls have bodies suitable to them? Therefore, for that soul which was to travel in life as a new world and perform miracles, how could a body fall to its lot, as Celsus thinks, from the adultery of Panthera and a virgin? For from such an incestuous union there ought rather to have been born some insane person, harmful to men, a master of intemperance, injustice, and other vices; not of temperance, justice, and the rest of the virtues. Concerning this, the Prophets of old predicted, not remaining silent about the miracle, that he would be born of a virgin, who should have his name from the fact, since when he is born God will be with men. Here I think I shall aptly object to the invented persona of the Jew the prophecy of Isaiah...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.
## E 2

...promising that Emmanuel would be born of a virgin. Celsus did not set this forth, either because he was ignorant of it—despite his boast of knowing all things—or, if he did read it, he intentionally suppressed it, lest he inadvertently support our view, which is contrary to his own purpose. The words of the prophecy are as follows: *And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of the underworld, or in the height above. And Ahaz said: I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord. And he said: Hear then, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to be troublesome to men, that you are also troublesome to the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted as God with us.* <note>This is the famous prophecy from Isaiah 7:14, central to the Christian argument for the divinity of Jesus.</note> I clearly conclude that Celsus maliciously omitted this prophecy because, although he alleges many things from the Gospel of Matthew—such as the star that rose at the birth of Jesus and other miracles—he made absolutely no mention of this one. But if a Jew, scrutinizing the vocabulary, should deny that it is written, *Behold, a virgin*, but rather *Behold, a young woman*; we shall say that the word *Alma* <note>original: "Alma" (Hebrew: עַלְמָה). Origen is engaging in a philological debate over whether this term specifically means a virgin or just a young woman of marriageable age.</note> is read there, which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated as "virgin," though others translated it as "young woman." That word, as they say, is also read in Deuteronomy signifying a virgin in these words: <margin>Deut. 22:23</margin> *If a man finds a young girl who is a virgin betrothed to a husband and lies with her in the city; they shall both be led out to the gate of their city, and they shall be stoned and killed: the young woman for the reason that she did not cry out in the city, and the man for the reason that he humbled his neighbor's wife.* And thereafter: *But if a man finds a betrothed woman in the field and ravishes her by force, you shall kill only the man who lay with her, but to the young woman you shall do nothing; there is no capital sin in the young woman.* But lest we seem to soothe with Hebrew readings those who are less able to grasp in their minds whether he should be agreed with or not, when we assert that the Prophet said Jesus would be born of a virgin—at whose birth it is also asserted, *God with us*—come, let us consider the meaning from the words themselves. The Lord is written to have said to Ahaz: *Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God in the depth or in the height.* And soon after the sign which is given is added: *Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb and bear a son.* Now, what kind of "sign" would it be for a young woman, and not a virgin, to give birth? And for whom is it more fitting to give birth to Emmanuel, which is *God with us*; for a woman who has experienced intercourse and is pregnant in the manner of women, or...

<column-break/>

Wherefore it is nothing absurd, that the Prophets of that nation were accustomed to answer even about certain chance events...

For among living creatures certain females are found who have no knowledge of a male's company, as those who have written on the nature of animals report concerning vultures; nevertheless, this animal perpetuates its kind by a succession of its own race. What wonder is it then, if God, wishing to send a certain divine teacher to the human race, caused the future birth to be provided for by some other means, instead of the sowing of seed that comes from the union of male and female? For even the Greeks themselves admit that not all men were born from a male and female. For if the world was created, as many of the Greeks also believe, it is necessary that the first humans were born not from coitus, but from the earth, in which the principle of seeds existed; which I consider more incredible than that Jesus was born half in the manner of men <note>i.e., having a human mother but not a human father</note>. 

Nor would it be absurd when dealing with Greeks to bring forward Greek histories, lest we seem to be the only ones to hold this miraculous history. For it pleased certain people—not only in ancient and heroic histories, but in those containing deeds done only yesterday or the day before—to report as a possible thing that Plato also was born of his mother Amphictione <note>Usually identified as Perictione; Origen notes the variant</note>, Aristo having been forbidden to lie with her until she had given birth to the child conceived from Apollo. But these are mere fables which have led some to invent such a thing for the sake of a man who, in the estimation of many, possessed a wisdom greater than the multitude.

# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...with insults that contain nothing serious. Next, using material from Matthew, or perhaps the other Evangelists, he attempts to slander the account of the dove that flew down upon the Savior when he was baptized by John, treating it as a fabricated story. Having finished—as he believes—his agitation against the narrative of our Savior’s birth from a virgin, he does not follow the subsequent events in order. Indeed, fury and hatred possess no sense of order; rather, when passion seizes those occupied by such emotions, they attack the objects of their hate with insults as the impulse strikes them, not permitted to weave their accusation with consideration or sequence. For if he had preferred order, he would have taken up the Gospel and begun his accusation there; after seizing upon the first history, he would have passed next to the second, and so on to the rest. 

But now, after the birth from a virgin, this Celsus—who boasts that he knows all our secrets—attacks the Holy Spirit seen in the form of a dove at the baptism. After this, he slanders the prophecies concerning the Savior’s coming; then he turns his course backward to the narrative of the star, which was written as occurring just after Jesus’s birth, and to the Magi who came from the East to worship the child. You yourself may find many such instances by observing how confusedly Celsus has placed things throughout his entire volume. Thus, by those who know how to maintain order and seek the truth, he is convicted even by this of having acted with arrogance and overconfidence in giving his book the title *The True Word* <note>original: "verum sermonem" / "ἀληθῆ λόγον"</note>—a thing which no learned philosopher ever did. 

For Plato says that it is not the part of a wise man to speak with such certainty about things that are obscure. Likewise, Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his modesty in logic</note>, having frequently set forth the reasons by which he himself was moved, refers us to others, if perhaps we might find some who speak better on the matter. But this man, supposedly wiser than these and all other Greeks, is everywhere consistent with himself: just as he professed to know all things, so he titled his book *The True Word*. 

However, lest we seem to intentionally skip over his chapters because we lack an answer, we have decided to refute each of his objections to the best of our ability, taking into account not the natural series and consequence of events, but the order in which they are written in his own book. Therefore, come, let us see what he says while he slanders the Holy Spirit seen by the Savior in the form of a dove. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 1.

"...except that you say, and some one or other [has said] either entirely or with you of those who have been punished?" <note>Origen is quoting Celsus's mocking tone regarding the followers of Jesus.</note> Before we begin the defense, it must be said that regarding almost every history, even if it be true, the attempt to establish it as having happened and to produce a convincing impression of it is among the most difficult of tasks, and for some things, impossible. For suppose someone were to say that the Trojan War never happened, especially because of the impossible story intertwined with it concerning Achilles being born of a sea-goddess and a mortal, Peleus; or Sarpedon being the son of Zeus; or Ascalaphus and Ialmenus being sons of Ares; or Aeneas being the son of Aphrodite. How could we establish such a thing, especially when we are pressed by the fiction that has been introduced into the opinion that has prevailed among all people concerning the reality of the war at Ilium between the Greeks and Trojans? And suppose one were to disbelieve the story of Oedipus and Jocasta, and their children Eteocles and Polynices, because the Sphinx, a half-maiden creature, was intertwined in the account; how could we prove such a thing? Let it be the same regarding the <term>Epigoni</term> <note>The "After-born," sons of the Seven against Thebes.</note>, even if no such [mythical] element is intertwined in the story, or concerning the return of the <term>Heracleidae</term> <note>The descendants of Hercules returning to the Peloponnese.</note>, or countless other matters. 

But the person who reads histories with a fair mind, and who wishes to keep himself from being deceived in them, will judge which things he will assent to, and which he will interpret <term>tropologically</term> <note>Figuratively or metaphorically.</note>, searching out the intent of those who fashioned such things; and which things he will disbelieve as having been recorded to favor <margin>certain people.</margin> certain individuals. And having premised this regarding the entire history of Jesus found in the Gospels, we have spoken not to call the more simple-minded to a bare and irrational faith, but wishing to show that there is a need for a fair mind in those who read, and much investigation, and (if I may name it so) an entry into the intent of the writers, so that it may be found with what purpose each thing was written. 

We shall say first, then, that if the one who disbelieves the vision of the appearance of the dove happened to be a <term>Pythagorean</term> or a <term>Platonist</term> <margin>* or a follower of Democritus.</margin> or an <term>Epicurean</term> or a <term>follower of Democritus</term>, or a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>; the argument would have a consistent place <margin>* in the mouth of the character.</margin> in the mouth of the character being portrayed. But as it is, the seemingly most wise Celsus, in claiming that he is a Jew—one who believes more and more miraculous things in the prophetic writings than this story about the appearance of the dove—has put such a speech [into the Jew's mouth]. For if anyone were to say to the Jew who disbelieves the vision and thinks to accuse it of being a fiction: "But you, my good man, from what source could you demonstrate that the Lord God said to Adam, or Eve, or Cain, or Noah, or Abraham, or Isaac, or Jacob, the things recorded as having been spoken by Him to these men?" And so that I may compare history with history, I would say to the Jew, "And your...

<column-break/>

...except you and one or two others of your associates in crime and punishment." Before we undertake the defense, it must be stated that to assert the truth of almost all narratives, even if they are true, and to fix them in opinion, is a very difficult matter, and for some, impossible. For imagine someone denying that there ever was a Trojan War, especially since certain impossible things are mixed into that narrative, concerning Achilles the son of a sea-goddess and the man Peleus, concerning Zeus's Sarpedon, Mars's Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, and Venus's Aeneas; how shall we support such things if we are pressed by manifest fictions? Although the opinion has already prevailed that the Greeks truly waged war with the Trojans at Ilium. Suppose another does not believe concerning Jocasta and Oedipus and their common children Eteocles and Polynices because of the Sphinx, the half-maiden, inserted into the narrative; how shall we demonstrate this? The same is to be felt concerning the <term>Epigoni</term> as they are called, even if that narrative lacks similar fictions; and concerning the journey into the Peloponnese of the sons of Hercules, and countless others: but he who reads histories candidly and conducts himself cautiously lest he be deceived, will judge which he should assent to, and will interpret others in a tropological sense, having scrutinized the minds of those who devised them; again, he will withhold credit from others as written for the sake of certain people. And we have prefaced this for the sake of forestalling [objections] concerning the entire history of Jesus contained in the Gospels, not calling the sharper-minded to a naked and reason-less faith, but forewarning that there is need for prudence and diligent examination in the reader, and, so to speak, a certain introduction into the designs of those who composed it, so that it may be found in what sense each thing was written. <margin>Ezekiel 1:1 & 2:1</margin> Your own Ezekiel writes thus: *The heavens were opened, and I saw a vision of God.* In explaining this, he adds, *This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord: and he spoke to me.* For if the things written about Jesus are false—since, as you suppose, we cannot clearly prove their truth because they were seen and heard by him alone, and as you think you have observed, by one of his companions in punishment <note>original: "ex supplicii sociis." Surely, O Jew, you believe these things as indubitable and produced by the Divine Spirit, and that the Prophet not only saw them but spoke them and committed them to writing. Who, then, is more worthy of belief? Ezekiel, saying the heavens were opened to him and that he heard a voice; or Isaiah, writing that the Lord of Hosts was seen by him sitting on a high and exalted throne; or Jesus? Certainly, no work similar to theirs is found <note>i.e., no lasting physical monument of the vision itself</note>; but the virtues of Jesus were not only powerful at the time he lived in a body on earth, but even now the power of Jesus is effective for converting and correcting as many as believe in God through him. For that these things happen by his power is evidenced by his own word, and it can be perceived that although there is a total lack of workers for the harvest of souls, nevertheless a great crop of harvested grain is brought together from everywhere and carried into the threshing floors of the Church of God. <margin>Matthew 9:37</margin> And I say these things to the Jew—not taking away faith from Ezekiel and Isaiah, since I am a Christian—but by those things which we both believe equally, I am putting him to shame. For this man [Jesus] is much more worthy to be believed when he says such visions were seen by him, which it is probable he later recounted to his disciples, along with the voice which he had heard. Yet someone might perhaps say that not everyone heard Jesus narrating what they wrote concerning the appearance of the dove and the voice sent from heaven; but rather the Spirit who taught Moses the history of former ages from the creation of the world down to Abraham, the father of his race, this same Spirit also taught the Evangelists the miracle which occurred at the time of Jesus's Baptism. Furthermore, he to whom the gift of wisdom has fallen will also give the reason for the opening of the heavens, and what the appearance of the dove signifies, and why the Holy Spirit appeared in this form specifically to Jesus; but to discuss these matters now is not the time.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 1.

->**The Argument**<-

<margin>* Disobedience or Unbelief <note>Greek: *apeithia*</note></margin> For the task at hand is to refute Celsus, showing that he inappropriately puts words into the mouth of a Jew—as if a Jew would lack faith in these matters based on a precedent of words, when the events are actually more probable than the things believed by them. I remember once, in a discussion with those called the "wise men" of the Jews, using this argument while many were judging what was said: "Tell me, sirs, since two men have visited the human race about whom <margin>* Paradoxes or Marvels</margin> extraordinary things have been recorded—I mean Moses, your lawgiver, who wrote about himself, and Jesus our teacher, who left no writing about himself but has the testimony of his disciples in the Gospels—what is the logic in believing Moses speaks the truth (even though the Egyptians slander him as a sorcerer who performed his feats by trickery), yet disbelieving Jesus because you accuse him? For nations bear witness to both: the Jews to Moses, and the Christians—who do not deny the prophecy of Moses but use it to prove the facts about Jesus—accept the marvelous things narrated about him as recorded by his disciples. If you demand an account from us concerning Jesus, first give the account concerning Moses who preceded him, and then we will give ours in turn. But if you shrink back and flee from the proofs concerning him, we will do the same to you for the present and offer no proof. Nevertheless, even if you admit you have no proof for Moses, listen to our proofs for Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. And the marvelous thing is that the proofs for Jesus in the Law and the Prophets also demonstrate that Moses was a prophet, specifically a prophet of God; for the Law and the Prophets are filled with similar marvels to that recorded about Jesus <margin>* Note this.</margin> regarding his baptism, the dove, and the voice from heaven." I believe the appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove was a sign of the miracles performed by Jesus—which Celsus slanders, saying he performed them having learned them among the Egyptians. I will not use those alone; but also, as is likely, the miracles the apostles of Jesus performed. For without powers and marvels, they would not have moved those hearing new words and new teachings to the point of abandoning ancestral customs and accepting these teachings despite dangers even unto death. Furthermore, traces of that Holy Spirit which appeared in the form of a dove are still preserved among Christians: they cast out demons, perform many healings, and foresee certain future events according to the will of the Word. And even if—

—is the purpose. For we are dealing with Celsus and showing that he unsuitably invents a speech for a Jew, as if the Jew does not believe this, when he believes much more difficult things. Indeed, I remember that I once used these words in a certain dispute with the wise men of the Jews in the presence of many who might judge what I had said: "Tell me, O you, since two have appeared among men of whom certain incredible things are handed down that exceed human nature—I mean your legislator Moses, who wrote of himself, and Jesus our master, who left no writing of himself but has the testimony of his disciples in the Gospels: what reason requires that it be believed that Moses produced true things, although the Egyptians slander him as a magician and a charlatan; but Jesus is not believed because of your accusations? For both rely on the testimony of nations: Moses indeed on the Jews; but the Christians, not denying the prophecy of Moses, even from that source approve Jesus, and therefore more easily believe the miracles written by his disciples to be true. Now if you demand a reason from us concerning Jesus, first give yours concerning Moses, who preceded him, and then finally we also will give ours concerning Jesus. But since you are stalling and shrinking from proofs, we shall return like for like, which suffices for us at present; nevertheless, you have confessed that you have no proofs concerning Moses: but you, listen to ours concerning Jesus, taken from the Law and the Prophets. And, what is more wonderful, from the demonstrations concerning Jesus which are held in the Law and the Prophets, it is shown that Moses and the Prophets were Prophets of God. Moreover, the Law is full, the Prophets are full of miracles similar to this which is written concerning the dove and the voice sent from heaven." Furthermore, I think the Holy Spirit was signified through the appearance of a dove, and I gather this from the miracles of Jesus, against which Celsus builds a calumny, asserting they were done by Egyptian arts. Nor shall I take my argument from those alone, but also, as is right, from those things which the Apostles of Jesus performed: for they would not have moved the hearers of a new doctrine without virtues and miracles, so that, having left behind ancestral institutions, they would receive their doctrine and defend it even unto death, despising all dangers. # Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## F 2

Whether Celsus mocks what is about to be said, or the Jew whom he has introduced as a character mocks it, it shall nevertheless be stated: that many have been drawn to the Christian religion almost against their will, by a certain spirit suddenly changing their mind <note>original: "intellectum" / "hegemonikon" (the ruling faculty of the soul)</note> from the hatred with which they held the Word, so much so that for its sake they did not hesitate to meet death, after visions were presented to them either while sleeping or waking. But God is witness to our conscience that I am trying to commend the divine teaching of Jesus not through false little narratives, but through various examples. And since it is the Jew who calls into doubt what is written concerning the Holy Spirit descending upon Jesus in the form of a dove, it might rightly be said to him: "Hey you! For I do not suppose that the visible heaven was opened and its physical body divided so that Ezekiel might record such a thing. We say that just as it is believed that many have observed divine visions in sleep, forewarning either openly or through riddles about certain future things pertaining to life—and this is admitted among all who allow for providence—so it is consistent that the power which forms the intellect in sleep can also, while one is awake, imprint the same forms for the benefit of the person himself, or of those who are to hear the vision. And just as in sleep we seem to ourselves to hear by a striking of the sense of hearing, and to discern with eyes, while in the meantime neither the hearing nor the eyes of the body are touched, but the intellect is so affected; so it would be nothing absurd for the same to have happened to the Prophets, whenever we read that they saw certain things exceeding belief, or heard the words of the Lord, or beheld the heavens opened. For my part, I do not think this sensible heaven was opened, and its body divided, so that Ezekiel might write such things. ...sense, and touching the Word *with faith*, so that a certain flow emanated from him into them, bringing health; in this way they saw what they write that they saw, and heard what they say they heard. This can be seen in the character of Jesus, who had removed all boasting about himself, and therefore says: *Even if I myself speak of myself, my testimony is not true:* and so, with all boasting set aside, as he preferred to declare that he was the Christ by works rather than by words, the Jews addressed him thus: *If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.*

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book I.

<margin>

It is a Jew who, in Celsus’s writing, speaks to Jesus regarding the descent of the Spirit in the form of a dove, saying: "except that you are the one, and that you bring forward one witness from among those punished with you." <note>Celsus is mocking the idea that the only witness to Jesus's divinity was John the Baptist, who was also executed.</note> It is necessary to show him that this, too, is falsely devised and unsuited to the character of a Jew. For Jews do not link John with Jesus, nor John’s execution with that of Jesus. Even in this, therefore, he who promises to know everything <note>A jab at Celsus’s arrogance.</note> may be convicted of not knowing how to skillfully assign words to a Jewish character addressing Jesus. After this, I know not how, he intentionally passes over—as I suppose, because he is unable to meet the argument—the most important chapter concerning the establishment of Jesus: namely, that he was foretold by the prophets among the Jews, by Moses and those after him, or even those before Moses. Perhaps he did not even know the prophecies concerning Jesus. For otherwise, when attacking the Christian claim that many prophets foretold the Savior’s arrival, he would not have put into the mouth of a Jewish character words that would better suit a Samaritan or a Sadducee <note>The Samaritans and Sadducees only accepted the five books of Moses (the Pentateuch) and rejected the later prophets.</note> than a Jew. For he makes his character say:

> "But my prophet once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God would come, a judge of the holy and a punisher of the unjust."

For it was not just one prophet who foretold things concerning Christ, even if the Samaritans or Sadducees, who accept only the books of Moses, claim that Christ was prophesied in those. Furthermore, no prophecy had been spoken in Jerusalem at that time, for the city had not yet been named in the time of Moses. I could wish, then, that all accusers of the Word might attack Christianity in such great ignorance, not only of the facts but even of the bare letter of the Scripture, so that their discourse might not have even an ordinary plausibility capable of leading away those who are ungrounded and only temporary believers due to their little faith. A Jew, however, would never admit that any prophet said a "Son of God" would come; for what they say is that the "Christ of God" <note>The Messiah.</note> will come. And they frequently dispute with us directly about the "Son of God," as if no such person existed or had been prophesied. We do not say this because the Son of God was not prophesied, but because he [Celsus] inappropriately assigned to a Jewish character, who does not admit such a thing, the words:
<margin>
* falsely devised (Interpretation).
</margin>
> "my prophet once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God would come."

Then, as if this were the only thing prophesied—that he would be a judge of the holy and a punisher of the unjust—he says nothing of the place of his birth, nor of his suffering, or what he would endure at the hands of the Jews...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for scholars.</note>

Since, however, it is a Jew in Celsus's work who, speaking of the vision of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, addresses Jesus thus: *Except that you say so, bringing forward a single witness from among the partners of your punishment;* it is necessary to show how foolishly this also is attributed to the person of a Jew: for Jews do not connect John with Jesus, or their punishments. Therefore, here also this boaster of universal knowledge is proven not to have known what words should be attributed to the character of a Jew holding a conversation with Jesus. After this, I know not by what means, he deliberately skips over that by which Jesus is chiefly commended—namely, the prophecies of the Prophets accepted by the Jews, of Moses and those following, or even those preceding—doubtless because he has no answer, just as the Jews and all the sects who do not want the Prophets to have predicted Christ have no answer. Or perhaps he knew nothing of the oracles concerning Jesus; otherwise, in attacking that saying of the Christians, that many Prophets foretold the coming of the Savior, he would not have assigned to the person of a Jew words which are more suitable to a Samaritan or a Sadducee; nor would this fictional character of a Jew speak thus: *But my Prophet once sang in Jerusalem that the Son of God would come, the judge of the pious, the punisher of the unjust;* for it was not a single Prophet who prophesied concerning Christ. Moreover, even if the Samaritans or Sadducees, who receive only the books of Moses, say that it was prophesied of Christ in those; yet by no means was that prophecy issued in Jerusalem, of which city there was not even a name in the time of Moses. It is to be hoped, therefore, that all accusers of the Word may be in such great ignorance, not only of matters, but even of the bare letters of Scripture; and thus may they accuse the Christian religion, so that their speech may not have even a moderate power of persuasion, which could turn away even the poorly grounded and those who believe for a time, I do not say from faith, but from the smallness of their faith. Furthermore, a Jew never confesses that any Prophet predicted the Son of God would come; they predict this, that the Christ of God will come: and as often as they dispute with us, they immediately ask about the Son of God, as if nothing of this kind were found anywhere among the Prophets. Yet we do not say that it was not predicted by the Prophets concerning the Son of God, but that those words were not aptly assigned to the person of a Jew who denies this: *My Prophet once said in Jerusalem that the Son of God would come.* Then, as if only this had been prophesied, *that he would be the judge of the pious and the punisher of the unjust,* he says nothing of the place of birth, nor of the punishment which he was to suffer from...

# Book I. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...prophesied to each of his sons, and foretold to Judah, among other things, this: *The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him shall come.* <note>original: "Non deficiet princeps ex Juda..." quoting Genesis 49:10. This is a foundational Messianic prophecy used by early Christians to show that the Jewish right to rule would end only when the Messiah arrived.</note> Anyone who reads this prophecy—which is in truth much older than the age of Moses, though an unbeliever might suspect it was brought forth by Moses—will marvel at how Moses was able to predict that the kings of the Jews (though there were twelve tribes among them) would arise from the tribe of Judah and rule over the whole people. This is why the name "Jews" originated; the entire nation was named after the one tribe that held the royal power.

The honest reader of this prophecy will likewise marvel at how, after predicting the kingdom of the tribe of Judah, he also established its end with these words: *The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him shall come; and he is the expectation of the nations.* For he came for whom it was laid up: Christ of God, the prince of God's promises. He is the only one from all previous ages—and I would even dare to say from all subsequent ages—to whom the title *Expectation of the Nations* fits. For people of all nations have believed in God through him and have fixed their hope in his name, according to the oracle of Isaiah which says: *In his name the nations shall hope.* <note>Isaiah 42:4</note>

This is he who said to the captives—insofar as each is bound by the chains of their own sins—*Go forth*, and to those who are in ignorance, *Come into the light*. Just as these things were foretold by the Prophets: *I have given you as a covenant of the nations, to establish the things of the earth, and to inherit the heritage of the desert, saying to the captives, Go forth: and to those who are in darkness, Show yourselves in the open.* <note>Isaiah 49:8-9</note> And now one can see, at his coming, that this prediction is fulfilled through those who believe with simplicity: *In all ways they shall be fed, and in all paths shall be their pasture.*

However, since Celsus, having professed that he knows all our doctrine, mocks the Savior regarding his passion <note>The "Passion" refers to the suffering and crucifixion of Jesus.</note>—claiming he was not helped by his father, nor could he help himself—this must be added: his passion was foretold by the Prophets, as was the cause of the passion. Namely, that his death, undergone for them, would be useful to men, as would the welts <note>The Latin "vibices" refers to the marks of scourging or whipping.</note> which he endured as one condemned. Furthermore, it was foretold that he would be recognized by the nations among whom there were never Prophets, and that he would live among men in a contemptible appearance. The words of the oracle are these: *Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, he shall be lifted up, he shall be very high. Just as many shall be amazed at you: so shall your appearance be inglorious among men, and your glory shall be despised by men.* <note>Isaiah 52:13-14</note>

<column-break/>

...to each of the sons, and to have said to Judah, along with other things: *A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him shall come.* <margin>Gen. 49:10</margin> Anyone encountering this prophecy—which is in truth much older than Moses, though an unbeliever might suspect it was spoken by Moses—would marvel at how Moses was able to foresee that the rulers of the Jews (there being twelve tribes among them) being born from the tribe of Judah, would rule the people. Therefore the whole people are called Jews, being named after the ruling tribe. And secondly, the one who encounters the prophecy fairly would marvel at how, having said that the rulers and leaders of the people would be from the tribe of Judah, he also set the end of that same rule, saying: *A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him shall come; and he is the expectation of the nations.* <margin>Ibid. same verse.</margin> For he came for whom the things were laid up, the Christ of God, the ruler of the promises of God. And clearly he alone has become this, beyond all those before him—and I would boldly say even those after him—the *Expectation of the Nations*. For from all the nations they have believed in God through him, and according to that which was spoken by Isaiah, *In his name the nations shall hope.* <margin>Isaiah 42:4</margin> <margin>\* shall hope.</margin>

This is he who also says to those in bonds—inasmuch as each is tightened by the cords of their own sins—the word, *Go forth*, and to those in ignorance, *To come into the light*, according to the things spoken by the prophets: *And I have given you for a covenant of the nations, to restore the earth, and to inherit the inheritance of the desert, saying to those in bonds, Go forth, and to those in darkness, To be revealed.* <margin>Isaiah 49:8</margin> <margin>\* go forth.</margin> <margin>Ibid. v. 9</margin> And it is possible to see at his presence, through those everywhere in the inhabited world who believe more simply, the fulfillment of: *And in all the ways they shall be fed, and in all the paths shall be their pasture.*

But since Celsus, who claims to know all the things of our Word, reproaches the Savior regarding his passion, as <margin>Isaiah 49:8</margin> not having been helped by the Father, or not being able to help himself, it must be said that his passion was prophesied and also the cause: that his dying for them was useful to men, and by the welt of his suffering as one condemned. And it was also prophesied that those from the nations, among whom the prophets had not been, would know him; and it must be said that he would be seen in an appearance that seemed without honor among men. The text is this: *Behold, my servant shall understand, and shall be exalted, and shall be glorified exceedingly. In the manner that many shall be amazed at you, so shall your form be without glory from men, and your glory from men.* <margin>Isaiah 53:5</margin> <margin>Isaiah 52:13</margin> <margin>\* your.</note>

In that disputation I proved with many words that these things, which were predicted about some one person, they do not rightly refer to the whole people: and I inquired from whose person it is said, "This man carries our sins, and suffers sorrows for us"; and that, "He was wounded on account of our sins, and languishes on account of our iniquities": also from whose person is that: "By his bruise we are healed." For manifestly these who were lately in sins, being healed by the passion <note>The "passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> of the Savior, say these things in the Prophet who sees the future: whether they be from that people, or from the nations, the Holy Spirit adapting the words to the persons. But I was especially seen to urge them with this saying: "On account of the iniquities of my people he was led to death." But that I have lingered on these matters at some length, I believe I have done so out of necessity, because of the words of the Jew which are found in Celsus’s work. It escaped the notice of Celsus and his Jew, and all those who have not believed in Jesus, that the Prophets foretold two comings of Christ. The first was earlier, subject to human sufferings and more humble, so that while living among men he might teach them the way leading to God, and leave no person living in this life a place for excuse, as if they had heard nothing of the future judgment. The other coming, however, will be glorious and purely divine, having nothing of human suffering mixed with his divinity. It is likely, therefore, that at the birth of Jesus—since a multitude of the heavenly host (as Luke recorded, and I believe) praised God and said: *Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men*—for this reason the demons grew weak and were exposed, their sorcery being refuted and their power abolished. Therefore, when the Magi <note>The "Wise Men" or astrologer-priests from the East.</note> wished to perform their usual rites, which they previously did through certain incantations and magic tricks, they sought the cause, finding it by a great sign. And seeing a divine sign in the heaven, they wished to see what was signified by it. It seems to me, then, that having the prophecies of Balaam <margin>Numbers 24:17</margin> (which Moses also recorded, as he always set down such things as they happened), and having found there the oracle concerning the star and the words: *I shall point to him, but not now; I bless him, but he does not draw near* <note>Origen is quoting a version of the Septuagint/Greek Old Testament; modern Bibles usually read "I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near."</note>, they conjectured that the man prophesied by the star had arrived in this life. They came therefore to Judea, being persuaded that a certain king had been born, though not understanding what kind of kingdom he would rule, nor where he would be born, or [initially] knowing the place. And bringing gifts, they offered them to one who was (if I may name him so) a composite of God and mortal man: symbols, as it were—gold as to a king, myrrh as to one who was to die, and frankincense as to God. <margin>Matthew 2:11</margin> They offered these after learning the place of his birth. They came therefore into Judea, already taught that a certain king was born, but otherwise ignorant of what kingdom, or where the place of his birth might be; bringing gifts for one composed (so to speak) of a mortal and God: gold as a sign of royal power to a king, myrrh as to one about to die, frankincense as to God; and when they knew the place of birth, they offered these to him. But because he was God, who had come as the Savior of the human race, more powerful than the angels who help men, immediately an angel returned a reward to the piety of the Magi who had worshipped Jesus, and warned them by an oracle: *That they should not go to Herod, but return to their country by another way.* Moreover, it is no wonder that Herod laid snares for the newborn, even if Celsus’s Jew does not believe it: for malice is blind, and tries to conquer the fates, as if it were itself more powerful. Affected by this same evil, Herod believed the King of the Jews was born and firmly assented to this: not understanding either that he is altogether a king and will surely reign; or if he will not reign, then his death is unnecessary: he therefore decreed to kill him, because he had opinions fighting amongst themselves on account of his malice, being surely agitated by the evil and blind devil...

For he did not see the sleepless guardian power over those worthy of being guarded and kept for the salvation of men, of whom first of all and greater in every excellence for us was Jesus, who was to be a king—not as Herod thought, but as was fitting for God to give a kingdom, for the benefit of those ruled. He would benefit those subjected to him not with a middle or indifferent (if I may call it so) beneficence, but would educate and bring them under truly divine laws. Jesus, knowing this and denying that he was a king as the many understand it, but teaching the exceptional nature of his own kingdom, says: *“If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have struggled so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from this world.”* If Celsus had seen these things, he would not have said: *“But if it was so that you might not reign instead of him when you grew up, why, since you have grown up, do you not reign? This is clear to one who perceives that Jesus died for men; concerning which we have spoken according to our ability in the preceding parts. After these things, since he does not even know the number of the apostles, he says: *“Jesus, having attached to himself ten or eleven notorious men, tax-gatherers and the most wicked sailors, fled here and there with them, shamefully and greedily collecting food.”* Come then, let us discuss these things also as far as possible. Furthermore, let us reproach the profligacy of Polemon, the successor of Xenocrates, in his philosophy. Among the Greeks, there is one Phaedo, and I do not know if there is a second, and one Polemon, who, having changed from a profligate and most wicked life, practiced philosophy. But with Jesus, there were not only the twelve then, but always and many times more, who, having become a choir of temperate people, say concerning their former life: <margin>Titus 3:3</margin> *For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another. ...to be led by those raising him, arranged by divine angels. First, the one delivering the oracle said: *Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife; for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν, ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου"</note> And secondly: *Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child to destroy him.* In these accounts, nothing seems paradoxical to me. For in another part of the Scripture, it is said that an angel spoke these things to Joseph in a dream. That it is revealed to some in a dream to do certain things happens to many others as well; whether by angels or by visions appearing to the soul during sleep. What is absurd about the one who once became man, and was governed according to human upbringing, fleeing to avoid dangers? Not because it was otherwise impossible for such a thing to happen, but because it was necessary for the preservation of Jesus to be managed in an orderly and sequential way. And it was certainly better for the child Jesus to withdraw from *the plot of Herod* and to travel abroad with his guardians to Egypt until the death of the plotter, than for the providence surrounding Jesus to hinder the impulse of Herod who wanted to kill the child, or to use the so-called "Helmet of Hades" <note>A mythical helmet of invisibility mentioned by Greek poets like Homer and Hesiod.</note> mentioned by the poets, or to do something similar for Jesus, or to strike those coming for his murder just as those in Sodom were struck. For a completely miraculous form of help, being too obvious, would not have been useful for his desire to teach as a man witnessed by God, while having something more divine within the visible man—which was properly the Son of God, God the Word, and the Power and Wisdom of God, called Christ. Now is not the time to explain the nature of the composite, and of what elements the incarnate Jesus consisted; this is a matter of a specific (if I may call it so) inquiry for those who believe in this topic. After this, the Jew in Celsus' writing, acting like a learned Greek educated in Greek culture, says: "While the ancient myths assigned a divine seed to Perseus, Amphion, Aeacus, and Minos—whom we do not even believe in *ourselves*—they nevertheless displayed great and wonderful works of their own, truly beyond human capacity, so that they might not seem implausible. But you, what noble or wonderful thing have you performed in deed or word? You have shown us nothing, even though we challenged you in the temple to show a very clear and manifest sign that you were the Son of God." To this it must be said: let the Greeks show us any life-benefiting or brilliant work from those they have listed, or any benefit for later generations, or a work of such magnitude...

<column-break/>

...it was fitting that he be led by his guardians through divine dispensation, having been forewarned by an angel: first in these words; *Joseph, son of David, fear not to take Mary thy wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Ghost:* and secondly in these; *Arise, and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be there until I shall tell thee: for it will come to pass that Herod will seek the child to destroy him.* In this Scripture, nothing seems incredible to me: for in another place of Scripture we read that these things were said to Joseph in sleep by an angel. Moreover, it frequently happens to others also, that it is signified to them by a dream what is to be done, whether by an angel or by some other appearance observed by the mind. What then is absurd, if he who once was made man, should be led in a human manner to avoid dangers? Not that it was impossible for it to happen otherwise, but that it was necessary for the safety of Jesus to be dispensed in its proper order: certainly it was better for the child Jesus to yield to the snares of Herod, and to sojourn with his guardians in Egypt until his death, than that the providence which was had concerning Jesus should interrupt the onset of Herod, who wished to kill the child, or to employ that "Helmet of Orcus" <note>Latin: "Orci galeam" - the Roman equivalent of the Greek Hades' helmet of invisibility.</note> celebrated by the poets, or to consult for Jesus in a similar way, or to afflict those sent to his death with a Sodom-like destruction: for too much novelty in the assistance, and being illustrious beyond measure, was not suitable for him who wished to show himself as a man having testimony from God, while hiding something more divine under a human appearance, that which was properly the Son of God, God the Word, the power and wisdom of God, who is called Christ. But it is not the time now to discuss such a composite, and of what things the man-made Jesus consisted, since concerning this place a certain proper question, so to speak, is held among the faithful. After this, Celsus' Jew, as if he were some Greek and a student of Greek literature, says; *The fables of the ancients, attributing a divine birth to Perseus, Amphion, Aeacus, and Minos, although they are not likely, yet that the fiction might be more probable, they record certain wonderful things and things altogether exceeding human nature concerning them. But thou, he says, what distinguished or admirable thing hast thou produced for us in word or deed, although challenged in the temple to declare thyself the Son of God by a manifest sign?* To this it must be answered: Rather let the Greeks show us some distinguished utility proceeding from those whom you have enumerated, which would be profitable even for the future of the human race; or some deed...

He then addresses Celsus' comparison of Jesus to Greek heroes like Perseus, challenging the actual moral utility of those myths.</summary>

We affirm, therefore, that the work of Jesus stands out among the men of the entire inhabited world, as widely as the Churches of God founded through Jesus dwell among the nations, consisting of those converted to a better mind from countless evils. The name of Jesus also heals the frantic <note>literally "lymphatos," those driven mad or possessed</note> and drives out demons; it even brings present help to diseases. It also introduces a certain wonderful mildness and honesty of character, humanity, goodness, and placidity to all who embrace the preaching of God, of Christ, and of the future judgment—not hypocritically because of the cares of life or some human necessities, but from the soul. 

Next, Celsus, not being entirely ignorant of how much can be brought forward concerning the magnificent works of Jesus (of which we have mentioned a few out of many), pretends to concede that whatever has been handed down regarding healings, or the resurrection, or the multitude fed with a few loaves and their remains, is true; finally, whatever else he thinks the disciples narrate to exaggerate the magnitude of the miracles. And soon he adds: *“Come, let us believe these things were done by you.”* And immediately he makes this common to the works of sorcerers <note>term: "præstigiatorum" / "goētōn" — refers to street magicians or illusionists who used trickery</note> who promise more wonderful things, and to the deeds of jugglers performed in the middle of the marketplace, who learned these things from the Egyptians, selling those marvelous arts for a few obols <note>a small Greek coin</note>, and driving demons out of men, blowing away diseases, summoning the souls of heroes, and exhibiting the empty appearance of sumptuous dinners and rich delicacies, and phantoms of living creatures which seem to move when in truth they do not move. He asks: *“Therefore, because they do these things, must we believe them to be sons of God? Or should it rather be said that these are the arts of wicked and unhappy men?”* 

You see in these words that he almost concedes there is magic, though perhaps he is the same one who wrote many books against magic; and yet, because it is convenient for him, he compares magical operations with those things read about Jesus. And they would be similar, if he had shown that in them there was nothing beyond appearance; but as it is, no sorcerer invites the spectators to the correction of morals through the things he does, nor do spectacles of that kind instruct those struck by the fear of God, nor does the juggler

And sorcerers do none of these things, since they are neither able nor even willing to concern themselves with the moral correction of men; for they themselves are full of the most shameful and unspeakable sins. But as for him who, by the wonders he performed, called those who witnessed his deeds to the reformation of their character, how is it not reasonable to believe that he presented himself as an example of the best life, not only to his true disciples, but also to the rest? This was so that the disciples might be prepared to teach men according to the will of God, and that the others, having been taught more by his word and character than even by his wonders how one ought to live, might do everything with a view to pleasing the God over all. If, then, such was the life of Jesus, how could anyone reasonably compare him to the purpose of sorcerers, and not rather believe that, according to the promise of God, he appeared in a human body for the benefit of our race? After this, Celsus, confusing the argument and applying the claims made by a certain sect as common charges against all who follow the divine word, says: "A body such as yours could not belong to a God." But we, in response to this, say that he assumed a human body, having come into this life from a woman, and one capable of human death. Therefore, among other things, we say he was a great combatant <note>original: "agonisten" — referring to one who struggles or competes in a contest, here meaning the spiritual struggle against sin</note> because of that human body, having been tempted in all things just like all men, yet no longer like other men with sin, but entirely without it. For it is clearly manifest to us that *he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.* <margin>Isaiah 53:9</margin> And though he knew no sin, <margin>2 Corinthians 5:21</margin> God delivered him up as pure on behalf of all who have sinned. Yet let him consider that if (as it is written) he had been born, his body could in some way be more divine than that of the many, and in a certain sense be the body of God. But Celsus disbelieves the accounts written about his conception from the Holy Spirit <margin>Matthew 1:20</margin> [and believes that he was sown by a certain Panthera <note>A common anti-Christian slur in antiquity claiming Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera</note> who corrupted the virgin]; therefore he said, "The body of a God would not be so rotten as yours was sown." # ORIGEN

## AGAINST CELSUS

### BOOK II.

<margin>
* Against the work entitled "The True Word" by Celsus.
</margin>

In the first volume of the works we dictated in response to the treatise of Celsus entitled *The True Word* <note>original: "Alēthēs Logos"</note>, having concluded at the point where he introduces a Jewish character speaking to Jesus, and having provided a sufficient reply, we now purpose to compose this second volume. In it, we shall offer a defense against the accusations he brings against those from among the Jewish people who have believed in Jesus. And first, we must point out a flaw: Celsus, having decided to use the literary device of a fictional character <term>prosopopoeia: a rhetorical device where a speaker portrays an absent person or imaginary character</term>, has his Jew address those who believe from among the Jews, rather than those from the Gentiles. His argument would have seemed much more plausible had it been directed at us <note>i.e., Gentile Christians</note>. But perhaps this man, who claims to know everything, failed to see what was appropriate for the role he created. Let us, then, consider what he says to the believers from among the Jews.

<margin>
* he saw.
</margin>

**"He says that they, having been led astray by Jesus, have abandoned their ancestral law,"** **"having been deceived in a most ridiculous way, and have deserted to another name and another way of life."** He does not even understand this: that those from among the Jews who believe in Jesus have not abandoned their ancestral law. For they live according to it, having acquired a name that reflects the "poverty" of the law as they perceive it. For a "poor man" is called *Ebion* among the Jews; and those from among the Jews who have accepted Jesus as Christ are known as Ebionites <note>Origen is punning on the Hebrew word 'Evyon' (poor), suggesting the Ebionites were "poor in understanding" for clinging to the literal Law</note>. Even Peter appears for a long time to have observed the Jewish customs according to the Law of Moses, as one who had not yet learned from Jesus to rise from the letter of the Law to its spirit. This we have learned from the Acts of the Apostles. On the day after the angel of God appeared to Cornelius, suggesting to him that he send to Joppa for Simon, who is called Peter, Peter went up to the housetop to pray about the sixth hour. He became hungry and desired to eat. While they were preparing the meal, a trance fell upon him, and he saw heaven opened, and a certain object like a great sheet descending, bound at the four corners and let down to the earth, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the air.
