After the first book, in which we replied to Celsus's commentary—which bears the title *The True Word*—up to the place where the words assigned to the character of the Jew end, because that volume grew quite large, we determined to compose this second one. We respond here to the charges he brings against those of the Jewish people who believed in Jesus. And first, it is pleasing to ask why, once Celsus decided to introduce fictional characters, he preferred to make a Jew address his own countrymen rather than those who believed from the Gentiles. For his speech would have seemed more probable if he had written it to our people. But perhaps that man, who professes to know all things, did not know in this instance what was fitting for *character-portrayal* <note>Latin: "prosopopoiïis"</note>. We must consider, therefore, what he says to the faithful converts from Judaism: *he says they were enticed and deceived in a truly ridiculous manner by Jesus, and having left their ancestral institutions and laws, they fled to another name and a far different way of living.* He did not even understand this: that the Jews who believed in Jesus did not defect from their ancestral laws; for they live according to them, being named after the poverty of their law. For *Ebion* means "poor" in the Jewish tongue, and those who received Jesus as Christ are called Ebionites by the rest of the Jews. Indeed, even Peter seems for a long time to have observed Jewish rites according to the Law of Moses, as one who had not yet learned from Jesus to ascend from the literal law to the spiritual, which we know from the Acts of the Apostles. For on the day after Cornelius had seen the Angel, who advised him to send to Joppa for Simon surnamed Peter, Peter ascended to the upper room to preach <note>The Latin text says "prædicandū" (to preach), though the Greek and the Biblical source specify "to pray"</note> about the sixth hour; and when he was hungry, he wished to taste food. For truly it was untimely to apply a remedy to them of which they were not yet capable, and which could hinder the accepted opinion of Jesus, that he was the Christ, the son of the living God. And notice whether it should not probably be understood this way: *I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them at this time:* for there are many spiritual interpretations and declarations of the law, and the disciples could in no way have carried them at that time, as people born and educated among Jews. Moreover, I think that since those things were figures, but the truth was what they were to be taught by the Holy Spirit, it was therefore said; *After that spirit of truth has come, he will lead you into all truth:* as if he were saying, into all the truth of those things in whose figures you were occupied, thinking that you worshipped God with true worship. And according to the promise of Jesus, the Spirit of truth came to Peter, saying to him concerning the quadrupeds and reptiles of the earth, and the birds of heaven; *Rise Peter, kill and eat:* and it came to him even then laboring under superstition; for he says even after hearing the divine voice; *By no means, Lord, because I have never eaten anything common and unclean:* and then at last he was taught the true doctrine concerning true and spiritual foods, those words having been heard; *What God has purified, beware of calling common:* and after that vision the Spirit of truth, leading Peter into all truth, told him many things which he had not been able to bear for as long as he lived in the flesh with Jesus. But concerning these things there will be another time for discussing what pertains to the reception of the Mosaic law: now the purpose is to prove the ignorance of Celsus, in whose work a Jew asks his fellow Israelites believing in Jesus, how it happened that they deserted the ancestral law, and the rest. But how did they desert the ancestral law, who reproach those not listening to it with these words; *Tell me you, who read the law, why do you not hear it? For it is written; Abraham had two sons,* and so forth. How...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS Book 2.

<margin>Mark 1:1</margin>
<margin>* in his own [work]</margin>

The beginning of the Evangelist, Mark, says: *The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ; as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who shall prepare your way;* <note>original: "Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου..."</note> showing and pointing out that the beginning of the Gospel is linked to the Jewish scriptures. What, then, is said against us by the Jew in Celsus’s work, in the passage: *"For if someone predicted to you that the Son of God would come to men, was this not our prophet, and our God's [prophet]?"* And what sort of accusation against Christianity is it if John, who baptized Jesus, was a Jew? For Celsus concludes that because he was a Jew, it follows that everyone who believes—whether coming to the Word from the Gentiles or from the Jews—must observe the Law of Moses according to the letter. After this, Celsus repeats the same old arguments about Jesus, speaking as if he had already been overthrown, saying, *"having committed errors, he paid the penalty among the Jews."* But we shall not repeat our defense, being satisfied with what has been said previously. Then, since the Jew in his work treats the resurrection of the dead, the judgment of God, the honor for the righteous, and the fire for the unrighteous as stale ideas <note>original: "ἑωλὰ" - literally "leftovers" or "stale," implying the ideas are old and unimpressive</note> and belittles them, claiming that Christians teach nothing new in these matters, he thinks he can overturn Christianity. It must be said to him that our Jesus, seeing the Jews doing nothing worthy of the teachings in the prophets, taught through a parable that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to those from the nations <term>Gentiles: non-Jewish peoples</term>. Therefore, one can truly see that all the affairs of the Jews are full of myths and nonsense—for they do not have the light of the knowledge of the scriptures—while the affairs of Christians contain truth, capable of lifting up and elevating the souls and minds of men, and persuading them to hold a citizenship <note>original: "πολίτευμα" - referring to one's spiritual allegiance or "commonwealth"</note> not like that of the lowly Jews, but one in the heavens. Hence it is apparent to those who behold the magnitude of the thoughts in the Law and the prophets, and who are able to present them to others. Even granted that Jesus performed all the Jewish customs, even down to their sacrifices, how does this contribute to the idea that one should not believe in him as the Son of God? Jesus, then, is the Son of the God who gave the Law and the prophets; and we of the Church do not "Judaize," but having fled the mythologies of the Jews, we are disciplined and educated by the mystical contemplation of the Law and the prophets. For the prophets, as they did not stop the mind at the obvious historical narrative, nor at the legislation according to the words and the letter, say in one place, as if about to set forth histories: *I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter dark sayings from the beginning;* and in another place, praying about the Law as something obscure, [they ask for] the sense of it for themselves—

<column-break/>

Mark says: *The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the Prophet; Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who shall prepare your way before you,* showing that the beginning of the Gospel depends on the Jewish writings. What, therefore, does Celsus’s Jew bring against us, saying: *“For if someone announced to you that the Son of God would come to men, was this not our Prophet and our God’s?”* Or what kind of crime against Christianity is it that John, who baptized Jesus, was a Jew? For it does not follow that because he was a Jew, everyone who believes—whether approaching the Word from the Gentiles or the Jews—must keep the law of Moses according to the letter. After this, although Celsus babbles the same things about Jesus, repeating again that *“for his misdeeds he suffered punishment by the Jews,”* we will not repeat the answer, content with those things we have already said. Then, since his Jew makes little of the resurrection of the dead, the judgment of God, the rewards of the righteous, and the fire of the unrighteous as if they were trifles, and saying that Christians teach nothing new here, he thinks he can subvert Christianity in this way; it must be answered that our Jesus, seeing the Jews doing nothing worthy of prophetic doctrine, signified through a parable that the kingdom of God would be taken from them and handed over to those of the nations who would believe. Wherefore one can now see that all things among the Jews are delusions and trifles, for they do not have that light by which the Sacred Scriptures are understood: on the contrary, the doctrine of Christians possesses truth which can raise and lift up the mind and soul of man: and establish a certain form of citizenship, not such as the Jews have, humble and earthly, but heavenly, so that those who perceive the magnitude and sublimity of the prophetic meanings contained in the law may understand and be able to show them to others as well. But let us grant that Jesus observed all Jewish rites even unto the sacrifices; how does this lead to not believing that he is the Son of God? Jesus is therefore the Son of God who gave the law and the Prophets, which law we who are called by the name of the Church do not transgress: but having omitted the fables of the Jews, we are learned and instructed by the mystical understanding of the Prophets. For the Prophets, as those who do not stand within the obvious historical sense, nor within the words and letter of the law, speak thus elsewhere, surely about to relate histories; *I will open my mouth in parables, I will speak propositions from the beginning:* elsewhere [praying] for the sense of the law as something obscure and which cannot be understood without divine help—

He defends the Christian interpretation of the Law as a "mystical" rather than "literal" observance.</summary>

And that the one saying in Jesus, *I am the way and the truth and the life*, the Gospels do not know as being circumscribed [by the body], so as to be nowhere outside the soul and the body of Jesus, is clear from many things, and from these few which we shall set forth, being thus. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 2.

<margin>Matthew 28:20</margin>...to the disciples the promise, saying: *And behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age.* <note>original: "ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος"</note> We say these things, however, without separating the Son of God from Jesus. For in the highest sense of the divine economy, the soul and the body of Jesus have been made one with the Word of God. <margin>1 Corinthians 6:17</margin> For if, according to the teaching of Paul where he says: *He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit*; anyone who understands what it means to be joined to the Lord, and having been joined to Him, is in some way one spirit with the Lord—how much more, in a more divine and greater way, is that which was once a composite nature <note>referring to the human nature of Jesus</note> now one with the Word of God? And He demonstrated among the Jews the power of God through such wonders, which Celsus suspects were performed by sorcery <note>term: goeteia (sorcery/juggling), a common pagan charge against Christian miracles</note>, but which the Jews of that time <margin>Matthew 12:24</margin> (having learned about Beelzebub from I know not where) claimed were done by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, to cast out demons. Our Savior there refuted them for speaking most absurdly, as if the kingdom of wickedness had not yet reached its end. This will be clear to those who intelligently read the Gospel writings, which it is not the time to explain now. Furthermore, let Celsus produce and demonstrate what Jesus promised and did not <margin>* or "demonstrate, O Celsus"</margin> perform. But he will be unable to do so, especially since he thinks he brings his charges against Jesus and us from misheard reports, or from readings of the Gospels, or from Jewish stories. But since the Jew says again, "that after we had convicted and condemned him, we demanded he be punished," let him show how they convicted him, <margin>Matthew 26:59</margin> they who sought false witness and deceit against him—unless perhaps the "great conviction" against Jesus <margin>Ibid. v. 61.</margin> was that which the accusers spoke: "This man said, I am able to destroy the temple of God, and in three days to build it up." For while He <margin>* raise up</margin> <margin>John 2:21</margin> was speaking about the temple of His body, they—not knowing how to hear the words according to their intended meaning—thought the speech was about the stone temple, which was honored by the Jews more than was fitting for the true temple of God, the Word, Wisdom, and Truth. And let someone say, how did Jesus flee while hiding in a shameful manner? For one should demonstrate what the shame was. But since he also says that He was "caught": I would say that if being "caught" implies being taken against one's will, then Jesus was not caught. For at the fitting time He gave Himself into the hands of men, <margin>John 1:29.</margin> offering Himself as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Knowing, therefore, all things that were coming upon Him, He went out and said to them, "Whom <margin>John 18:5.</margin> do you seek?" They answered, "Jesus of Nazareth." He said to them, "I am He." And when again the Jew says that his people wanted to punish him after he was convicted and condemned: let them show how they convicted him, they who sought to suborn false testimonies; unless perhaps Jesus was greatly convicted by those words of the accusers; *This man said, I can destroy the temple of God, and in three days repair it*: which He Himself had said concerning the temple of His body, but they, as those who did not know how to understand the mind of the speaker, thought He spoke of the stone temple, which the Jews worshipped more than enough, while meanwhile despising the true temple of God, of truth and of wisdom. Let him also say who can, how Jesus sought escape by hiding shamefully; let him show what shamefulness can be reproached. Because he says *he was taken*, I am able to say; if being taken is of one unwilling, Jesus was not taken. For at the opportune time He allowed Himself to come into the power of men as the lamb of God, that He might take away the sin of the world. Knowing therefore all things that were to come upon Him, He went forward, and said to them; *Whom do you seek?* They answered Him; *Jesus of Nazareth.* Jesus says to them; *I am He.* Moreover, Judas who betrayed Him was standing with them. As therefore He said to them; *I am He:* they went backward, and fell to the ground. Again therefore He asked them; *Whom do you seek?* But they said again; *Jesus of Nazareth.*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...the Nazarene. *Jesus answered them; I told you that I am he; if therefore you seek me, let these go their way.* <note>original: "Respondit Jesus; Dixi vobis quòd ego sum..." quoting John 18:5-8</note> Furthermore, to the one who wished to bring him aid, and who had struck the servant of the High Priest and cut off his ear, he said; *Put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword. And why is it not the truth which those most closely associated with Jesus have handed down in writing, being so affected toward his word that they were ready to suffer anything for his sake? For to display such patience and constancy even unto death is not the mark of disciples who invent things about their teacher that never happened just as they pleased: and it is a manifest argument to honest readers that they knew what they were writing, since they endured all adversities with such tolerance for the sake of the Son of God, in whom they believed. 

But Celsus’s Jew learned that he was indeed betrayed by those whom he called disciples from the Gospels—mentioning "many disciples" where there was only one, Judas, so that he might seem to exaggerate the accusation—but he was not curious enough to know everything written about Judas. Judas was distracted by conflicting judgments about his teacher; he was neither entirely hostile to him in his soul, nor did he preserve the due reverence for his master with his whole heart. For he who betrayed him gave a sign to the crowd coming to seize Jesus; *Whomever I shall kiss, that is he; hold him fast:* <note>original: "Quemcumque osculatus fuero..." quoting Matthew 26:48</note> retaining some small amount of his former reverence; otherwise he would have betrayed him freely and without the pretense of a kiss. 

This certainly could persuade anyone regarding Judas’s purpose: that he had, mixed in his soul along with greed and the evil will to betray the Lord, a certain—so to speak—appearance of goodness innate from the words of Jesus, because it is written thus: *Judas the betrayer, seeing him condemned, moved by repentance, returned those thirty pieces of silver to the High Priests and elders, saying, I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

<margin>Matthew 27:4</margin>
<gloss>to the elders</gloss> It is clear that the teachings of Jesus were able to produce a certain repentance in him <note>Judas</note>, which shows that he did not entirely despise or trample upon what he had learned, but even his words, *I have sinned in betraying innocent blood*, were the confession of one acknowledging his sin. And see how burning and exceedingly vehement was the grief that came upon him from his repentance for his sins, so that he could no longer endure even to live; but throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he withdrew and went away and hanged himself. For he condemned himself, showing how much the teaching of Jesus was able to accomplish even in the sinner Judas—the thief and traitor—who was not able to utterly despise what he had learned from Jesus. Or perhaps those around Celsus will say that the details showing that Judas had not entirely abandoned Jesus, despite his daring crime against his teacher, are mere fictions; and that the only truth is that one of the disciples betrayed him. They would then falsely claim, contrary to what is written, that he betrayed him with his whole soul—which is implausible based on the writings themselves, to believe some parts and disbelieve others just as an enemy might. But if we must also put forward a persuasive argument concerning Judas, we shall say that in the Book of Psalms, the entire 108th Psalm <note>Psalm 109 in modern numbering</note> <margin>* Psalm 108:1</margin> contains the prophecy concerning Judas, which begins: *O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man are opened against me.* It also prophesies in that place that Judas would separate himself from the number of the Apostles because of his sin, so that another might be called into his place; <margin>Ibid. v. 8.</margin> and this is declared in the words, *And let another take his <margin>* grace or</margin> office <term>episkopēn</term> <note>original: ἐπισκοπὴν; refers to his position of oversight or "bishopric"</note>.* But even suppose <margin>Ibid.</margin> he was betrayed by a disciple who was worse than Judas, one who had cast out all the words he heard from Jesus; how does this contribute to an accusation against Jesus or Christianity? And how does this prove the Word to be false? We shall also defend what follows in the appropriate sections, showing that Jesus was not captured while fleeing, but willingly gave himself up for us all; from which it follows that even if he was bound, he was bound willingly, teaching us that we should undergo such things for the sake of piety without being unwilling. These other points also seem childish to me: "that a good general, leading many tens of thousands, was never betrayed; nor even a wicked leader of bandits and a most evil ruler, so long as he seemed useful to his associates; but he <note>Jesus</note> was betrayed by those with him, having neither ruled like a good general, nor—even if he deceived them—having gained the goodwill of those deceived, such as is shown toward a leader of bandits (if I may use such a term)." For one could find many histories concerning generals betrayed by their own people, and bandit leaders captured because their associates did not keep their agreements with them.

<column-break/>

It clearly appears that the discipline of Jesus was effective in him for stirring up repentance, which had not been altogether despised and trodden underfoot by the traitor: but even the words themselves, *I have sinned in betraying innocent blood*, were those of one confessing sin. And see how flaming and vehement a sorrow of repentance seized him, so that he could no longer endure to live, but having cast the money into the temple, he departed from there and strangled himself, being his own condemner and executioner: showing how much the doctrine of Jesus could do even in a sinner, a thief, a traitor, who was not able to totally despise what he had learned from Jesus: unless perhaps Celsus will say these things—which seem to indicate that Judas had not altogether defected even after his wicked audacity—are fictions, and that the only truth is that one of the disciples was his traitor, and will add to the Scripture that the betrayal was perpetrated with his whole soul; which would be quite absurd, to either believe or not believe the reading of the same commentary just as hatred dictates. But if we must also take something regarding Judas that may strike shame into our adversaries, we shall say that in the book of Psalms the entire hundred and eighth Psalm contains the prophecy concerning Judas, which begins thus: *O God, be not silent of my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man is opened against me*. There it is also prophesied that Judas, moved by his own fault from the order of the Apostles, had another substituted in his place, which is indicated by these words: *and let another take his office*. But suppose he was betrayed by some disciple who, being worse than Judas, had cast all the teaching of Jesus out of his breast: what does this pertain to the accusation of Jesus or of Christianity? How does it prove the falsehood of our religion? Those things which follow we have already refuted before: that Jesus was not captured while fleeing, but voluntarily delivered himself up for us all, so that consequently even if he was bound, he was bound of his own accord, teaching us that we should undergo such things for piety's sake, not against our will. Those things also seem to me childish which he adds next, that *never was a good commander and leader of many thousands betrayed; nay, not even a prince of robbers, an evil man and set over worse men, as long as he seemed useful to his own. But this man neither presided in the manner of a good commander, nor obtained from his deceived disciples even such goodwill as is shown by robbers to their prince*, if it may be so called. For one may find in histories many commanders betrayed by their companions, and princes of robbers captured by their associates because conditions were poorly kept.

<summary>Origen argues that Judas's suicide and confession prove that Jesus's teachings had a lasting moral impact even on a traitor, and he cites Psalm 108 as a prophetic fulfillment of these events. He further dismisses Celsus's claim that "good leaders are never betrayed" by pointing to numerous historical counter-examples of generals and bandit chiefs being turned upon by their followers.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Book 2

...nes. But suppose that no general or leader of robbers was ever betrayed by his own men: what does this have to do with the matter of Jesus being betrayed by one of his disciples? Since Celsus wishes to be considered a philosopher, let us ask him: was it a crime on Plato's part that, in the twentieth year after he had begun to hear him, Aristotle—revolting from his teacher—attacked his doctrine on the immortality of the soul and called Plato's "Ideas" mere <term>chattering</term> <note>original: "argutationes" / "τερετίσματα" - literally "twittering" or "empty talk," a derogatory term Aristotle used for Plato's Theory of Forms</note>? We might ask further, in doubt: Was Plato therefore no longer capable in Dialectic, nor fit to communicate his thoughts, simply because he was deserted by Aristotle? And are Plato's dogmas therefore false? Or is it perhaps possible—since it is established that Plato perceived the truth, as Platonists would easily grant—that Aristotle was ungrateful and wicked toward his master?

Furthermore, Chrysippus often seems to criticize Cleanthes in his writings, introducing innovations contrary to the doctrine he received from him, even though he had him as a teacher when he was still young and only held the first principles of philosophy. Yet Aristotle is said to have attended Plato's school for twenty continuous years, and Chrysippus also spent no small amount of time with the disciples of Cleanthes. Judas, however, was with Jesus for not even three full years. Moreover, in the commentaries on the lives of the philosophers, many such instances can be found, similar to what Celsus objects against our Jesus on account of Judas.

Besides, the Pythagoreans used to build <term>Cenotaphs</term> <note>Empty tombs erected as memorials for those whose bodies were lost, or in this case, for those "dead" to the community</note> for those who had defected from philosophy, having turned back to a <term>common life</term> <note>original: "vitam idioticam" / "ἰδιωτικὸν βίον" - the life of a private citizen or "layman" as opposed to the disciplined life of a philosopher</note>; yet Pythagoras was not on that account considered inferior in his doctrine and demonstrations, nor were his disciples. After this, the Jew in Celsus's writing proceeds thus: *“Although I could say many true things about the affairs of Jesus, and not similar to the writings of his disciples, I prudently pass them over.”*

What, then, are those "true things," dissimilar to the Gospel writings, which this Jew passes over? Is he perhaps using a rhetorical color, pretending to have something to say when he has nothing beyond the Gospels that could strike the listener as true, nor anything at all that could manifestly accuse Jesus and his doctrine? He then accuses the disciples, as if they had invented the claim that he foreknew and foretold everything that happened to him. On the contrary, we shall show that this also is true, even against Celsus's will, from many other things prophetically spoken by the Savior, in which he predicted what would happen to Christians in later ages. And who would not marvel at that which he foretold:

<column-break/>

...tombs. But let it be that no generals or bandit-leaders were betrayed; how does this contribute to the case against Jesus, namely, that one of his pupils became his betrayer? Since Celsus wraps himself in philosophy, we might ask him: what sort of accusation was it against Plato that Aristotle, after twenty years of listening to him, walked away and accused his discourse on the immortality of the soul, and called Plato's Ideas "twitterings"? Going further, we might say: was Plato then no longer powerful in dialectic, nor able to present his thoughts, because Aristotle walked away from him, and are Plato's dogmas false because of this? Or is it possible that while Plato was right (as those who philosophize according to him would say), Aristotle was wicked and ungrateful toward his teacher?

But Chrysippus also appears in many places in his writings to attack Cleanthes, innovating against his decrees, even though he was his teacher while he was still young and possessed only the beginnings of philosophy. And yet Aristotle is said to have studied under Plato for twenty years, and Chrysippus to have spent no little time in the schools of Cleanthes. But Judas did not stay with Jesus even three years. From what is written in the "Lives of the Philosophers," one could find many such things, for which <margin>* against Jesus</margin> Celsus blames Jesus on account of Judas. The Pythagoreans used to build cenotaphs for those who, after being embraced by philosophy, ran back to the common life; and the reason and proofs of Pythagoras and his followers were not weak because of this. After <margin>* The Jew</margin> these things, the Jew in Celsus says: *“That <margin>* true things about the affairs of Jesus</margin> although I have many true things to say about the events concerning Jesus, and not like those things written by the disciples of Jesus, I willingly leave those things aside.”*

What then are the truths, not like those written in the Gospels, which the Jew in Celsus leaves aside? Or will he seem, by using rhetorical skill, to pretend to have something to say, while having nothing to bring forward from outside the Gospels that is able to strike the listener as <margin>* it was * true</margin> truly true, or to clearly accuse Jesus and his teaching? He accuses the disciples of having faked the claim that he foreknew and foretold all that happened to him. But we shall present this as being true, even if Celsus does not wish it, from many other things prophesied by the Savior, in which he includes the things that happened to Christians in later generations. And who would not wonder at the thing foretold: *“You shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake,”* <margin>Matthew 10:18</margin>

He challenges Celsus's claim that there are "secret truths" about Jesus not found in the Gospels, dismissing it as a rhetorical bluff.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

...on account of me, for a testimony to them and to the nations; <note>original: "εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσι"</note> and whatever else he foretold concerning the persecutions his disciples would undergo? For what other doctrine moved among men causes others to be punished? One of the accusers of Jesus might say that, seeing impious or false doctrines being accused, he decided to dignify his own cause by "foretelling" things about it. For if people had to be brought before governors and kings because of their doctrines, who else should have been brought but the **Epicureans**, who entirely do away with Providence? Or those of the **Peripatetic** school <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, who claim that prayers and sacrifices to the Divine achieve nothing? 

But someone will say that the **Samaritans** are also persecuted for their own religion. To him we shall say this: that the **Sicarii** <note>A radical Jewish faction; here referring to those practicing circumcision against Roman law</note> are put to death because of circumcision, as they mutilate themselves contrary to established laws and those privileges granted to Jews alone. And one never hears of a judge asking a *Sicarius* if he might be acquitted by changing his mind and abandoning his supposed religion; rather, if he persists, he is led away to death. In that case, the mere evidence of circumcision is enough for the appropriate execution. 

But Christians alone (according to the words spoken by their Savior, saying: 
<margin>Matthew 10:18</margin>
**"You shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake"**) are permitted by the judges, until their very last breath, to renounce Christianity, sacrifice according to common customs, take the oath, and live safely at home. See then if it was not with great authority that he said: 
<margin>Matthew 10:32</margin>
**"Whoever confesses me before men, him will I also confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men,"** and so forth. 

Follow my argument back to Jesus speaking these things, and see them being prophesied before they had yet happened. Unless, in your disbelief, you say that he is talking nonsense 
<margin>* he says these things.</margin>
and * speaking in vain, or that these things will not happen. If you are hesitant to agree with his words, wait until they are fulfilled and the teaching of Jesus’s words is established—when governors and kings make it their business to kill those who confess Jesus. Then we shall believe that he received great power from God to sow this Word among the human race, and that he prevailed in persuading them. 

Anyone would be amazed, tracing the argument back to him, seeing what 
<margin>Matthew 24:14</margin>
he said then: **"This gospel shall be preached in the whole world for a testimony to them and to the nations,"** and observing that, according to his words, the Gospel of Jesus Christ has now been preached to all under heaven, both to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish. For the Word, spoken with power, has conquered every human nature...

<column-break/>

...for a testimony to them and the nations: and if he prophesied anything else regarding the future persecutions of the disciples? For on account of what other doctrine arisen among men are others punished? So that some detractor of Jesus might say that, seeing impious and false doctrines being accused, he snatched a magnificent reputation from such predictions. For if, because of the impiety of doctrines, some were to be led before Kings and princes, none ought to have been led sooner than the **Epicureans**, who remove providence entirely; or the **Peripatetics**, who deny that prayers poured out to God or sacrifices are of any use. 

But someone will say the **Samaritans** also suffer persecution because of their religion. To him we will reply that the **Sicarii** are killed on account of circumcision, because they mutilate themselves against the prescriptions of the laws which permit it to the Jews alone. Nor was it ever heard that a Judge gave a *Sicarius* accused of his religion the option of whether he preferred to be acquitted by changing his religion, or to be killed by persisting in it; rather, the display of circumcision is sufficient for his punishment. 

But to Christians alone (according to that prediction of the Savior: *Before Governors and Kings you shall be led for my sake:*) is it permitted by the Judges, as long as they draw breath, to abjure Christianity, and to sacrifice in the manner of others, and so live securely at home. And see if it is not said from the greatest authority which he possessed: *Whoever shall have confessed me before men, I also will confess him before my Father, who is in heaven: and whoever shall have denied me before men, I also will deny him before my Father:* 

And ascend in your mind to Jesus predicting these things before they happened; unless perhaps you are going to say, being unwilling to believe, *He trifles and achieves nothing;* for these things will not be. Or, being doubtful in mind whether you will assent to his words until the event approves the matter, and his doctrine is established by Kings and Princes taking care that those who confess Jesus are removed from the midst—which having been done, then at last we are to agree that, having received power from the Father, he was sent to disseminate the word among men, which indeed he brought forth since he was certain it would prevail greatly. 

Who likewise will not wonder, ascending in contemplation to that prophecy: *This Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, for a testimony to them and the nations;* when he sees that, according to that prediction, it is already preached in all lands which are under heaven, to Greeks and barbarians, both to the wise and the foolish? For the word preached with power has conquered all human nature...

<summary>Origen argues that the unique persecution of Christians—and the specific legal "out" offered to them to recant—proves the divine authority of Jesus's prophecies. He contrasts the Christian experience with that of philosophers and Samaritans to highlight the supernatural spread of the Gospel.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

...nor is there any race of men to be seen by whom this doctrine has not been received. But let that unbelieving Jew of Celsus, who thinks what has been handed down concerning the foreknowledge of Jesus is vain, consider how, while Jerusalem was still standing and the Jewish ceremonies were intact within it, Jesus predicted how it would be treated by the Romans. For they will not say that Jesus’s intimate hearers taught the Gospel without writings and left behind disciples uninstructed by any commentaries <note>original: "commentariis" – here meaning written records or memoirs</note>, for it is written in the Gospel: *But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near.* <note>Luke 21:20</note> Certainly, when these things were being written, no armies were besieging Jerusalem, nor attacking it with ramparts. For this began to happen under the reign of Nero and lasted until the times of Vespasian, whose son Titus leveled Jerusalem to the ground: as it seems to Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian</note>, this was on account of James the Just, who was called the brother of Jesus Christ; but as the facts themselves cry out, it was on account of Jesus Christ the Son of God. And yet Celsus, by not denying his foreknowledge, could have feigned contempt, just as he previously tried to diminish his power by attributing it to magical deceptions; he could have said that many have known what would happen to them through the sciences of divining, augury, soothsaying, and the stars; but he preferred to deny this entirely as something too excellent. Regarding the miracles performed, although he admits them to some extent, he nevertheless slanders them as being disguised by trickery. Phlegon <note>A 2nd-century Greek author</note> certainly, in the thirteenth or, if I am not mistaken, the fourteenth volume of his *Chronicles*, candidly confesses that Christ had foreknowledge of future events—confusing Peter with Jesus—and bears witness that whatever had been predicted came to pass. Nevertheless, there too, perhaps because of this foreknowledge, he almost unwillingly confesses that the discourse we received from our ancestors was not void of divine power. Celsus adds: *The disciples of Jesus, having nothing to invent in the face of an obvious fact, devised the claim that he foreknew all things.* This is because he has not read, or did not wish to read, what is most truthfully written, including that which was said by him to the disciples: *All of you will be scandalized this night.* As it truly happened, it was also predicted to Peter that before the cock crowed he would deny the Lord three times, and Peter denied him three times according to the prophecy. For if they had not been students of truth, or if (as it seems to Celsus) they had delighted in writing fictions, they would not...

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

<margin>John 10:18</margin>
No one takes my soul from me; but I lay it down of myself: I have the power to lay it down, and I have the power to take it up again. <note>original: "Nemo tollit animam meam..." / "Οὐδεὶς αἴρει τὴν ψυχήν μου..."</note> And perhaps for this reason he hastened his departure from the body, so that he might preserve it whole, and that his legs might not be broken, as were those of the robbers crucified with him. For the soldiers broke the legs of the first and of the other who was crucified with him; but when they came to Jesus, as they saw he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Now, therefore, we have responded to that point: *How is it credible that he foretold these things?* and furthermore, *how can he who died be immortal?* Let him who wishes learn that it is not the dead man who is immortal, but he who rose from the dead. Not only, therefore, is the dead man not immortal, but not even Jesus—before he died in that composite state <note>Referring to the union of divine and human natures</note>—was immortal, since he was destined to die; for no one who is about to die is immortal; but one is immortal when he will die no longer. *But Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more: death shall no longer have dominion over him;* <note>Romans 6:9</note> even if those who are incapable of understanding these things do not wish to. Now, how foolish is this: *What God, or demon, or prudent man, foreknowing such things would happen to him, would not, if indeed he could, have avoided them, but instead willingly fell into what he had foreseen?* And yet Socrates knew that he would die by drinking hemlock; and he could have, if indeed he had wished to obey Crito, escaped from custody unharmed; but he preferred, following a certain reasoning of his own, to die philosophically rather than to live a life unworthy of a philosopher. Moreover, Leonidas, the leader of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, knowing he was just about to die with the guards at Thermopylae, did not labor to live basely; but said to his companions, *Let us dine as if we are to sup among those in the underworld:* many such examples may be found in histories, if anyone cares to pursue such things. What wonder is it then, if Jesus, not being ignorant of future events, did not avoid them, but fell into what was foreknown? Since even Paul, his disciple, having heard what he was to suffer in Jerusalem, nevertheless exposed himself to dangers, even rebuking those weeping and standing in his way to prevent him from going up there. Indeed, even in our own time, many, knowing they must die if they confess Christianity—but that by denying it they would be acquitted and even receive back their confiscated goods—have despised life and voluntarily chosen death for the sake of piety. Next, the Jew in Celsus says another equally foolish thing: *How is it that if he foretold both the betrayer and the denier, they did not fear him as God, so that the one would abstain from betrayal and the other from denial?* Nor does this most wise man see—

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

<column-break/>

<note>The text begins mid-argument, addressing Celsus's claim that if Jesus were God and foreknew the betrayal, the disciples' actions were either forced by fate or the prophecy itself was a lie.</note>

...in the midst of the conflict, [Celsus argues] that because he foreknew it as God, it was impossible for him to be deceived. It was therefore impossible for the one known as the traitor not to betray, or for the one exposed as the denier not to deny. But if it were possible for this one not to betray and that one not to deny—since the act of not betraying or not denying remained possible for those who had been forewarned—then he who said "this one will betray" and "this one will deny" would no longer be speaking the truth. 

Furthermore, if he foreknew the betrayal, he saw the wickedness from which the betrayal would spring, which was by no means overturned by the foreknowledge. Again, if he understood the one who would deny, seeing the weakness from which the denial would come, he predicted the denial; yet this weakness was not going to be removed so suddenly just by the foreknowledge. 

And where does that claim come from: "*But they themselves both betrayed and denied him, caring nothing for him*"? For it has been shown that regarding the traitor, it is a falsehood to say he betrayed his teacher out of utter contempt. No less is this shown regarding the one who denied him, who <margin>Matthew 26:75</margin> went out and, because of his denial, wept bitterly. 

It is also superficial to say: "*Even a man, when he senses a plot against him and foresees he will be betrayed to the conspirators, turns away and guards himself.*" For many have been plotted against even when they foresaw the plots. Next, as if bringing his argument to a conclusion, Celsus says: "*Therefore, because these things were foretold, they happened; for it was impossible otherwise. But because they happened, the prediction is proven a lie; for it is altogether impossible that those who heard the warning beforehand would still betray and deny.*" 

We must overturn this by what has been said previously, along with the conclusion he draws: "because these things were foretold, they happened." We say that it did not happen [simply] because it was possible; rather, because it happened, the prediction is shown to be true. For the truth of future events is judged by the outcome. His proposition is false when he says the prediction is proven a lie; and Celsus speaks in vain when he says: "*it is altogether impossible that those who heard the warning would still betray and deny.*"

After this, look at what he says: "*These things (he says) he foretold because he was God, and it was absolutely necessary for the prediction to happen. Being God, he led his own disciples and prophets, with whom he ate and drank, to such a point that they became impious and unholy—he who ought to have been a benefactor to all men, and especially to his own table-companions. While no man would plot against one with whom he shared a table, here one who feasted with God became a plotter. And, what is even more absurd, God himself plotted against his own table-companions, making them traitors and impious.*" <margin>* so as to be impious.</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Page 73

frivolous. Celsus thinks that because someone with foreknowledge predicted an event, it happens *because* it was predicted. We, however, do not concede this, and we say that the one who foreknows is not the cause of the future event; rather, the future event—which would have happened anyway even if no one had predicted it—provided the cause for the foreknower to predict it. For the whole matter in the prophet's foreknowledge is this: since either of two things could happen, this specific one *will* happen. We do not say that the foreknower takes away the possibility of it either happening or not, as if he were saying: "This shall entirely be, and it is impossible for it to happen otherwise." This is understood universally regarding all things that can be foreknown about us, whether according to Holy Scripture or according to the histories of the Greeks. Otherwise, that fallacy which the Logicians call the <term>Idle Argument<note>original: *ἀργὸν λόγον* (argon logon). A famous Stoic puzzle: if it is fated you will recover from illness, you will recover whether you call a doctor or not; if it is fated you won't, you won't. Therefore, doing anything is "idle."</note></term> will not be a fallacy in Celsus's judgment, when in truth it is a fallacy. 

To understand this, I will bring forward prophecies from the Scriptures concerning Judas, and our Savior’s foreknowledge of him as the traitor; and from the histories of the Greeks, the oracle given to Laius—assuming for the moment that it was truly given, since it does not hinder the present discussion about Judas. In the 108th Psalm, the beginning of which is *O God, do not be silent to my praise*, it is said from the person of the Savior: *The mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me*. If you observe what is written in that Psalm, you will find it was foreknown that just as he would be the traitor of the Savior, so the cause of the treachery would be in himself, so that he is worthy of the imprecations contained in the prophecy. *Let him suffer these things*, it says, *because he did not remember to show mercy, and persecuted the beggar and the poor man*. Therefore, he was able to remember to show mercy, and not to persecute the one he persecuted; and although he was able, he did not do it, but betrayed him, so that he is worthy of the curses of the prophecy.

And this whole matter happens to be in the foreknowledge of the observer: while it is possible for [this or that] to happen, this one of them *will* be. And such a thing extends to all foreknowledge concerning things in our power, whether according to the divine scriptures or according to the histories of the Greeks. And the so-called "Idle Argument" among the logicians, being a fallacy, will not be a fallacy as far as Celsus is concerned, but according to sound reasoning it is a fallacy.

But being able, he did not do it, but betrayed him; so that he was worthy of the curses in the prophecy.

> *You have voided a great oath, and the salt and the table.*

After this, as if he had already demonstrated the point by most fitting logical consequences, he proceeds thus: *And, what is even more absurd, God himself lays snares for his own companions, making them traitors and impious.* How Jesus laid snares, or made his disciples traitors and impious, this man <note>Celsus</note> cannot show, except from this supposed logical consequence (as it seemed to him), which is very easy for anyone to refute. After this he says: *If it seemed good to him, and obeying his father he underwent punishment; it is clear that to one who is God, and who endures it willingly, none of those things which he suffered were painful or grievous.* He does not see that he is speaking contradictions: for if he grants that he was punished by his own and his Father's will, it is clear that he paid the penalty; and penalties cannot be inflicted without pains, for they are sweet and desirable to no one. But if he thinks pain and torture were absent because he did not bear them unwillingly, how does he grant he was punished? This man did not understand that he who once assumed a body through birth, certainly assumed one subject to pains, and to those troublesome things which happen to those clothed in bodies; if by the name "troublesome" we understand what no one wants for themselves. Therefore, just as he willingly assumed a body not different from the nature of human flesh, so he assumed with it whatever brings pain and trouble to it: which were then inflicted by the will of his enemies, not by the will of him who suffered. Moreover, it was answered before that he would not have come into the hands of men if he had not willed it; but he did come because of that immense utility which fell to the whole human race from his death. Then in the following parts, wishing to show that the things he suffered were troublesome and sorrowful to him, because he could not change their nature even if he had wished, he <note>Celsus</note> speaks thus: *Why then does he lament and grieve, and pray that the fear of destruction might pass away in these words; Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass.* See here also the malice of Celsus, that he does not embrace the truthfulness of the Evangelists, who could have passed over in silence those things which seem to these people worthy of reproach, but did not pass them over for many reasons to be stated in their proper place in the interpretation of the Gospels: but he tragically accuses the text of the Gospel, adding things which are not found there; for it is not written that Jesus lamented. <margin>Ibid. v. 42</margin>

But they also did not hear the part, *He makes one suffer, and again restores*; but only, *He makes one suffer*. Thus, therefore, the Jew introduced by Celsus, having set forth the words, *O Father, if only this cup could pass by*, suppressed the following words and those which show Jesus prepared for his passion with discipline and vigor. And these matters, which contain much discourse from the wisdom of God, we shall reasonably set before those whom 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:6</margin>

The weakness is in the words, *Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me*; but the readiness of the spirit is in, *Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.* And if one must also observe the order of what was said, notice that the prayer according to the weakness of the flesh (so to speak) is mentioned first; but later, the things according to the readiness of the spirit are more numerous. For there is one instance of, *Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me*; but then more numerous are, *Not as I will, but as You will*; and, *My Father, if this cannot...*

<column-break/>

*Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will:* and not even those words by which he accommodates his own will to the judgment of the Father, where declaring his obedience he speaks thus: *If this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, Your will be done.* Celsus does here what malicious and impious listeners of the divine Scripture are accustomed to do: for they do not hide that they have heard—indeed, they frequently reproach us with this word—*I will kill*; but they do not remember that which follows: *I will make alive.* Since that entire speech signifies that men living in public evil and practicing malice are killed by God, so that a better life may soon be restored to them by Him, that they might die to sin. Similarly, they heard that, *I will strike*; but not likewise that, *And I will heal*: just as if a physician speaks while cutting bodies and inflicting greater wounds so that he may remove something harmful, who nevertheless does not end in torture, but restores the body itself to integral health by his cure. But these people do not hear this whole thing, by which the same one who inflicts pain also restores to health, but only that he causes pain. In the same way, this Jew introduced by Celsus, after he recounted that; *Father, would that this cup could pass*, adds nothing more of those things which show the constant and prompt mind of Jesus toward his passion. But these things, having more recondite meanings to be opened through that divine wisdom which Paul writes is rightly delivered to the perfect, saying: *But we speak wisdom among the perfect:* deferring them for a little while, we will deal with certain things suited to the present business that now come to mind. We have said also in the sections above, that there are certain voices in Jesus of the firstborn of all creation, such as, *I am the way, the truth, and the life,* and others like these: but others of the man who is understood in him, such as that; *But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from my Father.* So here also he describes in his human nature both the weakness of human flesh and the alacrity of the spirit: the weakness in these words, *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me;* the alacrity of the spirit in those, *Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.* But if it pleases one to observe also the order of the sayings, attend to the fact that the word of weakness, of the flesh so to speak, was said first; but later those more numerous words from the alacrity of the spirit: for this is one, *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me;* but those are more, *Not as I will, but as You will,* and, *My Father, if it cannot...*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

...this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done. <note>Matthew 26:42</note> It should also be observed that he did not say, "let this cup depart from me," but spoke with a certain pious reverence, not without a condition, in this manner: *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.* <note>Matthew 26:39</note> Nor am I unaware of another interpretation of this passage: that the Savior, seeing what the people and Jerusalem would suffer in vengeance for the crime committed by the Jews against him, said—out of no other reason than the benevolence with which he regarded that people, wishing to avoid his future passion—*Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.* It is as if he were saying: "Since, because of my drinking this cup of punishment, the entire nation will be deserted by you, I pray, if it be possible, that this cup may pass from me, so that my portion <note>The Jewish people, often referred to as God's portion in the Old Testament.</note> may not be entirely deserted by you because of their daring crime against me." Furthermore, if, as Celsus says, *Jesus felt no pain or distress at the time of his passion*, how could his followers use his example in enduring bitter things for the sake of piety, when he only appeared to suffer, but in reality suffered nothing human? The Jew in Celsus's writing goes on to rebuke the disciples of Jesus as fabricators of such narratives, adding that *they were not even able to give their lies a plausible appearance.* To this it will be answered, that it would have been easy either to disguise such things or not to write them at all. For who, if these things were not contained in the Gospels, could reproach us for Jesus having spoken such things during his passion? Celsus does not understand, however, that it is not possible for the same men to be so deceived as to hold Jesus as the God foretold by the oracles of the Prophets, and yet to invent things about him which they themselves know to be untrue. Either, therefore, they did not invent them, but wrote the truth from their hearts; or if they produced falsehoods against their own conscience, they were not so deceived as to hold him for God. After this, he says that some of the believers, as if from a fit of drunkenness, allow themselves to change the Gospel scripture in three or four or more ways, so that by such revisions they might be able to deny the text whenever they are challenged. Indeed, I know of the Gospel being changed by no one else except the disciples of Marcion <note>A 2nd-century dualist who rejected the Old Testament and edited the Gospel of Luke.</note> and Valentinus <note>A prominent Gnostic teacher.</note> and perhaps those of Lucanus: which is a crime not of the Gospel, but of those who dared to recklessly corrupt it. And just as the crime of the Sophists, Epicureans, Peripatetics, or whoever professes false dogmas is nothing to philosophy; so the crime of those corrupting the Gospels and introducing new sects in the name of Jesus does not fall upon true Christianity.

<column-break/>

...pass, unless I drink it, let your will be done. <note>original Greek: παρελθεῖν, ἐὰν μὴ αὐτὸ πίω, γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου</note> And it must be noted that it was not said, "let this cup depart from me"; but all this was spoken piously and with humble hesitation: *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.* And I know of a certain explanation of this place: that the Savior, seeing what the people and Jerusalem would suffer for the punishment of the things dared against him by the Jews, for no other reason than his love for mankind toward them, wishing not to suffer the things he was about to suffer, says, *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.* As if he were saying, "Since from my drinking the cup of punishment, the whole nation will be abandoned by you; I pray, if it be possible, for this cup to pass from me; so that your portion, having dared [to act] against me, might not be altogether abandoned by you." But even if, as Celsus says,
> "neither anything painful nor distressing happened to Jesus at that time, how could those after him have used Jesus as an example for enduring evils for the sake of piety, if he did not suffer human things, but only seemed to have suffered?"

<margin>1 Peter 2:21</margin>
Furthermore, the Jew in Celsus says to the disciples of Jesus, as if they had fabricated these things, that
> "even in lying, you were not able to cover your fabrications with plausibility."

And to this it must be said, that it was easy not to cover such things in this way, but not to record them in the first place. For who, if these things were not lying in the Gospels, would have been able to reproach us on the grounds that Jesus spoke such things according to the [divine] economy? <note>term: economy (oikonomia) — the divine plan for salvation, often used to explain why God acts in human ways.</note> But Celsus does not understand that it is not possible for the same person to be both deceived about Jesus—viewing him as God and as prophesied—and to fabricate things about him, clearly knowing that the fabrications are not true. Either, then, they did not fabricate, but wrote thus, and recorded without falsehood; or they recorded while lying, and did not believe these things, nor were they deceived into thinking him God. After these things, he says that some of the believers, as if coming from a state of drunkenness to the point of being beside themselves, alter
> "the Gospel from its first writing in three-fold and four-fold and many-fold ways, and transform it, so that they might have [means] to deny it in the face of criticisms."

But I do not know of others who have altered the Gospel, other than those from Marcion, and those from Valentinus, and I think also those from Lucanus. But this being said is not an accusation against the Word, but against those who dared to tamper with the Gospels. And just as the Sophists are not an accusation against philosophy, nor the Epicureans, nor the Peripatetics, or whoever they may be who hold false opinions; so those who alter the Gospels and introduce strange heresies against the will of Jesus are not an accusation against true Christianity.

He also addresses Celsus's claim of textual corruption, attributing such changes only to specific heretical groups rather than the Church at large.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

...of Jesus's teaching. Since, after these things, the Jew in Celsus's writing also reproaches the "good Christian" for proclaiming the things concerning Jesus through the prophets, we shall say—in addition to what was said above on this matter—that he ought (as he says) out of consideration for men to have set forth the prophecies themselves. By advocating for what seemed to him more plausible, he should have attempted to overturn the accepted use of the prophetic interpretations. For he would then have seemed not to be snatching away such a major topic with a few words, especially since he says: "The prophetic writings could be applied to ten thousand others much more plausibly than to Jesus." <note>Celsus argues that Messianic prophecies are vague enough to fit anyone, a common skeptical trope.</note> He certainly ought to have addressed those Christians who hold this as their strongest proof, and for each individual prophecy, set forth how it can be applied to others much more plausibly than to Jesus. 

But Celsus did not even realize that he put into the mouth of his Jewish character words that would perhaps be plausibly said by someone entirely alienated from the prophetic writings. For a Jew would not concede that the prophetic words could be applied to "ten thousand others" more plausibly than to Jesus; rather, by providing his own specific interpretation for each passage, he would attempt to oppose the Christian interpretation. Or, at least speaking with persuasion, let us attempt to do such a thing. 

We have already stated in the preceding sections that the Christ is prophesied as having two visitations <term>advents: the first in humility, the second in glory</term> for the benefit of the human race. Therefore, there is no longer a need for us to defend ourselves against the statement made by the Jew: "that the prophets say the one who is to visit will be a great and powerful lord of all the earth, and of all nations and armies." 

I think he also spoke in a "Jewish" manner <note>Origen implies a stubborn or dismissive tone</note> regarding the necessity of that point, when—without proof, even if plausible—he reviles Jesus. Indeed, neither a Jew, nor Celsus, nor anyone else can demonstrate with proof that he announced such "destruction." For no such "destructive" man ever turned so many people away from the flood of evils toward a life according to nature, self-control, and the rest of the virtues. 

Celsus also tossed aside this point: "No one establishes a God or a son of God from such symbols and misheard rumors, nor from such ignoble evidence." He ought to have set forth these "misheard rumors," refuted them, and presented the "ignoble evidence" through reasoning; so that if he seemed to say anything plausible, the Christian might attempt to contend against it and overturn the argument. What he said about Jesus, he simplified as if speaking of a great man, but he did not wish to see that this...

<margin>
* having made two.
* having visited.
</margin>

<column-break/>

...introducing his doctrine. And since, as the speech proceeds, that Jew also objects to the Christians: *That they use the prophecies of the Prophets concerning Jesus;* we shall respond beyond what was already said above; that he ought, if, as he says, he spares men, to explain the sense of those Prophecies; and having brought forth more likely reasons, only then convict our people of misusing the Prophecies. For in this way he would have taken care lest he seem to constrain such a long chapter into too few words: especially when he writes; *That the Prophetic sayings can be taken in countless other ways much more aptly and likely than if they are referred to Jesus.* 

He ought also to have stood bravely against the very strong reasons of the Christians, and accurately declared through each individual Prophecy how they fit others better than our Jesus, and with how much more probability. But he does not understand that if these things had been said against Christians by someone a stranger to the Prophetic scriptures, they might perhaps have been more plausible: now Celsus fashions words for the persona of the Jew which a Jew would never say. For a Jew will not agree that the Prophetic sayings can be fitted to countless others more probably than to Jesus; but bringing forward some interpretation of his own for each one, he will endeavor to oppose it to the one received by Christians; not saying things that are entirely credible, yet giving effort so that he might do this. 

Moreover, we have already said before how it was prophesied concerning the two comings of Christ to the human race: for which reason there is no need for us to respond to the Jew saying; *That a certain most powerful king and Lord of the whole earth and of all nations and armies is foretold by the Prophets as the one who is to come.* That is Jewish enough and suited to their resentment, that, omitting demonstrations, he prefers to attack Jesus with insults adapted for persuasion. 

As for what he says, that such a "pestilence" was never foretold: neither a Jew, nor Celsus, nor anyone else will be able to teach that a "pestilential" man turned so many men from the filth of vices to the study of virtues, and to leading a life temperately according to the prescriptions of nature. Celsus also added that; *But no one proves a God and a son of God from such signs and rumors and such cold arguments.* But he ought to have proved those rumors dragged out of falsehood, and refuted those cold arguments with reasons: so that if he seemed to bring anything likely, the Christian would have material for contending, and reasons for trying to subvert him. But that which he said about Jesus as if about an excellent man happened, yet he did not want to acknowledge it, although...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

->The evidence of the matter itself asserts this concerning Jesus. *Just as the Sun*, he [Celsus] says, *while illuminating all other things, first shows itself; so it behooved the son of God to do*. We are able to say: he has indeed done so. For in his days justice has dawned, and an abundance of peace was created immediately from the time he was born, with God preparing the nations for his teaching, so that all might obey the one king of the Romans. This was so that the commerce of nations might not be interrupted by a multitude of kingdoms, which would have made it more difficult for the Apostles of Jesus to carry out that command of his: *Going forth, teach all nations* <note>original: "Euntes docete omnes gentes" - Matthew 28:19</note>. It is well established that Jesus was born during the reign of Augustus, who, as a prince, leveled most of the lands of the earth by bringing them under a single empire. For it would have been an obstacle to the distribution of the teaching of Jesus's disciples throughout the whole world if there had been many kingdoms—not only for the reasons mentioned above, but because everyone would have been forced to perform military service and fight for their own fatherland due to wars. This was the case before the age of Augustus and in earlier times, such as when the Athenians were at war with the Peloponnesians, and others similarly with other nations. How then could that peaceful doctrine, which does not even permit one to repel the violence of enemies, have gained strength unless the affairs of the world had been changed into a milder state upon the arrival of Jesus? After this, he accuses the Christians of *arguing sophistically when they say that the Word itself is the son of God; and he thinks it a heavy crime that, having promised the Word as the son of God, we soon present not a pure and holy Word, but a man affected by the most shameful punishment, beaten with whips, and driven to the cross*. Regarding these slanders of Celsus, a brief response was given above, where it was shown that the first-born of all creation assumed a human body and soul, and that by the command of God so many creatures were created, and that the Word, being God, received that command. And since it is a Jew who speaks in Celsus's work, we shall not absurdly use that saying: *He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their corruptions* <note>original: "Emisit verbum suum..." - Psalm 107:20 (Vulgate 106:20)</note>, which we also mentioned above. Indeed, though I have debated with many Jews, even those considered wise, I have heard no one who approved of the Word being the son of God, as Celsus claims. He makes his Jewish character speak thus: *If the Word is the son of God to you, we also approve*. We have already said before that Jesus can be considered neither a boaster nor a sorcerer; therefore, it is not necessary to repeat the same things, lest in responding to Celsus we ourselves repeat his wordiness. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 2.

Attacking the genealogy, Celsus fails to mention those points which are actually debated among Christians—those discrepancies in the lineages that some bring forward as accusations. For Celsus, truly a boaster who claims to know all things concerning Christians, wisely kept silent regarding the actual Scripture. “He says that the genealogies were fabricated to trace Jesus back to the first light <note>original: "φωτὸς" (light), though the Latin and context suggest "man" (φωτός/φωτός confusion or "first man")</note> and to the kings of the Jews. And he thinks he brings forward a noble point: that the wife of a carpenter, being of such a birth, would not have been ignorant of it.” What does this matter to the argument, even if she were not ignorant? How does it hurt the premise? But let it be that she was ignorant; how does he know she was? Was she not descended from the first man? And was her lineage not traced back to those who reigned in Judea? Or does Celsus think it necessary that the poor must always be born from the poor, or kings from kings? It seems to me a waste of time to dwell on this point. For it is clear, even in our own times, that some from wealthy and famous families have become poorer than Mary, and from those more obscure than Mary, kings have arisen. “And what noble deed,” he asks, “did Jesus perform as a God, looking down on men and mocking and playing with what was happening to him?” To him asking this, how should we reply? We could present the noble and miraculous events that accompanied his passion from the <margin>Matthew 27:51; Luke 23:45</margin> Gospels: that the earth shook, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, and darkness occurred during the day when the sun failed. But if Celsus trusts the Gospels only where he thinks he can accuse Christians, but utterly disbelieves them where they establish the divinity of Jesus, we shall say to him: “O man, either disbelieve them entirely and do not bring charges, or if you believe them, marvel at the Word of God who became man, wishing to benefit the entire human race.” A noble work of Jesus is that, even to this day, those whom God wills are healed in his name. Regarding the eclipse in the time of Tiberius Caesar, under whose reign Jesus appears to have been crucified, and regarding the great earthquakes that then occurred, Phlegon also wrote, I believe, in the thirteenth book of his *Chronicles*. Mocking Jesus, as he thinks, the Jew in Celsus’s writing is recorded as knowing the words of Euripides’s *Bacchus* <note>The character Dionysus in the play *The Bacchae*</note> saying:
<margin>Euripides, *The Bacchae*</margin>
> The deity himself will free me, whenever I wish.
<margin>* study philosophy.</margin>
Now, Jews are not at all fond of * Greek literature. But let it be that some Jew was more literary; how then does it follow that because Jesus did not free himself when bound, he was therefore unable to do so?

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the preceding Greek text, provided in the original manuscript for scholars.</note>

...genealogy, he by no means mentions those things which come into discussion among Christians and are blamed by some as if the genealogies were discrepant. For that truly boastful Celsus, having professed to know all things of the Christians, did not know how to hesitate prudently in the Scriptures: but he says the weavers of the genealogy please him too much, because they make the first king of the Jews the head of Jesus's pedigree: and he seems to himself to bring in something great, that the wife of a carpenter should be ignorant of such a prince of her own race. For what is this to the matter? What if she did not ignore it, what does it matter? But suppose she did ignore it, how is this established to you? Was she not descended from the first man? And was she not joined by blood to the kings of the Jews? Unless perhaps Celsus thinks it necessary that all ancestors of the poor were poor, or all ancestors of kings were kings. Therefore, it is not pleasing to linger in vain on these things, since it is manifest even in our times that some from the rich and illustrious have become poorer than Mary, and on the contrary, from the most obscure have come kings and governors of nations. He adds: *What magnificent thing did Jesus do as a God looking down from on high upon men, and playing and laughing at that which happened to him?* To this inquirer, what ought we to respond? Even if we could bring forward the miraculous thing which happened in the passion, even from the Gospels, when the earth moved, rocks were scissored, monuments opened, the veil of the temple torn from the highest even to the lowest, and darkness made during the day with the sun failing. But if Celsus believes the Gospels whenever they seem to him to act against Christians, but would not believe the same ones asserting the divinity of Jesus: we will say to him, hey you! either do not believe them in general, and cease to criminalize, or, if you believe all that they contain, admire the Word of God made man, with that purpose, that he might profit the universal human race. A magnificent work of Jesus stands today, while even today the ill-affected are healed by his name, whom God wishes to be healed. Concerning the failure of the sun under Tiberius Caesar, by whose command it is certain Jesus was crucified, and concerning the great earthquakes of that time, even Phlegon wrote in the thirteenth, or (unless I am mistaken) the fourteenth volume of his *Chronicles*. But playing, as it seems to him, against Jesus, the Jew of Celsus recognizes Euripides's Bacchus saying:
> *God himself will solve me, when I myself shall wish.*
But Jews are not accustomed to be curious in Greek letters: but suppose some of the Jews were so literate, was Jesus therefore unable to release himself because he did not release himself?
