# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

How could he? For either Celsus must believe what is contained in my writings—that Peter was bound in custody and went out when an angel loosed his chains, and that Paul, together with Silas, was bound in wooden stocks at Philippi in Macedonia and was set free by divine power when the doors of the prison were opened—though Celsus may laugh at these things, or perhaps he has never read this history at all. Otherwise, he would have said that the chains were loosed and the doors opened by magic spells, so that he might make our affairs appear common to those of sorcerers <note>Celsus frequently attempted to categorize Christian miracles as mere "goeteia" or low-level street magic.</note>. But not even the one who condemned him <insert>Jesus</insert> suffered anything such as Pentheus did, who was driven to madness or torn to pieces <note>In Greek mythology, King Pentheus was torn apart by his mother and aunts for opposing the god Dionysus. Celsus argues that if Jesus were a god, Pilate should have suffered a similar fate.</note>. He does not know, however, that he was not so much condemned by Pilate—who knew he had been handed over by the Jews out of envy—as by the nation of the Jews themselves. That nation has certainly been condemned by God, torn apart and scattered over the whole earth even more than the limbs of Pentheus. And why did he intentionally pass over what was written concerning the wife of Pilate, who was troubled by dreams so that she sent word to her husband, saying: <margin>Matthew 27:19</margin> *Have nothing to do with this just man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.* And again, keeping silent about the things that show the divinity of Jesus, Celsus hurls insults at him, bringing forth from the Gospel writings the mockeries of the scarlet robe, the crown of thorns, and the reed placed in his hand. From where, Celsus, did you learn these things, if not from the Gospels? Therefore, you saw these things as worthy of reproach; but those who wrote them did not realize that they would be a derision to you and those like you, while others would take from them an example of despising those who mock and revile the one who willingly underwent death for the sake of piety. Marvel rather at their truthfulness, and at him who willingly suffered these things for humanity, and bore them with the greatest long-suffering and patience. For it is nowhere written that he lamented after his condemnation, or did or said anything abjectly. But to those words: *Why does he not, if not before, at least now exert his divinity, and deliver himself from this ignominy, and treat those who are injurious to both himself and his Father according to their merit?* it must be said that the Greeks could similarly be asked, who assert providence and attribute something to portents: why does God not likewise take notice of the impious who do away with the providence of the deity? For whatever the Greeks might answer to these things, we also shall answer similar or better things, since by celestial portents, the eclipse of the Sun, and other miracles, it was sufficiently declared that there was something divine and not common in the one crucified. Celsus continues: *What of the blood of the crucified one...*

<column-break/>

<margin>Acts 12:7; 16:24-26</margin> ...or how shall he be persuaded from my own writings that Peter, being bound in prison, went out when an angel loosed his bonds; and Paul with Silas in Philippi of Macedonia, being bound in the stocks, was loosed by divine power, when also the doors of the prison were opened? But it is likely that Celsus laughs at these things, or has not read the history at all; for he would have seemed to say against it that certain sorcerers also loose bonds with incantations and open doors, in order to make the wonders of the virtuous among us common with the stories told among us. "But not even the one who condemned him," he says, "suffered anything, such as Pentheus, being driven mad or torn asunder." <margin>Matthew 27:18</margin> But he does not know that it was not so much Pilate who condemned him—who knew that the Jews had delivered him up through envy—as the nation of the Jews; which has been condemned by God, being torn asunder and scattered into all the earth, more than the tearing asunder of Pentheus. And why did he intentionally pass by the things concerning the wife of Pilate, who had seen a vision in a dream and was moved by it, so as to send to her husband and say: <margin>Matthew 27:19</margin> *Have nothing to do with this righteous man, for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him.* And again, keeping silence about the things that manifest the divinity of Jesus, Celsus reviles him from the things written in the Gospel concerning Jesus, citing those who mocked him and put on him the scarlet robe and the <margin>Matthew 27:28-29</margin> crown of thorns and the reed in his hand. From where then, O Celsus, did you learn these things, except from the Gospels? Did you then see these things as worthy of reproach, while those who recorded them did not perceive that you would mock them, and as many as are like you? But others will take an example of despising those who laugh and scoff at one who is ready to die for the sake of or through godliness. Rather, wonder at their love of truth, and at him who suffered these things voluntarily for men, and endured them with all forbearance and long-suffering. For it is not recorded that he wailed, or did anything humble <note>original: "ταπεινόν" (tapeinon) - meaning groveling or lacking dignity</note> because of being condemned. And to the point: "Why does he not, if not before, at least now show something divine, and deliver himself from this shame, and judge those who insult both himself and the Father?" it must be said that it is possible to say the same to the Greeks who introduce providence and accept divine signs: why then does God not punish the impious who insult the divine and do away with providence? For as the Greeks would defend themselves against these things, we also shall say the same or even better, since even a divine sign from heaven, the eclipse of the sun, and the other wonders, showed <margin>Luke 23:45</margin> that the crucified one had something divine and more than the many. Then Celsus says: "What, he says, as the body was being impaled, what kind of ichor <note>In Greek mythology, ichor is the ethereal fluid that flows in the veins of the gods instead of blood.</note>..."

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

They are able to believe in him who was clearly foretold by the Prophets; who, after taking on flesh, taught his disciples that he bore these things for the benefit of mankind. For in this first coming, he did not come to judge us before teaching us what ought to be done, nor to immediately distribute punishment to the wicked and salvation to the good. Instead, he came to miraculously sow his doctrine throughout the entire human race, not without a certain divine power, just as the Prophets had also predicted. Furthermore, we bring a charge against them <note>The critics of Christianity, specifically the Jews mentioned by Celsus</note> because they did not believe in him when he declared his power, but said that he cast out demons from the souls of men by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. <margin>Matthew 12:24</margin> Likewise, they slander his humanity—he who did not disdain any city or village in Judea with the preaching of the kingdom of God, spreading it everywhere—as the wandering of a vagabond in a lazy body. For it is not the mark of a lazy man to undertake such great labors for the sake of men who, anywhere his doctrine is heard, are able to be converted to a better harvest. Now, however, that which Celsus’s Jew says next is a manifest lie: *That he, having persuaded no one while he lived, not even his own disciples, suffered punishment and the cross.* For how were the Jewish High Priests, Elders, and Scribes moved against him in envy, unless it was because he was drawing the crowds after him, even into the deserts? He moved them not only by words most suited to their understanding, but also by performing wonders which would surely strike even those who did not give credit to his words with amazement. It is an equally manifest lie which he adds, *that he did not even persuade his own disciples.* They did indeed suffer something through human infirmity <note>referring to their fear during the crucifixion</note>; for they were not yet trained in fortitude. However, they did not change their judgment concerning Christ. For Peter, immediately after his denial, sensing into how great an evil he had fallen, went outside and wept bitterly. <margin>Matthew 26:75</margin> The rest, though struck with sorrow—as those who even then marveled at him—were soon confirmed in their faith by his appearance, believing more firmly than before that he is the Son of God. <margin>Luke 24:31; John 20:19</margin> Here, Celsus thinks in a way that is hardly philosophical, imagining that the excellence of a man consists not in saving doctrine and pure morals, but in this: if, not responding to the persona he assumed by taking on mortality, he should not die; or if he should die, but not by that death which could serve as an example to others, so that those taught by the reality of the event might in no way be burdened to die for the sake of piety,

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the passage translated above.</note>

...to believe in the one clearly prophesied, who declared among those who were his disciples, even after the time of his incarnation, that he endured these things for the benefit of men. His purpose in the first advent was not to judge the affairs of men before teaching and initiating them into the mysteries of what must be done; and not to punish the wicked and save the good, but to sow his word in a marvelous way, and with a certain more divine power, for the whole race of men, as the prophets also foretold these things. And further, we accuse them, since they did not believe in him when he displayed his inherent power, but said in Beelzebub, the prince of demons, <margin>Matthew 12:24</margin> that he cast out the demons from the souls of men. And we accuse them because they disparage his love for mankind—he who did not overlook any city, but visited every part of Judea so that he might announce the kingdom of God everywhere—charging him with wandering as a vagrant, and elsewhere as being in an ignoble body. For it is not ignoble to endure such labors for the benefit [to Celsus] of those who are able to be inspired from every quarter. And is it not an outright lie, that which is said by the Jew in Celsus’s writing, that "having persuaded no one while he lived, * that <margin>* or "not even"</margin> "not even his own disciples, he endured punishment and such things"? For from where did it arise that the Jewish High Priests and elders and scribes were moved against him, if not from the fact that the multitude was persuaded to follow him, even being carried out into the deserts? This was not only by the sequence of his words, which were always suited to those hearing them, but also by his power, which astonished those who did not believe in following his word. And is it not an outright lie "that he did not even persuade his own disciples, who suffered something human from cowardice" at that time (for they were not yet sharpened for courage), yet they did not cast aside their convictions concerning Christ. For Peter, after the denial, perceiving what sort of evils had occurred, went out and wept <margin>Matthew 26:75</margin> bitterly. And the rest, being struck by despondency over him (for they still marveled <margin>Luke 24:31</margin> at him), were confirmed through his appearance <margin>John 20:19</margin> toward believing even more and more firmly than before, that he is the Son of God. And Celsus, having suffered something unphilosophical, imagines that excellence among men is not in the word * of salvation * <margin>saving</margin> and in pure morals, but in not doing anything appropriate to the role he assumed, and having assumed mortality, not to die; or to die indeed, but not a death which was able to become an example to those who through him are strengthened to die for the sake of piety, and to speak with boldness concerning piety and impiety...

the records written about the philosopher Democritus, who abandoned his estate; and about Crates, who freed himself by gifting to the Thebans the money resulting from the sale of all his possessions. Moreover, Diogenes, due to his extreme frugality, lived in a tub; and among those who possess even moderate sense today, Diogenes was not considered to be "in evils" for this reason. Furthermore, **"since Celsus wishes that Jesus should not even have been beyond reproach,"** let him say: who among those pleased by his word has recorded that Jesus was truly subject to reproach? Or, if he does not accuse him as being subject to reproach based on these records, let him show from where he learned it so as to call him "not beyond reproach." For Jesus performed what he promised to persuade those whom he benefited. And we, always seeing the things spoken by him being fulfilled before they happen—

<margin>
Matthew 24:14; 28:19.
</margin>

such as this Gospel being preached in the whole world, and his disciples being delivered up to all the nations, and his having announced the Word itself; 

<margin>
Ibid. 10:18.
</margin>

and further, that they would be brought before governors and kings for no other reason than his teaching—we are struck with awe of him, and every day we are confirmed in our faith in him. By what greater or more manifest proofs did Celsus wish him to create faith? Unless, as it seems, not understanding the Word <note>original: "λόγον" - the Logos</note> who became man in Jesus, he wished him to suffer nothing human, nor to become a noble example for us humans to always bear what happens to us—even if these things seem piteous <gloss>he only says this.</gloss> and shameful to Celsus.

...ignorant of the distinction, who think the pious are profane, while they consider those wandering in their thoughts—and worshipping anything rather than God—to be religious; especially whenever they drive to death men who have devoted themselves from the heart to the one and most manifest God. Celsus proceeds to accuse Jesus from the persona of a Jew: **"that he did not show himself pure from all evils."** Let this discourse of Celsus say: from what evils did Jesus not show himself pure? For if he denies he was pure from "evils" properly so called, let him openly bring forward some evil deed of his. But if he calls poverty, the cross, and the snares prepared for him by evil men "evils," without a doubt he will also admit that Socrates was subject to evils; for he will not be able to show him immune from these. Furthermore, how great is the chorus of the poor who, among the Greeks, embraced philosophy along with voluntary poverty, is commonly known among the Greeks from their own commentaries; in which it is established that Democritus left his lands as pasture for sheep, and Crates, that he might philosophize more freely, bestowed upon the Theban people the money he had made from selling his goods. But also Diogenes, on account of excessive frugality, lived in a jar; yet he was not held to be subject to evils by anyone even moderately prudent for this reason. Moreover, **"because Celsus contends that Jesus was not even irreproachable,"** let someone from those who are delighted by that famous discourse of his show where it was truly written that he was reproachable; or, if he considers something besides what has been said to be deserving of reproach, let him declare from where he learned that he was worthy of blame. Certainly, he gave credit to his promises by exhibiting great advantages to all those who showed themselves teachable to him: especially since they see daily the fulfillment of those things which had been predicted by him so long before, such as: *That the Gospel shall be preached in the whole world;* and that regarding the departure of the disciples into all nations to announce his word to them; furthermore, that they were to be led before Governors and Kings for no other cause than the profession of Christian doctrine. Let us admire him, and daily be confirmed in faith and confidence. Indeed, I do not see by what greater arguments Celsus demands faith be built for him; except that it appears he was ignorant that the Word of God was made man in Jesus, and therefore wished that he should suffer nothing human, nor become an example to men for enduring the truth bravely: namely, because these things seem most shameful and miserable to Celsus, as one who [fears] pain...

...considers pain to be the greatest evil, and pleasure to be the absolute good: a view which no philosopher has ever held—at least among those who assert the existence of Providence, and who count courage, endurance, and magnanimity among the virtues. Therefore, Jesus did not make his faith void through the things which he suffered, but rather confirmed it in those brave men who learned from him that the "blessed life" <note>original: *beata vita* / *μακάριον ζῆν*</note> properly and truly so-called is not here, but in the coming age (as he himself said); whereas to live in the present (so-called) age is a calamity and the greatest struggle for the soul. After this, Celsus speaks to us thus: *“Surely you will not say of him that, when he could not persuade those living here, he set out to the lower world <note>original: *inferos* / *ᾅδου* (Hades)</note> to persuade those dwelling there?”* Indeed, even against Celsus's will, we say that while he was in the body, he persuaded so many that for this reason he was sought out by conspiracies; and when he became a soul stripped of the body, he held discourse with other souls similarly stripped of their bodies <margin>1 Peter 3:19</margin>, so that he might convert even from among them as many as were teachable, or who, for certain reasons known to him, were more fit for this.

Next, however, Celsus speaks in a way that I find quite foolish: *“If, being ridiculously deceived, you think you are truly defended by certain absurd defenses you have devised, what forbids others—as many as have perished miserably under condemnation—from being regarded as supreme and divine angels?”* It is manifest to anyone that Jesus, having suffered what has been recorded of him, is entirely unlike those miserably condemned for sorcery <note>original: *maleficas artes* / *γοητείαν*</note> or other crimes. For no one can show that the souls of men have been converted from sins and the filth of vice by the arts of magic. 

And since Celsus’s Jew, comparing him to robbers, says: *“one could similarly, with a hardened brow <note>meaning: with shameless impudence</note>, say even of a robber or a murderer who has been punished: 'this was not a robber but a God; for he predicted to his fellow-robbers that he would suffer what he did suffer.'”* It can be answered: first, it is not because he predicted he would suffer these things that we believe concerning Jesus what we freely profess—that he himself came as one sent from God. Secondly, we confess that these things were long ago recorded in the Gospels: that he was "counted among the lawless" <margin>Mark 14:28</margin>. God was among the lawless, while they preferred that a robber imprisoned for murder <margin>Luke 23:19</margin> be released to them, but that Jesus be crucified; and they soon fixed him to a cross between two robbers. And so it is always read among the true disciples of Jesus and witnesses of the truth: he is condemned by men along with robbers and subjected to the same punishment of the cross. And we say: if these men have anything similar to the character of robbers, and do not rather suffer for the sake of piety toward the Creator <note>original: *rerum opificem* / *δημιουργὸν* (Demiurge/Creator)</note>...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

### Page 86

...and that they preserve the teaching of Jesus pure and sincere, enduring all manner of torture and every kind of death. It is clear that Jesus himself, the father of such teaching, is reasonably compared by Celsus to robber-chiefs <note>Celsus argued that Jesus was a mere leader of a rebel band</note>. But while those others die for a common cause, these men suffer these things for the sake of piety; and they alone of all men are plotted against because of the way toward the divine that was revealed to them. They are not killed without the wickedness of their persecutors, nor was Jesus plotted against in an unholy manner <note>Origen argues the plot against Jesus was a violation of divine law by the Jews</note>. 

Celsus also speaks very superficially regarding the words of Jesus's disciples at that time, saying: "Furthermore, those who were with him while he was alive, hearing his voice and following him as their teacher, when they saw him being punished and dying, they neither died with him nor died for him, nor were they persuaded to despise punishments; instead, they even denied him. If these were his disciples, why do you now die along with him?" 

In these remarks, Celsus selects the sin of the disciples—who were then still beginners and imperfect—as it is written in all the Gospels, so that he might accuse the Word. But he is silent about how they corrected themselves after that sin, how they spoke with boldness <margin>Acts 4:13</margin> <margin>\* having spoken boldly</margin> before the Jews, how they suffered countless things at their hands, and finally died for the teaching of Jesus. 

For he did not wish to hear what was prophesied to Peter: <margin>John 21:18</margin> "But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands," and so forth. To which <margin>Ibid. v. 19</margin> the Scripture adds: "This he said, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God." Furthermore, he ignores that James the brother of John—an Apostle and the brother of an Apostle— <margin>Acts 12:2</margin> was put to death by Herod with a sword for the sake of the word of Christ. <margin>Ibid. 13:46</margin> 

<column-break/>

Nor does he mention the things Peter and the rest of the <margin>Ibid. 5:41</margin> Apostles did, speaking freely for the sake of the Word, and how they departed from the presence of the council after being scourged, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name. In this, they far surpassed many of the stories told by the Greeks regarding the endurance and courage <margin>\* courage</margin> <margin>\* this especially</margin> of those who practiced philosophy. 

Therefore, from the very beginning, this was a primary part of Jesus's teaching for those who heard him: it taught them to despise the life so loved by the many, and to strive instead for a life that closely approaches the life of God. 

How, then, is the Jew in Celsus's writing not lying when he says: "That when he was present, he only took ten sailors and tax-collectors of the most abandoned sort, and did not even persuade all of them?" For it is manifest, even by the confession of the Jews themselves, that he did not take only ten, nor a hundred, nor a thousand; but all at once, sometimes five thousand, <margin>John 6:10</margin> and at other times four thousand. <margin>Mark 8:9</margin> And he drew so many that they followed him even into the deserts—places that could only accommodate the multitude of those believing in God through Jesus.

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS
## Book II
->N<-

...we have performed many mighty works: *and I will say to them; Depart from me, for you are workers of iniquity.* <note>Matthew 7:22-23</note> But Celsus, wishing to disparage the miracles of Jesus by comparing them to the tricks of men, says these words exactly: *“O Light and Truth! He proclaims with his own voice, just as your own Scriptures testify, that others will come to you using similar tricks, wicked men and sorcerers; and he names a certain Satan as the author of these arts. So that not even he himself denies that these things have nothing divine about them, but are the works of the wicked; and, compelled by the truth, he at once uncovered the arts of others and exposed his own.”* Is it not therefore a wretched and unworthy thing that from the same works, this one is considered a God, but the others are considered sorcerers? For why, taking a guess from such arts, should we believe others to be evil rather than this one, even by his own testimony? Certainly, he himself confessed that these are signs not so much of a divine nature, but of impostors and wicked men. Consider whether Celsus is not clearly caught here maliciously distorting the argument; since Jesus speaks in one way about the future performers of signs and wonders, but this Jew introduced by Celsus speaks in another. For if Jesus had simply warned his disciples to beware of those who display miracles, and had not added what they would boast themselves to be, perhaps his suspicion would have had a place. But since those whom Jesus wants us to avoid claim to be the Christ—which sorcerers do not do—but rather, living wickedly in the name of Jesus, they say they will perform certain powers and cast out demons: <margin>cast out.</margin> indeed, if one must speak thus, all suspicion of magical vanities is removed in this place, and the divine power of Christ and his disciples is commended, under the pretext of whose name others might sell themselves as the Christ, who, with a far different power working in them, present a certain likeness to the genuine disciples of Christ. Which also Paul, in the second epistle to the Thessalonians, indicates, how *that man of sin will be revealed, the son of perdition, who is the adversary and is exalted against everything that is called God or an object of worship, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God;* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:3-4</note> and again he says to the Thessalonians; *And now you know what withholds, namely that he may be revealed in his own time, for the mystery of iniquity is now at work, only he who now holds, let him hold, until he is taken out of the way; and then that wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord will consume with the spirit of his mouth, and will abolish* <margin>the lawless one, whom * the Lord will consume, will rise up with the spirit <note>original Greek: ἄνομος, ὃν ὁ Κύριος ἀναλώσει</note></margin>

<column-break/>

...we have performed many; and I will say to them, depart from me, because you are workers of unrighteousness. But Celsus, wishing to make the wonders of Jesus common to the sorcery found among men, says in these very words: “O light and truth, he explicitly declares with his own voice, just as you have written, that others will appear to you using similar powers, who are wicked men and sorcerers; and he names a certain Satan as the author of such things; so that not even he himself denies that these things are not at all divine, but are the works of the wicked. And being forced by the truth, he both revealed the deeds of others and convicted his own. How then is it not miserable to consider the one a God and the others sorcerers from the same works? For why should we consider the others wicked from these things rather than this one, using him as a witness? For he himself admitted that these were the marks not of a divine nature, but of certain deceivers and utterly wicked men.” See then if in these things Celsus is not clearly <margin>* clearly Celsus</margin> convicted of misrepresenting the argument; for Jesus says one thing about those who will perform signs and <margin>* will perform.</margin> wonders, but the Jew in Celsus says another. For if Jesus had simply told the disciples to beware of those promising wonders, as if we were passing them by—what shall we say of ourselves? 1) perhaps his suspicion would have had a place. But since those from whom Jesus wishes us to be on guard promise to be the Christ—which sorcerers do not do—but even while living wickedly in the name of Jesus, they say they will perform certain powers and cast out demons from men; <margin>* cast out.</margin> rather (if one must say it this way) <margin>* or etc.</margin> all suspicion against them is renounced; and the divinity of Christ is introduced, and the divinity of his disciples, because it is possible for someone using his name, even if the things are enacted by powers from a certain disposition, to claim and pretend that he himself is the Christ, and to seem to do things similar to those who perform them for Christ, and others in the name of Jesus, things as it were similar to his genuine disciples. And Paul also, in the second epistle to the Thessalonians, declares in what <margin>2 Thess. 2, 3</margin> manner the man of sin will one day be revealed, the son of perdition, the adversary <margin>* of lawlessness.</margin> and one who exalts himself against everything called [either] God or an object of worship, so as to sit himself in the temple of God, showing himself off, that he is God. And again he says to the Thessalonians: And now <margin>Ibid. v. 6</margin> you know what withholds, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only he who now withholds until * the Lord comes from the midst. # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

->N 2<-

From miracles we gather that it is necessary for there to be other things performed by divine power in the life of men: and it follows that either both must be denied, granting neither, or if one is granted—especially the inferior kind—one must also confess that which is more excellent. For if anyone were to confess that prodigious miracles occur, while denying that any are performed by divinity, he would seem to act just as if he were to deny that there exist among men any true and logical arguments, far different from sophisms, simply because there are certain false sophisms <note>original: "sophismata"</note> and probable reasonings which possess a likeness to the truth while having nothing of the truth in them. But if we once admit—since the existence of the magical art is manifest in world affairs—that through wicked men, evil spirits <note>original: "genios malos"</note> enticed by curious incantations are drawn out to perform miracles, it follows that operations of divine power must also be found among men. Indeed, we examine the promisors of such miracles by certain signs; namely, those taken from their life and character, as well as from the effects of the miracles themselves, discerning whether they bring harm to men or a correction of morals. Thus we may know which are done by an enchanter through the service of demons, or by a soul pure and holy and inspired by the divine spirit, whose very body, from its commerce with that same spirit, is effective for the utility and instruction of men, and for confirming true faith in God. But if miracles are not to be approved before they are distinguished by whom they are rightly performed or otherwise—lest we either condemn all or marvel at all as if they were divine—is it not clear from the miracles of Moses and Jesus, by which entire nations were drawn to religion, that those things recorded in the Scriptures were not done by them without divine power? For never by evil arts and impostures could the Republic of an entire nation have been established, which at once despises all idols <note>original: "simulacrorum"</note> and, having transcended all created things, strives toward God, the prince and author of this universe, who is without beginning. And since it is a Jew who speaks these things in Celsus' work, it is pleasing to address him thus: "But you, good man, why do you so believe those things recorded in your Scriptures as having been performed by God through Moses, and endeavor to stop the mouths of those who compare them with the tricks of the Egyptian sages; yet you yourself deny that those things which you confess were performed by Jesus were done divinely, in this imitating the obstinacy of the Egyptians?" For if the result of the works—namely, the entire nation of the Israelites originating under these auspices—sufficiently declares that God worked through the ministry of Moses, why then—

<column-break/>

—that it is absolutely necessary that there are also things occurring in life from divine beneficence. And the same follows by sharp logic: either to do away with both and say <margin>* neither one.</margin> that neither occurs, or, by positing the one and especially the inferior, to confess also concerning the superior. If someone were to posit things arising from sorcery <note>original: "goeteia"</note>, but not posit those from divine power, he seems to me <gloss>to confess</gloss> that to some there are indeed sophisms and persuasive words that miss the truth, while he <gloss>seems</gloss> to deny that truth exists to educate among men, and that a dialectic foreign to sophisms is in operation. But if we once accept, as a consequence of there being <gloss>certain</gloss> magic and sorcery worked by evil demons charmed by curious invocations and obeying human sorcerers, that it is also necessary to demonstrate things from divine power among men; then let us examine those powers which are led and confirmed by their promises, based on the life and character and the things following the powers: whether they lead to the harm of men or to the correction of morals? Who is it that, being served by demons through painful incantations and sorceries, does such things? And who is it that, being in a pure and holy place according to his own soul and spirit? I think also that for the body that has received God, a certain divine spirit performs such things for the benefit of men and for the inquiry of those turning to believe in the true God. If we must once inquire, not being carried away by the powers, which one performs such things from a superior source and which from an inferior? So that we may neither speak ill of all things, nor marvel at and accept all things as divine. How will it not be manifest from the outcomes of Moses and Jesus—the establishment of whole nations after their signs—that they performed them by divine power, namely those things which <gloss>to the</gloss> [Scripture] it is recorded they performed? For he would not have established a whole nation by wickedness and sorcery, so as to flee not only statues and the foundations of idols, but also all sorcery, and to ascend to the unbegotten God, the beginning of all things. Since it is a Jew who says these things in Celsus' work, we would say to him: "You there, why ever do you believe <gloss>to the</gloss> things written among you as being performed by God through Moses to be divine, and try to refute those who disparage them as having happened according to sorcery similar to those performed by the sages of the Egyptians; yet you accuse the things confessed by you to have happened by Jesus as not being divine, in this yourself imitating the Egyptians? For if the end, and the whole nation established through the wonders of Moses, <gloss>belies</gloss> [the claim of sorcery] and shows the energy of God who did these things, agreeing that they were of Moses—"

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book 2 of Origen's "Against Celsus," where Origen uses a "mirroring" technique to defend Christianity. He shows that the same skeptical arguments Celsus's Jewish character uses against Jesus could be used by a skeptic against Moses and the foundations of Judaism.</meta>

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

And just as Celsus’s Jew says of Jesus: *Therefore, not even he himself denies that these things have nothing of divinity, but are the works of evildoers,* so anyone who does not believe in Moses would say in the very same words: *Therefore, not even Moses himself denies that these things have nothing of divinity, but are the works of wicked men.* In a like manner, those words—*forced by the truth, he exposed his own arts and those of others at the same time*—could be twisted against Moses. Likewise, those words of the Jew—*Is it not therefore shameful that from the same works, this one is considered a God, but others are considered sorcerers?* <note>original: "praestigiatores" – literally those who use sleight of hand or illusions</note>—could be turned back against him like this: *Is it not therefore shameful that from the same works, Moses is considered a Prophet of God and his servant, but others are considered sorcerers?* And since Celsus lingered on this point, adding to what has already been said (which can be applied to both equally): *For why, taking a guess from such arts, should we believe others to be evil rather than this man, even by his own testimony?* let us also add a similar speech: *For why, since Moses forbids giving credit to those who perform portents and miracles, should we think the others are wicked rather than the one who condemned this class of men?* And to exaggerate the matter further, he says: *He himself confessed that these are signs not so much of a divine nature as of impostors and wicked men.* Who is that "he"? You, O Jew, will answer "Jesus"; but your adversary, throwing the same charges back at you, refers it to Moses. The Jew of Celsus proceeds (so that I may follow what he proposed from the beginning) in his speech addressed to his fellow citizens converted from Judaism, speaking thus: *What then won you over to him? Was it because he predicted he would rise again after death?* But this, like the previous points, will be transferred to Moses: *What then won you over to him? Was it because he wrote of his own death thus: "And Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of the Moabites by the word of the Lord; and he was buried in that land near the house of Phogor: and no one knows his grave unto this day."* <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 34:5-6</note> For just as the Jew falsely claims that Jesus predicted his own resurrection, in the same way one may say of Moses that he himself wrote (for Deuteronomy is also his) that his grave was known to no one unto this day, so that he might make it more venerable by being unknown to the human race. After this, the Jew, dealing with his fellow citizens converted to the faith of Jesus, continues his speech thus: *Come, let us grant you that this was predicted by him: but how many others have used such miraculous tricks...*

<column-break/>

The Jew in Celsus says concerning Jesus: "so that not even he himself denies that these things at least are nothing divine, but are the works of the wicked." Thus, one who disbelieves Moses will say to him, setting out the aforementioned points, the same things: "so that not even Moses himself denies that these things at least are nothing divine, but are the works of the wicked." He will do the same regarding the claim <margin>that he, being forced by his own [deeds]</margin> *that being forced by the truth, he at once revealed the arts of others* and exposed his own. And when the Jew says: "How then is it not wretched, that from the same works one is thought a God, and others sorcerers?" one might say to him, using the words set out concerning Moses: "How then is it not wretched that from the same works, one is thought a prophet of God and His servant, and others sorcerers?" Since Celsus, having previously discussed this place, added to the things examined and shared: "For why should we rather think from these things that they are evil, or that he is a witness using them?" we also will apply such things to what is said: "For why should we rather think from these things—by which Moses forbids us to be persuaded when they show signs and wonders—that those men are evil, rather than Moses, based on the things for which he slandered others regarding signs and wonders?" Saying more on the same point, so that he might seem to increase the argument, he says: "He himself at least confessed these things were not of a divine nature, but were the marks of certain deceivers and utterly wicked men." Who was "he himself"? You, O Jew, say it was Jesus. But the one accusing you as being subject to the same charges will bring the "he himself" back to Moses. Does the Jew in Celsus not say these things to us (so that I may maintain the character suitable to the Jew from the beginning) in the speech to his fellow citizens who have believed: "By what were you persuaded, <margin>\* were you led.</margin> or was it because he foretold that having died he would rise again?" And this will be shared in the matter concerning Moses similarly to the previous points. For we shall say to him, by what <margin>\* were you led.</margin> <margin>Deut. 34. 5</margin> <margin>\* such things.</margin> were you led, or was it because he wrote about his own end: "And so Moses [the] servant of the Lord died there, in the land of Moab, by the word of the Lord, and they buried him in Moab, near the house of Phogor. And no one knows his burial place until this day." For as the Jew slanders [Jesus], saying he foretold that having died he would rise again; the one saying the same thing about Moses will say that Moses also wrote (for Deuteronomy is his) that no one knows his burial place until this day; solemnizing and exalting his burial as not being known to the nature of men. After these things, the Jew says to his fellow citizens who believe in Jesus: "Come now, let us even believe you that he had said [this]. But how many others use such portents..."

Or do you think that the stories of others are merely myths and appear as such, while you have invented a 'grand finale' to your drama that is elegant or plausible—the cry upon the cross <term>skolops</term> <note>original: "σκόλοπος" - referring to the stake or cross of crucifixion.</note> as he breathed his last, the earthquake, and the darkness? That he who while living could not help himself, arose when dead and showed the marks of his punishment, and his hands just as they had been pierced. Who saw this? A frantic woman, as you yourselves say, or perhaps someone else belonging to the same sorcery, or someone dreaming in such a state, deceived by a wandering imagination according to his own desire—a thing which has happened to countless people. Or, what is more likely, wanting to strike others with amazement by such a portent, and through such a lie to provide an opportunity for other beggars and charlatans."

Since it is a **Jew** who says these things, we shall defend ourselves as if against a Jew. We shall apply the arguments regarding our **Jesus** to the account of **Moses**, saying to him: "How many others have performed such portents as Moses did, employing deceitful trickery for the sake of persuading simple-minded listeners?" Indeed, it would be more fitting for one who disbelieves Moses to use the examples of Zamolxis and Pythagoras, who performed portents, than for a Jew—unless he is very fond of learning Greek histories. An Egyptian, too, disbelieving the wonders concerning Moses, might plausibly cite **Rhampsinitus**, saying it is far more credible to them (that he descended to the underworld, played dice with Demeter, and snatched a golden hand-cloth from her as a token of having been in the underworld and ascending from there) than the account of Moses, who wrote of himself that he entered into the thick darkness where God was, and that he alone drew near to God, while the rest did not. For he wrote thus: *And Moses alone shall come near unto God, but the rest shall not come near.* <note>Quoting Exodus 24:2.</note> We, the disciples of Jesus, shall therefore say in defense against the Jew who says these things: "Answer us, you who always accuse our faith in Jesus—what will you say to the Egyptian and the Greeks regarding Jesus? What will you say to these charges you bring against Jesus if someone were to argue against Moses in the same way? If you struggle mightily to defend Moses—as he can indeed be defended—you will, even against your will, establish the case for Jesus by the very arguments with which you defend Moses."

<column-break/>

...they are used to impose upon foolish listeners; *Zamolxis* among the *Scythians*, the servant of *Pythagoras*: and *Pythagoras* himself in *Italy*; and in *Egypt Rhampsinitus*, who is also said to have played at dice with *Ceres* <note>The Roman equivalent of Demeter.</note> among those below, and to have brought back a golden napkin as a gift from her: such also were *Orpheus* among the *Odrysians*, *Protesilaus* among the *Thessalians*, and at *Taenarum Hercules* and *Theseus*. But it must be considered whether any dead man ever truly rose with the same body: unless perhaps you hold the stories of others to be fictions, but think you have found a beautiful and credible "catastrophe" <note>In the sense of a dramatic resolution or climax of a play.</note> for your own story—the voice of the one dying on the cross, the earthquake, and the darkness: then that he, who living was unable to help himself, when restored to life showed the traces of his punishment, his hands just as they had been pierced: and that this was seen by a furious woman, as you yourselves confess, and if there was any other follower of that magical vanity, or otherwise a dreamer, deluded by his own accord by empty ghosts, which often happens to innumerable people: or rather wishing to strike others senseless with such wonders, and to provide matter for lies to other traveling quacks. 

We shall respond as if to a Jew, since a Jew speaks these things, and transferring his words about Jesus to Moses, we shall say: "But how many others have abused such deceits of miracles to impose upon foolish listeners?" And one estranged from the religion of Moses would more properly use the examples of Zamolxis and Pythagoras than a Jew who is not a very careful reader of Greek history. An Egyptian also, not believing in the miracles of Moses, would aptly here cast in a mention of Rhampsinitus, saying that his descent to the underworld and game with Ceres is more credible, and the golden napkin brought back from there as proof of his infernal pilgrimage and happy return, than what Moses wrote of himself—that he entered into the darkness in which God was, and alone out of so great a multitude had a meeting with Him. For he wrote thus: *And Moses alone shall come closer to God, but the others shall not come closer.* We the disciples of Jesus shall therefore say to that Jew objecting these things: "Answer us, whose faith in Jesus you accuse, what will you report to this Egyptian, what to the Greeks? What will you say to these things which you reproach our Jesus with, if someone should also accuse Moses in the same way? But if you contend strongly for Moses, just as indeed he can be effectively and clearly defended, by the same effort you will unintentionally defend Jesus much more..."

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 2.

<margin>Concerning Heroes</margin>
...more divine than Moses. And since the Jew in Celsus’s writing claims that the histories told concerning the descent of Heroes to the underworld and their subsequent return from there are "monstrous fictions"—suggesting they merely hid themselves from human sight for a time and then reappeared as if returned from the dead (for his words seem to indicate this regarding Orpheus among the Odrysians, Protesilaus in Thessaly, Hercules at Taenarum along with Theseus)—come, let us demonstrate that these accounts written about the resurrection of Jesus cannot be compared with such fables. For it was possible for any of the aforementioned Heroes to withdraw themselves from the sight of mortals and return to them again at their own will. But Jesus was crucified in the sight of all the Jews, and after death was taken down from the cross in the presence of that same people; how can he be accused of having feigned anything like the stories boasted about the Heroes' descent to and return from the underworld? For we say that in defense of the crucified Jesus, one can never assert what is recorded in the histories of those Heroes whom you believe descended to the underworld by force. For if, as we have supposed, Jesus had died an obscure death—so that in dying he had not been visible to the entire Jewish people—even if he had afterwards truly risen from the dead, there would still be room for the same suspicions held about the Heroes to be applied to Jesus. It is for this reason, among others, that he was publicly subjected to punishment: so that no one could claim he had intentionally withdrawn from human sight to be falsely regarded as dead, only to come forward when it suited him, as if miraculously returned to life from the dead. Moreover, I would consider the following a clear argument for a non-fictitious resurrection: the evidence taken from his disciples, who gave themselves over to a teaching of such great danger and preached the word with such constancy. They not only made others more ready to despise death, but were the first to undergo it themselves. Observe, however, how recklessly Celsus’s Jew speaks—as if it were an impossible thing for someone to rise from the dead with the same body—saying, *“But this must be considered: whether anyone who has truly died ever rose again with the same body.”* A Jew who believes the Scriptures of the third and fourth books of Kings <note>original: "tertii quartique Regnorum libri" — in modern Bibles, these are 1 and 2 Kings</note> concerning the boys would never say this; one of whom Elijah called back to life, and Elisha the other. And for this reason, I think Jesus appeared among the Jews rather than among other nations...

<column-break/>

...more divine than Moses. Since the Jew in Celsus’s work says that the heroic histories <margin>*</margin> concerning those said to have descended into Hades and to have ascended from there are "mumbo-jumbo" <note>original: "τερατείας" — wonders, portents, or tall tales</note>; suggesting that the heroes became invisible for a time, stealing themselves away from the sight of all men, and afterwards showed themselves as having ascended from Hades (for his language seems to imply such things about Orpheus among the Odrysians, Protesilaus in Thessaly, Hercules at Taenarum, and also about Theseus); come, let us establish that the event of Jesus being raised from the dead cannot possibly be compared to these. For each of the heroes mentioned in those places, had he wished, would have been able to steal himself away from the sight of men and, having decided to do so, return to those he had left behind. But since Jesus was crucified in the presence of all the Jews, and his body was taken down <margin>*</margin> in the sight of their people, how can they think <margin>*</margin> to [fabricate] something similar, saying that he, like the heroes in the histories, descended into Hades and ascended from there? We say that, perhaps, this might be said especially in defense of Jesus having been crucified, because of the histories told of the heroes who <margin>*</margin> forced their way into Hades. For if, by hypothesis, Jesus had died an obscure death, so that he had not <margin>*</margin> been manifest to the whole people of the Jews, and then after this he had truly risen from the dead, there would have been room for the suspicion held about the heroes to be said of him as well. Perhaps, then, in addition to other reasons for Jesus being crucified, this also contributes something: that he died conspicuously upon the cross, so that no one might be able to say that he voluntarily withdrew from the sight of men and seemed to have died without having died; <margin>*</margin> and that when he came out again, appearing once more, he "faked" <note>original: "ἐτερατεύσατο" — performed a deceptive wonder</note> the resurrection from the dead. And I think the argument <margin>*</margin> of his disciples is clear and manifest, <margin>*</margin> in that they gave themselves up to a teaching that was dangerous to human life. They would not have taught this so reasonably if they had fabricated the raising of Jesus from the dead; especially since they not only prepared others to despise death, but did this themselves first. But Celsus’s Jew—unless he is completely deaf—speaks as if he posits it as something impossible for someone to rise from the dead with the same body, saying: <margin>*</margin> “But that must be considered, if anyone who truly died ever rose again with the same body.” A Jew would not have said these things if he believed the things recorded in the third [book] of Kings, <margin>3 Kings 17 <note>Modern 1 Kings 17</note></margin> and in the fourth concerning the boys; one of whom Elijah raised up, and the other Elisha. <margin>4 Kings 4:34 <note>Modern 2 Kings 4:34</note></margin> Because of this, I think Jesus did not stay among any other nation but the Jews, who had become accustomed...

<summary>Origen argues that Jesus's resurrection is historically superior to Greek myths because his death was a public execution, preventing any claims that he merely hid himself. He also points out the hypocrisy of Celsus's Jewish character, who denies bodily resurrection despite it appearing in the Hebrew Scriptures (the stories of Elijah and Elisha).</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

...you might consider the paradoxes <note>original: *τὰ παράδοξα* - things contrary to expectation or miraculous</note> in the tradition of those who believed the things done by him, or recorded about him; so that they might accept those things, concerning which greater things have happened, and by which they were fulfilled more credibly, he being greater than all of them. Furthermore, after the Jew <note>Celsus writes in the persona of a Jewish critic of Christianity</note> set forth Greek histories about those who supposedly performed wonders and those said to have risen from the dead, he says to those from among the Jews who believe in Jesus: <margin>Let it be.</margin> "**Or do you think that while the stories of others are and appear to be myths, for you the catastrophe of the drama <note>Celsus uses theatrical language to imply the Crucifixion was a staged play</note> has been elegantly or plausibly invented—the cry he uttered upon the stake <note>original: *σκόλοπι* - refers to the cross</note> when he breathed his last?**" We shall say to the Jew that we consider the stories you set forth to be myths; but the things in the scriptures common to you and us, in which not only you but we also join in prayer, we by no means say are myths. Therefore, we do not doubt the things written about those there who rose from the dead as if they were myths. And what of this, as also concerning these things and concerning his own resurrection? This is more paradoxical than those who rose from the dead: the prophets Elijah and Elisha raised those men, but no one of the <margin>Acts 2:24</margin> prophets raised him, but rather the Father in heaven. Therefore, his resurrection worked greater things than the resurrections of those others. For what so great thing happened to the world from the children raised by Elijah and Elisha, compared to what has happened through the preached resurrection of Jesus, believed by divine power? <margin>upon the stake.</margin> It [the account] includes the earthquake and the darkness; concerning which, as far as possible, we defended in the preceding sections, citing Phlegon <note>Phlegon of Tralles, a 2nd-century secular historian who recorded an eclipse and earthquake</note>, who recorded that such things occurred at the time of the Savior's passion. "**And that while living he did not help himself, but having died he rose and Jesus showed the signs of his punishment, and his hands, as they had been pierced;**" and we ask him, what is this: *He helped himself*? For if we speak regarding virtue, he helped himself very much indeed. For he did nothing unseemly because of his enemy; but truly *as a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is <margin>Isaiah 53:7</margin> silent;* <margin>Matthew 26:63 & 27:12, 14</margin> and the Gospel bears witness that he thus did not open his mouth. But if he takes the phrase *He helped himself* from the realm of indifferent and bodily things, we say that we have demonstrated from the Gospels that he came to these things willingly. Then, following these things, having mentioned from the Gospels that he showed the signs of punishment after rising from the dead, and his hands as they had been pierced, he [Celsus] inquires and says: "**How was this seen?**" and slandering the account of Mary Magdalene, <margin>John 20:18</margin> who is recorded to have seen him, he then says, "**a frantic woman, as you say.**" And since not

<column-break/>

...led such a life, that those already accustomed to believe such miracles, as they saw him perform, were persuaded by the comparison of both that he was so much greater, as he performed greater things than those of whom sacred history tells. Then, after the Jew brought forward what the Greeks report concerning those who by wondrous arts brought it about that they were believed to have returned to life from the underworld, he thus addresses the Jews who followed the faith and discipline of Jesus: "Unless perhaps you consider external things as fictions, but you think you have found a beautiful and credible catastrophe for your own fables—the words of the one expiring on the cross." To which we will answer him: those things indeed which you have brought forward we plainly hold as fables: but the things contained in the Scriptures common to us and you, and for which there is no less religion among us than among you, those we truly deny are fables. Wherefore we believe those miracles are not feigned, which are written there concerning those raised from the dead, and that our [Lord] rose again, as he who performed this according to his own promises and those of the Prophets, is so much more worthy of admiration than those previously returned to life, because the Prophets Elijah and Elisha raised them; but none of the Prophets raised him, but the heavenly Father himself: by which it happened that greater effects followed his resurrection than theirs. For what such thing proceeded from the boys raised by Elijah and Elisha for the benefit of the whole world, as from the preaching of the resurrection of Jesus believed through divine power? But that man [Celsus] also considers the earthquake and the darkness as fictitious portents: concerning which matter we have already responded above as best we could, citing the testimony of Phlegon narrating that these things happened at the time of the passion of the Lord Savior. But as for what he adds, *That he who living was not able to help himself, being returned to life displayed the traces of his punishment, the hands as they had been pierced:* we ask of him, what he wishes to be said by this word *help*. For if he speaks of virtue, we will say he helped himself in no small measure: for he neither said nor did anything unbecoming, but truly *as a sheep he was led to the slaughter and as a lamb before its shearer he was silent*, the Gospel attesting that he did not open his mouth. But if he wishes this word to be understood of indifferent and bodily things: we say we have already shown from the Gospels that he underwent such things voluntarily. Then, having mentioned from Scripture the traces of punishment which he displayed after the resurrection, namely the hands, as they had been pierced by iron: he inquires who saw this, and in passing slandering Mary Magdalene, who is written to have seen this, "A woman," he says, "by your own confession..."

<meta>catchword: confession</meta>

<summary>Origen defends the historical reality of Jesus's resurrection and the accompanying portents (darkness and earthquake) against Celsus's claims that they are mere "theatrical" inventions. He argues that Jesus's resurrection is superior to those performed by Elijah or Elisha because it was enacted by God the Father and resulted in the transformation of the world.</summary>

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...fanatical confession: and because it is written that Jesus after the resurrection was seen not only by this woman, but also by others; here too Celsus’s Jew, acting as a detractor, says, *And if there was any other follower of that same magical vanity.* And soon after, as if it were impossible for a dead man to appear in the likeness of a living one, so that you may recognize him as an Epicurean <note>The Epicureans denied the immortality of the soul and the possibility of post-mortem appearances.</note>, he says, *Or otherwise, he dreams, being deceived of his own accord by empty specters, a thing which has often happened to countless people.* Although this seems to him to be a powerfully stated point, it nevertheless necessarily follows from it that the souls of the dead survive, nor did he who accepted this dogma believe in their immortality or certainly their permanence without reason; as Plato relates in his book *On the Soul* <margin>Plato in the Phaedo.</margin>, that images in the likeness of shadows have been seen by some around monuments. Therefore, those specters of ghosts do not appear out of nothing, but because the souls of the deceased also have a certain body of their own, which is called by the Greeks <term>augoeides</term> <note>original: "αὐγοειδές" — meaning "lucid" or "luminous-form," a Neoplatonic concept of a spiritual vehicle for the soul.</note>. 

But Celsus, while assenting to this opinion, nevertheless says that some people dream while awake and are deceived of their own accord by empty specters; the sort of delusions observed during sleep are not new: but that the same should happen to those who are awake does not seem likely to me, unless perhaps they are out of their minds, or suffering from frenzy or melancholy; not being ignorant of this, Celsus called the woman "mad." It is uncertain where he found the occasion for this slander, since nothing of the sort is found in the Scriptures. Therefore, Jesus also appeared after the resurrection, displaying the images of the wounds received on the cross, though he was not at all wounded in the way Celsus thinks, but as the Gospel teaches (to whose words Celsus sometimes gives credit when it pleases him to accuse, and sometimes not). He summoned one of the disciples who was incredulous and who thought the matter impossible; for he agreed with the woman who told him she had seen him, as if it were not a new thing for the soul of a deceased person to be seen. However, he could not bring himself to believe that he had risen with the same body. For this reason he did not merely say, *Unless I see, I will not believe*: but added also those words; *Unless I put my hand into the print of the nails, and touch his side, I will not believe.* Now Thomas said these things because he thought it possible that there might present itself to the eyes a body of the soul, similar in all respects to the one laid aside,

> —the voice, the beautiful eyes, and the very habit of the body:
> And often clothed in a similar garment. <note>Origen is quoting Homer's Iliad (23.66-67) regarding the ghost of Patroclus to illustrate the concept of a "soul-body."</note>

Therefore, having called Thomas, Jesus said, *Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.*

<column-break/>

...only she is recorded to have seen the risen Jesus, but others as well; and slandering these things, Celsus’s Jew says, "if there was any other of those from the same sorcery." Then, as if it were possible for it to happen then—I mean for a phantom to appear to someone of a dead man as if living—he adds, like an Epicurean, or says, "According to some disposition, someone dreaming, or according to his own will by a wandering opinion, has been haunted by such a phantom; which the boy," he says, "reported has already happened to thousands." Even if this seemed to be very cleverly said, it is nonetheless a confirmation of a necessary doctrine: that the soul of the dead truly exists. And he who has taken up this doctrine has not believed in its immortality, or at least its duration, in vain; just as Plato in his <margin>Plato in the Phaedo.</margin> discourse on the soul says that shadow-like phantoms of the dead have occurred somewhere around tombs. Therefore, the phantoms that occur concerning the souls of the dead arise from some underlying subject, namely the soul existing in what is called the "luminous" body. 

But Celsus, wishing to undermine such a thing, wants some to dream while awake, and by their own will to be haunted by a wandering opinion; which is not very likely to happen while awake. Unless, that is, in the case of those who are not entirely in their right minds and are delirious or melancholic, which is rare. And Celsus represented this as being observed by calling the woman [mad]. From where the recorded history does not show, he took the occasion to accuse the matter. Jesus, therefore, coming—not as Celsus thinks, sending out a phantom of the wounds on the cross, and not truly being so wounded—but as the Gospel teaches (which Celsus sometimes <margin>John 21:5 <note>Likely a citation error in the original for John 20:25.</note></margin> believes in parts, where he wishes to accuse, and sometimes disbelieves), Jesus called to him one of the disciples who was disbelieving and thought the marvel impossible. For he agreed with her who said she had seen him, as it was not impossible for the soul of a dead man to be seen; but he no longer thought it was true that he had been raised in a solid body. Hence he did not say, "Unless I see, I will not believe"; but he <margin>Ibid.</margin> also added, "Unless I put my hand into the print of the nails, and touch his side, I will not believe." These things were said by Thomas, judging that it is possible for a body of the soul to appear to the physical eyes, in every way like the former form:

> —in stature and beautiful eyes, and voice;
> And often she wears such clothes about her skin.

And having called Thomas, Jesus <margin>John 21:27 <note>Citation error for John 20:27.</note></margin> said, "Reach hither thy finger, and see my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and put it into my side, and be not faithless, but believing."

<summary>Origen refutes Celsus's claim that the Resurrection was a mere hallucination or "waking dream," arguing instead that the soul possesses a "luminous body" (augoeides) that can manifest after death. He uses the account of Doubting Thomas to prove that Jesus rose with a physical, tangible body, not just a spectral one.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

<margin>Psalm 16:9 <note>original: "Pfal. 15. 9." following the Septuagint numbering.</note> and following.</margin>
...and following this, I see that in all the things prophesied about him (among which was this) and the things proclaimed beforehand by him, and the events that occurred, this happened most paradoxically of all. For it had been spoken beforehand in the person of Jesus by the prophet: *My flesh shall dwell in hope; for you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.* And indeed, after his resurrection, he existed in a state midway between the density of the body before the passion and the soul appearing naked of such a body. Hence, when *his disciples were together and Thomas was with them, Jesus came, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst, and said, "Peace be to you"; then he said to Thomas, "Reach your finger here,"* and so forth. And in the *Gospel according to Luke, while Simon and Cleopas were talking to one another about all the things that had happened* to him, Jesus stood by them and traveled with them. And their eyes were kept from recognizing him; but he said to them, "What are these words that you exchange with one another as you walk?" And immediately their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; then the Scripture says in these very words, *And he vanished from their sight.* Even if Celsus wishes to make common the events concerning Jesus and those who saw him after the resurrection with other phantoms and apparitions, yet to those who examine the matters fairly and wisely, the paradoxical nature of the event will be clear. After this, Celsus, maliciously slandering the writings, says: "If Jesus truly wished to breathe a divine power into himself, he ought to have appeared to those who insulted him, and to the judge who condemned him, and generally to everyone."

<margin>* His disciples. John 20:26.</margin>
<margin>Luke 24:13 * to them.</margin>
<margin>Ibid. v. 13.</margin>
<margin>* the judge.</margin>

<margin>John 20:26.</margin>

For truly it appears even to us, according to the Gospel, that he was not seen after the resurrection in the same way as he appeared publicly and to everyone before. But in the Acts it is written that, being seen by the disciples over forty days, he announced the things concerning the kingdom of God. In the Gospels, he did not stay with them continually; but sometimes he appeared after eight days, the doors being shut, in their midst; and at other times in similar ways. And Paul, in the final parts of his letter to the Corinthians, says—indicating that he was by no means seen in the same way as in the time before the passion—he writes as follows: *For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was seen by Cephas; then by the twelve; then he was seen by over five hundred brothers at once, of whom the majority remain until now, but some have fallen asleep; then he was seen by James; then by all the apostles; and last of all,*

<column-break/>

...fittingly. Moreover, it beautifully matched both the prophecies by which he was foretold, and his own deeds, and the things that happened to him, that this last greatest miracle should be added: for it had been predicted by the Prophet in the person of Jesus, *And my flesh shall dwell in hope, and you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption.* And after the resurrection, he had a certain body intermediate between that thickness which was in it before the passion, and the soul stripped of that body: wherefore when his disciples were together, and Thomas with them, Jesus came, the doors being closed, and stood in the middle, and said, *Peace be to you;* and soon he added these words toward Thomas, *Put your fingers here,* and the rest. Furthermore, in the Gospel according to Luke, while Cleopas and Simon were talking among themselves about these things which had happened, Jesus suddenly intervening made the journey with them, *and their eyes were held, lest they should recognize him: but he said to them, what are these speeches which you confer among yourselves walking?* then after their eyes were opened they recognized him, then the Scripture speaks thus to the word, *And he vanished from their sight.* Therefore, although Celsus tries to compare these appearances of Jesus after the resurrection with common ghosts and visions: yet whoever shall have examined these things candidly and prudently, will see the matter is far otherwise. After this, as if having found a handle for rebuking the Scriptures, he speaks thus, *If Jesus wanted to truly declare his divine power, he ought to have shown himself to his insulters, and to the governor himself, who had brought the capital sentence against him, and finally to all others.* For it is clear also to us from the Gospels, that he did not provide himself so commonly visible after the resurrection as before, since in the Acts it is read that being seen by the disciples for forty days he taught about the kingdom of God: likewise in the Gospel he is not continually occupied with them; but sometimes after eight days, the doors being closed, he was suddenly seen in their midst; sometimes in other similar ways. Paul also near the end of the first to the Corinthians, indicating him not commonly seen as before the passion, writes thus, *For I delivered to you in the first place what I also had received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was seen by Cephas; then by those twelve; afterwards he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once; of whom many remain to this very day, but some also have fallen asleep; then he was seen by James; then by all the Apostles; but last of all,*

<summary>Origen argues that Jesus's post-Resurrection body was a "middle" state between physical flesh and pure spirit, explaining why he appeared only to select followers rather than to his enemies like Pilate. He cites the accounts of Thomas, the road to Emmaus, and Paul's list of witnesses to support this specialized form of divine manifestation.</summary>
