<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s critiques of Christianity. Here, Origen addresses the theological problem of why the resurrected Jesus did not appear to everyone in the same way he did before his death.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.
## O 2

...as to one born out of due time, he appeared also to me <note>original: "velut abortivo, visus est & mihi" / "ὥσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί" — a reference to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:8</note>. A truly great and wonderful matter presents itself at this point, which could challenge not only the common sort of believers, but even the more perfect: namely, why the Lord after his resurrection did not offer himself to be gazed upon in the same way as in former times. Nevertheless, as an extra measure in a work written against the adversaries of the Christian religion, let us see if we can bring forth some probable argument that might move the minds of those hearing this defense. Though Jesus was one, he could be thought of in more than one way, and he was not seen similarly by all who looked upon him. That he could be thought of in many ways is manifest from those words, *I am the way, and the truth, and the life*; then from those, *I am the bread*; then from those, *I am the door*, and countless others. Moreover, that he was not seen in the same way by all who looked upon him, but according to what they were capable of receiving, will be manifest to those who understand why, when he was about to be transformed <term>Transfigured: the event where Jesus's divine glory became visible on a mountain</term> on the high mountain, he did not take all the disciples, but only Peter, James, and John. This was because they alone were capable of beholding such a glorious spectacle, and were able to contemplate Moses and Elijah in that brightness, and hear their conversations, and even the voice brought down from heaven out of the clouds. Indeed, I am of the opinion that even before he ascended the mountain—where he taught those beatitudes to the disciples alone—when he was in the plain below in the evening healing those brought to him suffering from various ailments, freeing them from all diseases, he did not appear the same to those who were ill and in need of his help as he did to those who, being healthy, were able to follow him as he ascended the mountain. And just as whenever he explained parables to them privately, which the common crowd of listeners heard under veils <note>original: "sub involucris" — meaning wrapped in mystery or allegory</note>, those who heard them explained without veils possessed a more excellent hearing; so also certain souls excelled in sight, and as I believe, even in the body. Furthermore, this is indicated by the fact that he was not always accustomed to appear in the same way, because Judas, when about to betray him to the crowd he brought with him, said to those who did not know him, *Whomever I shall kiss, that is he*. And the Savior’s own words seem to point to this: *I was with you daily teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me*. Since, therefore, Jesus was such a person—not only according to that deeper divine nature not visible to everyone, but also according to the varying form of his body, by which he was seen by whom he willed and as often as he willed—we say that Jesus, who had not yet [stripped off] the principalities and powers...

<column-break/>

...as to one born out of due time, he appeared also to me. I suppose that the matter in this place is something great and wonderful, and beyond the capacity not only of the many among the believers, but even of those who have made great progress; wherein the reason might be shown why, having risen from the dead, he did not appear in the same manner as in former times. But from several points—as in this treatise written against the argument against Christians and their faith—see if we shall be able, by reasonably setting forth a few things, to reach those who hear the defense. Jesus, being one, was many in conception, and was not seen as the same by all who saw him. And that he was many in conception is clear from: *I am the way and the truth and the life*; <margin>John 14:6</margin> and from: *I am the bread*; and from: *I am the door*; and ten thousand other things. <margin>John 6:35. John 10:9.</margin> And that when seen he did not appear in the same way to those seeing him, but as the beholders had capacity <margin>* had capacity.</margin>, will be clear to those who consider why, when he was about to be transfigured on the high mountain, he did not take all the apostles, <margin>Matthew 17:1</margin> but only Peter, and James, and John; as they alone were able <margin>* to be able.</margin> to behold his [then] glory, and were able to perceive Moses and Elijah appearing in glory, and to hear them talking with him, and the voice sent from the cloud. And I think that even before going up into the mountain, where only the disciples came to him and he taught them concerning the beatitudes, <margin>Matthew 5:1</margin> when he was still below the mountain and crowds were present, he healed those brought to him, delivering them from every disease and every infirmity; he did not appear the same to those who were sick and needing his healing, and to those who, because of being healthy, were able to go up with him into the mountain. But also when he privately explained the parables to his own disciples, <margin>Mark 13:34</margin> which were spoken to the crowds outside under a veil, just as those hearing the explanation of the parables were superior in their hearing to those hearing the parable without the explanation; so also in sight, certainly that of the soul, but I believe also that of the body. And that he did not always appear the same is shown by the fact that Judas, being about to betray him, said to the crowds following him who did not know him: *Whomever I shall kiss, that is he*. <margin>Matthew 26:48</margin> And the Savior himself seems to indicate this through the saying: *I was with you daily in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me*. <margin>Ibid. v. 55</margin> As we do not always perceive Jesus as being of such a nature, not only according to the divinity within and hidden from the many, but also according to his body which was transformed when he willed and to whom he willed; we say that he who had not yet stripped off the principalities and powers...

<summary>Origen argues that Jesus's physical appearance was not static but changed based on the spiritual and physical capacity of the observer, explaining why he appeared differently after the Resurrection. He uses the Transfiguration and the betrayal by Judas (who needed a sign to identify Jesus) as evidence for this "polymorphic" nature.</summary>

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

[For if we believe that] Jesus died and rose again: *even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus: for this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord, shall by no means precede those who are asleep.* <note>Quoting 1 Thessalonians 4:14-15</note> We have set forth our interpretation of these passages in our commentaries on the first epistle to the Thessalonians. Nor should you wonder if the entire multitude of those believing in Jesus does not behold his resurrection, since Paul, writing to the Corinthians as if they were not capable of receiving more, says: *I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:2</note> Such also is that saying: *For you were not able, nor even now are you able, for you are still carnal.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:2-3</note> Thus, with the divine will moderating the style of the narrative, it is written of Jesus that before his passion he was seen by the multitude without distinction, though not always; but after the passion, he was no longer seen equally by all, but with a selection according to each person's capacity. Just as it is read in the Scriptures, <margin>Genesis 12:7; 48:3</margin> *God appeared to Abraham*, or to one of the saints; yet this was not a perpetual occurrence but happened at intervals, and he did not appear to everyone. In the same way, it must be understood that the Son of God was seen by these men with the same distinction by which God was seen by those [patriarchs]. Therefore, a sufficient answer has been given, as far as is possible in a writing of this kind, to that objection: *"If Jesus truly wished to declare his divine power, he ought to have shown himself to his revilers, and to the governor himself, and finally to everyone else."* On the contrary, it was not fitting for him to be beheld by the one by whom he had been condemned, nor by his revilers; for he spared both groups lest they be struck with such blindness as that which once struck the Sodomites when they plotted against the beauty of the angels received into Lot's hospitality. As the Scripture relates, <margin>Genesis 19:11</margin> *But the men reached out their hands and pulled Lot into the house to them, and shut the door; and they struck the men who were at the doorway with blindness, from the small to the great, and they wore themselves out seeking the door.* Truly, Jesus wished to show his divine power only to those fit to see it, and according to the measure of their capacity. He avoided being seen everywhere for no other reason than that not everyone could bear the sight of him. Therefore, Celsus rashly puts forward the claim: *"Surely he feared no one any longer, having died once, and being now a God, as you say;"* and that he had not been sent for the purpose of remaining hidden. On the contrary, he was sent not only to be known, but also to be hidden; for even by those by whom he was known, he was not known in his entirety, remaining partially unknown; to some...

<column-break/>

...[likewise], that Jesus died and rose; so also God will bring those who have fallen asleep through Jesus with him. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we the living who are left behind until the presence of the Lord shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. We have set forth the explanation of these places that appeared to us in the commentaries we dictated on the first epistle to the Thessalonians. And do not wonder if all the believing crowds do not see the resurrection of Jesus; since even when writing to the Corinthians as those not containing more, Paul says, *I decided to know nothing among you, except Jesus <margin>1 Cor. 2:2</margin> Christ, and him crucified.* And such is also the, *For you were not yet able; but not even now are you able, for you are still carnal.* <margin>1 Cor. 3:3</margin> Thus, the Word, doing all things by judging with the divine [will], recorded concerning Jesus: before the passion appearing simply to all, and this not always; but after the passion no longer appearing in the same way, but with a certain judgment of what was fitting for each participant. And just as it is recorded, *God appeared to Abraham*, or to some of the saints; and this "appearing" did not happen always, but at intervals, and did not appear to all; so understand also the *appearing of Jesus <margin>* already of the</margin> [Son] of God by a similar judgment regarding the divine as that by which God appeared to them. We have therefore defended as much as was possible for us, in such a treatise, against the: *"He ought, if he really wanted to manifest divine power, to have appeared to those very people who insulted him and to the one who punished him and altogether to everyone."* It was not fitting, then, for him to appear to the one who punished him, nor to those who insulted him. For Jesus spared both those who punished and those who insulted, so that they might not be struck with "unseeingness" <note>original: ἀορασίᾳ (aorasia) - a specific term for spiritual or physical blindness</note>, such as those in Sodom were struck with, when they were plotting against the beauty of the angels who were guests with Lot. And this is shown through these [words]: *But the men stretching out their hands, drew Lot to themselves into the house, and shut the door. And the men who were at the door of the house, they struck with blindness from small to great; and they were paralyzed seeking the door.* And Jesus displayed his power, being divine, to each as they had the power to see it, and according to the measure they were able to contain. And for no other reason did he guard against being seen, than because of the powers of those not able to contain the sight of him. And in vain was it taken up by Celsus that, *"Surely he feared some man after dying, and (as you say) being God;"* nor was he sent for this at the beginning, that he should be hidden. For he was sent not only that he might be known, but also that he might be hidden. For even all that those who already knew him did know, was known, but even that was hidden from them; and sometimes not even...

<summary>Origen argues that Jesus appeared only to those with the spiritual capacity to perceive him after the Resurrection, comparing this selective revelation to Old Testament theophanies and the blindness of the Sodomites.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 2.

The treatment of these matters will be as follows: for now, the pure linen cloth is sufficient for us, in which it was fitting for the pure body of Jesus to be wrapped, and the new tomb cut out of the rock by Joseph, where no one had yet lain, or (as John writes) *In which no one had yet been placed.* Here, consider whether the consensus of the three Evangelists might move someone, as they record so accurately the tomb being cut or carved out of the rock: so that he who examines the reason of the Scripture may see matters of great importance both in the novelty of the tomb, which Matthew and John mentioned, and in the fact that no one had ever been buried there, as is related by Luke and the same John. For it was fitting that he who did not die in an ordinary way, but even after death brought forth vital signs from his body—water and blood—and being, so to speak, a "new" corpse, should be laid in a new and pure tomb. Just as his birth had been purer than all births, because he was born of a virgin and not from sexual union: so also his burial should possess a distinguished purity, his body being deposited in a new tomb, not constructed by art from gathered stones, but cut out of the living rock. 

<margin>
Luke 23:53.
John 19:41.
Matt. 27:60.
Luke 23:53.
John 19:41.
</margin>

Therefore, a more hidden meaning of this sacred narrative could receive a more venerable and divine treatment, if that were the purpose. But as for what pertains to rendering the reason of the context for the present, it fit beautifully that he who by a fixed purpose endured the punishment of the cross should also maintain decorum in the subsequent events: so that he who had died as a man, should likewise as a man be taken down from the stake <note>original: "stipite" - referring to the upright post of the cross</note> and be buried. Nevertheless, even if it had been written in the Gospels that he vanished from the cross, Celsus with the unbelievers would have found fault with it; and carping at this too, they would have said, *Why did he disappear in this way after he was crucified, and not rather take care before then that he should not come to the punishment?* Therefore, if they think this very thing should be rebuked—that the Evangelists preferred to relate the truth rather than to feign that he disappeared from the cross—how are they going to believe the resurrection, and that by his own will he suddenly appeared standing in their midst while the doors were closed, or that after giving bread to two of his acquaintances and holding a conversation with them, he vanished from their sight? Furthermore, how did it come into the mind of Celsus’s Jew to say that Jesus was hiding? For he says, *What messenger ever sent, when he ought to report his commands, hid himself?*

<column-break/>

...we shall describe. For now, the pure linen cloth is sufficient, in which it was necessary for the pure body of Jesus to be wrapped, and the new tomb, which Joseph hewed in the rock, in which no one was lying, or (as John says) *in which no longer had anyone been placed.* And consider if the agreement of the three Evangelists is able to move anyone, they having taken care to record the tomb hewn in the rock; so that he who examines the words of the Scripture with scrutiny [may see] both concerning the novelty of the tomb, which Matthew and John established, and concerning the fact that no dead person had been there, according to Luke and John. For it was necessary that he who was not like the rest of the dead, but showed vital signs even in death—the water and the blood—and being a "new" (if I may name it so) dead man, should be placed in a new and pure tomb; so that, just as his birth was purer than all birth, by not being from union but from a virgin; so also the burial might have purity, through that which is symbolically shown in his body being deposited in a new tomb... not built from selected stones and having a natural union, but hewn and carved in one continuous rock.

For it was written in the earlier sections: "Either, while he was constrained in a body, he preached openly to all; but when he rose from the dead, he appeared secretly to only one little woman and to his own band of followers." <note>Celsus uses the diminutive "muliercula" or "γύναιον" (little woman) to mock the testimony of Mary Magdalene.</note> But it is not even true that "he appeared to only one woman"; for it is written in the Gospel according to Matthew, that "late on the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb, and behold, there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven [and] coming, rolled away the stone." Something has also been said regarding the claim: "While being punished he was seen by all, but having risen, he was seen by only one." We have already defended the point that "He did not appear to all." And now we shall say that his human qualities were visible to all; but his more divine qualities (I mean those regarding the radiance poured out—not just regarding the body) were not capable of being perceived by everyone. <note>Origen argues that the resurrected body required a certain spiritual "capacity" or "receptivity" in the witness to be seen.</note> 

Let us next contend against the point Celsus has at hand. For he says "he appeared secretly to one little woman and his own disciples," and immediately adds: "While being punished he was seen by all, but having risen, by only one"—which is a strong contradiction. For why is it called "it ought to have been the opposite," namely that the one being punished was seen by all, but the one risen by only one? Where he says this to himself, he desires both the impossible and the irrational: that he be punished in the sight of [only one?], but rise before all. Or how would he explain "it ought to have been the opposite"? 

Jesus taught us who the one who sent him was, in the passage: "No one knows the Father except the Son," and "No one has ever seen God." And being the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he explained him; he, speaking of divine things, reported the things concerning God to his true disciples. From their writings, we have the most devout starting points for speaking of God, hearing in one place that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all," and in another, "God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." But also, the reasons for which the Father sent him are myriad...

*hiding places?* Certainly he was not hiding at all, who said to those seeking to seize him: *Daily I taught freely in the temple, yet you did not seize me.* As for what Celsus soon repeats from his previous babbling, let it be enough that it has already been answered once: for those things he objects to again can be refuted from what we wrote in the preceding pages: *While he moved in a body among the unbelieving, he thrust his preaching everywhere to all; now when faith was to be built upon the resurrection from the dead, he offered himself to be seen secretly by only one little woman and his own companions.* 

And yet it is false that he appeared to only one woman: for it stands written in the Gospel according to Matthew: *On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns on the first of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and that other Mary came to see the tomb, and behold a great earthquake occurred: for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and approaching, rolled back the stone.* And a little later the same Evangelist adds: *And behold Jesus met them, namely the aforementioned Marys, and greeted them: but they, approaching, held his feet and worshipped him.* 

An answer has also been given to that: *That he suffered punishment before all, but after the resurrection was seen by one;* and we have rendered the cause of both: and now also we say, that his human nature was conspicuous to all; but of the divine (I speak however of these natures, not insofar as one is referred to the other, but insofar as they differ between themselves) the eyes of all were not capable. And here notice for me how Celsus speaks things contrary to himself, for when he had just said that he appeared secretly to one woman and his companions, he soon adds: *Therefore, bearing punishment he was seen by all, but revived by one, when it was necessary to do the opposite.* Let us hear what that "opposite" might be; he says he suffered with all looking on, but was seen revived by a single woman. Therefore, as much as can be gathered from his own words, Celsus wanted that which is absurd and impossible: that his punishment be watched by a single person, and his resurrection by all—or how else are those words to be taken, *When it was necessary for the opposite to happen?* 

Furthermore, Jesus taught us by whom he was sent, when he said: *No one knows the Father except the son;* and, *No one has ever seen God: the only-begotten God indeed, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has told of him,* he discussed divine discourses concerning God among his true disciples: finding the traces of whose discipline in the Scriptures, we have the occasion therefrom of disputing concerning God, while we hear that: *God is light, and there are no darknesses in him;* then that: *God is spirit, whom those who worship, must worship in spirit and truth.* Moreover, why he was sent by the Father, from innumerable places...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

->**P**<-

One may learn of these matters, if they wish, both from the prophecies of the Prophets and from the Gospels, and no small part from the writings of the Apostles, especially those of Paul. It is He who shines before the pious on the path to salvation, and takes notice of sinners; concerning which the ignorant Celsus said, *That he leads the pious on the way, and has mercy on sinners turned toward repentance.* After this, he asks, *If he wished to be the son of God? But if he did not wish to remain hidden, why did he suffer and die?* and he thinks that he has thus refuted the inconsistency of the Scriptures, not understanding that He wished neither to become known to everyone at random, nor for his affairs to be entirely unknown. Certainly, the proclamation of the heavenly voice, declaring Him to be that beloved son in whom the father is well pleased <note>original: "Hunc esse illum dilectum filium, in quo pater sibi placeat" - Matthew 3:17</note>, is not written as having been heard by the common crowd, as Celsus’s Jew supposes; just as that voice which came from the cloud on the high mountain was heard only by those who had ascended with him. For such is the voice of God, that it is heard only by those whom He Himself wishes to hear it—not to mention for the moment that the voice of God, of which the Scripture speaks here, is not struck air, or a percussion of the air, or whatever else is said about the voice <note>Origen is using Platonic/Stoic physics to argue that God's voice is a spiritual perception rather than a physical sound wave</note>, and therefore it is perceived not by this sensory hearing, but by one far more excellent and divine. And whenever He who speaks does not wish it to be heard by all, those who have those exceptional ears hear God; but those who have become hardened in the ears of the soul do not perceive the word of God. Let this be the response to the one asking, *Why was a voice heard from heaven proclaiming him the son of God?* Furthermore, as to what he asks next, *Why, if he did not wish to remain hidden, did he suffer and die?* sufficient answer was given above, where we treated his passion at length. After this, Celsus’s Jew gathers as a logical consequence something that does not follow at all: for it does not follow from the fact that he taught us to despise death by his own passion, that he ought to have called the human race openly to a new light of doctrine after his resurrection from the dead, and taught the cause of his coming. For he had already previously called all to the light with these words, *Come here all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.* <note>Matthew 11:28</note> And for what cause he descended was related in that long sermon on the beatitudes, and the promises that follow them, as well as in the parables and the discussions which he had with the Scribes and Pharisees. Now indeed, according to the Gospel of John, how many things he taught is clear to those who notice his magnificence, situated more in deeds than in words; for it appears from the Gospels how much authority his words had, even unto miracles—

<column-break/>

—which things let him who wishes learn, both from those who proclaimed him beforehand, the prophets, and from the gospels; and he will know not a few things also from the apostles, and especially Paul. But he is also a light-bringer to those who act piously, while punishing those who sin; which Celsus, failing to see, has written, “and to lead the pious as a light-bringer, <margin>\* he wished</margin> but to have mercy on sinners through repentance.” After these things he says, “If he wished to remain hidden, why was the voice from heaven heard, proclaiming him the son of God? But if he did \* not wish to remain hidden, why was he punished, or why did he die?” And he thinks in these points to expose a disagreement in the things written about him, not seeing that he neither wished all things about himself to be known to everyone and to just anyone; nor did he wish his affairs to be entirely hidden. Therefore, the voice from heaven, proclaiming him the son of God, and saying, “This is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased,” <margin>Mat. 3. 17.</margin> is not recorded to have happened in the hearing of the crowds; which is what Celsus’s Jew thought. But also the voice on the highest mountain \* from the cloud <margin>\* from the cloud.</margin> was heard only by those who went up with him. And <margin>Mat. 17. 5.</margin> the divine voice is of such a kind, being heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear. For I do not yet say that the recorded voice of God is altogether struck air, or a blow of the air, or whatever is said in the treatises concerning the voice; wherefore it is heard by a hearing better than the sensory one and more divine. And whenever the speaker wishes his own voice not to be heard by all, the one who has the better ears hears God; but the one who is deafened in the ears of the soul does not perceive God speaking. These things then are for the question, “Why was the voice from heaven heard, proclaiming him the son of God?” And as for, “If he did not wish to remain hidden, why was he punished? or why did he die?” what was said by us at greater length in the previous parts concerning the passion is sufficient. And after these things Celsus’s Jew sets forth as a consequence that which is not a consequence; for it does not follow from the fact that he wished to teach us through the punishments he suffered and through death to despise death, that after he rose from the dead he should have called all men clearly into the light and taught the reason why he had come down. For he had already previously called all into the light, saying, “Come unto me all <margin>Mat. 11. 28</margin> you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” And for what reason he came down is recorded <margin>Ibid. 5. 3.</margin> in the words he set forth in the beatitudes, and the things announced following them, and in parables, and in the conversations with the Scribes and Pharisees. And as for the Gospel according to John, how many things he taught is set forth to those who have been \* persuaded <margin>\* persuaded.</margin> by Jesus, not in words, but in deeds. His magnificence; and it is clear from the gospels that his word was also in authority; at which they also wondered <margin>Mat. 7. 29.</margin>

...should they say, is the providence and love of God toward man wonderful to you, while you are being punished and deprived of Jerusalem, and of what is called the sanctuary, and of the most venerable worship? For whatever they may say in defense of the providence of God, we shall establish it even more firmly and for the better, saying that it was a wonderful providence of God <margin>* making use of.</margin> *making use of the sin of that people for the purpose of calling those from the nations <note>Gentiles</note> through Jesus—those who were strangers to the covenants and foreign to the promise—into the kingdom of God. And these things the prophets foretold: that because of the sins of the Hebrew people, God would choose not a single nation, but chosen ones from everywhere; and having chosen the foolish things of the world, He would cause a senseless nation to become learned in the divine oracles; while the kingdom of God is taken away from the former and given to the latter. It is sufficient from many examples, for the present, to set forth the prophecy from the Song of Deuteronomy concerning the calling of the nations, which is as follows, spoken from the person of the Lord: <margin>Deut. 32:21</margin> *For they have moved me to jealousy with those who are not gods; they have provoked me to anger with their idols: and I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a nation; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.* Then the Jew’s epilogue on these matters says again concerning Jesus: "That man, then, was such as truth itself reveals, and as reason shows. But by the teaching of a man, having dared to sow all the ordinances of his own religion and teaching, he is able to choose to do what he wishes, and to become stronger than all those who oppose the law of his teaching—both kings and governors, and the Roman Senate, and rulers everywhere, and the common people. For how could a human nature, having nothing superior in itself, turn such a multitude? And it is not surprising if it were of the wise; but even of the most irrational, and those given over to passions, and who, as far as irrationality goes, are more difficult to transform into a more temperate state." But since Christ is the power of God <margin>1 Cor. 1:24.</margin> and the wisdom of the Father, for this reason He has done these things, and still does them, even if neither Jews nor Greeks, who disbelieve His word, wish it. We, therefore, shall not cease believing in God according to the precepts of Jesus Christ, and wishing to turn those who are always blind toward the worship of God. And even if those who are truly blind revile us as being blind and "leading them astray" <note>original: βουκολοῦντας (boukolountas) - literally "tending like cattle," used here to mean deceiving or hoodwinking</note>, whether they be Jews or Greeks who charge us with leading men astray—it is a noble "leading astray," so that instead of being licentious they become temperate... when we lead men who have been charmed by an honest deception, so that instead of being intemperate they become temper-

<column-break/>

...ate, or did the providence and clemency of God seem admirable to you, when you were both afflicted with punishments and deprived of the city of Jerusalem and the Sanctuary, as it is called, and the most magnificent worship? For whatever they say in defense of divine providence, we shall confirm more fully and for the better by saying that the counsel of God is to be wondered at, because He used the sin of His own people to call the nations <note>Gentiles</note> who were foreign to the covenants and promises concerning the kingdom of God. This had already been predicted long ago by the Prophets: that on account of the sins of the Hebrew people, God would choose not some one nation, but select individuals out of all: <margin>1 Cor. 1:25</margin> *after those things which are foolish of this world were chosen*, He would turn a brutish nation to the oracles of God, the kingdom of God having been taken from the former and delivered to the latter. It will suffice for the present to bring forward one oracle out of many, which sings in this manner in Deuteronomy concerning the future calling of the nations, from the person of the Lord; <margin>Deut. 32:21</margin> *They have moved me to jealousy with those who are not gods, and provoked me to anger with their idols: I also will move them to jealousy with those who are not a nation, and will move them to anger with a foolish nation.* Finally, the Jew concludes thus concerning Jesus: "Therefore he was that man, such as both words and the facts themselves indicate. But I do not know whether a man, having dared to draw the whole world to his own worship and his own doctrine, could have had such success without God, and overcome all the obstacles to his doctrine, even Kings and Emperors, the Roman Senate itself, and all the Princes of all peoples. For how could one born a man and partaking of no superior nature turn such a multitude to himself? If it consisted only of the wise, it would perhaps not seem a wonder; but it is composed of a rabble of men who are led by no reason, but are mostly devoted to vices, and who, being void of reason, are the more difficult to lead to self-control." But because Christ was the power of God and the wisdom of His Father, therefore He did such things and does them even now. Though Jews and Gentiles may hesitate to believe his words, we certainly shall never cease to trust in God according to the doctrine of Jesus Christ, and to convert others who are blind to the worship of God, if they are willing: even if those truly blind ones repeatedly say that we are blind, and whether Jews or Greeks, accuse us of the same crime of being deceivers of those who have joined them...

# Book 2. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...that they might become <note>The text describes the moral transformation of converts.</note> [temperate], or at least make progress toward temperance; that instead of being unjust, they might become righteous, or at least advance toward justice; that instead of being foolish, they might become prudent, or at least enter upon the path of prudence; and likewise, that instead of being cowardly and timid, they might become brave and steadfast, especially whenever they must strive for the sake of piety toward God, the creator of all things. Therefore, Jesus Christ came, having been foretold not by a single prophet, but by the proclamation of them all. In this matter, Celsus betrays his own ignorance when, speaking through the character of a Jew, he claims that only one prophet predicted the Christ. And since Celsus has, up to this point, made his Jew speak as if according to his own law—except for some remarks added at the end which are not worthy of mention—I myself will also finish here and close this second book. With God’s favor and the power of Christ assisting our soul, we shall endeavor to respond to Celsus’s remaining arguments in the third volume to follow.

<column-break/>

...that they might live [righteously], or at least make progress toward temperance; and instead of being unjust, become righteous, or progress toward justice; and instead of being foolish, become prudent, or travel the road toward prudence; and instead of being cowardly, untrained, and unmanly, become brave and enduring, especially demonstrating this in the struggles for the sake of piety toward God who created all things. Thus Jesus Christ came, having been proclaimed beforehand not by one prophet, but by all. And this too is a mark of Celsus’s ignorance: to have his Jewish character believe that only one prophet spoke in advance concerning the Christ. And since the Jew in Celsus’s work was introduced saying these things, supposedly according to his own law, and has paused his discourse there—except for other things he said that are not worth remembering—I too will here bring to a close the second of the volumes dictated by me against his treatise. God granting it, and the power of Christ dwelling within our soul, we shall attempt in the third book to present the appropriate arguments against the next part of Celsus’s writings.

In the first volume—written against the arrogantly titled book by Celsus, who inscribed his work against us as *The True Word* <note>original: "alēthē logon"</note>—we ran through his preface and the sections following it to the best of our ability, most faithful Ambrose, examining each of his statements until we reached the public speech he fabricated from the persona of a Jew addressing Jesus. In the second volume, we refuted as much as we could all the points made by that same speech-making Jew against us who believe in God through Christ. Now, we begin this third book, in which we intend to grapple with the points Celsus asserts in his own person. He says * indeed, "that Christians and Jews argue with one another most foolishly," and he claims that our dispute with one another concerning Christ differs in no way from the proverbial "fight over the shadow of an donkey" <note>A Greek idiom for arguing over something completely worthless or non-existent.</note>. He thinks there is nothing dignified in the inquiry between Jews and Christians, where both believe that a Savior for the human race was prophesied by the Divine Spirit to visit the world, but they no longer agree on whether the one prophesied has come or not. For we Christians have believed in Jesus as the one who has come according to the prophecies; but the majority of Jews are so far from believing in him that those of that time even plotted against Jesus. Even now, those who approve of the daring deeds committed by the Jews against him then continue to revile Jesus, claiming he used some kind of sorcery <note>term: goēteias (sorcery/magic) — Celsus frequently accused Jesus of being a mere magician who learned tricks in Egypt.</note> to fashion the claim that he was the Christ announced by the prophets to visit the world, in opposition to the ancestral customs of the Jews. Let Celsus and those who are pleased with his arguments against us tell us: does it seem like a "shadow" that the prophets of the Jews foretold the place of birth of the one hoped for by those who lived well and <margin>Micah 5:2</margin> those who are counted as God's portion? And that a virgin <margin>Isaiah 7:14; 35:5</margin> would conceive Emmanuel? And that such signs and wonders would be performed by the one prophesied? And <margin>Psalm 18:5; Isaiah 53:7; Psalm 15:10</margin> that his word would run so swiftly that the sound of his apostles would go out into all the earth? And what he would suffer, being condemned by the Jews, and how he would rise again? For was it at random that these things were poured—

In the first volume, which we wrote against the book titled with the arrogant name of *The True Word* with which Celsus attacks us, we ran through it with all our strength, just as you requested, most faithful Ambrose, examining his preface and what follows, scrutinizing his individual sayings until we left off at the fabricated speech to Jesus from the persona of a Jew. He says * foolishly that Christians and Jews contend among themselves, and that this concertation of theirs concerning Christ differs in no way from that proverbially celebrated contention over the shadow of a donkey: and that this whole question has no weight; since both believe the advent of the Savior of the human race was foretold through prophets inspired by the divine spirit, but they disagree in this: has he who was designated by the oracles come, or not? # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

Did the Prophets pour forth these things moved by no probable cause, not only to predict them, but even to commit them to writing? Therefore, did so great a nation of Jews, who once inhabited their own region, attribute the honor of Prophets to some and reject others as false seers based on no likely reason? Or was there nothing that invited them to number the writings of the later Prophets along with the volumes of Moses, which were always held as sacred? How will those who object to the "folly" of Jews and Christians show us that the Jewish nation could have endured without any promise of foreknowledge? For while each of the neighboring nations sought oracles in the shrines of their own gods (as they were then regarded), these people alone—who had learned to hold external deities in contempt, not as gods but as demons <note>The Latin text uses *dæmonum*, referring to lesser spirits or deceptive entities rather than the modern concept of "demons."</note> (surely warned by the voice of the Prophets that *all the gods of the nations are demons* <margin>Psalm 95:5 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 96:5.</note></margin>)—had no one who, professing himself an interpreter of the divine mind, might draw them back from those vain soothsayers to himself? Otherwise, in their desire to know the future, they would have defected to the demons worshiped by others. Consider, therefore, whether it was not necessary for them to have a supply of seers at home who, by their foreknowledge of events, exhibited greater things, surpassing all the prophecies that were then everywhere among others; since they were instructed to hold the gods of other nations in contempt. Therefore, while miracles were happening everywhere—just as he <note>Celsus</note> soon mentions Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine.</note> providing healings and oracles to entire cities dedicated to him, such as Tricca <margin>Tricca</margin>, Epidaurus, Cos, and Pergamum; and Aristeas of Proconnesus; and a certain man of Clazomenae; and Cleomedes of Astypalaea—was there among the Jews alone, who took pride in being the peculiar people of God the creator of all things, no sign or prodigy to confirm faith in Him, joined with the hope of another, better life? And yet, how could anyone think this? For they would have immediately defected from their God (whom they would have believed to bring them help in word only) to those external fate-telling and health-giving gods, if they had felt no presence of their own God in doubtful matters. But if they did not do this, but preferred to endure innumerable calamities rather than abjure Judaism and their ancestral laws—afflicted now by the Assyrians, now by the Persians, now by Antiochus—how is it that these critics, who do not deign to believe in the miracles of the histories and the Prophets, think these are fictions rather than that the most holy souls of those seers were inspired by the divine spirit through their love of virtue

...did the prophets say these things by chance, with no persuasiveness, which was present in them so as to not only speak but also to deem the things said worthy of being recorded? And was it with no persuasiveness that the Jewish nation, having long ago received its own land to inhabit, proclaimed some as prophets but rejected others as false prophets? And was there nothing among them that called for the words of those considered to be subsequent prophets to be arranged with the sacred and trusted books of Moses? Indeed, those who usually charge Jews and Christians will appear to us to say that the Jewish nation could have existed without any promise of foreknowledge being present among them; and that while each of the surrounding nations received oracles and divinations according to their ancestral customs from those they considered gods, these alone—who were taught to look down upon all the gods recognized by the nations as not being gods but demons (since the prophets said to them, *All the gods of the nations are demons*)—had no one promising divine prophecy and able to pull them away from the desire for foreknowledge of the future to keep them from deserting to the demons of others? Consider then if it were not necessary, for a whole nation taught to look down upon the gods of the rest, to have an abundance of prophets manifesting something greater and excelling the oracles everywhere. Furthermore, powers were working in many places or in many ways; as he himself <note>Celsus</note> sets forth in the following passages, Aesculapius doing good and foretelling the future to whole cities dedicated to him, such as Tricca, and Epidaurus, and Cos, and Pergamum; and Aristeas the Proconnesian; and a certain Clazomenian, and Cleomedes of Astypalaea. For they would have immediately turned to the worship of the demons who give oracles and healings, leaving behind the God believed to help them only as far as words go, but in no way bringing about His own manifestation. But if this did not happen, but they even endured ten thousand things so as not to swear away Judaism and the law according to it—at one time being enslaved in Assyria, at another in Persia, and at another by Antiochus—how is it not more reasonable, being struck by the most incredible and marvelous histories and prophecies, to believe that such things are not fictions, but some divine spirit being present in pure souls...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

...those concerning the prophets, who took up every labor upon them, some things regarding their own times, others regarding how things would be later, and especially concerning the arrival of the Savior to the human race. If these things are so, how is it not a "shadow of an ass" <note>A Greek proverb meaning a dispute over something utterly worthless or non-existent.</note> for Jews and Christians to seek against one another, examining from the prophecies—as they both commonly believe—whether the one prophesied has come, or has not yet arrived, or is still expected? Even if it were granted to Celsus for the sake of argument that Jesus is not the one whom the prophets announced, even so, the inquiry into the prophetic scriptures is no less than a search for the "shadow of an ass" <note>Origen is being sarcastic here, mirroring Celsus's insult to show that the subject matter—divine prophecy—is inherently weighty, regardless of the conclusion.</note> so that it might be clearly demonstrated who the one being proclaimed was, what kind of person he was prophesied to be, what he would do, and if possible, when he would arrive. In the preceding sections, we have already spoken, setting forth a few prophecies out of many, concerning Jesus being the prophesied Christ. Therefore, neither Jews nor Christians are mistaken in the premise that the prophets spoke by divine inspiration; rather, do those who are mistaken about the expected one of prophecy hold a false opinion as to who and what kind of person was proclaimed by the prophets according to the true word? Following these points, Celsus—thinking that the Jews were Egyptians by race and had left Egypt after revolting against the Egyptian community and despising the customary Egyptian religious rites—says: **"They [the Jews] suffered the very same thing from those who joined themselves to Jesus and believed in him as the Christ, which they themselves had previously done to the Egyptians; for both groups, the cause of their innovation was a revolt against the community."** We must consider what Celsus has done in this passage. Long ago, the Egyptians, having subjected the Hebrew race to many hardships when they arrived in Egypt as guests and suppliants due to a famine in Judea, committed injustices that a whole nation was destined by divine providence to suffer, having conspired against a race that was a guest among them and had done them no wrong. Stricken by divine plagues, they finally and not long after released those who had been unjustly enslaved to go wherever they wished. But being lovers of themselves, and favoring their own kin of whatever sort over even the most righteous strangers, there is no accusation they have left out which they have not spoken against Moses and the Hebrews—either entirely denying the miraculous powers displayed through Moses, or claiming they occurred through sorcery <term>goeteia: sorcery or jugglery, as opposed to divine miracles</term> and not by divine power. But Moses [recorded what happened] not as a sorcerer, but as a pious man, devoted to the God of all things, and sharing in a more divine spirit, he also established laws.

...shunning no hardships, while agitated by the divinity dwelling within them, they reveal public and private fates both to their own age and to future centuries, and especially concerning a certain coming Savior of the human race? Since these things are so, how can Jews be seen to contend with Christians over the "shadow of an ass," inquiring from the Prophets (whom both believe in equally) whether he of whom the Prophets sing has come, or not yet, but is to come? And even if it be granted to Celsus for the time being that Jesus is not the one foretold by the Prophets; nevertheless, not even so would those who examine the prophetic Scriptures be inquiring about the "shadow of an ass," so that it might be more evidently shown who was designated by the oracles of the Prophets, or what he would do, and, if it can be done, where or when he would come. The Egyptians once, when they afflicted the Hebrews with many injuries (who had been brought into their region because of famine as guests and suppliants), it was necessary that their whole nation suffer those things which they endured (since they had conspired against guests without receiving any injury) by a certain divine providence. Finally chastised by the punishment of God, with difficulty and not long after, they manumitted them from unjust servitude to go wherever they pleased. Therefore, as lovers of their own kind, and more favorable to their own relatives of whatever sort than to guests, they omitted no calumny with which to attack Moses and the Jews; not entirely denying the wonders performed by him, but attributing them to magic arts, not to divine power: but Moses, not a magician, but a pious man, referring all his affairs to the God of the universe, and a partaker of the divine Spirit, by his instinct [established] laws...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

->Q 2<-

He <note>Moses</note> brought laws to the Jews and truly committed their history to writing. But Celsus is not a fair examiner of the controversy between the Egyptians and the Hebrews; instead, being already captivated by the charms of Egypt, he preferred to believe the oppressors of his guests. He claims that the Hebrews, who were the ones suffering injury, left Egypt through an act of sedition <note>original: *seditionem*; a violent uprising or political rebellion</note>. He fails to see, meanwhile, that it is impossible for such a small number—once a faction had arisen while the Egyptians held the kingdom—to establish a nation through rebellion and, by that same effort, change their language. It is unthinkable that those who had spoken Egyptian until then should suddenly be skilled in Hebrew. But even if it were granted that, upon leaving Egypt, they felt a loathing for their native tongue, why did they not assume the language of the Syrians or Phoenicians instead of Hebrew, which differs from both? By all these reasons, it is gathered that it is falsely believed that some people of the Egyptian race once withdrew into Palestine from the rest of the Egyptians, and that a colony was born from them which is now called Judea. For the Hebrews had their own ancestral language before they went down into Egypt, and the Hebrew letters were different from the Egyptian ones; using these, Moses wrote those five sacred books held among the Jews. Therefore, both claims are equally false: either that the Hebrews, having once been part of the Egyptians, withdrew from them by sedition; or that in the time of Jesus, a sedition having arisen in the Jewish Republic, a part torn away from the rest of the people defected to Jesus. For Celsus and those who think like him will be able to show nothing seditious among the Christians. Certainly, if the Christian religion had arisen by cause of sedition—having made a defection from the Jews, who were permitted both to take up arms for their defense and to kill an enemy—the Legislator of the Christians would not have forbidden all homicide. He willed that such a crime against any human being, even the most wicked, be a sin for his disciples (for he thought it unbecoming to his divine laws to permit the slaughter of any man whatsoever). Nor would Christians, if they had their beginning from a rebellion, have accepted such gentle laws, which offer their enemies the opportunity to slaughter them like unresisting sheep. However, if we look more deeply into the matter, we can say regarding the departure from Egypt, that it was not without a miracle and divine grace that the entire people received back their original language which is called Hebrew; just as one of their own Prophets sings: *That in their exit from Egypt, they heard a language they did not know.* <note>A reference to Psalm 81:5</note>

<column-break/>

...to the Hebrews, as the Divine obeyed him; and he recorded the events as they truly were. Therefore Celsus, not being a just judge examining the accounts told differently by the Egyptians and differently by the Hebrews, but being preoccupied as if by the charms of the Egyptians, agreed with those who wronged the strangers as if they spoke the truth. He says the Hebrews, who were wronged, <margin>* having revolted.</margin> left Egypt after having revolted. He does not see how it was possible for such a rebellious multitude—while the Egyptians <margin>* held.</margin> held power <margin>[throughout]</margin> the whole land—to establish a nation at the same time as revolting, and to change their dialect; so that those who until then used the speech of the Egyptians should suddenly fill out the dialect of the Hebrews. But let it be granted for the sake of argument that, having left Egypt, they hated even their foster-speech. Why then did they not rather use the dialect of the Syrians or that of the Phoenicians, but instead the Hebrew, which stands apart from both? This is what my argument wishes to conclude: that it is a lie <margin>* that some who were by race from Egypt.</margin> that certain people, being Egyptians by race, revolted against the Egyptians and left Egypt, and having come to Palestine, inhabited that which is now called Judea. For the dialect of the Hebrews was ancestral before their descent into Egypt, and the Hebrew letters were different from those of the Egyptians; using these, Moses wrote the five books believed in among the Jews. Likewise, it is a lie that the Hebrews took their beginning from a revolt, "being Egyptians"; and that "being Jews" again in the times of Jesus, they revolted against the community of the Jews and followed Jesus. For Celsus, or those who agree with him, will be able to point to no act of sedition by Christians. And yet, if sedition was the cause of the Christians' establishment—having taken their beginning from the Jews, who were allowed to take up arms for their own people and to destroy enemies—the Legislator of the Christians would not have altogether forbidden the destruction of man, <margin>†</margin> teaching that the daring act against a man is never right for his own disciples, even if <margin>Matthew 26:52. * and unjust.</margin> that man be most unjust. For he did not think it consistent with his own laws of piety to allow the destruction of any man whatsoever. Furthermore, if Christians had started from a revolt, they would not have accepted laws so mild that it resulted in them being slaughtered like sheep <margin>Romans 8:36.</margin> and never defending themselves against their persecutors. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

<margin>Psalm 81:5</margin> They heard a language which they did not know <note>original: "Αἰγύπτε γλῶσσαν, ἣν οὐκ ἔγνω, ἤκουσαν" / "linguam audierunt quam non noverint"</note>. And it must be established in this way: that those who departed Egypt with Moses were not Egyptians. For if they had been Egyptians, they would have used Egyptian names, just as every dialect has names related to its own tongue. But if it is clear from their names being Hebrew (for the Scripture is full of Hebrew names, even those given to children by their parents while in Egypt), it is evident that the claim made by the Egyptians is a lie—namely, that being Egyptians, they were driven out of Egypt with Moses. It is clearly [manifestly] seen that they were descended from Hebrew ancestors, and following the history recorded by Moses, the race used their own dialect, from which they also gave names to their sons.

But to speak of the Christians: because they were taught not to defend themselves against their enemies, they observed this mild and philanthropic law of their author. Through this, they achieved more than if they had received authority to commit any offense, even if they had been quite powerful. For God took up their cause, always checking those who warred against the Christians at the appropriate times, so that the race might remain, even when people wished to destroy them. For they endure for this reason: so that a few, being easily numbered, might struggle for the sake of piety, become more approved, and despise death. Only a few at certain intervals of time, and easily numbered, have died for the Christian religion, as God prevented the entire nation from being warred against. For He willed that this nation should be established, and that all the earth should be filled with this saving and most pious teaching. Again, on the other hand, so that the weaker ones might rest from the anxiety concerning mortal things, God provided for the believers, scattering by His will alone every plot against them, so that neither Kings, nor local governors, nor the common people could be further incensed against them.

These are the responses to the things said by Celsus concerning how "the beginning arose from sedition, formerly for the communities of the Jews, and later for these Christians of ours." <note>Celsus argued that both Judaism and Christianity began as rebellious break-away movements.</note> Since in what follows he manifestly lies, come, let us set forth his own words where he says: "If all men wished to be Christians, these people would no longer desire it." That such a thing is a lie is clear from this: that as far as in them lies, Christians do not neglect to sow the Word throughout the whole inhabited world. Indeed, some have made it their business to travel around not only through cities, but also villages and farmsteads, so that they might prepare others to be pious toward God. And one could not say that they do this for the sake of wealth, since sometimes they do not even accept the necessities for food. If they are ever forced to do so by this poverty, they are content with their immediate need alone, even if the voluntary liberality of many is not lacking

they heard a language which they did not know. There is also another argument that they were not Egyptians who departed that region under the leadership of Moses: for if they had been, they certainly would have had Egyptian names, just as every language has its own names. But if it is established that their names are Hebrew or of foreign origin (for the Scripture is full of Hebrew appellations, which even in Egypt the parents had bestowed upon their children), it appears sufficiently that it is a fiction of the Egyptians that they were once driven out of Egypt with Moses. And no further doubt is left that they were born of Hebrew ancestors, as was handed down by Moses, and consequently used their own language, and also had Hebrew names bestowed by their parents.

Furthermore, to speak also of the Christians: these, because they were taught not to fight back against their harassers, constantly preserved this gentle and humane law of their author; they attained more than if they had received license to resist their enemies. Doubtless, this was because God fought for them and at opportune times restrained the persecutors of the Christian name. For so that by looking collectively at a few athletes of piety, they might become proofs and despise death, only a few at intervals of time and easily countable have died for the Christian religion, as God forbade that this race of men be utterly cut off. For He willed it to subsist, and all lands to be filled with this saving and pious doctrine. On the other hand, so that the weaker might breathe again from the fear and anxiety of death, God looked out for the faithful, dissipating all the attempts of adversaries by His nod alone, so that neither Kings, nor governors of provinces, nor the people could be further exasperated against them.

Let these be the answers to Celsus asserting *that both for the Jews formerly, and for the Christians later, the beginning came from sedition.* <margin>Matthew 5:39</margin> <margin>* Jews</margin> <margin>* Christians</margin> <margin>* by men</margin> Since, however, in the following parts he manifestly lies, come, let us set down his words: *If all men wished to be Christians, these people would no longer admit this.* That this is false is evident from the fact that Christians, as much as is in them, do not neglect to sow this doctrine of theirs throughout the whole world. Certainly, some have taken up this one business for themselves: to wander not only through towns, but even villages and villas, so that they might draw others also to piety and the true worship of God. Nor can it be objected that they do this for the sake of gain, since they often refuse to accept the necessities for living; and if by chance they are sometimes compelled to do so by poverty, they are content with present use only, even if the voluntary liberality of many is not lacking.

For since medicine is useful and necessary to the human race, and there are many things sought within it concerning the manner of healing bodies; for this reason, many sects in medicine are admittedly found among the Greeks; and I think also among the barbarians, as many as profess to use medicine. And again, since philosophy, promising the truth and knowledge of existing things, suggests how one ought to live and attempts to teach what is beneficial to our race; and since the matters to be managed involve many inquiries; for this reason, very many sects have been established in philosophy. But even Judaism provided a pretext for the birth of sects, due to the different interpretation of the writings of Moses and the words of the prophets. Let it be so, then, since Christianity appeared as something venerable to men—not only (as Celsus thinks) to those of a slavish nature, but also to many of the learned among the Greeks—sects necessarily arose, not entirely * due to sedition and a love of strife, but because more of the learned were eager to understand the teachings of Christianity. * And from this it followed, as they interpreted the divine words—which were believed by all—in different ways, that sects arose named after those who admired the antiquity of the Word, but were moved somehow by certain probabilities toward disagreements with one another. ...the things already said, can we not in the same way excuse the sects among Christians? Regarding these, the opinion of Paul seems wonderful to me when he says, <margin>1 Cor. 11:19.</margin> *There must be sects among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.* <note>original: "Oportet sectas in vobis esse..." Origen argues that diversity of opinion is a natural byproduct of any serious intellectual or spiritual pursuit.</note> For just as a physician is only truly "approved" who, having examined the various medical sects, has practiced skillfully in many of them; and as one is understood to have made progress in philosophy who, exercised in the discussions of various opinions, follows the more powerful reasons among them: so I would dare to affirm that he is the wisest among Christians who has most diligently looked into the sects of both Jews and Christians. 

But he who blames our teaching because of its sects would also have to condemn the Socratic teaching, because several different schools arose from the discussions of that philosopher; he would also condemn the decrees of Plato <margin>Book 1.</margin> because of Aristotle’s disagreement with them and his indulgence in new opinions—a matter we have already spoken of before. 

Moreover, Celsus seems to me to know of certain heresies with which even the name of Jesus is not held in common with us. For perhaps he has heard of the so-called Ophites <note>A Gnostic sect that gave special importance to the serpent (Greek: ophis) in the Garden of Eden.</note> and the Cainites, <note>A group that revered Cain as a victim of the inferior creator-god.</note> and if there is any other similar opinion that differs in every way from the teaching of Jesus: truly, those things have nothing to do with the blaming of the most blameless Christian religion.

# Book 3. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

To those who approach them, there are offered splendid sacred precincts with groves, and temples with vestibules and porches of extraordinary size and beauty, wonderful to behold, and ceremonies that are quite religious and mystical; but having entered, one will see the worship of a cat, or a monkey, or a crocodile, or a goat, or a dog. For what is there among us similar to the Egyptian sanctuaries, so beautiful at first sight? Or what can be compared with the brute animals worshipped within? Or perhaps the Prophecies, and God the Lord of all, and the contempt for idols, also seem to him to be magnificent things; but Jesus Christ crucified similar to a worshipped brute beast? If he says this—for I do not think he will say anything else—we will reply with the many things mentioned by us above in defense of Jesus: that even those things which seem to have happened to him in the human manner were useful to the whole world and salutary. And afterwards, regarding those venerable things of the Egyptians—who affirm that in brute animals there exists some symbol of divinity, or whatever name their prophets like to call these things—he says they hold out a certain appearance of non-empty rites, at least to those skilled in such matters. But as for the spiritual gifts <note>original: "charismata"</note> which our discipline possesses (to speak in the manner of Paul) granted through the spirit of wisdom and spiritual knowledge, which Christians are studious of, I guess that they have not even entered into Celsus's thought, not only from these words of his, but also from what follows: where he accuses the Christian fellowship, saying <margin>He drives away all wise men from the doctrine of faith, and only the foolish and those endowed with a servile nature are admitted: concerning which we shall see after we have come to that place. among whom, to one approaching, there are very splendid sacred precincts, and groves, and greatness and beauty of gateways, and wonderful temples, and proud tents around, and ceremonies very <margin>* Superstitious.</margin> superstitious and mystical. Or <margin>* Truly the prophecies, and the God over all.</margin> the prophecies, and the God over all, and the things concerning the statues, that these are solemn even according to him; but Jesus Christ crucified is the analogy to the worshipped brute animal? But if he says this—for I think he will say nothing else when challenged—[we say] that more has been said by us in the preceding parts for the establishment of the facts about Jesus: that even the things which seem to have happened to him according to man occurred usefully in the universe, and salvifically for the whole world. Then, regarding the solemn talk of the Egyptians, even through <margin>* other animals.</margin> brute animals, and their claiming that they are certain symbols of God, or however it is pleasing to name them to those of them who are called prophets, he says "it draws out an imagination to those who have learned these things, that they have not been initiated in vain." But the things in our words, arising from that gift mentioned in Paul <margin>1 Corinthians 12:8</margin> in the word of wisdom through the Spirit, and in the word of knowledge according to the Spirit, presented to those who are well-learned in Christianity, Celsus does not seem to me to have even imagined, not only from these things, but also from what he says in the following parts, accusing the system of the Christians. Concerning whom, as being sufficient to hear the wisdom in Christianity, Paul teaching says: *But we speak wisdom among the perfect; yet a wisdom not of this world,* <margin>1 Corinthians 2:6</margin>

...then, nor of the rulers of this world who are coming to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this world knew. <note>Origen is quoting 1 Corinthians 2:6-8 to prove that Christianity has a "hidden" intellectual depth for the mature, contrary to Celsus's claims that it is only for the ignorant.</note> And we say to those who agree with Celsus, that Paul did not promise to speak a wisdom he merely imagined, but he promised to speak wisdom among the "perfect" <note>The "perfect" or "mature" (teleioi) refers to advanced believers capable of higher philosophy.</note>. And when they say—as they do—that he promised these things while having nothing of substance, we answer them by saying: First, let those who say these things explain the Epistles, and having looked closely at the intent of every word in them (for example, in the letters to the Ephesians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Philippians, and Romans), let them demonstrate both that they have understood Paul’s words and that they can prove them to be foolish or senseless. But if a man gives himself to an attentive reading, I know well that he will either wonder at the mind of the man who perceives great things in common language; or, if he does not wonder, he himself will appear ridiculous—whether he is explaining what he thinks he understood of the man's intent, or wishing to contradict and overturn what he imagined he understood. And why should I speak yet of the things in the Gospels which are so worthy of observation? Each of these contains much for contemplation, offering a challenge not only to the common people but even to the more intelligent, containing the explanation of very deep parables which Jesus spoke to those outside, while reserving their clarity for those who had surpassed "external hearing" and approached him privately in the house. He will wonder, once he understands, what reason there is for some to be named "outside" and others "in the house." And again, who would not be struck with awe seeing the power of the transitions of Jesus, ascending the mountain for such words or deeds, or for his own Transfiguration; and then below, healing those who had fallen ill and were unable to ascend to where his disciples went? To explain now the truly solemn and divine things of the Gospels, or those in the "Pauline Christ"—that is, of the Wisdom and the Word—is not the right time. But even these points are sufficient against the unphilosophical mockery of Celsus, who compares the internal and mystical things of the Church of God to the Egyptians' cats, or apes, or crocodiles, or goats, or dogs. And leaving nothing out in his mockery and ridicule of us, this buffoon Celsus, in his discourse against us, names the Dioscuri <note>Castor and Pollux, twin deities in Greek mythology.</note>, and Hercules, and Aesculapius, and Dionysus, who were once men among the Greeks and became Gods; and he says: "You do not endure that we consider these to be Gods, because they were formerly men, even though they displayed many...

<column-break/>

...I say, not of this world, nor of the vanity of those who are the princes of this world: but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God pre-ordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the princes of this world knew. Let those now like Celsus say whether Paul imagined no more excellent wisdom when he promised he would speak wisdom among the perfect: for if anyone will dare to say with a hardened brow <note>A Latin idiom for "shamelessly."</note> that the Apostle promised such things while possessing no wisdom, we shall bid him interpret the epistles of this writer, having inspected the mind of each individual word as diligently as possible (namely those to the Ephesians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Philippians, Romans): and let him show both that they have been understood by him, and that they are stupid and fatuous. For I know enough that if he gives himself to an attentive reading of them, he will either admire the mind of a man who encompassed extraordinary sentiments in common speech, or unless he admires them, he himself will seem ridiculous: whether he tries to narrate them as if understood, or to refute what he himself imagined in his writings. I am silent now concerning those things which are worthy of observation in all the Gospels: each of which has much contemplation, difficult not only for the unskilled and common people, but even for the talented, because of the very profound meanings of the parables which Jesus used among the profane, keeping their understanding for disciples endowed with no common ears, and who called upon him privately at home. There he who understands will wonder by what reason some are said to be at home, others outside. Again, who would not be stunned, who is only able to perceive the frequent transitions of Jesus, now seeking the mountain for the sake of saying or doing this or that, as in his transfiguration: now again descending to heal the sick, who were not able to follow him into the mountain together with the disciples? But it is not of the present time to narrate the divine meanings of the Gospels or the Pauline letters, that is, of the wisdom and word of God; let it be enough to have said even these things against the unseemly slander of Celsus, a philosopher, who compares the mysteries of the Church of God with the Egyptians' cats, monkeys, crocodiles, goats, and dogs. And, so that he might leave no kind of derision remaining, that scoundrel, in his speech by which he attacks us, mentions the Castors, Hercules, Aesculapius, and Bacchus, Gods made as the Greeks believe from men: saying, that we do not bear for them to be held as gods, because they were once men: although they were more excellent than others...

# Book 3. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...and those who have deserved most highly of the human race. But regarding Jesus, Celsus asserts that we claim he appeared to his own companions after being put to death; he adds to this accusation that we, who say he appeared, were merely looking at a ghost <note>original Latin: *umbram*; Greek: *σκιάν* (shadow/specter)</note>. To this we say that Celsus has craftily concealed the fact that he himself does not worship these gods, fearing the opinion of his readers lest they believe him impious. If he had any regard for the truth he perceived, he would never have pretended to hold them as gods, so that we might answer him on either ground. 

Come then, let us argue with those who do not think they are gods. Therefore, they do not exist at all; but as is the opinion of some concerning the human soul—that it perishes immediately upon being released—the souls of these figures have also perished. Or, if according to the opinion of others, souls survive the body and enjoy immortality, then these figures also survive, but either as heroes and not gods, or not even that, but as mere, pure souls. Therefore, if you think they no longer exist, you support that former opinion about the soul. But if they still exist, you must agree with the immortality of the soul, not only according to those excellent Greek disputes on this matter, but also according to the decrees of divine doctrine. 

We shall show from history that it is impossible for those whom they wish to have increased the number of the heavenly beings to have migrated to better seats after death, since so many things have been handed down concerning the lusts of Hercules—even to the point of enduring female domination while he did not disdain to serve Omphale <note>A reference to the myth where Hercules was enslaved to Queen Omphale and forced to do women's work</note>—and concerning Aesculapius being struck down by the lightning of their own Jove.
