# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 3.

<margin>\* Phantasms.</margin>
...can have a real existence, and are worthy of worship and adoration; let us tear them apart like **Titans**, or gods cast down from heaven. But our **Jesus**, having appeared to his own followers (for I will use the term used by **Celsus** <note>Celsus used the Greek word *thiasōtais*, meaning members of a religious cult or troupe, likely as a slur</note>), was seen in truth. Celsus slanders the account, saying he was seen only as a **shadow**. Let the histories concerning their gods be examined alongside those concerning Jesus. Does Celsus wish those to be true, while these—reported by those who saw them, who showed by their deeds the clarity of their grasp of what they witnessed, and who presented their disposition in what they suffered for the sake of his Word—are merely fictions? And who, wishing to act according to reason, would arbitrarily agree with the former, yet rashly rush to distrust the latter without examination? 

<margin>\* Concerning those gods.</margin> 
<margin>\* Of the multitude.</margin> 
Again, when he says that a great multitude of people, both **Greeks** and **barbarians**, confess to having often seen, and still see, not a mere ghost of this person <note>Referring to Aesculapius, the god of medicine</note>, but the god himself healing, doing good, and foretelling the future—Celsus expects us to believe this. He accuses those who believe in Jesus for believing on such grounds; yet when we agree with the disciples and eyewitnesses of the wonders of Jesus, who clearly presented the integrity of their own conscience, we are called "foolish" and "wicked" by Celsus. 

<margin>\* As many Greeks and barbarians.</margin> 
He claims he can present an unspeakable multitude of Greeks and barbarians who believe in **Aesculapius**. For our part, if it is considered a noble thing to believe such things, we clearly show an unspeakable multitude of Greeks and barbarians who believe in Jesus. Some show signs of having received something more miraculous through this faith in the way they heal; they call upon nothing else over those needing healing than the **God over all** and the name of Jesus, along with the history concerning him. For by these means, we ourselves have seen many delivered from grievous symptoms, and fits, and madness, and countless other ills which neither men nor **demons** <note>In the ancient sense, *daimones* were intermediate spirits, not necessarily evil, though Origen views them as deceptive</note> could cure. 

<margin>\* A physician.</margin> 
Even if I grant that some medical demon called Aesculapius heals bodies, I would say to those who admire such a thing, or the prophecy of **Apollo**: if the healing of bodies is a "middle" thing <note>A technical term from Stoic philosophy meaning something morally neutral, neither good nor evil in itself</note>, and the foreknowledge of causes is also a middle thing—for the one who foreknows is not necessarily a virtuous person—then demonstrate how those who heal or prophesy are in no way wicked. Show that they display a virtuous character in every way, so as to be rightly considered blessed gods. But they will not be able to show them to be virtuous...

<column-break/>

...even the gods must be weighed to see whether they truly exist and are worthy of being worshipped, since they were torn apart by **Titans** and shamefully cast down from heaven. But our **Jesus**, seen by his companions (as that man puts it), was truly seen; and it is a calumny of **Celsus** that only his **shadow** was seen. Now let those celebrated histories be compared with these things which have been committed to writing concerning Jesus: unless Celsus demands that those be believed as true, while these—even though written by those who saw them, and who showed by the facts themselves that they were prepared to testify to the faith they had in what they had seen, constantly even unto death—are nevertheless held to be fictions. And who, if he only follows reason, would be so rashly credulous of those things, examining nothing, yet with equal rashness reject the faith of our people? 

Likewise, when it is said of **Aesculapius** that a great multitude of both Greeks and barbarians assert that he has often been seen, and is seen today—not as a ghost, but as the god himself exhibiting the benefits of health and oracles—Celsus wants this to be believed even by Christian men. But if we should agree with the disciples of Jesus, the spectators of his miracles, who candidly profess their conscience (considering the simplicity of the **Scripture**, which lacks all craftiness), he does not fear to stamp us with the mark of "folly." Yet he cannot produce that multitude of Greeks and barbarians believing in Aesculapius; whereas we, if Celsus thinks it proper, can show an inexpressible number of both Greeks and barbarians believing in our Jesus. 

Among these, some—as a sign of the power received through faith—miraculously heal the sick, having only invoked over them the **God of the universe** and the name of Jesus, and having recited some part of the history of his deeds. For we ourselves have seen many thus freed from heavy evils: from alienation of the mind, from insanity, and from countless other things which neither men nor demons ever brought help to. Now, even if we concede that some physician-demon who is called Aesculapius cures diseases of the body, we will object to the admirers of this one, and likewise to the admirers of the prophet **Apollo**, that skill in medicine is an "indifferent" thing <note>Latin: *indifferentem*, translating the Greek *meson*</note>, which falls to the wicked just as much as to the good. For he who foreknows the future is not immediately a good man. Therefore, another proof is required: that those healers and soothsayers are not wicked, but upright in all ways, and such as may not undeservedly be held as gods. But they will not be able to declare them...

Then in the seventh year, when he appeared in Proconnesus, he composed those verses which are now called the Arimaspea by the Greeks: which being finished, he disappeared again, as it is told in those cities I mentioned. But I know those things happened to the Metapontines, who are in Italy, three hundred and forty years after he disappeared a second time, as much as I gather from a comparison of the accounts I heard from the Proconnesians and Metapontines. The Metapontines themselves say Aristeas was seen among them and ordered an altar to be dedicated to Apollo, and a statue to be erected nearby which should have the surname of Aristeas of Proconnesus: because he said that Apollo had come to them alone of the Italians into their land, with him following; and he who was now Aristeas, when he followed the God, had been a raven, and having spoken these things he vanished. They, having sent legates to Delphi, consulted the oracle as to what that ghost of a man might be: then the Pythia ordered them to obey the ghost, for this would be to their advantage. And having received the response, they did what was commanded, and today there stands a statue with the surname of Aristeas, near the very altar of Apollo with laurels surrounding both. Moreover, that image is in the forum: thus far concerning Aristeas.*

I respond to these things: if Celsus had left the credit of this history to its author <note>Herodotus</note>, I would have dealt with him differently. But now, since he reports it as true, saying that he disappeared divinely and appeared again openly in many regions of the world, and announced many wonders—and even mentions the oracle of Apollo, which commanded the Metapontines to worship the man with divine honors—being clearly persuaded that these things are so, I wish to challenge him thus: You, who regard the miracles produced by the disciples of Jesus as fictions, and accuse the credulity of others, how is it that you do not consider these things to be fictions, and indeed prodigious ones? How can you charge others with believing the wonders of Jesus without any reason, when you yourself show that you believe fables that have nothing probable which you can bring forward? Unless perhaps Pindar and Herodotus are truthful to you...

# Book 3. ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

Indeed, men who were accustomed to die for the teachings of their master, Jesus—teachings which, being fully persuaded of their truth, they handed down in writing to posterity—struggled so constantly for what you consider "fictions," that, living according to that standard, they preferred to be killed rather than to renounce them. Therefore, having placed yourself in the middle between the accounts written about Aristeas and those about Jesus, suspend your judgment for a while until you can discern from the outcome—regarding the correction of morals and piety toward God the creator of all things—whether the things told about Jesus were not done with divine power, rather than those told about Aristeas of Proconnesus <note>Aristeas was a 7th-century BCE Greek poet said to have the ability to leave his body and appear in different places simultaneously.</note>. For what purpose would divine providence have wished those fabulous miracles to be published through Aristeas? You cannot even say what benefit would have come to the human race from those things which seem so wonderful to you.

We, however, when we narrate the deeds of Jesus, do not bring forward common reasons for them: we say that God willed to establish a saving doctrine for men through Jesus, confirmed in the Apostles as the foundation for building up Christianity, and further to be increased in later times by greater additions, when healings and other manifest proofs of the present and favorable heavenly power are performed by invoking the name of Jesus.

What kind of being is this Apollo, and what does he mean by severely commanding the people of Metapontum <note>A Greek city in Southern Italy.</note> to hold Aristeas in such honor as is given to the heavenly gods? What benefit, I ask, were they to obtain from this, if they believed that he, who had just been a man, had suddenly become a God? Yet the recommendation of Apollo—who in our opinion is a demon <note>original: "daemonis"; Origen uses the term to mean a fallen spirit or pagan deity, not necessarily a "demon" in the modern horror sense.</note>, though honored by your esteem with the smell of sacrifices and libations—has weight in adorning Aristeas. On the other hand, the testimonies of the supreme God and his holy Angels and Prophets—published not only after the birth of Jesus, but even long before his birth—do not move you to admire either the seers inspired by the divine spirit, or the one foretold by them, whose coming into this life happened to be signified by the proclamation of many people so many centuries before.

So much so, that the entire nation of the Jews, which for a long time hung upon the expectation of the one to come, disputed among themselves about this after the arrival of Jesus; a great part believed and contended that this was the Christ designated by the oracles of the Prophets. The others did not believe, and having despised the gentleness of his disciples—who did not pursue sedition even in word—dared to commit such a great crime against Jesus, as is narrated in the most truthful and candid writings of his disciples. In these writings, not even those things are omitted which might seem to bring—

—shame <note>The Greek text at the top of the second column begins with the word for "shame" or "disgrace," matching the catchword from the previous page.</note>. Standing in the middle, look at the events concerning Aristeas <margin>* Aristeas.</margin> and the history of Jesus, and see if it is not possible to say from the result—and from those who are benefited in the correction of their morals and their reverence toward the God over all—that one must believe that the history of Jesus did not happen without God's help, whereas the history of the Proconnesian Aristeas did. For what purpose did Providence manage the wonders concerning Aristeas? And what benefit did it wish to provide to the human race <margin>* to the human race.</margin> by displaying such great things (as you think)? You cannot say.

But we, when we relate the things concerning Jesus, offer no ordinary defense for these things having happened: namely, that God willed to establish the word through Jesus as a means of salvation for men. This was confirmed by the apostles as if they were the foundations <margin>Ephesians 2:20.</margin> of the building of Christianity being laid down, and it increased in the following times, in which not a few healings and other not-to-be-despised manifestations are performed in the name of Jesus.

These did not just happen when Jesus was born, but before he resided in human life <margin>* life.</margin>, they foretold him and moved you to wonder at both the prophets who were granted the divine spirit and the one prophesied by them. His arrival in life happened to be proclaimed many years before by many people, so that the whole nation of the Jews, hanging on the expectation of the one hoped for to arrive, came to a dispute with one another when Jesus arrived. A great multitude of them confessed him to be Christ and believed <margin>* believed.</margin> him to be the one prophesied. But those who did not believe, despising the gentleness of those who, because of the teachings of Jesus, did not wish to revolt even in the slightest degree, dared such things against Jesus as his disciples recorded truthfully and with good judgment, not stealing away from his wonderful history the things that seem to the many to be—

For it was not sorcerers <note>Latin: *Magi*; Greek: *γοήτες* (goētes). Origen distinguishes between mere magicians and divine power.</note> who, at the command of some King or Emperor, gathered together and by their own decree enrolled Him in the number of the Gods; but the Creator of the world Himself, in accordance with the wondrously persuasive power of His teaching, commended Him to be worshipped with divine honor in the hearts of believers. Even to this day, these powers manifest a fear of the name of Jesus as something more powerful, whether compelled by fear or by the laws of their own Master. Otherwise, if He did not have a power given from God, the demons would by no means yield at the mere invocation of His name and depart from the bodies they once possessed.

The Egyptians, therefore, having been taught to worship Antinous <note>A youth deified by Emperor Hadrian; Origen uses him as a foil for the true divinity of Christ.</note>, will bear it with a calm mind if you compare him with Apollo or Jupiter; indeed, they honor Antinous more for the very reason that he is numbered among such great Gods. And in this, Celsus is caught in a notorious lie when he says, *If you compare Apollo or Jupiter with him, they will not endure it.* But Christians, who know that eternal life consists in the knowledge of the only true God and of Jesus Christ whom He has sent <margin>John 17:3</margin>; and who have learned that all the gods of the nations are demons <margin>Psalm 95:5</margin> greedy for the blood of victims, hovering around the smells of such sacrifices to deceive all those who do not have a refuge in the God of all creation; and that the angels of God differ greatly from earthly demons in both nature and will—and that these angels are known to very few men who prudently and diligently seek such things—these Christians will not suffer Jupiter or Apollo to be thrust upon them, nor will they seek any other who requires sacrificial smells and bloody offerings.

Some of the simpler folk, not even knowing how to give a reason for what they do, are content to keep in good faith what they received from their ancestors; but others will even give reasons that are not to be despised, but rather are deep and to be looked into "internally" (as the Greeks say). In these reasons, there is frequent mention of God and of those who are dear to God as partakers of the only-begotten Word of God and adopted into His name. There is also frequent mention of the good spirits who are God's messengers, and of those who are different from them—the enemies of truth who, imposing upon mortals with deceitful tricks, show themselves as gods or angels of God, or good spirits, or heroes into whom it is believed the good souls of men are changed. These more learned Christians will be able to show that just as many of the philosophers seem to themselves to hold the truth,

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

We say that the human soul in him <note>Jesus</note>, not only through communion with that Word <note>The Logos</note> but even through union and intermingling, has received the greatest elements and, having shared in His divinity, has passed over into God. But if anyone is offended when we say these things even concerning his body, I shall direct him to the accounts given by the Greeks concerning "unqualified matter" <note>original: *idias logō apoias hylēs* — a philosophical concept of matter as a blank slate without inherent properties</note>, which, while lacking its own quality, is clothed in whatever quality the Creator wishes to bestow upon it; and often, laying aside its former qualities, it takes on others that are better and different. For if these things are so, what is surprising if the mortal quality of the body of Jesus—God’s providence so willing it—changed into an ethereal and divine quality? 

It is not as Celsus argues with his dialectical subtleties, comparing the human flesh of Jesus to gold, silver, and stone, claiming that the former is more corruptible than the latter. For according to strict reasoning, no incorruptible thing is "more incorruptible" than another, nor is one corruptible thing "more corruptible" than another. But even if it were more corruptible, we shall say this: if it is possible for matter, which underlies all qualities, to change its qualities, how is it not also possible for the flesh of Jesus to have changed its qualities and become such as was fitting for one living in the ether and the highest regions, no longer <margin>* of flesh.</margin> pouring out the traits of * fleshly weakness and those things which Celsus called "foul"—doing so in a way that is hardly philosophical? For that which is properly "foul" is such because of vice. By the nature of the body, it is not foul. <margin>* The nature of the body is to have [the capacity for] foulness.</margin> For the * nature [of the body] is either the producer of foulness or it possesses the evil of foulness. 

Then, whispering a potential defense from our side, he says regarding the change of his body: "But having laid these things aside, he will surely be a God. Why then not rather Aesculapius, and Dionysus, and Hercules?" We shall reply: what so great thing did Aesculapius, or Dionysus, or Hercules perform? And whom can they point to as having been improved in character and made better by their words and life, so that they should become Gods? For having read many histories about them, let us see if they purified anyone from licentiousness, or injustice, or folly, <margin>* such a thing.</margin> or cowardice. And if no * such thing should be found in them, then perhaps Celsus would be right to compare the aforementioned to Jesus. But if it is clear—even if some better things are reported of them—that they are recorded to have done myriad things contrary to right reason, how is it still more reasonable that they, rather than Jesus, became Gods after laying aside the mortal body? 

After this he says of us: "that we laugh at those who worship Zeus, since his tomb is shown in Crete; and yet we nonetheless worship the one <margin>* such a thing.</margin> from the tomb, not knowing how and why the Cretans do * this." See then that in these matters...

<column-break/>

...the human soul in him, not only by communication with that Word, but even by union and mixture, assumed so much of divinity that it became God. But if it offends anyone that we say these things even of his body, let him go to the writings of the Greeks who discourse on matter, which, since it properly lacks all quality, puts on whatever kind the creator wishes to wrap around it, and frequently, having laid aside the former ones, assumes others and still better ones. If their opinion is sound, what wonder is it if the mortal quality of Jesus's body, by the providence of God so willing it, was changed into an ethereal and divine quality? 

But it is not as Celsus argues with dialectical sharpness, comparing the human flesh of Jesus with gold, silver, and marble, on the grounds that the former are more corruptible; for if it is investigated exactly, neither is an incorruptible thing more incorruptible than another incorruptible thing, nor a corruptible more corruptible than a corruptible. Nevertheless, let it be that they are more corruptible; we will say even to this: if it is possible for matter, which receives any qualities whatsoever, to change qualities, is it not also possible for the flesh of Jesus, its qualities having been changed, to have been rendered such as was fitting to dwell in the highest ether, retaining nothing of the innate carnal weakness, and of those things which Celsus calls "impure"—and that with little philosophy? For that is properly impure which is contaminated by vice. But the nature of the body is not impure, for the nature of the body and of impurity are not the same, but it has malice as the mother of its impurity. 

Then, hinting at what might be answered by us, he says of the change of the body, that "having laid aside weaknesses he will certainly be God; why then not rather Aesculapius, and Bacchus, and Hercules?" We shall say, what so distinguished a thing did Aesculapius do, or Bacchus, or Hercules? Who by their doctrine or example was made a hair's breadth more corrected, so that they ought to be referred to among the Gods? Let us see in the histories which exist concerning their deeds, whether they were pure from lust, injustice, timidity, or foolishness. If nothing of these shall be found in the character of those men, Celsus's speech making them equal to Jesus will not be vain; but if it is well known—even if some better things are reported of them—that nevertheless innumerable things done by them not rightly are remembered; how do you say that these men, more probably than Jesus, became Gods after leaving the mortal body? After this he objects to us, that we laugh at the worshippers of Jupiter, whose sepulcher is shown among the Cretans, yet we ourselves worship him who was buried, not knowing why the Cretans do that. See how in this part...

He further argues that Jesus is superior to Greek heroes like Hercules and Aesculapius because his life and teachings actually improved the moral character of his followers.</summary>

[Left Column]

On one hand, he <note>Celsus</note> acts as an advocate for the Cretans and for Jove <note>Latin: *Jovi*, referring to Zeus</note>, and his tomb, dragging the whole matter toward figurative interpretations by which the fable of Jove might stand. But against us, he turns it into a crime that, while we admit our Jesus was buried, we say he rose again from the tomb—something the Cretans do not add concerning Jove. Therefore, since you seem to plead the cause for the tomb of the Cretan Jove while saying *that we do not know why the Cretans do this*, we shall answer that even Callimachus of Cyrene—who examined almost all the histories of the Greeks and all their poems—knew of no "tropology" <note>figurative or metaphorical interpretation</note> in those things reported about Jove’s tomb. For this reason, in a certain distich written in praise of Jove, he accuses the Cretans thus, saying:

> *Cretans are always liars; for they have built*
> *Thy tomb, O King: but thou art not dead, for thou livest forever.*

And yet, he whose words these are—*but thou art not dead, for thou livest forever*—although he denies Jove was buried in Crete, nevertheless tells of the beginning of death for Jove. For an earthly birth is the beginning of death. Thus he speaks:

> *Rhea bore thee among the Parrhasians.*

Now, since he denied he was born in Crete because of his tomb there, he ought to have considered that it necessarily follows that one who was born in Arcadia has also died. For so says the same Callimachus:

> *Jove, they say thou wast born on the Idaean mountains,*
> *Jove, they say in Arcadia. Which father lies?*
> *Cretans are always liars, etc.*

We have been led to bring these things forward by the speech of Celsus, who, being little fair toward Jesus, agrees indeed that he died and was buried, but thinks it a fiction that he rose from the dead—even though this was predicted by so many Prophets and is established by many signs that he appeared alive again. Celsus goes on, and taking what is said about the doctrine of Jesus by a few who are considered Christians—not the more prudent ones, as he thinks, but the more unrefined—he says these are the precepts of our men: *"Let no educated man approach, no wise man, no prudent man (for these are considered evils among us); but if anyone is unlearned, foolish, or an infant, let him come boldly."* By openly confessing that such people are worthy of their God, they clearly declare (he says) that they only wish and are only able to win over the stupid, the low-born, the senseless, slaves, silly women, and little children. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 3.

...to refute, so that he may stop the mouths of those who speak vanities and deceive good minds through his own wisdom. And just as he prefers a man of one wife over one who marries again in the selection of Bishops <note>original: "Episcoporum"</note>, the blameless over the blameworthy, the sober over the opposite, the temperate over the intemperate, and one adorned with orderly character over the even slightly disorderly: so he wishes the one to be properly appointed to the Bishopric to have the faculty of teaching and the power to stop the mouths of those who contradict. What reason, then, moved Celsus to charge us as if we were accustomed to say, *“let no educated man approach, no wise man, no prudent man”? On the contrary, let the educated, or the wise, or the prudent approach, whoever wishes: but nonetheless let the unlearned, and the foolish, and the unrefined, and the infant also approach.* For to such as these, if they approach, the word of God promises a cure, making them all fit for God. Moreover, that other claim is false: *“that only the fatuous, the lazy, the senseless, slaves, women, and children are sought after by the preachers of the divine word.”* Indeed, the preaching calls even these, so that it may make them better; but it also calls those far superior to them: since Christ is the Savior of all men, especially of the faithful, whether they be intelligent or more simple; and he is the propitiation before the Father for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world. It would be superfluous, therefore, for us to wish to respond further to such sayings of Celsus; otherwise, what evil is there in being learned in the best disciplines, in having cultivated one's natural talent, or in being and being held to be prudent? How do these things hinder the knowledge of God? Do they not rather lead to the attainment of the truth? True education <note>original: "eruditio"</note> is therefore not a bad thing, since it is a path to virtue; but no wise man, not even a Greek, counts those having erroneous dogmas among the educated. Again, no one would fail to admit that it is good to study the best disciplines: but which disciplines, pray, do we call the best, if not those that are true and which rouse one toward virtue? Prudence also is an excellent thing—though not necessarily "seeming" prudent, as Celsus says. And so far are education, the study of the best disciplines, and prudence from hindering the knowledge of God, that they even assist it: which is more fittingly said by us than by Celsus, especially if he should be detected to be an Epicurean <note>Origen frequently accuses Celsus of being an Epicurean (a philosophy often associated with atheism or materialism in this period) to undermine his religious critiques.</note>. Let us now see what he adds next in these words: *“We certainly see these market-place charlatans displaying those most celebrated tricks of theirs, not in the assemblies of prudent men—for they would never dare that—but wherever they notice a crowd of youths, house-slaves, and stu—”*

How then does Celsus reasonably charge us, as if we say:

And it is a lie that “the teachers of the divine Word wish to persuade only the silly, the low-born, the senseless, and slaves, and women, and children.” For the Word calls even these, in order to make them better, but it also calls those who differ greatly from them; since Christ is the Savior of all men, and especially of the faithful, whether they be intelligent or simpler, and he is the propitiation before the Father for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for the whole world.
<margin>1 John 2:2</margin>
> It is therefore superfluous to wish to defend ourselves further against the words of Celsus which run as follows: “For what else is bad about being educated, and having cared for the best discourses, and being and appearing to be prudent? What indeed does this hinder regarding the knowledge of God? How would it not rather be a benefit, and the means through which one might reach the truth?” Now, to be truly educated is not an evil, for education leads toward virtue; but as for counting those who hold mistaken dogmas among the educated, not even the wise among the Greeks would say that. Again, anyone would agree that to have cared for the best discourses is a good thing; but which shall we call the best discourses, except those that are true and exhort one toward virtue? But also to be prudent is a beautiful thing; though not necessarily to “appear” so, which is what Celsus said. And education, and caring for the best discourses, and being prudent do not hinder the knowledge of God, but even cooperate with it. And it is more fitting for us to say this than for Celsus; especially if he is refuted as being an Epicurean. But let us look at the following words themselves:
> “But we certainly see those most notorious performers in the marketplaces showing off and gathering a crowd, who would never enter a gathering of prudent men, nor would they dare to show off their own wares among them; but wherever they see youths, and a crowd of house-slaves, and foolish men—”

<summary>Origen defends Christianity against Celsus's claim that the faith only targets the ignorant, arguing that while the Gospel is open to the simple, it highly values education and prudence when directed toward virtue. He asserts that Christian leadership (Bishops) requires the highest intellectual and moral standards.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

“...crowd of [your own] people, there to push themselves forward and **show themselves off**.” See now in these matters also how he slanders us, likening us to those in the marketplaces who display the most infamous wonders and collect a crowd. What "infamous" things do we actually bring forward? Or what do we do similar to them? We who, through both the readings <note>Scripture readings</note> and the explanations of those readings, exhort people toward piety toward the God of all things and the virtues that sit as companions to her; turning them away from contempt for the divine and from all things done contrary to right reason. Even the philosophers would surely pray to gather so many listeners to words encouraging them toward what is noble. This is exactly what some of the **Cynics** <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophers known for their public, often provocative, street preaching</note> have done, speaking publicly to whoever happens to be there. Shall they then say that these men too—who do not assemble those considered "educated" but call upon and gather listeners from the common folk—are similar to those in the marketplaces who display infamous things and collect crowds? But neither Celsus, nor anyone who thinks like him, will accuse those who, out of apparent love for humanity, stir up discourse even for the unlearned masses. If those men are not to be accused for doing this, let us see if Christians do not do even better in calling the multitudes toward **moral excellence**. For the philosophers who speak publicly do not scrutinize their listeners; anyone who wishes stands and listens. But Christians, as much as they are able, having first tested the souls of those who wish to hear them and having privately "enchanted" <note>original: προεπάσαντες / incantatos; likely referring to preliminary catechetical instruction</note> them, only introduce them once they seem sufficiently moved toward the desire to live well. At that point, they introduce them, having created a separate * **rank** <margin>* of ranks</margin> for those who are just beginning and being introduced, who have not yet received the **symbol of purification** <note>The "symbol of purification" refers to Baptism</note>; and another rank for those who have, as far as possible, demonstrated their intention to desire nothing other than what Christians approve. Among these, some are appointed to inquire into the lives and conduct of those approaching, so that they may prevent those who commit forbidden acts from coming to their common assembly; but receiving those who are not such with their whole soul, they make them better day by day. And what a discipline they have regarding those who sin, especially the lustful, whom they drive out from the community—those whom Celsus says are like the men in the marketplaces displaying infamous things! The venerable school of the **Pythagoreans** used to build **cenotaphs** <note>Empty tombs built to signify that a member who abandoned the philosophy was "dead" to the community</note> for those who fell away from their philosophy, considering them to have become dead. [Christians] likewise mourn as lost and dead to God those who have been overcome by licentiousness or any absurdity; as dead, they lament...

<column-break/>

...crowd of your own, there to push themselves in, and there to sell themselves. Consider how here also he constructs a calumny against us, whom he compares with peddlers babbling speakable and unspeakable nonsense. But what [nonsense] exactly? Or what do we do that is similar? We who, by readings and their interpretations, exhort the people to piety toward God, the Best and Greatest, and the other virtues that are the inseparable companions of piety; and we lead them away from contempt for the deity, and from other passions that wander outside the rule of reason. Indeed, even philosophers should wish that they could rouse so many listeners with speeches calling them to honesty, which has been done by certain of the **Cynics** especially, who discourse publicly before a chance audience. Will they then compare these men too—who do not dispute before gatherings of the learned, as it seems, but seek out audiences for themselves from the crossroads—with the peddlers showing off their loquacity in the circles of the marketplaces? But neither Celsus nor his like find fault with what they consider a duty of humanity: to instruct the unlearned common folk with speeches. But if the philosophers are not to be blamed while they do these things, let us see whether the Christians do not far better provoke the plebeian multitude toward honesty? For those [philosophers] discoursing openly among the common herd of men are not careful in discerning their listeners, but anyone who wishes stands by and listens indiscriminately. Christians, however, as much as they can, pre-examine the minds of those desiring to hear them; and first having been privately "enchanted" <note>instructed</note>, before they are received into the assembly, when they seem to have progressed so far as to be desirous of an honest life, then at last they introduce them, with **distinct ranks**: one of those recently admitted and not yet having attained the symbol of lustration <note>Baptism</note>; the other of those who, as much as is in them, demonstrate that their purpose is to will and feel nothing other than with the Christians. Among these, some are put in charge to inquire into the life and manners of those who are admitted, so that they may keep the candidates of religion who do forbidden things away from their assemblies: the others, unlike these, they receive from the heart, and make them better by daily advances. Now, how severe is the discipline toward those who sin, especially those contaminated by lust, whom our people reject from their communion, however much Celsus makes them similar to babbling peddlers? And indeed the venerable school of the **Pythagoreans** placed **Cenotaphs** for the deserters of their discipline, surely because they held them for dead: these [Christians] truly mourn as lost and dead to God those who, by lust or some other [vice]...

For we, as much as we are able, take pains in every way that our assembly consists of prudent men; and whatever we have that is excellent and divine, we only then bring forth into the midst of popular discourses when there is an abundance of wise listeners present. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

For from what prudent fathers, or from what masters teaching serious things, do we alienate young children and women? Moreover, we restrain adolescent boys who are itching for lust, not only by reminding them how shameful it is to indulge in libido, but also how much danger threatens the soul therefrom, and what punishments await such things. Furthermore, who are those teachers whom we call crazy and out of their minds, whom Celsus defends as teaching better things than we do? Unless perhaps he thinks those are excellent instructors of women—and by no means crazy—who invite them to superstition and obscene spectacles; and that those are not out of their minds who carry and sweep away youth into all the disgraces which we know are very often committed by them. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

...of philosophical doctrines, with all our power, we invite men to our own piety, demonstrating its excellence and its purity. But since Celsus has presented a charge, asking why we do not do this, but instead "call only the foolish," we would say to him: if you were accusing us of turning away from philosophy those who were already occupied with it, you would not be speaking the truth, though your argument might have some plausibility. But now, when you say that "we turn away those who approach good teachers," show us teachers other than the teachers of philosophy, or those who teach something useful. But nothing of this sort is shown. We say that those who live according to the Word of God <note>Greek: *Logos*</note> will be blessed—freely and with boldness of speech, and not in secret—looking always to Him, and performing everything they do as if before God as their spectator. From what source are these the lessons of wool-workers, shoemakers, laundry-men, and the most uneducated rustics? He will not be able to justify this. "But those who, according to Celsus, are like the wool-workers in houses, and similar to shoemakers and laundry-men and the most uneducated rustics, in the presence of a father and teachers (he says) will not even wish to speak, nor will they be able to explain anything good to the children." And to this we shall say: what kind of father do you mean, O man, and what kind of teacher? If you mean one who displays virtue, and shrinks from vice, and embraces the better things—know that with great confidence, as being well-pleasing to such a noble person, we will speak our truths to the children. But if we remain silent in the presence of a father <margin>\* who is prejudiced.</margin> \* who is prejudiced against virtue and nobility, and who teaches things contrary to your own reason, do not bring this as a charge against us; for you do not charge us reasonably. For you yourself, when you wish to impart the beginnings of philosophy to the young and to sons whose fathers consider philosophy a rustic and useless thing, would do so as a side-teacher, not in the presence of such base fathers; but wishing to separate those persuaded by you toward philosophy from their wicked fathers, you would watch for opportunities so that the words of philosophy might reach the young. And we shall say the same regarding teachers: for if we look at teachers who teach the indecencies of comedy, and the licentious parts of iambic poetry, and whatever other things neither benefit the speaker nor the listeners—unless they know how to hear poems philosophically and to select from each what contributes to the benefit of the young—in doing this, we are not ashamed to admit the matter at hand. But if you point out to me teachers trained in philosophy and exercised in philosophy, we will not turn the young away from them, but we will try...

<column-break/>

...imbued with philosophical decrees, we recall them to our religion as much as we can, commending to them its sincerity and excellence. Because Celsus denies this, saying *that only fools are enticed by us*, I would say to him: If you objected to us that we lead away those already occupied with the decrees of philosophy, although it would not be true, it would perhaps be plausible. But now, since you say *that through us good youths are alienated from their instructors, so that they listen to them less*, produce other teachers besides philosophers or professors of useful arts. But you will be able to produce no such thing. Furthermore, we promise blessedness freely, not secretly, to those who regulate their lives according to divine precepts, and who always have God before their eyes, and desire whatever they do to be approved by His eyes. Is this the discipline of wool-workers, shoemakers, laundry-men, and the most illiterate rustics? But he will not be able to show this. Furthermore, he slanders *that these sedentary workers, an uncultivated and rustic race of men accustomed to chatter in their shops and workshops, when the heads of families or teachers happen to be present, neither wish nor are able to interpret anything good to the boys.* We will respond: Hey you! What teachers are you telling us about, what heads of families? If they are students of virtue, shrinking from vices, and desirous of better things, know that in the presence of such men we will intrepidly speak our message to the boys, as they will be our judges and praisers. But if we are silent in the presence of a father who is unjust to honesty and virtue, and in the presence of teachers who are adversaries of sounder doctrine, that truly is not to be made a crime for the undeserving: since you yourself, when about to deliver the mysteries of philosophy to youths whose parents are despisers of such doctrines, are not going to do this in the presence of evil fathers, but having seized an opportunity, you will instruct the sons privately. The same reasoning applies to instructors: for if we turn youth away from those teaching comedies and iambic obscenities, and whatever other things neither make the teacher himself better nor profit the listeners—unless one understands poems philosophically and interprets individual parts for the utility of the young—we are not ashamed to confess these things. But if you give me instructors teaching and practicing philosophy, we will not deter the youth from such men: but when they have been in the schools of these...

# Book 3. ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

After this, Celsus, touched by a consciousness of his own rather bitter insolence, speaks as if making an excuse: *“That I do not charge anything more bitterly than the truth demands, it is easy to guess; for to other mysteries, those about to be initiated are usually summoned by a herald thus: 'Whosoever is pure of hands and wise of speech'; and again elsewhere: 'Whosoever is pure from every crime, and whose soul is conscious of no evil, and whosoever has lived well and justly'; and these things they proclaim, promising sacred rites of purification. Now, by contrast, let us hear whom these people call: 'Whosoever is a sinner, whosoever is foolish, whosoever is like a child, in short, whosoever is miserable, him the Kingdom of God will receive.' Since we are not ignorant of this distinction, we first call those in need of healing, so that having heard the salutary doctrine, sinners may learn not to sin, the foolish may acquire understanding, the childlike a manly mind, and finally the miserable may find happiness—or rather blessedness, to speak more properly. # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Those who possess a better conscience desire that the things preached concerning the rewards to be given by God to the virtuous be true; thus, they assent to this doctrine more easily than the wicked, who are held back by a conscience burdened with evils. To those who contemplate that universal judgment, their conscience threatens a well-deserved penalty. Nor is that terror of the final judgment, before which all men shall stand, set forth without cause: for sometimes even the most deeply lost are seized by a love for this doctrine, invited by the sole hope of repentance <note>original: "pœnitentiæ"</note>, however much they may be pulled back by an inveterate habit of sinning. Being imbued with malice, they are not easily able to leave their former ways and apply themselves to a more corrected life.

Celsus also seems to have understood this in some way, for as his oration proceeds, he speaks thus: *“Now it is clearly evident that vices which are innate and confirmed by habit cannot be corrected even by punishment, much less by showing mercy; for to change nature entirely is extremely difficult. But those who do not sin are participants in a better life.”* In this, however, Celsus seems to me to be greatly mistaken, because he does not grant a perfect transformation to those who are sinners by nature and habit, thinking that they are not curable even by penalties. For it is clear enough that we are all sinners by nature, and some indeed also by habit; yet not all are incapable of a perfect change for the better. For there are found both in all the sects of philosophy and in Holy Scripture those who, having changed their life for the better, have progressed so far that they can serve as an example to others.

Something of this sort is even told of certain heroes, such as Hercules and Ulysses; and in later ages of Socrates; and just yesterday or the day before <note>A Latin idiom "nudiusfertiùs" meaning very recently</note> of Musonius <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher known as the "Roman Socrates."</note>. Therefore, Celsus has not only lied against us, saying, *“it is clearly evident that vices innate and confirmed by habit are not corrected even by chastisement and the restraint of penalties;”* but he also speaks against those seriously devoted to philosophy, who do not despair of recovering virtue <note>original: "virtutem"</note> as a thing impossible for man. But even if we grant that he has sufficiently proved his point to us, nevertheless, if we listen to his words with fair ears, we shall find them to be unsound. For he said *“vices innate and confirmed by habit are not corrected even by punishments”*: the sense of which words we have refuted as best we could. Yet it is possible that he wished to say there are certain crimes and those driven to ruin, whom—if a most wicked habit is added to their native proclivity—no one

<column-break/>

those who are conscious of better things in themselves, praying that the proclamations regarding the recompense from God to the better sort be true, more readily agree with what is said, compared to those who have lived altogether wickedly. These latter are prevented by their very conscience from imagining [the truth], because they will be punished by the Judge of all with a punishment that befits one who has committed such great sins. And it is not contrary to right reason to fear the Judge of all. But sometimes even the utterly destroyed wish to accept the word concerning punishment because of the hope found in repentance; though they are persistently stained, and their habits prevent them from moving toward better things, as if they were being mastered by malice and were no longer able to depart from it easily toward a settled life according to right reason.

And Celsus perceived this, I know not how, saying in the following passages such things as: “And indeed it is clear to everyone, I suppose, that those who are prone to sin by nature and habit, no one could entirely transform, not even by punishing them, much less by showing mercy; for to change nature completely is very difficult. But the sinless are sharers of a better life.” And in these matters Celsus seems to me to be quite mistaken, not granting to those prone to sin and accustomed to doing so a complete transformation; he thinks they cannot be healed even by punishments. For it is clearly seen that we are all prone to sin by nature, and some are not only prone but also accustomed to sinning. But not all men are closed off from a complete transformation; for there are in all the philosophical schools, and according to the Divine Word, those recorded to have changed so much that they themselves are set forth as examples of the best life. And some of the heroes are cited, such as Hercules and Odysseus; and of those later, Socrates; and of those who lived yesterday and the day before, Musonius.

Therefore, Celsus lied not only against us, saying, “It is clear to everyone, I suppose, that those prone to sin and accustomed to it could be led by no one, not even those punishing them, to a complete transformation for the better”; but also against those who have nobly practiced philosophy and have not despaired of the attainment of virtue as being possible for men. But, even if he did not wish to present the whole matter with precision, nonetheless, listening to him with a fair mind, we shall even convict him of not <margin>* speaking</margin> healthily. For if “no one could entirely transform those prone to sin and accustomed to it, even by punishing them,” we have overturned the meaning understood from the text as far as we are able. It is likely he wished to show this: that those [inclined] toward such sins, and moved by

<margin>the most destructive [impulses], being not only prone by nature but also accustomed, no one could entirely transform, not even by punishing them,</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

-> [Response] to what has been said. <-

For according to us, God can do all things; but in being able to do all things, He does not depart from being God, nor from being good, nor from being wise. But Celsus says (as if not understanding in what sense it is said that God can do all things) "that He will not will anything unjust," implying that He is *able* to do what is unjust, but simply does not *will* it. We, however, say that just as that which is naturally sweet cannot, by the very fact of its being sweet, produce bitterness—unless it acts against its own nature—and just as that which is naturally light-giving cannot, by being light, produce darkness; so also God cannot act unjustly. For the power of acting unjustly is contrary to His divinity and to every power inherent in it. If any existing thing is able to act unjustly, it is because it has a nature capable of injustice; but God has it in His nature to be utterly unable to act unjustly.

This would be most unjust. For according to us, God relieves no wicked man who has not changed his mind toward virtue, and He casts off no one who is already good. Moreover, He does not relieve or show mercy to anyone simply because He is "judged" (to use the common term for mercy); rather, those who are exceedingly angry with themselves for their sins, so as to mourn and lament themselves as lost because of their deeds, and who display a noteworthy change—these God accepts for the sake of their repentance <term>metanoia: a transformative change of heart and mind</term>. For virtue gives life to such people, desiring to dwell in their souls and having cast out the wickedness that previously occupied them. To this we might say: Who among us, O Greeks, are the ones who do not see? Therefore, we do not say that those who see sharply have eye diseases or are blind; rather, we say that those who have grown weary in ignorance of God and turn toward temples, statues, and so-called sacred rites, have a blinded mind. How can self-control and temperance be practiced from a wicked disposition, or the spirit of giving and community? Rather, this fear toward the Divine—to which the Word calls as something useful for the many who are not yet able to see that which is choice-worthy for its own sake, and to choose it as the greatest good and beyond every promise—is what this <margin>* he/himself.</margin> man himself [possesses].

...that honor is rendered to true gods through works of this kind, often by the most worthless of craftsmen. After this, he compares the teacher to one suffering in the eyes, and likewise the learners to those having eyes corrupted by inflammation: and he says that among such people *that man* speaks against those seeing sharply, as if they were *blind*. Let us therefore ask the Greeks, who are those not seeing? Surely those who are not warned by such magnificent beauty of the world and of the things encompassed by this circuit, that the founder of all is to be looked up to; that He alone is to be adored, admired, and worshipped; and nothing besides Him, or with equal honor to Him. **For to compare things that are to be matched by no proclamation with Him who far excels every created creature, is truly the work of those blind in the eyes of the mind.** Therefore, we do not cast the reproach of dullness or blindness upon those seeing sharply, but those who, ignorant of the celestial divinity, wallow among temples and images and festivals recurring in fixed months, we say are blinded in soul: especially if to their impiety is added a life most lost in luxury and lusts, having no regard for honesty, but serving only shameful desires. And after so many atrocious accusations which he has hurled against us, he wishes to seem to have many other things to turn into a crime, which he nevertheless passes over in silence. For thus he speaks: *These things are worthy of accusation, and others of that kind, lest I perceive them individually, and indeed that they themselves speak ill of God, by enticing men with the vainest hope, and teaching them to despise better things, as if it were better to let those things go.* To this also there is no lack of a response taken from the effective powers of Christian doctrine: that wicked men do not so readily submit themselves to it as do the simple, and (so to speak) the rustic. For these, terrified by the dread of the denounced punishments—which most moves and exhorts them to be without those things for whose sake they are brought—endeavor to devote themselves entirely to the Christian religion, and are so restrained by this doctrine that, fearing the eternal penalties declared through it, they despise whatever tortures and labors men have devised against them, and death itself, which no wise man would say falls upon a bad man. For who that is bad by purpose will exercise prudence, and temperance, or liberality, and beneficence, and the fear of God, to which as something useful for many the divine Scripture calls those who are not yet able to discern what that thing is which is to be sought for its own sake; and to choose the same as the highest good and greater than every promise;

He asserts that the fear of eternal punishment is a useful tool for moral reformation, leading even "simple" people to live lives of virtue and courage.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 3.

...against Celsus, who has philosophized concerning the immortality or the continued existence of the soul. Regarding those with whom we hold certain things in common, we shall demonstrate at a more opportune time that the future blessed life will belong only to those who live according to the piety of Jesus, and who maintain a sincere and pure devotion toward the Creator of all things, unmixed with anything mortal <note>original: "θνητὸν" / "profanis religionibus" - Origen contrasts the eternal nature of God with the "mortal" or "profane" nature of pagan idols</note>. 

Let anyone who wishes point out and compare our teachings—which we hold before God in Christ (that is, in the Word, Wisdom, and every virtue)—with any "better" path they claim we persuade men to reject. We promise a final blessedness to those who have lived blamelessly and purely, having taken up an undivided and unattached love toward the God of all things; a blessedness that will be met as a gift from God. Let them compare this with the final goal promised by every sect of philosophers among the Greeks or barbarians, or any mysterious promise; and let them show if any of the others have a goal truly better than ours. Let them show that their path follows as the truth, while ours is unsuited to the gift of God or to those who have lived well—or that these things were not spoken by the Divine Spirit filling the souls of the pure Prophets. 

Let anyone who wishes show that there are arguments more powerful and universally acknowledged among all men than those demonstrated to be divine and announced through divine inspiration <note>original: "θεοφορίας" - literally "God-bearing" or "divine breathing"</note>. It is immediately apparent (if it be not offensive to say so) that nothing better can even be conceived than to entrust oneself to the God over all, and to devote oneself to a teaching that turns away from everything else and leads us—through the ensouled and living Word, who is both living Wisdom and the Son of God—to the God over all. 

But since a sufficient amount has been outlined in these pages and in this third volume of our dictated response to the treatise of Celsus, let us end our discourse here. In the following books, we shall continue the struggle against the subsequent writings of Celsus.

### BOOK 4.

In the three preceding books, holy Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Alexandria (d. c. 251), Origen's wealthy patron who provided the stenographers and copyists for this massive undertaking.</note>, we have covered whatever we thought necessary to say against the writings of Celsus; we now proceed to the fourth, having called upon God through Christ. <meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s philosophical attacks on Christianity, specifically addressing the problem of divine intervention and human free will.</meta>

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

He says that Christ descended into this life to inspect the affairs of men. Then, as if this reason for the descent had been given to him by others, he objects from the opposite side: *Did he not know all things?* Then, as if having received the answer *that he did know,* he moves another question: *Therefore he knew indeed, but did not correct, or was he unable to correct by divine power?* In all of this he speaks foolishly. For God, in every age, descending into holy souls through his Word <note>original: "verbum suum" / "λόγου". Origen refers to the Logos or Divine Reason.</note> and making them friends of God and Prophets, corrects all who obey; just as since the birth of Christ, he amends through Christian teaching—not, however, those who are unwilling, but those who betake themselves to a better life pleasing to God. 

Furthermore, I do not know what kind of "correction" Celsus desires when he goes on to ask: *Therefore was it not possible to correct by divine power, unless someone born for this purpose were sent?* Perhaps that man demanded that God, appearing present to men, should at once take away all malice and insert virtue in its place. One might rightly doubt whether such a thing could even happen. But suppose it were possible: where then would be our will? Where would be that praiseworthy belief in the truth, or that commendable turning away from falsehood? 

But even if we grant that this were possible and even fitting, by the same logic someone like Celsus might ask: *Why rather did he not make men such by divine power that they did not even need correction, being good and perfect from the very beginning, with no malice admitted?* Such thoughts easily creep into the minds of the unlearned, but not into those who consider the nature of things; for unless virtue is spontaneous <note>meaning: voluntary or of one's own free will</note>, it will not even be virtue. 

Truly, these matters require a specific treatise, concerning which many things are found even in the discussions of the Greeks regarding providence <note>original: "providentia" / "προνοίας"</note>. They would never say such things as Celsus: *He knew, but did not correct, or he was unable to correct by divine power.* We also, in many places, have discussed these things as much as we were able; and the divine Scriptures explain such matters, provided a suitable reader approaches them. 

Yet these words, with which Celsus deals with us and with the Jews, can be reflected back against him in this way: Hey you! Does the supreme God know the affairs of men or does he not? But if you establish that God exists, and providence exists—as your writings suggest—it necessarily follows that he knows. If he knows, why does he not correct them? Unless perhaps a reason is demanded from us as to why he does not correct; while from you—who hide your Epicureanism <note>The Epicureans were often accused of believing God existed but did not care about human affairs.</note> and feign an acknowledgment of providence—it is not permitted to inquire: Why does God know human affairs, yet not—

<column-break/>

<margin>himself</margin>
—he says that, *In order to learn what is among men, Christ visits life.* Then, as if some had said, *"In order to learn what is among men,"* he <margin>himself</margin> retorts to this: *"For does he not know all things?"* Then, as it is assumed that he knows, he attacks again, saying: *"Does he then know, but not <margin>correct</margin> correct, or is it not possible for him to correct by divine power?"* And all these things he says quite simply. For God, always passing through his own Word into holy souls throughout the generations, and preparing friends of God and prophets, corrects those who hear what is said. And in the visitation of Christ, he corrects through the word of Christianity—not those who are unwilling, but those who have chosen the better life and what is pleasing to God. 

And I do not know what kind of correction Celsus wishes to happen, when he attacks saying, *"Is it not possible for him by divine power to correct, unless he sends someone naturally for this purpose?"* For did he want men to be transformed by God—who would have taken away wickedness all at once and implanted virtue—for the correction to happen? Another person might ask if such a thing were consistent or possible for nature. But we would say, let it be so, and that it is possible. Where then is our "what is up to us" <note>original: "τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν". A technical term in Greek philosophy for free will or moral agency.</note>? And where is the praiseworthy assent to the truth? Or the rejection and turning away from falsehood? 

But even if it were granted once that this is both possible and becomingly done, why would someone not rather ask from the beginning—saying something analogous to Celsus—that it was not possible for God by divine power to make men not even needing correction, but straightway upright and perfect, with wickedness having no substance from the start? These things might be able to snatch away the unlearned and senseless, but not the one who looks into the nature of things: for if you take away the voluntary from virtue, you take away its very essence. 

There is need of a whole treatise on these things; about which not a few things have been said by the Greeks in their works on providence—who would not have said what Celsus set forth, saying, *"He knows indeed, but does not correct, or it is not possible for him by divine power to correct."* And we also in many places have spoken about these things according to our ability; and the divine words have presented it to those able to hear. But it shall be said now, regarding what Celsus brought against us and the Jews, to him: "Look here, does God know the things among men, or does he not know?" But if you grant that there is a God and a providence, as your book indicates, it is necessary for him to know. And if he knows, why does he not correct? Or is it necessary for us to defend why he does not correct while knowing, but for you—not quite revealing the Epicurean through your book, but pretending to know providence—it shall not likewise be said: Why, since God knows all things among men, does he not <margin>correct</margin> <margin>himself</margin>

<summary>Origen defends the Christian concept of divine intervention against Celsus, arguing that God corrects humanity through the Word and human free will rather than by overriding human nature. He asserts that virtue must be voluntary to be meaningful, rejecting Celsus's suggestion that God should simply "implant" goodness.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

Does he reform them, or by divine power rid all men of vice? But we are not ashamed to say that he is always sending those who will act as reformers; for the arguments that exhort men to the best things—God having given them—are present among humanity. Now, among those ministering to God, there are many differences, and there are few who entirely and purely champion the cause of truth and work toward a complete reformation; such men were Moses and the prophets. But in addition to all these, the reformation through Jesus was great, as he did not wish for only those in one corner of the inhabited world to be healed, but, as far as depended on him, those everywhere; for he came as a savior of all men. After this, the most noble Celsus, having taken some occasion I know not where, raises a doubt against us as if we were saying, "that God himself comes down to men." He thinks it follows from this that God must leave his own seat <note>throne or dwelling place</note>. For he does not know the power of God, and that "the spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world," and "that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice."

<margin>Jeremiah 23:24</margin>

<margin>Acts 17:28</margin>
Paul also taught in his speech to the Athenians. Therefore, even if the God of the universe descends by his own power with Jesus into the life of men, and even if the Word who was "in the beginning with God,"

<margin>John 1:1</margin>
being himself also God, comes to us; he does not become "out of his seat," nor does he desert his own throne—as if one place were made empty of him and another filled which previously did not have him. The deity of God visits by power through whom he wills, and in whomsoever he finds a place, without changing location, nor leaving a place itself empty and filling another.

<margin>* that is</margin>
* For even if we say that he "leaves" one and "fills" another, we would not be declaring this concerning a physical place; rather, we would say that a wicked soul, poured out in vice, is "deserted" by God, while the soul of one who wishes to live according to virtue—or who is making progress, or already living by it—we declare to be "filled" by or participating in the divine spirit. There is no need, therefore, for the descent through Christ, or for the return of God to men, for a greater seat to be deserted and for things here to be changed <insert>disturbed</insert>, as Celsus thinks when he says, "For if you were to change even the smallest thing on earth, all things would be overturned and vanish for you." Now truly, there is also a great variety of God's ministers, with few handling the truth purely in all things and striving for perfect correction, such as were Moses and the Prophets. Beyond all these there approached the great correction through Jesus, the physician not only of one corner of the lands, but of all, as much as in him lies; for the Savior came for all men. Furthermore, having found an occasion from I know not where, the eminent Celsus makes it a matter of controversy, as if we affirmed that *God himself would descend to men; because if that happens, he fears lest he desert his throne there:* for he does not know the power of God, that *the spirit of the Lord fills the orb of the earth*, and he who contains all things has knowledge of the voice: nor does he understand those words, *Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?* nor does he see, that according to the reasoning of Christians, *we all live, move, and are in him*, just as Paul teaches in the speech held to the Athenians. Therefore, whether the God of this universe descends by his power with Jesus into the life of men, or the Word of God, which was in the beginning, and which is itself God, comes to us; he will not lack a seat, nor will he desert it, so that another place becomes empty of him, and another full which before had been empty; but the power and Deity of God proceeds where it wills, and in whomsoever it finds a place, without migration, nor leaving a place empty by its absence, and filling another by its presence. For when we say this is filled, that deserted, it is not to be understood of a place; but we say a bad soul, lost in vices, is deserted by God; but him, who desiring to live with virtue, either profits toward this, or has already attained it, we pronounce to be full of the divine spirit, or a participant. There is no need, therefore, on account of the descent of Christ, or the presence of God among men, for that eminent throne to be deserted, or for anything here to be changed, as Celsus dreams while he speaks thus, *For if you change even the least thing here, all things will fall in ruin.* But if anything is changed in human affairs by the presence of the power of God and the advent of his word to men, we will candidly confess, that he is changed from evil to good, from intemperate to sober, from superstitious to pious, whosoever shall have received the word of God into the hospitality of his soul. But we must also respond to his ridiculous trifles; hear what he says: *“Unless perhaps God was unknown to men, and because he seemed to be in a lower condition, he wished to become known, and to make a trial of those who believe as well as those who disbelieve, just like men who have recently acquired great wealth, who thrust their much and altogether mortal ambition upon God by their own testimony.”* <note>Celsus is comparing God to a "nouveau riche" social climber who shows off his status because he is insecure.</note> Indeed, I confess that God was unknown to wicked men: yet not because he wished to become known as if he lacked anything, but so that, being known, he might deliver the wretched from their miseries. Nor is it a wonder that in certain ages there existed prophets more outstanding in receiving divinity, because they had led a life by far the most upright in one and the same tenor, than even—

—even to the most ridiculous things of Celsus we must nevertheless respond; hear him saying: “Or perhaps, being unknown among men, and appearing then to have less, he wished to be known and to test those who were persuaded and those who disbelieved; just like the newly-rich among men, displaying a great and altogether mortal ambition, they bear witness against God.” We say, therefore, that God, being unknown by wicked men, did not wish to be known because he himself appeared to have less, but because the knowledge of him delivers the one who knows him from misery. But neither wishing to test those who believe or those who disbelieve, he either visits all himself with unutterable and divine power, or he sends his Christ; but so that those who are persuaded and have understood his divinity might be delivered from all misery; and that there might no longer be a place for an excuse for unbelief, as if they had not been persuaded because they had not heard or been taught. What argument then presents itself that we follow the idea that God is, according to us, “like the newly-rich among men, making a display?” For God does not make a display toward us, wishing us to soberly perceive his excellence; but wishing to implant in us the blessedness that comes to us from <margin>* him</margin> knowing him, he busies himself through the coming of Christ and the constant presence of the Word, so that we might take up an intimacy with him. <meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of the philosopher Celsus, specifically addressing the nature of divine judgment and the "conflagration" of the world. Origen is arguing that biblical descriptions of God "descending" or using "fire" are metaphorical rather than literal, physical events.</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 4.

Moses and some of the prophets, who lived in ancient times, did not receive their ideas about the conflagration <note>original: *ekpyrosis* — a Stoic term for the periodic destruction of the world by fire</note> of the world from others. Rather—if one must speak by comparing the timelines—it is others who have misheard them. Failing to accurately grasp what was said by the prophets, these others invented the idea of identical cycles, where things return exactly as they were in their specific qualities and circumstances. We, however, do not attribute floods or conflagrations to cycles and the revolutions of stars. Instead, we say the cause of these events is wickedness spreading ever further, which must be purified by a flood or a fire. 

And if the prophetic voices speak of God "descending"—He who said, <margin>Jeremiah 23:24</margin> *Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord*—God descends figuratively from His own greatness and height when He manages the affairs of men, especially those of the wicked. Just as in common speech we say that teachers "descend" to the level of infants, or that the wise and advanced "descend" to young people who have just begun to crawl toward philosophy—not meaning a physical descent of their bodies—so too, if <margin>Genesis 11:5, 7; 18:21. Exodus 3:8; 19:20. Genesis 17:22. Psalm 46:5.</margin> God is said in the Holy Scriptures to "descend," it is understood in a way analogous to this humble use of the word; and the same applies to "ascending." 

But since Celsus mocks us, saying that we claim "God descends like a torturer bringing fire," he forces us to examine these matters more deeply. Having said a few things—just enough to give the listeners a taste of a defense that clears away Celsus’s mockery against us—we shall turn to what follows. The divine <margin>Deuteronomy 4:24. Daniel 7:10. Malachi 3:2.</margin> Word says that our God is a *consuming fire*, and that a *river of fire* flows before Him; but also that He comes like a *refiner’s fire* and like *fuller’s soap*, so that He may refine His people. <margin>Deuteronomy 9:3.</margin> Therefore, when He is said to be a consuming fire, we ask: what is it appropriate for God to consume? We say that God, like a fire, consumes wickedness and the deeds resulting from it, which are figuratively called <margin>1 Corinthians 3:12</margin> "wood, hay, and straw." Indeed, the wicked man is said to build wood, hay, and straw upon the previously laid rational foundation. Now, if someone can show that the author intended these things differently, and can prove physically that a wicked man builds with actual wood, hay, or straw, then clearly the fire would also be understood as material and perceptible to the senses. But if the works of the wicked are clearly a figure of speech, being called wood, hay, and straw, how is it not immediately <gloss>brought to mind</gloss> <margin>* bringing.</margin> what kind of fire is being received to consume such "wood"? For the Scripture says, <margin>1 Corinthians 3:13</margin> *the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.*

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for scholars.</note>

...that those most ancient men, Moses and certain Prophets, did not take this opinion concerning the burning of the world from others; indeed, if the account of the times is weighed, others rather heard these things incorrectly. Since they held what was said with no certain knowledge, they fashioned identities according to cycles returning in a circle, very similar both in their own qualities and in those things which were accustomed to happen. We, however, do not accept that either floods or burnings are produced by fixed periods and the recursions of stars into the same form of stations; but we refer the cause of these things to the malice of men increased to an immense degree, not to be purged except by flood or fire. 

But if the oracles of the Prophets recognize God descending and saying, *Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?* we accept that as said figuratively. For God descends from His majesty and height whenever He disposes the affairs of men, especially of the evil: and just as common speaking custom says teachers "condescend" to children, and those advanced in philosophy to novice disciples—by no means wishing this to be understood of the body—so if God is said anywhere in Holy Scripture to descend, it must be understood in a like manner, according to the received custom of speaking; as also concerning "ascending." 

But because Celsus censures us, who say *God descends in the manner of a torturer with fire*, and compels us somewhat unseasonably to scrutinize deeper discourses; when we have said a few things, as much as the hearers of this apology (which removes Celsus's derision against us) can taste; we shall return to the rest which follow in order. Divine Scripture says, *our God is a consuming fire; and rivers of fire precede him; he himself also comes like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's herb, that he may refine his people.* Therefore, since he is said to be a consuming fire, let us ask, what is it most fitting to be consumed by God? Truly I would say malice, and whatever its works, which are figuratively named wood, hay, stubble, are consumed by God as if by fire: certainly it is said of the evil man that he builds wood, hay, stubble upon the laid rational foundation. If anyone can teach that these are accepted otherwise by Paul, and that it is to be understood corporally that the evil build wood, hay, stubble: it will also appear that a material and sensible fire is to be understood: but if the speech is evidently figurative, while the works of the evil man are signified by the name of wood, hay, and stubble, how does it happen that it does not immediately occur how the fire is to be accepted, which consumes wood of this kind? *For the fire (says Scripture) shall prove what sort of work each one's is...*

<summary>Origen argues against a literal interpretation of divine fire and God's "descent," explaining that these are metaphors for the spiritual purification of human wickedness rather than physical or cyclical cosmic events.</summary>
