# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

*...of what sort it is: if any man’s work which he has built thereupon remains, he shall receive a reward; if any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss.* <note>original: "si cujus opus superædificatum permanserit..." quoting 1 Corinthians 3:14-15</note> And what else can be called a "burned work" than the work of wickedness? Is not our God, therefore, a *consuming fire*, as we have shown? And he comes as a *refiner’s fire* to refine the rational nature which is full of the "lead" of wickedness and other impure materials that adulterate the golden (so to speak) or silver nature of the soul. Thus, rivers of fire are also said to go before God, abolishing whatever vice is mixed throughout the entire soul. But let this be a sufficient answer to the charge: *This was the reason they said, by error, that God would descend like a torturer with fire.*

Let us see what Celsus brings forward next with a great display of words: *He says, "Let us repeat the argument from a higher level with more proofs. Nothing new will be said, but things long since granted by all. God is good, beautiful, happy, and in the most beautiful and best form. If he descends to men, he must undergo change; he would change from good to evil, from beautiful to ugly, from happy to unhappy, and from the best to the most wicked. Who would choose to be so changed? Certainly, this change and transformation belongs to a mortal man; but it is fitting for an immortal being to remain always in the same state. Therefore, God would never accept such a change."*

To these things it will be a sufficient answer (as it seems to me) if I explain how the "descent" of God to men is understood in the Holy Scriptures. For Him, there is no need for change, as Celsus thinks we believe, nor a turning from good to evil, or from beautiful to ugly, or from happy to unhappy, or from best to worst. For remaining immutable <note>unchanging</note> in His essence, He condescends to human affairs by His arrangement <term>dispensatione: the Greek 'oikonomia', referring to God's plan for managing the world</term> and providence. We certainly learn from the sacred writings that God is immutable, where it is read: *But you are the same*; and, *I am not changed.* <note>quoting Psalm 102:27 and Malachi 3:6</note>

The gods of Epicurus <note>a Greek philosopher who taught that the world is made of atoms and gods are indifferent</note>, however, being composed of atoms and therefore dissolvable into them, have work to do in shaking off those atoms which cause corruption to their bodies. Nor is the God of the Stoics <note>philosophers who believed God was a physical "pneuma" or spirit pervading matter</note> any different; since He is a body, He is sometimes the mind which possesses the whole substance when the universal conflagration <note>the Stoic belief that the universe is periodically consumed by fire</note> occurs; but at other times He exists only in a part of that substance when the ordering of the world takes place. For these thinkers were not able to clearly understand the nature of God—that He is altogether incorruptible, simple, neither composite nor divisible. But that which descended to men was in the form of God, and out of love for the human race, He emptied Himself...

<column-break/>

<margin>Daniel 7:10</margin>
...of what sort it is: *if any man’s work remains, which he has built thereupon, he shall receive a reward; if any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss.* And what work could be said to be burned among these things, other than everything done out of wickedness? Therefore our God is a *consuming fire*, as we have rendered it; and He comes as a *refining fire*, refining the rational nature, which is filled with the lead of wickedness and other impure materials that have clouded the golden (if I may name it so) nature of the soul, or the silver one. And so <margin>these things</margin> rivers of fire are said to be before God, vanishing everything of the wickedness mixed into the whole soul. But indeed, these things are enough regarding the claim: "These things caused them to say, by a mistaken opinion, that God will descend like a torturer bringing fire."

But let us see also what follows; Celsus says, with a great promise, in this manner: "Furthermore," he says, "let us take up the argument from above with more demonstrations. I say nothing new, but things long ago decreed. God is good, and beautiful, and happy, and in the most beautiful and best state. If indeed he comes down to men, he has need of change; and change from good to evil, and from beautiful to ugly, and from happiness to unhappiness, and from the best to the most wicked. Who then would choose such a change? For indeed, it is the nature of the mortal to be altered and reshaped; but for the immortal, to stay according to the same things and in the same way. Therefore, God would not accept even this change."

It seems to me then that the necessary things are said in response to this, by explaining a certain "descent" of God to human affairs mentioned in the Scriptures; in which He has no need of change, as Celsus thinks we say, nor a turning from good to evil, or from beautiful to ugly, or from happiness to unhappiness, or from the best to the most wicked. For remaining unchangeable in essence, He condescends by providence and by His divine plan <term>oikonomia</term> to human affairs. We, on the one hand, according to the divine writings, speak of God as unchangeable, in the passage: <margin>Psalm 101:28; Malachi 3:6</margin> *But you are the same*; and in: *I have not been altered.* But the gods of Epicurus, being composed of atoms, and as far as their constitution goes, being dissolvable, busy themselves with shaking off the soul-destroying atoms. But also the God of the <margin>indeed</margin> Stoics, being a body, sometimes has the whole substance as the leading principle, when the conflagration occurs; and sometimes He comes to be in a part of it, when the ordering of the world occurs. For these men have not been able to conceive the natural concept of God, as being entirely incorruptible, and simple, and uncomposite, and indivisible. But that which descended to men, *existed in the form of God*; and through His love for mankind, He emptied Himself— <margin>Philippians 2:6</margin>

Regarding the claim that Moses—or whoever recorded the story of the fire <note>referring to the destruction of Sodom</note> and the confusion of dialects—corrupted the stories told about the *Aloadae <note>Giant sons of Aloeus in Greek myth who tried to storm heaven by piling mountains on top of each other.</note> when he wrote about the Tower: it must be said that I do not think the story of the sons of Aloeus was told by Homer alone. However, the account of the Tower is much older, not only than Homer, but even than the invention of Greek letters; I am persuaded that Moses recorded it first. Who, then, is more likely to have corrupted the writings of the other? Was it those who tell the story of the *Aloadae who corrupted the account of the Tower? Or was it the one who recorded the Tower and the confusion of dialects who corrupted the story of the *Aloadae? To impartial listeners, it is clear that Moses is more ancient than Homer. 

Furthermore, the history of Sodom and Gomorrah recorded by Moses in Genesis—how they were wiped out by fire because of sin—is compared by Celsus to the story of Phaethon <note>A youth in Greek myth who lost control of the Sun's chariot, nearly burning the Earth.</note>. In this, he falls into the same error of failing to observe the antiquity of Moses, acting consistently in his mistake. For those who tell the story of Phaethon seem to be younger than Homer, or at least much younger than Moses. 

We do not, therefore, deny the cleansing fire and the destruction of the world for the sake of abolishing wickedness and the renewal of the universe; we say we have learned this from the prophets and the sacred books. For as we said above, the prophets, in speaking many things about the future, *are proven to have spoken the truth about many things in the past, giving proof that the Divine Spirit was within them. It is clear, then, that they should be believed regarding the future, or rather, the Divine Spirit within them should be believed. 

"But the Christians," according to Celsus, "adding certain words to those spoken by the Jews, say that because of the sins of the Jews, the Son of God has already been sent; and that the Jews, by punishing Jesus and giving him gall to drink, drew the wrath of God upon themselves." Let anyone who wishes challenge this statement as a falsehood, if the entire nation of the Jews has not been overturned, and if they have not suffered this very thing within a single generation of Jesus. For forty-two years, I believe, passed from the time they crucified Jesus until the destruction of Jerusalem. And it has never been recorded, since the Jews have existed, that they were cast out from their venerable sanctuary and worship for so long a time, even when conquered by more powerful nations. Even if they ever seemed to be abandoned because of sin, they were nonetheless looked upon with favor, and returning, they recovered their own possessions and performed their customary rites without hindrance. One of the facts, then, that proves Jesus was something divine and sacred is that the Jews have already suffered so many and such great things for so long a time on his account. And we shall say with confidence that they will not be restored. But...

So also the things which Moses narrates in the book of Genesis concerning Sodom and Gomorrah, deleted by fire on account of sin, Celsus compares with the history of Phaethon, striking again against the same stone because he did not observe the antiquity of the times of Moses. For those who tell fables about Phaethon seem to be later than the age of Homer, who followed a long time after Moses. Therefore, we do not deny that a purifying fire will consume all wickedness along with the world itself, since we have learned this from the sacred books of the Prophets. Since many events (as we have already said) have approved their truthfulness in predicting, by a manifest argument of their commerce with the divine spirit, it is left beyond doubt that faith is owed also to future things, whatever are expected according to the same oracles, or rather to the Spirit of God which possessed their breast. 

Furthermore, "the Christians" (says Celsus) "*adding certain things to the dogmas of the Jews, say that on account of the sins of the Jews the son of God has already come: and that the Jews, having driven Jesus to punishment and given him gall to drink, stirred up the bile of God against themselves.*" If that is false, let him who wishes refute it, if the whole Jewish race has not been expelled from its seats, not even one full century having elapsed after Jesus suffered, being condemned by them. For forty-two years, I think no more, intervened between the cross of Jesus and the destroyed Jerusalem: nor does it stand in any monuments of the Jews that they lacked divine worship for so long a time, and were ejected from their ceremonies by more powerful men; but, if ever they seemed to be deserted on account of sin, nevertheless, God looking back at them, they returned to their own and performed their sacred solemnities with no one prohibiting them. This is one of the arguments that Jesus was something divine and sacred, because the Jews, having harmed him, are afflicted with so many and such great evils for so long a time: and we dare to say, <note>original: "δ’ ἐροῦμεν, ὅτι οὐδ’ ἀποκατασταθήσονται. ἀλλ’"</note> "that they shall not be restored. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

<margin>Matthew 5:48.</margin>
But if one were to listen to the word in a healthy way, he might say, "First there is God, and then after Him, us." And we would interpret this "us" to mean rational beings, and even more so, those rational beings who are virtuous. For according to our doctrine, the same virtue belongs to all blessed beings, so that the virtue of man and God is the same. Therefore, we are taught: *Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.* <note>Origen argues that humans share a capacity for divine virtue, distinguishing them from the animals Celsus uses in his analogy.</note> Thus, no good and virtuous person is a "worm wallowing in filth"; no pious person is an "ant"; no righteous person is a "frog"; and no one whose soul is illuminated by the bright light of truth could reasonably be compared to a "bat."

<margin>Genesis 1:26.</margin>
It seems to me that Celsus has also misunderstood the passage: *Let us make man according to our image and likeness.* Because of this, he has invented his "worms" who say, "Having been made by God, we are in every way like Him." For if he had known the difference between man being made *according to the image* of God and being made *according to the likeness*; and that it is recorded that God said, *Let us make man according to our image and likeness*, but that God [actually] made man *according to the image of God*—and not yet also *according to the likeness*—he would not have represented us as saying, "We are in every way like God." <note>Origen makes a technical distinction common in early Greek theology: the "image" is the innate potential/reason, while the "likeness" is the final perfection achieved through virtue.</note> Nor do we say that the stars are subjected to us; although the so-called resurrection of the righteous, as understood by the wise, is compared to the sun,

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:41.</margin>
moon, and stars by the one who says: *There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory, so*

<margin>Daniel 12:3.</margin>
*also is the resurrection of the dead.* Daniel also prophesied these things long ago. He further claims that we say, "All things have been appointed to serve us." Perhaps he heard this from some among us who speak such things thoughtlessly; or perhaps he does not understand

<margin>Matthew 20:27.</margin>
how it is said that the one who is "greater" among us is to be the "servant of all." And if the Greeks say,

<margin>Euripides, Phoenician Women. * "The sun," in the edited books.</margin>

And see how, like a buffoon, this "solemn philosopher" has turned the announcement of divine judgment—the punishment of the unrighteous and the reward of the righteous—into mockery, laughter, and derision. He adds to all this: "These things would be more tolerable if said by worms and frogs than by Jews and Christians disputing with one another." Wherefore we learn that precept: *Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.* Therefore, no good man is a worm swimming in mud, no pious man an ant, no righteous man a frog, and no one illustrated in the soul by the splendid light of truth is rightly compared to a bat. It seems to me Celsus understood well enough that passage, *Let us make man in our image and likeness*, and from there he fashioned the words of the worms: *We were made by God similar to Him in all things.* If he had known the difference between a man made in the image of God and one made in His likeness, and that it was written that God said, *Let us make man in our image and likeness*, but that man was made by God in His image, and it does not add "also in the likeness," he would not have feigned that we say, *we are like God in all things.* Nor do we say the stars are subject to us, because the resurrection of the righteous, as understood by the wise, is compared to the Sun, Moon, and stars by him who says: *there is one glory of the Sun, another glory of the Moon, another glory of the stars; for star is surpassed by star in glory, and in the same way is the resurrection of the dead;* just as Daniel sang of these things long ago. <meta>This page continues Origen’s refutation of Celsus, specifically addressing the power of the names of the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) in prayer and exorcism. Origen argues that the efficacy of these names proves the sanctity of the Jewish ancestors.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

...be called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; but indeed, nearly all those who occupy themselves with incantations and magic use these names. For such an invocation of God is found in many places in magical writings, and the names of these men are taken up as being particularly effective against demons. These facts, therefore (which are brought forward by Jews and Christians to prove that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the fathers of the Jewish nation, were holy men), seem to me not to have been entirely unknown to Celsus, though he did not set them out clearly because he was unable to answer the argument. For we ask of all those who use such 

<margin>* invocations.</margin>

invocations: Tell us, O good sirs, who was this Abraham? And how great was Isaac? And of what power was Jacob, that the name of God, when joined to their names, should perform such great miracles? From whom have you learned, or can you learn, the history of these men? Who was it that recorded their history—whether it be a plain history, or one of those who celebrate these men in secret mysteries, or one that hints at great and wonderful things through allegories <note>original: "hyponoiai" - deeper meanings or undercurrents of thought</note> for those able to contemplate them? Then, when 

<margin>* we.</margin>

we ask, and no one is able to produce anything from any history whatsoever—except perhaps for mythical accounts—concerning these men, we shall bring forward the book entitled Genesis. This book contains the deeds of these men and the divine oracles given to them. We shall ask: if you have received from us these three names of the founders of the Jewish race, and if we clearly perceive that God, when invoked by these names, exerts a power that is not to be despised, does this not prove the divinity of these men? For we have no knowledge of them from any source other than the sacred books of the Jews. Furthermore, "the God of Israel," "the God of the Hebrews," and "the God who drowned the King of the Egyptians and the Egyptians in the Red Sea" are names often used in spells against demons or certain evil powers. We learn the history of these names and their interpretation from the ancestral writings of the Hebrews and in their native dialect, where these things are celebrated and narrated. How then can Celsus suppose that the Jews—who trace their genealogy from these first ancestors—are the lowest of men and wanderers? He shamelessly attempts to argue against their very origin. Their names, being Hebrew, bear witness to those who possess the sacred books in the Hebrew language and script, showing that their nation is truly related to those an-

<margin>Exodus 5:1, 3, 18; 15:4</margin>

<margin>* their origin.</margin>

<column-break/>

...be called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but they are used by all who practice incantations and magic. For in magical literature, this title of God is often found invoked, and the names of these men are joined to it as being familiar to Him and terrifying to demons. These things, therefore (which are usually cited by Jews and Christians as a most certain proof of the holiness of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the fathers of the Jewish people), Celsus seems to me not to have been entirely ignorant of; yet he could not address them openly because he was unable to respond to these statements. For we shall inquire of all who use such invocations: Tell us, O good men, who was this Abraham? What was the great virtue of Isaac and Jacob, that the name of God joined with their names performs such miracles? From what men did you learn, or can you learn, about the affairs of these men? Who took care to commit them to writing, whether celebrating them in secret or indicating certain wonderful and excellent things through the veils of riddles <note>Latin: "involucra aenigmatum" - the wrappings of mysteries</note>, provided one is able to behold them? Then, when at our questioning no one can produce anything from any monuments of the Greeks or barbarians or from sacred letters regarding these men, we shall produce that volume which is titled Genesis, containing their deeds and the divine oracles delivered to them. And so we shall ask again: If you have received from us these three names of the authors of the Jewish race—we who openly know that God, when invoked through these names, exercises a power not to be looked down upon—would that not indicate the divinity of these men, of whom we have no knowledge except from the sacred volumes of the Jews? Indeed, "the God of Israel," "the God of the Hebrews," and "the God who submerged the Egyptians," who were killed with their king in the waves of the Red Sea, is often included as a surname in songs effective against demons and evil powers. We have the knowledge and interpretation of these names from the ancestral letters of the Hebrews, celebrated in their own native tongue. How then can the Jews, having set out to weave their genealogy from these first authors—whom Celsus thinks were impostors and wanderers—be seen to act imprudently? Their names, since they are Hebrew, attest to those who have their sacred books written in the Hebrew language, so that it appears beyond controversy that they are not strangers to that lineage.

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Bb

->tion: for even in our own age, the names of the Jews are brought forth in the Hebrew tongue, because they have been taken from their own scriptures; or certainly fashioned from them, and turned through interpretation, signifying the same as those originals. Now see, whoever happens upon the writings of Celsus, whether he does not hint at these things in these words: *Having set out to weave their own genealogy, they dared from the first offspring of deceptive and wandering men to bring forward obscure and ambiguous voices into testimony?* For these names are obscure and not known to many, though to us they are not ambiguous, even if they are used by men foreign to our worship. But by Celsus, since he does not understand their ambiguity, they are—I know not how—rejected. And yet he ought, if he wished to attack without malice the genealogy of the Jews (which he thinks was imprudently fabricated by those boasting of Abraham and his grandsons as the authors of their race), to have cited the passage of Scripture pertaining to this and convinced them with probable reasons; and by bringing forth the truth, as he thinks it to be, and his assertions regarding the passage, to have proved the error. But neither Celsus nor anyone else will be able, by discussing the names which are employed for the working of powers <note>original: "virtutes" / "δυνάμεις" - referring to the use of Hebrew names in ancient exorcisms or mystical rites</note>, to give an account of this matter: or to demonstrate that those men were common and contemptible, whose names alone obtain such great power both among their own people and among foreigners. He ought also to have shown how we, interpreting those names to the unlearned and senseless, deceive our listeners, as it seems to him; let he himself, who boasts that he is not among the number of the unlearned and senseless, bring forward their true interpretation. Furthermore, he added this in his mention of the Jewish names contained in the genealogy: *that for so many ages before there was no controversy concerning men of this sort; but now the Jews contend about them with certain others*, whom nevertheless he does not name. Let anyone who wishes show who raises even a probable controversy against the Jews on this matter, or who refutes their opinion, or even that of the Christians, as far as these names are concerned; and let him bring forth a better opinion of others regarding the men so named. But we are certain that no one can do this, since nothing is more evident than that these names are taken from the Hebrew language, which is found among the Jews alone. After this, Celsus, bringing forward from profane histories the contentions of certain people concerning the antiquity of their race, such as the Athenians, Egyptians, Arcadians, Phrygians, and some—

<column-break/>

established forms. For even until now, the Jewish names, using the dialect of the Hebrews, were either taken from their very letters, or simply from the things signified by the Hebrew voice. And see, you who encounter the writing of Celsus, if he does not hint at this: "And they attempted to trace their genealogy from the first seed of sorcerers <note>original: "γοήτων" - can mean impostors or magicians</note> and wandering men, witnessing to obscure and ambiguous voices, hidden in darkness." For these names are hidden, and not in the light and knowledge of many, though according to us they are not ambiguous, even if they are adopted by those foreign to our piety. But according to Celsus, <margin>\* as it was judged</margin> \* setting out the ambiguity of the voices, I know not how, they are cast aside. And yet it was necessary for him, if he wished fairly to overturn the genealogy which appeared to be most shamelessly adopted, where the Jews boast of Abraham and <margin>\* how from.</margin> \* those from him, to set out the whole matter according to the place, and whether it was previously conceded or thought probable, and through this to nakedly overturn the facts of the place with the truth as it appeared to him and the arguments for it. But neither Celsus, nor any other, will be able, in treating the nature of names adopted for powers, to present the accurate account concerning these things; and to prove how they have become contemptible men, whose names alone are powerful not only among their own, but also among foreigners. It was necessary for him to set forth <margin>\* much is missing.</margin> how we, misinterpreting the things concerning these names to the ignorant and foolish, <margin>\* much is missing.</margin> deceive (as he thinks) the listeners; but he himself, who boasts of being neither ignorant nor foolish, should tell the true interpretation of the places. And he cast aside in the matters regarding these names, from which the Jews trace their genealogy, "that never yet in the long time before has there been a dispute concerning such names; but now Jews dispute about these with certain others," whom he did not name. For let him who wishes show who the claimants are, even using probability, against the Jews, so that it is not you Jews and Christians who have understood these things. But we are persuaded that <margin>\* some to do.</margin> some will not be able to do such a thing, it being most manifest that the names were taken from the Hebrew dialect, which is found among the Jews alone. ...of those who say that certain people were born among them, and providing evidence for each of these, Celsus says, "that the **Jews**, huddled together in some corner of **Palestine**, being utterly uneducated and having never seen these things celebrated long ago by **Hesiod** and countless other inspired men, composed a most improbable and crude story: how a certain man was formed by the hands of God and *breathed into*, and a woman was *brought forth* by God from his side, and a serpent *acting against* them, and God being too weak to overcome the serpent <note>original: "ἐφεσματισμένην" - Celsus mocks the idea that the serpent's counsel prevailed over God's command</note>; **narrating** a kind of myth as if to old women, and most impiously making God weak right from the start, unable to persuade even the one man whom he himself had formed." By these words, this "man of great learning" and "polymath," who charges Jews and Christians with ignorance and lack of education, clearly teaches us how accurately he knew the dates of various writers, both Greek and barbarian. For he thinks that Hesiod and countless others, whom he calls "inspired men," are older than **Moses** and his writings—Moses, who is proved to be much older than the **Trojan War** <note>original: "Ἰλιακῶν" - the events of the Iliad</note>. It was not the Jews who composed an improbable and crude story about the earth-born man; rather, it was those whom Celsus calls "inspired men," Hesiod and his countless others, who—having neither learned nor heard the much older and most venerable accounts in Palestine—wrote such histories about ancient things as are sung in the *Theogony* <note>The "Birth of the Gods" by Hesiod</note>, where they attribute births to gods and countless other things. These are the men whom **Plato** rightly expelled from his Republic as corrupters of youth—namely **Homer** and those who write such poems. But it is clear that Plato did not believe those who left behind such poems were "inspired men." Yet Celsus the **Epicurean**, who is a more capable judge than Plato (if indeed *this* is the same man who composed two other books against the Christians), perhaps out of a desire to quarrel with us, calls those "inspired" whom he did not actually believe to be so. He further charges us with introducing a man "formed by the hands of God." While the book of **Genesis** does not mention the hands of God in the making or the forming of man, **Job** and **David** do say: *Your hands have made me and formed me.* There is much to be said to clarify the meaning of those who spoke these words, not only regarding the difference between "making" and "forming," but also regarding the "hands of God." Those who do not understand such expressions in the Divine Scriptures think that we attribute to the God of all a physical shape such as the human one—just as they might think he has wings—

<column-break/>

...of those among them who assert that some were born from the earth, and who offer arguments for each of these, he says: *The Jews, having conspired in a corner of Palestine, being unlearned men who had never before heard the same things celebrated by Hesiod and countless other divine men, composed an incredible and unpolished fable: that a certain man was fashioned by the hands of God and inspired by him, and a woman was produced from his side, and they received commands from God, and a serpent was their adversary; and finally, that the serpent was more powerful than the commands of God. This is an old wives' tale, which with the highest impiety makes God weak from the very beginning, having no authority over the man he himself fashioned.* In this manner, the "multifaceted and most learned" Celsus, objecting to the rudeness and lack of skill of Jews and Christians, shows clearly how exactly he holds the account of the times in which two writers lived, one Greek and the other barbarian. He thinks Hesiod and countless other "divine men," as he calls them, are older than Moses and his writings—Moses, I say, who is well known to be far superior in age to the Trojan affairs. Therefore, it was not the Jews who invented an incredible and unpolished fable about the earth-born man, but those who, in Celsus's opinion, were inspired by God—Hesiod and the rest—who, not having heard the ancient and venerable narrations of the Palestinians, wrote such histories of ancient things as the *Generation of the Gods*, to whom they attributed births and countless other things according to their ability. These men Plato deservedly ejected from his Republic as a plague to youth, specifically the poems of Homer and similar writers. Certainly, Plato did not consider those who left such songs to posterity as being inspired by God. But Celsus the Epicurean, a judge more fit than Plato (if indeed he is the one who also composed two other books against the Christians), pronounces them inspired by God, doubtless out of a spirit of contention and to our insult, though he does not truly think them inspired. He further accuses us *that we introduce a man fashioned by the hands of God,* although the book of Genesis makes no mention of God's hands when man is made or formed; but Job and David say, *Your hands have made me and fashioned me.* Regarding these words, in what sense they were spoken, what the difference is between "making" and "fashioning," and how the "hands of God" are to be understood, a long disputation could be established. For those who do not understand these and similar voices in the sacred letters think that we add a human form to God, the Best and Greatest; they could by the same effort...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

## Book IV

...to suspect that we are equipped with other works even when we believe these things, since these expressions are also found literally in our Scriptures speaking of God: to interpret these is not the business of the present moment; for we have devoted a special labor to the interpretation of Genesis, as far as we were able. <note>Origen refers to his now largely lost *Commentary on Genesis*.</note> See now the malicious mind of Celsus in what follows: when our Scripture says concerning the formation of man, *And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul:* <note>Genesis 2:7</note> this man, wishing maliciously to carp at the phrase, *He breathed into his face the breath*, which he does not even understand how it was spoken, wrote that they composed a fable about a man fashioned by the hands of God: so that someone, thinking that breathing is to be understood in the same way as with wineskins, might laugh at the breathing performed into the man's face: which is to be interpreted thus, that God imparted to man an incorruptible spirit, just as it is written, *For your incorruptible spirit is in all things.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 12:1</note> Then, after he has once decided to carp at the Scriptures, he also blames that passage, *God sent a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and filled up the flesh for it, and built the rib, which he had taken from Adam, into a woman*, and what follows thereafter: nor does he add any interpretation which might warn the listener of figurative speech, preferring to ignore the allegory. Although in the progress of his discourse he says that the more moderate among both Jews and Christians, out of shame, take refuge in allegory. To which it is permitted to respond: Therefore, does the fable of your divinely inspired Hesiod admit allegory concerning the woman whom Jupiter gave to men as a great evil in place of fire? <note>The myth of Pandora.</note> But does this woman, taken from the side of the sleeper after an ecstasy and built by God, seem to cover nothing of a more recondite sense beneath an external covering? But what kind of fairness is it, not to laugh at those things as trifles, but to admire them as a philosophical mystery veiled by a fable: yet to hang these things from the nose <note>A Latin idiom meaning "to turn up one's nose" or mock.</note> by sticking only to the words, and to estimate them as of no value? For if it must be accused because of the simplicity of the words, because it touched upon an excellent latent sense: see whether Hesiod, inspired by a deity (as you say), might be more subject to your sneers, who sings thus:

> *You are glad, and revolve a celebrated triumph in your heart,*
> *Because you have craftily deceived the highest Jove with art.*

But it is not consistent to not laugh at those things as a myth, but to wonder at them as philosophy in a myth; yet to sneer at these things, resting the meaning only on the literal word, and to think they will be of no account. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

*Hope alone, while she chanced to linger at the lowest lips of the jar,*

<note>original: "Sola, labris urnæ..." Origen is quoting Hesiod’s myth of Pandora’s box (or jar) to show that Greeks also use myths to convey deeper truths.</note>

To those who contend that these matters are filled with solemn allegories—whether they hit the mark in their interpretation or not—we shall ask: Is it then permitted only to the Greeks to philosophize in deeper meanings, or perhaps to the Egyptians, and any other barbarians who boast that they possess truth hidden in mysteries? But do the Jews alone, and their lawgiver, and their other writers, seem to you the most foolish of all mortals? And is this nation alone devoid of divine power, though it has been stirred by such excellent teachings to pursue through contemplation that sublime nature of God, to gaze upon Him alone, and to hope for nothing good from any source other than Him? 

Furthermore, because Celsus mocks with a "comic tooth" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to ridicule or sneer, like a satirist in a comedy.</note> what is written therein concerning the serpent who opposed the commands of God given to man—thinking the story similar to the ravings of old women—he has deliberately avoided naming the "Paradise of God." Nor did he mention that it was planted by God in Eden toward the East, and that there soon sprang up from the earth every tree pleasing to the sight and sweet to the taste, and the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and likewise the much-celebrated tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and what follows. These things are capable of moving a candid reader to seek something serious beneath the figurative language. 

We shall set against him, in opposition, what Socrates tells of Cupid <note>original: "Cupidine" / "Eros". Origen uses the Latin name for the Greek god Eros.</note> in Plato’s *Symposium*; these words were assigned to Socrates to speak because he was more elegant than the others disputing about love. The words of Plato are as follows: 

"When Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> was born, the gods sat down to a prepared banquet, and among the rest was Porus, the god of Plenty, son of Metis. After dinner, Penia <note>Poverty</note>, coming to beg for food, lingered about the doors of the hall where they were feasting. Meanwhile Porus, drunk with nectar (for there was not yet wine), entered the garden of Jupiter and fell into a heavy sleep. Then Penia, seeking a remedy for her own want, took it into her mind to secretly and by ambush lie with Porus for the sake of procreating children; so she lay down beside him and conceived by him. From this was born Love <note>Eros</note>, a follower and servant of Venus, as he was begotten on Venus’s birthday; moreover, by nature he is seized by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is beautiful. Because Love is the son of Porus and Penia, he has obtained a lot of this kind: First, he is always poor and squalid, with bare feet, without a home, fluttering about the ground, without bedding, lying at doors and in the streets under the open sky, and not degenerating from his mother, as he is perpetually in want. But he resembles his father in this, that he plots against the beautiful..."

In response to these things which are solemnly allegorized—whether the allegory is successful or not—we shall say: is it only permitted to the Greeks to philosophize with hidden meanings? Is it also permitted to the Egyptians, and as many of the barbarians as pride themselves on mysteries and truth? But did the Jews alone seem to you, and their lawgiver, and their writers, to be the most senseless of all men? And that this nation alone has no share in any power of God, though it has been taught by the most noble minds to ascend to the uncreated nature of God, and to look to that alone, and to expect hopes from it alone? 

And since Celsus also ridicules the story of the serpent, as opposing the commands of God to man, regarding the account as a myth similar to those taught by old women; and he intentionally did not name the "Paradise of God," nor how God is said to have planted it in Eden toward the east, and after this to have made to spring up from the earth every tree fair to the sight and good for food, and the tree of life in the midst of the paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the things said after these, which are able at once to move one who reads with natural intelligence to see that all these things are allegorized with significant meaning. Come, let us compare the things said about Love by Socrates in Plato’s *Symposium*, which were attributed to Socrates as being more solemn than all those who spoke about him in the *Symposium*. Plato’s wording is thus: "When Aphrodite was born, the gods were feasting, both the others and Porus the son of Metis. And when they had dined, Penia came to beg, as there was a feast, and she was about the doors. Now Porus, being drunk with nectar (for there was not yet wine), went into the garden of Zeus and, being heavy, slept. Then Penia, plotting because of her own poverty to have a child from Porus, lay down by him and conceived Love. Wherefore also Love has become a follower and servant of Aphrodite, having been begotten on her birthday, and being at the same time by nature a lover of the beautiful, since Aphrodite is beautiful. Since then Love is the son of Porus and Penia, he is in such a condition. First, he is always poor, and far from being tender and beautiful, as many think; but he is hard and parched, and shoeless and homeless, always sleeping on the ground and without bedding, lying at doors and in the ways under the open sky; having always his mother’s nature, a housemate with want. But on the other hand, after his father, he is a schemer against the beautiful."

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

> "...with the noble and the good; being brave, and headstrong, and intense; a formidable hunter, always weaving some new device; a seeker after wisdom and full of resources; philosophizing through his whole life; a powerful sorcerer, a dealer in drugs <note>original: *pharmakeus*, which can mean a poisoner or a magician</note>, and a sophist. By nature, he is neither immortal nor mortal; but sometimes on the same day he flourishes and lives, when he is in abundance; at other times he dies; then again, he comes back to life through his father’s nature. But that which he gains always slips away; so that Love is never in want, nor is he ever rich."

<margin>* The edited books read "of wisdom."</margin>
"Furthermore, he stands in the middle between wisdom and ignorance." Now, will those who encounter these words—unless they share Celsus’s malice—blame the Christian, or will they mock and scoff at the myth <margin>* of the myth.</margin> of so great a man as Plato? Or rather, if they examine the philosophical meaning spoken enigmatically within the myth, will they be able to find Plato’s intent? Will they see how he was able to hide the great doctrines that appeared to him by using many forms within the framework of a myth, yet spoke them in such a way that those who know how to find the truth from myths could understand the author's purpose? I have set out this myth from Plato because his "Garden of Zeus" seems to have something in common with the "Paradise of God." In this comparison, *Penia* <note>The personification of Poverty</note> corresponds to the serpent, and *Porus* <note>The personification of Plenty or Resource</note>, who is plotted against by Penia, corresponds to the man who is plotted against by the serpent. It is quite clear whether we should suspect that Plato hit upon these things by chance, or (as some believe) that during his travels in Egypt he met with Jewish philosophers and learned something from them. In that case, he preserved some things but altered others, being careful not to offend the Greeks by following the Jewish philosophy <margin>* of wisdom.</margin> in every detail—since the Jews were slandered by the masses because of the strangeness of their laws and their peculiar way of life. However, now is not the time to explain Plato’s myth, nor the details of the serpent and the Paradise of God and what is recorded to have happened there. For we have already worked through these matters as far as possible in our inquiries into *Genesis*. But when Celsus claims, "that the word of Moses introduced God as most impious, being weak right from the start and unable to persuade even one man whom He Himself had formed," <margin>* from the beginning.</margin> we shall say in response that this is similar to someone complaining about the existence of evil, as if God were unable to prevent it even in a single human being, so that at least one man might be found among men who was good and stripped of evil. For just as those who care to defend Providence offer a defense on this point—

<column-break/>

> *...then he delights in honorable things, and lays snares for them, being manly, industrious, and a skilled hunter, always weaving new machinations; a seeker of prudence and a gatherer [of knowledge] philosophizing through his whole life; a distinguished magician, a sorcerer, and a juggler; neither ranked with the immortals nor the mortals; sometimes on the same day now living and flourishing, if there is an abundance of desired things, now dying, and again revived because of his father’s nature; but what is gained by him quickly slips away: wherefore Love is never a beggar nor wealthy, learned in an uncertain way or unlearned.* Whoever reads these things, if they are like Celsus in malice—which far be it from Christians—will mock that greatest of men, Plato. But if they examine the philosophical doctrine under the appearance of the fable, they will grasp his mind: how he concealed his excellent opinions from the common folk with figures, yet in such a way that they might be understood by those who know how to extract truth from fables. I have more willingly applied this fiction of Plato because the Garden of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> which he mentions seems to have something similar to the paradise of God; just as the treacherous Penia reflects the serpent, and Porus, deceived by her snares, reflects the circumvented man. It is not entirely clear whether the philosopher fell into this similarity by chance, or whether, as some think, he learned it from conversations with wise Jews while traveling in Egypt, rendering part as he received it and changing part so as not to offend the Greeks by departing in no way from the wisdom of the Jews—who were infamous among the common people for laws differing from the institutions of other nations and for a certain private way of living. But it is not the time now to explain Plato’s fable nor what is written of the serpent and the paradise of God; for we have already dedicated a specific treatise to the explanation of Genesis. As for his claim that *Moses impiously fabricated this, because he makes God weak from the very beginning, not being strong enough to save the man whom He Himself had created:* we reply that this is just as if someone were to find fault that malice was admitted into human affairs, which God could not ward off even from one man, so that at least one might be free of it even at the very origin of things. For just as this has been sufficiently answered by those—neither few nor contemptible—who patronize providence: so also will they philosophize concerning Adam and his sin, who know that in the Greek tongue the name of Adam—

Divine Scripture speaks not so much about one particular individual as about the entire human race: for the curse which is said to have been inflicted on Adam is common to all; just as that which was laid upon the woman does not pertain to her alone. Those coats of skins also (which God put upon the man and his wife when they were cast out of paradise because of sin) signify a certain hidden mystery <note>original: "arcanum quoddam mysterium"</note>, more profound than that which Plato relates concerning the soul losing its wings and falling headlong here until it reaches something solid. After this, he [Celsus] proceeds in this manner: *Add to these the flood and the absurd ark containing all things within itself, then the dove and the crow as messengers, which tell of them distorting here also, by way of a joke, the story of Deucalion.* <note>Deucalion was the hero of the Greek flood myth; Celsus argues the Jews simply copied and ruined the Greek story.</note> For they did not think (I suppose) that these things would come to light, but were plainly telling a fable to children. Here, see the unphilosophical hatred of this man toward the most ancient scripture of the Jews. For since he had nothing to say against the history of the flood, nor did he know how to argue against the measurements—how it could be that the ark, according to the common understanding, being three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, could hold fourteen of the clean land animals and four of the unclean—he simply called it "absurd," containing all things in itself. For what is absurd, when it is said to have been built over a hundred years, that from three hundred cubits of length and fifty of width, it was sloped to a height of thirty cubits, ending in a single cubit of length and width? Was not the structure rather to be admired, like a great city, whose base extended ninety thousand cubits in length and twenty-five thousand in width? <note>Origen is using a mathematical defense to show the internal volume was vast enough for all species.</note> Is not the genius of the builder to be admired? Who so joined it together and fastened the joints so that it could withstand a storm as great as would suffice for a flood? Unless, perhaps, he does not even think the writing belongs to Moses, but to several people; for this is indicated by his saying, "falsifying and tampering with the story of Deucalion." For it is even prophesied that this piety would be preached to all nations. And when Jesus said to the Jews, <margin>Matthew 21:43</margin> *The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof*, what else did he hint at, than that by divine power he would bring into the light the whole of Jewish scripture containing the mysteries of the kingdom of God?

If we believe that God is present in all these affairs, what absurd thing do we do, being persuaded never to separate from His divinity those who have dedicated to Him a life lived well and vigorously? He also mocked the "acquisition of Jacob while with Laban" (not understanding what <margin>Genesis 30:43</margin> it refers to), namely, *And the unmarked ones belonged to Laban, but the marked ones to Jacob*; and he says that "God bestowed donkeys and sheep and camels upon his sons." # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

->Cc<-

<column-break/>

God also gave wells to the righteous. For Celsus did not observe that the righteous do not prepare cisterns <note>Latin: *lacunas*; Greek: *λάκκους*. These refer to stagnant pits or man-made reservoirs for rainwater, contrasted here with "wells" of living water.</note> for themselves, but dig wells in the earth, seeking some beginning of drinkable waters; as those who have received such a figurative precept: *Drink water from your own vessels, and from the springs of your own wells: let not the waters from your spring be poured out, and let your waters run within your streets; let them be for you alone, and let no stranger be a partaker with you.* <margin>Proverbs 5:15</margin> Often, however, Scripture uses the narration of events to signify something greater to those who understand: such as the things handed down concerning the wells, and concerning the marriages of the righteous and their various unions. All these things would be treated more seasonably in commentaries illustrating the Scriptures themselves. Moreover, that those righteous men adorned wells in the land of Palestine, just as it is written, is clear from the wonderful wells shown at Ascalon, which are worth visiting for a style of structure that varies greatly from other wells. Furthermore, that wives and handmaids are referred to through tropology <note>A method of interpretation that finds moral or spiritual lessons in historical accounts.</note> is not our own invention, but we have received it from the wise who were before us. One of them, raising the listener toward tropology, speaks thus: *Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear what the law narrates, that Abraham had two sons, one from a handmaid and the other from a free woman? But he who was born of the handmaid was born according to the flesh; but he who was from the free woman, through the promise; which things are spoken through allegory: for these are the two testaments, one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating into servitude, which is Hagar.* <margin>Galatians 4:21</margin> And a little after: *But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother.* <margin>Galatians 4:26</margin> And he who will not find it a burden to take the Epistle to the Galatians into his hands will know how the marriages and the unions with handmaids are to be understood allegorically: then, that Scripture wishes us to emulate not those things which were done physically, but those which were done spiritually, as the Apostles of Jesus are accustomed to speak. This man [Celsus], when he ought to embrace the truthfulness of the author of Divine Scripture—who, by not remaining silent about things having an unseemly appearance, shows that he does not fabricate the rest of the wonders—does the contrary. Regarding what is related of Lot and his daughters, having neither scrutinized it according to the literal words nor according to the higher sense, he says it is more monstrous than the crimes of Thyestes. <note>In Greek mythology, Thyestes unwittingly ate his own children; Celsus compares the biblical account of Lot's incest to this extreme pagan taboo to mock the Bible.</note> <margin>Genesis 19:33</margin> However, it is not necessary now to explain the tropology of this place; what Sodom may be; and what the angels warn the one saved from there, saying: *Look not behind you, nor stay in any of the surrounding countryside.* <margin>Genesis 19:19</margin>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 4.

<margin>Genesis 19:17, 26</margin>
"Escape to the mountain, lest you be overtaken by the same calamity as the others"; then who Lot was; who his wife was, who turned into a pillar of salt because she looked back; and who those daughters were, who made their father drunk so that they might become mothers by him: we shall briefly defend these historical accounts so that they do not offend the reader. Even the Greeks have investigated the nature of good, evil, and indifferent things <note>The Stoic concept of *adiaphora* (indifferent things) refers to actions that are neither inherently virtuous nor vicious.</note>; and they found that good and evil reside in the will alone, and that all other things, if not examined by the will, are otherwise indifferent. Furthermore, they say the will that uses these things as it ought is to be praised, while that which does otherwise is to be blamed. In this category of "indifferent things," they have said that lying with one's daughters is an indifferent matter, even if it should not be allowed in well-ordered Republics. And, to teach by example that it is an indifferent thing to couple with a daughter, they proposed the case of a wise man left alone with his daughter as the sole survivors after the entire human race had been destroyed; they ask whether it would then be his duty to come together with his daughter so that, in such dire circumstances, the human race might not utterly perish. Therefore, if these things are discussed and approved among the Greeks by the highly respected sect of the Stoics, why should these girls be judged more harshly? They had learned of the conflagration of the world (though not precisely), and seeing their city and lands devastated by flames, they believed that only their father and themselves were left as the seedbed for the human race. If, moved by this suspicion, they wished to come to the aid of a perishing world, are they to be held worse than that "wise man" of the Stoic judgment, who thinks it his duty to couple with his daughter if the safety of the universe is the reward for his labor? Nor am I unaware that some, offended by this will of Lot’s daughters, consider their deed impious; and therefore the nations of the Moabites and Ammonites, born from this incestuous union, are cursed. Indeed, the divine Scripture is not found to explicitly approve or disapprove of this deed; nevertheless, however it stands, it is reduced to a tropology <note>term: tropology (an allegorical or figurative interpretation of scripture focusing on moral lessons)</note>, and it has some excuse from the circumstances themselves. Celsus further adds the hatred of Esau toward Jacob—a man who is openly evil by the testimony of Scripture—and he accuses Levi and Simeon, the avengers of the rape committed against their sister by the son of the king of Shechem, yet he does not indicate the cause of their deed. Furthermore, he mentions the brothers who sold their sibling as the sons of Jacob; and the sold brother as Joseph; and the deceived father as Jacob, because he suspected nothing—

"Escape to the mountain, lest perhaps the same calamity that befell the others overtake you"; then who Lot was; who his wife was, turned into a pillar of salt because she turned herself backward; also who those daughters were, who intoxicated their father so that they might become mothers from him: we shall offer a brief defense of the history only so far as it might not offend the reader. The Greeks also sought the nature of good and evil and indifferent things, and they found that good and evil are situated in the will alone, which if not examined, otherwise all things are indifferent: furthermore, the will, which uses these as it ought, is to be praised; that which does the opposite, is to be blamed. In this reasoning of indifferent things, they said that intercourse with daughters is indifferent, even if it is not to be admitted in well-constituted Republics. And, to show by example that it is an indifferent thing to meet with a daughter, they proposed a wise man left alone with his daughter as a survivor after the destruction of the entire human race: and they ask whether he would then meet with his daughter out of duty, lest in such afflicted circumstances the human race perish fundamentally through this occasion. Therefore, if these things are correctly discussed among the Greeks, and approved by the not-to-be-despised sect of the Stoics: truly the girls, who had learned of the burning of the world, even if not exactly, seeing their city with its fields devastated by flames, and thinking their father and themselves left for the nursery of the human race, if moved by this suspicion they wished to succor the perishing world, shall they be held worse than that wise man in the judgment of the Stoics, who thinks it his duty to meet with his daughter, if the safety of the university of things be the reward of his work? Nor am I ignorant that some, offended by this will of Lot's daughters, think their deed impious; and therefore that the nations of the Moabites and Ammonites were born from incestuous intercourse as cursed: and in truth the divine Scripture is not found to manifestly approve or disapprove this deed: yet however this holds itself, it is reduced to tropology, and has that by which it may be excused somewhat from the circumstances themselves. Observe, however, how Celsus—moved more by hatred of us than by a zeal for the truth—collects these stories: he touches only upon those parts which seem to serve his accusation. But where the remarkable temperance of Joseph is commended, who did not yield to his mistress's love, neither for her threats nor her prayers, Celsus does not make mention of it by even a single word. After this, Celsus mentions—piously now, but quite obscurely—the dreams of the cupbearer and the chief baker of Pharaoh, and the interpretation of them, by which occasion Joseph was released from custody and obtained the second throne among the Egyptians after the King. What evil does that narrative contain, that it should be placed in the section of accusations by this man, who added the title of "True Word" to his writing, yet does not hand down doctrines but merely accuses Christians and Jews? He adds that Joseph showed favor—I know not what, for he does not explain—to his brothers who had sold him, when they set out with their donkeys for Egypt to seek grain because of the famine. What absurdity would the account of the history have in itself, that he should set these things out as part of an accusation—he who entitled his work "The True Word," yet does not teach but attacks to accuse Christians and Jews? "And to the brothers who sold him, being hungry and having come for trade with donkeys," he says, "the one who was sold performed favors," which things Celsus also set forth. And it was more necessary to ask him what he intended, and what absurdity he shows in the recognition; for it is not possible, so to speak, even for **Momus** himself to reasonably accuse these things, which even without the tropology have much that leads to good character. In which way also, "Joseph, who had gone down into the dwelling of the dead <note>original: "ᾅδου" (Hades/the pit), referring here to his slavery or the prison.</note>, being freed and processing with the burial of his father," Celsus does not think the account provides an accusation, saying "by whom (clearly Joseph) the 'illustrious and divine' race of Jews, multiplying in Egypt, was ordered to dwell somewhere outside as aliens and to shepherd in **vile places**." And he added from his own hateful disposition that they were "ordered to shepherd in vile places," without asking how the Egyptian departure of the people was called a "flight"; silencing at the start the things written in Exodus about the departure of the Hebrews from the land of Egypt. Having examined these things also, and having shown that not even according to the literal sense do they appear worthy of accusation, Celsus placed them in the category of accusation and nonsense, without adding—

...when our scripture is considered poor in its wording. Then, as if he had devoted himself solely to hating and shaming the affairs of the Jews and Christians, he says, "that even the more moderate of the Jews and Christians interpret these things allegorically." He would say that they, being ashamed of these things, * flee to allegory. But one might say to him: if things which, according to their first appearance, must be called myths and fictions—whether written with a hidden meaning or in any other way—are worthy of shame, to whom should this be applied if not to the Greek histories? In those, sons castrate their father-gods, and father-gods swallow their son-gods. And a mother-goddess gives to the son, the father of both men and gods, a stone in place of his child; and a father lies with his daughter; and a wife binds her husband, taking as accomplices in the chains both the brother of the one being enslaved and his daughter. And why must I list the absurd histories of the Greeks concerning the gods, which are inherently worthy of shame even when allegorized? Where * indeed Chrysippus of Soli <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) known for his vast writings.</note>, who is thought to have adorned the Porch <term>Stoa: the school of Stoic philosophy</term> of the philosophers with many * intellectual writings, misinterprets a painting in Samos in which Hera was depicted performing an obscene act with Zeus. For that solemn philosopher says in his own writings that matter, having received the generative principles <term>spermatikoi logoi: the creative seeds or formative forces in Stoic physics</term> of God, contains them within itself for the adornment of the whole. For in the painting at Samos, Hera is matter and Zeus is God. And for these reasons indeed, because of such myths and ten thousand others, we do not wish to call the God over all by the name of Zeus, even as far as the name goes, nor the Sun Apollo, nor the Moon Artemis. But practicing pure piety toward the Creator, and speaking well of His beautiful creations, we do not defile divine things even by a name; accepting the word of Plato in the *Philebus*, who did not wish to accept Pleasure as a God. "For my fear," he says, "O Protarchus, concerning the names of the Gods is of such a kind." We, therefore, truly have a fear concerning the name of God and His beautiful creations, lest even under the pretext of figurative language <term>tropology: a method of ethical or figurative interpretation</term> we should admit some myth harmful to youth. But if Celsus had read the scripture without prejudice, he would not have said "that our writings only admit of allegory * because of [shame]." For from the prophecies, in which historical events are written, * one ought to approach the histories not merely as history, but as being written with the goal of figurative meaning, and * arranged most wisely, aimed both at the multitude of those who believe more simply, and at the few who wish to examine matters with understanding.

...doing nothing to refute us, which is what that man attempts. Then, acting only so that he might harass the Jews and Christians, whom he hates, with slanders, he says that both *Jews and Christians, at least the more moderate ones, pull these things toward allegory, and therefore take refuge there because of shame. To this slander it can be answered: If stories are worthy of shame because of the appearance they present—whether they were fashioned to cover a more hidden sense, or in whatever way—that shame falls upon no stories more than those of the Greeks. If you read them, you will find among the Gods sons who castrate their parents, and parents who devour their children; there also a mother-Goddess substitutes a stone for her son to the father of men and Gods; a father sleeps with his daughter; a wife casts chains upon her husband, having brought the husband's own brother and daughter into the partnership of the crime. And why is it necessary for me to enumerate the absurd stories of the Greeks about the gods, shameful in the first place even when they are explained allegorically, when Chrysippus of Soli, who is believed to have adorned the porch of the philosophers with very many writings, interprets a picture in Samos where Juno is depicted submitting to the unmentionable lust of Jupiter? For that grave philosopher writes in his Commentaries that matter, receiving the feminine <note>The Latin 'feminalem' here likely refers to the receptive nature of matter in Stoic thought.</note> word of God, contains it in itself for the adornment and order of all things. For in the Samian inscription, Juno is matter, and Jupiter is God. Wherefore we, offended by these and similar myths, in no way allow the greatest God to be called by the name of Jupiter, nor the Sun by the name of Apollo, nor the Moon by the name of Diana: but by exercising pure piety toward God and praising His most beautiful works, we do not contaminate divine things even by name, approving the doctrine of Plato in the *Philebus*, who was unwilling for Pleasure to be received into the register of the Gods. "I am scrupulous," he says, "Protarchus, regarding the names of the Gods." We, therefore, are truly scrupulous regarding the name of God and His excellent works, so much so that we do not admit any myths that would be harmful to the morals of youth, even under the pretext of figurative interpretations. But if Celsus had read our Scriptures with a sincere mind, he would not have denied that they can admit allegory. For from these Prophecies, which contain histories, one may proceed from the mere narration of events to the histories which were written with the express purpose of being interpreted allegorically, and were most wisely dispensed with this purpose: that they might suit either the simple crowd of the faithful, or those distinguished ones wishing to search more deeply.

->and those who are capable.<- For if even those who today are considered by Celsus to be the more moderate among the Jews and Christians did not interpret the writings through **allegory** <note>original: "allegoriam" / "ἠλληγόρουν" — the practice of interpreting texts to reveal a hidden spiritual or moral meaning</note>, perhaps his argument would seem more plausible. And what are the "rivers in Egypt" about which the aforementioned boastful Pharaoh says, <margin>Hosea 14:10</margin> "The rivers are mine, and I made them"? <note>Origen is quoting from the Septuagint tradition; modern Bibles attribute the "rivers are mine" quote to Ezekiel 29:3.</note> And who is the dragon <term>dragon: here referring to a great sea monster or crocodile</term> that corresponds to these rivers as shown by interpretation? And who are the fish in his scales? Why should I provide further evidence for things that are not easily understood? Regarding these things it is said: *Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or intelligent, and will know them?*

I have extended this argument further because I wanted to show that Celsus was wrong to say, "that the more moderate Jews and Christians try somehow to allegorize <term>allegorize: to interpret a text as having a hidden spiritual meaning beyond the literal words</term> these things, but they do not admit of any allegory, being instead outright and most true myths." For the myths of the Greeks are much more not only very foolish, but also most impious. Our scriptures, however, are aimed even at the multitude of the simpler folk; a precaution which the creators of the Greek fictions did not take. Therefore, Plato was not unkind when he expelled such myths and such poems from his own Republic.

It seems to me that Celsus has heard that there are writings containing allegories of the Law; if he had read them, he would not have said, "at any rate, the allegories which seem to have been written about them are much more shameful and more absurd than the myths themselves, attempting with a certain wonderful and totally senseless folly to join together things that can in no way and by no means be harmonized." He seems to be saying this about the writings of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who used allegory to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note>, or even older ones, such as those of Aristobulus. But I guess that Celsus has [not] read the books, since in many places they seem to me to be so successful that even the philosophers among the Greeks would be won over by what is said; for not only is the style polished, but also the thoughts, the doctrines, and the use of what he considers myths from the scriptures.

I know also that Numenius the Pythagorean—a man who interpreted Plato much better than others and who <margin>* excelled.</margin> championed the Pythagorean doctrines—in many places in his writings sets forth the words of Moses and the prophets, and allegorizes <term>tropology: a figurative or moral interpretation of a text</term> them not unconvincingly, as in the work called *Epops*, and in those *On Numbers*, and in those *On Place*. And in the third book *On the Good*, he even sets forth a certain story about Jesus, mentioning his name, and interprets it figuratively; but whether he did so successfully or unsuccessfully is for another time to say.

But what need is there for me to bring forward more things which require no proof? Concerning which it is said, *Who is wise and will understand these? Who is intelligent and will know them?*

I have been more wordy here to declare that Celsus did not speak correctly when he said, *That the more modest among the Jews and Christians attempt to interpret such things allegorically, which nevertheless cannot receive allegory, but are the purest fables.* But the fables of the Greeks are not only most foolish, but truly most impious: for our Scriptures accommodate themselves even to the simple common people; a thing which the fashioners of Greek fables did not care to do. Wherefore Plato does not act inhumanely when he ejects such fables from his Republic, and such poems.

And it seems to me Celsus has heard that there exist somewhere commentaries on the allegories of the law, which if he had read, he would not say, *The allegories therefore written about these are much more foul than the fables themselves, and even more absurd, attempting by a marvelous stupidity to fit together things which in no way cohere.* He seems to say this about the writings of Philo, or even older ones, such as those of Aristobulus. However, I am led by certain conjectures to think that Celsus has not read those volumes: since very often they so attain the mind of Scripture that it would not shame Greek philosophers to pluck certain things from there, in which sayings not only is the style refined, but deeper meanings and doctrines are present, and the use of storytelling from the sacred letters, as Celsus thinks.

Indeed, I know Numenius the Pythagorean, who discussed many matters better than Plato, and gave primacy to Pythagorean doctrines, inserted many things into his commentaries taken from the books of Moses and the Prophets, treated through a plausible figurative interpretation, just as in the book titled *Epops*, likewise in the books *On Numbers*, and *On Place*: and in the third book *On the Good* he even tells a certain story about Jesus, without adding the name, bringing also a figurative interpretation of it: but whether he hit the mark or not, it is not for this time to offer an opinion. # Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

## Page 199

It spoke of Moses and Jannes and Jambres <note>original: "Moſe & Janne ac Jambre"; these are the traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in Exodus</note>: yet we do not mention this for our own glorification; rather, we approve of this man <note>referring to a previous author mentioned by Celsus</note> more than Celsus and other Greeks, because he deigned to investigate even our Scriptures for the sake of learning, and held them not to be foolish, but figurative. After this, bringing forward from various authors of allegories certain things that are not entirely unpolished—which might, however, persuade the simple-minded more quickly than the prudent—*Celsus says: "I know of a certain dispute between Papiscus and Jason, which is not so much worthy of laughter as of pity and hatred. Truly, to refute these things is not my purpose, since they are clear to anyone, especially if one can bear to unroll the writings themselves. I prefer," he says, "to teach men that God made nothing mortal: but that all the works of God are immortal, while mortal things are the works of others. Accordingly, the soul is the work of God, but the body has a different nature: and in this respect a human differs nothing from a bat, or a worm, or a frog: for the matter of all these is the same, and their corruptibility is the same."* I, however, would desire anyone—after hearing the grand words of Celsus saying that the writing titled *The Dispute of Jason and Papiscus concerning Christ* is worthy not of laughter but of hatred—to take the little work into his hands and spend some labor in reading it, so that, being truly taught, he may condemn the empty talk of Celsus, finding nothing there worthy of hatred. For if he approaches the reading with an incorrupt mind, he will find nothing even ridiculous in it, in which a Christian is introduced disputing with a Jew, and proving from the very letters of the Jews that whatever was predicted concerning Christ by the Prophets applies to Jesus, even though the adversary contradicts him strenuously and in a sufficiently Jewish manner. Furthermore, I do not know how he joined things which nature does not allow to coexist in the human mind, calling the book worthy of both pity and hatred: since it is certain that he who is pitied cannot meanwhile be held in hatred, nor conversely can he who is hated be deemed worthy of pity for that time. Celsus further denies that it is his purpose to refute those things because, even without a refutation, it is manifest that they are worthy of both pity and hatred. We, however, pray that all who happen upon this our apology against him will not find it burdensome to attend to the writings of our people, and as much as possible, to gather their meaning from the writings themselves, as well as their conscience and purpose: for he will find men fervently contending for those things of which they are persuaded
