<margin>* to me at least.</margin> <note>The Greek margin contains a variant or emphasis of the phrase "to me at least" (ἐμοὶ γ’ οὖν).</note>

...is set forth, as is the history concerning Moses, and Jannes, and Jambres. But we do not pride ourselves in that; rather we accept him more than Celsus and other Greeks, as he wished to examine our affairs with a love of learning, and was moved by them as writings that were allegorized <term>tetropologemenon: interpreted figuratively or through tropes</term> and not foolish. Next to these things, having selected from all writings those containing allegories—not having related them in a contemptible style, but rather something simpler and able to contribute something for the sake of faith to the many and the simpler sort, yet not giving enough to move the more intelligent—he says, "such as the dispute of a certain Papiscus and Jason which I have known, worthy not of laughter, but rather of pity and hatred." *To me at least* it still remains to refute these things. "For everything is clear to everyone, and especially if one would endure and read the writings themselves above all. But I wish rather to teach concerning nature, that God made nothing mortal; but whatever is immortal is the work of God, while mortal things are the work of those others. And the soul, indeed, is the work of God; but the body is of another nature. And in this, the body of a human will differ nothing from that of a bat, or a worm, or a frog. For the matter is the same, and the corruptibility is identically similar." I would desire anyone at all, having heard Celsus speaking grandly and claiming that the writing entitled *The Dispute of Jason and Papiscus concerning Christ* is worthy not of laughter but of hatred, to take the little book into his hands and endure to read and hear what is in it, so that he may immediately condemn the vanity of Celsus, finding nothing worthy of hatred in the book. And if one reads it without prejudice, he will find that the book does not even move one to laughter, in which a Christian is recorded conversing with a Jew from the Jewish scriptures, and showing that the prophecies concerning the Christ fit Jesus; and indeed the other party stands against the argument in a manner not ignoble nor unbefitting the Jewish persona. I do not know how he brought together things that are unmixed, and which by nature do not happen to a human at the same time, saying "that book is worthy of pity and hatred." For everyone will agree that the one being pitied is not hated when he is pitied, and the one being hated is not pitied when he is hated. Because of this, Celsus says he does not take it upon himself to refute these things, since they are somehow clear to everyone, even regarding the titled refutation, as being base and worthy of both pity and hatred. But we exhort the one who happens upon this apology written against the accusation of Celsus, to read and listen to our writings, and, with all one's power, to judge from what has been written the purpose of those who wrote them, and their conscience, and their disposition; for he will find men fervently contending for those things which they have understood;

Celsus thinks this is an argument that none of these things are the work of God, but rather that qualities arise from one another in some unknown order, and that the wisdom of God does nothing in their alteration. 

Furthermore, when Celsus says, "the soul is indeed the work of God, but the nature of the body is something else," he not only puts forth this doctrine without proof, but he does not even distinguish whether he means *every* soul is the work of God, or only the *rational* soul. We respond: if every soul is the work of God, then without doubt even the souls of brutes or the most vile creatures are His work, so that the nature of every body is different from that of the soul. Certainly, in the following discourse, where he even says that brutes are dearer to God than we are, he attributes to them a purer understanding of divinity than we possess; from which it follows that the souls of brutes are no less the work of God than our own. 

But if only the rational soul is the work of God, first of all, you did not express this clearly. Secondly, because you spoke indefinitely, implying not every soul but only the rational one is God's work, it follows that it is not the case that every body has a nature different from that of souls. But if not every body has a different nature, but rather the body of each living thing is appropriate to the reason of its own soul, then it follows that the animal whose soul is the work of God has a body that differs from a body inhabited by a soul which is *not* the work of God. And thus, it will be false to say there is no difference between the body of a man and the body of a bat, or a frog, or a worm. For it is absurd to hold that stones differ from stones and buildings from buildings—some being considered purer or more defiled because they were built either in honor of God or as a receptacle for vile and impure bodies—and yet to claim that bodies do not differ whether they are inhabited by rational or irrational beings, or even that human bodies do not differ among themselves, whether they belong to the good or the worst of men. But if, distorting the concept of immortality, he says that the world is immortal for this very reason—that although it is corruptible, it is nevertheless not destroyed, as if it were capable of death but does not die—it appears that according to his opinion there will be something simultaneously mortal and immortal, since it is capable of both; and it will be a mortal thing that does not die, and though not immortal by nature, it will be called immortal because it does not die. In what sense, then, does he wish it to be understood when he says that *nothing immortal is produced from matter*? Do you see how, if his opinions are examined, nothing solid is found in them that cannot be contradicted? Having said these things, he remarks, *that enough has been said on this for now, and if anyone desires to hear more, it should be sought in what follows.* Let us therefore, we who are "senseless" in his opinion, see what follows if for a little while we can listen more diligently to the varied and not-to-be-despised question concerning the nature of evils, which he explains quite remarkably in a few words—to speak more easily—in this manner: *Evils in things can be neither more nor fewer, neither before, nor now, nor in the future. For the nature of all things is one and the same, and the generation of evils is always the same.* These things also seem to be translated from the *Theaetetus* in other words, where Plato introduces Socrates speaking thus: *But it is not possible for evils to be removed from among men, nor for them to take hold among the Gods*, <note>original: "Sed neque ut ex hominibus mala tollantur potest fieri, neque ut apud Deos hæreant"</note> and what follows. Although it seems to me that he has not even listened sufficiently to Plato, he who thinks to embrace the truth in this one little book, to which he gave the title *The True Word* <term>True Word: Origen refers to Celsus's lost work, 'Alethes Logos'</term> written against us. For those words in the *Timaeus*, *As often as the gods purge the earth with water*, indicate that the earth, having been purged by water, has fewer evils than it had before it was purged. And we say this according to Plato’s opinion: that evils are sometimes diminished, since they cannot be removed entirely from men, just as we heard him teaching previously in the *Theaetetus*. Furthermore, I do not know how it happens that, while he seems to favor providence <term>providentia: the divine care or guidance of God/nature</term> at least in this volume, he now says that evils become neither more nor fewer, but are always as if in a fixed number—meanwhile doing away with that most beautiful doctrine, that wickedness is not circumscribed, and that evils by their own nature are innumerable. Therefore, if there were, are, or will be neither more nor fewer evils, it seems to follow that—just as according to the opinion of those who say the world will never perish, providence maintains the equilibrium of the elements, not allowing any of them to prevail, lest the world fall into danger—

<column-break/>

the work will be destroyed; then, in the destruction of the world, what will the soul, the work of God, do? Let Celsus say. But if, perverting the notion of the immortal, he says that the world, though corruptible, is not destroyed and is thus immortal—as being receptive of death, yet not dying—it is clear that according to him there will be something at once mortal and immortal, being receptive of both; and it will be a mortal thing not dying, and that which is not immortal by nature, by virtue of not dying, is uniquely called immortal. According to what meaning, then, does he assert that *no offspring of matter is immortal*? And you see that when the thoughts in his writings are pressed and tortured, they are proven not to admit of [necessary] irrefutable consistency. And having said these things, he adds, "that these things concerning this are sufficient; and if anyone is able to hear and seek more, he will know." Let us then, the "foolish" ones according to him, see what will follow, and how we might be able to hear and seek these things even for a little while. Following these, the things sought through many and not-to-be-despised arguments in various ways concerning the nature of evils, and interpreted differently, he thinks to teach us to learn in a few words, saying, "Evils among existing things could become neither fewer nor more, neither before, nor now, nor again. For the nature of the whole is one, and the same generation of evils is always the same." And these things seem to have been paraphrased from the passage in the *Theaetetus*, in which the Socrates of Plato said, <margin>Plato's Theaetetus.</margin> "But it is neither possible for evils to perish from among men, nor for them to be established among the gods," and so forth. It seems to me that he has not accurately heard even Plato, he who supposes the truth to be in this one composition of his, which he entitled *The True Word*, the book against us. For the passage in the *Timaeus* saying, "Whenever the gods <margin>Plato's Timaeus.</margin> purge the earth with water," will show that the earth being purged by the waters has fewer evils than in the time before the purging. And we say this according to Plato, that evils are sometimes fewer, because of the passage in the *Theaetetus* saying that evils cannot perish from among men. But I do not know in what manner, while positing providence—at least as far as the words of this book go—he says that evils are neither more nor fewer, but as it were fixed; destroying a most beautiful doctrine concerning the fact that wickedness is undefined, and that evils, by their own definition, are infinite. And it seems to follow from the idea that neither fewer nor more evils have been, or are, or shall be, that just as according to those who say the world is by nature incorruptible, the equilibrium of the elements occurs by providence, not permitting one of them to take more than its share, lest the world be destroyed;

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4

->Thus, as if by a kind of providence, a limit is set upon evils and their quantity, so that they become neither more nor less.<- Celsus’s argument regarding evil is also refuted by those who have philosophically examined the nature of good and evil, and who have demonstrated from history that, originally, courtesans <note>Greek: *hetairai*</note> lived outside the city and wore masks when they hired themselves out to those who desired them. Later, out of contempt for decency, they laid aside their masks; yet, because the laws did not permit them to enter the cities, they remained outside. But as moral corruption increased daily, they eventually dared to enter the cities themselves. **Chrysippus** <note>A famous Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BCE) known for his extensive writings on ethics and logic.</note> says this in his *Introduction to Good and Evil*. From this, since evils increase and decrease, one can see that those called "ambiguous" <note>Greek: *amphiboloi*; a term for those who took both active and passive roles in sexual acts</note> were once outcasts, both suffering and performing indecencies, and serving the lusts of those who came to them. Later, they were driven out from there by the market inspectors <note>Greek: *agoranomoi*; officials who policed public order and markets</note>. Why need I mention the countless instances of overflowing wickedness that have crept into human life which did not exist before? Certainly, the most ancient histories, though they accuse sinners of countless faults, know nothing of "unspeakable acts" <note>Greek: *arrhetopoiia*; likely referring to specific sexual perversions or taboos not mentioned in older records</note>. How then, from these and similar facts, does Celsus not appear ridiculous for thinking that evils never become more or less? For even if the nature of the universe is one and the same, it does not follow that the production of evil is always the same. Just as the nature of an individual human is one and the same, yet the state of his governing mind, his reason, and his actions are not always the same—sometimes he is less mature, sometimes he adopts evil with reason (and this evil is either more or less widespread), and sometimes he progresses toward virtue, either to a greater or lesser degree—so it is better to say of the nature of the universe: that even if it is one and the same in kind, the same things do not always happen throughout the whole. For there are not always fertile seasons, nor always heavy rains, nor always droughts. In the same way, there are no fixed seasons of "fertility" or "barrenness" for better souls, nor a constant spread of worse ones. It is necessary for those who wish to accurately understand the nature of bodies to realize that the state of evils does not remain the same, because of the Providence that either maintains abundance on earth or purifies it with floods and conflagrations <note>Refers to the Stoic and Platonic ideas of periodic destruction by water (cataclysm) or fire (ekpyrosis) to cleanse the world.</note>. And perhaps it is not only the things on earth, but also the things in the whole world that require purification when wickedness has spread too far within it. After this, Celsus says: "The nature of evils is not easy to know for one who has not studied philosophy, but it is sufficient for the multitude to be told..."

<column-break/>

...to the truth: so also a certain providence presides over evils, which commands them to maintain an equality, without increases or decreases. There is also another argument by which Celsus's opinion on evils is refuted, taken from the disputation of philosophers on goods and evils, who teach from histories that at first, masked harlots prostituted themselves to the lust of passers-by outside the cities; then, along with their shame, they laid aside their masks; yet they remained outside, kept away by the laws; finally, as discipline became more depraved day by day, they dared to penetrate inside the cities. **Chrysippus** says these things in his introductory book on goods and evils; from which it is permitted to gather that evils increase and diminish according to the time: since there were once those who were called "ambiguous," excelling at enduring or inflicting disgrace, and serving the lust of those entering to them, who were finally cast out by the aediles <note>Latin: *aedilibus*; Roman officials in charge of public buildings and regulation of public order</note>. Furthermore, innumerable examples of most profuse malice have crept into the life of men, of which it can truly be said that they were not there before. Certainly, ancient histories, although they may charge men with innumerable sins, do not know of the unspeakable lusts of the mouth. Is not Celsus therefore shown to be ridiculous through these and similar things, thinking that evils never increase or decrease? For though the nature of things be one and the same, the crop of evils is not always the same. For just as when the nature of any man is one and the same, yet he does not always act or understand in the same way—but he who was just now scarcely in possession of reason, has now with reason assumed malice also, and that now more contracted, now more diffused; likewise in virtue he now advances, now fails, and sometimes may profit excellently in the contemplation of it with greater or lesser zeal—so it is permitted to pronounce concerning the universal nature of things, that although it be one and the same in kind, yet similar things do not always and everywhere happen; for there are not always fertilities, nor sterilities, nor rains, nor droughts: so neither is there always a good crop of good souls, or always a bad one, with evils also reigning now more widely, now more narrowly. And this persuasion concerning evils not always remaining in the same state is necessary for the searchers of truth, because of the providence caring for earthly things, and purging them now with fires, now with floods: and perhaps not only these, but also the whole world, when malice grows so strong in it that it has need of a purging. After this Celsus proceeds: "To know the nature of evils is difficult for those not philosophizing, and it is enough that the common people be taught..."

<summary>Origen argues against Celsus's view that evil is a constant quantity in the universe, citing the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus and historical shifts in public morality to prove that wickedness increases and decreases over time. He suggests that God uses natural disasters like floods and fires to periodically purge the world of excessive evil.</summary>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 4.

->*Evil does not come from God, but matter is occupied with evil; and the cycles of mortal things are similar to one another from the beginning to the end, following appointed revolutions: therefore it is necessary that the same things have always been, are now, and shall be.*<- Here Celsus says that the origin of evils is not easily known by those who do not practice philosophy, as if a student of philosophy could easily know their origin, while one void of philosophy could not easily contemplate the source of evils—though he might, albeit with difficulty and great labor. We, however, in responding, add that the origin of evils is not easily known even by those who practice philosophy, unless by the breathing of divine favor <note>Latin: *divino favore aspirante*; Greek: *Θεοῦ ἐπιπνοίᾳ*. Origen emphasizes that grace, not just intellect, is required for true understanding.</note> the evils are brought to light, and it becomes manifest from where they subsist, and it is understood how they are to be removed. Since, therefore, among other evils is the failure to know God, and what is worst, to be ignorant of piety and the manner of worshipping the celestial deity; it is established, even by Celsus’s own testimony, that students of philosophy have been ignorant of these things, as is clear from their disagreeing sects. In our opinion, moreover, no one who is ignorant that it is an evil to think that piety consists in those common laws of cities <note>Origen is critiquing "civil religion" or the idea that following local pagan customs constitutes true worship.</note> will be able to understand the origin of evils. Furthermore, no one who is ignorant of the one they call the devil, and his angels—who this devil was before, and how he became the devil, and for what cause those who are called his angels revolted with him—will be able to know the origin of evils. It is also necessary for him who is to arrive at the knowledge of this origin to treat diligently of demons, and to know that they are not the work of God insofar as they are demons, but insofar as they are rational beings; and from where they fell so as to become such, and how their rational nature was brought into the order of demons. Therefore, if there is any other topic in human affairs difficult for our nature to scrutinize, the origin of evils may rightly be numbered among them. Then, as if he held some other more secret thing concerning this origin, which he passed over to speak words suited to the common multitude, he says it suffices to preach to the common people about the birth of evils: that they are not from God, but adhere to matter and dwell among mortal things. It is indeed true that evils are not from God, for our Jeremiah clearly teaches: *Out of the mouth of the Lord shall not proceed evil and good:* <margin>Lamentations 3:38</margin> <column-break/> but that matter, which dwells among mortals, is the cause of evils, is false in our opinion. For each person's own reason <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *ἡγεμονικόν* (hegemonikon). In Stoic and Christian thought, this refers to the "commanding faculty" or the seat of the will.</note> is the cause of the wickedness existing in him, which is itself the evil; as are the evil actions which <margin>* [Greek note regarding a textual variant in the word "origin"]</margin> <margin>* [Greek note correcting "evilly" to "evil"]</margin>

...and another thing besides that, according to a precise account, is what we consider to be evil. But I know that this argument requires much elaboration and preparation (by the grace of God illuminating the ruling faculty <note>original: *hegemonikon* — the Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul</note>) for those judged by God to be * worthy of this level of knowledge. I do not know why it seemed useful to Celsus, in writing against us, to present a doctrine that requires much—even if only apparent—demonstration to be at all * persuasive: namely, that "the cycle of mortal things is the same from beginning to end, and according to fixed revolutions, it is necessary that the same things have always happened, are happening, and will happen." If this were true, our free will is destroyed. For if, according to fixed revolutions, it is necessary that the same things always have happened, are happening, and will happen in the cycle of mortal things, it is clear that it is necessary that Socrates will always practice philosophy, and will be accused for * introducing new deities and for the corruption of the youth. And Anytus and Meletus will always accuse him; and the council of the Areopagus will * condemn him; and he will die by hemlock. In the same way, it is necessary that according to fixed periods Phalaris will always act as a tyrant, and Alexander of Pherae will commit the same cruelties, and those condemned to the bull of Phalaris will always bellow within it. If these things are granted, I do not know how our free will can be saved, or how praise and blame can be reasonably assigned. It will follow first from such a hypothesis of Celsus—"that if the cycle of mortal things is always the same from beginning to end, and according to fixed revolutions it is necessary that the same things always have happened, are happening, and will happen"—then it is necessary that according to fixed periods Moses will always go out of Egypt with the people of the Jews, and Jesus will again reside in this life to do the same things, which he has done not once, but infinitely many times according to the cycles. Furthermore, the same Christians will exist in the fixed revolutions; and Celsus will write this book again, having written it infinitely many times before. Now, if Celsus says that "only the cycle of mortal things and the fixed revolutions necessarily have always happened, are happening, and will happen," most of the Stoics say that not only is the cycle of mortal things such, but also that of the immortals and of those they consider Gods. For after the conflagration of the universe <note>original: *ekpyrosis* — the Stoic belief that the world is periodically consumed by fire and reborn</note>, which has happened infinitely many times and will happen infinitely many times, the same order of all things from beginning to end has occurred and will occur. However, attempting to somehow heal the contradictions, the followers of the Porch <note>The Stoics</note> say, I know not how, that in each cycle all people will be "indistinguishable" from those in previous cycles; so that it is not Socrates who is born again, but someone "indistinguishable" from Socrates, who will marry an "indistinguishable" Xanthippe, and be accused—

<margin>* new [deities].</margin>
<margin>* condemn.</margin>

...arise from it: nor is there anything else that is evil according to our most exquisite examination. But I know this dispute has need of many exercises and confirmations which (by divine grace illustrating the mind) can be present in him whom God judges worthy of it, and of this knowledge which regards this place. I do not know, however, why it seemed expedient to Celsus, writing against us, to make mention of a dogma which has need of at least a likely proof, so that, as far as possible, it might be confirmed: *that from the beginning even to the end the circuits of mortal things become similar among themselves, and it is necessary by fixed revolutions that all the same things which have already been done, be done again, and shall be in the future.* By which it happens that it is necessary always for Socrates to philosophize and be accused on account of new demons and the depravation of youth: and for Anytus and Meletus always to accuse him, and the senate of the Areopagites always to condemn him to drink the hemlock: by the same reason it will be necessary always, the turns having been revolved, for Phalaris to exercise tyranny, and Alexander of Pherae to be the rival of his cruelty: always for the condemned to bellow in the bull of Phalaris. Which if it be granted, I know not how our will shall be preserved, or what place will be left for deserved praise or blame. And it will be necessary, if Celsus speaks the truth, by certain turns of recurring times that all the same things were, are, and shall be again, so that Moses, by returning turns, may more often go out from Egypt together with the people of the Jews: Jesus also may come again into the life of men, about to do all the same things which he had done before, not once, but many times, as often as the time of his advent shall have been revolved. The Christian religion also will have its vicissitudes of rising and falling at fixed times, and again Celsus will write his book, already written by him a thousand times before. And Celsus indeed asserts only the circuits of mortal things and fixed revolutions, so that necessarily all the same things have been, are, and are to be: but most of the Stoics bring these same circuits even into immortal things and those of the Gods, whom they themselves imagine: for after the universal conflagration having been made and to be made infinitely, in the same order from the beginning even to the end all the same things already done shall recur again to be done. The Stoics however, that they may heal the absurdity, I know not how, say that those similar in all things to the prior ones return with the circles of times, so that not Socrates is born again, but one similar to Socrates in all things, about to marry one similar in all things to the prior...

Truly, I do not understand how, since the world is always the same and not merely another world similar in all respects to the previous one, the things contained within it are not the same, but only of an indistinguishable similarity. But to discuss these matters more at length against Celsus and the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that believed in the periodic destruction and rebirth of the universe (ekpyrosis).</note> is neither the purpose of this work nor the present time. After this he says, *that these things we see were not given for the sake of man, but that each thing exists and perishes for the preservation of the whole, one after another in the successions already mentioned*; an opinion already overturned, which it would be superfluous to attack further. Likewise, an answer has been given to his claim that *neither more nor fewer goods or evils are produced*. It has also been said that there is no need for God to correct anything made by Himself, as if He were a human craftsman mending something made with less skill, restoring the world to a better state through burnings <note>original: "exustiones" / Greek: "ekpyrosis"</note> and floods; rather, He does this to restrain the widely spreading malice <note>The term "malitia" here refers to moral evil or wickedness.</note>, and perhaps He will remove it entirely from the midst when it is advantageous for the universe. Whether it is probable that evil will return again after it has been extinguished requires its own discussion. God, therefore, wishes to restore what has collapsed through new corrections: for although He ordained all things most beautifully when He founded the world, He nevertheless had need of a certain medicine against the diseases of malice with which the whole world is infected. God neglects nothing, nor will He neglect it, but through each individual age He does what is fitting for Him to do in a world that is versatile and changeable. And just as a farmer performs various rustic labors upon the field and its crops according to the variety of the seasons of the year; so God dispenses the ages as if they were certain "years" (so to speak), doing through each of them whatever the order of this universe demands, which He alone accomplishes as He understands it most truly and clearly. In this consideration of evils, Celsus speaks among other things thus: *Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil: for you do not know what is beneficial to you, or to the whole world.* This saying, although it does not display open impiety, nevertheless suspects that the nature of evils is not entirely wretched, because it might be that what is evil for individuals is useful for the whole. It would be excessive to teach the falsehood of these things by their reversal, as the argument has already been set forth by us in principle. But whether after the vanishing of wickedness there is a reason for it to exist again or not; such things will be sought in a primary discourse. God, therefore, wishes to always take up the failings through a newer correction; for even if all things were ordered by Him most beautifully and securely according to the creation of the whole, yet there was a time when He had need of a certain medical art <margin>* for those.</margin> for those who are sick with wickedness, and for the whole world which is, as it were, defiled by it. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

<margin>

...at least a part of what is useful. It shall be said that, while the free will of each of us is preserved, even if God makes use of the wickedness of the depraved for the arrangement of the whole, assigning them to a use for the whole—nevertheless, such a person is still blameworthy. As one who is blameworthy, he has been assigned to a role that is to be avoided by the individual, yet is useful to the whole. It is as if one were to say of cities: someone who has committed certain crimes and is condemned to certain public works for those sins is useful to the whole city; he performs something useful for the entire city, yet he himself is in a state to be avoided, and one in which no person of even moderate sense would pray to be. And the apostle of Jesus, Paul, also teaches us that while even the most wicked are preserved for the use of the whole, they themselves will be among those things to be avoided; whereas the most earnest and excellent are most useful to the whole, and by their own cause will be stationed in the most beautiful place. He says: *“In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some for honor, and some for dishonor. If anyone, therefore, cleanses himself [from these], he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the master, prepared for every good work.”* I suppose it was necessary to set these things out in response to the claim: “Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear if it is evil; for you do not know what is profitable for you or for another.” This is so that no one might take an occasion for sinning from this topic, thinking they will be useful to the whole through their sin. 

Since, after this, Celsus—not understanding the expressions in Scripture about God as if they were human passions <note>The term here is "anthropopathism," attributing human emotions like anger or regret to God.</note>—mocks those passages in which voices of anger are spoken against the impious, and threats against those who have sinned; it must be said that just as we, when talking to very young children, <margin>* It is possible to [speak] from our own [strength].</margin> do not aim for the [full] extent of our own power in speaking, but adapting ourselves to the weakness of our subjects, we say these things, and even do what seems useful to us for the conversion and correction of children as children. In this way, it seems the Word of God has administered the things recorded, measuring the fitness of the promise by the capacity of the hearers and by what is useful to them. And generally <margin>Deut. 1:31. * "He carried as a nurse" & "He endured his manners." In the published book of Origen the reading is confirmed, Acts 13:18 & elsewhere.</margin> regarding such a manner of the promise concerning God, it is said in Deuteronomy: *“The Lord your God carried you as a nurse, just as a man might carry his son.”* <note>Origen notes a linguistic variant here between "carrying as a nurse" (etrophophoresen) and "bearing with manners" (etropophoresen). He argues God adapts His "manners" to human capacity.</note> Thus, having "borne with their manners"—as if the Word had assumed the manners of a man for the benefit of men—He says such things. Even so, the many who claim to know God do not see that these things are spoken in a way fitting to Him; but whoever cares for the clarity of the divine Scriptures will find that He elevates the things said to a spiritual level, comparing the will of those things to the "spiritual" ones, as they are called...

<column-break/>

...certainly able to contribute: I say that, while the will of each of us remains intact, even if God uses the malice of wicked men for the order of the things of this world, so that they contribute something to the worldly Commonwealth; nevertheless, whoever is such a person is to be blamed, and as one disapproved, he is reduced to his own rank for some use—one to be deprecated by anyone, yet contributing something to the sum of things. Just as in cities it can be shown that this or that person, condemned for crimes to public labor, is indeed useful to the Commonwealth, but in a function which everyone who is even moderately wise finds abominable. Furthermore, the apostle of Jesus, Paul, teaching us, says that even the most wicked are indeed of some use to the universe, yet in their own place among the abominable; but that every best man is likewise most useful to the universe, and for that reason is established in a most excellent place, saying: *“In a great house, he says, there are not only vessels of gold or silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, others for ignominy: if anyone therefore shall have purged himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to his lord, prepared for every good work.”* And so I think enough has been answered to that saying: *“Even if something seems evil to you, it is not yet clear whether it is evil; for you do not know what it contributes to you, or to another, or to the whole world”*: lest perhaps someone should seize an occasion for sinning from the investigation of this topic, as if by sinning he could contribute something to the university of things. After this, since Celsus, not understanding, censures the words of Scripture for attributing human affections to God, as it seems, whenever He makes Him attacking the impious angrily and threateningly; it must be said that just as we, dealing with small children, do not look to our own powers of speaking, but adapt our words to their sense as much as we can, and we educate and instruct children in a childish way, as we think suitable for them: so the divine wisdom seems to have woven the Scriptures to the measure of the hearers, judging that to be decorous for itself which is useful for them. Concerning this custom of God addressing men, these things are read in Deuteronomy: *“The Lord your God accommodated Himself to your manners, just as a father accommodates himself to his son.”* Surely the Scripture speaks in the manner of men for the utility of the multitude, for it would not have been for the benefit of the common multitude if the person of God were introduced speaking according to His own majesty. However, he whose study it is to look clearly into the divine Scriptures will find spiritual things being said to the spiritual (as they are called), comparing among themselves the mind of those things which...

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

things which are said either to the weaker sort or for the sake of exercise, are oftentimes so blended that both types are found in the same context. Therefore, when we name the "wrath of God," we do not mean an emotional effect in Him, but rather something employed for the purpose of a harsher discipline to instruct men who are subject to so many and such great sins. For it is manifest that the so-called wrath and fury of God educates men—and that this is pleasing to the Divine Word—from what is said in the sixth Psalm: *O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor instruct me in thy wrath.* <note>original: "Domine, nè in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua erudias me." Origen argues that "wrath" is a tool for education, not a loss of control.</note> So also Jeremiah says: *Instruct us, O Lord, but in judgment; and not in fury, lest thou bring us to a small number.* Now, if anyone should read in the second book of Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 24:1.</note> that the wrath of God persuaded David to number the people, and in the first book of Chronicles that it was the Devil; and if he examines and compares these texts with one another, he will see in what sense "wrath" is used—of which Paul says all men were children, saying: *We were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.* Furthermore, that wrath is not an emotion of God, but that each person brings it upon himself by his own sins, Paul will teach in these words: *Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, and tolerance, and gentleness, not knowing that the goodness of God invites you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, in which the righteous judgment of God shall appear.* How, then, can anyone "treasure up" wrath for himself in the day of wrath, if you understand wrath as an emotion? Or how can an emotional state of wrath provide instruction? Moreover, the Word which teaches us by no means to be angry, saying in the thirty-sixth Psalm: *Cease from anger and leave off fury;* and in Paul: *Put away all these things: anger, fury, malice, slandering, and foul language;* would it ever attribute to God an emotion from which it wishes us to be free? It is apparent, then, that the wrath of God is spoken of figuratively, even from the fact that in the same Scriptures His "sleep" is also recorded, from which the Prophet speaks as if awakening Him: *Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?* Again, elsewhere it says: *The Lord arose as if from sleep, like a mighty man recovering from a hangover.* <note>original: "tanquam robustus à crapula." A bold biblical metaphor comparing God's "awakening" to a man shaking off the effects of wine.</note> If, therefore, "sleep" signifies something other here than in daily use, what forbids "wrath" also to be understood figuratively? Indeed, even threats are announcements of coming calamity to sinners, no differently than if one were to call "threats" the words of a physician forewarning a patient: "I will cut you, and apply cauteries to you, unless you obey my prescriptions, and unless you use this diet and conduct yourself in this manner." Therefore, these are not human...

<column-break/>

...things said to the weaker ones, and those announced for the sake of exercise, often hearing each of the forms lying in the same expression. We say, then, that the named "wrath of God" is not a passion in Him, but something taken up for the leading of a more somber discipline, educating those who have sinned in such ways and to such an extent. For that the so-called wrath of God and His named fury educates—and this is pleasing to the Word—is clear from it being said in the sixth Psalm: *Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor instruct me in your wrath.* And in Jeremiah: *Instruct us, Lord, but in judgment; and not in fury, lest you make us few.* And if one reads in the second book of Kings of the wrath of God persuading David to number the people, but in the first book of Chronicles, the Devil; and examining the sayings together, he will see to what "wrath" is assigned; of which Paul also says all men have become children, saying: *We were by nature children of wrath, as also the rest.* And that wrath is not a passion of God, but each one prepares this for himself through the things he sins; Paul will show in: *Or do you despise the wealth of his kindness, and forbearance, and longsuffering, being ignorant that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath in a day of wrath, and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* How then can one treasure up for himself wrath in a day of wrath, if we consider wrath the passion? And how can a passion of wrath be able to educate? But also the Word teaching us in no way to be angry, and saying in the thirty-sixth Psalm: *Cease from anger, and abandon fury;* and saying also in Paul: *Put away also all things: anger, fury, malice, blasphemy, shameful speaking;* would the passion be attributed to God himself, which he wishes to rid us of entirely? It is indeed clear that the things concerning the wrath of God are spoken figuratively, from the fact that "sleep" is also ascribed to him, from which as if awakening him the prophet says: *Arise, why do you sleep, Lord?* And again he says: *And the Lord was awakened as one sleeping, as a mighty man who has been overcome with wine.* If therefore sleep signifies something else, and not that which the obvious reception of the word shows; why shall not wrath be understood similarly? And the threats are announcements concerning the things that will meet the wicked; as if one called "threats" the medical words of such a doctor, saying to the sick man: *I will cut you, and I will bring cauteries to you, if you are not persuaded by the rules, and in such a way by diet, or lead yourself in such a way;* not human...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s "True Word." The previous section likely dealt with the nature of God’s immutability; here, Origen addresses Celsus’s mockery of divine "anger" and the purpose of creation.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

...we do not attach passions to God, nor do we hold impious opinions about Him, nor do we lead anyone astray with such narratives; rather, we attempt to draw out the true meaning by comparing passages of the Scripture itself with one another. Nor is there any other purpose for those among us who skillfully represent the Word than to free the listeners from ignorance <note>original: "conscience" or "shared ignorance"</note> as much as possible and to make them wise. 

Following this, because he has not understood what has been written regarding the "anger" of God, Celsus says: **"Is it not ridiculous? When a man was angry with the Jews, he destroyed them all from youth up and burned their city, so utterly were they reduced to nothing; yet the 'Greatest God,' as they say, being angry and moved to wrath and threatening, sends His own Son, and he suffers such things?"** 

Certainly, if the Jews were destroyed from youth up and burned with fire, it was not from any other "anger" than that which they stored up for themselves <note>A reference to Romans 2:5</note> after they dared to commit such a deed against Jesus. This judgment of God against them—occurring by God's decree—is called "anger" according to a certain educational custom of the Hebrew nation. Furthermore, the Son of the Greatest God suffered willingly for the salvation of mankind, as we have stated to the best of our ability in the preceding pages.

After this he says: **"But so that my argument may not be about the Jews alone (for that was necessary to say), but about the whole of nature, as I promised, I will make what was said before more clear."** 

Now, any moderate person reading these things, being aware of human weakness, would not accept the offensive weight of one "promising to give an account of the whole of nature," a boastful claim similar to the arrogance with which he dared to title his book <note>Celsus titled his work "The True Word," which Origen considers peak arrogance</note>. Let us see, then, what these things are which he promises to say about the whole of nature, and what he will reveal. 

Through many subsequent points, he accuses us of claiming that God made all things for the sake of man. He wishes to show—from the history of animals and the cleverness <term>sagacity: the apparent intelligence or instinctual skill shown by animals</term> displayed by them—that all things were made no more for the sake of humans than for the sake of irrational animals. It seems to me he is doing something similar to those who, out of hatred for their enemies, accuse them of the very things for which their own dearest friends are praised. For just as hatred blinds these people so that they do not see they are accusing their own friends while they think they are speaking ill of their enemies; in the same way, Celsus, his reasoning being muddled, has not seen that he is also accusing the philosophers of the **Stoic** school. They rightly prefer man—and rational nature in general—above all irrational creatures, saying that Providence made all things primarily for the sake of rational nature. For rational beings hold the primary place, like children; while irrational and inanimate things are compared to the status of a household possession <note>original: "comparable to the place of property or furniture"</note> in relation to the children.

* indeed
* to him
* need and of needs
* being compared
</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for scholars.</note>

...we do not feign passions for God, nor do we conceive impious opinions of Him, nor do we deceive anyone with narrations of this kind, since we elicit the true sense from the passages of Scripture itself compared among themselves. Nor is there any other purpose for our teachers than to remove raw simplicity from the listeners and to bring in wisdom as much as they can. 

Then, as one not understanding what has been written about the anger of God, he says: *“Is it not ridiculous, when a man, angry at the Jews, killed all the youths and even burned their cities, so utterly were they overthrown: that the supreme God, angry as they say, and stirred by fury and threatening, would send His son to suffer such punishments?”* 

Certainly, because the city of the Jews was destroyed by flames and the youths slain after such a bold crime was perpetrated against Jesus, this happened to them from no other anger than that which they long accumulated for themselves, finally poured out upon them at once by God the just judge, called "anger" according to the idiom of their native language. Furthermore, the Son of God suffered willingly and knowingly whatever he suffered for the salvation of men, as we have shown above to the best of our strength. 

After this he says: *“But lest I deal only with the Jews, for this was not my purpose, but I shall speak of the whole nature of things, as I promised, I will more plainly declare what has already been said.”* 

Who, being modest and conscious of human infirmity, would not marvel at this promiser boastfully promising that he would render an account for the entire nature of things, with the same arrogance with which he previously dared to prefix such a magnificent title to his writing. But let us see what this is that he promises he will say for the whole nature of things, and what that declaration is. 

He accuses us at length, *“Because we say God made all things for the sake of man:”* and he attempts, from the history of animals and the skill which they display, to show that all things were made no more for the sake of men than for the sake of brutes; and he seems to me to speak just like those who, out of hatred for enemies, disparage even those things which are most praiseworthy in their own friends. For just as hatred blinds these men, lest they see that in the meantime they are accusing their closest friends while they think they are speaking ill of their enemies; in the same way Celsus, whose reason is disturbed, did not see that he was attacking the **Stoics**, who rightly place man and rational nature in general before all brutes, since they say all things were made by providence for the sake of this nature: wherefore rational beings, as the more powerful, obtain the place of children, but the brute and inanimate things that of a possession compared to the children.

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...the grace of children. Indeed, it seems to me that just as in cities the clerks of the market <note>original: "ædiles" / "ἀγορανόμοι" — officials in charge of public order and the monitoring of markets</note> take care of the marketplace and the goods for sale, yet the dogs and other brute animals also enjoy that abundance; so by providence the rational animal is primarily cared for, while the brutes consequently enjoy those things prepared for the use of humans. And just as he errs who says that the market clerks take no more care for men than for dogs, because the dogs also enjoy the abundance of the market along with the men; so Celsus and those who think like him are impious toward the God who provides for the rational creature, by saying that He nourishes men no more than stalks, trees, herbs, and thorns. For he opines first that *thunder, lightning, and rain are not the works of God*, now more openly playing the Epicurean <note>Epicurus taught that the gods do not intervene in human affairs and that natural phenomena have purely physical causes</note>: then he says, *even if we grant that these are the works of God, they are no more made for the nourishment of us humans than for stalks, trees, herbs, and thorns*. A true Epicurean thinks these things happen by chance, not according to providence: for if these things benefit us no more than stalks, trees, herbs, and thorns, it is manifest that they do not come from providence; or if they do come from it, it provides no more for us than for stalks, trees, herbs, and thorns. To believe either is impious: and it is folly to try to find us guilty of impiety with such arguments. For it is clear enough from what has been said who is truly impious. *But if*, he says, *you say these things grow for men, namely stalks, trees, herbs, and thorns, why do these grow more for men than for brutes or even the most savage wild beasts?* Therefore, let Celsus say with a hardened brow <note>A Latin idiom meaning "shamelessly"</note> that such various species of things growing from the earth are produced not by the operation of providence, but by a fortuitous collision of atoms: and that it is also a matter of chance that so many various forms of stalks, trees, and herbs are similar to one another by kind, and that there is no craftsmanship in them, nor do they have their beginning from a Mind that surpasses all admiration. But we Christians, who attribute these things to the one God as author, and give thanks to Him as the creator of all, who has prepared such a dwelling for us, and for the animals that serve us for our sake, He who *makes grass grow for the cattle, and green herbs for the service of men, and brings forth bread from the earth, and wine to gladden the heart of man, and makes his face shine with oil, and strengthens his heart with bread.* <margin>Psalm 103: 15, 16, 17 <note>In modern bibles, this is Psalm 104:14-15</note></margin> But if He has also prepared food for the most savage of beasts, it is no wonder, since even

And just as he is in error who says the market-wardens care no more for men than for dogs, since the dogs also enjoy the abundance of the goods; so much more do Celsus and those who hold the same views as he act impiously toward the God who provides for rational beings, saying: "Why are these things produced for the food of men any more than for plants, trees, herbs, and thorns?" For he thinks first that thunder, lightning, and rain are not the works of God—now more clearly playing the Epicurean—and secondly he says, "that even if one were to grant these are the works of God, they are produced no more for the food of us men than for plants, trees, herbs, and thorns." For if these things are no more useful to us than to plants, trees, herbs, and thorns, it is clear that they do not come from providence; or they come from a providence that cares no more for us than for a tree, a herb, or a thorn. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

<margin>

...certain philosophers have said that these things were created for the sake of exercising the rational animal <note>i.e., humanity</note>. And one of our own wise men says somewhere: *Do not say, "What is this for?" for all things have been created for their own use; and do not say, "What is this for?" for all things will be sought out in their own time.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ εἴπῃς, εἰς τί τοῦτο; ... πάντα γὰρ ἐν καιρῷ αὐτῶν ζητηθήσεται.</note> Following this, Celsus—wishing to show that Providence has not produced the things that grow upon the earth for us any more than for the wildest of irrational animals—says: "For we, with toil and great suffering, can scarcely and with difficulty feed ourselves; but for them, all things grow without sowing or plowing." He fails to see that God, wishing human intelligence to be exercised everywhere so that it might not remain idle and ignorant of the arts, made man a creature of needs. It was through this very need that man was forced to invent arts—some for food, others for shelter. For it was better for those who were not yet ready to seek divine things and practice philosophy to be in want, so that they might use their intelligence to discover the arts, rather than to have such abundance that they neglected their intellect entirely.

Indeed, the lack of life's necessities gave rise to agriculture, viticulture <note>the cultivation of grapevines</note>, and the gardening arts; likewise the arts of the carpenter and the smith, which create tools for the arts that serve our nourishment. The lack of shelter introduced the art of weaving—following the carding and spinning of wool—as well as the art of building; and thus intelligence ascended even to architecture. This same lack of necessities caused the products of other places to be transported by the arts of seamanship and navigation to those who lacked them. Thus, for these reasons, one might admire Providence for making the rational being more needy than the irrational animals for its own benefit. For irrational animals have their food ready at hand, as they are not equipped for the arts; they also have natural protection, being fortified with fur, or feathers, or scales, or shells. Let these things be said in our defense against Celsus's statement: "For we with great labor and suffering are scarcely fed, while for them all things grow without sowing or plowing."

<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s arguments which attempt to lower the status of humanity to that of irrational animals. Origen is specifically addressing the claim that the universe was not made for man any more than for ants or flies.</meta>

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

not only for us the Sun and celestial bodies; but even the **stage-philosopher** <note>original: "Scenicus philosophus" referring to Euripides, known for embedding philosophy into his plays</note> says the same, he who was once a pupil of Anaxagoras the natural philosopher. Through a **synecdoche** <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>, he wishes all rational nature to be understood by the name of "man," while he says this entire machine of the world serves him. Again, he signifies this synecdochically by the terms "Sun" and "Night": unless the tragic poet took the cause for the effect, because those things which are beneath the Moon have the greatest need of day and night, whereas other creatures do not require them in the same way as those inhabiting the earth. Therefore, both day and night serve mortals, having been made for the sake of rational beings. But if ants and flies also enjoy these things with us—working by day and resting by night—it must not immediately be said that day and night exist in the world for the sake of ants and flies, or other living creatures, but rather that they were provided for the uses of men.

He [Celsus] continues: *“If anyone should call us the masters of the animals because we hunt them and prepare feasts from the entrails of those we catch, why do we not rather believe we were made for their sake, since we are intercepted and devoured by them? Moreover, we require nets and the weapons of many men and the work of dogs to catch wild beasts; but they are armed by nature with weapons by which they easily destroy us.”*

Yet even from this you can see how great a protection **intellect** has been given to us, which is more powerful than any kind of physical equipment with which wild beasts may be fortified. Thus, although we are of much weaker body than the animals, and even vastly inferior to some in size, we overcome the beasts by **reason**. We capture elephants of such great mass in the hunt, and we even tame those that can be domesticated by us, teaching them to live more mildly. Furthermore, regarding those whose nature cannot unlearn ferocity, or which, even if tamed, cannot serve our uses: consulting our own safety, we shut them up for as long as we have need of the meat of slaughtered animals for food. Just as the Creator of the world prepared the milder brutes for the service of rational man—and we have dogs for other uses, such as guarding flocks, herds, and homes; oxen for others, such as the cultivation of fields; and beasts of burden for carrying loads—so too the race of boars, bears, leopards, lions, and the like was given to us to exercise our innate courage. Then, addressing men who recognize their own excellence above other living creatures, he says: *“If you say that the power of catching and killing wild beasts was given to you by God, we shall reply that before cities were built and civil customs and arts established...”*

Athenaeus and Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 5: "The philosopher of the stage, Euripides."

...and the things in heaven; but also a certain **stage-philosopher**, the sweet-speaking listener of the natural philosophy of Anaxagoras, who, starting from the one rational being, man, says by synecdoche that all things in the universe are appointed to serve all rational beings, expressing again by synecdoche... the sun and the night. Or perhaps the tragic poet named the day from the action of the sun; teaching that those things most in need of day and night are those under the moon, and not [just] the horse, but those upon the earth. Day and night, therefore, serve mortals, having come into being for the sake of rational beings. And if ants and flies also enjoy them, being active by day and resting by night, these things having already been made for the sake of men; it must not be said that day and night exist for the sake of ants and flies; nor for nothing, but according to **Providence**, for the sake of men, one must believe these things have happened.

And he [Celsus] says, "that if anyone should call us rulers of the animals, because we hunt the other animals and dine on them; we shall say that we were no more made for them, since they hunt and eat us; but we even need nets and weapons, and the help of many men, and dogs, and the craft of hunting; but to them, immediately and by themselves, nature has given weapons, easily bringing us under their power." And here you see in what way **intelligence** has been given to us as a great aid, and better than every weapon which the wild beasts seem to have. We, at least, who are much weaker in body than the animals, and in some cases excessively smaller, prevail through intelligence over the wild beasts, and we hunt even such great elephants, subduing those naturally inclined to be tamed to our gentleness; and as many as are not so inclined, or do not seem to provide us use from taming, we keep for our safety so that, when we wish, we have such great beasts shut up; and when we need the food from their bodies, we may slay them, just like the non-wild animals. It is clear that the Creator prepared all things for the rational animal and for his natural intelligence. And we need dogs for some things, for example, for the guarding of flocks, or herds of cattle, or goats, or houses; and oxen for other things, such as for farming; and for others we use beasts of burden or carriers. So that for the exercise of the courage sown within us, the race of lions, and bears, leopards and boars, and such things, is said to be given to us. Then he says to the race of men who perceive their own superiority over the irrational animals, "that if you say God has given you the power to take wild beasts and to use them, we shall say that (as is likely) before there were cities and arts, and such..."

He counters Celsus's claim that animals are superior due to their natural weapons by highlighting that human reason and intelligence are far more effective tools for dominion and survival.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

“...their very interactions, and weapons and nets; men were snatched away and eaten by wild beasts, while beasts were hardly ever captured by men.”
Now look at this: even if we grant that there is a mutual snatching—men by beasts and beasts by men—there is a great difference in the intelligence of those who prevail through their vessels <note>original: ἀγγεῖα; likely referring to tools or traps</note> and those who prevail through cruelty or by using their intelligence to suffer nothing from the beasts. But when he speaks of cities and arts and such social interactions, he seems to have forgotten what he asserted above: “that the world is uncreated and indestructible, and that only things on earth suffer floods and conflagrations, and not all things perish at once in these.” Just as it is impossible for those who maintain the world is uncreated to name its beginning, so too there was no time when there were no cities at all, nor when arts had not yet been invented. But let us concede these points to him, even if he is inconsistent with himself and his previous statements. If, in this regard, it were absolutely the case that men were snatched and eaten by beasts, and beasts were no longer captured by men—well, if the world was indeed made according to Providence, and God stands over the whole, it is necessary that the first animals of the human race were under some protection or from a superior nature, so that in the beginning there was an interaction of the divine nature with men. This is what the poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod</note> had in mind when he said:

<margin>* seats.</margin>
> For then feasts were shared, and shared were the * seats,
> Between the immortal gods and mortal men.

And the divine word according to Moses introduced the first people hearing a more divine voice and seeing oracles, and sometimes the visits of angels of God <margin>* human nature.</margin> happening to them. For it is likely that at the beginning of the world * human nature was helped more; until, progress having been made in intelligence and the other virtues and the invention of arts, they were able to live by themselves, no longer needing those who always acted as guardians and managed them by the miraculous appearance of those ministering to the will of God. It follows from this that it is a lie that in the beginning men were snatched and eaten by beasts, while beasts were hardly ever captured by men. From these things it is clear that what is said by Celsus is false: “so that in this way at least God subjected men more to the beasts.” For God did not subject men to the beasts, but gave the beasts to be capturable by the intelligence of men and by the arts established according to that intelligence. For not without God did men devise for themselves safety from the beasts and mastery over them. But this excellent man, not noticing how many philosophers who introduce Providence...

<column-break/>

...invented, and nets and other instruments of hunting, men were often snatched and devoured by beasts, while wild animals were not usually captured by men. But see, although it is mutual between beasts and men to capture and be captured, there is nevertheless a great difference for those living by reason and the invention of arts, whether they are overcome by forgetfulness or by violence. Moreover, regarding what he says about the time before cities were founded and the gatherings of men together—I think he has forgotten that he said above the world was uncreated and incorruptible, and that only those things on earth suffered floods and fires, and not all things fell into these calamities at once. Therefore, just as the proponents of an uncreated world cannot show its beginning, so neither can they show a time when there were no cities, nor when arts were not yet invented. But let us agree with him here, even though he differs from himself; he will not immediately prove there was once a time when men were seized by beasts, and not conversely beasts by men. For, since the world was made through providence, it is necessary that the seeds of the human race were, right from the beginning, under the protection of some more powerful nature, and even then God was present to men: which the poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod</note> understanding, said:

> Common feasts and shared seats
> The gods placed with men.

Sacred Scripture also in Moses introduces those ancient men hearing the oracles of the divine voice, and seeing sometimes angels coming to them as guests. For it was right that at the beginning of the world human nature should be more assisted, until it should profit in intellect toward virtues and arts; which being invented, they could protect their life by themselves, lest they always need guardians coming frequently and miraculously to their service by the command of God. Whence it follows that those are deceived who believe that formerly men were accustomed to be devoured by beasts, while they themselves in that age made no captures of beasts. And from this it appears that what Celsus says is not true: that in this part God rather subjected man to the beasts. For he did not subject man to the wild animals, but gave reason to man, and arts, by which he could bring them into his power: for not without divine help did men think out how they might make their safety secure from the cruelty of beasts, and exercise command over them. But this distinguished man, not noticing how many philosophers who introduce providence...

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...many philosophers assert the existence of providence, and say that all things were made for the sake of rational nature. <note>original: "providentiam... propter rationalem naturam"</note> Celsus, as far as he is able, destroys not only the excellent doctrines of the Christians but also their agreement with the philosophers. He fails to see how great an impediment to piety it is if one admits that ants and bees are no less dear to God than humans. *What*, he says, *if on this account humans seem to stand above the brutes because they dwell together socially in founded cities and administer republics through magistrates: this should count for nothing, for the same is observed in ants and bees.* Certainly, he claims, bees have their own kings who are honored with royal attendance, under whose leadership they wage war, conquer, and cast out the defeated. He says there are also cities and suburbs, <note>original: "pomœria" - the open space within and without the walls of a city</note> successions of labor, and finally judgments and punishments for laziness; for the drones are slaughtered or driven away by them. But here he does not see how much difference there is between the works of reason and those of nature alone. The cause of these insect behaviors is not any internal reason (for the creatures that do these things have none), but that ancient Son of God, the King of the universe, who created irrational nature to assist, in an irrational way, those who were not deemed worthy of reason. Therefore, the cities of men consist of many legal prescriptions and many arts. Republics, empires, and powers among men are properly so called when they are honest habits and actions—or, as the common people now name them, those things which are fashioned as far as possible in imitation of the ideal. For those who brought forth the best laws, looking upon those ideals, established the forms of the republic, the magistrates, and the powers. You will find nothing of the sort among the brutes, however much Celsus attributes names to them which only suit rational beings, applying "cities," "republics," "magistrates," and "powers" to ants and bees. None of these apply to ants or bees, since they lack reason and therefore do nothing by the guidance of reason. Rather, one should admire the kindness of God extending even to the brutes, to such an extent that they can serve as an example to men and strike them with shame; so that by observing ants, men might become more industrious and less wasteful; likewise, by considering bees, they might learn to obey magistrates and distribute functions and labors among citizens for the preservation of the public safety. Perhaps even their wars teach us to wage war justly, if the situation should so demand. They do not truly have cities and suburbs, but hexagonal hives and honey-making, in which they work by turns in

<column-break/>

...and saying that she [Providence] does all things for the sake of rational beings, he [Celsus] destroys (as much as in him lies) the useful doctrines in this agreement between Christians <gloss>Christians</gloss> and philosophy. Nor does he see what a hindrance to piety arises from accepting that man differs nothing from ants or bees in the eyes of God. For he says, "If on this account humans seem to differ from the irrational animals, because they inhabit cities and use a constitution, and offices, and leaderships; this is nothing to the point, for so do ants and bees." <margin>* furthermore.</margin> For bees, at least, have a leader, and there is a following, and service, and wars, and victories, and the taking of the defeated. There are "also cities, and even suburbs, and a succession of labors, and judgments against the idle and the wicked; for they drive out and punish the drones." Even in these things he has not seen the difference between things accomplished by reason and logic, and those produced by irrational nature and mere physical equipment. The cause of these things is not any reason residing in the doers (for they do not possess it), but the most ancient [and] Son of God, the King of all things subject to Him, who made irrational nature, helping in an irrational way those not deemed worthy of reason. Cities among men were established by many arts and the arrangement of laws; and constitutions, and offices, and leaderships among men are either those properly so called—certain virtuous habits and energies—or those named more loosely according to an imitation, as far as possible, of the former. For the most excellent lawgivers, clearly seeing those ideals, <margin>* established.</margin> established the constitutions, the offices, and the leaderships. None of these are to be found in irrational creatures; even if Celsus applies rational names, and those assigned to rational beings—"city," "constitutions," "offices," and <margin>* thoughts/notions.</margin> "leaderships"—even to ants and bees. In these cases, one must by no means accept the ants or the bees as rational, for they do not act by reasoning. But one must wonder at the divine nature, which has extended as far as the irrational animals a sort of imitation of rational things. Perhaps this is for the shaming of rational beings; so that looking at ants they may become more industrious, and more careful in storing what is useful for themselves; and observing bees they may obey leaderships, dividing the works useful to the community for the safety of the cities. And perhaps even the so-called wars of the bees contain a teaching for the waging of just and orderly wars among men, should it ever be necessary. And as for cities and suburbs among bees, <margin>* hives.</margin> they are rather hives, and hexagonal structures, and the works of bees, and the succession among them...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Unless perhaps Celsus secretly intends by these remarks (as he follows Plato in many things) to suggest that there is one single species for all souls, and that the soul of an ant or a bee does not differ from that of a human. This is the view of one who brings the soul down from the vaults of heaven <note>original: "cœli convexis" / "ἁψίδων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ". This refers to the Platonic idea of the soul descending from the celestial spheres into material bodies.</note> not only into human bodies, but also into those of the remaining animals. Truly, this does not seem plausible to Christians, who are persuaded that the human soul was made in the image of God. They see it as impossible that the features of that image, once impressed, could ever be entirely erased from the soul, or that others could succeed them which reflect I know not what other image made in brutes.

But since he says that *when ants die, the living ones set apart a certain specific place, and that this is for them their ancestral tombs:* it must be said that the more praises he heaps upon the brute animals, the more—whether he wishes to or not—he extols the work of the Creator and Arranger of all things. He shows the great dexterity of humans, which is able to adorn even the gifts of nature in brutes with reason; although Celsus does not even consider those to be "brutes" which are called "devoid of reason" by the common sense of everyone. 

Thus, this man—who promises he will speak about the whole nature of things and boasts of his truthfulness in the very title of his book—does not even count ants among the brutes. For he affirms that they even talk among themselves, saying: *“Furthermore, when they meet, they converse, which is why they do not wander from the path.”* Therefore, they are perfectly rational, as if endowed with common sense and a significant voice like anyone else. For conversations are carried out by a voice having the power of signifying, reporting whatever chance has brought; would it not be utterly ridiculous to attribute such things to ants? 

Nor is he ashamed, while handing down most foolish dogmas even to posterity, to close this discourse on ants thus: *“Come now, if someone were to look down from heaven to earth, what would seem to him to be the difference between our labors and those of ants or bees?”* But this "observer" of Celsus, surveying with his eyes from heaven what humans and ants do, does he look only at the bodies of both? Does he not likewise look at the intellect moved by reasoning, whereas, on the contrary, ants are carried along devoid of this, wherever a certain natural imagination <note>The term "imaginatio" or "φαντασίας" here refers to instinctive sensory impressions rather than creative imagination.</note> drags them? Yet it would be absurd for one who deigns to look from so far off—from heaven all the way to earth—at the bodies of humans and ants, not to look much more at the natures by which they are led, and—

Then, as if striving even more to cast down the human race, and make it like the brutes, and to leave nothing untouched from the history of animals—at least what might serve to persuade one of their excellence—he says that in some there are even **magical arts** (so that men should not glory in this as if it were unique, or please themselves as being superior to brutes). *“But if,”* he says, *“on account of the secret science of magical arts man seems to himself extraordinary, even in this part snakes and eagles are wiser than he: for they know many remedies against diseases and other evils, and the virtues of certain small stones, which they insert into their nests as amulets to protect the safety of their chicks; which stones, when men obtain them, they think they have added not a little to their own resources.”*

First, I do not know how he can call the knowledge of natural remedies—whether animals attain it through experience or by their own innate character—"magic"; for commonly this name is taken in a worse sense: unless perhaps, as an Epicurean, he wishes secretly to calumniate this whole class of things, and all who use such things, as if they belong to the profession of magi. Nevertheless, let it be granted to him that men please themselves with the knowledge of such things, whether they be magi or not: How are snakes better than men in this? Is it because they seek the faculty of seeing sharply and the agility of the whole body from fennel, using a remedy not thought out, but ready and found everywhere, as something which nature holds out? But men do not handle remedies by the instinct of nature, like snakes, but partly they learn by experience, partly by reason, and sometimes from reasoning and science. Similarly, even if eagles carry the stone which they call *aetites* [eagle-stone], once found, into the nest for the protection of their chicks, are they therefore wise and wiser than men, who by reasoning have found the help imparted to eagles by nature, and have used it intelligently? Granted, let living creatures have notice of other remedies, it does not immediately follow...
