# Book 4. ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

It follows that they owe their discoveries to nature rather than to an innate sagacity. For if they had discovered these things by the benefit of reason, the discoveries would not be limited to a single thing found in serpents, and then a second or third in the eagle, and so on for the rest of the animals; rather, they would have discovered as many things as humans have. As it is, when we see that nature has assigned certain specific remedies to individual animals, it is sufficiently clear that neither wisdom nor reason resides in them, but rather a natural disposition for the sake of preserving these or those animals, produced by the Divine Reason <note>original: "à ratione factum," referring to the Logos or Universal Reason</note>. 

However, if I wished to agree with Celsus, I could use the saying of Solomon from the Proverbs, which goes like this: *There are four smallest things of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise: the ant, a weak people, who prepare their food in the harvest; the rock-badgers <note>original: "erinacei," often translated as hedgehogs or hyraxes</note>, an infirm folk, who make their beds in the rock; the locust has no king, yet it goes out in a single column; the lizard crawling with its hands, easy to catch, yet it dwells in the palaces of kings.* 

But I do not bring these forward as literal truths; rather, as is fitting for a book pre-titled with such a name—namely, *Proverbs*—I examine them as enigmas <note>riddles or allegories</note>. For it is the custom of these [inspired] men to divide into many categories those things which present one appearance but signify something else to those looking deeper; among these categories are proverbs. Therefore, we read in our Gospels that our Savior said: *These things I have spoken to you in proverbs: the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs.* <note>John 16:25</note> Thus, it is not these ants which we see that are wiser than the wise, but those signified by the proverb. The same must be said of the other animals. 

Celsus, however, thinks the books of the Jews and Christians are written in the simplest possible way, and thus he thinks those who interpret them allegorically are doing violence to the text and twisting it against the intention of the authors. Therefore, his slanders are refuted by these points, as is his opinion concerning serpents and eagles being wiser than man (as it seems to him). Furthermore, wishing to prove that humans do not even surpass the other animals in religion, but that God is understood even by certain brutes—even though there is such great variation in opinions about God even among the sharpest men, both Greeks and barbarians—he speaks thus: 

<margin>* "But if man is thought superior to the other animals for this reason, because he understands and acknowledges God; let those who say this know that even here many animals will not yield to him: and rightly so, for what is more divine than to foreknow and fore-show the future?"</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Greek text of the passage translated above. Key variations or notes in the Greek margin are included below.</note>

...against the idea that it is nature, and not reason, that finds these things in animals? For if it were reason that was the discoverer, it would not be that only this one thing was found among serpents, and a second and third thing in the eagle, and so on with the rest of the animals; but there would be as many as are among men. Now it is clear, from the fact that certain helps have been devised for each animal in a fixed way, that wisdom is not in them, nor is reason <margin>* a way.</margin> but rather a certain natural preparation for the safety of the creature, produced by Reason. 

And indeed, if I wanted to grapple with Celsus on these points, I would have used the words of Solomon from the Proverbs, which are as follows: *There are four smallest things upon the <margin>Proverbs 30:24</margin> earth, and these are wiser than the wise: the ants, who have no strength, yet prepare their food in summer; and the rock-badgers, a nation not strong, who made their houses in the rocks; the locust is without a king, and <margin>* marches, printed edition.</margin> marches out in an orderly way at a single command; and the lizard, supporting itself with its hands, and being easy to catch, <margin>* dwells out, printed edition.</margin> dwells in the strongholds of a king.* 

But I do not follow these as if the literal words were plain; following the title (for the book is titled *Proverbs*), I seek these things as enigmas. For it is the habit of these men to announce one thing in the literal narrative and another in the underlying meaning, dividing them into many types, of which proverbs are one. Wherefore also in our Gospels it is written that our Savior said: *These things <margin>John 16:25</margin> I have spoken to you in proverbs, but the hour comes when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs.* Therefore, it is not the ants perceived by the senses that are wiser than the wise, but those shown in the form of proverbs. 

The same must be said about the rest of the animals; but Celsus, thinking the books of the Jews and Christians are entirely too simple and unlearned, thinks that those who treat them as allegory are forcing the will of the writers. Let Celsus therefore be refuted through these things for slandering us in vain, and let his opinion about serpents and eagles be refuted, where he declares them wiser than men. And wishing <margin>* and further.</margin> to show through more points that humans are not even exceptional among all mortal things in their notions about the divine, but to declare that even some of the irrational animals have notions about God—concerning whom there has been such disagreement even among the sharpest of all men, Greeks and barbarians—he says: *"But if, because man has grasped divine notions, you think he excels the rest of the animals; let those who say this know that many of the other animals will also lay claim to this; and very reasonably so, for what would anyone say is more divine than to foreknow and fore-show what is to come?"*

See here how many questions among those who practice philosophy (not only among the Greeks, but also among the barbarians, whether they discovered these things or learned them from certain demons <note>original: *daimonōn* - in this context, spiritual entities or intermediaries, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> concerning augury and the other animals from which men are said to practice divination) he snatches up and sets down as if they were agreed upon. For first, it is questioned whether there is such a thing as the art of augury <term>augury: the practice of foretelling the future by observing the flight or calls of birds</term>, and simply whether divination through animals exists or not. Second, for those who have accepted the reality of divination through birds, there is no agreement on the cause or the manner of the divination. For some say that the movements are produced in the animals by certain demons or prophetic gods—in birds by various flights and various cries, and in the rest by such and such movements. Others hold that their souls are more divine and naturally suited for this, which is the most improbable claim of all.

If Celsus, wishing through the preceding points to show that irrational animals are secondary <insert>to God</insert> and wiser than men, wanted to establish through more arguments that such divination exists, he should have demonstrated his defense with clearer evidence. He should have refuted with proofs those who reject the arguments of those who do away with such divinations, and demonstratively overturned the arguments of those who say that the movements in animals for the purpose of prophesying come from demons or gods; and after that, he should have established that the soul of irrational animals is more divine. For then, against his plausible arguments, we might have overturned them as decently as possible, as he would have displayed a philosophical examination of such great matters. But now, he makes the claim that irrational animals are wiser than men, and that they have more sacred conceptions of divine things than we do, and that they have certain sacred conversations with one another. Now, this man who accuses us because we believe in the God over all, demands that we believe that the souls of birds have more divine and clearer conceptions than men—which is not...

<column-break/>

*...but men learn that foreknowledge from other animals, especially birds: and as many as attend to their significations, these are prophets. Because if birds and similar creatures indicate to us by signs whatever they foreknow from God, it appears that a much greater familiarity exists between them and the powers above, and that they are so much wiser and most dear to God. Furthermore, prudent men say that even conversations occur among birds, without doubt more sacred than ours; and that they understand these, and declare what they understand, when, having predicted those things which the birds had said—that they were going somewhere, and would do this or that—they show they have gone there and done what they predicted: moreover, nothing seems more religious regarding an oath, nothing more faithful toward the Gods, than elephants, surely for the reason that elephants have a notice of the Gods.*

See here how he seizes as confessed truths many things pertaining to divination from birds and other animals—whether they are human inventions or from demons—concerning which there is no agreement either among Greek philosophers or among barbarians. For first it is asked, is there an augural art, and is there any divination at all through animals, or is there none? Then, those who grant there is divination through birds do not agree on its cause and the mode of divination; since some say they are moved by demons or the Gods presiding over this art—birds indeed to various flights or voices, but the remaining living creatures to such or such movements: others think the very souls of the brutes are fit for this by some divinity of their own; which is incredible. Therefore, if Celsus wished to ascribe such divinity and wisdom to brutes, he ought to have more extensively proved to us the augural science, and more strongly built his defense, and refuted those who abolish it with weighty arguments, and with no less weight those who say animals are moved by demons or gods for the purpose of signifying; and only then contend for the soul of brutes being capable of divinity. For thus, as against a man imbued with philosophy bringing forward likely reasons, we would have resisted with all our strength, denying that brutes are wiser than men; and showing it to be false that they have thoughts more holy than ours, or that they celebrate certain sacred conversations among themselves. Now this man, who turns it into a crime for us that we believe in God the lord of the universe, demands that we believe the souls of birds have more divine and more excellent thoughts than those of men: that...

# Book 4. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

If that is true, then birds have a better sense of God than Celsus does. Nor is it a wonder, since Celsus so greatly belittles mankind: for in his opinion, birds possess more sublime and divine thoughts, not only than us Christians and the Jews who use the same scriptures, but even more than the theologians of the Greeks, for they were merely men. Therefore, according to Celsus, the swift-winged birds and those that sing omens <note>Latin: *alites praepetes & oscines* — technical terms in Roman augury for birds that give omens by flight or by voice</note> are more capable of understanding the divine nature than Pherecydes, Pythagoras, Plato, or Socrates. It would follow that we ought to frequent the schools of birds for the sake of learning, so that—just as Celsus believes they can teach us the future through prophecy—they might also free men from doubt concerning God by communicating the clear opinion they have perceived about Him. It would therefore befit Celsus, who thinks birds are superior to men, to use birds as his teachers rather than any of the Greek philosophers.

But we shall answer him briefly, by exposing his most ungrateful vanity toward the Creator. For Celsus was a man who, "being in honor, did not understand" <margin>Psalm 48:21 (Vulgate numbering; Psalm 49:20 in English Bibles)</margin>; for this reason, he is not merely compared to the birds or other creatures he thinks participate in divinity, but he has actually granted them the first place. Surpassing even the Egyptians—who worship irrational animals as gods—he has subjected himself and, as far as he was able, the entire human race to irrational animals, as if man had a worse and lesser sense of God than they.

We must therefore ask, above all, whether there is any true divination from birds or other animals said to prophesy, or whether in truth there is none. For there are arguments on both sides that are not to be despised. On one hand, it seems a shameful thing if men endowed with reason should prefer to consult birds rather than the oracles of the divine spirits <note>original: *daemonum* — in the classical sense of "daemons" or intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>. On the other hand, many testimonies support the idea that many have escaped the greatest dangers by obeying auspices. But even if we grant that there is some art of the augurs, let those who believe this learn that even with this concession, man is far superior to irrational beasts—even those consulted by augurs—so much so that they are not even to be compared.

For it must be said that if they possessed such divinity and were conscious of the future, so that from their abundance they could even provide counsel to men, they would without a doubt look out for themselves first of all. They would fly cautiously and not fall into the snares or nets set for them by men, nor would they become targets for archers. And eagles, if they foresaw the ambushes of serpents or the designs of men <margin>...flying over this place, where men have set snares and nets against them; or archers using them as a target and releasing arrows at them as they fly. Surely eagles, if they foreknew the plot against their young, whether by men climbing up to them, and destroy—</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek translation of the preceding Latin text, following the same arguments.</note>

...is true, birds have clearer conceptions of God than Celsus. And it is not surprising if Celsus, when he so greatly debases man; but rather, as far as Celsus is concerned, birds have greater and more divine conceptions, I do not say than us Christians, or the Jews who use the same scriptures as we do; but even than the theologians among the Greeks, for they were men. Rather then, according to Celsus, the race of so-called prophetic birds has understood the nature of the divine better than Pherecydes, and Pythagoras, and Socrates, and Plato. And we ought to go to the birds as teachers; so that, just as in Celsus’s notion they teach us the future by prophecy, so also they might deliver men from doubting the divine, and impart clear conceptions about it by handing them down. It follows for Celsus, <margin>* to think that man differs from birds [in a negative way], and that we should use birds as our teachers, and none of the others who have practiced philosophy among the Greeks.</margin> to lead us to use birds as teachers, and none of the others who have practiced philosophy among the Greeks.

But we must say a few things out of many regarding the matters at hand, refuting his ungrateful impiety toward the one who made him a man. For he, being Celsus, "being in honor did not understand," wherefore he was not even compared to the birds and the other animals which he considers to be prophetic; but he yielded the first place to them, even beyond the Egyptians who worship irrational animals as gods. He subjected himself, and as far as he could, the whole race of men, as being worse and having less mind concerning the divine than the irrational animals.

First, then, we must inquire whether there is any divination believed to be through birds and the rest of the animals, or if it does not exist. For the argument on each side is not to be despised: the one side being ashamed to accept such a thing, lest the rational being use birds instead of the divine oracles, leaving those behind; but on the other hand, <margin>* being persuaded by the evidence testified by many, that many were saved from dangers by prophecy, being persuaded by divination through birds, evidence...</margin> being persuaded by the evidence that many were saved from dangers by prophecy. Even if this is granted, I will show to those who have been deceived that even then, the superiority of man over irrational animals—even those very prophetic ones—is great and in no way comparable to them. It must be said, then, that if there were some divine nature in them that foreknew the future, and was so rich as to reveal the things to come from its abundance to any man who wished it, it is clear that much earlier, knowing the things concerning themselves, they would have guarded against flying over this place where men have set snares and nets against them; or archers using them as a target and releasing arrows at them as they fly. Surely eagles, if they foreknew the plot against their young, whether by men climbing up to them, and destroy—

<meta>This page continues Origen’s polemic against Celsus regarding the nature of divination through animals (augury). Origen argues that animals do not possess prophetic souls, but are manipulated by lower spirits.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Therefore, was the eagle divine, but the dragon (for the augurs <note>Ancient Roman or Greek officials who observed bird behavior to predict the future.</note> observe this creature as well) not so? But since what happens by chance is certain, could it not be argued that both were prophetic? For if the dragon possessed the power of divination, would it not have taken care not to fall into the clutches of the eagle? There are many other examples from which it is gathered that foresight does not reside in the souls of brute beasts, but, as the poet speaks and the common folk believe, "the Son of Saturn <note>Jupiter/Zeus. Origen is quoting Homer here.</note> sends these things into the sight of men." Furthermore, Apollo signifies certain things by the omen of a hawk, and it is called the "swift messenger" of this God. 

Our opinion, however, is that certain evil demons—"Titanic" (so to speak) and "Gigantic"—rebelled against the true God and His angels through impiety. Having been cast down from heaven, they wallow on the earth around thicker and more impure bodies; yet they are perceptive in great matters because they are stripped of earthly bodies. Occupied with such business, in order to lead the human race away from the true God, they insinuate themselves into wild animals noted for their greed and craftiness, and move them to whatever they wish at their own will; or they present certain phantoms of these very animals flying or otherwise moving before human eyes, so that men, preoccupied with divinations of this kind, might not seek God, the Lord of all things, nor examine true piety, but cast their minds down to the earth toward birds, dragons, foxes, and wolves. 

For it has been observed by those skilled in such matters that more evident omens are made through animals of this kind, because demons cannot exercise their power in tamer creatures as effectively as in those, on account of a similar malice—which, however, in animals is not strictly "malice," but something resembling it. 

Wherefore, I consider this also, if anything else, worthy of admiration in Moses: that having considered the differences of animals—whether taught by God what kinship each animal has with which demons, or having investigated their orders by his own wisdom—he declared all those to be "impure" from which the Egyptians and other men take omens; but the rest, which are not of this kind, are almost all "pure." And in the order of the impure, he counts the wolf, the fox, the dragon, the hawk, the eagle, and similar creatures. And for the most part, not only in the Law but also in the Prophets, one may find this genus of animals presented as examples of the worst things, and never for a good purpose.

<column-break/>

<margin>\* being prophetic.</margin>
Was the eagle then prophetic, but the dragon—since the bird-watchers <note>Greek: *oionoskopoi*, those who look at birds for signs.</note> use this animal too—not prophetic? And what of this: since a random choice is easily refuted, could it not be proven that both are prophetic? For if the dragon \* were prophetic, would it not have guarded against suffering what it suffered from the eagle? One might find ten thousand such examples, showing that animals do not have a prophetic soul within themselves; but, according to the poet and the majority of men, "the Olympian himself sent it to the light." <note>original: "αὐτὸς Ὀλύμπιος ἧκε φόωσδε" - a reference to Zeus in Homer's Iliad.</note> And according to a certain sign, Apollo also uses the hawk as a messenger: "the hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo." <note>original: "κίρκος Ἀπόλλωνος ταχὺς ἄγγελος" - a reference to Homer's Odyssey.</note> 

But according to us, certain base demons—and (if I may name them so) Titanic or Gigantic—having become impious toward the truly Divine and the angels in heaven, and having fallen from heaven, wallow upon the earth around the thicker and impure parts of bodies. They have a certain foresight concerning future things, inasmuch as they happen to be naked of earthly bodies; and being engaged in such work, wishing to lead the race of men away from the true God, they slip into the more predatory and licentious of animals, and others more crafty, and move them toward what they want, when they want; or they turn the appearances of such animals into such flights and movements. This is so that men, being caught by the divination found in irrational animals, may not seek the God who governs the universe, nor investigate pure worship, but may fall in their reasoning to the earth, to birds and dragons, and further to foxes and wolves. 

For it has been observed by those clever in these things that the most vivid foreknowledge occurs through such animals; since the demons are not able to work as much in the tamer animals as they can through those that have a similarity of wickedness—not actual wickedness, but as it were "wickedness" existing in such animals. 

Hence, if I have wondered at anything else of Moses, I show that I also wonder at this as being worthy: that having understood the different natures of animals—whether having learned from God the things concerning them and the demons akin to each animal, or having found it himself by ascending through wisdom in his arrangement of animals—he said that all those considered by the Egyptians and the rest of men to be prophetic are "impure," but generally the "pure" are those that are not so. And among the impure according to Moses are the wolf, the fox, the dragon, the eagle, the hawk, and things similar to these. And generally, not only in the Law but also in the Prophets, you would find these animals taken as examples of the worst things, and never for a useful matter.

<margin>Iliad 12.209; Odyssey 15.526.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 11:6, 13, 15.</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 4.

...named a wolf or a fox. It seems, therefore, that each species of demon has a certain fellowship with each species of animal. And just as among men some are more powerful than others, though not necessarily because of their moral character, in the same way, among the "intermediate" beings <note>referring to beings between gods and men</note>, some demons may be more powerful than others. Some of these use certain animals to deceive men, according to the will of the "Prince of this World" <note>original: *kosmokrator*, a term for the devil or a ruling worldly power</note>—as our scriptures call the ruler of this age—while others reveal things through different forms. And see how foul these demons are, since even weasels are used by some to reveal the future! Consider for yourself which is the better view: that the God over all and His Son move birds and other animals for divination, or that those who move such animals (and not humans, even when humans are present) are wicked and—as our sacred writings name them—"unclean" spirits. For if the soul of birds is divine because the future is foretold through them, why should we not rather believe this of humans? Shall we say the soul of that person is divine through whose chance words omens are heard? According to such logic, the servant girl at the mill in Homer was divine when she spoke concerning the suitors:

The truth is that the Divine, for the knowledge of future things, uses neither irrational animals nor the chance occurrences of men. Instead, He uses the most holy and pure souls of men, whom He fills with His spirit and makes into prophets. Therefore, if anything else is wonderfully stated in the Law of Moses, such things must be classified here: *You shall not practice augury, nor shall you observe the flight of birds.* And elsewhere: *For the nations, which the Lord your God will destroy from before your face, listen to omens and divinations; but to you the Lord your God has not granted this.* Then he says immediately after: *The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you...*

...partly understood as a wolf or a fox. It appears, therefore, that each species of demon has a certain species among animals similar to itself. And just as among men some are more powerful than others, not always because they are better: so it can happen that demons are more powerful than other demons in indifferent matters; some using certain animals to deceive men, according to the will of the prince of this age, as the Scripture names him, while others signify through another species. And see the malice of demons, how some even adapt prophecies from weasels: and reflect within yourself, whether it is better to confess that the God and Lord of things, and His son, move birds and other living creatures for the purpose of augury, or that those who move these animals (and not men, even in the presence of men) are evil demons, and, as our sacred letters name them, impure. But if the soul of birds is divine because future things are predicted through them, why do we not rather think this of the soul of man, when omens are taken from their words? Therefore, according to these people, the servant girl at the mill in Homer was divine, thus prophesying to the suitors:

> *May Jupiter command this to be their last meal.*

And she indeed was divine; but not so Ulysses, the friend of Homeric Minerva, but having understood the omen of the divine servant, he rejoiced, as the Poet says:

> *Divine Ulysses rejoiced in the omen of the miller-woman.*

Now therefore see, that if birds have a divine soul, and perceive God, or the Gods, as Celsus speaks, then surely we men, as often as we sneeze, do so from a certain divine affection of the soul. For so it is believed by the testimony of many: whence that of the Poet:

> *--he sneezed an omen to the one praying.*

And Penelope says thus:

> *Do you not see how my son sneezed an omen at the words.*

But the true God, to signify the future, uses neither brutes nor those things which happen to man by chance, but chose the purest and holiest souls of men for this use, whom, seized by His divine power, He renders prophetic. Wherefore, among the first things wonderfully commanded in the law of Moses: *Let there be no augur or soothsayer among you:* and elsewhere: *For the nations, which the Lord your God will delete from His face, they observe omens and auguries: but to you the Lord your God has not so given:* and soon after is added: *The Lord your God will cause a Prophet to arise...*

from among your brothers. And once, when God wished to abolish faith in augurs <note>original: "auguribus" — Roman religious officials who observed bird flight to predict the future</note> through an augur himself, He commanded him, being inspired by His spirit, to break forth into these words: *For there shall be no omens in the lineage of Jacob, nor divinations among the Israelites; in due time Jacob shall be warned, and God shall make His word known to Israel through prophets.* <margin>Numbers 23:23</margin> Since we are not ignorant of these and similar things, we take care to keep that secret command: *With all watchfulness guard your heart,* <margin>Proverbs 4:23</margin> lest by chance some demon should creep into our mind, or some opposing spirit should turn our thoughts according to its own pleasure. We pray that the light of the knowledge of the glory of God may illuminate our hearts, <margin>2 Corinthians 4:6</margin> as the Spirit of God visits our imaginative faculty and suggests thoughts worthy of God; *For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.* <margin>Romans 8:14</margin>

Furthermore, it must be known that the foreknowledge of future events is not an entirely divine thing; for in itself it is an intermediate matter <note>original: "indifferens" / "μέσον" — a Stoic term for things neither inherently good nor evil</note>, as it falls to the wicked as well as the good. Thus, even physicians, by their art, foresee certain things even if they are of evil character; likewise, pilots, even if they are worthless men, have their own prognostications from which they gather future changes in the weather, being taught by experience and long-term observations. Yet they are not considered divine for this reason if they possess impure morals. Therefore, what Celsus says is false: *“What is more divine than the foreknowledge and foretelling of the future?”* It is likewise false that *“many of the brute animals attempt to think about God,”* for no brute understands anything about God. It is also false that *“brutes have the greatest familiarity with God,”* since even men who are otherwise excellent, if they are wicked, are very far removed from that intimacy with God which is granted only to the truly wise and sincerely pious. Such were the Prophets among us, and among them Moses, of whose great purity the Scripture testifies, saying: *Moses alone shall come near to God, the others shall not come near.* <margin>Exodus 24:2</margin>

Now, how impiously has this man—who accuses us of being impious—stated that *“brute animals are not only wiser than men but also dearer to God than men?”* Who would not detest the idea that a dragon, a fox, a wolf, an eagle, or a hawk is more beloved by God than the nature of humans? For if this were true, it would necessarily follow that Socrates, Plato, Pythagoras, and Pherecydes—divine men so greatly praised—are less dear to God than these creatures. May such "happiness" turn back upon Celsus’s own head, so that he might be equally dear to God as they are, and become just like them himself!

...from among your brothers. In due time it shall be told to Jacob and to Israel what God will accomplish.*
<margin>Proverbs 4:23</margin>

<margin>2 Corinthians 4:6</margin>
And we pray that the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God may shine in our hearts, as the Spirit of God dwells in our imagination and presents to us the things of God; since
<margin>Rom. 8:14</margin>
*as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.* One must know that to foreknow the future is not altogether divine; for in itself it is a middle thing, and it happens to the base and the refined alike. Even physicians, at any rate, foreknow certain things from medicine, even if they happen to be base in character. So too pilots, even if they happen to be wretched, foreknow signs, and the violence of winds, and seasonal changes, and such things; but they are not already divine because of this foreknowledge, even if their character be <margin>* he says.</margin> base. Therefore, the statement made by Celsus is false: *“What would anyone say is more divine than foreknowing and declaring the future?”* And it is false that *“Many of the animals lay claim to divine conceptions”*; for none of the irrational creatures has a conception of God. And it is false that *“The irrational animals are closer to divine conversation”*; whereas even those men who are still base, even if they make the greatest progress, are far from divine conversation. Only those who are truly wise and sincerely pious are closer to divine conversation; such as the prophets among us, and Moses, to whom the Word testified because of his great purity, saying:
<margin>Exodus 24:2</margin>
*Moses alone shall draw near to God, but the rest shall not draw near.* And how impiously has it been said by him who accuses us of impiety: *“The irrational animals are not only wiser than the nature of men, but also dearer to God?”* And who would not be repelled by listening to a man saying that a dragon, a fox, a wolf, an eagle, and a hawk are dearer to God than the nature of men? It follows for him to say that, if these animals are dearer to God than men, then clearly Socrates, Plato, Pythagoras, and Pherecydes, whom <margin>* speaking of divine things.</margin> he recently lauded as *theologians* <note>original: "θεολόγων" — here meaning those who speak of the gods</note>, are less dear to God than these animals. And one might pray for him, saying: *“If these animals are dearer to God than men, may you become dear to God along with them.”*

For God cares for the whole; providence never deserts this, nor allows it to suffer harm; nor does He visit it only after certain intervals of ages, nor is He angry with men, with whom He is no more indignant than with monkeys or mice; nor does He threaten any of His works, since each has been distributed in its own order.* Come then, let us answer him at least in a few words. It is not because we are pursuing a forbidden talkativeness—which cannot escape the stain of sin <note>original: "peccatum effugere" / "φυγεῖν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν". A reference to Proverbs 10:19: "In the multitude of words sin is not lacking."</note>—that we now begin this fifth book against the writings of Celsus, holy Ambrose. Rather, we strive with all our might to leave none of his statements unexamined, especially where he seems to accuse us or the Jews with some degree of plausibility. Certainly, if we were able to penetrate the consciences of any who have happened upon his books, and pull out the arrows that wound those not sufficiently protected by the armor of God, and apply a rational remedy to the injury inflicted by Celsus, we would do so most gladly. 

But since this is the work of God alone—to visit through His Spirit, together with the Spirit of Christ, those whom He deems worthy of His presence—it is our task, as we attempt to bring men to faith through words and writings, to take care in all things that we may be called *workers who need not be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth* <note>original: "operarii sine ignominia, rectè secantes sermonem veritatis" / "ἐργάτας ἀνεπαισχύντους, ὀρθοτομοῦντας τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας". A citation of 2 Timothy 2:15.</note>. One task among all seems most vital: to refute to the best of our ability the arguments that Celsus thought were likely true, faithfully following your instructions. 

Come then, let us proceed to tear down the remainder, setting forth his words in the order they follow after those already refuted; let the fair-minded reader judge whether we do so rightly or otherwise. May God grant that our mind does not handle this dispute void of His inspiration, so that the faith of those we wish to benefit may not rest in human wisdom <note>original: "in humana sapientia" / "ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων". A citation of 1 Corinthians 2:5.</note>. A citation of 2 Corinthians 10:5.</note>, as well as the pride of Celsus, which he raises against our Jesus, Moses, and the Prophets.

A reference to Psalm 68:11.</note> provide the same to us, granting us great power so that we may obtain faith among our readers through the word and power of God. "No God or son of God has either descended, or could ever descend. But if you speak of certain angels, who do you say these are? Gods, or some other race?" But as is likely, <note>Celsus suggests they are actually demons.</note> "demons." However, out of many points, we shall set forth a few which we think harmonize well with what was said before, though they do not have entirely the same sense as those. In what we have previously stated, by declaring universally that no God or son of God has descended to men, he also does away with the appearances of Gods <note>The Greek term is 'epiphaneia', referring to a visible manifestation of a deity.</note> believed in by the many, and the same things mentioned in the passages above. For if the statement, "No God or son of God has descended, nor could descend," is truly spoken by Celsus, then clearly it is done away with that any God has descended from heaven to earth, either to prophesy to men or to heal through oracles. Both the Pythian <note>Apollo, the god of the Delphic oracle.</note> and Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine and healing.</note>, and any other of those believed to do such things, would be a God having descended from heaven; or he would be a God <margin>would be.</margin> who had always been allotted to dwell on the earth, and as it were, an exile from the place of the Gods. Or how would it not be that they do not have the power to commune with the divine beings there? Either Apollo and Aesculapius are gods, and as many as are believed to do something on earth; or they were certain demons among wise men, and far worse than those who ascend through virtue because of the unsparing nature of heaven. See then that wishing to do away with our doctrines, he who has not acknowledged himself an Epicurean <note>Follower of Epicurus, who believed gods exist but do not intervene in human affairs.</note> throughout the whole treatise is caught deserting to Epicurus. It is time then for you, the reader of Celsus’s words, if you agree with the propositions, either to do away with the idea of God visiting to benefit the human race in any single case; or to prove Celsus’s argument false in every such instance. If, on the one hand, you do away with providence entirely, you will make his argument false in those places where he posits God and providence, so that you may say these things are true; but if you nonetheless posit providence, as one not agreeing with Celsus when he says "neither God nor a son of God has descended or does descend to men," why will you not diligently examine what we have said concerning Jesus, and the things prophesied concerning him? Which one should rather be thought to be God and a son of God having descended to men: Jesus, who administered and performed such great things; or those who, under the pretext of oracles and divinations, do not correct the morals of those being healed, and who, having promised to save them, fall away from the sincere and pure worship of the Creator of all things, and lead others into the same defection by their authority...

<column-break/>

*...no son ever descended, nor can descend;* but if you speak of his angels, *who do you say they are; gods, or some other race? It is a wonder if they are not demons.* Thus far, regarding Celsus’s talkativeness, which blunts us by repeating the same things so many times, and which has already been answered frequently in the preceding parts, there is no need for many words, for what has already been said suffices. However, we shall add a few things out of many tending toward the same point, though not exactly the same; by which we shall show him that, while he totally denies that any God or son of God descended to mortals, he also removes the common opinion about God being seen among men, just as he himself admitted above. For if it is universally true what Celsus said, *neither God, nor any son of God ever descended, nor can descend:* it is manifestly vain that there are certain Gods who glided down from heaven to earth, either to give oracles to men, or to bring remedies for diseases. Neither the Pythian, nor Aesculapius, nor any other of those who are thought to do such things, will be a God proceeded from heaven; or even if he be a God, destined forever to inhabit the earth, and as if an exile from the seats of the Gods, he will be unworthy of the fellowship of the Gods. And Apollo, together with his Aesculapius and those like them, stripped of deity, will be held far inferior to men who excel among humans, consecrated by grace of virtue and received into the number of the heavenly ones. See how, wishing to subvert our decrees, although throughout his whole commentary he has disguised that he is a follower of Epicurus, he is now caught stealthily deserting into his camp. Therefore, it remains that the reader, assenting to his writings, must either deny that any God has come to look after any of the mortals; or, if it pleases him to receive this as true, he must brand Celsus’s book with the mark of a lie. Therefore, if you take away providence altogether, in this way you make him a liar in his own writings, in which mention is made of providence and of the Gods. But if you grant providence, differing here from Celsus who denies that *any God, or son of God descends or has descended to men:* why do you not diligently weigh by examining what we say of our Jesus, and what the Prophets predicted of him, which of the two is rather to be believed to be God and the son of God descended to mortals: Jesus, who dispensed and perfected such great things, or those who, under the pretext of prophecies, not only do not heal from their vices those whom they undertake to cure, but even themselves fall away from the sincere and chaste worship of God, and draw others also into the same defection, following their authority, away from the one, only, true, and manifest...

<summary>Origen argues that Celsus's denial of any divine descent contradicts the pagan belief in gods like Apollo and Aesculapius, effectively exposing Celsus as a closet Epicurean who denies divine providence.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.
## Hh

...alienated from the worship of the manifest God, by seducing their souls to the religion of many Gods. But since shortly after, as if the Jews or Christians had answered that those who descended to men were angels, he says: *If you speak of angels,* and proceeds to ask: *are they gods or another race?* and again, as if receiving the answer that *it is another race pertaining to demons:* come, let us consider these things as well. We confess indeed that there are angels who are certain ministering spirits <note>original: "ministratorios quosdam spiritus"</note>, frequently sent by God to travel to those men for whom the inheritance of salvation waits. We find that these spirits sometimes ascend to the purest celestial places, and even to the purer super-celestial regions, to offer the prayers of men; and then again they descend to men, bringing back from there something for the use of individuals, according as each is worthy of a benefit. Having been taught to name these spirits "angels" <note>The word "angel" literally means "messenger" in Greek.</note> because of their office, we find that on account of a certain divinity they are sometimes called *Gods* by the sacred Scripture; but not in such a way that we are commanded to adore them, or to worship them with divine honors, even though they bring the gifts of God to us. For all vows, all petitions, intercessions, and thanksgivings must be directed to God, the Lord of all things, through the High Priest who is greater than all angels, the living Word and God. We shall pray to that Word, we shall make intercession to him, and give thanks to him, and offer prayers, provided we understand how these terms are used either in an improper or a proper sense. For to invoke angels without a knowledge of them—of which man is not capable—does not seem consistent with reason. And even if we grant that a certain wonderful and secret knowledge of them, and of the offices which each performs, could be comprehended by a man: this very knowledge would restrain him from daring to offer prayers to anyone except the Lord God alone, who alone is abundantly sufficient for all, through our Savior the Son of God, who is the Word, Wisdom, Truth, and whatever else the writings of the Prophets and Apostles of Jesus proclaim concerning him. And this makes the angels of God sufficiently favorable to us, so that they willingly do all things for us, because, as far as human nature allows, we are well-disposed toward God, imitating in this the angels, who themselves also imitate God; and because we embrace his Son, the Word, as much as we can, though he is better understood by the holy angels; yet we strive daily toward a clearer knowledge of him. But that man <note>Referring to Celsus.</note>, as one ignorant of our scriptures, answers himself on our behalf, *that they are a race other than that of the gods*

<column-break/>

...of the souls usurped by them under the pretext of honoring many Gods, away from the one and only manifest and true God? But since after this, as if Jews or Christians would have answered concerning those descending to men that they were angels, he says, "but if you say certain angels," and further asks, saying, "whom do you call these? Gods, or some other race?" then again as if we would have answered— <margin>Hebrews 1:14. *ministry. Psalm 49:1. 81:7. 95:4. 135:2. John 1:1. 14:6. 1 Corinthians 1:24. *human.</margin> <insert>he says</insert> "that it is likely some other kind, namely demons," come, let us consider these things too. For we confess that we call them angels, being "ministering spirits," and "sent out for service" <note>original: "διακονίαν"</note> for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation; ascending indeed, bringing the prayers of men in the purest celestial regions of the world, or even in the super-celestial regions; and descending again from there, bringing to each according to their merit something of those things commanded by God to be ministered to those who are being benefited. Having learned to call these "angels" from their work, we find them, because of their being divine, sometimes named "Gods" in the holy Scriptures; but not so that it is commanded to us to revere and worship those who minister and bring to us the things of God, instead of God. For every petition, and prayer, and intercession, and thanksgiving is to be sent up to the God over all, through the High Priest who is over all angels, the living Word and God. And we will petition the Word himself, and intercede with him, and give thanks, and pray, if we are able to distinguish between the proper and improper use of the term "prayer." For to call upon angels, without having grasped the knowledge concerning them which is above humans, is not reasonable. And even if, for the sake of argument, the knowledge concerning them—being something wonderful and secret—were grasped; this knowledge, having presented their nature and the things over which each is appointed, would not allow one to venture to pray to another than the God over all who is sufficient for all, through our Savior the Son of God; who is Word, and Wisdom, and Truth, and whatever else the writings of the prophets of God and the apostles of Jesus say about him. It is enough to have the holy angels be propitious to us, and that they do all things for us, that our disposition toward God is as much as <insert>human</insert> nature is able to imitate God; and our perception of his Son the Word, as far as is attainable by us, which is still inferior to the clearer perception of him by the holy angels, but daily hastening toward that clarity and distinctness. Since Celsus does not endure our holy scriptures, he answers himself as if from us, "that we say those descending are some other race than God..."

He emphasizes that all prayer should be directed to God through the Word (Christ), rather than to angels whose nature is beyond full human comprehension.</summary>

Book 5. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
Hh 2

He introduces another absurdity, accusing those who, while they adore the heavens, are reluctant to yield the same honor to the Sun, Moon, and stars; as if it were possible that what is God as a whole should have parts devoid of deity: calling the whole heaven, as it seems, the "whole," and the Sun, Moon, and stars its "parts." And yet, neither Jews nor Christians pronounce the heaven to be God. But let us grant it were true what he says, that the heaven is held by the Jews to be God; let us also grant that the parts of heaven are the Sun, Moon, and stars (which is by no means true, for neither terrestrial animals nor plants are "parts" of the earth): how will he prove, even from the doctrines of the Greeks, that if the whole be God, its parts must also be deities? Certainly the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that the universe itself is a rational, divine being.</note> say the whole world is God—the primary God; while the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who often viewed the cosmos as a "secondary" created god.</note> say it is the secondary; and there are those who assign it the third place among the gods. Therefore, according to their opinion, because the entire world is God, the parts will also be gods: not only men, but also brutes and plants. But if among the parts of the world there are both mountains, and rivers, and seas, and the whole world is God; then the rivers are gods and the seas are gods: something which not even the Greeks are likely to say; rather, they name the presidents over them either gods or demons. And so, even according to the sentiment of the Greeks—at least those asserting a providence—that universal proposition of Celsus will be false: "Whatever is God as a whole, its parts are also deities." Otherwise, if it were conceded that what he says is true—that the world is God—it would follow that whatever is in it increases the number of gods, since it is a part of the world; even animals, not even excluding flies and gnats <note>original: "sciniphibus," referring to stinging insects or lice mentioned in the plagues of Egypt.</note>, and worms, and every species of serpent; and much more the birds and fishes: things which not even those who assert the world is God would say. Moreover, the Jews, who live according to the law of Moses, even if they admit nothing of what is hidden and secret in the law, would neither say that the heaven is God, nor the angels. But since we have said that he was confused by certain things poorly understood: come, let us also declare these things according to our strength, and let us show that Celsus is mistaken, who thinks the heaven is adored by the Jews, or the angels, since that is most foreign to their religion; just as the adoration of the Sun, Moon, stars, and statues is forbidden by their own laws. There exists in Jeremiah the word of God, expostulating through the Prophet with the Jewish people because they adore such things, and make sacrifices to the queen of heaven, and to all the host of heaven. The writings of the Christians also [bring] the same charge against the Jews

Whence indeed is it true, even according to the Greeks, that if a whole be God, then its parts are already divine? Clearly they say the whole world is God—the Stoics the first; those from Plato the second; and some of them even a third. Is it then according to these, since the whole world is God, that its parts are already divine? Divine, not only men, but also all the irrational animals, being parts of the world, and in addition to these, the plants. And if the rivers, and the mountains, and the seas are parts of the world; then since the whole world is God, <margin>then since.</margin> are the rivers and the seas already gods? It follows from Celsus's argument that if the world be God, all things in it are divine, being parts of the world. Which things not even those who say the world is God would say. <meta>This page continues Origen’s defense of Christian and Jewish monotheism against the philosopher Celsus, specifically addressing why the Hebrews do not worship the heavenly bodies (sun, moon, and stars) despite their beauty.</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 5.

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:19, 20.</margin>
In Deuteronomy <note>original: "nomio," likely a truncated "Deuteronomio"</note> it says: *Take heed, lest when you lift up your eyes to heaven and see the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars with which the world is adorned, you fall into error and adore them, and worship them as gods; which the Lord your God has assigned to all the nations that live under heaven. But God has taken us and led us out of Egypt, that iron furnace, so that we might be his peculiar and inherited people, as it is on this day.* Therefore, since the Hebrews have been called by God a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a purchased people—of whom it was foretold to Abraham by the voice of the Lord himself: *Look up at the heaven and count the stars if you can, so shall your offspring be*—having the hope that they would be made equal to the stars in number, they could not worship those things, to whose multitude they could only attain through the observation of the Law. For it was said to them: *The Lord our God has multiplied you, and behold! today you are as many as the stars of heaven.* The Prophet Daniel prophesies such things concerning the resurrection: *And at that time every person shall be saved who is written in the book, and many of those who slept in the dust of the earth shall awaken, some to eternal life, and others to eternal reproach and shame; but those who have been taught shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many in justice, like the stars for perpetual eternities and beyond.* From this is also taken what Paul says: *There are heavenly bodies, and there are earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and the earthly another: there is one brightness of the Sun, another brightness of the Moon, and another brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness: so also is the resurrection of the dead.* Therefore, it was not fitting for those who had learned to nobly transcend every created thing, and to hope for the magnificent rewards of a well-spent life from God, and who had heard that voice: *You are the light of the world*, and *Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your heavenly Father*, and who were striving with fervent zeal for that unfading wisdom—or had already perceived it, I say, which is the brightness of eternal light—to be so struck with awe at the sensible light of the Sun, Moon, and stars, that they would consider themselves inferior because of it, when they themselves possess such great intelligible light, the true light, the light of the world, the light of men. Nor should they adore those things which, if they were to be worshipped at all, ought not to be worshipped because of the sensible light which many admire, but because of that true and intelligible light; if indeed even the heavenly stars <unclear>possess sensible</unclear> light <unclear>to be adored</unclear>: <unclear>but</unclear> <unclear>on account of</unclear> <unclear>that</unclear> <unclear>true</unclear> <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>intelligible</unclear> <note>The Latin text here becomes fragmented and difficult to read in the original manuscript.</note>.

[The stars] are rational and virtuous living beings, and they have been enlightened with the light of knowledge by Wisdom, which is the radiance of the eternal light. <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 7:26, often applied to Christ.</note> Indeed, their physical light is the work of the Creator of all things; but their intellectual light is perhaps also their own, proceeding from the free will within them. Therefore, it is not right for that light to be worshipped in itself by one who sees and understands the true light—nor should one attach "participation" and so forth to it—nor by one who sees the Father, the God of the true light. For it has always been well said that, *God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.* And just as those who, because of the physical and heavenly light, worship the sun, moon, and stars, would never worship a spark of fire or a lamp on earth (seeing the incomparable superiority of those things deemed worthy of worship over the light of sparks and lamps); so also those who have understood how God is light, and have grasped how the Son of God is the true light which enlightens every man coming into the world, and who understand how he says, *I am the light of the world*, would not reasonably worship what is, as it were, a tiny spark compared to God, the true light of light, found in the sun, moon, and stars. This is not because they dishonor such great works of God—as Anaxagoras did, calling the sun, moon, and stars a "glowing mass of metal" <note>Anaxagoras was a Pre-Socratic philosopher famously prosecuted for claiming the sun was a hot stone rather than a god.</note> and speaking disparagingly of them—but because they perceive the ineffable superiority and incomparable divinity of God, along with the superiority of his Only-begotten Son over all other things. We are persuaded that even the sun, moon, and stars themselves pray to the God over all through his Only-begotten Son, judging that we ought not to pray to those who themselves are praying. For they themselves wish rather to send us upward to the God to whom they pray, rather than * to lead us down to themselves, or to divide our power of prayer between God and themselves. We shall also use an example concerning them in this place: our Savior and Lord, having once heard himself called "Good Teacher," referred the one saying this back to his own Father, saying, *Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God the Father.* If, therefore, the Son of the good Father said this reasonably, being the image of the goodness of God, how much more reasonably would the sun say to those who worship it: "Why do you worship me? You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve; whom I and all those with me worship and serve." And even if someone is not of such high standing, let such a person nonetheless pray to the Word of God <note>The *Logos*.</note>, who is able to heal him; and much more to his Father, who in former times sent out his Word to the righteous and healed them, and delivered

they are rational animals, endowed with virtue, illustrated by the light of knowledge from that wisdom which is the splendor of eternal light. For their sensible light is the work of the creator: but the intelligible light is perhaps also from themselves, proceeding from their own will. And yet, it is not to be adored by him who sees the true light, to which light all things owe whatever they participate in, nor by him who sees God the father of the true light, of whom it is beautifully said, *God is light, and there are no darknesses in him.* And just as those worshippers of the Sun, Moon, and stars, and admirers of their light, would never adore a spark of fire or a lamp on earth, seeing the incomparably more excellent things whose light they deem worthy of adoration: so those who understand how God is light, and how his son is the true light, enlightening every man coming into this world, and understand also that saying, *I am the light of the world*, would undeservedly adore a small spark, as it were, of the Sun, Moon, and stars, if it be compared to that true light which is God. Not that they despise such an excellent handiwork of God, or like Anaxagoras think the Sun is a fiery globe, and the Moon and other stars likewise: but moved by the unspeakable excellence by which God has left all other things far behind him, as also has his only-begotten son. Nor being ignorant that the Sun itself, the Moon, and the stars offer prayers to God the Lord of all things, through his only-begotten, we judge there is no need that we should solicit with prayers those who themselves pray: since it is more pleasing to them if, being about to pray, we rather approach God, to whom they themselves offer prayers, than that we should bring [prayers] down to them, or impart to them our powers of supplication separated from God. In this place it is pleasing to bring forward an example: our Savior and Lord, being called at one time "Good Teacher," sending back the one who had so called him to his father, said, *Why do you call me good? no one is good, except one God, my father*, because if the most beloved son of the father said that rightly, as the image of the goodness of God, would not the Sun more justly say to its worshippers, *Why do you adore me? You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve*, whom both I and all who are with me adore and worship. But if anyone is not so great, nevertheless let such a one approach with prayers the Word of God, who is able to heal him, and even more his father, who also sent out his word to the ancient righteous ones, and healed them, and delivered [them].

Even if you, in your wretchedness, should desire something loathsome according to your own lust, God will not be able to do it, nor must one believe immediately that it will happen. For God is the author not of disordered desire, nor of wandering disorder, but of a right and just nature. He might be able to provide eternal life for the soul; but 'corpses,' as Heraclitus says, 'are more fit to be cast out than dung.' As for the flesh—filled with things not even honorable to mention—God will neither will nor be able to declare it eternal against all reason; for he himself is the Reason <term>Logos: the divine word or logic governing the universe</term> of all things that exist, and therefore he can do nothing contrary to reason or contrary to himself." # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.

->The Word <note>original: ὁ λόγος (ho logos); here referring to the Christian teaching or the Divine Reason</note> has called those who are foolish in the eyes of the world, the low-born, and the despised.<-

For such people, a simple acceptance of punishments is appropriate, as they are not capable of other means of correction beyond the fear and the mental image of punishments to turn them away from the many evils they commit. Therefore, the Word says that only those who have kept their doctrines, their morals, and their <term>governing faculty<note>original: ἡγεμονικὸν (hegemonikon); the Stoic and early Christian term for the seat of the mind and will</note></term> perfectly purified will remain untouched by the fire and the punishments. But those who are not of such a character, and who according to their deserts require the discipline of punishment by fire, will find themselves in those trials for a certain end—an end which it is fitting for God to impose upon those made in His image who have lived contrary to the will of that image-bearing nature. And this is my answer to your claim that "the rest will be roasted by fire, but they alone will remain."

Then, following this, having overheard something either from the Holy Scriptures or from those who have failed to understand the Holy Scriptures, Celsus says that we claim "only we shall remain at the time of the purification of the world by fire—not only those living then, but also those who died long ago." He did not grasp that these things were spoken with a certain hidden wisdom by the Apostle of Jesus:

<margin>1 Cor. 15:51, 52.</margin>
*We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.*

He ought to have considered the meaning of the one saying these things, how he by no means separated himself from those people, nor those like himself, when he said, *And the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.* To confirm that the Apostle wrote such things with this meaning in the first letter to the Corinthians, I will also set forth the passage from the first letter to the Thessalonians, in which Paul speaks as one living, awake, and distinct from those who sleep:

<margin>1 Thess. 4:15, 16, 17.</margin>
*For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, shall by no means precede those who have fallen asleep; for the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God.*

Then again, following these words, knowing that there are others dead in Christ besides himself and those like him, he adds: *The dead in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.* But since Celsus has further mocked the resurrection of the flesh as it is preached in the churches—though it is understood more skillfully by the more sensible members—and since there is no need to repeat his words which were already stated once: come, let us treat this problem as well (as far as is fitting in a dispute with one outside the faith).

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text provided in the left column.</note>

Scripture calls them the fools of this world, of no reputation, and ignoble; this straightforward doctrine concerning punishments and chastisement is suited to them, as they admit no other improvement than that which scares them away from vices through fear and the imagination of evil. Therefore, this doctrine promises that only those will be immune from the fire who have preserved uncorrupted opinions, pure morals, and finally a preeminently pure mind. But for the rest who are unlike these, who have need of the chastisement of fire to be dispensed according to their merits, it must be brought upon them for a certain time—that which is fitting for God to bring upon those who, though made in the image of the divine nature, have despised the will of God and did not strive for their life to correspond to that same image. And let these things be said in response to that claim: *the rest of men will be scorched, while ours alone remain unharmed.*

Next, having either drawn from the sacred writings without understanding them, or having heard from those who do not understand them, he says that we say, *in the conflagration of the world we alone shall escape, not only as many living as that disaster shall overtake, but even those long since dead;* not grasping the words of the Apostle of Jesus, which reveal through a secret wisdom: *That we shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a point of time, in the moment of an eye, at the last trumpet: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we also shall be changed.* Yet he ought to have known the mind of the one saying these things, that he by no means separates himself and those like him from the dead, subjoining after these words, *And the dead shall rise incorruptible,* those others, *And we shall be changed.*

And that the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians in that sense, I will confirm through those things which the same man writes in the first to the Thessalonians, as one living, watchful, and different from those sleeping: *For this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we who live, and shall remain until the coming of the Lord, shall by no means precede those who sleep: because the Lord himself with the signal of the voice of the Archangel and with the trumpet of God shall descend from heaven:* then, since he knew others besides himself and his peers were dead in the Lord, he also added this: *And the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we who live, who shall remain, shall be snatched up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.* And since he mockingly bites at the resurrection of the flesh preached in the Churches—which is understood more clearly by the wiser—nor is there need to repeat his sayings again: come, let us also handle this question (as far as is proper in a conflict with a profane man).

<summary>Origen defends the Christian doctrine of the resurrection and the "purifying fire" against Celsus's mockery, explaining that while the simple-minded require fear of punishment, the wise understand these as spiritual refinements. He uses Paul's letters to the Corinthians and Thessalonians to clarify the nature of the "change" that occurs at the end of the world.</summary>

# Book 5. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

(taking into account the little ones <note>original: *parvulorum* / *νηπίους*; referring to those young or immature in faith</note>, who are tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine by the trickery of men who lead others into error) we are, as much as we can, adapting ourselves to the capacity of the common reader. Therefore, neither we nor the Divine Scriptures say that the dead emerging from the earth will live again with their very same flesh, unchanged for the better; rather, this is a mere calumny <note>A false and malicious accusation</note> of Celsus. For we hear many Scriptures speaking of the resurrection in a way that is worthy of God, their author. From these, it will suffice for the present to bring forward one passage of Paul from the first epistle to the Corinthians, where he writes: *But someone will say, "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?" Foolish man! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare seed, for example, of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.* You see how he says that the body which is to be born is not the one sown; rather, a bare seed is cast into the earth, and God gives each seed its own body. A sort of resurrection occurs from that sown seed: an ear of corn rising up, or in the case of a mustard seed, a larger tree; or from the stone of an olive or some other fruit-bearing tree. God, therefore, gives to each a body according to His will, just as He does with seeds; so too with those who, when they die, are as it were "sown," they shall receive in due time from that sowing a body according to their merit, in whatever form it pleases God to clothe them. For we hear the Scripture teaching in many words the difference between that which is sown and that which rises, when it says: *It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body.* Now let him who can understand these things, when he says: *As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust; and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the man of heaven.* In this passage the Apostle (although concealing certain secrets <note>original: *arcana* / *ἀπόῤῥητα*; hidden or mystical truths</note> that exceed the grasp of the simple and are not suitable for the unrefined who are still being instructed in the faith; yet, lest we should misunderstand his words) after he said, *let us bear the image of the heavenly*, adds: *I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.* And soon, as if providing a secret in his writings for posterity—

For we say that just as an ear of corn rises from a grain of wheat, so a certain principle <term>logos: a formative or rational principle</term> is implanted in the body, from which—since it is not destroyed—the body is raised in incorruption. And we do not retreat to a most absurd refuge by saying that "everything is possible for God"; for we know how to hear the word "everything" as not applying to things that do not exist, nor to things that are inconceivable. We also say that God cannot do shameful things, since then God would be able to not be God; for if God does anything shameful, He is not God. But since Celsus posits that "God does not even will things contrary to nature," we distinguish what is being said: if by "contrary to nature" one means "wickedness," we also say that God does not will things contrary to nature, neither things arising from wickedness nor things done irrationally. But if things are done according to the reason of God and His will, they are necessarily not contrary to nature; things done by God are not contrary to nature, even if they are marvelous, or seem marvelous to some. But if it is necessary to use names in a forced way, we will say that, in respect to nature as it is more commonly understood, there are some things "contrary to nature" which God will sometimes do, raising man above human nature, and making him change into a better and more divine nature...

But if violence must be done to names, we say that by taking the word *nature* as the common people understand it, there are certain things above nature, which God sometimes does by lifting man above human nature, and changing him into a more excellent and divine nature, and preserving him as such...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic refutation of the pagan philosopher Celsus. The discussion transitions from the nature of God’s power and the resurrection of the body to Celsus’s sociological arguments regarding Jewish law and national customs.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.

...such a person, as long as he presents himself as such, is easily preserved and fit. And because we have said once for all that God can do nothing that is unbecoming to Himself—since this would be a denial of His own deity—we also say that if a man, through his own wickedness, should foolishly will something, God cannot do that. Indeed, we are not so contentious, but rather examine Celsus’s words with a zeal for the truth, that we agree with him that God is not subject to immoderate desires, nor to erring disturbances, but is the presiding guardian of a right and just nature and of all virtue. We confess that He is able to grant eternal life to souls; and not only is He able, but He actually grants it. Therefore, the saying of Heraclitus cited by Celsus, that *corpses are more to be cast out than dung*, does not obstruct our view. <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change; here Celsus uses him to mock the Christian hope for the resurrection of the body.</note> Although someone might say that while dung is indeed to be held in contempt, the corpses of men—on account of the soul that inhabited them, especially if it were a good soul—are not to be cast out. For more civilized laws command that they be buried with appropriate honor, lest if they be thrown out like beasts, an injury be done to the soul that has departed from its dwelling. Far be it, therefore, from God to wish even a grain of wheat to be eternal, but rather the ear of corn grown from it; nor that which is sown in corruption, but that which rises from it incorruptible. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15, where Paul compares the resurrection of the body to a seed growing into a plant.</note> Now, as for Celsus saying that God Himself is the Reason <term>Logos: the Greek word for 'word' or 'reason', used here to bridge Greek philosophy and Christian theology</term> of all things, we say it is the Son of God, concerning whom we philosophize: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.* <note>original: "In principio erat verbum..." quoting John 1:1</note> But we do agree on this: that God does nothing contrary to reason, nor contrary to Himself. Now let us see what follows next in the context of Celsus’s words, which are as follows: *Therefore the Jews, having become a distinct nation and having established laws which they still circulate today along with a religion of whatever sort—but at least one belonging to their fathers—act in the manner of other men, each of whom follows the institutions of his own fatherland, whatever they may be. This seems even useful, not only because different laws have occurred to different people, and it is necessary to observe whatever has once been publicly decided; but also because, as is credible, the parts of the earth were distributed from the beginning to different overseers, and having been divided into certain prefectures, are administered in this way. Thus, in each place, that which is received by custom is rightly done, and it is not holy to violate the institutions of the inhabitants established there from the beginning.* Here Celsus indicates that the Jews, having made a secession from the Egyptians (of whom they were once a part), established their own nation and their own laws...

<column-break/>

...preserving <margin>* such a thing</margin> more quickly, as much as even he who is able to be preserved <margin>* for most, whatever you wish</margin>. Having said once that God wills nothing unbecoming to Himself, which would be destructive to the very nature of God, we say that if a man, having planned wickedness for himself, wills something, God will not be able to do this. Thus we are not quarrelsome toward the things said by Celsus; but examining them with a love for truth, we will agree that God is not of a faulty desire, nor of wandering disorder, but of a right and just nature, being the author of every good thing. And we will confess that He is able to provide nothing other than the eternal life of the soul; and not only is He able, but He provides it. Therefore, because of the things said before, we are not at all distressed by the saying of Heraclitus which Celsus has taken up, that *corpses are more to be cast out than dung*. And yet one might say even concerning this, that while dung is to be cast out, the corpses of men, because of the soul that dwelt within—and especially if it were of a more noble sort—are not to be cast out. For according to the more noble of the laws, they are deemed worthy of burial with the honor possible in such matters; so that we may not insult by our power the soul that dwelt there, by tossing away the body after that soul has departed, as we do the bodies of cattle. Let God not wish, then, contrary to reason, to make eternal the grain of wheat, but rather the ear of corn from it; nor that which is sown in corruption, but that which is raised from it in incorruption. But also, the Reason <gloss>Logos</gloss> of all things is, according to Celsus, God Himself; but according to us, it is His Son. Concerning Him we philosophize, saying: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.* <margin>John 1:1</margin> But, according to us also, God does not administer anything contrary to reason, nor is He able to work anything contrary to Himself.
