And this seems to be advantageous, not only because it entered the minds of different people to legislate differently, and it is necessary to guard the things ratified for the common good; but also because, as is likely, the parts of the earth were from the beginning assigned to different overseers of the world, <margin>* so that it might be</margin> and having been divided into certain domains, are governed in this way. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5

<margin>
* It is beneficial to worship according to ancestral customs.
</margin>

...to these men. And so that we do not have to repeat the very words of Celsus, he says that it is beneficial for these people to worship according to their ancestral traditions, just as it is for other nations to embrace their own. He sets forth a somewhat deeper reason why it is beneficial for the Jews to observe their ancestral customs, hinting that the overseers <note>Greek: *epoptai*; Latin: *praesides*. These are the guardian spirits or lesser gods Celsus believes govern specific nations.</note> who were allotted the various parts of the earth and acted as lawmakers established these things in cooperation with the original legislators. He seems to indicate, then, that both the land of the Jews and the nation upon it are overseen by someone or some group, by whom or with whose cooperation the laws of the Jews were established or given to Moses. "And it is necessary," he says, "to keep the laws, not only because it occurred to different people to think differently, and because one must guard what has been ratified for the common good; but also because, as is likely, the parts of the earth were from the beginning assigned to different overseers and divided into certain domains, and are governed in this way." Then, as if Celsus had forgotten what he previously said against the Jews, he now includes them in his general praise of all who keep ancestral traditions, saying, "And certainly, things would be done rightly among each people if performed in the way that is pleasing to those overseers." And see if he does not outright—as far as he is able—wish for the Jew to live in his own laws and not depart from them, as if he were acting impiously if he did depart; for he says, "it is not holy to violate the customs established from the beginning according to locality." I would like to ask him next, or those who agree with him: Who is it, then, who divided the parts of the earth from the beginning to different overseers? It is clear that the land of the Jews and the Jews themselves were given to the one or those to whom it was allotted. Did Zeus, then—as Celsus would name him—assign the Jewish nation and their land to someone or some group? And did he wish for the one who was allotted Judea to establish such laws for the Jews? Or how did such a will of his come to be? Whichever way he answers, you see that his argument will be backed into a corner. For if the parts of the earth were not distributed to their overseers by a single spirit, did each one distribute the earth to himself by lot and without a supervisor, just as it happened? But this too is absurd, and is a reduction of the providence of the God over all, even tending toward its destruction. Let anyone who wishes explain how and according to what domains the parts of the earth are divided and governed by those overseeing them, promising us also how the things done among each people are "rightly" done when they please the overseers. And tell me if they are "right," for example, the laws of the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia, often used in Greek literature as examples of "barbarians."</note> which allow for the killing of fathers; or those of the Persians, which do not prevent mothers from being married to their sons, nor fathers to their own daughters. Why should I need to select from those who have labored over history...

* to himself, then.

...to retain from that time: and not to repeat his same words, it is useful for them to use their own rites, just as other nations each use their own. And soon he brings forward a certain more hidden cause why it is expedient for the Jews to preserve their ancestral institutions: suggesting that there are certain presidents <note>Latin: *praesides*, translating the Greek *epoptai*.</note> of the lands, who assist the legislators of those lands in bringing forth laws. Therefore he seems to signify that the region of the Jews also, and the nation, is subject to some one president or many, by whose help Moses brought his laws to the people. *It is necessary, he says, to keep the laws, not only because it pleased others to bring them forth differently, and whatever the consensus of the people approved must be observed: but also because it is credible that the parts of the earth were distributed from the very beginning to different presidents, and are governed by them as if they were provinces.* Then, as if Celsus had forgotten how many things he said against the Jews, he now includes them also in a universal praise of those who keep ancestral laws, saying, *And certainly, whoever lives by the customs of his own nation does rightly. And see whether he does not, as much as in him lies, accuse the Jew who deserts his ancestral law of impiety; for he says it is a crime to violate the ancient laws of the regions.* Wherefore I would gladly ask him, and those who feel as he does, Who is he who from the beginning distributed the parts of the earth to his presidents, so that among the others the province of the Jews also fell by lot to someone or to several? Did Jupiter <note>Latin: *Jupiter*, translating the Greek *Zeus*.</note>, as Celsus would say, attribute the Jewish nation and region to one or several, and did he wish that he who had been allotted the Jewish province should write such laws for the Jews? Or was this perhaps done against the will of Jupiter? Whichever he might answer, his speech is stuck in straits. But if the regions of the earth were distributed to their presidents by no one person, then each one seized his own rashly, with no one dividing them: which itself would be absurd to believe, surely taking away all providence from affairs. How, moreover, and into what provinces the distributed earth is administered by presidents, let him who wishes tell us, and show how rightly those things are done in each which are done at the will of the presidents: then how right are the laws of the Scythians concerning the killing of fathers, which may be said for the sake of example, or those of the Persians not restraining mothers from marriage with sons, nor fathers with daughters. But what need is there for me to [recount] various...

# Book 5. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...to collect the various laws of nations from writers, and to ask whether the laws which pleased the presiding powers are rightly observed by each? Let Celsus tell us how it is not a violation of holiness to break ancestral laws concerning the marrying of daughters or mothers; or concerning a "blessed" end of life (as they think) by hanging, or by the funeral pyre—into which, if someone throws himself alive, they say the soul is purged and all sins are consumed along with the body. How could it be a crime to dissolve the laws of the Tauri, for example, who slaughter guests as victims for Diana <note>original: "Artemis"</note>; or of the Africans <note>original: "Libyans"</note> who sacrifice their sons to Saturn <note>original: "Cronus"</note>? By the same reasoning of Celsus, it follows that the Jews act impiously if they transgress their ancestral laws about not worshiping any other God except the Creator of this world. Thus, according to his opinion, holiness <note>term: *pietas/hosiotēs* — a sense of duty toward the divine and one's community</note> will not be natural but arbitrary (for it is holy among some to venerate the crocodile, and to eat animals consecrated by others; among others to venerate the calf; and again others to worship the goat as a God). And so it will happen that one and the same man is holy according to the laws of some, but conversely impious according to others: which is by far the most absurd thing. They will perhaps respond that piety consists in this: if it is done according to ancestral laws, because foreign laws bind no one; nor is he immediately impious who is held impious by others, provided he does not depart from his ancestral rite; and that it is permitted for this man to oppose the laws of others and to devour their sacred things. See whether this does not introduce great confusion into law and right, if these things have no nature of their own by whose formula piety in actions may be examined. Therefore, if piety, holiness, and justice are relative to something else—so that the same thing is holy and impious according to which different laws it refers to—see if it does not follow that temperance is also counted among those things which are called relative, as well as fortitude, and prudence, and knowledge, and the rest of the virtues; than which nothing more absurd can be imagined. And let these things suffice as a response to the sayings of Celsus for those who understand matters more simply and in the common way. But since we think these words will come into the hands of the more diligent and accurate, come, let us bring forth a few things from more recondite matters, which contain a secret and abstruse contemplation concerning that attribution of the parts of the earth from the beginning to certain inspectors <note>term: *epoptai* — overseers or guardian spirits assigned to specific regions</note>; and having commemorated and collected the absurdities, let us finally, as far as possible, hand down the true reason. It seems to me that Celsus has not rightly understood this more secret doctrine of the division of the lands, which even Greek history touches upon somewhat, introducing certain of those who are believed to be gods

And how is it not holy to dissolve the laws, for example, among the Tauri where they slaughter strangers as sacrifices to Diana; or those of the Libyans concerning the sacrificing of children to Saturn? However, it follows for Celsus that it is not holy for Jews to dissolve ancestral laws, those concerning the necessity of worshiping no other God besides the Creator of all things. And according to him, holiness will not be by nature, but by some position and custom it will be divine; (for it is holy among these to worship the crocodile, and to eat from those things which are religiously observed among others; and it is holy to others to worship the calf; and among others, to consider the goat a God.) And he himself will be doing holy things according to these laws, but unholy things according to others. Which is the most out of place of all things. But it is likely they will say to these things, that he who keeps ancestral customs is holy, and in no way unholy, since he does not observe the things of others. And again, that he, though thought unholy among certain people, is not unholy when he worships his own things according to ancestral custom, but <margin>is able to sink/overcome.</margin> devours and * feasts upon the things held by those with contrary laws. Now, for the simpler and more common sort, the things said are a sufficient enough response to the words set forth by Celsus. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 5.

<margin>
* holy things.
</margin>

...among the poets, it is admitted that certain of those called gods have certain places more peculiarly their own. Even barbarian history, and especially that of the Egyptians, shows something similar regarding the division of Egypt into the districts they call "nomes"; they say, for instance, that Sais fell to Athena, who also possesses Attica. The learned among the Egyptians will tell countless such stories. I do not know if they also include the Jews and their land in this distribution along with others. However, enough has been said for the present regarding accounts outside of the divine words. 

But we say that our prophet, the genuine servant of God, Moses, in the Song of Deuteronomy, sets forth something concerning the division of the earth, speaking thus: "When the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and the Lord's portion became his people Jacob, the allotment of his inheritance Israel." <note>original: Deuteronomy 32:8-9. Origen uses the Septuagint Greek version, which mentions "angels of God" where modern Bibles often say "sons of Israel."</note> The same Moses, in the book entitled Genesis, speaks in the form of a history about this same distribution of nations. Thus: "And the whole earth was of one lip and one voice for all; and it happened as they moved from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there." And a little later, he says: "The Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the sons of men built; and the Lord said, Behold, they are one race and have one lip; and they have begun to do this, and now nothing will fail them of all they intend to do. Come, let us go down and there confound their tongue, so that they may not hear each other's voice. And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they ceased building the city and the tower. Because of this, its name was called Confusion <note>original: "Sygchysis" (Confusion), translating the Hebrew "Babel."</note>, because there the Lord God confounded the lips of all the earth, and from there the Lord God scattered them over the face of all the earth." <note>original: Genesis 11:1-9.</note> 

And in the work entitled the Wisdom of Solomon, concerning wisdom and the confusion of dialects by which the division of those on earth occurred, these things are said of wisdom: "She also, when the nations were confounded in a conspiracy of wickedness, knew the righteous man, and preserved him blameless before God, and kept him strong against his compassion for his child." <note>original: Wisdom of Solomon 10:5. This refers to Abraham and the sacrifice of Isaac.</note> 

The discourse on these matters is long and mystical, to which the saying applies: "It is good to keep the secret of a king." <note>original: Tobit 12:7.</note> This is so that the discourse concerning souls—which are clothed in bodies but not through transmigration <note><term>metensomatosis</term>: the Greek term for the migration of a soul into a new body, similar to reincarnation, which Origen is distinguishing from his own views.</note>—is not tossed into the ears of just anyone, nor that "holy things be given to dogs," nor "pearls be cast before swine." <note>original: Matthew 7:6.</note> For such a thing would be impious, involving a betrayal of the secret things of the wisdom of God—

# Book 5. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Kk 2

<margin>Wisdom 1. 4.</margin>
It is beautifully written: *Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin.* <note>Origen quotes the Book of Wisdom to argue that spiritual understanding requires moral purity.</note> It is sufficient to set forth the historical account of those things hidden beneath the surface of history, so that those who are able may seek out the deeper meaning of this passage for themselves. Let it be understood, then, that all people upon the earth once used a certain single divine language; as long as they agreed with one another, they were preserved in this divine language, and they did not move away from the East <note>In Origen's allegory, the "East" represents the source of divine light and eternal truth.</note> so long as they grasped those things which belong to the light and the radiance of the eternal brightness. But when these people moved away from the East, thinking thoughts that do not belong to the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar (which is interpreted as *shaking out of teeth*, symbolizing that their nourishment had perished) <note>A typical Origenist etymology: losing teeth means losing the ability to "chew" or process spiritual food.</note> and there they dwelt. Then, wishing to gather together material things and join to heaven those things not born for such a purpose—striving to reach immaterial things through material ones—they said, *Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.* <margin>Gen. 11. 3.</margin> And now, hardening the clay-like matter, they fashioned bricks instead of stones, and using mud for mortar instead of bitumen, they built a city and a tower, the top of which, in their own opinion, reached unto heaven. Let each person be handed over—according to how much they have receded more or less from the East, and how much more or less labor they put into shaping bricks into stones and clay into bitumen in that building—to angels who are more or less severe, until they have paid the penalty for their audacity. Then, by these angels, each of those who created their own language shall be led away to various parts of the earth according to their merits: some, for instance, to a burning region; others to a region heavy with cold; some to a land harsh and difficult to cultivate, others to one more mild; some to a place swarming with wild beasts, others to one more free from such harm. If anyone can consider these things as a history that partly narrates actual events and partly veils something more secret, let him see that those who preserved the original language—because they had not departed from the East, but remained there and kept the Eastern tongue—alone became the "portion of the Lord." <margin>Deu. 32. 9.</margin> They were called his people by the name of Jacob, and the Israelites were the "cord of his inheritance." These alone had a protector <note>The Lord himself, rather than a subordinate or punishing angel.</note> not for the purpose of punishment like the others. Here it must be observed, as far as human weakness allows, that even in the city of those who were assigned to God as his excellent portion, sins were committed—at first bearable, and such as did not merit...

This must be understood as occurring over a long period of time, with healing remedies constantly being applied, and these people returning from their lapses. Thus they were left to themselves in proportion to their sins against those who had fallen to the other regions—first being punished less severely <note>original: *αὐτοῦ κολασθέντας*</note> and paying the penalty as if they were being disciplined, so that they might return to their own home. Later, however, one sees them delivered over to harsher rulers, whom the Scriptures would name the **Assyrians**, and then the **Babylonians**. Then, even as treatments were being applied, one sees them nonetheless increasing their sins, and because of this, they were immeasurably plundered by the rulers of the remaining nations in the other portions. But their own Ruler <note>Origen refers here to the Logos or the God of Israel</note> intentionally allowed them to be plundered by the rulers among the rest of the nations; so that He Himself, rising up to avenge Himself with good reason, might take authority over all the remaining nations as far as He is able, and might do this: both establish laws for them and show them the way of life by which they must live. This was in order to lead them back to the same end to which He was leading those of the former nation who had [not] sinned. Through these things, let those who are able to see such great matters learn that He who obtained the former people who had not yet sinned is much more powerful than the rest of the gods. For He has been given the power to draw out from every portion those who were chosen, snatching them away from those who had taken them for punishment, and leading them to laws and a life that contributes to the forgetting of their former sins. But since those who moved from the east, because of the things in which they sinned, were delivered over to a "reprobate mind," and to "vile passions," and to "impurity in the lusts of their hearts," so that being sated with sin they might hate it; we do not submit to **Celsus** when he pleases to assert that because the parts of the earth have been assigned to overseers, the affairs among each people are done rightly. On the contrary, we do not wish to do their things just because it is pleasing to them. For we see that it is a holy thing to dissolve the ancient customs established in various places in favor of better and more divine laws, which **Jesus** established as the most powerful one, "delivering us from this present evil age" and from the "rulers of this age who are coming to nothing." ...not entirely abandoned for that reason; then more punishments, yet tolerable ones, and that over a long time with remedies never failing to be applied, so that they might recover their senses through intervals. Then, whenever they were forsaken according to the magnitude of their sin—not unlike the other regions allotted to others—they were first punished more lightly, so that, as if warned by a childish chastisement, they might return to their own. But afterward, they were truly handed over to more cruel masters, such as the Scripture names the **Assyrians**, then the **Babylonians**. Observe furthermore how finally, when despite the applied cures their malice nonetheless grew, they were carried away by plundering princes and dispersed among distant nations into the portions of foreign governors. However, their own governor <note>Latin: *praeses*</note> intentionally looked the other way while they were being plundered by the governors of the other nations; so that He Himself, by the best right, as if avenging the injuries brought upon Himself, having obtained power in turn, might invade the nations of others and lead away from there as many as He could. Having brought them under His laws, He might prescribe a way of living; and thus lead them to that end to which He would have led the men of His own nation formerly assigned to Him, had sins not stood in the way. By this, He might instruct those who are able to notice these things: namely, that this One who obtained those immune from sin even then is far more powerful than the others; since He is able to take the chosen ones from all the portions, dragged back from those who had received them to be punished, and lead them to useful laws of life, their former sins being given over to oblivion. But these things, as I have prefaced, are said by us in a covered way, whereby it appears that Celsus and his like have not rightly understood the division of the earth and the provinces assigned, as it were, to their own governors. But since those who set out from the East, on account of their sins, were "given over to a reprobate sense," and "shameful passions," and "impurities according to their own lusts," so that being sated they might loathe sin, we shall not assent to the opinion of Celsus when he says that, because of those governors placed over the parts of the earth, all things in each place are done in the best manner; nor do we wish to approve such things as Celsus proclaims them. For we see it is lawful to change the ancient laws of regions for better and more divine ones, which **Jesus** brought to His own by His power, "snatching them from this present evil world" and from the "princes of this world who are already vanishing." And it is impious not to subject oneself to the most powerful Prince exalted above all others, whom God Himself addressed thus, as is held in the writings of the ancient Prophets...

He refutes Celsus's claim that national traditions should never be changed, asserting that Jesus has the authority to replace old local laws with a superior divine law.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.

Those who drink from the Nile must observe the Egyptian laws regarding female oxen. On this point, Celsus mockingly compares the angels who serve as God's messengers among the Jews <margin>* and worse.</margin>—saying "and is Ammon worse" than the angels of the Jews at delivering divine messages? This he says without investigating the meaning of the words or the appearances of these angels. For he would have seen that God is not concerned with oxen <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note> where He appears to legislate for oxen or irrational animals; rather, these things were written for the sake of men, under the guise of irrational animals, to demonstrate a certain <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>original: "physiologia," meaning the study of the inner nature of things.</note>. Celsus, then, claims that no one does wrong by wishing to observe their own ancestral customs. It follows, according to him, that the Scythians do nothing wrong when they feast on human flesh according to their ancestral traditions. And the Indians who eat their fathers would be acting piously, according to Celsus, or at least not unjustly. He even cites a passage from Herodotus to support the idea that everyone should cherish their ancestral laws, and he seems to approve of those Indians called Callatiae under King Darius, who ate their parents; for when Darius asked them for what price they would be willing to abandon this custom, they cried out loudly and told him to speak of better things. Therefore, since two types of law are set before us—one being the law of nature, which God would legislate, and the other being the written law of cities—it is good, when the written law does not oppose the law of God, for citizens not to abandon it on the pretext of foreign laws. But where the law of nature—that is, <margin>* always far away.</margin> the law of God—commands the opposite of the written law, see if reason does not tell us to bid a long farewell to the written codes and the will of the legislator, and to give oneself to God the Legislator, choosing to live according to His word, even if this must be done amidst dangers, countless labors, deaths, and dishonor. For it would be absurd, when the things pleasing to God are different from those pleasing to the laws in cities, and it is impossible to please both God and those who champion such laws, to despise the actions by which one pleases the Creator of all things, and instead choose those by which one will be displeasing to God but pleasing to the laws and their friends. And if it is reasonable in other matters to prefer the reason of nature, which is the law of God, over the written law enacted by men in opposition <margin>* honored. * or for now.</margin> to the law of God, how much more should this be done in laws concerning God? * Thus, we will not worship only Jupiter and Bacchus (as they please) like the Ethiopians who inhabit Meroe; nor will we honor Ethiopian gods in the Ethiopian fashion at all; * nor will we consider only the Heavenly Queen and Bacchus as gods, like the Arabs; indeed, not at all will we consider these as gods

those who drink from the Nile are bound by the law of the Egyptians regarding cows. Presently Celsus, attacking with insults the angels who are the intermediaries of the Jews with God, denies that Ammon is inferior in administering divine affairs *to the angels of the Jews*; yet he understands neither their words nor what their appearances signify; otherwise he would have seen that oxen are not a care to God where He is thought to establish laws about cattle and brutes: but in these things, which are written for the sake of men, a certain <term>Natural Philosophy</term> lies beneath the pretext of brutes. Therefore, Celsus denies that he who lives by ancestral laws acts unjustly: from which it follows that, according to his own opinion, the Scythians do not act unjustly when, by ancestral custom, they prepare feasts from human entrails: likewise the Indians devouring their own fathers would act piously by this reasoning, or certainly not unjustly. Here he brings forward in his favor the opinion of Herodotus, *that everyone rightly uses the laws of his own fatherland*: and he seems to approve of those Callatian Indians, who, when asked by Darius for what reward they would allow themselves to be induced to abolish their law about eating parents, cried out that he should speak of honorable things. Therefore, since there are two kinds of laws in general, one the law of nature, of which God is the author, the other written and valid in cities: wherever the written law does not oppose the law of God, it is proper to adapt oneself to the citizens, nor to affect foreign laws: but where the law of nature, that is of God, commands the contrary to the written law, see whether reason does not dictate that, having bid the written law be gone, committing yourself to God the legislator, you should live according to His precept, even if it must be done with innumerable dangers, labors, deaths, and ignominies. For it would be absurd for men, while approving things that displease God—if it becomes impossible to please God and men who protect such laws at the same time—to behave so that, having despised the actions by which you can please God the Creator, you choose those by which God is offended for the sake of unlawful laws and their friends. But if in other matters it is fair to prefer the reason of nature, which is itself the law of God, to the written law brought forth by men against the sentiment of divine law: how much more must that be done in laws pertaining to religion? Wherefore we shall neither adore Jupiter and Bacchus as the only gods (as it seems to them), like the Ethiopians inhabiting Meroe; nor shall we honor any Ethiopian gods in the manner of the Ethiopians; nor shall we hold the Heavenly Queen and Bacchus as the only gods like the Arabs; indeed, this whole [class] of gods...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s rebuttal against Celsus’s argument that all people should remain in their ancestral religions. Origen uses the specific examples of Egyptian and Arabian deities to demonstrate the logical inconsistencies of such cultural relativism.</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

We shall not condemn a race distinguished by gender; (for the Arabs worship Urania <note>The Greek name for the "Heavenly" goddess, often identified with Aphrodite or Al-Lat</note> as a female, and Liber <note>The Roman name for Dionysus/Bacchus</note> as a male). Nor, like all the Egyptians, shall we decree divine honors to Osiris and Isis; nor, like the people of Sais, to Minerva. And if it seemed fit to the ancient people of Naucratis to worship other Gods, while the younger generation chooses to venerate Sarapis—who was never before ranked among the Gods—they certainly shall not find us to be rivals in worshiping a "new" God, one not even known to men. For the Son of God, the firstborn of all creation, although he appears to have become man only recently, is not for that reason "new": for Holy Scripture knows him to be the oldest of all creatures; and that God the Father said to him, *Let us make man in our image and likeness*. <margin>Colossians 1:15.</margin> <margin>Genesis 1:26.</margin>

I will show, moreover, that Celsus does not speak rightly when he says that everyone must remain in the religion of their fathers. For he says that *the Ethiopians, inhabitants of Meroe, know only two Gods, Jupiter and Liber, and worship them alone: likewise the Arabs know two, Liber—whom they have in common with the Ethiopians—but their own goddess, Urania*. Consequently, the Ethiopians do not hold Urania as a deity, nor do the Arabs hold Jupiter. If, therefore, an Ethiopian, brought by some chance into Arabia, were to be accused of capital impiety because he does not worship Urania, should he rather die, or should he adore her against his ancestral rites? For, if he must transgress his country's religion, he acts impiously according to Celsus’s own opinion; but if he allows himself to be led to execution, let Celsus explain why he should choose death, since it is nowhere taught that the Ethiopians philosophize about the immortality of the soul or the reward for keeping one's ancestral religion inviolate. 

The same may be said of an Arab traveling by chance among the people of Meroe: for he too, having been taught at home to venerate only Liber and Urania, will not adore Jupiter with the Ethiopians; and if, condemned for impiety, he is led to death, let Celsus explain to us what he ought to do. Furthermore, regarding Osiris and Isis, it would be superfluous to recount the fables and foreign to our present business, even if these stories are pulled toward a "Tropology" <note>A method of interpretation that treats myths as metaphors for moral or physical truths</note> teaching us to venerate the lifeless element of water and the earth spread beneath men and other animals. For thus, I believe, they take Osiris to mean water, and Isis to mean earth. Regarding Sarapis, however, the history is long and inconsistent, brought into the light only yesterday or the day before by certain deceptions of Ptolemy, who wished to make this God famous at Alexandria.

Neither do the Ethiopians worship Urania, nor the Arabs Zeus. If then an Ethiopian, by some circumstance being among the Arabs, should be considered impious for not worshiping Urania, and should face the danger of death among them; must the Ethiopian die, or act against his ancestors and worship Urania? For if he must act against his ancestors, he will not be doing what is right according to Celsus’s words; but if he presents his composure in the face of death, he must have a reason for choosing death. The traditions of the Ethiopians do not teach one to philosophize about the immortality of the soul, or the honor given for piety in keeping the ancestral laws of the recognized gods. 

One can say the same thing about the Arabs, if by some circumstance they were staying with the Ethiopians near Meroe. For either, having been taught to worship only Urania and Dionysus, they will worship Zeus, or being considered impious by the Ethiopians, if they were led away to death, let Celsus say what they would reasonably do. It is not the right time for us now to list the myths concerning Osiris and Isis. Even if the myths are interpreted metaphorically, they will teach us to worship lifeless water and the earth that lies beneath humans and all animals; for they interpret, I believe, Osiris as water and Isis as earth. Regarding Sarapis, there is a long and discordant history, he having come into the midst only yesterday or the day before through certain sorceries of the one called Ptolemy, as if to show a manifest God to those in Alexandria.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

We Christians, recognizing that natural law as the queen of all—which is itself the law of God <note>original: "τῇ φύσει πάντων βασιλέα ἐπιγνόντες νόμον, τὸν αὐτὸν ὄντα τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>—endeavor to live according to it, bidding a long farewell to all unlawful laws. But let us see what Celsus says next, where he touches very little upon the Christians, but a great deal upon the Jews. He speaks thus: *“Truly, that the Jews embrace their own law with their whole heart in this manner is not to be blamed; rather, those are to be accused who, having deserted their own institutions, defect to the Jews. If these people pride themselves on the knowledge of some higher wisdom, and therefore disdain the company of others as if they were not equally pure, let them hear that even their opinion concerning heaven is not their own; but, to say nothing of others, the Persians (as Herodotus reports) have felt the same for a long time. It is their custom,” he says, “to sacrifice to Jupiter on the highest mountains, calling the whole circle of the heavens Jupiter.” I think, therefore, they know that this is merely a difference of names: the Supreme, or Diespiter <note>An archaic Latin name for Jupiter, meaning "Father of Day."</note>, or Jupiter, or Adonai, Sabaoth, or Amun (as the Egyptians call him), or (as the Scythians say) Pappaeus. But they are not more holy than others because they are circumcised; for the Colchians and Egyptians did this first. Nor because they abstain from swine’s flesh; for this is a custom of the Egyptians, who moreover are known to spare sheep, goats, oxen, and fish. Pythagoras and his disciples forbade themselves beans and all living things; yet it is not credible that they are therefore more to be praised or dearer to God than others, while others are not; nor that He sends His angels to them alone, as if to a region of the blessed which they have obtained. For we see both who they are and what sort of region they have been deemed worthy of. Therefore, let that arrogant choir depart far away where it deserves; not knowing that great God, but deceived by the tricks of Moses, and having embraced his teaching to their own misfortune.* It appears here that the Jews are accused of falsely believing themselves to be the peculiar portion of the Supreme God, selected above all other nations; and that they arrogantly boast of Him whom they do not know, having been deceived to their own hurt by the tricks of their teacher Moses. But we have already spoken in large part above concerning the venerable and excellent Republic of the Jews, while the temple—the symbol of the city of God—still stood, along with the altar and its ceremonies. If anyone, with a mind raised to contemplate the design of the Lawgiver, should examine the institutions of that nation compared with the customs of the rest, which they use even today, he will admire no race of men more; as a people who, having rejected all things useless to the human race—

It is clear that in these words he accuses the Jews of falsely supposing themselves to be in a chosen portion above all the nations on earth before God. # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

[Celsus claims that the Jews] differ from the true opinion concerning God, and he says that *the Persians, in the manner of the Jews, perform sacred rites to Jupiter upon the highest summits of the mountains*; not seeing that the Jews, just as they knew only one God, so also they had only one holy house of prayer, one altar of burnt offerings, one altar of sacred incense, and one high priest of God. Therefore, the Jews had nothing in common with the Persians, who climb very high mountains—and many of them—for the sake of sacred rites far dissimilar to the Mosaic sacrifices. These [Mosaic rites] were performed by the priests of the Jews according to a certain likeness and shadow of heavenly things, while they explained in secret the understanding of the lawful rites and what was signified by them. <margin>* in secret</margin> <note>The Greek margin notes "in secret" or "mystically," emphasizing that the Jewish law had hidden spiritual meanings.</note> The Persians call the whole circuit of heaven by the name of Jupiter; but we believe the heaven to be neither Jupiter nor God, as we are those who know that certain beings inferior to God have ascended above all heavens and above every nature perceptible to the senses, thus understanding that passage: *Praise God, ye heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.* <margin>Psalm 148:4</margin> And because Celsus thinks it makes no difference whether you say Jupiter or "Father of Day" <note>original: *Diespiter*, an archaic Latin name for Jupiter</note>, or Adonai, or Sabaoth, or Amun (as the Egyptians do), or Pappaeus (as the Scythians do); let us discuss these things for a little while. Only let the reader remember what we said previously regarding this same question, on the occasion offered to us by Celsus; and now we repeat the same: that the nature of names is not according to the whim of men, which was the opinion of Aristotle. For the languages of men did not take their beginning from men, as is clear to those who notice the properties of incantations in various languages, and the various accents of names according to different regions. We treated this briefly above, saying that words which have a genuine power in a certain language, if they are translated into another, do not retain the same power. The same is found regarding men: for if you take a man called by this or that Greek name from birth, and change the name into a Roman or Egyptian one, or that of any other nation, and try to enchant him, the incantation will not be effective, though it would have been if he were called by the name long ago imposed upon him. The same happens with a Roman name; if you attempt an incantation after changing it into Greek, it will not have the strength it would have had if the man's original name had not been changed. If this is true regarding human names, what must be thought of the attributes assigned to God for whatever reason? For example, if you signi—

<column-break/>

—[signify] a difference in the opinion concerning God, he says "similarly to the Jews, the Persians perform sacrifices to Zeus upon the highest of the mountains," not seeing that just as the Jews knew one God, so they knew one holy house of prayer, and one altar of whole-burnt offerings, and one altar of incense, and one high priest of God. [He does not see] that in climbing the highest of the mountains, which are many, to perform sacrifices, they have nothing similar to the rites according to the law of Moses; according to which the priests of the Jews served a "copy and shadow" of heavenly things, looking into the secret <margin>* in secret</margin> narration of the law concerning sacrifices, of which the rites themselves were symbols. The Persians, then, call the whole circle of the heaven "Zeus," but we do not say the heaven is Zeus, nor do we say it is God; for we know that even some of those inferior to God have ascended the heavens and all sensible nature. And thus we understand this: *Praise God, ye heavens of heavens, and let the water above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.* <margin>Psalm 148:4</margin> But, since Celsus thinks it makes no difference to call him Zeus the Highest, or Zen, or Adonai, or Sabaoth, or (as the Egyptians) Amun, or (as the Scythians) Pappaeus; come, let us discuss a few things about these, reminding the reader at the same time of what was said above on such a problem when the text of Celsus called us to such matters. And now we say that the nature of names is not a matter of established laws <note>i.e., arbitrary human convention</note>, as Aristotle thinks. For the dialects among men do not have their origin from men, as those who focus on the powers of natural incantations can conclude, according to the different dialects and the different sounds of the names provided by the dialects. We have dealt with these briefly in the preceding parts, saying that things which are naturally powerful in a certain dialect, if changed into another dialect, no longer have the same strength as they perhaps had in their own sounds. And already such a thing is found even among men: for if we change the name of a certain person called in the Greek dialect from birth into the dialect of the Egyptians or Romans or anyone else, <margin>* to do</margin> we would not make him experience or do <margin>* it will do</margin> what he would have experienced or done if called by the only name first given to him. Nor if we translated the name of one called from the beginning in the Roman tongue into the Greek dialect, would it do what the incantation promises to do, if the first name named for him were not preserved.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.

...the Greek language from the name of Abraham, and is signified by the designation of Isaac, and is manifested by the voice of Jacob. And if the one calling upon or adjuring names the **God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob**, he might perform certain things, either through the nature of these names or their power, with demons being conquered and subjected to the one speaking these things. But if he says, "the God of the chosen father of the resonant sound," and "the God of laughter," and "the God of the supplanter," <note>These are the literal etymological meanings of the names Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in Greek/Hebrew. Origen argues the power lies in the specific sound of the name, not its translated meaning.</note> the name performs nothing in this way, just like anything else that possesses no power. In the same way, if we translate the name **Israel** into Greek or another dialect, we shall accomplish nothing; but if we preserve it, attaching those things which those skilled in these matters have thought to weave together with it, then something might happen according to the promise of such invocations, though not in just any voice. We shall say the same also concerning the word **Sabaoth**, which is employed in many places in incantations; for if we translate the name into "Lord of powers," or "Lord of hosts," or "Almighty" (for those interpreting it have received it in various ways), we shall accomplish nothing. But by preserving it in its own sounds, we shall accomplish something, as those skilled in these matters say. We shall say the same also concerning **Adonai**. If, therefore, when *Sabaoth* or *Adonai* are translated into what they seem to signify in the Greek tongue, they achieve <margin>* will perform nothing, nor be able.</margin> * anything; how much more will it *perform nothing, nor be able to do so, as if it made no difference whether one calls the name **Zeus** or **Most High**, or **Zena**, or **Adonai**, or **Sabaoth**. Knowing these and similar secrets, Moses and the prophets forbade the naming of the name of other gods with [one] mouth, <margin>* having practiced. S. G.</margin> *having practiced praying to the one God over all, and remembering in a heart taught to be pure from all vanity of thoughts and words. For these reasons, one must choose to endure every outrage rather than confess **Zeus** to be God. For we do not suppose Zeus and Sabaoth to be the same; indeed, we do not consider Zeus to be anything divine at all, but rather a certain demon who rejoices in being so named, who is no friend to men, nor to the true God. And if the Egyptians proffer **Ammon** to us, <margin>* punishment.</margin> threatening *death, we will die rather than proclaim Ammon to be God, as he is used (as is likely) in certain Egyptian incantations; or this demon in incantations. And let the Scythians say that **Pappaeus** is the God over all; but we will not be persuaded, while acknowledging the God over all, yet not naming God by the proper name of Pappaeus, as if he were a friend of those who were allotted the Scythian wilderness and their nation and dialect. For the common name for "God" in Scythian, and in Egyptian, and

<column-break/>

...achieves anything, if you translate it: "God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob"; if someone adjures by the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, he will effect something, either through the nature or the virtue of those names, with the demons yielding and doing the bidding of the victor. That same adjurer, if he should say, "By the God of the chosen father of the sounding," "By the God of laughter," "By the God of the supplanter," will effect just as much as if he employed any most inert name. Likewise, if we change this name **Israel** into the Greek or another language, we shall effect nothing: but if we keep it as it is, and join other things which those skilled in these arts are accustomed to; then at last the outcome will answer the hope, the force of such names exerting itself. The same must be said of this word **Sabaoth**, which is frequent in incantations; if you substitute for it "Lord of virtues," or "Lord of armies," or "Omnipotent" (for it has been variously translated by interpreters), you will do nothing: but if you keep the Hebrew word itself, it will not be ineffective, if we believe those skilled in such arts: which can also be said of this name **Adonai**. Therefore, if neither *Sabaoth* nor *Adonai*, having preserved their significance but changed into the Greek language, is effective, how much less will it avail among those who think it matters nothing whether you say **Jupiter Most High** or **Zena**, **Adonai** or **Sabaoth**. Because Moses and the rest of the Prophets knew these and other secrets in a similar way, they forbid the name of other gods to be in the mouth of him who intends to supplicate the God of the universe, lest it be recollected by a heart taught to be pure from all vanity of words and thoughts. Wherefore we endure any tortures rather than confess Jupiter to be God: for we do not believe Jupiter and Sabaoth to be the same: indeed, we do not even believe Jupiter to be a God, but a certain demon, who delights in this name, hostile to men and an enemy to the true God. And if the Egyptians thrust their **Ammon** upon us, even threatening punishments, we will die sooner than call Ammon "God," though he be invoked by Egyptian incantators. Let the Scythians also affirm that **Pappaeus** is that God of the universe; they will never persuade us of it—believing indeed that there is one God of this universe, but not intending to name this God "Pappaeus" as if by a proper name, namely by the will of that presiding spirit of the Scythian solitudes and nations and languages: otherwise, by the appellative name of God either in Scythian, or Egyptian, or...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

or in whatever language each person was raised. If someone names him <note>referring to God</note>, he will have committed no sin. However, the reason for circumcision is not the same for the Jews as it is for the Colchians or Egyptians, and consequently, it is not the same circumcision. For just as one who sacrifices does not sacrifice to the same being, even if he seems to perform similar rites; and he who prays does not offer prayers to the same being, even if he asks for the same things; so too it must not be said of a circumcised man that he differs in no way from any other circumcised persons. For the purpose, the law, and the will of the one being circumcised makes it a different matter. 

And, so that this point may be better understood, it should be said that although the name of "justice" is the same among all Greeks, it appears that justice according to Epicurus <note>the philosopher who emphasized pleasure and avoided pain</note> is one thing; justice according to the Stoics—who deny the three-part division of the soul—is another; and justice according to the Platonists—who say it consists of the proper duties of each part of the soul—is yet another. In the same way, the courage of Epicurus is one thing, enduring labor to escape greater labor; the courage of a Stoic is another, seeking all virtue for the sake of virtue itself; and the courage of a Platonist is another, referring this virtue to the "irascible" <note>spirited or emotional</note> part of the soul and assigning it a place in the chest. 

Thus, as the doctrines of those circumcised are diverse, so too is the circumcision; about which it is not necessary to discourse in this treatise. If anyone desires to know our opinion on this place, let him read our commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. Therefore, the Jews will not allow this circumcision, in which they boast, to be common to them and the Colchians or Egyptians, nor even with the Ishmaelites of the Arabian race, although they descend from a common father, Abraham, through Ishmael, who was circumcised together with his father. 

The Jews say, moreover, that the circumcision of the eighth day is the primary one, and others are superfluous. And perhaps it was devised because of some angel hostile to the Jewish race, who could harm those not circumcised, but not those who were; which can be gathered from the books of Exodus, where the angel prevailed against Moses before the circumcision of Eliezer; but once he was circumcised, that power was made void. Zipporah, not being ignorant of this, snatched up a sharp stone and circumcised her son, saying according to the common edition <note>the Septuagint Greek translation</note>, *The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped*, but according to the Hebrews, *A bridegroom of blood you are to me*: for she knew such an angel was powerful before the blood, but was to be restrained by the gore of circumcision; wherefore she said, *A bridegroom of blood you are to me*. Truly, these things [require] a certain curiosity...

<column-break/>

...in every dialect in which each was nurtured, naming him, he shall not sin. But the cause of the Jews' circumcision is not the same as the cause of the <margin>Egyptians</margin> circumcision, or the Colchians'; wherefore the same circumcision would not be legislated. For just as he who sacrifices does not sacrifice to the same, even if he seems to sacrifice similar things; and he who prays does not pray to the same, even if he requests the same things in his prayers; so neither, if someone is circumcised, is it entirely indifferent to the circumcision of another. For the intention, and the law, and the will of the one being circumcised makes the thing different. 

But so that the whole may be understood even more according to the passage, it must be said that the name of justice is the same among all Greeks; but it is already demonstrated that justice according to Epicurus is one thing; and another is that according to the Stoics who deny the three-part nature of the soul; and another is that according to the Platonists who say that justice is the "proper-acting" of the parts of the soul. And so also the courage of Epicurus is one thing, enduring pains for the sake of fleeing more pains; and another is that of those from the Porch <note>the Stoics</note>, choosing all virtue for its own sake; and another is that from Plato, who say that courage is the virtue of the spirited part of the soul, and who place its location around the chest. 

Having said this, I would also call the circumcision different according to the different doctrines of those being circumcised. Concerning which it is not now necessary to speak in this work. But to whom it is dear to see what moved us on this place, let him read what is recorded by us concerning it in the [commentaries] on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans. Even if the Jews pride themselves in circumcision, they will separate it not only from the circumcision among the Colchians and Egyptians, but also from that of the Ishmaelite Arabs, even though they were born from their patriarch <margin>Gen. 17. 23.</margin> Abraham through Ishmael, and were circumcised with him. 

The Jews say that the eighth-day circumcision is the principal one, and that which is not such is by circumstance; and perhaps it was devised because of some angel hostile to the Jewish nation, being able to hurt those of them not circumcised, but being weak among the circumcised. Which someone might say is shown from the things written in <margin>Ex. 4. 24.</margin> Exodus; in which the angel, regarding the circumcision of Eliezer, was able to act against Moses; but when he was circumcised, he had no strength. And having learned these things, Zipporah, taking a stone, circumcised her own child; and according to the common copies she is recorded to say, *The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped*; but according to the Hebrew, this: *A bridegroom of blood you are to me*. For she knew the angel around the child was empowered before the blood, and ceased because of the blood of circumcision; whereupon it was said to <margin>* her.</margin> him, *A bridegroom of blood you are to me*. But [this belongs] to her...

He uses philosophical definitions of "justice" and "courage" to illustrate how the same word or action can have different meanings based on the underlying belief system.</summary>

Then, when it was said to His disciple <note>Referring to the Apostle Peter</note>, who did not yet understand the reason for these things and was saying, *Nothing common or unclean has entered my mouth*, the response was: *What God has cleansed, do not call common.* <margin>Acts 10:14. *He cleansed.</margin> Therefore, the fact that Egyptian priests abstain not only from swine, but also from goats, rams, oxen, and fish, pertains neither to the Jews nor to us. Since we examine the points in this place with a love of truth, we shall say that Apelles, <margin>Theodoret, Book 1</margin> an acquaintance of Marcion and father of a certain heretical sect, and considering the writings of the Jews a myth, says that Christ alone has visited <margin>Epiphanius, Book 1, p. 166</margin> the race of men. No one, therefore, convicts us as false witnesses who set down opposites: both that our Savior alone came, and that yet many others have often come. But very confusedly in the inquiry about the angels who came to men, he sets down the things that came to him unclearly from the things written in Enoch. Which things he does not even seem to have read himself, nor to have known that the books inscribed with the name of Enoch are not at all carried in the churches as divine. From which it might be thought that the [statement] was cast out, that sixty or seventy together descended and became evil. But so that we may look upon him more fairly, [let us look at] what he has not seen from the things written in Genesis, that 'The sons of <margin>Gen. 6:2</margin> God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took for themselves wives from all whom they chose.' # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 5.

And Numenius the Pythagorean <note>original: "Pythagoricus Numenius". Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who sought to link Plato with Pythagoras and even Jewish thought.</note> in the second book *On the Immortality of the Soul*: unless perhaps, whenever the Greeks relate such things, especially their philosophers, it is not permitted to laugh, to criticize, or to consider them fictions and fables; but when men consecrated to God—for whom it is a mortal sin to be driven even by tortures or the fear of death to lie about God—say they have seen visions of angels, they are to be considered vain and unworthy of belief, and their discourses are not to be reckoned among truths. But such a judgment concerning truths and falsehoods is not consistent with reason. For those who take care not to be deceived, only after inquiry and examination do they safely pronounce that this is true and that is false in miraculous narrations: because neither do all deserve credit among men, nor should all be rejected as fabricated fables. 

Furthermore, concerning the resurrection of Jesus from the dead, this too must be said: it is not strange that one or two angels announced that he, now restored to life, cares for the affairs of those who trust in him. Indeed, it seems likely to me that the faithful, continually perceiving fruit from that resurrection and emerging from the mire of vices through conversion to God, and living with integrity, are assisted by the help of angels. 

Celsus, however, did not leave even this un-slandered: that an angel rolled away the stone from the monument in which the body of Jesus had been placed. Seizing the opportunity in the manner of schoolboys declaiming under the rod <note>A metaphor for immature or forced rhetorical exercises in ancient schools.</note>, he says, *“Therefore”* (as if he had devised something quite clever), *“the son of God was not strong enough to open the tomb, but had need of another's service to move the rock.”* 

At this point, lest I act too inquisitively or philosophize unseasonably under the pretext of tropology <note term="tropology">A method of biblical interpretation that looks for moral or figurative meanings rather than just the literal history.</note>, I will speak of the history itself: it is more in keeping with the dignity of the one rising for the benefit of the human race that the stone was rolled away by an inferior minister than if he had done it himself. I say nothing now of the fact that those who lay snares for the Word of God, after they showed him to the people as slain, lifeless, and reduced to nothing, do not want his tomb opened, lest anyone behold the living Word after their nefarious plots. But God’s messenger, who had descended for the salvation of men—a helper of the angel <note>The Latin text here suggests the messenger is a "helper of the angel," while the Greek clarifies the angel is a "fellow-worker" (synergos) of God.</note> stronger than the plotters—rolled away that heavy rock; so that those who thought the Word was dead might learn he is no longer among the dead but lives, and leads all who are willing to follow him, so that to these he might demon—

—to the Pythagorean Numenius in the second book *On the Incorruptibility of the Soul*. But it is not reasonable to judge in this way concerning those who speak truth or falsehood. For those who practice being undeceived, after much and accurate research and examination of the specific places, only then slowly and safely declare that some are speaking the truth, while others among the faithful speak falsely in the wonders they relate. Thus, while not all demonstrate what is worthy of belief, nor are all clearly proven, they have not handed down fictions and myths to men. 

Furthermore, regarding the resurrection of Jesus from the dead, this must also be said: that at that time either one or a second angel was seen, announcing that he had been raised, and was already caring for the benefit of those believing in such things, which is wonderful. And it seems to me not irrational that always to such people who believe Jesus has been raised—showing the robust life that is the fruit of believing through their transformation, and the change from the flood of evils—angels become helpers in their holier deeds toward God, even without [men] touching them.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 5.

->**Gnostics**<- <note>original: Γνωστικοὶ / scientiam. Origen is discussing those who claim "special knowledge."</note>, are analogous to those among the philosophers who call themselves **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus, often criticized in antiquity for denying divine providence.</note>. But just as those who do away with providence could hardly be true philosophers, so those who introduce strange fabrications—which are not pleasing to the successors of Jesus—could hardly be Christians. Suppose there are some who accept Jesus and boast of being Christians on that account, yet still desire to live according to the law of the Jews like the Jewish multitudes; (these are the two types of **Ebionites** <note>An early Jewish-Christian movement. Origen notes their internal division over the Virgin Birth.</note>, either confessing like us that Jesus was born of a virgin, or that he was not born that way, but like other men.) What charge does this bring against those of the Church, whom Celsus has named "the multitude"? He also mentioned certain **Sibyllists**; perhaps having overheard some people mocking those who believe the **Sibyl** <note>A legendary female prophetess of the ancient world.</note> was a prophetess, and calling such people "Sibyllists." Then, pouring out a heap of names upon us, he says he knows of certain **Simonians** <note>Followers of Simon Magus.</note>; who, because they worship **Helena**, or a teacher named **Helenus**, are called **Helenians**. But it escapes Celsus’s notice that the Simonians by no means confess Jesus as the Son of God, but rather call **Simon** the "Power of God" <note>See Acts 8:10.</note>; telling certain wonders about him, thinking that if he performed things similar to what Jesus seemed to have done, he himself would have as much power among men as Jesus has among the many. But neither Celsus nor Simon could understand how Jesus, like a good husbandman of the Word of God, has been able to sow and fill so much of Greece and so much of the barbarian world with words that transform the soul from every evil and lead it back to the Creator of all things. Celsus, then, knows of **Marcellians** from **Marcellina**, and **Harpocratians** from **Salome**, and others from **Mariamne**, and others from **Martha**; but we—who through our love of learning have, as far as possible, examined not only the matters within the Word and the differences among them, but have also, with all our might, searched through the writings of those who have philosophized with a love for truth—have never associated with these people. Celsus also mentioned **Marcionists**, who follow **Marcion**; then, so that he might seem to know others besides those he named, he says in his usual way, "that others, wandering wickedly after different teachers and demons, and wallowing in great darkness, are more lawless and foul than the devotees of **Antinous** <note>The deified favorite of Emperor Hadrian; Origen finds the comparison to Jesus offensive.</note> in Egypt." And it seems to me he repeats something similar to a truth when he says that some, wandering wickedly after different demons and wallowing, *found for themselves a great darkness of ignorance on the earth. He also makes mention of I know not what Sibyllists; perhaps because he had heard from certain people that those who consider the Sibyl a prophetess are disapproved of, and marked by the name of Sibyllists. But in this Celsus is mistaken, since the Simonians refuse to confess that Jesus is the son of God, but say that Simon is the power of God, telling certain prodigious things about a vain man, who thought that by emulation of miracles he would prepare for himself a reputation among men no less than that of Jesus. But neither Celsus nor Simon could understand how Jesus, in the manner of a good farmer, could fill a great part of Greece and Barbarism with the seed of the word, leading souls away from vices to the founder of all things. Celsus furthermore knows both Marcellians from Marcellina, and Harpocratians descended from Salome, then others from Mariamne, others from Martha: but we, who out of a zeal for learning have not only searched out the various opinions of our own doctrine, but have even shaken out the writings of philosophers tracking the truth, have never fallen in with those people. # Book 5. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...and they skirmish with one another with insults, both speakable and unspeakable, never in agreement because of their mutual hatreds. To this also a response has already been given before: that among philosophers one can likewise find sects hostile to other sects, and among physicians as well. However, we who have meditated upon the words of the Lord Jesus, and have learned to think, speak, and act in accordance with his doctrine, "bless those who revile us, endure our persecutors, and encourage our detractors" <note>original: "benedicimus... toleramus... admonemus" / 1 Cor. 4:12</note>. We do not hurl "speakable and unspeakable" insults at those who hold opinions different from our own; rather, if we are able, we attempt everything possible to persuade them to change for the better, so that they might attend to the Creator of all things alone, and do everything as those who must render an account to the Supreme Judge. But if we achieve nothing, we observe that precept: *Avoid a heretical man after one or two warnings, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned* <note>Titus 3:10-11</note>. Furthermore, those who understand that saying of the Savior, *Blessed are the peacemakers*, and that other, *Blessed are the meek*, will not pursue either the deceived or the deceivers with hatred, nor will they mockingly call them "alluring Circes" <note>A reference to the sorceress from the Odyssey who turned men into swine; Celsus likely used this to mock Christian teachers.</note>.

It seems to me that Celsus did not even sufficiently understand that Apostolic saying: *In the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared with a hot iron, forbidding marriage, and commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful* <note>1 Timothy 4:1-3</note>. Nor did he understand those who use these words of the Apostle against people who introduce novelties and falsehoods into sacred doctrine. For this reason, Celsus says that some among the Christians are called "cauteries of the ears" <note>original: "aurium cauteria" / Greek: "ἀκοῆς καυτήρια". Likely a misunderstanding of the "seared conscience" passage.</note> and others "enigmas," something which we have not yet seen. It is certain that the name "stumbling block" <note>term: scandalum (stumbling block) — a common biblical term for something that leads a person into sin or error.</note> is frequent in our writings, which we are accustomed to use regarding those who corrupt sound doctrine and deceive simpler men. However, we have never found them called in those writings "dancing Sirens," or "sophistries plugging ears with wax," or "imposing pig heads instead of human ones." And, unless I am mistaken, they are not so named in our scriptures nor in those of the heretics. Only this man [Celsus], who professes to know everything, asserts this. And soon he adds: *But you will hear all of them, though they differ so greatly among themselves and refute one another with the foulest contentions, boasting of that saying: "To me the world is crucified, and I to the world."* For this seems to be the only thing Celsus retained from the letters of Paul; otherwise, he would object to us regarding countless other things, such as: *Though we live in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh: for the weapons...*

<column-break/>

“...against one another these people say all sorts of things, speakable and unspeakable; and they would not yield even a little if you asked for harmony, hating each other entirely.” And to these things we have said that even in philosophy it is possible to find sects warring against sects, and in medicine too. However, those of us who have been disciplined by the Word of Jesus, and have practiced thinking, speaking, and doing things in harmony with His words, when reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we encourage. And we do not say "speakable and unspeakable" things to those who hold different opinions than what we have received; but, if possible, we would do everything to change them for the better, so that they look only to the Creator and do all things as those who will be judged. But if the heterodox <note>term: heterodox — those holding different or "other" opinions, often used for heretics.</note> are not persuaded, we keep the Word that commanded us such things: *Reject a heretical man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.* Furthermore, those who have understood "Blessed are the peacemakers" and "Blessed are the meek" would not hate those who forge the things of Christianity, nor would they call the deceived "Circes" or "alluring mixers of potions."

It seems to me that he has misheard the Apostolic phrase saying: *In the latter times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to wandering spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars, having been seared in their own conscience, forbidding to marry, and to abstain from foods which God created for participation with thanksgiving for the faithful.* He also misheard those who used these Apostolic words against those who forge the things of Christianity; therefore Celsus said that some are called "cauteries of hearing" among Christians. He himself says some are called "enigmas," which we have not recorded. It is true that the name of "stumbling block" <note>Greek: σκανδάλου (skandalou)</note> is frequent in these writings, which we are accustomed to say about those who distort the simpler and easily deceived from sound doctrine. But we do not know of any being called "dancing Sirens" and "sophistries sealing the ears" and "turning those persuaded into pig-heads." I think that no one else among those in the Word, nor among the sects, [uses these names]. But this man, who promises to know all, says such things: "And you will hear all of them," he says, "who differ so much and most shamefully refute themselves with strife, saying: 'To me the world is crucified, and I to the world.'" For Celsus seems to have remembered only this from Paul; for why do we not also say a myriad of other things, such as: *Living in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh; (for the...*

The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God <note>Origen is quoting 2 Corinthians 10:4-5 to describe the intellectual and spiritual nature of Christian defense</note>. Therefore, in this also Celsus lies, and he goes on at length accusing the differences found among the various heresies. Indeed, it seems to me that he speaks quite indistinctly, having neither carefully observed nor understood how Christians—who have established laws for themselves—claim to know more than the Jews; and whether they agree with the Jewish books but interpret them differently, or whether they do not agree with their writings at all. He wishes to argue that whatever good things are thought to be said by Christians are expressed better and more clearly by the philosophers, so that he might draw those captured by the apparent virtue and piety of Christian dogmas back toward philosophy. ...our warfare is not fleshly, but powerful in God for the destruction of all structures and thoughts raising themselves on high against the knowledge of God. Furthermore, regarding this very thing—that he says everyone boasts of these words, "To me the world is crucified, and I to the world"—we shall prove it false. After these things he speaks thus: "Therefore come, even if they have no suitable principles for their dogma, let us examine their doctrine itself: and first we must speak of those things which, being poorly understood, they corrupt through ignorance, ineptly usurping for themselves things they are ignorant of: and these are the things..." and soon, reviewing the decrees of the Christian faithful, he opposes philosophical ones to them: contending that whatever is thought to be well said by Christians is both better and more clearly handed down among the philosophers, so that he might pull back toward philosophy the honesty and piety displayed in their dogmas. We shall make an end of the fifth book here, and begin the sixth from the remaining parts.

# ORIGEN
## AGAINST
# CELSUS

-> BOOK 6 <-

As we begin this sixth book, holy Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Alexandria (d. c. 251), Origen's patron who encouraged and funded the writing of this work.</note>, we must strive against the slanders of Celsus, rather than against philosophical opinions, as it might seem to some. For Celsus cites many things, especially from Plato, which can even persuade the prudent among those who read the Holy Scriptures; and he tries to show that these things are common to us and others, asserting that they are expressed more aptly among the Greeks, yet without that commanding proclamation of God, or the Son of God. To this we reply: since the purpose of those who profess the truth <margin>* the truth.</margin> <margin>* [the things] of the truth</margin> is to benefit as many mortals as possible, and by the duty of humanity to attract anyone at all, whether wise or foolish; and not only to convert Greeks or mild-mannered barbarians, but even any of the wilder peoples—it is undoubtedly necessary for this purpose to use a common form of speaking which accommodates itself to the ears of everyone. On the other hand, those who bid farewell to common people, and who despise them as unliberally educated and incapable of well-ordered doctrine, taking account only of the literate, circumscribe their own kindness within narrow limits. I say this because Celsus and others find fault with the simplicity of our Scriptures in their expression, which, when compared to the splendor of more refined oratory, seems to be obscured; whereas our Prophets, and Jesus himself, and his Apostles, were attentive primarily to a mode of speech that was not only most true, but also most suitable for attracting the multitude; so that each person, having been finally converted and attracted, might perceive according to his ability the secrets hidden beneath the simplicity of the language. Indeed, if the truth may be told, the refined and accurate speech of Plato and those like him has benefited few (if indeed it has benefited any); but much more have been benefited by that simplicity of men who, in both style and doctrine, tempered themselves to the common understanding. Thus, one may see Plato only in the hands of those who seem to be lovers of learning; but Epictetus is read even by the common sort

<column-break/>

As we enter upon this sixth book, holy Ambrose, we find it necessary to contend against the accusations of Celsus against the Christians, rather than against the philosophical views set forth by him, as one might suppose. For Celsus has set forth many things, especially from Plato, making common those things which are able to win over even a wise man from the Holy Scriptures; claiming, "these things are better said among the Greeks, and without the arrogance and the promise of being from God, or a Son of God." We say, therefore, that if the goal of those who represent <margin>* the truth.</margin> <margin>* [the things] of the truth</margin> is to benefit as many as possible, to the best of their power, and to bring in, as far as is possible through love of humanity, anyone at all—not only the wise, but also the foolish; and again, not only Greeks, but also barbarians (for it is a great thing if one is able to convert even the most rustic and unlearned)—it is clear that he must be concerned with a style of speaking that is of common benefit and able to reach every ear. But those who say a long farewell to the unlearned as if they were slaves, and as if they were unable to listen to the sequence of things announced in the phrasing and order of words, have cared only for those brought up in <margin>* writing.</margin> words and learning; these men have gathered the spirit of community into a very narrow and small space. These things have been said by me in defense of the simplicity of the Scriptures which is accused by Celsus and others—a simplicity which seems to be darkened by the brilliance of the composition of their words. For our prophets, and Jesus, and his apostles, looked toward a manner of announcement that not only contained the truth, but was also able to win over the many. Thus, having advanced and been led in, each person according to his power may take up the things spoken in secret within the words that seem to be simple. And, if one must dare to say it, the beautiful and labored style of Plato and those who write similarly has benefited few (if it has benefited any); but the style of those who taught and wrote more simply, and at the same time practically and with an aim toward the many, has benefited more. One can see, at any rate, that Plato is in the hands of those who seem to be scholars only; but Epictetus <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 50–135 AD) whose teachings on ethics were widely popular and accessible.</note> is read even by the ordinary people
