...and woe: and having been commanded, he devours the book, so that he might not write it down and publish it to the unworthy <note>referring to Ezekiel 3:1</note>: a similar thing is written concerning John, that he saw and did the same. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

And concerning Pythagoras, they have told a great many marvels, showing that he displayed an ivory thigh at a general assembly of the Greeks, and claiming that he recognized the shield he used when he was Euphorbus <note>Pythagoras claimed to remember past lives, specifically as the Trojan hero Euphorbus.</note>, and that he appeared in two cities on one and the same day. If he said the narratives about Jesus were marvels, his own genuine disciples did not write such accounts about him. 

But Celsus, who professes to know everything and has cited many things from Plato, intentionally, I believe, keeps silent about the discourse concerning the Son of God mentioned by Plato in his <margin>Plato, Epistle 6.</margin> letter to Hermias and Coriscus. The passage from Plato is as follows: "And swearing by the God of all things, the leader of both things that are and things to come, and the Father and Lord of that leader and cause; whom, if we truly practice philosophy, we shall all know clearly <margin>* in a leading manner. * all to whom.</margin> as far as the power of happy men allows." ...their opinion, nor seeks understanding from God, nor knocks at closed doors, the word of God is not immediately void of all wisdom. Then, after quoting from Plato to the effect that the highest good can be known by only a few, he adds these things: *There are those who, by rashly despising others, are themselves full of a magnificent but empty hope, as if they had learned I know not what excellent thing; they say some true things, but which Plato taught much earlier: yet he does not speak in portents, nor does he stop the mouth of those inquiring what this is that he promises, nor does he command before all things to believe that God is such, or has such a son, and that he himself drew his knowledge from a conversation with him.* 

To these things I respond, that concerning Plato, Aristotle, unless I am mistaken, wrote that he was not the son of Ariston, but of a phantom which, resembling Apollo, embraced Amphictione; to which most Platonists who have handed down the life of their master to posterity bear witness. Why should I mention Pythagoras, about whom many prodigious things are reported, such as that he bared an ivory thigh in a gathering of Greeks, and that he recognized a shield as his own equipment when he was formerly Euphorbus, and was seen on the same day in two cities. Now, he who wishes to criticize the prodigious narrations about Socrates and Plato will bring forward the swan commended to Socrates through a dream, and the voice of the master himself, saying that Plato was that swan when the youth was commended to him the next day. Similarly, that also, that Plato seemed to himself to have a third eye, he will refer to among the portents: nor will there ever be lacking to those who are not candid, and who feel maliciously toward every most excellent man, some calumny, since they even make sport of the spirit of Socrates as if it were a fictitious thing. Therefore, we do not speak in portents when we narrate the acts of Jesus, but his genuine disciples wrote such things about him. 

But that Celsus, as he professes, "all-knowing," while bringing forward so many things from Plato, by deliberate effort, I believe, conceals that which he [Plato] wrote concerning the Word as Son of God, in his epistle to Hermias and Coriscus, in these words: *Calling to witness the God, the ruler of all things that are and will be, and the father and lord of that ruler and cause, whom indeed, if we truly philosophize, we shall all clearly know, as far as that knowledge can fall within the capacity of happy men.* Celsus also adduces other words from the same [Plato] thus: *Now indeed it seemed to me also worth the effort to indulge in a slightly longer discourse on these matters; for perhaps, if these things shall have been set forth, something of those things which I signify will appear more clearly: for there is a certain discourse...*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...indeed *the opposite of that man who, in writing on these matters, dares to occupy himself even a little—a point I have often noted before, and which seems necessary to mention again now. In every subject there are three things through which knowledge must be acquired; the fourth is knowledge itself; and the fifth must be placed as that which is both an object of the intellect and is true;* <note>Origen is quoting or paraphrasing Plato’s Seventh Letter regarding the stages of cognition.</note> of all these, the first is the name, the second the definition, the third the image, and the fourth knowledge. According to this reasoning, we might say that the "voice of one crying in the wilderness," John, was introduced before Jesus, corresponding in a certain proportion to the "name" found in Plato. In the second place after John, Jesus was revealed by him, to whom the phrase *The Word was made flesh* <note>John 1:14</note> applies, responding to the "definition" <note>original: "logos" (word/reason/definition)</note> found in Plato. Furthermore, Plato says the third is the "image" <note>original: "eidolon"</note>; because we use this word in a different sense, we shall speak more clearly by saying that after the Word has produced compunction in the soul, the figure of Christ is imprinted in each person by the Word of Christ. Whether, by the same analogy, the fourth—which is knowledge—is Christ as the "wisdom of the perfect" among us, let him who is able discern. Then, Celsus says, *“You see how Plato, although having prefaced that the matter is ineffable, nevertheless, lest he seem to flee to the unconvincing, gives a reason for this difficulty: perhaps nothing is explainable.”* Since these remarks seem to suggest that one should not believe simply, but give a reason for what we believe, we shall also bring forward Paul, who rebukes those who believe rashly when he says, *Unless you have believed in vain.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:2</note> Here Celsus, repeating the same things again as much as he can, forces us also to repeat the same. For when mention is made of the arrogant, he denies *that Plato was arrogant or a liar, as one who does not profess to have discovered something new himself, nor that he comes as a messenger from heaven, but shows from whence he took his own ideas.* To this it can be answered that Plato is indeed arrogant and puffed up, who in the speech of Jupiter in the *Timaeus* speaks thus: *“Gods of Gods, of whom I am both the creator and father,”* and the rest that follows. But if anyone attempts to defend these things because of the meaning of Jupiter speaking in Plato, why does he not with the same effort investigate the meaning of the words of the Son of God or the Creator in the prophetic Scriptures? He would find greater things than in the speech of Jupiter read in the *Timaeus*. For the character of divine speech is the prediction of future events, which does not fall within human nature and is judged by the outcomes, when the foretelling of the Divine Spirit becomes evident. Therefore, we do not say to everyone who approaches, "First believe that he whom I teach you is the Son of God," but—

Of which one is the name; second is the definition; the third is the image; the fourth is knowledge.” And according to these we might say, that the "voice of one crying in the wilderness" John was introduced before Jesus, analogous to the "name" in Plato. ...to address the discourse to each person according to what is appropriate for their character and disposition; having learned to know how we ought to answer every man. # Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Because this doctrine did not proceed from God, they perished, and soon all who had followed them were scattered. Therefore, we do not cast lots <note>original: "tesseris fortunae" - literally dice or tokens of fortune</note> to decide where we ought to turn or whom to follow, as if there were many who could pull us in different directions by claiming to be sent by God to the human race. But enough on these matters for now: we must move on to another of Celsus’s slanders. He does not even know our actual sayings, but through a misunderstanding, he asserts that we say, *the wisdom of men is foolishness with God*; whereas Paul actually says, *The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.* <margin>1 Corinthians 3:19</margin> Here Celsus says the reason for this has long since been given: he thinks the reason is that we wish, through these words, to allure only the uneducated and the foolish to ourselves. But he himself indicates that he has said this before, and we have responded to this to the best of our ability. Nevertheless, he attempts to show that we have borrowed this also from the wise men of the Greeks, who say that there is one kind of wisdom that is divine and another that is human. Accordingly, he brings forward the sayings of Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrines on change and the Logos</note> into the discussion; one being, *For human nature has no power of understanding, but the divine nature has*; the other, *A foolish man hears from a deity just as a child hears from a man.* He also brings forward from Plato’s *Apology* written for Socrates: *Indeed, men of Athens, for no other reason than a certain wisdom have I gained this name. But for what kind of wisdom? Perhaps for that which is human wisdom: for in this I truly seem to be wise.* <margin>Plato's Apology</margin> Celsus cites these, but I will add one more to them from Plato’s letter to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus: *To Erastus and Coriscus, in addition to that most beautiful wisdom of the forms, I say—even though I am an old man—that there is need of another wisdom; namely, that by which we can be wary of the attempts of the wicked and provide a timely defense against them, and thus protect ourselves safe and sound from their violence. For they are inexperienced in fraud, because they have lived a long time among you with moderate and least-evil men; therefore I say they need such aids, lest they be forced to despise true wisdom while meditating more than is right on human and necessary knowledge.* <margin>The same, Letter 6 <note>The Latin text says "ep. v." (5th), but the Greek margin and standard citations usually refer to the 6th Letter.</note></margin> Therefore, according to these men, there is one human wisdom and another divine: the human is indeed what is called by our people the "wisdom of this world," which is foolishness with God; but the divine, being different from the human since it is truly divine, happens by the grace of God, bestowed upon those who have made themselves fit to receive it by preparation: especially to those who, knowing the difference between the two, in their prayers to God...

<column-break/>

...because the teaching was not from God, they were destroyed, and all who were persuaded by them were immediately dispersed. We do not cast lots to divine where we should turn and to whom we should hold fast, as if there were many capable of persuading us by the promise of having arrived from God to the race of men. But enough of these things; let us therefore pass to another accusation of Celsus, who does not even know our words, but spoke from hearsay: "that we say the wisdom among men is foolishness with God." <margin>1 Cor. 3:19</margin> Paul says, *The wisdom of the world is foolishness with God.* And Celsus says, "that the <margin>for which reason.</margin> cause of this has also been stated long ago; for he thinks through this cause" "that we wish through this saying to attract the uneducated and the idiots alone." But, as he himself noted, he said the same thing above; and we met the argument as far as we were able. Nevertheless, he again professes to show this willingly to us, as having been taken from the wise among the Greeks, who spoke in one way of human wisdom and in another of divine. And he sets forth the words of Heraclitus; one which says, "Human nature does not have insights, but the divine has;" and another, "An infant man <note>meaning a foolish or immature man</note> hears from a divinity, just as a child from a man." And he sets out from the *Apology of Socrates* written by Plato these things: "For I, O men of <margin>Plato's Apology of Socrates</margin> Athens, for no other reason than a wisdom, have obtained this name. What kind of wisdom is this? That which is perhaps human wisdom; for in truth I risk being wise in this." These are the things Celsus sets out, but I from the letter of Plato to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus <margin>The same, Letter 6.</margin> will also set these things out: "To Erastus and Coriscus, in addition to this beautiful wisdom of the forms <margin>of images.</margin> I say, even though I am an old man, there is additional need of the wisdom that is protective against the wicked and unjust, and of a certain defensive power. For they are inexperienced, because of having spent their lives with you who are moderate <margin>us.</margin> and not evil. Therefore I said they need these things, so that they are not forced to neglect true wisdom, and to care for human and necessary wisdom more than is necessary." <margin>already.</margin> Therefore, according to these things, one is divine wisdom and the other human. And the human is the one called by us the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God; but the divine, being different from the human, since it is divine, comes by the grace <margin>bestowed.</margin> of God, who gifts it to those who have prepared themselves to be suitable for its reception; and especially to those who, from knowing the difference of each wisdom from the other, say in their prayers to God: for even if one be perfect...

<summary>Origen defends the Christian distinction between "worldly wisdom" and "divine wisdom," arguing that Celsus misrepresents the concept as a trap for the ignorant. Origen uses Greek philosophers like Heraclitus and Plato to show that even the pagans recognized a similar distinction between human and divine knowledge.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

<margin>Hebrews 5:14</margin>
...among the sons of men, if the wisdom that comes from You is absent, he shall be accounted as nothing. <note>Origen is quoting Wisdom of Solomon 9:6 here, though the margin refers to the related concept in Hebrews.</note> And we say that human wisdom is an exercise <term>gymnasion; a place of training</term> for the soul, but the end <note>the ultimate goal</note> is divine wisdom. This is what is called the "solid food" of the soul by him who said: *But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.* And this view is truly ancient; it is not, as Celsus thinks, an antiquity of wisdom to be referred back to Heraclitus and Plato. For long before these men, the Prophets distinguished between these two kinds of wisdom. It is enough for the present to speak from the words of David concerning the one said to be wise in divine wisdom, who says: *who shall not see corruption, when he sees the wise dying.* <margin>Psalm 48:9</margin> Therefore, divine wisdom, being distinct from faith, is the first of what are called the "spiritual gifts" of God; and after that, second—for those who know how to define such things accurately—is what is called "knowledge" <term>gnosis</term>; and third (since even the simpler folk, approaching godliness according to their ability, must be saved) is faith. Therefore it is said by Paul: *For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit.* <margin>1 Corinthians 12:8, 9</margin> Therefore, you would not find just any ordinary person participating in divine wisdom, but rather those who excel and stand out among all those who adhere to Christianity. Nor does anyone explain the matters of divine wisdom to the most uneducated, or to slaves, or to the most ignorant. And yet, Celsus says that we are "most uneducated, slaves, and most ignorant"—those of us who do not embrace his views nor are educated in the learning of the Greeks. But we say that the "most uneducated" are those who are not ashamed to talk to lifeless objects, and who call upon the weak for health, and ask the dead for life, and petition the most helpless for aid. And even if some say that these [idols] are not gods, but rather imitations of the true ones and symbols of them, nonetheless even these people—imagining that imitations of divinity exist in the hands of common craftsmen—are uneducated, slaves, and ignorant. We say that even the lowest among us are free from this kind of lack of education and ignorance, and are considered and found to be most prudent because of their divine hope. What we say is that it is not possible to grasp the more divine wisdom without having first exercised oneself in human wisdom; yet we confess that all human wisdom is foolishness when compared to the divine. Next, when he ought to argue with reason, he calls us "sorcerers" <term>goētas; charlatans or magicians</term> and says that we flee from the more refined people standing around, as they are not easily deceived, but we "snare the more rustic." He does not <gloss>know.</gloss> know...

<column-break/>

...among the sons of men, if he lacks the wisdom given by You, he shall be counted as nothing. Accordingly, we call human wisdom the training ground of the soul, but the target and end is the divine, which is also called the solid food of the soul by him who speaks thus: *But solid food is for the mature, those who by habit have their senses exercised to discern good from evil.* This opinion is indeed ancient, but not, as Celsus thinks, to be referred to Plato or Heraclitus: for long before their age the Prophets made this distinction between both wisdoms, which can be made manifest enough even by the testimony of David: who says of one endowed with divine wisdom, *he shall not see corruption, when he sees the wise dying.* Therefore divine wisdom, since it is different from faith, holds the first place among the "charismata" (as they call them) of God; the second indeed, as those who know these things more exactly judge, is what is called "knowledge"; then third, because it is necessary that even the simpler people approaching piety according to their strength be saved, is faith: for which reason Paul says, *To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge through the same Spirit, to another indeed faith in the same Spirit.* Wherefore, one cannot find common men as partakers of divine wisdom; but rather the outstanding, and those far superior to the rest, who study the Christian religion. Nor do they narrate this wisdom to every most ignorant, most vile, and most rude person—as Celsus names those who do not know profane letters and Greek disciplines. But we call those the most unlearned who are not ashamed to address inanimate things, and to seek health from the weak, life from the dead, and help from the helpless. But if anyone should say that those things are not gods, but images and signs of the true gods: nevertheless these people are also ignorant, vile, and unlearned, who imagine gods in the handiwork of craftsmen, so much so that not even the lowest of our men labor under this kind of ignorance. Yet we confess that even the most prudent are capable of divine hope: but we do not say it is impossible for one to perceive divine wisdom who has not first exercised himself in human wisdom, as we consider all human wisdom, if compared to the divine, to be foolishness. Here, where he should have dealt with arguments, that man calling us "juggling-tricks" <note>Latin: *praestigiatores*, referring to deceivers or stage magicians</note> says that all the more elegant people are avoided by us, because they are not rashly deceived; only the more rustic are ensnared: for he has not known for a long time...

<summary>Origen refutes Celsus's claim that Christianity is for the ignorant by distinguishing between human wisdom (preparatory) and divine wisdom (the goal). He argues that true ignorance lies in pagan idolatry, while Christians of all levels possess a higher spiritual prudence.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

of old we had wise men educated in foreign disciplines; that famous Moses, learned in all the Egyptian doctrine; Daniel, Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael, skilled in all the literature of the Assyrians, so much so that they surpassed all the wise men of that nation tenfold. Indeed, even today the Churches, among such a multitude of common people, possess some who are excellently learned; these, turning away from what we call "carnal wisdom" <note>original: "sapientia carnali" — worldly or secular knowledge as opposed to spiritual insight</note>, have joined themselves to us, and among them are those who have ascended from that wisdom to divine wisdom. After this, Celsus—as if touched by some light rumor concerning Christian humility, and not even understanding this sufficiently—admits indeed that it exists among us. However, he thinks that this too was wrongly taken from the doctrine of Plato, who in his books *On Laws* speaks somewhere thus: *God, as the ancient saying also witnesses, holding in Himself the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things, completes a straight path, unfolding His force and power through this nature of the universe, and passing through all its parts on every side: justice follows Him, the avenger and punisher of those who fall away from the divine law; to which justice he who is to be happy adheres with a modest and composed mind, and constantly follows its lead and guidance.* <note>Quoting Plato, Laws, Book IV, 715e–716a</note> Nor does he see that among many older than Plato there exist those voices in prayers: *Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes raised up, nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders above me, except humbly.* <note>Psalm 131:1-2 (Vulgate 130)</note> From which we are also taught this: that it is not humility if someone unseemly and abjectly casts themselves on the ground with bent knees, or lies prostrate dressed in the clothing of mourners and having their head sprinkled with ashes. For whoever is humble in the way of this Prophet, walking in great and wonderful thoughts exceeding his own intellect, humbles himself under the mighty hand of God. But if some, through lack of skill and understanding little of this dogma of humility, frequently do those abject things we mentioned: the doctrine is not at fault, but common ignorance, which follows the worse things while neglecting the better. For he is more humble and composed than the one in Plato who composes himself by the fact that he walks in great and wonderful things above himself, and yet voluntarily humbles himself—not under just anyone, but under the mighty hand of God, according to the doctrine of Jesus, the teacher of such disciples: *who did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man, he showed himself humble, becoming obedient...* <note>Philippians 2:6-8</note>

<column-break/>

...from above and from the beginning, those among us who are wise were educated in external studies: Moses in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; Daniel, and <margin>Acts 7:22; Dan. 2:4, 20.</margin> Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael in all the letters of the Assyrians, so that they were found to be ten times wiser than all the wise men there. And even now the churches have, in proportion to the multitudes, a few wise men who have approached us, even from that which is called among us "wisdom according to the flesh" <margin>1 Cor. 1:26.</margin>; they also have those who have advanced from that to divine wisdom. Then, as if Celsus had heard these things about humility, and not having carefully understood them, he wishes to speak ill of our practice; he thinks it is a mere offshoot <note>original: "παρεκύσμα" (parekysma) — a side-growth or imitation</note> of the words in Plato, who says in the *Laws*: "God, as the ancient <margin>Plato book 4 of the Laws. * straight. passes through. * those left behind.</margin> "saying goes, holding the beginning and the end and the middle of "all things that exist, completes a straight path, *moving "according to nature. And with Him always follows Justice, the "punisher of *those who fall short of the divine law; he who "intends to be happy, clinging to her, follows humble and "orderly." He does not see that among those much more ancient than Plato, it was said in prayer: *Lord, my heart was not exalted, nor <margin>Ps. 130:1, 2, 3.</margin> were my eyes raised high, nor did I walk in great things, nor in wonders above me; unless I was humble-minded.* At the same time, it is shown through these things that the one who is truly humble-minded is not the one who is humbled in an unseemly and ill-omened way, groveling on the knees and cast prostrate, clothed in miserable garments and heaping up dust. For the one who is humble-minded according to the prophet, walking in great and wonderful things—those which are above him, the truly great dogmas and the <margin>1 Pet. 5:6.</margin> wonderful thoughts—humbles himself under the mighty hand of God. But if some, through their commonness <note>original: "ἰδιωτείαν" (idioteian) — lack of education or "lay" status</note>, not having clarified the dogma concerning humility, do such things: one must not blame the Word, but the commonness of those who overlook the better things and, through their lack of skill, miss the mark; they should be forgiven. For he is more "humble and orderly" than the one according to Plato, who is orderly because he conducts himself in great and wonderful things above him; and humble because, while being in these things, he willingly humbles himself, not under any random person, but under the mighty hand of God, <margin>Phil. 2:6, 7, 8.</margin> through the teacher of such disciples, Jesus; who did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death...

<summary>Origen argues that Christian humility is not a poor imitation of Platonic philosophy, but a biblical virtue predating Plato, exemplified by figures like Moses and Daniel and perfected by Jesus.</summary>

...even unto death, even the death of the cross. And this institution of humility is so excellent that it does not have a common author, but our Savior himself says, *Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.* After these things, that saying against the rich, *It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man into the kingdom of heaven,* he says that Jesus took it entirely from Plato with a few things changed: since his [Plato's] sentiment is, *It is impossible that the same man be exceedingly good and remarkably rich.* Who would not laugh at Celsus, even if only moderately sensible, whether he be a Christian or one of the rest of men, when he hears that Jesus (born and educated among the Jews, thought to be the son of Joseph the smith, who never learned even Hebrew letters, much less Greek, as the truthful Scriptures testify of him) had read the books of Plato: and being delighted by his sentiment concerning the rich, *It is impossible that the same man be exceedingly good and remarkably rich,* twisted it somewhat and made a new one from it, *It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man into the kingdom of God?* But if Celsus had turned over the gospels with a candid mind and a zeal for truth, he would have learned why a camel is chiefly used for this comparison, and a distorted animal compared with a rich man: then what that narrow eye of a needle means? But truly, these things so far. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

our own writings: come then, let us bring forward a few points to be compared with the Platonic sayings—which, though spoken with likelihood and probability, did not have as much influence even upon the philosopher himself as they ought to have had, to turn him toward true piety and the worship of the Creator of this universe, by casting away that which corrupts and contaminates religion, whether it be called *idolatry*, as we name it, or *superstition*, as the common people speak. Certainly, in a Hebrew figure of speech in the seventeenth Psalm <note>original: "decimo septimo Psalmo"; modern Bibles usually cite this as Psalm 18:11</note> God is said to have *made darkness his hiding place*: by which is signified that no one can think of God in a manner worthy of Him, as if He were lurking in darkness, insofar as it concerns men who cannot bear the splendor of His knowledge; nor are they able to gaze upon Him, partly because of the impurity of the mind bound to this lowly body, and partly because of its narrowness, which is by no means capable of containing such great divinity. Moreover, so that it may be known how rare it is, and granted to few mortals, to know God: it is written that *Moses entered into the thick darkness where God was*: and again concerning the same, *Moses alone shall come near to God, the rest shall not come near*. And again, so that the Prophet might indicate the depth of divine doctrines, incomprehensible to those who lack the Spirit that searches all things, even the deep secrets of God, he says, *The abyss is like a garment, his covering*. Furthermore, our Savior and Lord, the Word of God, indicating the magnitude of the knowledge by which His Father is known—and that He is known worthily by Himself alone in the first place, and in the second place by minds illuminated through the Word of God—says, *No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son shall reveal him*. For no one can worthily know the one begotten from eternity, the firstborn of all created nature, except the Father Himself who begot Him: nor can anyone know the Father as well as His living Word, who is Truth and Wisdom. For whoever participates in Him—who removes from the Father the darkness which He placed as His hiding place, and reveals the abyss with which He is clothed, as far as is possible—that person shall know Him. These few things out of many I have discussed, taken from the meditations of holy men concerning God, showing that there is more weight in these than in the Platonic discourses, provided you bring eyes capable of looking into the majesty of the Scriptures. The words of Plato, which Celsus cited, are as follows: *All things are around the King of all, and all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all good things. The second things are around the second, and the third* <unclear>for the sake of</unclear> *all things, and that is the cause of all beautiful things.*

<column-break/>

our own writings; come, let us compare a few things to those which were spoken persuasively by Plato, yet were not able to lead the philosopher to a worthy piety toward the Maker of all things; which piety he ought not to have adulterated nor defiled with (as we call it) *idolatry*, or as the many might say instead of the proper term for worship, with *superstition*. In a certain Hebrew manner it is said in the seventeenth Psalm, *that God made darkness his hiding place*; in order to show that the things worthily understood concerning God are invisible and unknown, He having *hidden* Himself as if in darkness from those who cannot endure the rays of His knowledge, nor are able to see Him; partly because of the pollution of the mind, which is bound in the body of man's humiliation, and partly because of its too-limited power for the comprehension of God. And to show that the knowledge of God reaches men rarely and is found in very few: Moses is recorded *to have entered into the thick cloud where God was*. And about Moses again, *Moses alone shall draw near to God, but the rest shall not draw near*. And again, so that the prophet might represent the depth of the doctrines concerning God, which are unattainable to those who do not have the Spirit that searches all things, even the depths of God, he said, *The abyss is like a garment, his covering*. But also our Savior and Lord, the Word of God, representing the greatness of the knowledge of the Father—that it is primarily received and known worthily by Him alone, and secondarily by those whose leading faculty is enlightened by the Word and God Himself—says, *No one fully knows the Son except the Father; nor the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son reveals him*. For neither can anyone know the Unbegotten and the Firstborn of all created nature worthily, as the Father who begot Him knows Him, nor the Father, as His living Word and His Wisdom and Truth; by participation in whom, He removes from the Father the so-called darkness which He made His hiding place, and His so-called covering, the abyss, and thus reveals the Father. I thought it well to set forth these few things from the very many conceived by holy men about God, showing that what is admired by Celsus in the Platonic words has something more venerable in it for those who have eyes able to see the venerable things of the Scriptures, the holy writings of the prophets. The passage of Plato, which Celsus set out, is in this manner: *Around the King of all are all things, and for his sake are all things, and he is the cause of all beautiful things. And the second is around the second things, and the third...*

He asserts that true knowledge of the Father is only possible through the revelation of the Son (the Word).</summary>

# Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Page 289

...acting thus, he writes in the second epistle to the Corinthians: *For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory; while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.* <margin>2 Cor. 4:17, 18</margin> Here it immediately occurs to the fit listener: that "things seen" refers to sensible objects <note>original: "res sensibiles"; things perceived by the physical senses</note>, while "things not seen" refers to intelligible objects <note>original: "intelligibiles"; things understood by the mind or intellect</note>. Thus, he understands by the name of "temporary" those sensible things which are seen; but by "eternal," those which are understood and not seen. Desiring to obtain the contemplation of these, out of great longing he considers any afflictions as nothing and light, bearing them without grievance even when most heavily afflicted, as the hope of that contemplation relieves all his anguish. *Since we have a great high priest, who by the greatness of his power and understanding has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God*, <margin>Heb. 4:14</margin> promising to his true disciples and those living worthily of divine instruction, that he will raise them above all worldly things: for he says, *That where I go, there you may be also.* <margin>John 14:3</margin> Therefore, after our completed labors and struggles, we hope to escape to the highest heaven, and by drawing from the fountains of water springing up into eternal life according to the teaching of Jesus, <margin>John 4:14</margin> and by perceiving the rivers of contemplations, we shall dwell with those super-celestial waters of which the Scripture speaks, praising the name of the Lord. <margin>Ps. 148:4</margin> And as long as we praise him, we shall not be carried around by the rotation of the heaven, but shall be ever intent upon the invisible things of God; no longer knowing him through the created things of the world, <margin>Rom. 1:20</margin> but face to face, as that true disciple of Jesus says: and again elsewhere, *When that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be done away.* <margin>1 Cor. 13:12, 10</margin> Furthermore, "seven heavens," or any fixed number of them, is nowhere accepted in the Scriptures received by the Church of God: but rather "heavens," whether they be the spheres of the planets (as the Greeks call them) or whether something more secret is signified by them. Celsus, following Plato, says the path of souls to the earth and from the earth passes through the planets; but Moses, the most ancient of the Prophets, narrates in the dream of Jacob a divine vision: *A ladder reaching into heaven, and the angels of God descending and ascending by it, and the Lord leaning upon the top of the ladder*; <margin>Gen. 28:12, 13</margin> whether he was indicating this very thing by the ladder, or something greater: concerning which Philo composed a book, worthy to be examined by the wise. <margin>Philo, *On Dreams being sent from God*, p. 384 Paris edition.</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

<margin>Psalm 104:24, 25, 26. <note>The Greek text cites Psalm 103, following the Septuagint numbering.</note></margin>
...in the diagram. Indeed, although we have traversed many regions of the earth and sought out those everywhere who profess to know something, we have nowhere found any who advocate for the contents of this diagram. In it, there was a drawing of ten circles, separated from one another but bound together by a single circle, which was said to be the Soul of the Universe and was named **Leviathan**. The Jewish scriptures—whatever they may be hinting at in their riddles—say that this was created by God as a plaything. For in the Psalms we find: *In wisdom you have made them all; the earth is full of your creatures. Here is the sea, great and wide; there ships travel, and small animals with great; this dragon, whom you formed to play with him.* <note>original: "δράκων οὗτος, ὃν ἔπλασας ἐμπαίζειν αὐτῷ"</note> In the Hebrew text, the word **Leviathan** stands in place of "dragon." This impious diagram, then, which was clearly condemned by the prophet, claimed that Leviathan was the soul that permeates all things. We also found in it one named **Behemoth**, <note>original: "Βεημὼθ"</note> stationed as it were after the lowest circle. The creator of that foul diagram inscribed this Leviathan both upon the outer circle and at its center, putting his name twice. Furthermore, Celsus says that "the diagram is divided by a thick black line," and he claimed that this was called by him "Gehenna, which is also Tartarus." <note>Tartarus: a deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment.</note> Having found **Gehenna** written in the Gospel as a place of punishment, we searched to see if it was named anywhere in the ancient writings, especially since the Jews also use the name. We found that in the Scripture it is named the "Valley of the Son of Hinnom," <note>original: "Φάραγγι υἱοῦ Ἐννὸμ"</note> where we learned that in the Hebrew, instead of "Valley," the same subject was called both the Valley of Hinnom and Gehenna. Observing the readings, we also find Gehenna, or the Valley of Hinnom, located in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, where Jerusalem also was. Examining the connection of the heavenly Jerusalem with the lot of Benjamin and the valley of Hinnom, we find that those who partake in the places of perpetual punishment are led into a purification of such souls through torments, according to the passage: *Behold, the Lord enters like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap; and he shall sit refining and purifying as silver and gold.* <note>Malachi 3:2. This reflects Origen's view of "purgatorial" fire rather than eternal damnation.</note> And so, punishments occur around Jerusalem for those being refined, who dissolve away the products of wickedness from the substance of their soul—wickedness being figuratively called "lead." For this reason, in Zechariah, "Iniquity" sat upon a talent of lead. Whatever might be said on this topic is not for everyone, nor is the present time suitable for explaining it; indeed, it is not even safe to entrust the clarity of these matters to writing, since the masses do not require more teaching...

Therefore, although I have traveled through many regions, seeking everywhere those who professed to know something, I have nowhere found supporters of that diagram; in which there were ten circles embracing one another, with one circle surrounding them all, which was said to be the universal soul named **Leviathan**: which the Jewish scriptures, indicating something hidden, say was created by God for mockery. For thus we read in the Psalms, *In wisdom you have made all things, the earth is filled with your creatures; the sea is great and very spacious; there the ships pass through, small and great animals, that dragon, whom you fashioned to mock him.* In the Hebrew, the word **Leviathan** is held in place of "dragon." And this Leviathan, so clearly condemned by the Prophet, the maker of that impious drawing turned into the soul penetrating all things: in it we also found a certain one named **Behemoth**, placed below the lowest circle of all. Moreover, the fabricator of that impious diagram wrote this Leviathan both in the circumference and in the center, placing his name twice. Celsus adds that the diagram is *divided by a thick black line, and that it is called Gehenna, which is Tartarus:* but we, when we found Gehenna in the Gospel as a place of punishments, sought whether it was held anywhere in the writings of the ancients, especially since the Jews also use this word; and we found in them the valley of the son of Hinnom named in some places, for which in the Hebrew letters it is read indifferently now as *Valley of Hinnom*, now as *Gehenna*: and while reading we observed that Gehenna is reckoned in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin: or the valley of Hinnom, where Jerusalem also was. And when we examined further why the heavenly Jerusalem is thus associated with the Benjamite tribe, in which the valley of Hinnom also is, we found that place of punishments to be understood as the purgatory torments of the soul, according to that: *Behold! The Lord comes as a refining fire, and as fullers' herb; and he shall sit refining and cleansing as silver and gold.* Which fits well that there are punishments around Jerusalem for those who would come to be refined; because they have admitted some degree of malice into the substance of the soul, which is figuratively called lead: whence in Zechariah iniquity sits upon a talent of lead. For those people, it is not useful to ascend to higher philosophy, since they are barely restrained from the rush of every kind of vice by the fear of eternal punishment. Therefore, neither that diagram nor Celsus has understood the teaching regarding **Gehenna** <note>original: "Gehenna"; the valley of Hinnom, used as a metaphor for hell or purgatorial fire</note>. Otherwise, those painters would not have sketched those diagrams as if they were teaching the truth through them; nor would Celsus, in his slanderous writing against the Christians, have inserted things that are never said by Christians, but perhaps by some of whom either no remains now exist, or very few. And, just as it is not the place of those who follow **Plato’s** philosophy to offer a defense for the impious dogmas of **Epicurus** <note>Epicurus taught that the gods do not intervene in human affairs and the soul is mortal, views Origen considers the opposite of Christianity</note>; so it is not our task to answer for that diagram regarding the things Celsus objects to. For this reason, we pass over these things as superfluous and rashly mentioned by Celsus, since we ourselves are far more vehement accusers of such monstrosities than he is.

He has not even learned these from the slight teachings of others, but fancies certain new things for himself concerning the mutual words of *the one marking with the seal, who is called the father, and the one being sealed, who is called the junior or the son*. The one being sealed answers to his sealer: *I have been anointed with white ointment from the tree of life.* This is something we have never heard of, even among heretics. And soon he adds a certain number of seven angels, as proclaimed by the sealer, standing on either side of the soul as it departs from the body; some of whom are of light, while others are called "principal" <note>original: "principales" / "ἀρχοντικῶν"; likely referring to the Archons or planetary rulers in Gnostic cosmology</note>. He says that the prince of these "principals" is called the **Accursed God**. In attacking those who teach such things, he rightly condemns their audacity. Therefore, we are no less indignant than their accusers, if indeed there are those who say the God of the Jews is execrable—He who sends rain and thunder, the Creator of the world, the God of Moses and of the creation described by him. Here Celsus seems to feel little candor toward us, having taken into his counsel a hatred unbecoming of a philosopher, and that quite ungenerously. For he wished to make those ignorant of our affairs hostile to us by the reading of his commentary, as if we said that the God who is the good Creator of this world is "accursed." It seems to me he has done the same thing as the Jews did at the beginning of the Christian teaching, when they spread the rumor that men of this sect ate the flesh of slaughtered children, and that whenever they wished to indulge in hidden lusts, they extinguished the light

<column-break/>

concerning the punishment of those who sin. For it is not useful for them to ascend to things beyond that, because they are barely restrained to some extent from wickedness and the flood of sins resulting from it by the fear of eternal punishment. Neither the diagram, then, nor Celsus, knows the discourse concerning Gehenna. For if they did, those men would not have marked out paintings and diagrams as if they were educating people in the truth through them; nor would Celsus, in his treatise against the Christians, have included in his accusation against Christians things never said by Christians, but by people who—though they may still exist—have either entirely disappeared or have been reduced to a very small and easily counted number. <margin>* by those things</margin> And just as it does not befit those who philosophize according to Plato to apologize for Epicurus and his dogmas, so it does not befit us to apologize for the things in the diagram and the things said about it by Celsus. Because they are set forth as superfluous and vain, we leave aside what Celsus has said on these matters. For we shall accuse those who have been mixed up in these discourses more than Celsus does. <margin>* reduced</margin> Next to the things about the diagram, not even having heard correctly <margin>* not even having heard</margin> about what is called the **seal** by the churchmen, he fancies for himself some strange things and alternating voices: "as if some things were said to the sealer, called the father; and others to the one being sealed, called the son and Christ, who answers: 'I have been anointed with white chrism from the tree of life.'" This is something we have not heard happening even among the heresies. Then he also shows a number of seven angels mentioned by the one delivering the seal, standing on either side of the soul departing from the body; some of light, and others named "archontic." And he says that the ruler of those named "archontic" is called the **Accursed God**. Then, having fabricated these expressions, he reasonably accuses those who then dared to say such things. But why should we not also be indignant along with those who blame such people, if indeed there are any who say the God of the Jews is "accursed"—He who rains and thunders, and is the **Demiurge** <note>term: Demiurge; from the Greek 'demiourgos' meaning craftsman. In Gnosticism, a lesser, often hostile deity who created the physical world, distinct from the supreme God.</note> of this world, and the God of Moses and of his account of the creation? But Celsus seems to have intended even through these things to be not fair-minded, but most ignorant out of an unphilosophical hatred toward us. <margin>* spread</margin> For he wished to make those who are inexperienced in our affairs, upon encountering his writing, at war with us, as if we called the good Creator of this world an "accursed God." And he seems to me to have done something similar to the Jews, who at the beginning of the teaching of Christianity spread a foul rumor against the Word: that after sacrificing a child they partake of its flesh; and again, that those of the Word, wishing to do the works of darkness, extinguish the light, and each... <margin>Tertullian, Apology, ch. 7.</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

<margin>* to destroy.</margin>
...that he mentions this with madness. This slander, which unreasonably prevailed long ago over so many, persuaded outsiders of the reports that Christians were of such a character; and even now it still deceives some, who are deterred by such things from even coming into a conversation of simpler words with Christians. Something of this sort seems to me to be what Celsus is managing to set forth: namely, that Christians say the Creator God is "accursed." He does this so that anyone believing him when he says these things against us might, if possible, <margin>Ophites.</margin> be moved to *destroy Christians as the most impious of all people, dragging matters along and setting forth the reason why the God of the creation-story according to Moses is called "accursed." He claims "that he is worthy of such a title, according to those who hold these opinions about him, because he cursed the serpent, who introduced the knowledge of good and evil to the first humans." But he ought to have known that those who chose the side of the serpent—believing he gave good advice to the first humans, and thus surpassing the mythical Titans and Giants—are called **Ophites** <note>From the Greek 'ophis' meaning serpent; a Gnostic sect that revered the serpent of Genesis as a bringer of knowledge.</note> for this reason. They are so far from being Christians that they accuse Jesus no less than Celsus does; they do not admit anyone to their assembly unless they first place curses upon Jesus. See then how most irrationally Celsus has acted: in his arguments against Christians, he has compared us to those who do not even wish to hear the name of Jesus, even if he were merely a wise man, or moderate in character, or simply a human being. What could be more foolish or more insane—not only on the part of those who wish to be named after the serpent as the author of good things, but also on the part of Celsus, who thought that <margin>Diogenes the Cynic.</margin> accusations against the Ophites were accusations against Christians? Long ago, among the Greeks, a philosopher who loved simplicity <note>Referring to Diogenes of Sinope.</note> and set forth an example of a happy life—showing that happiness is not hindered by total lack of possessions—called himself a **Cynic** <note>Meaning 'dog-like'; Origen contrasts the Cynics' harmless name with the Ophites' choice of a dangerous animal.</note>; but these impious men, as if they were not humans (to whom the snake is an enemy) but snakes themselves, pride themselves on being called **Ophites**. They have a certain Euphrates as the introducer of their impious doctrines. Then next, as if insulting Christians and accusing those who called the God of Moses and his Law "accursed"—thinking that those who say these things are Christians—he says: "What could be more foolish or more insane than this shameless wisdom? In what way did the lawgiver of the Jews err? Or how is his world-creation formed? You yourself take it to be allegorized figuratively through sources, as he says, and you praise the Law of the Jews; and unwillingly, even if you are most powerful, you praise the Creator of the world, who promised everything to them, who [promised] to increase their race—"

—would defile whichever woman he first encountered: which false and unjust opinion for a long time kept very many people alienated from our religion, persuaded that Christians were such; and to this time it deceives some, because for that reason they so turn away from Christians that they do not even wish to have a simple conversation with a Christian man. Celsus, as it seems to me, preparing something of this sort, said that the Creator God is called "accursed" by Christians, so that whoever believes his slanders might pursue Christians with hatred unto destruction as being extremely impious. Here, mixing and confounding everything, as if to give the reason why that God, the creator of the world according to Moses, is called "accursed" by the authors of this opinion, he says: *He was deservedly cursed, according to those who believe such things about him, because he cursed the serpent, who brought the knowledge of good and evil to the first humans.* And yet he ought to have known that those people, to whom the serpent is pleasing as a good counselor to the first humans—more impious than the Titans and Giants, and called **Ophites** for that reason—are so far from being Christians that they accuse Jesus no less than Celsus does; nor do they admit anyone into their fellowship unless he has first cursed Jesus. See how absurdly Celsus acts in his speech against Christians, since he compares the men of our religion with those who cannot even endure to hear the name of Jesus, whether as a wise or good man, or simply as a human. What therefore is more stupid or more insane, either for those holding the serpent as the author of good things, or for Celsus, who thinks that what he hurls at the Ophites falls upon Christians? There was among the Greek philosophers a lover of frugality, who wishing to show by his example that poverty is no obstacle to happiness, declared himself a **Cynic**: but these impious men, as if they were not humans (to whom the serpent is an enemy) but were themselves serpents, rejoice to be named **Ophites** after the serpent, which is most hostile and horrific to humans, having a certain Euphrates as the author of this impiety. Then, as if making a reproach against Christians, and accusing those who curse the God of Moses and the law brought through him—thinking they are Christians who say such things—he says: *What is more stupid or more insane than this foolish wisdom? Did the lawgiver of the Jews err? # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

[Celsus says of God:] "Promising to expand [his kingdom] to the ends of the earth, and a resurrection from the dead together with the very body and blood, and breathing inspiration into the Prophets: and then soon after, do you conversely revile him? Surely when you are compelled by these facts, you acknowledge him as the God to be worshipped; but whenever your teacher Jesus establishes laws contrary to those of Moses of the Jews, you abandon this God and Father and seek another." Here indeed Celsus, as befits a distinguished philosopher, openly slanders the Christians, saying they are hardly consistent with themselves—now, when Jews wring a confession from them, acknowledging the same God as they do; and now, when Jesus establishes laws contrary to the Mosaic ones, seeking another God in his place. For we, whether we are debating with Jews or conversing among ourselves, know one and the same God, whom the Jews worshipped of old and now claim to worship, and we are in no way impious toward Him. We do not preach that He will raise the dead together with the very flesh and blood, as has already been said above: for we do not say that this "animal body," which is "sown in corruption, and dishonor, and weakness," rises in the same state as it was sown. <note>Origen is referencing 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 to argue for a spiritual rather than a literal physical resurrection.</note> But we have discussed these matters sufficiently above. Next, he again brings up those seven principal demons, who are never named among Christians; I think, however, he took them from the Ophians <note>The Ophians or Ophites were a Gnostic sect that revered the serpent (ophis) as a symbol of knowledge.</note>, and indeed in that diagram which we acquired for their sake, we found the entire series laid out exactly as Celsus described. He says the first is formed in the likeness of a lion, not adding how those truly impious men name him; we, however, found that this wicked diagram calls Michael, the angel of the Creator praised in Holy Scripture, "the lion-faced." Second, Celsus says is a bull; the diagram which we had, however, names this bull Suriel. Third, Celsus describes as a horrific hissing creature living on land and in water alike; the same diagram in the third place calls Raphael "the serpent-formed." Likewise, Celsus says the fourth has the appearance of an eagle, whom the diagram says is Gabriel, equally "eagle-formed." Next, the fifth Celsus says has a bear's face, named Thauthabaoth, "bear-formed" in the diagram. The sixth has a dog's face, who among those people is named Erathaoth in the same order of description. Furthermore, the seventh Celsus says has the face of an ass and is named Thaphaoth or Onoel; we found in the diagram that he is called Onoel or Thartharaoth, to be seen in "asinine form." # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...and finally, they name the last one **Horæus** <note>A Gnostic archon or planetary spirit, often associated with Venus or the Moon</note>, and they believe these words must be spoken to him: *"Having fearlessly passed over the barrier of fire, and having obtained the lordship of the first gate, O Horæus, let me pass, seeing as you do the symbol of your power, destroyed by the type of the tree of life, an image assumed according to the likeness of innocence. May grace be with me, O father, let it be with me."* To these things we have been driven by the supposed vast learning of Celsus—though more truly it is his meddlesomeness and trifles—while we wish to show the reader of his writings and of our response that we are not ignorant of those "learned" matters which he falsely charges against us. For none of our wise men hold such views, nor are they found among our people. Nevertheless, I myself wished to learn and explain these things, lest impostors, professing to know more than we do, should deceive some who are struck with awe by the imagination of these names. I could have declared even more to show that we both know these deceptions and turn away from them as alien and impious, not fitting for the truly Christian doctrine which we defend even unto death. It must be known, however, that those who composed these things, neither understanding magic nor discerning the sacred Scriptures, have mixed everything together: from magic they took **Ialdabaoth**, **Astaphæus**, and **Horæus**; and from the Hebrew Scriptures **Iaoia** <note>original: "Iaoia," likely a corruption of Yahweh</note>, whom the Hebrews name, as well as **Sabaoth**, **Adonæus**, and **Eloæus**. These names taken from the Scriptures are titles of the one and only God. Not understanding this, as professed enemies of God, they thought that **Iao** was one, **Sabaoth** another, and a third different from these was **Adonæus** (whom the Scriptures call **Adonai**), and yet another was **Eloæus** (whom the Prophets in Hebrew call **Eloi**). After this, Celsus sets forth other myths in succession about *certain ones returning into the forms of the ruling powers, so that some are said to breathe like lions, others like bulls, others like dragons, or eagles, or bears, or dogs.* In the same diagram we also found a quadrangular shape, which Celsus mentions as being located at the gates of paradise, as those wretched people say. In the same place, a flaming sword was painted as the diameter of a certain fiery circle, as if standing guard over the tree of knowledge and of life. Furthermore, Celsus either did not wish or was not able to set forth the speeches which, according to the myths of those impious men, are spoken by those who pass through each gate. We, however, have done this as well, so that we might show to Celsus and to our readers the end of this profane mystery, which we know to be utterly foreign to Christian piety. After what has already been said, and what we have added...

Even if we have gone through these things to know and set them out, it is so that sorcerers might not deceive those who are snatched away by the fantasy of names through their promise of knowing more than we do. We could have presented even more to show that we know the ways of deceivers, but we reject them as alien, impious, and not co-existing with the truly Christian words confessed by us even unto death. For as the use of the oracles of the Prophets is ours, who prove that Jesus is that Christ announced by them, then from the Gospel histories we show the outcome of the prophecies. But as to his saying "circles in circles," it is either of the already mentioned heresy, embracing seven principal circles in one circle (which they say is the soul of the universe and Leviathan): or it is taken from Ecclesiastes, the meaning of the speaker not being sufficiently understood: *The spirit proceeds circling through circles, and returns into its circles.* Furthermore, the "outpourings of the terrestrial Church and of circumcision" seems to be taken from certain people asserting that this terrestrial Church is a flowing forth from a certain Aeon of the celestial Church: and that the circumcision written in the law is a sign of a certain purgatory circumcision which happens there. Moreover, the Valentinians name a certain wisdom "Prunica" according to their erroneous wisdom: they want her symbol to be that woman who labored for twelve years with a flow of blood: which having been heard, but not understood, this man, who heaps all things of the Greeks, barbarians, and heretics into one mass, called the "flowing power of a certain virgin Prunicus." But "living soul" is perhaps said somewhere...

## Book VI

in the secret mysteries of the Valentinians <note>A prominent Gnostic sect in the 2nd century known for complex cosmic hierarchies.</note> concerning the creator, whom they call "soulish" <note>original: *animalem* / *psychikon*. In Gnostic thought, the creator of the material world was inferior to the supreme God.</note>: or perhaps, in contrast to a dead soul, a *living soul* is rightly said by some to belong to one who has attained salvation. However, a *slaughtered heaven* is nowhere mentioned that I know of, nor a *earth slaughtered by a knife*, nor many slaughtered so that they might live: so I can easily believe that Celsus invented these things himself. But that *heaven* <note>meaning the worldly order</note> shall undergo death in the world after sin has died, that indeed is our doctrine; we who have read this mystery in the Apostle, who says: *When he shall have put all enemies under his feet, then the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed.* It is also written: *When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory.* Now, as for the *narrow descent*, perhaps those who assert the migration of souls into various bodies <note>reincarnation or metempsychosis</note> might say this; but it is likely that *spontaneously opened gates* are mentioned by some alluding to that passage in the Psalm: *Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter into them and praise the Lord: this is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter into it.* And again in the ninth Psalm it is read: *Thou who liftest me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all thy praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion*: where the gates of death signify sins, which lead to destruction; just as, on the contrary, by the gates of Sion are understood good works. In the same way they are called gates of righteousness, as if they were gates of virtue: these are opened spontaneously to those who pursue virtue. Regarding the *tree of life*, it would be more appropriately discussed in the commentaries on Genesis, where it is told that God planted a paradise. But Celsus, not content with having frequently mocked the resurrection—though he does not understand it—now says that the *resurrection of the flesh from a tree* is spoken of: because, I suppose, he did not rightly hear that figurative saying: *Through a tree, death; and through a tree, life*: death in Adam, life in Christ. Then, playing with quibbles about the "tree" <note>original: *lignum*, which means both wood and the Cross</note>, he says frequent mention is made of it either because our master was fixed to a cross, or because he practiced the trade of a carpenter: not seeing that the *tree of life* is found in the writings of Moses; nor noticing that nowhere in the Gospels received by the Church is it read that Jesus himself was a carpenter. <note>Origen here follows a specific textual tradition; other manuscripts of Mark 6:3 do call Jesus a carpenter.</note> He thinks that we, through allegory, have invented that tree of life from the cross; and, consistent with his aforementioned error, he adds: *That if he had happened to be thrown from a cliff, or pushed into a pit, or strangled with a noose: they would have invented a cliff of life above the heavens,*

But we would speak of death ceasing in the world when sin in the world dies, pointing out the mystery found in the Apostle: "But when he has subjected all enemies under his feet, then the last enemy, death, is abolished." Again, those who introduce the doctrine of reincarnation <note>original: *metensomatosis*</note> will perhaps speak of a "narrow descent." And it is not improbable that "gates opening of their own accord" are mentioned by some hinting at the specific passage: "Open to me the gates of righteousness, that entering into them I may give thanks to the Lord; this is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter into it." And again in the ninth Psalm it is said: "Thou who liftest me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all thy praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion." The Word calls the "gates of death" those sins which lead to destruction; just as the "gates of Sion" are the opposite, namely good deeds. In this way also the "gates of righteousness" are the same as the "gates of virtue"; and these are opened readily to the one who pursues acts according to virtue. Concerning the "tree of life," it would be more fittingly explained when interpreting the account in Genesis of the paradise of God planted by Him. Celsus, having already often mocked the partial resurrection, now, not satisfied with what he has said, claims that "a resurrection of the flesh from a tree" is spoken of—having misunderstood, I believe, the symbolic saying that "through a tree came death, and through a tree, life": death in Adam, and life in Christ. Then, playing with the matter of the "tree," he mocks it from two angles, saying: "For this reason it is used, either because our teacher was nailed to a cross, or because he was a carpenter by trade"—not seeing that the "tree of life" is recorded in the writings of Moses; and also not seeing that nowhere in the Gospels circulating in the churches is Jesus himself recorded as being a carpenter. He thinks that we have allegorized the tree of life to fit the cross. Following his own error, he says: "that if he had happened to be thrown down a cliff, or pushed into a pit, or strangled by a noose, a 'cliff of life' would have been invented in heaven,"

# Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Celsus claims to know [our secrets]: not as one who gathers facts, but by collecting uncertain fables, and we likewise condemn such things. Whether those who boast of such matters promise certain magical arts, and whether this constitutes the height of their wisdom, we have no certain knowledge; for we have never witnessed any of these things. Let Celsus see to it—he who has already been frequently convicted of lying and calumny—whether he is lying here as well: or whether he has inserted into his own commentaries things he discovered among those who are strangers to our religion. He rightly says that such magicians and tricksters, who use the foreign <note>original: "barbaricis"</note> names of demons, are like certain people who, among those who do not know that the Greeks call them one thing and the Scythians another, show off certain portentous voices. He then lists these, taken from Herodotus: that *Apollo* is called *Aetosyrus* by them, *Neptune* is *Thamimasades*, *Venus* is *Artimpasa*, and *Vesta* is *Tabiti*. 

However, let him who is able examine whether perhaps Celsus, along with Herodotus, is lying about these matters; just as the Scythians do not know that these same things are established by the Greeks concerning those who are thought to be gods. For how is it likely that Apollo is called *Aetosyrus* among the Scythians? For I do not think that by a Greek interpretation of the word *Aetosyrus* an etymology for Apollo is produced; or that what *Aetosyrus* sounds like in the Scythian tongue is signified by Apollo. The same must be said of the rest: for the Greeks were moved by certain reasons to give names to their deities, and the Scythians by others; in the same way the Persians by others, and the Indians, or Africans, or Ethiopians by others still: according to how it seemed fit to each, after they once fell away from the true and first religion, the Creator of which we worship. 

We have already sufficiently declared before that Jupiter and Sabaoth <note>Sabaoth: A Hebrew title for God meaning "of Hosts," which Celsus tried to equate with Zeus/Jupiter.</note> are not the same, at which time we also brought forward certain things concerning languages from the sacred scriptures: wherefore I intentionally decline the opportunities to repeat the same things to which Celsus calls us. Then, again mixing in something from the magical arts—which perhaps applies to none of us, since those who do such things under the pretext of this religion are not sorcerers—but perhaps mentioning certain things for the sake of those wishing to appear to have the power of divine words at hand to deceive the simple, he says: *Why should I list*, he says, *those who taught purifications, and incantations for driving away or warding off diseases; or various hissing sounds and forms of demons, and besides these things in garments, numbers, stones, and plants.*

<column-break/>

...into the discourse against Celsus, so that we may demonstrate to those who read it that he has understood these things in a more monstrous way, and not from mere hearsay, the things charged against us. But if those who pride themselves on such things promise some magical sorcery, and this is for them the sum of wisdom; we do not affirm it, for we have never yet investigated such a thing. But Celsus would know—he who has already been caught many times in false witness and irrational accusations—whether he is lying in these matters too; or whether, having obtained information from other strangers and those foreign to the faith, he set it forth in his own writing. 

Then, as if speaking to those who use, [as] he says, some magic and sorcery, and who call upon foreign names of certain demons; he says such things <margin>these things.</margin> as that those who perform wonders regarding the same subjects act similarly toward those who do not know that their names are one thing among the Greeks and another among the Scythians. Then he sets it forth, taking it from Herodotus, “that the Scythians call Apollo <margin>Herodotus book 4</margin> “Oitosyros, and Neptune <margin>* Gongosyros.</margin> “Thamimasadas, and Venus <margin>Thasimasada.</margin> “* Artimpasa, and Vesta Tabiti. <margin>* Argimpasa.</margin> Let him who is able examine whether perhaps Celsus is lying about these things along with Herodotus; since the Scythians do not understand the same underlying subjects as the Greeks concerning those who are considered gods. 

For how is it reasonable that Apollo is called * Oitosyros among the <margin>* Gongosyros.</margin> Scythians? For I do not think that the word * Oitosyros, <margin>* Gongosyros.</margin> when translated into the Greek tongue, presents the etymology of Apollo; or that 'Apollo' in the dialect of the Scythians signifies * Oitosyros. <margin>* Gongosyros.</margin> The same thing must also be said concerning the rest; for the Greeks, starting from different origins, have fashioned etymologies for how they named the gods recognized among themselves; and the Scythians from others; and indeed the Persians from others; and the Indians, or Ethiopians, or Libyans from others; or however it pleased each to name them, they having not remained in the ancient and pure conception of the Creator of all things. 

It has been sufficiently said by us in the passages before these, wishing to demonstrate that he [God] is not the same as Sabaoth or Jupiter. At which time we also cited certain things concerning dialects from the divine scriptures. We therefore intentionally pass over these things, in which Celsus calls us to tautology [repetition]. Then again, mixing up matters from magical sorcery, and touching perhaps upon no one—since he who practices trickery is not nourished by the godliness according to our character—but perhaps bringing forward those who deceive by using such things, so that they might seem to do something by divine power, he sets forth certain things, saying: “Why must I list how many “taught purifications, or healing songs, or “hissing sounds, or noises, or shapes of demons, whether perceived by the senses, or in garments, or stones, or plants.”
