# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

> "...or with a plant, or with roots, and generally with all sorts of <term>amulets</term> <note>original: "ἀλεξιφάρμακα" / "amuleta" — objects intended to ward off evil or disease</note> for children? It is therefore necessary for us to offer a reasonable defense against such a threat; especially since we have not yielded even slightly to such suspicions. After this, he seems to me to do something similar to those who, out of great hatred toward Christians, assert to those who know nothing of Christian affairs, that they have <margin>M. Minucius Felix to Octavius <note>A reference to the Latin apologist Minucius Felix, who recorded similar pagan slanders.</note></margin> caught Christians eating the flesh of children, and shamelessly engaging in sexual unions with the women among them. For just as these things—though said by the many and entirely foreign to our piety—are condemned as lies against Christians; so also might those things be found to be lies spoken by Celsus, in which he claimed to have seen among certain elders of our persuasion "barbaric books, containing the names of demons and monstrous wonders." And he claimed that "these supposed elders of our persuasion promise nothing good, but everything for the harm of men." And if only all the things said by Celsus against Christians were such that their falsehood could be proven by the experience of the majority, who have associated with Christians and have never heard any such thing about them. After this, as if forgetting that his purpose is to write against Christians, he says that "a certain Dionysius, an Egyptian musician who associated with him," said regarding his own magic, "that it has power over the uneducated and those with corrupt morals, but has no power against those who have studied philosophy, because they have been careful to maintain a healthy way of life." If it were our purpose now to teach about magic, we would have added a few things to what we said about it above; but since we must say what is most relevant to Celsus's treatise, we say regarding magic: let anyone who wishes to investigate whether even philosophers are ever susceptible to it or not, read what was written by Moeragenes concerning the memoirs of Apollonius of Tyana, the magician and philosopher. In these, a man who was not a Christian but a philosopher said that some not ignoble philosophers were captured by the magic in Apollonius, having approached him as a sorcerer. In these accounts, I believe, he also narrated quite a bit about Euphrates and a certain Epicurean. But we, who have learned by experience what kind of people they are who through Jesus worship the God over all in the Christian way and live according to His Gospel, using the appointed prayers more frequently and properly by night and day, affirm that they are not susceptible to magic or demons. For truly, <margin>Psalm 33:18 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 34:7.</note></margin> "the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear Him, and will deliver them" from every evil; even if the...

<column-break/>

...roots or amulets of various kinds? To which accusation it would be unjust for us to respond; since there is not even a slight suspicion regarding us as if we handled such things. After these things, he seems to me to act like certain people most hostile to the Christian name, who among those ignorant of what the Christian religion is, assert that they have experienced firsthand that this race feeds on the flesh of infants, and promiscuously without shame handles the women of the same sect. For just as it is well known that these lies were fashioned by the profane out of hatred for Christians: so also can the lies of Celsus be detected, when he says he saw among certain elders of our religion "barbaric volumes, containing the names of demons and deceptions." He adds that these same elders profess nothing good, but everything harmful to men. And would that all the things which Celsus objects against Christians were such that their vanity was refuted by the experience of many who live with Christians and never hear anything of the sort regarding their morals. Then, as if forgetting he is writing against Christians, he says, "a certain Dionysius, an Egyptian musician, his familiar friend, used to say regarding magic, that it can do something against the rude and ill-mannered; but against those devoted to philosophy it has no strength, because their way of life is healthily established." If it were now the intention to discourse on magic, I would add not a few things to those which we said above on this matter: but since those things must be said which pertain more to Celsus's commentary, we say only this of magic; whoever wishes to know whether even philosophers can be captured by it or not, let him read the writings of Moeragenes, who handed down the memorable deeds of Apollonius of Tyana, the magician and philosopher: where, not a Christian but a philosopher, says that not ignoble philosophers were captured by the magic of Apollonius, when they had approached him as if to a deceiver: and in these, I think, he also tells of that famous Euphrates, and a certain Epicurean. But we affirm this for certain, having experienced it ourselves, that those who in the Christian rite through Jesus worship God, the Lord of all, and live according to His Gospel, using solemn prayers by night and day, are conquerable neither by magic nor by demons. For it is true, that "the angel of the Lord will surround those who fear Him, and will rescue them from all evil":

Next, Celsus begins another slander against us: *They are deceived*, he says, *impiously through the greatest ignorance of a doctrine they do not understand—divine enigmas—while they make a certain devil an adversary to God, naming the same in Hebrew as Satan. For it is entirely a mark of mortal weakness, and utterly foreign to piety, to say that the greatest God, wishing to do good to men, is unable to do so because of a resisting adversary. Is the Son of God then conquered by the devil? And, having been tormented by him, does he teach us to despise his torments, foretelling that Satan will likewise come and perform great miracles, usurping for himself the glory of God, to whom, as a deceiver, one must not pay attention, but believe in him alone. This is clearly the act of an impostor, laboriously taking precautions against those of a contrary doctrine.* And soon, intending to point out those enigmas by which he thinks we were deceived into introducing Satan, he says that the ancients handed down a "war of the Gods" enigmatically: such as Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher known for the idea that change is central to the universe.</note>, when he writes thus, *That if it must be said that war is a common thing and a strife, and all things are produced from strife and administered by it:* or as Pherecydes <note>An early Greek thinker from Syros, often cited as one of the first to write in prose.</note>, much older than Heraclitus, who fabulously describes opposing battle lines, over one of which he places Saturn as leader, and over the other Ophioneus <note>A serpent-like giant in Greek mythology who fought Saturn (Cronus).</note>, writing of various challenges and contests, and certain conditions, so that the party which was cast into Ogenus <note>The primeval ocean or abyss.</note> should be held as defeated, while the victors, having driven off their adversaries, should possess heaven. Furthermore, he claims that the mystical wars of the Titans and Giants against the Gods belong to the same sentiment: as well as whatever the Egyptians tell of Typhon, and Horus, and Osiris. After he had recounted these things, yet without explaining them according to a better sense than they are understood by us, he reviles us, saying that these things are far different from our fictions about the devil-demon, or (what he himself thinks more true) about an impostor man acting as an adversary. Indeed, he even understands Homer in this way, as singing things not foreign to Heraclitus and Pherecydes, and the mysteries of the Titans and Giants, in whose work Vulcan suggests something of the sort to Juno:

Then, following this, wishing to show the enigmas from which he thinks we, having misheard, introduced the things concerning Satan, he says "the ancients hinted at a certain divine war, Heraclitus saying thus: 'If it is necessary to say that war is common, and justice is strife; and all things happen according to strife and necessity.' And Pherecydes, who was older than Heraclitus, tells a myth of an army drawn up against an army, and gives Saturn as the leader of one, and Ophioneus of the other, and relates their challenges and struggles; and that agreements were made between them, that whichever of them fell into Ogenus, these should be the defeated ones, but those who pushed them out and conquered should hold heaven. And he says the mysteries concerning the Titans and Giants, being reported as a war of gods, follow this same purpose; as do the stories among the Egyptians concerning Typhon, and Horus, and Osiris." Then, having set these things out, and not having explained in what way those things are reasonable, but rather that "these things of ours are mishearings of those," he insults us, saying, "those things are not well-suited to be like the stories about a devil-demon, or (which they say is truer) a sorcerer man who holds contrary opinions." And let us hear also from Homer, as he introduces things similar to Heraclitus and Pherecydes, and the mysteries concerning the Titans and Giants, hinting at such a thing in these words where Vulcan speaks to Juno:

### The Nature of the Adversary

<margin>Revelation 12:9; 20:2.</margin>

...divine things of the ascent, being drawn up by the Word <note>The *Logos* or Christ</note> toward the highest blessedness of all, and (if I may name it so) the very summit of good things. Now, he who is called "Satan" in the Hebrew dialect—and by some named more Greek-like as "Satanas"—when translated into the Greek tongue means "the Adversary." Everyone who chooses wickedness and the life according to it, as one doing things contrary to virtue, is a "Satan," that is, an adversary to the Son of God, who is righteousness, and truth, and wisdom. 

But more properly, the Adversary is he who was the first of all those living blessedly in peace to lose his wings <note>A Platonic metaphor for the soul losing its divine nature</note> and fall away from blessedness. He, according to Ezekiel, walked blameless in all his ways until *iniquity was found in him*; and being the seal of likeness and a crown of beauty in the paradise of God, as if sated with good things, he came into destruction, according to the word spoken mystically to him: *You have become destruction, and you shall not exist forever.* 

Let these few things be ventured, having trusted in this writing even at some risk. But if any scholar were to examine the sacred line from every side with a touchstone, he might <insert>give a body to</insert> the discourse concerning wickedness—how it first arose and in what manner it may be destroyed. He would see that neither Celsus, nor anyone else whose soul is dragged down and pulled away from God and the right conception of Him by the evil demon, has grasped even in a dream the intent of Moses and the Prophets regarding Satan.

Since Celsus also tosses aside matters concerning the one called Antichrist—whether having read what is said of him in Daniel, or by Paul, or the prophecies of the Savior in the Gospels regarding his coming—a few things must be said of this as well. Just as faces are not born identical, so too the hearts of men are not identical to one another. It is *clear* that there are differences in the hearts of men: some lean toward the good, being more fully shaped and formed toward it than others, while some, through neglect of the good, depart toward its opposite. Among these, <insert>in some</insert> it is to a lesser degree; or rather, it is not absurd that two (if I may call them so) extremes, one of good and one of the opposite, should arise among men. Thus, the extreme of good is found in the man understood to be Jesus, from whom such great conversion, healing, and improvement flowed to the human race; while the opposite extreme is in the one named the Antichrist. But God, having known all things by His foreknowledge and seeing the nature of both these men, willed concerning...

<column-break/>

...found, they are raised up through the Word to the supreme blessedness and the citadel (so to speak) of good things. Furthermore, Satan, so called in the Hebrew language, and by some named in a more Greek form *Satanas*, is interpreted as "adversary." Moreover, everyone who pursues malice in life, as an opponent of virtue, is a Satan—that is, an adversary of the Son of God, who is justice, truth, and wisdom. 

But more properly, the adversary is he who, first of all those living blessedly in peace, fell from his blessedness after losing his wings. He, as Ezekiel says, walked blameless in all his ways until iniquity was found in him; and since he was as it were an image expressed by a seal and a crown of beauty in the paradise of God, he perished as if from a fullness of good things, according to the word of him who said to him mystically: *You have become a destruction, and you shall not be forever.* 

These few things, therefore, we have boldly committed to these writings as if by a toss of the dice, yet perhaps we have accomplished nothing. If anyone, however, should apply himself to scrutinizing the sacred letters, and should collect those passages speaking everywhere of malice as if into a body, he would see how it first arose and how it perishes. He would surely see that Celsus—or anyone whose mind is torn away from God, His right understanding, and the Word of God by an evil demon—has not imagined even in a dream what the mind of Moses and the Prophets was concerning Satan. 

Since Celsus also interjects certain things about the Antichrist, as he is called—having read neither the testimonies of Daniel nor Paul about him, nor the prophecies of the Savior in the Gospels concerning his arrival—a few things must also be said about these. Because, just as the various faces of men are very different from one another, so their hearts are not similar; from which it appears that there is a very great difference in them. While those inclined toward the good are not all equally made and formed for it, so among the despisers of virtue, some rush into evil more or less than others: for there are some most profuse in every kind of vice, and again there are those who are carried into them more moderately. It is not absurd, therefore, to say that there are two extremes (to name them so) in all things, one of good, the other of opposites: so that the extreme of good is understood in him who is according to Jesus, the man from whom such great conversion, medicine, and progress toward the better flowed into the human race; but the extreme of the opposite in him who is according to the one called Antichrist. But God, who comprehends all things by His foreknowledge and sees both, willed...

# Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...to signify these things to men through the Prophets: so that those who understand their words may cling to better things and flee from their opposites. And since malice then most greatly overflows, reaching its highest peak when it is cloaked in the appearance of good, therefore it shall come to pass through that most wicked one—with his father the devil cooperating with him—by performing signs, wonders, and false powers. For the cooperation of the devil himself will leave far behind those common deceptions of sorcerers <note>original: "magorum præstigias"</note> which are done by the help of demons, in order to deceive the human race. Paul speaks of this Antichrist, showing, not without a certain veiling <note>i.e., using figurative or mysterious language</note>, how he is to come, and when he will come to the human race, and for what reason. Speaking thus: <margin>2 Thess. 2: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.</margin> *Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him, that ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as if the day of Christ were at hand. Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition; who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God. Remember ye not, that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things? And now ye know what withholdeth that he might be revealed in his time. For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way. And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming: even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.* To explain each of these points is not the purpose of the present treatise. Furthermore, the Prophecy designating him is found in Daniel, which is effective for moving the prudent and candid reader <unclear>to faith</unclear>.

<column-break/>

...to signify these things through the prophets to men; so that those understanding their word might lay hold of the better things, and guard themselves from the opposites. It was necessary that the one of the extremes, being the best, should be proclaimed the Son of God because of his pre-eminence; and the one diametrically opposite to him, the son of the evil demon, and Satan, and the devil. And since then especially the foulness of malice is poured out, even at its height, when it takes on a character <note>original: "charakter"</note> and hypocritically mimics the better; for this reason, through the worse one it shall happen, by the cooperation <margin>2 Thess. 2: 9</margin> of his father the devil, with signs, and wonders, and powers of falsehood. For while all the wicked deeds of sorcerers performed by the cooperation of demons bring about the deception of the lowest of men, this shall happen by the cooperation of the devil himself, for the deception of the human race. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

*but one flesh*: <note>original: "sed caro una"</note> concerning the perfect man, who is joined to the true Lord, the Word, and Wisdom, and Truth, because *he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit*. <margin>1 Corinthians 6:17</margin> For if he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit: how much more is the soul of Jesus joined to the Lord, to the Word itself, to Wisdom itself, to Truth itself, and to Justice itself; and thus the soul of Jesus and God the Word—the firstborn of all creation—are not two. But when Celsus hears the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that virtue is the highest good and based on reason.</note> asserting that the supreme God is no happier than their own wise man, since the virtue of God and the virtue of man are the same, and the happiness of both is equal, he does not mock or disparage that dogma. Yet when divine teaching says that the perfect man is joined by virtue and united to the Word itself, and hears from us that the soul of Jesus has been raised to such heights of sublimity that it is not separated from the firstborn of all creation, he laughs at the idea of Jesus being called the Son of God; not seeing what is said about him in the hidden mysteries of the divine Scriptures. However, so that we may persuade one who yields to consistent doctrines and consult his benefit, we say on the authority of Holy Scripture that the Son of God is like the soul to the body of Christ, which is the Church of God, while the individual believers are members of the whole body. <margin>Colossians 1:24</margin> For just as the soul gives life to and moves the body, which of itself has no living motion, so that Word, urging his body with wonderful energy <term>energy: from the Greek 'energeia', meaning active power or operation</term> toward those things it ought to do, moves each individual member of the Church, doing nothing without reason. If these things, as I believe, cohere beautifully, what prevents the soul of Jesus, and Jesus as a whole, from cohering so indivisibly with the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation <margin>Colossians 1:15</margin> through the highest and incomparable communion, that he is no longer distinct from Him? But enough on these matters; let us now look at what follows, in which, without proof and with a single word, he pronounces judgment on Moses describing the beginnings of the world, saying that this generation of the world is utterly foolish. If he had brought forward reasons and probabilities as to why it seemed foolish to him, we would have contended with him on this; for it is not reasonable for us to argue against his mere opinion to prove how the creation is not to be accused of foolishness. But if anyone wishes to consider the causes by which we are moved, or the clearer arguments by which we establish the creation of the world as delivered by Moses: let him take into his hands our commentaries on Genesis, from the beginning of the book until that text, *This is the book* <margin>Genesis 5:1</margin>

<margin>1 Cor. 6:17</margin>
*but one flesh*; and concerning the perfect one, and the one joined to the true Lord, the Word, and Wisdom, and Truth, that "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." And if he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit, how much more is the soul of Jesus, which has been joined to the Lord in a most touching way, to the Word-itself, and Wisdom-itself, and Truth-itself, and Justice-itself? If this is so, the soul of Jesus and the God-Word, the firstborn of all creation, are not two. Then, if the philosophers from the Porch <note>The Stoics, named after the 'Stoa Poikile' or Painted Porch in Athens where they met.</note> say that the God over all is no more blessed than the wise among men, but that the happiness of both is equal, Celsus does not laugh, nor does he mock the dogma. But if the divine Word claims that the perfect man is joined by virtue and united to the Word-itself, as one who has ascended, and that we do not separate the soul of Jesus from the firstborn of all creation, he laughs at Jesus being called the Son of God; not seeing what things are said about him in secret and mystically in the divine scriptures. But so that we might persuade the one who accepts what is said and wishes to follow the consistency of doctrines for his benefit, we say that the divine words call the whole Church of God the body of Christ, animated by the Son of God; and the members of this body as a whole are the individual believers. Since, therefore, just as a soul gives life to and moves the body, which is not naturally suited to move itself with life, so the Word, moving it toward necessary things and acting within it, moves the whole body—the Church—and each member of the Church, doing nothing without the Word <note>original: "logos", meaning both 'the Word' and 'reason'</note>. If these things do not seem absurd but, as I think, have consistency, what is difficult in the idea that by the extreme and unsurpassable communion with the Word-itself, the soul of Jesus—and Jesus once and for all—is not separated from the only-begotten and firstborn of all creation, nor happens to be anything other than Him? But let these things be as they are; let us look also at the next points, in which, speaking without evidence and not even saying anything plausible, he accuses the creation-story of Moses, saying, "Furthermore, the creation of the world is also very foolish." If he had stated the manner in which it appeared foolish to him and set forth some probabilities, we would have struggled against them; but it does not seem reasonable to me to construct a defense against his mere decree to show how it is not foolish. But if anyone wishes to see the things that moved us <margin>* prevailed over us</margin> and the proofs that appeared to us establishing the creation of the world according to Moses, let him take up what we have previously labored on regarding Genesis, from the beginning of the book until the passage, "This is the book of the generation of men—" <margin>Gen. 5:1</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

...of the generation of men: wherein we endeavored to establish from the divine scriptures themselves what that heaven was which existed in the beginning, and what the earth; and what was that invisible and unformed earth, and what the abyss and the darkness upon it; and what the water was, and the Spirit of God which moved upon it; and what the created light was, and what the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sky or dome of the heavens in ancient cosmology.</note>, being a light in the heaven that came to be in the beginning, and so on in order. Next to these things, having heaped together in bare assertions the differences among the ancients concerning the generation of the world and of men, he says: *Leaving aside your writings for a moment, Moses and the prophets, as if they knew what the nature of the world and of men ever is, composed deep nonsense.* If indeed he had stated in what way the divine scriptures appeared to him to be deep nonsense, we would have endeavored to refute the arguments that appeared persuasive to him regarding their being deep nonsense; but now, doing the same as he and jesting, we also shall declare that Celsus, in no way knowing what the nature of the words in the prophets is, composed deep nonsense, arrogantly entitling it "The True Word." ...of the generation of men: where we have attempted to build up from the divine letters what heaven was in the beginning, what earth, what was its "invisible and uncomposed" state, what the abyss and the darkness above, what the water and the Spirit of God carried over it, what light is, what the firmament is (distinct from the heaven which was founded first of all), and the rest in succession. # Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

We shall seek from him something worthy of note: whether Moses, having forgotten that he said the world was created in six days, then adds, *This is the book of the generation of men, in the day that God made heaven and earth.* <note>original: "Hic est liber generationis hominum..." quoting Genesis 2:4 and 5:1</note> But it is in no way probable that Moses spoke without sense when, after enumerating the six days, he said, *In the day that God made heaven and earth.* If anyone thinks those words can refer to that earlier statement, *In the beginning God made heaven and earth*, he should know that before those words, *Let there be light, and there was light*, and *God called the light Day*, those other words were spoken: *In the beginning God made heaven and earth.* 

However, to discourse at present concerning sensible and intelligible things <note>The distinction between the physical world perceived by senses and the spiritual world understood by the intellect</note>, and how the nature of days is divided into two species, is not our current purpose, nor is it the place to scrutinize these matters as strictly as some might require; for each point requires its own specific treatise for an exposition of the creation described by Moses. Indeed, this was done by us to the best of our ability long before this conflict with Celsus, having meditated on this contemplation of the works performed in the six days for several years. 

Yet it should be known that in Isaiah, the word of God promises the righteous that they shall live *in a perpetual day, for whom the Lord himself shall shine instead of the Sun, and God shall be their glory.* <note>original: "in perpetua die degant..." referencing Isaiah 60:19</note> But this man [Celsus], because he perhaps happened upon some interpretations of heretics who take these voices, *Let there be light*, as if spoken by a creator who desired it as a favor, says: *What?* he asks, *did the maker of things thus borrow light from above, just as we light lamps from our neighbors?* Just as he took from another impious heresy those words: *If there was some detestable God opposed to the great God, and making these works without his consent: how did he receive the use of light from him?* 

Far be it from us to answer such things; rather, we prefer to accuse those errors by insisting on their teachings—not being ignorant of them, as Celsus is, but knowing them exactly, partly from men of that sect and partly from having diligently studied their commentaries. After this, Celsus speaks thus: *Indeed, concerning the generation of the world and its corruption—whether it is uncreated and incorruptible, or created but incorruptible, or the opposite—I say nothing now.* Therefore, we shall not discourse on these things either, as they are foreign to the present argument. We do not grant that the spirit of God intruded into the affairs of another when we read that *the spirit of God moved upon the waters*: nor even that some other creator of the world besides the great God, by evil arts against his spirit (with even the superior God himself enduring it), prayed for its destruction.

<column-break/>

<margin>Genesis 1:31. Exodus 20:11. Genesis 2:4.</margin>
<note>The right column provides the original Greek text of the passage translated above.</note>
...we shall point out to him how it escaped Moses' notice that he had previously said the creation of the world was completed in six days; and contradicting himself, he adds, *This is the book of the generation of men, in the day that God made the heaven and the earth.* But there is no likelihood that Moses, without understanding, said again after the six days, *In the day that God made the heaven and the earth.* If anyone thinks these things can be referred to the, *In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth*; let him consider that before the, *Let there be light, and there was light*, and the, *God called the light day*, it was said, *In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.* 

But now to relate the discourse concerning the intelligible and the sensible, and in what way the senses of the days are divided into both kinds, is to examine the topics according to their places; for we have need of entire treatises for the narration of the making of the world according to Moses; which we have done according to our ability, many years before the present composition against Celsus, from the habit of many years which we then took up, treating of the six-day creation according to Moses. 

It is necessary to know, however, that to the righteous, through Isaiah, the Word promises they shall be in a state of day, in which there is no sun, but the Lord himself shall be to them an eternal light, and God his glory. But having satisfied himself with certain wicked heresies, which badly interpreted the *Let there be light* as if spoken by the creator as a prayer, he said, "Why then," he says, "like those who light lamps from neighbors, did the creator use light from above?" And having misheard another impious heresy, he also said, "If there was some God opposed to the great God, a cursed one, who made these things against his will, why did he use his light?" 

To which we are so far from making a defense, that we wish more clearly to denounce their opinions as mistaken, and we know the things which he does not know, like Celsus, but which we know accurately, partly having followed them, and partly having diligently read their writings. After these things Celsus says, "I, concerning the generation of the world and corruption, whether as uncreated and incorruptible, or as created but incorruptible, or all the reverse, say nothing to them now." Therefore neither do we speak of these things now, as they are not included in the present work. But neither do we say the Spirit of the God over all used the things here as if they were another's, according to the, *The Spirit of God moved upon the water*; nor do we wickedly devise some other creator besides the great God, and a sparing of his spirit, enduring the God above, to have received a subversion.

...of the soul. Therefore, let those who say such things be gone, along with Celsus, who accuses them in a flawed manner. Then, I believe, mixing up sects with other sects, and not noting that some things belong to one sect and some to another, he brings forward against us arguments to repel Marcion <note>A 2nd-century heretic who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a different, inferior being from the God of the New Testament</note>. He snatches up as a consequence for us—who say that this world is the work of the God over all—the idea that according to us, God is the maker of evils. Let him see how the matter of evils stands, whether God made them or not; but [not] as a consequence—

...is. Therefore, let those who say these things be gone, together with Celsus himself, who rebukes them not very skillfully. For he ought either to have passed over them entirely in silence; or, as he himself considers a duty of humanity, to have brought their errors into the open to sharply refute them as impious. For we have never received that the greater God, who had delivered the spirit to the creator, sought it back from him. And soon, foolishly accusing their speeches as impious, he says: "What God gives something in such a way that he asks for it back? For it belongs to one in want to ask back: but God is in want of nothing." To these he added, as if about to bring forth a very wise saying against certain people: "Why, when you gave it to be used, did he not know he was giving it to a bad person?" Furthermore, he adds this: "Why does he neglect this wicked creator who opposes him?" Then, mixing, I believe, heresies with heresies, yet not distinguishing what he has taken from each, he objects to us the errors of Marcion which are unknown to us, perhaps heard from some unlearned person and not even understood; and he accuses us, their accusers; doing that very thing with little eloquence. Therefore, reciting the sayings of Marcion, but with the name of the author kept silent, he says: "Why does he send secretly and destroy his works? Why does he break in secretly, suborn, and deceive? Why does he entice those banished and cursed by this one, as you say, and snatch them away in the manner of a kidnapper? Why does he teach them to flee from their master? Why to flee their father? Why does he adopt them against the father's will? Why does he profess himself the father of those belonging to another?" And soon, as if wondering, he adds: "Behold a God to be feared for his singular majesty, who desires to be the father of sinners condemned by another, of outcasts, and (as they themselves say) of excrement!" And he whom he himself had sent, departing from his duty, he is unable to pull back and punish. And soon, as if turning toward us who deny that this world belongs to some other new God, he speaks thus: "But if these are his works, how was God making evil things? How can he not persuade and exhort? How does it happen that he repents because of the ingratitude of the wicked, and that he accuses and hates his own craftsmanship, and threatens that he will destroy his own progeny? Or where at last does he lead the man made by himself out of this world?" Here also he seems to me to declare too little what those evils are, although even among the Greeks there have been various opinions concerning goods and evils, snatching it up as if already confessed and proved, that, since according to our decrees, the creator of this world is the best and greatest God, he is also the maker of evils. However those opinions about evils may hold themselves, whether God made them or not; yet not—

# Book 6. ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

...[things] were made by God as a consequence of preceding events. I wonder then if Celsus—just as he gathers from our writings that evils were also made by God when He founded the world—does not see that it follows from his own arguments that evils were established by God. For someone might ask: "If all these things are His works, how did God make evils? How is it that He cannot warn and persuade?" It is, moreover, the greatest fault in arguing if someone accuses the opinion of others as being unsound, when his own opinions are found to be not far from the same crime. Let us therefore look for a moment at what the Divine Scripture thinks about goods and evils: and what we must answer to those asking how God made evils, and how He profits nothing by warning and persuading. 

Certainly, speaking according to the custom of Scripture, "goods" are properly the virtues and the operations that proceed from them; likewise, "evils" are properly their opposites. To confirm this, a testimony from the thirty-third Psalm <note>Modern numbering: Psalm 34</note> will now suffice: *Those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing. Come, children, listen to me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, and loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil, and do good.* For *Turn away from evil, and do good* is not said concerning the "goods" of the body, as they are named by some, nor concerning external things; but concerning the goods or evils of the soul. And he who does goods of this kind out of a desire for true life will attain it, led by the love of seeing good days—for which the Word of Justice <note>original: *verbum justitiæ* / *logos tēs dikaiosynēs*</note> is as a Sun—and he will reach them by divine help, having been delivered from this present evil age and from the evil days of which Paul says: *Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.* 

Nevertheless, bodily and external things are found to be called "goods" in an abusive sense <note>term: *abusivè* (Greek: *katachrēstikōteron*) — a rhetorical term meaning to use a word outside its strict, proper definition, such as calling wealth a "good" when only virtue is truly good.</note> when they contribute to this natural life, and their opposites are called "evils." For thus that famous Job speaks to his wife: *If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?* Since, therefore, it is found elsewhere in the Divine Scriptures, spoken from the person of the Lord: *I am He who makes peace and creates evils;* and elsewhere again concerning Him: *That evils came down from the Lord to the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen;* and since these things have disturbed many readers of Holy Scripture because they were not able to perceive what is signified by the naming of "goods" and "evils," it is probable that Celsus, hesitating here, also asks how God made evils—or perhaps because it was necessary for Celsus to have said these things from this [source]...

But we say that God did not make "evils"—meaning wickedness and the actions resulting from it. For how could the proclamation concerning judgment have any boldness, teaching as it does that the wicked are punished for their deeds of wickedness according to the proportion of their sins, while those who have lived according to virtue or performed virtuous deeds will be blessed and approved by the rewards of God, if God had actually made the *real* evils? And if there are certain literal sayings from the scriptures which those who do not wish to dare to say these things come from God—being unable to show in the heights of Scripture that it blames those who sin and accepts those who do well—nevertheless, it also says those things which seem to spare <note>original: φείσασθαι; perhaps "to trouble" or "to give pause to"</note> the few who read the divine writings ignorantly. We are now setting forth these "troubling" words, which happen to be many, and their interpretations require much preparation; I did not think it appropriate to arrange them in the present work. Therefore, if one does not understand these things as they are strictly named, God has not made them; rather, they followed upon His primary works as a few things—as it were—occurring in the whole for the sake of order. Just as spiral shavings and scraps follow the primary works of a carpenter, and as the things lying next to a building seem to be made by the builders—such as any refuse of stones or mortar required for the thing being constructed—so especially physical and external evils, which are said *to be given* by God, have happened to be made by God so that through these He might turn some back to Him. And what absurdity can this reasoning hold? For just as if we were to use the term "evils" loosely for the pains brought upon those being disciplined by fathers, teachers, and tutors, or by doctors who cut or cauterize for the sake of healing, we might say the father, tutor, teacher, or doctor "does evil" to the sons; yet those who strike or cut would not be accused. Thus, if God is said to bring such things for the sake of the turning back and healing of those needing such pains, the reasoning would hold nothing absurd. Even when "evils come down from the Lord to the gates of Jerusalem," they have their substance in the pains brought by enemies, being brought upon them for their conversion; and when He "visits their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges"; and when He says, "You have coals of fire, sit upon them, these shall be a help to you." In this way we also explain the verse, "He who makes peace and creates evil"; for He creates physical or external evils, cleansing and disciplining those who did not wish to be disciplined by reason and healthy teaching. And these—

<column-break/>

—perhaps he heard someone unskillfully interpreting this passage. But we say that God did not make evil—that is, vice and its works. Otherwise, how would the preaching of the future judgment stand, in which the wicked are to pay the penalties according to the nature of their crimes, while the followers of virtue will enjoy the rewards destined by God? Would this be so if God were the author of evils, at least in this sense? I know there will not be lacking certain people who, paying little attention to the whole context of the Scriptures (which perpetually blames sinners and approves the well-doers), will dare to pluck snippets from them from anywhere to assert that even in this sense evils are made by God—an argument that will have some weight with unlearned readers. Truly, it would be laborious to interpret such sayings that seemingly favor them now, nor is it proper to this present treatise. Therefore, if evils are understood strictly, God did not make them. But a few such things have followed His primary work, yet they have their place in this universe; just as shavings and twisted scraps follow the primary work of a craftsman, and as the fragments of small stones and lime lie near the ruins when masons are building. But if anyone speaks of external things and those pertaining to the body, which are called "evils" in an abusive <note>term: *abusivè* - a technical term in rhetoric and logic meaning to use a word in a loose, non-literal, or extended sense</note> sense, we will grant that these are sometimes made by God for the purpose of converting some people. For what is absurd here? For in taking the name of "evil" with this meaning—just as we say children disciplined by parents, teachers, and tutors are "badly treated," and others who are cut or burned by surgeons for the sake of medicine—yet no one accuses the parents, teachers, or tutors of being cruel, or the surgeons of cutting. Thus, as often as God is said to convert certain people by these or those "evils" because they have need of such harsh remedies, nothing seen to be said is inconvenient. Neither when "evils descend from the Lord into the gates of the inhabitants of Jerusalem" while the enemy is imminent for the sake of their chastisement; nor when He "visits the iniquities of those bringing the law with a rod, and their sins with whips"; nor when He says, "You have coals, sit upon them, these will be a help to you." In the same way we interpret that also: "Making peace, and creating evils." For He creates the evils of the body and external evils, purging and chastising those who refuse to be chastised by words and sound doctrine. Thus far regarding those things which Celsus objects. How God is said to create evils, we have already said: for He creates those things which are corporal or external evils, purging and instructing those who were unwilling to be instructed by reason and sound doctrine. # Book 6. ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Sf 2

How does God make evil? <note>Origen is addressing Celsus's claim that if God is the source of all things, He must be the source of evil.</note> Furthermore, regarding his claim that God is unable to warn and persuade, we have already said that if this is to be an accusation, it could be leveled against all who assert the existence of providence. However, it must be answered that it is not impossible for God to warn men, since He warns through the whole of Scripture and through those who have divinely received the grace of teaching. This is true unless the word "warning" is taken in a different sense than the commonly accepted one, to mean an admonition that is automatically effective in the mind of the listener. Similarly, the question of persuasion has been tossed about among all who assert providence. And since "to be persuaded"—Celsus's word *peithesthai* <note>original: πείθεσθαι</note>—is a passive verb related to its active form, just as one is said "to be shorn" if he offers himself to be shorn; therefore, there is a need not only for the work of the one persuading, but also for the one who shows himself compliant to the persuader, admitting the things being urged. Thus, it must be said that it is not by the fault of the persuader that persuasion fails, but by the fault of those who do not receive the trustworthy words of God. This is true even of human masters of the art of persuasion: for it can happen that someone, even one advanced to the highest degree in Rhetorical studies, falling upon another who is obstinate and stubborn, may be eloquent and silver-tongued in vain. Moreover, even if persuasive words proceed from God, the act of believing does not come from God <note>i.e., it is an act of human free will</note>; Paul clearly teaches this in these words: *Persuasion is not from Him who calls us* <margin>Galatians 5:8</margin>. Such also is this: *If you are willing and obedient to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and disobedient, the sword shall devour you* <margin>Isaiah 1:19, 20</margin>. For in order that someone might want what the monitor says, and by obeying become worthy of God's promises, there is need of the listener's assent and purpose. For this reason, that which is said in Deuteronomy seems weightily spoken: *And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God, and to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to keep all His commandments?* <margin>Deuteronomy 10:12, 13</margin> Now the sequence of words requires that we also respond to that which he asks: *How can it be that God, because of the ingratitude of the wicked, feels regret, and blames His own handiwork, and hates it, and threatens that He will destroy His own offspring?* In this place, not without slander and falsehood, he takes this scripture from Genesis: *But when the Lord saw that the wickedness of men had increased immensely on the earth, and nothing but evil continually...* <margin>And he falsely represents the things written in Genesis in this manner: "And the Lord God seeing that the evils were multiplied on the earth, and everyone thinks in his heart..."</margin>

<column-break/>

"And indeed as to the point, 'God makes all evils.' And as to, 'How is He unable to persuade and warn?' it would appear that if such a thing were a crime, the wording of Celsus would be brought against all who accept providence. But one might defend it by saying that it is not that God is unable to warn; for He warns through all scripture, and through those who by grace teach the things of God to those who hear. Unless perhaps some peculiar meaning is understood <margin>* some meaning</margin> in 'to warn,' <margin>he understands 'to warn'</margin> namely that of also succeeding in the one being warned, and that the listener hears the word of teaching; for this definition signifies the concept as it is achieved in common usage. And as to the point, 'How is He unable to persuade?' (which itself is brought against all who admit providence), these things must be said. Since 'to be persuaded' is, as it were, a reciprocal passive, analogous to a man 'being shorn' by offering himself to the one shearing; for this reason, it does not require only the energy of the persuader, but also (if I may name it so) a submission toward the persuader, and an acceptance of the things said by the persuader. Therefore, it must be said that it is not through God's inability to persuade that those who are not persuaded do not yield, but through those people not receiving the persuasive words of God. And if one were to say this even of men who are called 'craftsmen of persuasion,' he would not be wrong; for it is possible that even one who has perfectly mastered the theorems of rhetoric and uses them properly, while doing everything to persuade, might seem not to persuade because he does not happen upon the choice of the one who ought to be persuaded. And though the persuasive words come from God, the act of being persuaded is not from God; Paul clearly teaches this, saying, 'Persuasion is not from Him who calls <margin>Galatians 5:8</margin> us.' <margin>* you, i.e.</margin> Such then is also, 'If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you are not willing and do not hear me, the sword shall consume you.' <margin>Isaiah 1:19, 20</margin> For in order that one may want the things the warner says, and by hearing them become worthy of the promises of God, there is need of the choice of the listener, and of his assent to the things said. Wherefore in Deuteronomy it seems to me to have been emphatically said, 'And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God <margin>Deuteronomy 10:12, 13</margin> ask <margin>* asks</margin> of you, but to fear the Lord your God, [and] to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to keep His commandments?' <margin>i.e.</margin> 'And if it is next to answer the point, 'How is it that over these <margin>* ungrateful</margin> ungrateful and wicked ones they acknowledge regret, and He blames His own art, and hates, and threatens, and <margin>* to destroy</margin> destroys <margin>Interpreter</margin> His own offspring?' He slanders in these matters <margin>Genesis 6:5, 6, 7</margin>..."

And to this we say, that He does not altogether withdraw those perishing in the flood from the entire world—which consists of heaven and earth—but He releases them from life in the flesh; and having loosed them from their bodies, He looses them at the same time from being upon the earth, for which <margin>Matt. 26:13; Mark 16:15; 1 Tim. 6:7; John 1:9; Ibid. 16:33 * you shall have.</margin> the name "world" is held in many places of Scripture. Especially in the Gospel according to John, one can often find the "world" being the name for the region around the earth; just as in the passage: *He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world;* and, *In the world you *have* tribulation, but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.* If, therefore, one understands the phrase "withdraws from the world" as referring to the region around the earth, it would not be absurd to say so; but if one names the "world" as the system of heaven and earth, those who suffered in the flood were certainly not withdrawn from the world so named. And yet someone might say, having understood the passage: <margin>2 Cor. 4:18; Rom. 1:20.</margin> *While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen;* and, *For His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made;* that being among the invisible things, and those once and for all simply named "unseen," he departed from the world, the Word having withdrawn him <margin>* under the celestial.</margin> *from here, and toward the *celestial realm, having been transferred to the place of beautiful things. ...that they turned their minds to them, He reconsidered that He had so made man on the earth, thus determining within Himself: *I will destroy man, whom I created, from the face of the earth, from man even to the animals, from the creeping thing even to the birds; for I have reconsidered that I made them;* gathering from the unwritten as if it were written: for nowhere here is "repentance" of God named, nowhere is He said to hate or accuse His own workmanship. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.
->Rr 3<-

It is by far the most foolish thing, <note>Origen is quoting Celsus's critique here.</note> that certain days are attributed to the creation of the world before there were any days at all: for how could days exist before the heavens were made, and the earth established, and before the sun moved in its course? How do these things differ from these other words of the same Celsus? *Let us repeat*, he says, *the matter from a higher perspective, and consider how it befits the first and supreme God to command, "Let this be," and again "this or that": and on one day to complete a certain thing, on the second again something more, and then on the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth likewise?* But concerning these commands, *Let this be, and again this or that*, a response may seem to have been given according to our strength already at that time when we cited that passage; <note>Psalm 33:9 (32:9 in the Vulgate/Septuagint numbering).</note> *He spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created*: by saying that the immediate Maker <term>Opifex/Demiurge: the craftsman or worker who brings a design into material reality</term> is the Son of God, the Word <note>original: "verbum" / "logos"</note>, who as if with his own hands fashioned the world: but the Father of the Word, by whose command the world was founded through the Son himself, is the primary Maker. Furthermore, concerning the order of creation—how on the first day light was made, on the second the firmament, on the third the waters under the heavens were commanded to flow together into one place, and so the earth by its own nature brought forth various sprouts, and on the fourth finally its lights were added to the world, on the fifth the swimming creatures were produced, on the sixth the land animals, and lastly man—we have spoken as much as we were able in our commentaries on Genesis; and indeed in the preceding sections, by rebuking those who, searching into nothing deeply, say the creation of the world was finished in six literal days, we presented to them those words of Scripture, <margin>Gen. 2:4.</margin> *This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when the day was made; in which day God made heaven and earth.* Then again, Celsus, not understanding those words, <margin>Ibid. v. 2, 3.</margin> *God completed on the seventh day his works which he had made, and he ceased on the seventh day from all his works which he had made, and he blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it, because in it he had ceased from all his works which God began to do*, and thinking that "he rested on the seventh day" and "he ceased on the seventh day" are the same thing, says, *Just as if some unskilled craftsman, now exhausted, had need of a holiday for rest.* For he does not know what that Sabbath day is which is to follow after the six days of the world's founding; in which all who have perfected their works in those six days, and have omitted nothing of those things which pertained to their duty, shall keep holiday with God, ascending to the contemplations and the assembly of the righteous and blessed. Then, as if either the Scriptures said, or we their interpreters, that God rested because he was weary, Celsus denies that *it is lawful for the first God to be weary, or to work with his hands—*

<column-break/>

—"It is even more foolish to distribute certain days to the making of the world before there were days; for when the heavens had not yet been made, nor the earth yet fixed, nor the sun <margin>*</margin> yet carried in this way, <margin>* yet.</note> how were there days? And how do these things differ from those taken from above? Let us consider how it would not be unsuitable for God, the first and greatest, to command, 'Let this be,' and another 'this and that'; and on one day let so much be completed, and on the next again so much more, and on the third, and fourth, and fifth, and sixth." But one can speak with power also regarding the "Commanding, Let this be, and another this and that"; when we cited the passage, <margin>Psa. 32:9.</margin> *He spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created*; saying that the immediate Creator is the Son of God, the Word, and as it were the actual worker of the world, but the Father of the Word, by having commanded his own Son the Word to make the world, is primarily the Creator. And concerning the light being made on one day, and on the second the firmament, and on the third the waters under the heaven being gathered into their gatherings, and thus the earth having sprouted those things governed by nature alone, and on the fourth the luminaries and stars, and on the fifth the swimming things, and on the sixth the land animals and man; we have spoken according to our ability in the treatises on Genesis; and in the earlier parts, having brought a charge against those who, according to the more superficial interpretation, say that periods of six days passed for the making of the world, we cited the passage, *This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it was made; in the day that God made the heaven and the earth.* Then again, not having understood the passage, *And God finished on the sixth day* his works which he made, and he rested on the seventh day from all his works which he made, and God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God began to make; and having thought that "He rested on the seventh day" and "He took repose on the seventh day" were the same, he says, and this indeed "just like some utterly clumsy craftsman <margin>*</margin> having become exhausted, and needing a rest <margin>* of idleness.</margin> from idleness." For he does not know what the day of the Sabbath and of the rest of God is, which follows after the world has existed for six days, in which those who have done all their works in the six days shall feast together with God, and because of having left out nothing of their duties, ascending to the contemplation and the assembly of the righteous and blessed therein. Then, as if either the scriptures spoke thus, or we ourselves interpreted thus concerning God, that having become weary he rested, he says, "that it is not lawful for the first God to be weary, nor to work with his hands—"

You might ask whether this applies to being in any body whatsoever, or specifically in an earthly one, or perhaps one slightly better. If you understand ‘working with hands’ <note>Greek: *cheirourgein*, literally "hand-working" or surgery/manual labor</note> in a literal sense, then neither does the second God <note>A reference to the Logos/Son in Origen's terminology</note> do so, nor any other of the divine beings. <margin>Psalm 19:1</margin>
<margin>Psalm 102:25</margin>
And if in these passages things are spoken of in a similar way—we speaking figuratively of the hands and members of God—what would be absurd about God ‘working with his hands’? Just as it was not absurd for God to work with his hands in this way, so it is not absurd for him to command, so that the things commanded by him are accomplished as beautiful and praiseworthy acts for the God who is to be worshiped by the one who received the command. Again, Celsus (perhaps having heard the saying, *For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things*,
<margin>Isaiah 1:20</margin>

<margin>Aristotle, On the Soul, Book 2, Ch. 8</margin>
But the so-called voice of God is said to be *seen* by the people in the passage: *All the people saw the voice of God*; where ‘seeing’ is taken (to use the custom of the Scripture) spiritually.
<margin>Exodus 20:18</margin>
But Celsus says, “nor is there anything else in God of the things we know.” He does not clarify what things ‘we know.’ For if he means members, we agree with him, asserting that God does not possess in a bodily way what are commonly named as such. But if we should understand ‘the things we know’ universally, we know many things [attributed to Him]: for He possesses virtue, and blessedness, and divinity. But if one understands ‘the things we know’ in a higher sense (since everything we know is less than God), it is not absurd for us to admit that nothing of what we know belongs to God; for He is better than all things, not only those which human nature can provide, but also those of every nature that transcends it,
<margin>\* equal.</margin>
namely the things fitting for God. \* If he had read the words of the prophets, such as the saying in David, *But you are the same*;
<margin>Psalm 102:27</margin>

<margin>Malachi 3:6</margin>
he would have seen that none of us says there are changes in God, either in deed or in thought. For while remaining the same, he administers changeable things according to their nature, and by his Word <note>original: *Logos*</note>
<margin>\* sacred.</margin>
he chooses to administer them.

<column-break/>

*to work, or to command.* Celsus therefore says, *it is not fitting for the first God to labor:* to which we respond, that neither the Word of God is exhausted, nor those who belong to a better and more divine order; for to be exhausted belongs to those living in a body: and it is asked whether this applies to any body at all, or only to an earthly one, or one slightly more excellent. *But neither is it lawful for the first God to work with his hands.* Indeed, if you take this word literally, neither the second, nor any divine nature does so. But suppose "working with hands" is said improperly or figuratively: just as one interprets that: *The firmament announces the works of your hands;* and, *The heavens are the works of your hands;* and if anything is said in the same manner, when we figuratively explain the hands and members of God, what absurdity do we preach about God, calling them the works of his hands? And just as it is not absurd for God to have worked with hands, if understood correctly: so neither is it to command; since his commands are honorable and praiseworthy, and most worthy of God. But Celsus again (*not understanding that passage of Scripture, The mouth of the Lord has spoken these things, or taking it according to a common sense, nor knowing that the names of bodily members are used for the powers of God*) says, *Neither has he a mouth, nor a voice.* It is true that he has no voice, if a voice is struck air, or a striking of the air, or a form of air, or however those whose profession this is define a voice: but what is called the voice of God, is read as *the voice of God seen* by the people, where the Scripture says, *All the people saw the voice of God:* in which place even *to see* (according to the custom of the sacred letters) is understood spiritually. *Indeed, he says, nor is there anything else in him of these things which you attribute to him;* yet he does not explain what we attribute to him. If he speaks of members; we do not understand them corporally; but by accepting them according to common custom more broadly: but if he said in general whatever we attribute to him, those things are many, virtue, happiness, divinity. But if what he said is to be understood more sublimely (since all things we attribute to him are less than his dignity) we confess that none of those things are present in him which we recognize: for what is in him surpasses all knowledge, not only human, but also that of more excellent natures. If Celsus had read the sayings of the Prophets, such as that of David, *But you are the same:* and in Malachi, *I am the same, and I am not changed:* he would have seen that none of us preach any changes concerning God, either of thoughts or of works; for remaining immutable himself, he disposes changeable things according to their nature and that of his word...

Now, the discourse concerning "essence" <note>original: *ousia* (οὐσία); a central philosophical term meaning being, substance, or reality</note> is long and difficult to contemplate. This is especially true if one seeks to know whether the "primary essence"—that which is stable and incorporeal—is God, who is beyond essence in dignity and power, communicating essence to those to whom He imparts it according to His own Word and to the Word Himself; or whether He Himself is essence, though He is called invisible by nature in the discourse concerning the Savior which says:
<margin>Colossians 1:15.</margin>

We must also inquire whether we should call the Only-begotten and "firstborn of all creation" the "essence of essences," the "Idea of ideas," and the "Beginning," while His Father and God is beyond all these. Now Celsus says of God "that all things are from Him," though I know not how he releases all things from Him <note>Origen is critiquing Celsus's vague philosophical phrasing</note>; but our Paul 
<margin>Romans 11:36.</margin>
says the same: "From Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things," placing the beginning of the existence of all things in the phrase "from Him," their cohesion in "through Him," and their end in "to Him." For truly, God is from One. But since he [Celsus] says "that He is not even reachable by reason," I distinguish the meaning and say: If he means the reason within us, whether internal thought or spoken word, we too shall say that God is not reachable by reason. But if we understand the passage, "In the beginning was the Word, 
<margin>John 1:1.</margin>
and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and we declare that God is reachable by *this* Word (being grasped by Him alone, and also by whomever He reveals the Father), then we prove Celsus to be speaking falsely when he says, "God is not even reachable by reason." And as for his claim that "He cannot be captured by a name": if he means that nothing in words and meanings can represent the unique qualities of God, what he says is true; for indeed, many qualities are not nameable. For who can distinguish by names the difference in quality between the sweetness of a date and the sweetness of a dried fig? Who can distinguish and represent the specific quality of each by a name? It is no wonder, then, if God is "unnameable" in this way. But if you take "nameable" to mean that it is possible to represent something about Him with names in order to guide the listener by the hand <note>A metaphor for introductory teaching</note> and make them understand things about God, according to what is attainable by human nature, then it is not absurd to say He is "nameable." In this way we also distinguish his statement, "nothing has happened to Him that is graspable by a name." For it is true that God is outside of all passion <note>In the sense of being "impassible" or unaffected by external change</note>. So much for these matters; let us see his next passage, in which he, as it were, creates a character who, after hearing these things...

<column-break/>

...rather than participating; and is participated in by those having the Spirit of God. And our Savior is not a participant in justice; but, since he himself is justice, he is participated in by the just. Furthermore, the inquiry concerning essence is difficult and long, especially concerning that which is proper, firm, and incorporeal: so that it may be found whether God, superior to all essence, through power and administration communicates essence to those to whom he communicates according to his word, and to the word itself; or whether he himself is essence, although by nature he is called invisible, where the Scripture says of the Savior, *Who is the image of the invisible God*, that is, of the incorporeal. It must also be asked whether the only-begotten and firstborn of every creature should be called the essence of essences, and the idea of ideas, and the principle, but his Father and God superior to all. Celsus indeed says of God, *that all things are from him*, I know not how releasing all things from him: but our Paul says, *from him, and through him, and in him are all things*, showing the principle of the substance of all things by these words *From him*, the preservation by these *Through him*, the end by these *In him*. But God himself has essence from nowhere else than from himself. Moreover, since he says, *him to be neither comprehensible by reason*: I distinguish the meaning, and say, If it be understood of the reason which is either implanted in us, or exerts itself from us, by this God is not comprehensible. But if of that which was in the beginning, and was with God, and was itself God, we say here God is comprehensible (not known by the word alone, but to whomsoever he shall have revealed the Father) therefore we shall prove to be false what Celsus affirms, *that he is by no means comprehensible*. Furthermore, as to his thinking him *innominable* <note>unnameable</note>, there is need of a distinction. For if he wants this, that in the meanings of words nothing can express the properties of God, it is true: since many qualities are not nameable. For who can discern by names the quality of the sweetness of a small palm-fruit, and the sweetness of a dried fig? Who could distinguish the proper qualities of individual things by names? It is no wonder therefore, if in this way God is innominable. But if "nominable" be taken insofar as he can lead the hearer by the hand with names to some knowledge of God, as much as it is permitted to human nature to comprehend, it would not be absurdly called nominable. Similarly we distinguish also what he says, *that nothing happens to God comprehensible by a name*: and we confess him to be outside all affections. Certainly, Christians in no way think themselves blinded by the impious speeches of Celsus or others. But let those who feel themselves blinded, attacked by the examples of the common crowd and the customs of men worshipping demons in their celebrations, approach the Word that bestows eyes: so that, just as formerly the blind, begging on the ground by the way, obtained health from Jesus, having obtained mercy because they implored the merciful Son of David; so also they themselves may receive new and good eyes, such as it is fitting to be created by the Word of God. Whoever has contemplated these things is able to say, *We have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the father: full of grace and truth* <margin>John 1:14</margin>. Celsus, therefore, in a manner not very philosophical, has invented what he thought we would answer to his questions—namely, how we believe we shall come to know God, and how we shall obtain salvation through him. We, however, would answer nothing other than what I have already said. But Celsus, like a "good guesser," fashions such a response for us: *Since God is great and difficult to behold, he therefore sent his own spirit into a body similar to ours and dispatched him here, so that from him we might be able to hear and learn.* According to our doctrine, however, it is not only the God and Father of all things who is great; for he shared his greatness with the only-begotten and first-born of all creation <margin>Colossians 1:15</margin>; so that, since he is the image of the invisible God, he might also reflect the image of the Father in his greatness. Otherwise, the image of that invisible God would not have had a beautiful (so to speak) proportion, unless greatness was also added to it. Furthermore, according to our opinion, since God is incorporeal <term>incorporeal: lacking a physical body</term>, he is invisible; yet he is seen by men who are contemplative in heart—that is, in mind. But he is seen by a heart that is not common, but pure; for it is a sacrilege for a polluted heart to gaze upon God; rather, it must be pure to be held worthy of the contemplation of the Pure One. We also admit that God is difficult to behold; but not he alone, rather his only-begotten as well. For God the Word <note>original: "Deus verbum" / "Theos Logos"</note> is difficult to behold, as is the Wisdom through which God created all things <margin>John 1:3</margin>: for who is able to consider that Wisdom through each individual work of the Creator? Therefore, it was not because God was difficult to behold that he sent the Son as if he were easy to behold. Celsus, not understanding this, spoke as if on our behalf: *Since he himself was difficult to behold, he therefore sent his own spirit here, inserted into a body similar to ours, so that from him we might be able to hear and learn.* But, as we have shown, even the Son (since he was difficult to behold, as the Word of God through whom all things were made) lived among us.
