When it is said of God, *Our God is a consuming fire*, all such things are spoken figuratively <note>original: τροπικῶς (tropikōs) - meaning metaphorically or by way of a "trope"</note> to represent the nature of an intelligible being <note>intelligible: that which can be understood by the mind rather than perceived by the senses</note> through names that are familiar and bodily. And just as,
<margin>1 Corinthians 3:12</margin>
if sins are called *wood*, *hay*, and *stubble*, we do not say that sins are physical bodies; and if noble deeds are called
<margin>Ibid. same verse.</margin>
*gold*, *silver*, and *precious stone*, we will not claim that noble deeds are bodies. In the same way, even if God is said to be a *consuming fire* that burns up the wood, the hay, the stubble, and every substance of sin, we shall not understand Him to be a body. Just as we do not think of Him as a body when He is called fire, so also when God is called *Spirit*, we do not say that He is a body. For the Scripture is accustomed to name intelligible things "spirits" and "spiritual" in order to distinguish them from things perceived by the senses. For example, when Paul says, *But our sufficiency is from
<margin>2 Corinthians 3:5, 6</margin>
God, who also made us sufficient ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the spirit*; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. By "letter," he named the sensory interpretation of the divine writings, but by "spirit," the intellectual interpretation. Thus, regarding the phrase *God is Spirit*: since both Samaritans and Jews performed the commands of the law in a bodily and symbolic way,
<margin>John 4:21, 24</margin>
the Savior said to the Samaritan woman that *The hour is coming when neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain* will they worship the Father; *God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth*.
<margin>worshipping, in the same place</margin>
By these words He taught that one must not worship God in the flesh or with fleshly sacrifices, but in spirit. For He Himself would be understood as Spirit in proportion to one's ability to serve Him in spirit and intellectually. Furthermore, one must not worship the Spirit in symbols, but in truth, which came through Jesus Christ after the law was given through Moses. For
<margin>2 Corinthians 3:15, 16, 17</margin>
whenever we turn to the Lord (and the Lord is the Spirit), the veil that lies over the heart is taken away when Moses is read. Because Celsus did not understand these things concerning the Spirit of God (for
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:14</margin>
the natural man <note>original: ψυχικὸς (psychikos) - a person living only on a physical/emotional level without spiritual insight</note> does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot
<margin>* that, in the same place</margin>
know * that which is spiritually discerned), he draws his own conclusions. He imagines that when we say God is Spirit, we differ in no way from the Greek Stoics, who claim that God is a spirit that has permeated all things and contains all things within Himself. For while the oversight and providence of God do reach through all things, it is not like the "spirit" of the Stoics. And while His providence contains all things that are provided for, it does not contain them as a body contains a body, because that which is contained would also be a body; rather, it is as...

<column-break/>

...it is said by him who says, *Our God is a consuming fire*: for all these things are said figuratively, so that through the bodily names familiar to us, that intelligible nature may be indicated. And just as, when sins are said to be wood, hay, or stubble, we do not accept that sins are bodies; and when good works are called gold, silver, or gems, they are not immediately bodies; so when God is called a fire consuming wood, hay, and stubble, and every substance of sin, we do not immediately understand Him to be a body. And just as, whenever He is designated by the name of fire, we do not understand something corporeal; so, while we call Him *spirit*, we nevertheless do not say that He is a body. For to differentiate from sensible things, Scripture is accustomed to call intelligible things *spirits* and *spiritual*: as when Paul says, *But our sufficiency is from God, who made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit; for the letter kills, the spirit gives life*: where he named the letter when we receive the divine writings according to the sense <note>the literal/physical sense</note>, but the spirit when according to the intellect. So as far as God being *spirit* is concerned, since the Samaritans and Jews observed the mandates of the law corporally and according to figures, the Savior said to the Samaritan woman, *The hour comes, when neither in Jerusalem, nor on this mountain, shall they worship my Father: God is spirit, and those who worship him, must worship in spirit and truth*. By which words he taught that God is not to be worshipped carnally, nor cultivated with carnal sacrifices, but in spirit: that He Himself is spirit is also gathered from this, since it is equally valid if one worships Him in spirit and intellectually. Indeed, the spirit is not to be worshipped in figures, but in truth, which shone forth through Jesus Christ after the law was given by the ministry of Moses. For when we have been converted to the Lord (which Lord himself is the spirit) the veil will be taken away, by which the heart is covered when Moses is read. Wherefore Celsus, as one understanding nothing of the spirit of God (*for the natural man does not grasp those things which are of the divine spirit; for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know that they are judged spiritually*) assumes this for himself, dreaming that we, when we say God is spirit, differ in this part not at all from the Stoics of the Greeks, who affirm that God is a spirit who passes through all things, and contains all things in himself. The gaze of God and his providence does indeed penetrate through all things, but not like that spirit of the Stoics: and he contains all things, for which he looks out through his providence; but not corporally...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

-> [Latin and Greek Parallel Columns] <-

temporally encompasses all things, since the body is surrounded by divine power. And so, according to the opinion of the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that held that everything, including God and the soul, was composed of a refined form of matter or "body."</note> (who assert that the primary principles are corporeal and therefore corruptible—so that, unless the absurdity of the thing forbade it, even the supreme God would not be free from the danger of corruption), even the Word of God, reaching down to men and the smallest of things, is nothing other than a corporeal spirit. According to our doctrine, however (which endeavors to show that the rational soul is superior to every corporeal nature, being an invisible and incorporeal substance), God the Word <note>original: "Deus verbum" / "ὁ Θεὸς λόγος" — referring to the Logos or second person of the Trinity.</note> cannot be a body; He through whom all things were founded, who brings it about that all things happen according to reason—not only human affairs, but even the smallest things belonging to the realm of nature. Therefore, as far as we are concerned, the Stoics may have everything consumed by a universal conflagration; but we know that no incorporeal substance is capable of being burned, nor is the soul of man consumed by fires, nor the substance of angels, thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers.

For this reason Celsus, ignorant of spiritual matters, poured out those words in vain: *“If the son of God is a spirit clothed in a human body, then the son of God himself could not be immortal.”* And again, confusing his own discourse as if some of our people denied that God is spirit, yet confessed that the Son of God is spirit, he thinks he proves that *“it is the nature of no spirit to be eternal.”* Just as above, when we said that God is a consuming fire, he denied that there is *“any nature of fire that remains forever,”* not seeing in what way we proclaim God to be a fire, and of what things He is consumptive—namely, of sin and malice. For it is fitting for a good God that, after each of the contestants has declared what kind of man he was in his struggles, He should consume his vices with the fire of punishments.

And again, he assumes for himself things never granted by us: that *“it was necessary for God to breathe again; from which it follows that Jesus could not rise with his body; for God would not have received back the spirit he had given, which was now contaminated by the nature of the body.”* Since these are not our discourses, it would be foolish to defend them as if they were ours. Then, repeating the same things again, as if he had not previously mocked the birth of God from a virgin in many words (to which we have already responded to the best of our ability), he speaks thus: *“But if he wished to emit a spirit from himself, what need was there to breathe it into the womb of a woman? For he could, as one who already knew how to fashion men, have fashioned a body for this one also, so as not to send his own spirit into such great contamination; and in this way, having spoken from the heavens, he would have gained more credit for himself.”*

<column-break/>

by divine power, and that the things contained are encompassed by it. And not even among the Stoics (who say the principles are corporeal, and for this reason make everything corruptible, risking that even the God over all things is corrupted, unless this seemed entirely inconsistent to them) is the Word of God, which descends even to men and the smallest things, anything other than a corporeal spirit. According to us (who try to demonstrate that the rational soul is better than every corporeal nature, and is an invisible and incorporeal essence), God the Word would not be a body, through whom all things came to be, who reaches out so that all things happen through reason, not only as far as men, but even the smallest things considered to be governed by nature. Certainly, then, let the Stoics have their conflagration; but we do not know of an incorporeal essence being burned, nor the soul of man being dissolved into fire, nor the subsistence of angels, or thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers.

Therefore, it has been said in vain by Celsus, as one not knowing the things of the Spirit of God, “that since the spirit from God is that which has come to be in a human body, the Son of God himself would not be immortal.” Then again he muddles the argument for himself, as if some of us did not <margin>* confessed.</margin> confess God to be spirit, but only His Son, and he thinks to answer by saying, “that there is no such nature of spirit as to remain forever.” Just as if, when we say that God is a consuming fire, he said <margin>* as if.</margin> “that there is no such nature of fire as to remain forever.” Not seeing how we say our God is a fire, and of what things He is destructive: that is, of sins and wickedness. For it is fitting for a good God, after each has appeared having contended, and what kind of contender he has become is clear, to consume the wickedness with the fire of punishments.

Then again he takes for himself things not said by us, “that it was necessary for God to have breathed out,” and the consequence that Jesus was not able to rise with the body. For God would not have taken back the spirit He gave, if it were only defiled by the nature of the body. But you seem to be answering our words, as if they were ours, when they are not ours. Then next, repeating himself, after having spoken many times in the preceding parts and mocked the birth of God from a virgin, to which we answered as far as possible, he says, “If he wanted to send down a spirit from himself, why did he need to breathe into the womb of a woman? For he was able, already knowing how to mold men, to mold a body for this one too, and not cast his own spirit into such a defilement; for in this way he would not have been disbelieved, if he had been sown immediately from above.”

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

->**Page 326**<-

And he <note>Celsus, the critic of Christianity</note> said these things because he did not see the pure and virginal birth—free from any corruption—of the body that was to serve for the salvation of men. He thinks that we are setting forth the **Stoic** <note>A school of philosophy that believed God was a physical force pervading all matter</note> doctrine, and—by not maintaining that the divine nature remained forever incorruptible—that it was cast into defilement. He imagines it was polluted either by being in a woman’s body until that very body was formed, or simply by having assumed a body at all. In this, he acts similarly to those who think that the rays of the sun are defiled in mud and foul-smelling bodies, and do not remain pure even there. 

And if, according to Celsus’s hypothesis, the body of Jesus had been fashioned without a birth, those seeing the body would not have believed that it did not come from a birth. For that which is seen does not announce the nature of its origin. For example, if we suppose there were honey not made by bees, no one could tell from tasting or seeing it that it did not come from bees; just as that which *is* from bees does not show its origin to the senses, but experience teaches us that "this is from bees." In the same way, experience teaches that wine comes from the vine; the taste does not report the "from the vine" origin in the same way. Thus, drinking <note>or perceiving</note> the sensible body does not announce the manner of its existence. 

Let this point be taken from the things in the heavens, whose existence and brilliance we perceive by looking at them; yet our senses suggest nothing to us as to whether they are created or uncreated. Indeed, different schools of thought <term>sects/heresies: original Greek 'haireseis'</term> have arisen concerning these things. Even those who say they are created do not agree on *how* they are created; for the senses do not suggest it, and even if reason, by force, finds that they are created, it does not find the manner in which they were made.

Then, in what follows, he repeats what he has already said many times regarding the opinion of **Marcion** <note>A 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament God</note>. In truth, he attacks Marcion, but in some places he has also misunderstood him; it is not necessary for us to meet or refute these points. Then he again brings up the arguments by Marcion and those against him, asking what path he says escapes the accusations, or whether they simply keep silent. And when he wishes the argument to appear sound, he disregards it so that he may accuse Marcion and his followers, clearly saying: "For how shall he be proved to be the Son of God, he who suffered such punishment, unless this had been predicted about him?" 

Then again he plays and (as is his custom) mocks, introducing "two sons of Gods"—one of the Creator, and another the God according to Marcion. He paints a picture of their "single combats" <term>monomachias: hand-to-hand duels</term>, saying they are like the "god-battles" of quails or fathers; or that because of old age they are useless and babbling, doing nothing to one another, but letting their sons fight. To this we shall say what was said above:

<column-break/>

He said these things because he was ignorant of the pure, virginal, and incorrupt birth of the body, by whose service the human race was to be saved. He thinks, according to the opinion of the **Stoics**—ignoring the doctrine of "indifferents"—that the divine nature was sent into contamination and polluted; either because it remained in a woman’s body until the body itself was formed, or by the very fact that it had assumed a body. This is no different than those who think the rays of the Sun are polluted by contact with filth or a corpse, and do not preserve their purity even there. 

But if, according to Celsus’s proposal, Jesus had assumed a body without a birth, those who saw that body would not immediately believe it was made without a birth: for appearance does not indicate nature and origin. For example, suppose some honey did not come from bees; no one would pronounce from the taste or sight of it that it did not originate from bees. Just as that which is made by bees does not declare its beginning by taste, but we learn by experience; so the same experience teaches us that wine arises from the vine, for the taste does not report its origin from the vine. In the same way, therefore, the perceptible body does not indicate the reason for its subsistence. 

What we say is confirmed by the celestial bodies, whose splendor we perceive by sense: yet that sense does not teach us whether they are created or not; for on this point the sects do not agree. Even those who say they are made do not agree on how they are made: for though it may be proved by reasons that they are made, the senses do not teach how they are made. 

And again he repeats the so-often-insisted-upon opinions of Marcion, sometimes reciting them truly, sometimes not even understood; which, because they do not pertain to us, are unworthy of a response. And soon he returns again to Marcion, arguing for and against him, partly condemning him, partly freeing him from blame. And while he wishes to patronize those who say Christ was foretold by the oracles of the Prophets, he openly says: *Who would believe the son of God was afflicted with such punishment, unless it had been predicted by the Prophets?* 

Then in his usual way he mocks, introducing two sons of Gods—one of the Creator, the other of the Marcionites' God—and depicting their "single combats": which he says are like the contests of quails, which being now useless for fighting due to age, no longer rage against each other, but let their sons fight. Here we will sing back to him what he said above: <note>original: "this we shall say to him, 'What old woman...'"</note>

<summary>Origen defends the purity of the Incarnation against Celsus's claims of "divine pollution," using analogies of sunlight and honey to show that physical appearance does not reveal miraculous origins. He also dismisses Celsus's mockery of the theological conflicts between mainstream Christianity and Marcionism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus, specifically addressing Celsus’s mockery of Jesus’s physical appearance. Origen transitions from defending Christian doctrines to defending the person of Christ against claims of ugliness.</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 6.

What old woman, soothing a little child, would not blush to say such things as this man has in the work to which he inscribed the title *The True Word*? <note>original: "Veri sermonis" / "ἀληθεῖ λόγῳ". Celsus’s lost anti-Christian polemic.</note> For when he ought to have contended seriously, he leaves aside earnest matters to play and act the buffoon, thinking he is writing mimes or jests. He fails to see that this is foreign to the purpose of one wishing to lead us away from Christian piety to his own dogmas. If he spoke with gravity, perhaps he would say things more credible; now, because he mocks, plays, and acts the buffoon, we shall say he does this because he has nothing better to offer—otherwise he would not fall into such trifles. After this he says: *"Since a divine spirit was in a body, it ought to have been more outstanding than others in stature, or form, or strength, or voice, or majesty, or eloquence. For it is incredible that one in whom more of divinity resided was in no way more outstanding than others; yet this man was better in nothing; but, as they themselves confess, he was small and deformed and ignoble."* <note>Celsus argues that a god inhabiting a human body should look like a hero or a king, not a common person.</note> From this it is also clear enough that whenever it pleases him to accuse Jesus, he is a believer in our Scriptures <margin>* believing.</margin>—from which he seizes opportunities for accusation offered to him, as he thinks, by citing their testimonies—but where he perceives those same Scriptures to oppose his slanders, he pretends not to know them. We confess it is written concerning the body of Jesus that it was "despicable," although it is not openly recorded that it was "small" and "vile." There is, however, a passage in Isaiah <margin>Isaiah 53:1, 2, 3.</margin> foretelling that he would come without an exceedingly beautiful appearance, nor with excellent beauty: *Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? we have announced in his presence like a little child <margin>* a little child.</margin>, like a root in a parched, thirsty land: he has no form nor beauty: but his form is without honor, and failing above the sons of men.* These things, therefore, Celsus heard because he thought they were in his favor and served for the accusation of Jesus; but he did not likewise hear those things from the forty-fourth Psalm <margin>Psalm 44:4, 5.</margin>, how they say: *Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one, with your glory and your beauty, and bend your bow <margin>* bend your bow.</margin>, prosper and reign.* But suppose he has not read this Prophecy; or having read it, was led astray by bad interpreters and does not think it pertains to Christ: what will he say of the Gospel <margin>Matthew 17:1.</margin>, where, having ascended a high mountain, he was transformed before the disciples and was seen in glory? When also Moses and Elijah <margin>Luke 9:31.</margin> were seen in glory and spoke of his departure to be fulfilled in Jerusalem? Unless perhaps while the Prophet says, *We saw him not having beauty*, and the rest, Celsus agrees that this prophecy is to be referred to Jesus, but—

<column-break/>

[The Greek text mirrors the Latin above, providing the original phrasing for Origen's defense.] ...and soothing a little child, would he not be ashamed to say such things as are in the work entitled *The True Word*? For it was necessary for him to be serious, as if dealing with serious words, but he, having left the facts, plays and acts the buffoon, thinking he is writing mimes or some jokes, not seeing that such a conduct of words is foreign to his purposes, wishing to make us leave Christianity to attend to his dogmas. Which things, if he spoke solemnly, might perhaps be more persuasive; but since he mocks, and plays, and acts the buffoon, we shall say that for lack of solemn words (for if he had them, he would not have fallen away from them) he fell into such nonsense. Next to these things he says, "that since a divine spirit was in a body, it was altogether necessary for him to differ from the rest either in magnitude, or beauty, or strength, or voice, or striking appearance, or persuasiveness. For it is impossible that he to whom something divine was present more than others should differ in nothing from another; but this man differed in nothing from another, but (as they say) was small and unsightly and ignoble." It appears also in these things, that if he wishes to accuse Jesus, as if believing the writings which seem to provide him with grounds for accusation, he will say the things from them. But where the same writings would seem to say the opposite to those things taken for accusation, these he now pretends not to know. It is admittedly written, then, concerning Jesus's body having been unsightly; yet not as it has been set forth as "ignoble," nor is it clearly shown that it was "small." But the wording is thus recorded in Isaiah, prophesying that he would sojourn among the many in no fair form, but in a failing beauty: *Lord, who believed our report? and the arm of the Lord, to whom was it revealed? we announced before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He has no form, nor beauty; but his form is dishonored, and failing beyond the sons of men.* Which things Celsus heard among these, since he thought they were useful to him for accusing Jesus; but no longer those things said in the forty-fourth Psalm, in what way it says: *Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. In your bloom, and in your beauty, and bend [your bow], and prosper, and reign.* But let it be that he has not read the prophecy; or having read it, was persuaded by those misinterpreting it, that it was not prophesied concerning Jesus Christ; what will he say also about the Gospels, in which having gone up into a high mountain he was transformed before the disciples, and was seen in glory? When also Moses and Elijah, appearing in glory, spoke of his departure, which he was about to fulfill in Jerusalem. Or if the prophet says, *We saw him, and he had no form, nor beauty*, and so forth. [And] Celsus accepts this prophecy as referring to Jesus...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

...to be referred [to him], being blind to the meaning of the passage, and not seeing that it is a great proof of the glory of Jesus being the Son of God, that many years before his birth it was prophesied even concerning his appearance. But if another prophet speaks of beauty and comeliness concerning him, he <note>Celsus</note> no longer wishes the prophecy to be referred to Christ. And if indeed it were possible to clearly take from the Gospels that he had no form or beauty, but that his form was without honor and inferior to the sons of men, one might say that they <note>the Evangelists</note> spoke these things to Celsus according to the prophetic word. But according to the Gospel [account], now neither in the Gospels nor by the Apostles is it shown that he had no form or beauty. It is clear that he <note>Celsus</note> is forced by the prophecy to accept the word concerning Christ as true, which is why he proceeds with his accusations against Jesus. And again, he who says: "Since a divine spirit was in a body, it certainly ought to have excelled the rest either in stature, or voice, or strength, or striking appearance, or persuasiveness; how then does the body not have something excellent?" Does he not see that the body, according to what was possible for those seeing it, and for this reason useful, appeared in such a way as it was necessary for each to see it? And it is not <margin>* nature.</margin> surprising that the *nature [of the body], being changeable and alterable by nature, and a matter transformable into all things that the Creator wills, and receptive of every quality by the Craftsman, <margin>Isaiah 53:2</margin> should at one time have a quality according to which it is said, *He had no form nor beauty;* <margin>Matthew 17:6</margin> and at another time a quality so glorious and striking and wonderful, that the spectators fell upon their faces at such great beauty—namely, the three apostles who went up with Jesus. But he will say that these things are fictions, and differ in no way from myths, like the rest of the wonders concerning Jesus. And to this we have already defended ourselves at length in the preceding sections. But the account also has something <margin>* more mystical.</margin> *mystical, declaring that the different forms of Jesus refer to the nature of the Divine Word, which does not appear the same to the many as it does to those who are able to follow him to the high mountain (which we have explained). For to those who are still below and not yet prepared to ascend, the Word has no form or beauty; for to such people his form is without honor, and inferior to the sons of men—the Word being stripped [of glory], figuratively called in these passages the "son of man." For I would say that the words of the philosophers, being "sons of men," appear much more beautiful than the Word of God preached to the many, which even displays the "foolishness <margin>1 Corinthians 1:21</margin> of preaching"; because of the apparent foolishness of the preaching, those who look only at this say:

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a Latin translation of the Greek text provided in the left column, likely from a 16th or 17th-century edition.</note>

...striking about its understanding, nor seeing how much it builds faith concerning Jesus the Son of God, this very fact that so many centuries before his birth he was seen by the prophets as not having beauty: but if another Prophet predicts his form and beauty, he truly denies that to be a prophecy about Christ. Furthermore, if we clearly perceived from the Gospels that he had neither form nor beauty, but was of a more unhappy appearance than the rest of the sons of men; someone might say that Celsus followed the authority of the Evangelists here, not the Prophets: now, since neither the Gospels nor the Apostles signify any such thing as that he lacked appearance or beauty, he is forced to admit that he recognizes the truth of the Prophets, and he does not stop after this from abusing slanders against Jesus. What? That while he said these words, "If indeed a divine spirit was in a human body, it ought to have been more excellent than others in stature, or form, or strength, or voice, or majesty, or eloquence," he did not see his excellence, at least useful to those who can discern it according to their capacity. Nor is it a wonder, that matter by its own nature changeable, alterable, mutable into whatever pleases the founder, and capable of whatever quality its maker wished to add to it, should at one time have such a quality, according to which it is said not to have had form or beauty; at another time so glorious, wonderful, and stupendous, that the spectators fell on their face at such excellent beauty; I mean those three Apostles, who had ascended the mountain together with Jesus. But he will pretend that these are fictions, no better than fables, just like the rest of the miracles reported about Jesus, to which we have already responded copiously. Furthermore, this present history is not without mystery, signifying that the various forms of Jesus refer to the nature of the Word of God, not appearing in the same way to the common people, and to those to whom it is given to climb the mountain, which we look for, with him: for to those who still cling to lower things, not yet ready to ascend, the word has neither form nor beauty, for among such his appearance is despicable, and is placed after human dissertations, since they are called sons of men not without a figure of speech. For we would say that to such people the sermons of philosophers are much more pleasing and seem beautiful, as to the sons of men, judging the preaching of the divine word in a worse place, which those people think has a certain appearance of foolishness; which while they look at it alone, they speak thus with themselves;

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 6.
## V v

We have seen him, *and he had no form nor beauty.* <note>original Latin: "Vidimus eum, & non habebat speciem, nec pulchritudinem." Quoting Isaiah 53:2.</note> But for those who are able to follow him as he ascends the high mountain, he offers himself to be beheld in a divine form. Anyone is sufficient for this spectacle who, like Peter, is fit for the Church to be built upon him through the Word <note>The "Word" here refers to the *Logos* or Christ's divine nature.</note>, having acquired such a disposition that not even the gates of hell prevail against him; being exalted above the gates of death by the grace of the Word itself, so that he may announce all the praises of God in the gates of the daughter of Sion. Or, if there are any who, having been reborn through preaching, are now great-speakers and to be compared with the sons of thunder. <note>A reference to James and John, the Boanerges.</note> But how can it happen to Celsus and those like him—who read Christian writings only with the zeal of infecting them with spite—that they should understand what the variety of Jesus’s forms signifies? I add also the variety of his ages, and of his deeds, whether before his passion or after his resurrection from the dead. Next, Celsus speaks in this manner: *“Furthermore, if God wanted, like Jupiter in the Comedies waking up from a long sleep, to rescue the human race from evils, why did he send this spirit (whom you boast of) into one corner? When he ought to have similarly inspired other bodies, and sent them throughout the whole world. Surely the Comic poet, intending to move the spectators to laughter, makes Jupiter, having been excited from sleep, send Mercury to the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians; but do you not think it a ridiculous fiction that the son of God is sent to the Jews?”* Observe here also the "philosophical gravity" of Celsus, seeking material for laughter from a Comedy, and comparing our God, the creator of all things, to his Jupiter waking up and sending Mercury. Regarding this matter, we have already said before that God did not send Jesus to the human race as if waking from a long sleep; for though he has only now, for just reasons, undertaken the dispensation of the incarnation, he has nevertheless always been beneficent toward men. For nothing good has ever been performed among men unless the Word of God was present in their souls, for however small a time they were capable of his energy. Moreover, the coming of Jesus into one corner (as it seems) was not without reason: since it was necessary that he who had been foretold through the Prophets should come to those who had learned of one God, and who read His Prophets and the proclamations concerning Christ; especially at that time when he was to be made known from one corner to the whole inhabited world. Therefore, there was no need for many bodies to be created everywhere, nor many spirits like Jesus, to illuminate the world inhabited by men with the Word of God: for the one Word was enough, rising like the Sun of Righteousness—

<column-break/>

<margin>Isaiah 53:2</margin>
We have seen him, and he had no form nor beauty. <note>The right column provides the original Greek text of the same passage translated in the left column.</note> However, to those able to follow him as he ascends the high mountain, he is seen to have a more divine form, if one is a "Peter" (having room for the building of the church upon him by the Word) and having acquired such a habit that no gate of Hades prevails over him; having been exalted through the Word from the gates of death, so that he may declare all the praises of God in the gates of the daughter of Sion; or if there are some who take their origin from the Word, being "great-voiced" ones, such as the sons of thunder. But from where could Celsus, and the enemies of the divine oracles who do not examine the things of Christianity with a love of truth, know the purpose of the different forms of Jesus? And I say also of his ages, and of the things done concerning his suffering, and those after his rising from the dead. Next, Celsus says something like this: “Furthermore, if God wanted, like the Zeus in the comedy, waking up from a long sleep, to rescue the race of men from evils, why ever did he send this spirit (which you mention) into one corner? He ought to have breathed into many bodies similarly, and sent them over all the inhabited world. But the comic poet, making fun in the theater, wrote that Zeus, having been awakened, sent Hermes to the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians; but do you not think it has been made ridiculous <note>original Greek: *katagelaston*</note> that the son of God is sent to the Jews?” See then even in these things the "wit" of Celsus, unphilosophically taking up a comic poet who makes laughter, and comparing our God, the creator of all things, to the one who wakes up and sends Hermes. Let it be said in the things before these, that not as if starting up from a long sleep did God send Jesus to the race of men—he who has now been allotted the dispensation in bodies for reasonable causes, but has always benefited the race of men. For none of the beautiful things among men has happened without the divine Word visiting the souls of those who were able, even for a short time, to receive such energies of the divine Word. But even the seeming visit of Jesus to one corner happened reasonably; since it was necessary for him who was prophesied to visit those who had learned of one God, and who read his prophets and learn of the Christ being heralded, and to visit at a time when he was about to be poured out from there, from one corner, over all the inhabited world. Therefore also there was no need for many bodies to come into existence everywhere, and many spirits analogous to Jesus, so that the whole inhabited world of men might be enlightened by the Word of God. For the one Word was sufficient, rising as the Sun of Righteousness <note>original Greek: *dikaiosynēs hēlios*</note>—

<margin>Matthew 16:18</margin>
<margin>Psalm 9:14</margin>
<margin>Mark 3:17</margin>
<margin>* ridiculous.</margin>
<margin>Malachi 4:2</margin>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.

<margin>John 1:12</margin> ...from Judea, to send out rays to illuminate the soul of anyone willing to receive him. But if anyone desires to see many bodies filled with the divine spirit, ministering—in a manner analogous to that one Christ—to the salvation of all men everywhere, let him consider those who, in every place, teach the word of Jesus with a healthy and upright life. These are themselves called "Christs" <note>original: Χριστοὺς (Christous), meaning "anointed ones"</note> by the divine Scriptures <margin>1 Chronicles 16:22; Psalm 104:15</margin> in the passage: *Touch not my Christs, and do my prophets no harm.* For just as we have heard that Antichrist is coming, and nonetheless <margin>* less</margin> have learned that there are many Antichrists in the world; in the same way, having recognized that Christ <margin>John 2:18</margin> has come among us, we see that through him many "Christs" have come into being in the world—those who, in imitation of him, have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. For this reason, God—the God of Christ—has anointed them also with the oil of gladness. But because He loved righteousness and hated lawlessness more than his companions, He <margin>Hebrews 1:9</margin> received the first-fruits of the anointing and (if one may put it this way) the entire anointing of the oil of gladness. His companions, however, each <margin>* participates</margin> shared in his anointing according to their capacity. Therefore, since Christ is the head of the Church, so that Christ and the Church are considered as one body, <margin>Colossians 1:18; Psalm 132:2</margin> the ointment descending from the head onto the beard—the symbol of the perfect man, Aaron—reached even to the hem of his garment. These things I have said in response to the absurd remark of Celsus, who said: "He ought to have breathed into many bodies in a similar way and sent them across the whole inhabited world." Now, the comic poet <note>Likely a reference to Homer or a dramatist</note> created a most ridiculous Zeus, sleeping and then waking up and sending Hermes to the Greeks; but our doctrine, showing that the nature of God is sleepless, teaches us that God governs the affairs of the world according to the seasons, as reason requires. It is no wonder if—because the judgments of God are great and <margin>Wisdom 17:1</margin> difficult to explain—uneducated souls are led astray, and Celsus along with them. Furthermore, it is not a matter for laughter that the Son of God was sent to the Jews, among whom the prophets lived; so that starting from there in bodily form, he might rise with power and spirit in the souls of the inhabited world that no longer wished to be a desert void of God. Following this, Celsus thought it well to list certain "divine nations." First are the Chaldeans, from whom the deceptive art of astrology <term>genethlialogy: the casting of nativities or birth charts</term> was distributed to men. But Celsus also ranks the Magi among these nations, from whom the magic named after their tribe has traveled to the rest of the nations, to the corruption and ruin of those who use it. And the Egyptians, although in the earlier parts...

<column-break/>

...arisen from Judea, sending rays into the souls of those willing to receive him. But if anyone desires to see many bodies filled with the divine spirit, and, just like that unique Christ, ministering to the salvation of men living everywhere; let him consider those who everywhere shine before men with an upright life and the sound doctrine of Jesus, being themselves called "Christs" in the divine writings, where it is read: *Touch not my Christs, and do no malice to my prophets.* For just as we have heard that Antichrist comes, and nonetheless have learned that there are many Antichrists in the world: in the same way, acknowledging the advent of Christ, we behold many made "Christs" <note>The Latin text here uses "christianos" (Christians), while the Greek uses "Christous" (Christs/Anointed ones)</note> through him in the world, who according to his likeness have loved justice and hated iniquity; wherefore *God, I say the God of Christ, has anointed them with the oil of exultation.* But Christ, because he loved justice above his companions, and truly held iniquity in hatred, received both the first-fruits of this unction and (so to speak) the whole unction of this oil of exultation. However, his companions attained as much of his unction as each was able to hold: for which reason, since Christ is the head of the Church, so that Christ and the Church are reckoned as one body, the ointment of the head descends into the beard of Aaron, which is the mark of the perfect man, and by descending reaches even to the edge of the garment. And let these things be said to the unseemly joke of Celsus, *That he ought to have similarly inspired many bodies, and sent them through the whole world.* Therefore that Comic writer, seeking a laugh, feigned a sleeping Jupiter, and soon after, having awakened, sending Mercury to the Greeks: but our doctrine, which knows the nature of God to be ever-watchful, teaches us that God disposes the things of this world with the highest reason according to the opportunity of the times. It is not to be wondered at, if, since the judgments of God are great and inexpressible, the souls of the unskilled are deceived, and Celsus among the rest. Therefore it is not to be laughed at, that the son of God was sent to the Jews, among whom the Prophets were, so that a beginning having been made from there corporally, he might arise in power and spirit to souls no longer wishing to inhabit a land deserted by God. Next, however, it pleased Celsus to speak of "most divine nations," first of the Chaldeans, by whom the deceptive discipline of the astrologers was propagated among men: then of the Magi, from whom Magic was named, and having set out to other nations brought corruption and destruction into them. The Egyptians also, although he previously taxed their error...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 6.
## V v 2

-> [Latin Translation of the Greek] <-

<column-break/>

Furthermore, Celsus was previously mistaken when he claimed that although the Egyptians have majestic enclosures for their supposed temples, they keep nothing inside except monkeys, crocodiles, goats, asps, or similar beasts; yet now Celsus sees fit to rank the Egyptian nation among the most divine and holy from the beginning—perhaps because they have been the bitterest enemies of the Jews from the beginning. Into this rank of "most divine nations" he also admits the Persians, who practice the union of mothers and daughters, and even the <margin>* Indians.</margin> Indians, some of whom he previously said eat human flesh. Yet the Jews, who for so many centuries never did any such thing, he not only refuses to call divine, but says they will soon perish. He speaks this about them now as if he were a prophet, failing to see how much God once held their Commonwealth in His care, and that through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles; and their fall has brought riches to the world, <margin>Romans 11:25, 26. * until the fullness</margin> * until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, so that afterwards all Israel—whom Celsus does not understand—may attain salvation. 

I do not know how he can claim about God that, *“although He is all-knowing, He was nevertheless ignorant that He was sending His son to wicked men who would kill him through a supreme crime.”* It seems to me he has forgotten what is preached concerning Jesus Christ: that He foreknew by the divine spirit everything He was to suffer, and that all these things had been foretold by the prophecies of the Prophets. From this it follows that it is false *“that God did not know He was sending His son to wicked men who would inflict punishment upon him,”* even though Celsus himself soon says <margin>Luke 24:26, 27.</margin> that we take refuge in the claim that all these things were foretold by the oracles of the ancient seers. 

But, since this sixth book has already grown quite large, we shall begin the seventh, in which we will see what Celsus brings against us regarding our claim that all things concerning Christ were foretold by the Prophets. Because these matters require a more extensive response, and lest we be forced to interrupt the discourse, we wish to end the sixth book here, as it would otherwise exceed a reasonable size.

# ORIGEN
# AGAINST
# CELSUS

->BOOK 7.<-

<margin>
Psalm 54:5 (LXX 53:7). <note>Origen cites the Septuagint numbering; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 54:5.</note>
</margin>
Having contended in six books, holy brother Ambrose, to the best of our ability against the accusations of Celsus against the Christians, and having left nothing, as far as our power allowed, unexamined or uninvestigated, nor having passed over anything to which we have not responded as best we could—calling upon God through Jesus Christ himself, who is the one accused by Celsus, so that the Truth, which he is, might shine in our hearts to the overthrowing of falsehood—we now begin this seventh volume. We say that prophetic word in our prayer to God: *In your truth, destroy them* <note>original: "Ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ σου ἐξολόθρευσον αὐτούς"</note>, meaning clearly those arguments which are contrary to the truth. For when these are destroyed by the truth of God, <margin>* driving away.</margin> and when they are utterly wiped out, all those who have been delivered from * temptation may say what follows that verse: *I will freely sacrifice to you* <note>original: "Ἑκουσίως θύσω σοι"</note>, offering a <term>rational and smokeless sacrifice</term> <note>A "rational sacrifice" (logike thysia) refers to spiritual worship or prayer, contrasted with the "smoke" of animal sacrifices in pagan or Jewish ritual.</note> to the God of all things. <margin>Psalm 54:6 (LXX 53:8).</margin> Celsus, then, intends to accuse those who claim that the Word <note>or "the message"</note> concerning Jesus Christ was foretold by the prophets among the Jews. First, at the very beginning, let us examine his opinion that those who introduce another God <note>A reference to Gnostic groups like the Marcionites who believed the God of the New Testament was different from the God of the Old Testament.</note> besides the God of the Jews are completely unable to meet his objections; while we, who maintain the same God, flee to the defenses regarding Christ found in the prophetic oracles. Regarding this he says: "Let us see, then, what excuse you will bring? Those who introduce another God bring none; but those who hold to the same God will again say that same 'wise' thing: that it was necessary for these things to happen thus; and the proof is that these things were predicted long ago." We shall say to this, that the things said about Jesus and Christians a little before this are so weak that even those who introduce another God—and who represent this impiously—could very easily answer the things said by Celsus. If it were not improper to give an opening to the weaker sort to accept worse doctrines, we ourselves would have done this, in order to prove the falsehood of his claim that those who introduce another God have no defense against what Celsus has said. But now, let us proceed with what was said above concerning the prophets—

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a Latin translation of the Greek text provided in the left column, likely from a later early-modern edition (e.g., Spencer or Delarue).</note>

After a long struggle, in which we have contended in the six preceding books against Celsus, the slanderer of the Christians, as much as we were able, leaving nothing, as far as was permitted, undiscussed; having invoked the divine power through Christ himself, whom Celsus attacks with slanders, so that, since he is the truth, he may shine in our heart for the subversion of falsehood; we now begin the seventh book with that Prophetic prayer, *God, in your truth destroy them*, namely the discourses hostile to the truth: (for these are destroyed through the truth of God,) so that these being destroyed, all those liberated from temptation may say that which soon follows, *I will voluntarily sacrifice to you*, namely a rational and smokeless victim, most pleasing to God the Lord of the universe. It is now the purpose of Celsus to accuse those who say that the prophecies of the Jewish Prophets foretold concerning Jesus Christ. First we inquire into this: that he thinks those who introduce any other besides the God of the Jews are by no means able to respond to his objections; while we, also retaining the same God, in order to defend ourselves, flee to the oracles of the Prophets concerning Christ. His words are these: *“Let us see what they will bring forward for themselves; certainly these, who introduce another God, bring nothing: those who bring the same, will bring forward that wise saying, that it was necessary for these things to happen so; and this argument, that these things were predicted of old by the Prophets.”* To which we respond, that the things which that man brought into the open a little before concerning Jesus and the Christians are so weak, that they could easily be refuted even by the impious sect of those introducing another God; which we ourselves would do in their name, were we not afraid lest the weaker might take an occasion from there of declining toward worse dogmas; so that we might prove the statement of Celsus to be false when he asserts that those who introduce any other God are by no means able to respond to his objections. Therefore, these things being omitted, we shall speak of the Prophets, as we began before, and first to that—

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

He <note>Celsus, the 2nd-century critic of Christianity</note> says that the *Pythian*, *Dodonean*, *Clarian* oracles, those of the *Branchidae* and of *Ammon*, and countless others—by whose instructions colonies were settled across almost all lands—are held as nothing. Yet, he claims the sayings of the *Jews* (whether actually spoken or not, and ambiguous in the manner of that nation, just as those of the *Phoenicians* and *Palestinians* are today) are considered marvelous and most certain. I say, therefore, regarding the oracles just listed, that we could bring forth many arguments from the authority of *Aristotle* and the *Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> that strip away the credibility of the *Pythian* and the rest. We could likewise transcribe from *Epicurus* and his followers what they think of these things, and show that the Greeks themselves value the most celebrated oracles of Greece as nothing. 

But let us suppose that the stories told about the *Pythian* priestess being inspired by a deity, and other seers of that kind, are not human fictions. Let us see whether, if we diligently weigh the truth of the matter, it might be proven that even if these are indeed oracles, it does not necessarily follow that a deity presides over them. Rather, they may be certain evil demons and spirits hostile to the human race, who set themselves against souls striving toward heaven through the path of virtue and true piety, to prevent them from returning to God. 

Certainly, regarding the *Pythian* oracle, than which no other is more famous, it is told that the prophetess of *Apollo* sits over the opening of the *Castalian* cave, and receives the spirit ascending from there through her female womb. Filled with this, she utters those "excellent" and "divine" oracles, as they are thought to be. Consider now whether the impurity of that spirit is not abundantly understood by this very fact: it does not enter the prophetic soul through hidden channels much purer than a woman's womb, but through those parts which an honorable man would not endure to look upon, let alone touch. And this happens not just once or twice (which might perhaps be tolerable), but as often as she is believed to prophesy while inspired by *Phoebus* <note>Another name for Apollo</note>. 

Furthermore, the fact that she is driven out of her mind and maddened as if by magic arts, so that she does not understand what she herself is doing, is not the work of a divine spirit. For it is proper that anyone inspired by a divine power should first be helped, and should feel the divinity within them most clearly at that very time when others are being taught by the oracle what leads to a better life consistent with nature, or what is useful and expedient. We, indeed, gather from the holy Scriptures that the Prophets of the *Jews*, being enlightened

I do not understand how Celsus, after saying, *Moreover, the sayings of the Jews, after the manner of that nation*, added, *or not said*. This is why those who accepted the prophecies in their own time preserved them; so that later generations, by reading them, might marvel at them as the words of God, and be benefited not only by the rebukes and calls to repentance, but also by the predictions. Thus, being educated in piety concerning the divine prophetic spirit, they might continue to practice rational piety, being persuaded by the Law and the Prophets. Now, the prophets spoke whatever was useful to be understood immediately by their hearers and contributed to the correction of morals, without any concealment, according to the will of God. But whatever was more mystical and for higher contemplation, and involved a vision beyond the common hearing, they uttered through riddles and allegories, and what are called "dark sayings," and named parables and proverbs; so that those who are not lovers of labor, but rather those who take up every toil for the sake of virtue and truth, might find them after searching, and having found them, might manage them as reason dictates. But the "noble" Celsus, as if

But then it would have been a great task if he had wished to show that nothing divine was present in those speeches, which recall sinners from their sins and rebuke them, and predict future things: for this reason the authors of the Prophecies handed them down in writings to be preserved for posterity; so that readers might admire them as divine oracles, and profit not only from the rebukes and warnings, but also from the predictions, and, recognizing the divine prophetic spirit from their outcome, might exercise themselves according to the doctrine of piety by obeying the Law and the Prophets. Certainly the Prophets themselves set forth without any wrappings whatever was necessary to be understood immediately by the listeners, and whatever worked toward correcting morals, just as God willed: but whatever was secret, and to be discerned more deeply as being more sublime than the common grasp, they veiled with obscure figures, riddles, allegories, proverbs, and parables; so that it might not be found by the lazy and sluggish, but by the studious searchers for virtue and truth, and once found, might be turned to their own use according to divine doctrine. But this "illustrious" Celsus, as if powerless over his anger because he is unable to understand the Prophetic voices, attacks them with insults, saying *that certain uncertain, frantic, and obscure things are displayed, understood by no wise man; but providing an occasion for fools and jugglers to usurp them for any opinion they please.* It seems to me he spoke craftily, wishing, as much as he could, to keep readers from diligently discussing and examining the meanings of the Prophets: in which he imitates those who, when a certain Prophet had entered to someone to give an oracle, after he left, said: *Why did that madman come to you?* Here perhaps we would need someone wiser than ourselves to prove Celsus a liar by declaring how divine the Prophetic speeches are: nevertheless we also, according to our faculties, have done this, [regarding] *those obscure and (as Celsus calls them) frantic*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

-> [Latin Text] <-

...that these things were not predicted; or that what happened to Jesus occurred differently than had been foretold: and thus he would have inferred what he wished to conclude. For in that way it would be apparent which Prophecies we refer to Jesus, and how vigorously our adversary refutes us; and it would have been established whether he nobly overturns the words of the Prophets, by which we build our faith concerning Jesus, or whether he is caught impudently attempting to corrupt the truth, as if it were not the truth. And because, presupposing certain things that are impossible and unbecoming of God, he says, *If these things had been especially predicted of God, should we, on account of that prediction, believe such things about God?* and he thinks it follows from this that, even if it were certain that the holy seers had foretold these things about the Son of God, they nevertheless should not be believed, since it is impossible for him to suffer or do these things: it must be said that this presupposition is absurd, as it joins together things that are by nature in conflict with one another; which shall be demonstrated thus. If the true Prophets of God, the Lord of all, predicted that he would serve, or be sick, or die, we confess that these things would so happen: for it is necessary that the Prophets of God do not lie. But if these same Prophets prophesy these things about the Supreme God, since those things which are naturally impossible are false, the true foretellings of the Prophets will not happen concerning God. Whenever two joined premises result in things contrary to each other—which is called a theorem from two Prophecies—both antecedents do not stand: as in the present business, while the Prophets of the greatest God predict that he will serve, be sick, or die. From which it is gathered that the Prophets by no means predicted that the Supreme God would ever undergo servitude, or be affected by disease, or finally meet death. For thus we reason: If the first, then also the second; but if not the first, neither the second: Therefore, not even the first. So also the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized logic and ethics.</note> argue about material things, bringing forward this: *If you know you are dead, you are not dead;* soon it follows, *Therefore you do not know you are dead:* which connected things they arrange in this manner. If you know you are dead, there is that which you know: Therefore it is that you are dead: and again, If you know you are not dead, and there is that which you know, you are not dead: since, however, a dead man knows [nothing], it clearly follows that, though you know you are dead, you are not dead. It follows, however, as I said, from both reasonings: Therefore you do not know you are dead. Such a thing is also in Celsus’s proposition, which we recited above; although it is different regarding the Prophecies announcing Jesus: for not...

...they foretold; or otherwise, or just as they foretold, the things concerning Christ have been fulfilled; spoken in Jesus; and he would have brought in the things that seemed to him to prove it. But since, placing certain impossible and unbecoming things for God according to a hypothesis, he says, "If these things were prophesied concerning the God over all, then because it is foretold, must one believe such false things about God?" and he thinks to establish that even if the prophets were truly prophesying such things about the God over all, it was impossible for him to suffer or act, and one ought [not] to believe the things prophesied. It must be said, that his hypothesis is absurd, making connections that end in things opposite to one another; which is shown thus. If the true prophets say <margin>they will say</margin> that the God over all will serve, or be always sick, or die, these things will happen concerning God; for it is necessary for the prophets of the great God to speak the truth. But also if the true prophets say these same things about the God over all, since things impossible by nature are not true, even if they should happen concerning God, the things the prophets say are true. But when two connected premises end in things opposite to one another—the theorem called "through two conditionals"—the leading part in both connections is destroyed; which in these matters is: the prophets foretelling that the great God will serve, or be sick, or die. For it is concluded in this: therefore the prophets did [not] foretell that the great God would serve, or be sick, or die. And the argument is led in this way: If the first, then the second; if the first, then the second; therefore not the first. And those from the Porch <note>The Stoics, named after the Stoa Poikile or "Painted Porch" in Athens.</note> bring this mode of matter, saying: If you know that you are dead, you are dead; it follows: therefore you do not know that you are dead. And they establish the connections in this way: If you know that you are dead, there is something you know; therefore it is that you are dead. And again: If you know that you are not dead, and there is something you know, you are not dead. Since a dead man knows [nothing]; clearly if you know that you are dead, you are not dead. And it follows, as I said before, from both connections: therefore you do not know that you are dead. Such a thing is also the hypothesis concerning Celsus, speaking the word we set out before; but upon those things which we have taken up in <margin>hypothesis</margin>... they must [apply] to the prophecies concerning Jesus. ...they foretold that God was to be crucified, when they speak thus of the one assuming death: *We saw him not having form, nor beauty, but his form was without honor above the rest of the sons of men: a man established in a stroke and grief, and knowing how to bear infirmity.* See how openly they name him a "man," who suffered human things. And Jesus himself, well knowing that what was to die was a man, says to his ambushers: *But now you seek to kill me, a man, who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God.* But if there was anything of divinity in this one, whom we understand as a man by himself—that which was the only-begotten of God and the firstborn of every creature, whose words are: *I am the truth, I am the life, I am the door, I am the way, and, I am the living bread, who descended from heaven:* there is another consideration of this and of his essence, separate from that man whom we understand in Jesus. Wherefore not even the simplest Christian, and one unpracticed in more exquisite doctrine, would say that the truth had perished, or the life, or the way, or the living bread, which descended from heaven, or the resurrection: (for he says he is the resurrection, who in the appearance of the man Jesus taught saying: *I am the resurrection.*) nor is any of us so insane as to say, "life is dead," "the resurrection is dead." Such people would be found, however, if the supposition of Celsus had a place—if we confessed that the Prophets had foretold that the Word of God would die, or the truth, or the life, or the resurrection, or any of those things which the Son of God proclaims of himself. Therefore, Celsus has spoken truly in this place only so far as: *That the Prophets would never predict this;* for that would be evil and impious. For what is this, except that the great God would die or serve? Otherwise, what the Prophets predicted are worthy of God: that the splendor of the divine nature and its character would look upon the life of men in the holy human soul of Jesus, so that he might sow the word that would reconcile all to God the Lord of the universe, whoever would receive it into their soul and cultivate it, and perform all things they are able, with the Word of God being present in the body and soul of the man: which happens in such a way, if his rays are not shut up in his body alone, nor is God the Word believed to be a light flashing with such rays nowhere else. Therefore, in as much as the deeds of Jesus are thought of, which the Deity performed in him, they are pious, nor foreign to holy thoughts about God: but in as much as he was a man, adorned above all men by participation in the Word itself...

<summary>Origen distinguishes between Jesus's human nature, which suffered and died as prophesied, and his divine nature (the Logos), which is immortal and cannot die. He refutes Celsus's claim that Christians worship a "dead God" by explaining the theology of the Incarnation.</summary>

In the same manner, one may find many similar things in the Law as well, such as: *We left none of them alive as a survivor* <margin>Numbers 21:35; Deuteronomy 2:34</margin>. He <note>Celsus</note> soon adds that it was foretold to them with a threat that unless they obeyed the Law, they would be treated in the same way as enemies, just as they were accustomed to treating their own enemies. But, before we hear Celsus proceeding to compare among themselves whatever he thinks he has found in the institutions of Christ that are contrary to the Mosaic Law, we must respond to what has already been proposed. We say, therefore, that the Law is twofold: namely, one according to the letter, and the other according to the understanding <note>original: "intellectum" / "dianoian"; referring to the spiritual or allegorical meaning</note>, just as our ancestors taught. Now, that which is according to the letter, not so much we, but God through a certain Prophet calls "justice that is not good" and *precepts that are not good* <margin>Ezekiel 20:25</margin>; but that which is understood according to the spirit is called by the same Prophet, speaking in the person of God, both *good justice* and *right mandates* <margin>Ezekiel 20:21</margin>. For the Prophet does not say openly contrary things about the same matter. Following him, our Paul pronounced that *the letter kills* <margin>2 Corinthians 3:6</margin>; which is the same as if he had said the literal words kill. But *the spirit*, he says, *gives life*, which is equivalent to writing that we attain life through their spiritual understanding. Therefore, it is possible to find even in Paul, as in the Prophets, certain things that appear contrary. For just as Ezekiel says in one place, *I gave them justifications that were not good, in which they shall not live*; and elsewhere, *I gave them good justifications and good precepts, in which they shall live*; or certainly to this effect: so also Paul, in one place wishing to accuse the literal law, says, *But if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is passing away: how shall the ministry of the spirit not be more in glory?* <margin>2 Corinthians 3:7, 8</margin> Yet elsewhere, praising and looking up to the Law, he calls it spiritual in these words: *We know that the law is spiritual* <margin>Romans 7:14</margin>; likewise in these: *Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good* <margin>Romans 7:12</margin>. Therefore, when the words of the Law promise riches to the just, Celsus indeed, according to the "killing letter," thinks that these "blind" <note>Celsus likely mocked material wealth as "blind" or base</note> riches are promised; but we understand them as "keen-sighted" riches, by which someone is enriched *in all doctrine and all knowledge* <margin>1 Corinthians 1:5</margin>; in which sense we also command the rich of this world *not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the instability of riches, but in the living God, who kindly provides all things for enjoyment, that they may do good and become rich in good works, and be liberal in sharing—* <margin>1 Timothy 6:17, 18</margin>

We say then that the Law is twofold: one according to the literal word, the other according to the meaning, as those before us also taught. And the one according to the literal word is called—not so much by us as by the oracle of God in one of the prophets—*statutes that were not good, and ordinances that were not good*. But the one according to the meaning is called by the same prophet from the person of God *good statutes and good ordinances*. For the prophet does not say things that are manifestly contrary in the same place. Accordingly, Paul also said that the *letter kills*, which is equal to the literal word; *but the spirit gives life*, which is equivalent to the meaning. It is possible, then, to find in Paul something analogous to the contradictions in the legislation according to the prophet. But if by the name of wisdom Christ is understood, since *Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God*: we say that to such a wise man not only is free access open to the Father, but we also assert that he is far superior to others not adorned with the same grace of the spirit. ...will prepare dust <note>original: χνῆν (chnēn), an archaic word for fine dust or chaff</note>. But neither is that saying, *Do not worry about what you shall eat or what you shall drink; consider the ravens, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them; how much more are you worth than the birds? And why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field,* and so forth—these are not contrary to the blessings in the Law, which teach that the righteous shall be filled. It is also spoken by Solomon in this manner: *The righteous man eats and satisfies his soul, but the souls of the wicked are in want.* For one must see that the "food of the soul" is what is revealed in the blessing of the Law; it is not the composite man <note>the physical body joined with the soul</note> who is filled by this, but the soul alone. From the Gospel, one should perhaps take a deeper meaning, or perhaps a simpler one: that we should not be distracted by anxieties concerning the food and clothing of souls, but practicing frugality, we should trust in God’s providence, provided one cares only for what is necessary. 

Now Celsus, without comparing the apparent contradictions between the Law and the Gospel, quotes the saying: *"To him who strikes you once, offer yourself to be struck again."* But we shall say that we know it was said to those of old, *An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth*; and we have also read, *But I say to you, to him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also.* But since Celsus, I believe, followed those who divide the divinity of the Law from that of the Gospel <note>referring to Gnostic groups like the Marcionites who believed the OT and NT Gods were different</note>, claiming the Law and Gospel are not from the same God, he sets these things down. It must be said in response to his argument that even the ancient writings knew to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes the right cheek. For in the Lamentations of Jeremiah it is written: *It is good for a man when he bears the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has taken it upon himself; he shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he shall be filled with reproaches.* 

The God of the Gospel does not set himself against the God of the Law, not even regarding the literal matter of a blow. Neither lies—not Moses, nor Jesus. Nor did the Father, in sending Jesus, forget what he commanded Moses. Nor did he, condemning his own laws, change his mind and send a messenger with contrary instructions. If it is necessary to speak even briefly about the different "polity" <note>term: πολιτεία (politeia) - a system of government or way of life for a community</note> which the Jews of old followed under Moses, and that which Christians now live according to the teaching of Jesus: we shall say that it was neither fitting for the called Gentiles to live according to the letter of the Mosaic law while being subjects of the Romans; nor was it possible for the ancient Jews to maintain their own Republic...

Consider the lilies present before you,* and what follows, contrary to the favorable prayers in the law, which promise that it will come to pass that the righteous man is satisfied by eating; or to Solomon saying, that *the righteous man by eating fills his soul, but the soul of the impious labors in want.* For it is necessary to notice that the blessing of the law speaks of the food of souls, by which not this composite man is filled, but the soul alone. Furthermore, the Gospel passage perhaps contains something deeper, or perhaps is to be understood simply: that the soul is not to be stretched thin by various anxieties concerning food and dress, but frugality is to be studied with the confidence that God will provide for those who are content with necessities. 

Thus far Celsus has shown nothing in the Gospel contrary to the law: now he brings forward that saying, *To him who has struck you once, offer the bone <note>original: os (mouth/face), likely a Latin variation for cheek</note> again.* We respond, that we know it was said to the ancients, *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth:* and we have read this, *But I say to you, whoever has struck a blow on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.* But, since Celsus had heard those who are accustomed to distinguish the divinity of the Law and the Gospel, he brought these things forward; to whose words I have judged it must be answered thus: that even the Old Testament very well understood that principle, *Whoever has struck a blow on your right cheek, turn to him the other also:* since in the Lamentations of Jeremiah it is written, *It is good for a man when he has carried the yoke from his youth; he shall sit solitary and be silent, because he has lifted it upon himself: he shall offer his cheek to the one striking him, and he shall be saturated with reproaches.* 

The Gospel does not oppose itself to the God who is the author of the law, not even in this saying which pertains to the blow: neither lies, not Moses, not Jesus; nor had the Father, sending Jesus, forgotten what he commanded to Moses; nor, led by repentance, having condemned his own law, did he send the Gospel to teach things contrary to the former commands. But if it must be said in a few words concerning the difference in the manner of living, which the Jews once followed with Moses leading, and this one, toward which Christians now direct their morals with Jesus as teacher: we think that it was not suitable for the calling of the nations to live according to the law of Moses, just as its letter sounds, since they are subject to the Roman Empire; nor could the Jews preserve their own Republic in the same state...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

<margin>Haggai 2:6.</margin>
...those who live alongside the prophets and have lived uprightly, devoting all their time to the examination of the sacred scriptures, will present these matters to those who are fit for them by reason of their purity of life and their love of learning concerning divine things. Our purpose was to show that we have not received our teachings about the holy land from the Greeks or from Plato; rather, they—being younger than we are and having either heard some riddles about such things from the most ancient Moses and most of the prophets, or having encountered the sacred scriptures themselves—distorted them and spoke such things about a better land. Haggai clearly presented the "dry land" as one thing and the "earth" as another, calling this place where we are "dry land"; for he speaks thus: *Yet once more I will shake the heaven, and the earth, and the dry land, and the sea.* <note>original: "Ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὴν ξηρὰν, καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν." In the same way, we also defer the discussion concerning the holy and good land, and the city of God within it—thinking it a madness of the mind to seek the things of that place here—to the place for interpreting the prophets, having explained as much as we were able concerning the city of God in our previously published works on the forty-fifth Psalm and the forty-seventh Psalm. <note>In modern numbering, these are Psalms 46 and 48.</note> You know that the most ancient word of Moses and the prophets calls all true things by the same names as the more general things here; for example, the "true light," and another "heaven" besides the firmament, and another "sun of righteousness" besides the one perceived by the senses. And he says once and for all, in contrast to the things of the senses (of which none is "true"), that *God, his works are true*; <note>original: "Θεὸς ἀληθινὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ."</note> while in other cases the works of God are called the "works of his hands." Rebuking certain people through Isaiah, he says: *They do not look upon the works of the Lord, nor do they consider the works of his hands.* And so much for these matters.
