Those who have modeled their lives on the emulation of the Prophets, always occupied in examining the sacred letters, will explain these things to those fit to hear them through purity of life and study of divine matters. We act now to show that what we believe concerning the holy land was accepted neither from Plato nor from other Greeks; indeed, they, as later in age, borrowed from not only the most ancient Moses but also from other Prophets whatever they transferred into their own commentaries concerning this land, whether poorly understood because of riddles or otherwise corrupted from the Scriptures. Clearly, however, we learn from Haggai that the "dry land" is one thing and the "earth" another, while he calls this in which we live the "dry land": he speaks thus, *Yet once more, and I will shake the heaven and the earth, and the dry land and the seas.* Just as he refers this fable to the author Plato, in whose *Phaedo* it is read, saying, *But what these things signify is not easy for anyone to know: unless one could understand what it is that he says; that because of weakness and slowness they cannot penetrate to the furthest air; and, if only their nature were equal to such contemplation, they could know that this is the true heaven and the true light:* so also we, because we do not think it the present purpose to treat the holy and good land, will defer this labor to another time, in which we shall explain the Prophets; although we have already treated in some part the city of God in the explanation of the forty-fifth and forty-seventh Psalms. Moreover, the most ancient scripture of Moses and the Prophets knows all these true things, which are judged by the same name as the things used among us: such as the true light, and a heaven other than this firmament, and a Sun of justice other than this sensible one: and universally, in distinction from these sensible things, of which none is true, that was said, *God, true are your works;* the Prophet calling some things the works of God, others (namely the lesser) the works of his hands: whence through Isaiah he rebukes certain ones who *do not behold the works of God, nor consider the works of his hands.* And concerning these things, thus far. But since Celsus, not understanding the long and difficult sermon on the resurrection (which no less than any doctrine has need of an advanced and wise teacher, who may commend both the dignity of God and the magnitude of the doctrine, showing this "tent" of the soul, as Scripture calls it, to be like a seed, in which the righteous groan, not wishing to put it off, but to be clothed over), he mocks what he heard from the unskilled.

<summary>Origen argues that Christian concepts of a spiritual "holy land" predate Plato and are rooted in Hebrew prophecy, specifically distinguishing between the physical "dry land" and the spiritual "earth." He also begins to address Celsus's mockery of the resurrection, noting that Celsus misunderstood a complex doctrine by listening to uneducated believers.</summary>

# Book 7. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Because some are unable to give a rational account of it, he <note>Celsus, the 2nd-century critic of Christianity</note> mocks the whole matter. One thing must be added to what was said above: Celsus is mistaken in thinking that we understand the name of "resurrection" as the migration of souls from bodies into other bodies according to the opinion of the Greeks <note>original: *migrationem animarum ex corporibus in corpora juxta Græcorum opinionem*—referring to metempsychosis or reincarnation</note>. Rather, we know that the soul, being by its own nature incorporeal and invisible, requires a body suited to the nature of the place in which it happens to dwell. Sometimes it wears a body after setting aside a previous one—which was necessary for a time, but has become superfluous for what follows. At other times, it puts on a new covering over the previous one, needing a better garment for the higher, ethereal, and heavenly regions. Indeed, when about to be born, it received a body fit for inhabiting the womb for a certain time, and again what was necessary for one living on the earth. 

Next, since it is established that there is an earthly tabernacle <note>term: *tabernaculum*—a "tent" or temporary dwelling, used biblically to describe the mortal body</note> and a dwelling necessary for it, the Scripture says it is destroyed, and that the tabernacle shall put on a *house not made with hands* <margin>2 Cor. 5:1</margin> by the power of God. This corruptible nature shall put on incorruption (which differs from the "incorruptible" itself), and this mortal nature shall put on immortality (which likewise differs from the "immortal"). For just as wisdom is related to the wise person, justice to the just person, and peace to the peaceful person, so is incorruption related to the incorruptible, and immortality to the immortal. See where the Scripture invites us, saying, *Put on incorruption and immortality* <margin>1 Cor. 15:43</margin>. While these things serve as a garment, they do not allow the one clothed in and retaining such garments to be corrupted or to die. 

I have been emboldened to set these things forth by the ignorance of that man <note>Celsus</note>, who does not understand what is meant by the resurrection, and therefore mocks and cavils at what he does not comprehend. Thinking that we assert the resurrection merely so that we might know and see God, he gathers whatever arguments he wishes and speaks thus: *“Certainly, though refuted in every way and convicted, they return again to the same question as if they had heard nothing: ‘How then can we know and see God? How can we go to Him?’”* Let whoever wishes know, therefore, that even if we have need of a body for some purposes—because we inhabit a physical place in a physical way, and require a body suited to the nature of that place—and though we may be clothed in the aforementioned tabernacle, yet for the knowledge of God we have no need of a body at all. For that which knows God is not the eye of the body, but

<column-break/>

the mind, which sees according to the image of the Creator <note>original: *mens videns, facta ad conditoris imaginem*</note>. 

<margin>* in that place.</margin>
<margin>2 Cor. 5:1</margin>
<margin>1 Cor. 15:43</margin>
<margin>* which he does not know.</margin>
<margin>* physical.</margin>

<margin>Matthew 15:19; 6:23; 5:8.</margin>
...they have acquired, having received the power to know God through the wisdom of God. And that which sees God is a "pure heart," from which there no longer come forth evil thoughts, nor murders, nor adulteries, nor fornications, nor thefts, nor false witness, nor blasphemies, nor an "evil eye," nor any other improper thing. Because of these things it is said, *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* <note>Matthew 5:8</note> But since our own will is not sufficient to keep the heart entirely pure, we have need of God, who creates it as such; therefore it is said by one who prays with knowledge, *Create in me a clean heart, O God.* <note>Psalm 51:10</note> But even if God were in a place, as in a figure, toward whom we were somehow intended to go, how should we go to Him? For God is better than any place, and He contains all things; and there is nothing that contains God. Therefore, we are not commanded to go to God in a bodily sense, as in the command: *You shall walk after the Lord your God;* <note>Deuteronomy 13:4</note> nor did the Prophet, when clinging to God, speak in a bodily sense in his prayer when he said, *My soul has clung behind you.* <note>Psalm 63:8</note> Celsus, therefore, lies against us when he says: **"They say that we shall see God with the eyes of the body, and hear His voice with our ears, and touch Him with sensible hands."** For we know of eyes mentioned by the divine words that are named the same as the eyes of the body, and likewise ears, and hands, and (what is more remarkable than these) a "divine sense," <note>original: αἴσθησιν θειοτέραν / sensum diviniorem</note> which is different from that commonly named by the many. For when the Prophet says, *Open my eyes, and I will perceive the wonders of your law;* or, *The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes;* or, *Lighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;* there is no one of sound mind who thinks that the eyes of the body perceive the wonders of the divine law, or that the commandment of the Lord enlightens the physical eyes, or that the sleep of death always happens to the eyes of the body. Furthermore, when our Savior says, *He who has ears to hear, let him hear;* even a common person understands that these things are said concerning more divine ears. And if it is said that the *Word of the Lord came in the hand of Jeremiah* the prophet, or of some other; or the *law in the hand of Moses;* or that *With my hands I sought God, and was not deceived;* there is no one so foolish as not to understand that certain hands are called so figuratively, <note>original: τροπικῶς / figuratè</note> about which John also says, *Our hands have handled the Word of life.* And if you wish to learn from the Holy Scriptures about that better and non-bodily sense, hear Solomon saying in the Proverbs, *You shall find a divine sense.* <note>Proverbs 2:5. # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Celsus sends us to the oracles of Trophonius, Amphiaraus, and Mopsus <note>These were famous Greek "hero-oracles" where seekers would sleep in shrines to receive dreams.</note>: where he says, *that Gods are seen in human form, and that not as a deception, but clearly and conspicuously manifest*. For we know that these are actually demons, who feed on the blood and the stench exhaling from victims, and are held captive in those prisons which they have obtained through their own lusts. The Greeks consider these to be temples of the Gods, but we have found them to be the dwellings of deceptive demons. After this, Celsus speaks maliciously regarding the aforementioned "gods" who offer themselves in human form, *claiming that they do not merely fly past once, like the deceiver of these Christians; but are always familiarly present with anyone who seeks a conversation with them*. By these words, he seems to signify that he regards Jesus as a ghost <note>original: "spectrum" / "φάσμα" (phasma)</note>, seen by the disciples after the resurrection as if snatched away from their eyes in a swift flight. Furthermore, regarding those Gods to whom he attributes human form, he says they do not deny the abundance of their conversation to anyone who desires it. But could a "ghost" (as that man thinks), flying past to deceive men, work so effectively even after this illusion of the eyes, and convert the souls of such people, persuading them to do all things according to the pleasure of God, as if they were to give an account in judgment? How does a so-called "ghost" drive out demons and perform other virtues that are not to be despised? He is not allotted to one single place, like those gods in human form he describes, but passes through the whole inhabited world, gathering and drawing by his divine power as many as he finds inclined toward living well. After these things, to which we have responded as much as we were able, Celsus speaks again as follows: *They will ask again, "How shall God be known, unless he be perceived by the senses? Who can know him without the senses?"* and soon, responding to this, he says: *This is the voice not of a man, nor of a soul, but of the flesh. Yet let them listen if they are able to hear anything. O timid lovers of the body, if you would look upward with the mind, closing your eyes to the senses, and awakening the eye of the mind by turning away the eye of the flesh; only then will you see God. And if you seek a leader for this path, you must flee the impostors and sorcerers who recommend ghosts to you—lest you be ridiculous in every way, slandering the other gods as idols, while you yourselves worship one who is truly more wretched than idols, and not even an idol, but a dead man, and seeking a Father who is like him.* First, as it pertains to his Personification <term>Prosopopœia: a rhetorical device where a speaker provides a voice to an absent person or an imaginary character</term>, in which he fashions speeches for us...

<column-break/>

Celsus sends us to Trophonius, and to Amphiaraus, and to Mopsus; where he says that gods are seen in human form, and (as Celsus says) not as false gifts, but as manifest beings. For we know these are demons, nourished by the steam and blood and the vapors from sacrifices, and dwelling in the prisons prepared by their own desires; which the Greeks have considered temples of gods, but we know that such dwellings belong to deceptive demons. After this, Celsus says maliciously about the aforementioned gods who appear in human form according to him, "that it is not just once that one sees him slipping away, like the one who deceived these people; but they are always conversing with those who wish." And it seems through these words he has already considered Jesus a ghost, seen by the disciples after the resurrection from the dead, as if he had slipped away from them after being seen. Then he named them, saying "gods in human form," and thinks these "always converse with those who wish." But how could a ghost, as he says, slipping away to deceive those who saw it, work such great things after that vision, and turn the souls of such men, and persuade them that they must do everything to please God, as those who will be judged? And how does a so-called ghost drive out demons, and perform other not-contemptible works; not having been allotted one place, like his gods in human form, but reaching over the whole inhabited world, and gathering and drawing by his own divinity whomever he might find leaning toward the good life? After these things, following what we have said as far as possible, Celsus says such things again, ("To whom it will be said again,") "How will they know God by being grasped by sensation? What is possible to learn without sensation?" then, pretending to answer these, he says, "The voice is not of a man, nor of the soul, but of the flesh. Nevertheless, let them hear, if they are able to understand anything, as a cowardly and body-loving race, if closing your eyes to sensation * you look up with the mind, and turning away from the flesh * you awaken the eye of the soul; only thus will you see God. And if you seek a leader of this way, you must flee the deceivers and sorcerers, and the idols who smile upon you; so that you are not altogether ridiculous, slandering the other gods as idols, while worshipping * him who is truly more miserable than idols, and no longer even an idol, but as a dead man, and seeking a father like him." And first it must be said regarding his personification, which he fashions for us as words spoken by us in defense of the resurrection of the flesh, that virtue...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

<margin>
* Natural philosophy <note>original: "φυσιολογίαν"</note>
</margin>

...it is the duty of one who creates a persona <note>The Greek term is "prosopopoeia," the rhetorical technique of speaking as another person.</note> to preserve the will and the character of the person being represented. It is a vice, however, when one attributes words to a speaking character that are not fitting. Likewise, those are equally blameworthy who, in creating a persona, attribute **philosophy** to barbarians, the uneducated, servants, or those who have never heard philosophical discourses or spoken them well—things which the creator of the persona may have learned, but which the character represented would likely not know. And again, conversely, it is a fault to attribute the speech of common passions, the uneducated, and the ignorant to those who are supposed to be wise and to have known divine things. 

For this reason, Homer is admired by many for having preserved the characters of his heroes as he established them from the beginning—such as those of Nestor, Odysseus, Diomedes, Agamemnon, Telemachus, Penelope, or any of the others. Euripides, however, is mocked by the comic poet Aristophanes as an "untimely-chatterer" <note>original: "ἀκαιροῤῥήμων"</note> because he frequently attributed doctrinal discourses—which he had learned from Anaxagoras or other wise men—to barbarian women or servants. 

If, then, such is the virtue in creating a persona, and such is the vice, how can Celsus not be reasonably laughed at for attributing to Christians things that are not said by Christians? If he invented the speeches of common folk, from where would such people get the power to distinguish perception from the mind, or sensible things from intelligible things? <note>In ancient philosophy, "sensible" refers to things perceived by the senses, while "intelligible" refers to things understood by the intellect.</note> And how could they dogmatize similarly to the **Stoics**, who do away with intelligible substances and claim that sensible things are the only things grasped, and that all comprehension depends on the senses? 

But if he invented the speeches of those who are philosophical and who examine the things of Christ with all their might, he has still not made them consistent. For no one who has learned that God is invisible, and that there are certain invisible (that is, intelligible) creations, would say—as if defending the doctrine of the resurrection—"How shall they know God if he is not grasped by the senses?" or "What is possible to learn without the senses?" For it is written, not in obscure books read only by a few studious people, but in the most common ones: *The invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.* <note>A reference to Romans 1:20.</note> From these words it can be known that even if men in this life must start from the senses and sensible things when they intend to ascend to the nature of intelligible things, they must certainly not remain fixed upon sensible things.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.
<meta>catchword: it must be said</meta>

We confess that God is mind, or even something beyond mind and all substance <note>original: *substantia* / *ousia*. Origen is referencing the Platonic idea that God is "beyond being."</note>, simple, invisible, and incorporeal. We maintain that He cannot be grasped by any other than a mind made according to His own image. Now, indeed (to use the words of Paul), we see *through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face*. When I say *face*, let no one misinterpret the meaning because of the word; but let him learn what was said: *Reflecting the glory of the Lord as in a mirror with an unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory*. We do not understand a physical face here, but take it figuratively, just as we do with "eyes" and "ears" and whatever other members of the body we have previously shown are used as metaphors. Furthermore, man—that is, the soul using the body as an instrument, which is otherwise called the *inner man*—would not respond as Celsus writes, but as he has learned from the men of God. Moreover, a Christian would never use a carnal voice, as one who has learned to mortify the actions of the body by the spirit, and to always carry about the mortification <note>The "death" or "putting to death" of worldly desires.</note> of Jesus in his own body. He has heard that precept, *Mortify your earthly members*; knowing also what is signified by that saying, *My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh*; likewise, *Those who are in the flesh cannot please God*. Therefore, he does everything so that he is no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit alone. Now let us see where he calls us, so that we may hear from him how God is to be known; although he thinks no Christian can understand what he is about to say, remarking, *Let them listen, however, if they are able to hear anything*. What is it, then, that this "philosopher" wants us to hear from him? When he ought to be teaching, he instead hurls insults; and when he ought to show goodwill toward his listeners at the start of his speech, he instead addresses those who endure death rather than renounce the Christian religion even by a word—those who are ready for any kind of torture or death—and mocks them, saying, *O fearful race of men*. Soon after, he calls us *a race most loving of the body*, even though we say, *Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know Him so no longer*; and we lay down the body for the sake of piety as readily as a philosopher would hardly take off his cloak. Finally, he addresses us thus: *If, closing your senses, you look upward with the mind, and turning away the eye of the flesh, you awaken that of the mind, then you will see God*. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

<margin>Gen. 3, 6.</margin>
It must be said that Moses, in recording the creation of the world, introduces man before the transgression as being in one way seeing, and in another way not seeing. He was seeing in the sense that it is said of the woman, *The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes to behold, and beautiful to contemplate.* <note>original: "καλὸν τὸ ξύλον εἰς βρῶσιν... ὡραῖόν ἐστι τοῦ κατανοῆσαι"</note> But he was not seeing, not only in what was said as if to the blind 
<margin>Ibid. v. 5.</margin>
by the serpent to the woman: *For God knew that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened;* but also in 
<margin>Ibid. v. 7.</margin>
the phrase, *They ate, and the eyes of the two were opened.* Therefore, the eyes of their senses were opened—which they had previously done well to keep closed, so that they might not be distracted or hindered from seeing with the eyes of the soul. And he attributes being crucified to those who are not accustomed to suffer any such thing: while to us, who are crucified for the sake of piety, he reproaches the fables of those others concerning the lion-shaped and amphibious creatures along with their other inventions. Therefore, it is not because of Celsus’s warnings that we shall flee those lion-shaped beings, which were never accepted by us; but because of the teaching of Jesus we contradict such inventions, not agreeing that such is the face of Michael, or of the others who are listed. <note>Michael was often depicted in Gnostic diagrams with the head of a lion.</note> Now we must consider whom Celsus proposes we should follow, as if we did not have ancient and most holy men as leaders. But if he had set down their names, we would have contended—not without reason—that blind leaders are being given to us by him so that we might fall: or, if not altogether blind, certainly mistaken regarding many of the doctrines of truth. Whether, therefore, he wants Orpheus to be the God-inspired poet, or Parmenides, or Empedocles, or Homer himself, or even Hesiod; let whoever wishes show how those who use such leaders will make a better journey, or what utility for life they receive from them, more than others who, having left behind all sacred statues and even all Jewish superstition because of the teaching of Jesus, look up through the Word of God to His Father alone. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 7.

By a more divine grace, the knowledge of God reaches those who have been foreknown by God's providence <note>original: *προγνώσει Θεῶ* - foreknowledge of God</note> because they will live worthily of what they have learned. They do not turn aside from piety toward Him, even if they are led away to death by those who are ignorant of what piety truly is—those who imagine piety to be anything other than what it actually is—so that they might be mocked and judged. I believe God, seeing the arrogance and the contempt for others shown by those who pride themselves on knowing God and learning divine matters through philosophy, yet who behave similarly to the most uneducated by frequenting statues, temples, and the so-called "mysteries," chose the foolish things of the world. These are the simplest among Christians, who live more modestly and purely than many philosophers. He did this to put to shame the wise, who are not ashamed to address lifeless objects as gods or as images of gods. For what person of sound mind would not laugh at those who, after such great and numerous philosophical discourses about God or the gods, look upon statues and either offer prayers to them or, through the sight of them, imagine they must ascend from the visible symbol <note>original: *συμβολικοῦ*</note> to that which is perceived by the mind? 

But the Christian, even the unlearned <term>idiota: a common person or layman without specialized training</term>, is convinced that every place in the world is a part of the whole, the entire world being the temple of God. Praying in every place, closing the eyes of the senses and raising those of the soul, he transcends the entire world. He does not even stop at the vault of heaven, but passes beyond to the super-celestial place in his mind, guided by the Spirit of God. Being, as it were, outside the world, he offers prayers to God for no ordinary things. For he has learned from Jesus to seek nothing small—that is, nothing perceptible by the senses—but only the great and truly divine things which, when granted by God, contribute to the journey toward the blessedness found with Him through His Son, the Word who is God. 

Let us see what he <note>Celsus</note> says he will teach us, if indeed we are able to follow him, since he says we are entirely bound to the flesh. Furthermore, God, seeing (I believe) the arrogance and supercilious pride of those who despise others in comparison to themselves—puffed up as they are by a knowledge of God drawn from philosophy—while they meanwhile lead others to statues, temples, and those celebrated mysteries just like any ignorant person, chose the foolishness of the world. He chose those who were the simplest among Christians, living more modestly and purely than many philosophers, so that He might put to shame those "wise" men who do not blush to speak to inanimate things as if they were gods, or images of gods. For who of sound mind would not laugh at one who, after those excellent and highly philosophical disputes concerning God or the gods, looks back at statues and either offers prayers to them or, through the contemplation of them as some conspicuous sign, tries to raise his mind to the imagination of an intelligible deity? 

But the Christian, even the unlearned man, is most firmly persuaded that any place in the world is a part of the universe, and the universal world is the temple of God. In any place, he prays with his physical eyes closed but the lights of his soul raised up; and thus he ascends above the whole world. Nor does he stop at the curves of heaven, but having transcended the super-celestial places in his mind, led by the divine Spirit as if already snatched outside the world, he offers prayers to God concerning things that are not vulgar. ->reason, the intelligible and the visible: truth belongs to substance, while error belongs to generation. Therefore, science is concerned with truth, and opinion with the other; and while the intellect belongs to the intelligible thing, sight belongs to the visible thing. The mind knows the intelligible, but the eye knows the visible. Just as the Sun is in the realm of visible things—which is neither the eye nor sight, but the cause of seeing for the eye, and for sight so that it may exist through it, and for visible things so that they may be seen, and for all sensible things so that they may come to be, and even for itself so that it may be perceived—so in the realm of intelligible things is He <note>Celsus refers here to the Platonic "Form of the Good" or the Supreme Being.</note>, who is neither mind, nor intellect, nor science, but the cause of understanding for man, and for the intellect so that it may exist through Him, and for all intelligible things, and for truth itself, and for substance itself, so that they may be, He himself being superior to all these by a certain ineffable power of His own among the intelligibles. These things are said to men of sound mind; if you also understand any of this, it is well for you. And the spirit, if you think any spirit descending from God announces divine things, this would be the very spirit preaching such things, filled with which the men of old <note>Referring to the ancient Greek philosophers or poets.</note> announced many good things. If you cannot listen to these, keep silent, and hide your own ignorance; and do not say that those who see are blind, or those who run are lame, when you yourselves have lame souls and are mutilated, living life in the body—that is to say, among the dead.<-

To these things we respond (we who are not accustomed to be adversarial when something is well said even by those outside our faith, nor to contend or attempt to subvert things that are sound): that those who indeed revile the piety toward God practiced by those seeking it to the best of their ability—the unlearned <term>idiotis</term> <note>original: "idiotis" - here meaning simple or uneducated believers rather than a slur</note> who apprehend Him through faith, and the more prudent who offer prayers to the Creator of all with reason and thanksgiving, doing so through that High Priest <note>Jesus Christ</note> who taught men this sincerity of piety—and call them "lame in soul" and "mutilated," and who say that those who live in the body are dead, while they meditate in their hearts on that Apostolic saying: *For though we live in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty in God:* <margin>2 Corinthians 10:3, 4, 5.</margin> they ought to see whether, by this very act of speaking ill of the worshippers of God, they declare their own souls to be lame and their "inner man" mutilated. They punish themselves poorly while they rage with insults against those striving to live well, depriving themselves of equity and that good character which is naturally implanted in rational nature by the Creator. But those who, among other things, have learned from the Word of God—which they also practice—to bless when they are met with insults, to endure their persecutors, and to answer kindly those who speak ill of them... <margin>1 Corinthians 4:12, 13. See above, Book 5, p. 273.</margin>

If only they commit themselves to faith in God and receive the teaching of Jesus, they are so far removed from all licentiousness, uncleanness, and the foulness of lusts, that—in the manner of perfect priests who shrink from all sexual intercourse—many of them live in total chastity and purity, staying away even from lawful union with women. And indeed, among the Athenians, a single high priest <note>original: "hierophanta." The Hierophant was the chief priest of the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note>, not even trusting himself to be able to command his male desires, is thought fit to perform the solemn ceremonies of that city purely only after his virile parts have been numbed with hemlock <note>A poisonous plant used in antiquity to induce numbness or as a means of execution; here, Origen suggests it was used to suppress sexual desire.</note>. But among Christians, there are men who have no need of hemlock to serve God purely; instead of hemlock, the Word of God is sufficient for them to expel all lusts from their thoughts and to devote themselves to prayers. Among those thought by others to be gods, there are virgins, very few in number, whether guarded by men or not (for that is not the question now), who seem to persevere in chastity for the sake of religion. However, among Christians, the pursuit of virginity flourishes not for the sake of human honors, nor for monetary rewards, nor for vainglory; and as soon as they have approved of having God in their knowledge, they are preserved by God in this laudable mind and in the duties of piety, full of all goodness and justice. I say these things not because I contentiously oppose the good opinions of the Greeks, nor because I accuse their sound doctrines, but to demonstrate that both these and even greater and more divine things were spoken by the divine men, the Prophets of God and the Apostles of Jesus. These things are sought out by those tending toward a more perfect Christianity, who know that <margin>Psalm 36:30 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 37:30-31.</note></margin> *The mouth of the righteous shall meditate on wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment: the law of his God is in his heart.* Indeed, even among those who—either because of a lack of education, or because of simplicity, or because of a lack of teachers to exhort them to piety—understand these things less, yet believe in the supreme God and in His only-begotten Son, the Word and God, one may frequently find a greater gravity, purity, and simplicity of character. This is not shared by those who call themselves wise, who wallow with boys in an abominable manner, males practicing foulness with males <margin>Romans 1:27</margin>. And he <note>Referring to Celsus.</note> did not declare how there is error regarding generation, nor did he teach what he meant, so that we might consider these things in comparison with our doctrine. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 7.

-> [The text is presented in parallel columns: Latin on the left, Greek on the right] <-

...there is a difference between those who have a modest knowledge of God, and those who, more fully taught by divine inspiration, always dwell with God and are led by His Spirit. If Celsus had noticed this, he would not charge us with ignorance, nor would he forbid us from saying that those are blind who think that piety pertains to statues made by craftsmen out of various materials. For no one who sees with the eyes of the soul worships the Divine in any other way than as He Himself taught; namely, by seeing the Creator in His handiwork, directing all prayers to Him, and doing all things as if in His sight, from whom not even our thoughts are hidden. Therefore, we profess both to see and to be guides to the blind, until, coming to the Word of God, they receive back the eyes of the soul which were blinded by ignorance. And if we do things worthy of that precept, *You are the light of the world*, <margin>Matthew 5:14</margin> and that teaching that *the light shines in the darkness*; <margin>John 1:5</margin> we shall also be a light in the darkness, and we shall instruct the foolish and teach the little ones. Nor is there any reason for Celsus to be indignant because we say those are lame and crippled in the feet of the soul who run toward falsely esteemed sacred rites as if they were true, and do not see that nothing can be sacred in the works of craftsmen. Yet those who live piously according to the teaching of Jesus also run, until, having finished the race, they may say truly and from the heart, <margin>2 Timothy 4:7</margin> *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness*. And each of us runs in this way, not as if in uncertainty; <margin>1 Corinthians 9:26</margin> and so practices boxing against vices, not as if beating the air with vain blows, but attacking the "princes of the air" <note>original: *principes aeris*; referring to demonic spiritual hierarchies</note> and the spirits now working in the sons of disobedience. <margin>Ephesians 2:2</margin> Let Celsus say that we live in a dead body—we who have heard that saying, <margin>Romans 8:13</margin> *If you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live*; and have learned that, <margin>Galatians 5:25</margin> *If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit*. We are able by our works to prove our adversaries liars, by living with a mortified body. After these things, to which we have responded as best we could, he addresses us thus: *How much better it would have been, if you were pleased to innovate something, to have taken up the story of a consecrated divinity regarding someone else who died nobly and was worthy of such an opinion? If Hercules did not please you, or Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>, and the renowned virtue of the ancients, you had Orpheus, a man undeniably inspired by a holy spirit and killed by a violent death.* But he, perhaps, was already claimed by others before you. Certainly Anaxarchus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher</note>, who, when cast into a mortar and being most cruelly pounded to pieces, uttered a remarkable cry amidst his punishments, and truly divine...

<column-break/>

...a brief conception of God; and those who are more fully divinely inspired, and always stand by God, and are led through everything by the divine Spirit. If Celsus had thought to examine this, he would not have accused us of ignorance, nor would he have commanded us not to say that those are blind who think they exhibit piety toward the material arts of men or toward statues. For no one seeing with the eyes of the soul worships the Divine in any other way than that which points toward always looking to the Creator of all things, and offering every prayer to Him, and doing all things as if before the eyes of God, because He is a spectator who looks even into our inner reasonings. We pray, therefore, that we may both see and be guides of the blind, until, approaching the Word of God, they may recover the sight of their souls which had been blinded by ignorance. And if we also do things worthy of Him who said to the disciples, <margin>Matthew 5:14</margin> *You are the light of the world*, and of the Word who taught that <margin>John 1:5</margin> *The light shines in the darkness*; we shall be both light in the darkness, and we shall educate the foolish, and we shall teach the infants. Let not Celsus be indignant when we call those lame and maimed in the steps of the soul who hasten toward supposed holy places as if they were truly holy, and do not see that no work of men is truly holy. But those who live piously according to the teaching of Jesus also run, until, reaching the end of the race, they may say with strength and a true disposition, <margin>2 Timothy 4:7</margin> *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness*. And each of us runs thus, <margin>1 Corinthians 9:26</margin> *not as if uncertainly*; and so boxes against wickedness, *not as if beating the air*, but against the principalities and powers of the air, <margin>Ephesians 2:2</margin> the spirits of evil in the sons of disobedience. Let Celsus say of us that we live in a dead body, we who hear, <margin>Romans 8:13</margin> *If you live according to the flesh, you are about to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live*; and learning that, <margin>Galatians 5:25</margin> *If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit*; let it be <margin>* to us.</margin> that we show by our deeds that he who says of us that we live in a dead body is lying. After these things, therefore, to which we have replied according to our ability, he says to us: “How much better it would have been for you, since you desired to innovate something, to have been zealous about some other of those who died nobly, and who were capable of receiving a divine myth? Come, if Hercules did not please you, and Aesculapius, and those glorified of old, you had Orpheus, a man admittedly possessing a holy spirit, and who himself died violently. But perhaps he was preoccupied by others. Or Anaxarchus at least, who, being cast into a mortar and being crushed most lawlessly, thoroughly despised the punishment...”

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:4. 2 Corinthians 1:12.</margin>

And if the goal is to make the recipient of this rational food (if I may call it so) patient and gentle; how would it not be better to have a word so prepared that it produces multitudes of patient and gentle people, rather than one prepared for these virtues that makes—if we grant it—only a very few and easily counted people patient and gentle? For just as if a Greek wished to benefit Egyptians or Syrians with healthy bodies, he would take care to learn the dialects used among them, and (as the Greeks call it) to "speak like a barbarian" <note>original: "βαρβαρίζειν" - to speak a non-Greek language, often used disparagingly by Greeks.</note> for the sake of the improvement of the Egyptians or Syrians, rather than remaining a Greek and being unable to say anything useful to them; so the presiding Divine Nature, providing not only for those thought to be educated in Greek learning but also for the rest of the Greeks, condescended to the simple style <note>original: "ἰδιωτίᾳ" - the plain or unlearned manner of speech.</note> of the listening multitude. This was done so that by using words familiar to them, it might challenge the multitude of simple folk to listen, who are then able, after an initial introduction, to easily strive toward understanding even the deeper of the hidden meanings in the Scriptures. For it is clear to anyone reading these that the immediate meaning is much deeper for those who devote themselves to the examination of the Word, being revealed in proportion to the leisure one gives to the Word and the eagerness of their practice. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

That Jesus, speaking in this simple and rustic style (as Celsus calls it), saying, *To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and to him who calls you into judgment to take away your tunic, let him have your cloak as well* <margin>Matthew 5:39</margin>, has benefited the lives of men more than that famous disputation of Plato in the *Crito*. For the common people are far from being able to hear such things; indeed, they are scarcely studied by Greek philosophers even after they have completed the full circle of their disciplines. It must also be considered that the doctrine of patience does not become inferior through simplicity of words, but that this is merely a slander by Celsus, whose words are: *"But enough of these things, and of others which these people distort for their own use; whoever desires to know more of this will easily find out. Come now, let us see what follows in this manner. Let us pass to other things. They cannot bear to look upon temples, altars, and statues. Not even the Scythians <note>A nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note>, nor the Numidian nomads, nor the impious Seres <note>Ancient Greek/Roman name for the people of North China</note>, nor other nations who lack religion as much as they lack laws, do this."* Herodotus relates the same about the Persians. *“I know these rites of the Persians,”* he says, *“they do not dedicate statues, altars, or temples, and they consider those who do so to be fools; as I believe, because they do not think the Gods are born from men, which is the opinion of the Greeks.”* <margin>Herodotus, Book 1</margin> Yet Heraclitus pronounces thus concerning them: *“They offer prayers to these images just as if someone were to chatter with logs of wood, because they do not know who the gods or heroes are.”* What, then, do these people teach us that is wiser than Heraclitus? He suggests, quite obscurely, that it is foolish to place vows with statues unless one knows who the Gods and heroes are. Such is the opinion of Heraclitus; but these people [the Christians] utterly despise the statues of the Gods. If they do so because a stone, or wood, or bronze, or gold polished by this or that person is not a God, this wisdom is ridiculous; for who else, unless he be a total fool, believes these things are Gods, rather than statues dedicated to the gods? But if they think that they should not even be considered images of the Gods, and that the form of God is something else, as it also seems to the Persians; they unknowingly refute their own dogma when they say that man was created in the image of God, and similar to Him in appearance. But they will agree regarding the similarities, yet they will deny that those to whom these things are dedicated are gods; they will contend that they are demons, and that the worshiper of God must flee the veneration of demons. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

->**The same doctrines**<- <margin>Those who hold the same doctrines.</margin> are held by those who, starting from these principles, do not tolerate temples and statues—at least those who truly refuse them. This is so that if one refuses them based on sound doctrines, he may be praised; but if from erroneous ones, he may be blamed. For it is possible for the same action to arise from different doctrines. For example: those who follow the philosophy of **Zeno of Citium** <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> avoid committing adultery, but so do those who follow **Epicurus**, and even some of the completely unlearned common folk. Yet, look at how much disagreement there is in the reasons for avoiding adultery among so many people. The former [the Stoics] believe it is contrary to the social nature of a rational being to take a woman already claimed by another under the law, and thus corrupt another man’s household. But those from the school of **Epicurus** do not abstain for this reason, but because they have established pleasure as the ultimate goal; and many things occur that hinder pleasure in the pursuit of the pleasure of adultery itself—sometimes guards, or exile, or death. Often, even before these, there are dangers and the need to watch for the husband’s departure from the house, and the vigilance of those who share his views. So, if by hypothesis an Epicurean could commit adultery and escape the notice of the husband, all his relatives, and those who look down on adultery, he would commit adultery for the sake of the pleasure. And if the unlearned man sometimes does not commit adultery when he has the chance, he might be found doing so out of the present fear of the law and its punishments <margin>The adulterer.</margin> * while not committing the act; such a man might abstain from adultery only to hunt for greater pleasures. You see, then, that the act in question—the abstinence from adultery—is not the same but becomes different according to the intentions of those abstaining; for it arises either from sound doctrines or from wicked and most impious ones, as in the case of the Epicurean or such an unlearned man. Just as this matter of abstaining from adultery, while appearing to be one thing, is found to be many things depending on different doctrines and intentions; so too regarding the refusal to worship the Divine with altars, temples, and statues. The **Scythians**, the **Nomads of Libya**, the godless **Seres** <note>Likely referring to the Chinese or people of Central Asia.</note>, and the **Persians** do this from different doctrines than those which lead **Christians** and **Jews** to refuse such supposed service to the Divine. None of those [pagan] nations refuse altars and statues because they avoid pulling down and dragging the worship of the Divine to such matter shaped into forms; rather, it is because they have a certain understanding about demons—that they hover around such sacrifices and places, either summoned by certain incantations or otherwise being able to occupy places for themselves, where they greedily partake of the steam of the sacrifices, finding an unlawful pleasure and raising barriers. But Christians and Jews, because of—

**The same doctrines** <note>This column provides the Latin translation of the preceding Greek text.</note>, by which they are moved to abominate statues and temples: so that either he whose reason for the deed is established may be praised, or the rash hater may be blamed. For it is possible that they hold diverse opinions on these matters. For example, the philosophers who follow **Zeno of Citium** avoid adultery; those whom **Epicurus** pleases as a master also avoid it; and even some from the illiterate common people. But see how varied their wills are in fleeing adultery. The former think it a sin against nature and human society if anyone violates a woman legitimately joined to another and adulterates his family. But the **Epicureans** do not abstain for this reason, but because they direct all their actions toward one goal: pleasure. He who succumbs to this one pleasure defrauds himself of many others, sometimes falling into prison, exile, or death. And before the deed, he is not without danger while he observes the husband’s exit from the home and others who favor him. Therefore, suppose he could deceive the husband, his domestics, and the others from whom he fears reproach; as far as pleasure is concerned, even the Epicurean would become an adulterer. But if even the unlearned man does not commit adultery when he can, the cause is the fear of laws and punishments, not a contempt for pleasure. You see how, although the flight from adultery seems a simple matter, it is nevertheless varied according to the different wills of men: for it is born either from healthy decrees or from worthless and impious ones, as in the case of such an unlearned man and the Epicurean. Just as this abstinence from adultery, while appearing to be one, is discovered to be manifold according to the variety of opinions and wills: so also among those who shrink from the ceremonies of statues, temples, and altars—the **Scythians**, **Numidians**, the impious **Seres**, and the **Persians**—they are moved by other reasons than the **Christians** and **Jews**, for whom it is a matter of religion to worship the deity in this way. For none of those nations is averse to these things because they fear to drag the deity down to these vile ceremonies involving altars and matter fashioned into various images; nor because they understand that demons hang around fixed places and statues, either bound by certain magic songs or otherwise brooding over places once preoccupied, where like gluttons they delight themselves in the smells of victims, catching a pleasure that is nefarious and forbidden by divine and natural laws. But Christian men and Jews restrain themselves from these things because of that [commandment] of the law...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

<margin>Genesis 1:27.</margin>
...not only do they err by thinking they worship these objects out of mere social conformity, but they fall so far in their souls as to believe these things actually are gods; they cannot even bear to hear that these objects they pray to are not gods. Celsus, for his part, says: "They do not consider them gods, but rather offerings dedicated to the gods" <note>original: *anathemata* — in this context, objects set apart or dedicated in a temple</note>; yet he fails to show how these are not merely offerings of men, but (as he calls them) of the gods themselves. For it is clear that these are offerings made by men who are led astray concerning the divine. Furthermore, we do not even suppose that statues are divine images, since we do not define the invisible and incorporeal God by any physical shape. 

But since Celsus supposes that we fall into a contradiction when we say that the Divine is not human-shaped, while also believing that God made man as His own image, and made him "in the image of God," we must state (as has been said previously) that we claim the "Image of God" is preserved in the rational soul, specifically through its virtue. And at this point Celsus, failing to see the difference between being the "Image of God" and being made "according to the image of God," claims we say: "that God made man His own image and a form like unto Himself." This has also been addressed in the preceding sections.

Next, he says regarding Christians, that "they will grant that these [idols] exist in honor of certain beings, whether similar or dissimilar in form; but they deny that those to whom these are dedicated are gods, calling them instead demons <note>original: *daimones* — in Greek thought, these were intermediary spirits, but Christians viewed them as malevolent fallen angels</note>; and they say that one who worships God ought not to serve demons." If he had any true knowledge of the teachings concerning demons—how they act when summoned by those skilled in such arts, or how they offer themselves voluntarily to provide care or benefit as they please—and if he had grasped the discourse on demons, which is vast and difficult for human nature to comprehend, he would not have accused us for saying that one who worships the God over all must not serve demons. Indeed, we are so far from serving demons that we actually drive them out of human souls and from the places where they have established themselves—and sometimes even from animals—using prayers and the teachings from the Holy Scriptures. For demons often act even upon such creatures to do harm. 

Because many things have already been said by us above concerning Jesus, there is no need now to repeat ourselves in response to his claim: "that they are clearly convicted of worshipping not a god, nor even a demon, but a dead man." Let us leave this for now and look at Celsus's next words, in which he says: "First, I will ask, why must demons not be served? Is not everything governed according to the will of God? And is not all providence from Him? And whatever exists in the universe, whether it be the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons...

<column-break/>

...of these is led into error, having their souls so depressed by false religion that they cannot even bear to hear someone denying that these are Gods, whom they themselves have become accustomed to worship. Celsus certainly says he believes *these are not Gods, but offerings dedicated to the Gods*; yet he does not explain how these are not offerings of men, but of the Gods, as he calls them. For it is evident that these are dedicated by men holding a false opinion about God. Nor do we think statues are images of the divine, as we do not circumscribe the incorporeal and invisible God with any figure. 

However, because Celsus says our opinions conflict—while we deny a human appearance in God, yet believe man was made by Him in His own image—it must be answered, as above, that this image of God is preserved in the rational soul through virtue. Celsus, not understanding that the "Image of God" is one thing and being "according to the image of God" is another, says we claim *that God made man His own image, and a form similar to Himself*; to which an answer has already been given previously. 

After this he says, *Christians will concede that these are images of those whose likeness they either express or do not; yet they will deny these are Gods, since they are more truly demons, and that no worship is owed to demons by a man dedicated to piety.* If he had known what is handed down concerning demons and their individual operations—which they perform either when invoked by those skilled in such arts, or spontaneously as they wish and are able—and if he had perceived the discussion about them, which is surely lengthy and exceeding the grasp of human wit, he would not have rebuked those who deny that worship is owed to demons by the pious worshippers of the true God. And we are so far from venerating them that by prayers and the recitation of the sacred letters, we drive them out of possessed men, and from the places dedicated to them, and sometimes even from animals; for sometimes demons work so as to injure these as well. 

Since, however, many things were said by us above concerning Jesus, there is no need to repeat the same things in response to him saying, *Certainly they are convicted by manifest arguments that they worship not a demon, but a dead man*; therefore, omitting this, let us see what Celsus says next in these words: *And first I will ask, why are demons not to be worshipped? Are not all things dispensed by the judgment of God, and do they not depend on His providence? Is not everything that is done anywhere, whether through God or through Angels, or through other demons...*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

*...whether through Heroes, all of this has a law prescribed by the highest God;* <note>Origen is quoting Celsus's argument here.</note> has not each of these obtained that power of which he was deemed worthy? Therefore, when he who received power from God is a worshipper of God, will he not offer veneration? For is it not permitted to serve several masters? See here also how many things he takes for granted, which require no small investigation, and even a deeper and more secret knowledge concerning the administration of all things: for this very point, that all things are administered by the will of God, must be examined—namely, whether this governance extends even to sins, or not? For, if it extends to them also, it pertains not only to human affairs, but also to those of demons, and if there be any other nature besides the corporeal that is liable to sin. He who says this should see what a great absurdity follows this proposition: that all things are administered by the judgment of God. For it will follow that whatever is committed through malice happens by the will of God. Which is indeed a different thing from happening while God does not prohibit it. But if anyone understands "administration" strictly as applying to things done through malice, then surely all things will happen by the will of God, and no sinner will transgress against God’s administration. Similarly, a distinction must be made regarding providence: that all things proceed from divine providence is true when understood regarding good things. But if all things are taken simply, even evil things, it will be false that all things happen by the providence of God: unless one contends that even those things which happen as a consequence <note>original: "per consequens" / "κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν" — referring to the indirect results of free will or natural laws</note> happen from the providence of God. He likewise asserts, *that whatever is done either by God, or by angels, or by demons, or by heroes, all these have the law of God:* which, however, he does not truly assert; for the wicked do not act wickedly according to the law of the highest God. It is evident by clear reason that not only evil men act against this law, but also evil demons and evil angels. Furthermore, that there are evil demons is not said by us alone, but by almost all others who posit that demons exist. Therefore, not all things have the law of the greatest God. For whatever things, through their own inadvertence, malice, misery, or ignorance of good things, have fallen away from the law of God, do not have the law of God, but (to speak in the manner of the Scripture) they have the *law of sin*. <margin>Romans 8:2</margin> Therefore, according to the opinion of many who posit that demons exist, even evil demons do not have the law of God, but act against the law; our people, however, hold the same opinion regarding all demons—as many as have fallen away from the path leading to the highest good—since they were not previously demons, and this was the nature of their kind,

<column-break/>

"...or of heroes, all these have a law from the greatest God; and there has been assigned to each one who was deemed worthy, a power which he obtained. Would not he, then, who has obtained authority from Him, be rightly served by one who worships God? For he says it is not possible for the same man to serve several masters." <note>Origen is quoting Celsus in Greek here.</note> See then in these words how many things he snatches up, which require no contemptible examination, but even a deeper and more recondite science concerning the administration of the universe. For the statement, "all things are administered according to the will of God," must be examined as to how it is said; and whether the administration reaches even to sins or not. For if the administration reaches even to sins, not only among men, but also in demons, and if there be any other thing outside of bodies which is of a nature to sin, let him who says this see the absurdity of the claim that all things are administered according to the will of God; for it follows from the argument that even sins, and all things resulting from vice, are administered according to the will of God. Which is not the same as saying they happen without God preventing them. But if anyone should hear the word "administered" in its proper sense, then things resulting from vice are not administered; clearly all things are administered according to the will of God, and no sinner acts lawlessly against the administration of God. <note>Origen is using a "reductio ad absurdum" here to show that if Celsus is right, sin wouldn't be "lawless" because it would be part of God's plan.</note> And a similar distinction must be made concerning providence, and it must be said: that "All things are from that providence" signifies the truth when the providence is over excellent things. But if we say simply that all things that happen are providence, even if something happens badly, it is false that "All things are from that providence"; unless perhaps one should say that even things which happen by consequence of God's providence are "from the providence of God." And he declares "whatever there may be in the universe, whether it be the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes, all these have a law from the greatest God." And he does not declare a true word. For those who act lawlessly do not do so according to the law of the greatest God. For the argument shows that not only are there wicked men, but also wicked demons and wicked angels. <margin>Psalm 77:54; 2 Peter 2:4</margin> And we are not the only ones who speak of wicked demons, but almost all who admit the existence of demons. Therefore, not all things have a law from the greatest God. For as many things as, through their own inattention, malice, or wickedness, or ignorance, have fallen away from the divine law of good things, do not have the law of God, but (to call it by a common name, and that according to the Scripture) have the *law of sin*. <margin>Romans 8:2</margin> According to the many who admit the existence of demons, even the wicked demons do not have the law from God, but act lawlessly; but according to us, all demons are those who have revolted from the way to the good, not having been demons previously; and if their race were...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 7.

...of those who have fallen away from God: the race of demons. Therefore, whoever worships God must not serve demons. The nature of demons is made clear by those who invoke them for so-called love-charms, or hate-spells, or for the hindering of actions, or countless other such things; which those who have learned to call upon and draw in demons for whatever they wish do through incantations and <term>juggling-tricks</term> <note>original: μαγγανειῶν (magganeion) - refers to sorcery or deceptive magical arts</note>. Therefore, the worship of all demons is foreign to us who worship the God over all. And the worship of demons is the worship of those named as gods. For *all the gods of the nations are demons.* <margin>Psalm 95:5 <note>In modern Bibles, Psalm 96:5</note></margin> This is clear from the fact that curious <term>invocations</term> <note>original: κατακλίσεις (katakliseis) - literally "callings down" or "indwellings"</note> have taken place in what are thought to be the more active of the supposed holy places; and at the beginning of the founding of such statues, those who devote themselves to the service of demons through sorcery have produced certain movements and indwellings. Therefore, we have resolved to flee the worship of demons as a deadly destruction; and we say that all the religion practiced among the Greeks regarding altars and statues and temples of the gods is the worship of demons.

Then, as to what he [Celsus] says: "Each has been assigned his own power, having obtained his portion from the Great God, according as he was deemed worthy"—this is a strange claim. For it requires a very deep knowledge to be able to show whether, just as there are executioners in cities and those appointed over grim but necessary matters in states, so there are wicked demons appointed by certain powers under the Word of God who administers the universe; or whether, just as those who commit robbery in deserts and set up one of their own to rule them, so the demons, having formed themselves into groups according to regions of the earth, have made for themselves a certain ruler, who is unknown to those whom they chose for the purpose of *harming and plundering* <margin>* to steal and to see / to harm and to plunder</margin> the souls of men. 

But he who intends to speak well on these matters, in order to defend the Christians—who are prepared to worship nothing other than the God over all and His Word, the firstborn of all creation—must also explain that saying: *All who came before me are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not listen to them;* <margin>John 10:8</margin> and the saying: *The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy;* <margin>Ibid. v. 10</margin> and whatever else is said like these in the Holy Scriptures; just as this: *Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you;* <margin>Luke 10:19</margin> and this: *You shall step upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.* <margin>Psalm 90:13 <note>Psalm 91:13 in modern Bibles</note></margin> But Celsus was entirely ignorant of these things. For if he had known them, he would not have said: "For what is there in the universe, whether it be the work of God, or of angels, or of other demons, or of heroes..." <margin>* whether of demons</margin>

<column-break/>

...who have deserted God: wherefore whoever worships God ought not to serve demons. The affairs of demons are also evident from those who invoke them, who use their help to stir up loves and hatreds, or to hinder actions, and innumerable other similar things, which they do through magical incantations, having been taught to call and lead in demons for whatever they please: for which reason all worship of demons is foreign to us, the worshippers of the Most High God. Moreover, the worship of demons is also to worship those who are called Gods. *For all the Gods of the Gentiles are demons:* a fact which is clear from the temples, which are thought to be inhabited by a present deity as being more sacred, which from the beginning of their dedication received such demons into the shrines through curious and magical invocations. Therefore, it has seemed good to us to flee the worship of demons no differently than a most certain destruction: under which name we include all Greek religions which are occupied with the temples of the Gods, and altars, and statues. 

But as for what he says, *“By the ordination of the Greatest God, his own power has fallen to each, according as he was held worthy of this or that work,”* this requires no common wisdom, which might be able to teach whether—just as executioners in cities are perfected for gloomy ministries, yet necessary to the state of the Republic—so evil demons have their ministries assigned by God, the Lord of the universe: or whether, just as robbers in the wilderness having appointed a leader for themselves, so demons in certain regions roam in troops under some leader of their own kind, by whose guidance they prey upon and vex men. 

Furthermore, he who wishes to argue well concerning these things, and to answer for the Christians who refuse to worship anything except God the Lord of all, and His Word the firstborn of every creature, ought to explain also that Gospel saying, *“All, as many as came before me, are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not hear them;”* and that, *“The thief comes not, but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy;”* and if there is anything of this sort in the sacred writings, or that, *“Behold, I have given you all power of treading upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you;”* likewise that, *“Upon the asp and the basilisk you shall walk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.”* But these things Celsus did not know. For if he had known them, he would not have said, *“Is not everything that is done anywhere, whether by God, or by Angels, or by other demons, or by Heroes...”*

<summary>Origen argues that pagan gods are actually demons invoked through magic, and that Christians reject their worship because they serve only God and His Word. He contrasts Celsus's view of "allotted powers" with the biblical view of demons as spiritual "robbers" whom Christ has given believers the power to overcome.</summary>

# Book 7. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...powers, does not all of this have a law prescribed by the highest God? Has not each of these obtained the power of which he was deemed worthy? Therefore, shall the worshiper of God not venerate him who has received power from God? To these points he also adds this: *Because it is not permitted to serve two masters.* <note>A reference to Matthew 6:24</note> We shall treat these final words in the following volume, now that this seventh book, in which we have responded to the writings of Celsus, is finished.

->BOOK 8.<-

<margin>2 Corinthians 5:20.</margin>
<margin>* Glory.</margin>
I have already reached the completion of seven books, and I wish now to begin the eighth. May God and His only-begotten Word be present with us, so that the falsehoods of Celsus—vainly inscribed with the title *The True Word* <note>original: "ἀληθὴς λόγος" (alēthēs logos). Celsus titled his anti-Christian work "The True Word," which Origen frequently mocks as being neither true nor a word of wisdom.</note>—may be nobly refuted, and that the truths of Christianity may be powerfully demonstrated (as far as is possible in these dictated words). We pray to say with the same disposition as Paul, *We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us*, and to act as ambassadors for Christ to men, just as the Word of God invites them to friendship with Himself. He desires to make those who have lived in the darkness of ignorance regarding God and the Creator familiar with righteousness, truth, and the rest of the virtues through the acceptance of Christ’s teachings. And again I say, may God * grant us that noble and true Word, the Lord of the mighty and the one powerful in the war against vice. Now we must proceed to the next passage of Celsus and the response to it. He raised a difficulty against us regarding these matters, asking: why do we not worship demons? And he claims that what he said about demons was confirmed according to what appears to us to be the will of the divine Word. Then, following those points, he introduces us as saying in response to his inquiry—where he wants us to also worship demons—that it is not possible for the same person to serve several masters. "This," as he thinks, he says, "is the voice," as he himself named it, "of those **walling themselves off and breaking away from the rest of humanity.**" He thinks that those who say this are, as far as they are able, **projecting their own human passions onto God.** Therefore, he maintained that while it has a place among men that one serving a certain person should not likewise serve another man—since the one would be harmed by the divided service—nor should one who has already sworn an oath to one person swear to another; so it would make sense that not serving different heroes and such demons at the same time would be harmful. But in the case of God, toward whom neither harm nor grief can appear, he considers it irrational to be on guard in the same way as one is with men, and heroes, and such demons—

<column-break/>

Having finished the seventh volume, and being about to attempt the eighth, I pray to God and His only-begotten Word, that He may be present with me as I bravely refute the lies of Celsus, which are disguised under the empty title of truth, and at the same time as I defend the Christian religion against its slanderer. For it is permitted to us also to say, *we act as ambassadors for Christ, God commanding us to use the words of Paul from the heart and to act as an envoy for Christ among men*, as the Word of God Himself invites to friendship those whom He desires to be reconciled to Himself through justice, truth, and the other virtues—those who, before knowing the teachings of Jesus Christ, were occupied in darkness, as if ignorant of God their founder and Lord. I pray, therefore, again and again, that God may give me that powerful and true word of His, strong in the war which is waged against vices. And now we must move on to the following context of Celsus, which we mentioned above, where he asks for what reason we are reluctant to worship demons? To which we replied by bringing forward whatever we have learned from the sacred Scriptures of God concerning the nature of demons. And soon therein he leads us to his questioning, demanding that we also worship demons, while we use that Gospel pretext, *It is impossible to serve several masters at the same time*. This voice he considers *seditious*, as he himself said, *of those breaking themselves off from the society of the rest of men*. And he thinks, *We, by this saying, rub our own vices onto God: since it may have a place among men, that he who serves one man, rightly abstains from serving another, lest perhaps he harm his master by the diversity of service, in which case also one who is joined to one cannot become the associate of another, without the inconvenience of the first associate: and for this reason it would be harmful to serve different masters and demons of this kind at the same time. But toward God, for whom there is no danger of being either offended or harmed, he deems it absurd that anyone should behave in that manner, lest he worship several Gods, just as if they were men, or heroes, or demons—*

# Book 8. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...you have taken up the duty of worshipping many gods. He <note>Celsus, the second-century critic of Christianity</note> also says, *“He who worships several gods, by the very fact that he worships one of those subjects of the most high God, does a thing pleasing to the supreme God”*; he adds furthermore, *“that it is not permitted to pursue anyone with honor, unless it is the will of that God that he be honored: therefore, he who worships His subjects does not offend Him to whom they all belong.”* Let us see then, before we come to what follows in Celsus’s argument, whether we may not rightly prove this sentiment to be false which denies that anyone can serve two masters, to which is subjoined, *“For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to this one and neglect the other”*; and thereafter, *“You cannot serve God and Mammon.”* <note>original: "Mammonæ" — a Syriac term for wealth or profit, personified here as a false god.</note> This point of our defense requires that we penetrate more deeply into the secret concerning gods and lords. Likewise concerning those who are Lords and those who are not, Paul says: *“For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords.”* Then, because the God of gods calls from the east and the west to His own portion through Jesus whomever He wills: and His Christ, since He is Lord, shows Himself superior to all those who exercise lordship, because He ascended above all boundaries to call people to Himself from all boundaries: therefore Paul, knowing these things, subjoins to the words just cited, *“Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him.”* And considering a certain wonderful and mystical doctrine in this place,
