# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

<margin>1 Cor. 8:7.</margin> *But not everyone possesses this knowledge.* <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡ γνῶσις." Origen quotes Paul to explain that while many claim to know God, true spiritual insight is rare.</note> When he says, *Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,* he uses the word "Us" to refer to himself and to all those who have ascended to the God of gods who is over all, and to the <margin>Deut. 10:17.</margin> Lord of lords who is over all. Now, he has ascended to the God over all who worships Him inseparably, indivisibly, and without distraction through the only Son who leads us to Him—the Word and Wisdom of God beheld in Jesus. This person strives in every way to make himself known to the God who is the Creator of all things through excellent words, deeds, and thoughts. And I believe that these things, <margin>* besides these.</margin> and things similar to them, were imitated by the ruler of this age <note>The "ruler of this age" refers to the Devil or a fallen spiritual power.</note> who transforms himself into an angel of light <margin>2 Cor. 11:4.</margin> when he fashioned the saying: "A host of gods and demons follows this one, arranged in eleven divisions." Regarding these, those who already philosophize about him say: "We are with Zeus, but others are under other demons." Therefore, although many are called or are indeed gods, and likewise lords, we do everything so that we may not only rise above those worshipped as gods by the nations on earth, but even above those whom the Scriptures call "gods." Of these, those who are strangers to the covenants of God delivered through Moses and our Savior Jesus know nothing, and they are alienated from the promises set forth through them. Moreover, he rises above the service to all demons who performs no work pleasing to demons; and he rises above the portion of those called "gods" by Paul, who looks *not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.* <margin>2 Cor. 4:18.</margin> He sees how *the whole creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God, not willingly,* <margin>Rom. 8:19, 20, 21.</margin> *but because of him who subjected it in hope.* He speaks well of the creation, seeing how it shall all be set free from the bondage of corruption and arrive at the freedom of the glory of the children of God. He does not serve anyone else alongside God, nor does he serve two masters. This is not the voice of sedition <note>Celsus accused Christians of being a "seditious" or rebellious sect; Origen argues their "rebellion" is actually a holy refusal to serve multiple masters.</note> among those who understand such things and do not wish to serve many lords. For this reason, being satisfied with the Lord Jesus Christ, those who serve Him are disciplined by Him, so that having been disciplined and made worthy of the Kingdom of God, He may hand them over to God the Father. Indeed, they separate and break themselves away from those who are strangers to the commonwealth of God and His covenants, so that they may live according to the citizenship of heaven, approaching the living God and <margin>Phil. 3:20. Heb. 12:22, 23.</margin> the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the festal gathering of myriads of angels, and the church of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven. But as if we were blaspheming...

...he thus introduces: *But not in everyone is there knowledge.* When, however, he says: *Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things:* he speaks this word, *Us*, concerning himself and all who have ascended to the highest God of gods, and to the highest Lord of lords. Moreover, he ascends to the highest God who worships Him inseparably and indivisibly through Jesus the Son of God, by whose sole guidance they reach the Father; those who, through the contemplation of the Word of God and Wisdom, strive in all ways to be reconciled to God the founder of all things, as much by doctrine as by works and thoughts. According to these and similar things, I suppose the prince of this world, accustomed to being transformed into an angel of light, feigned that saying: *A trained army of gods and demons follows this one in eleven orders:* where he says of himself and the followers of his wisdom: *We indeed are with Jove, but others are with other demons.* Therefore, since many are called or are gods, and similarly lords, there is nothing we do not do, so that we may not only ascend above everything worshipped as gods by the nations on earth, but even above those whom Scripture names "gods"; about whom those know nothing who are alienated from the Covenants of God produced through Moses and Jesus our Savior, to whom the promises signified in these pertain not at all. It is not, therefore, a seditious voice of those so feeling, and unwilling to serve many lords, being content with one Lord Jesus Christ, serving whom they are instructed by Him, so that He may deliver them, having been made worthy of the kingdom of God, to God and the Father. They are surely broken off and secede from those alienated from the Republic of God, and pertaining nothing to His Covenants, so that they may live according to the institutes of the celestial city, approaching the *living God, and the celestial city of God, Jerusalem, the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven.* Nor for that reason do we beware...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

->**Latin Text**<-

...we serve, lest we serve anyone besides God through His Word and in truth; not that God is harmed (as a man is harmed if his servant should serve another), but lest we ourselves be harmed by separating ourselves from our portion in God. He, according to His own blessedness, has made those living [righteously] intimate with Himself through the spirit of adoption; He is God among the sons of the heavenly Father, crying out not in words, but in reality and in secret, "Abba, Father." <margin>Romans 8:15</margin> Long ago, the ambassadors of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> refused to prostrate before the King of the Persians, even though his guards pressed them vehemently; they feared their only Lord, namely the law of Lycurgus. But those who perform a much greater and more divine embassy on behalf of Christ will prostrate neither to the prince of the Persians, nor of the Greeks, nor of the Egyptians, nor of any nation whatsoever—even if the demons and angels of the devil, acting as the guards of these princes, should attempt to compel them here and persuade them to bid farewell to that Law which is more excellent than all laws upon the earth. For Christ himself is the Lord of Christ’s ambassadors, for whom they perform their embassy: *the Word, which was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God.* <margin>John 1:1</margin> Next, since it pleased Celsus to stir up a discourse—deeper than he thinks—concerning heroes and certain demons, after he said *In the service of men, the first master is harmed if anyone wishes to serve another in addition*, he says, *the same must be thought concerning heroes and such demons.* We must ask of him what he wishes to be understood by "heroes," and what he calls "demons of this kind"; so that one serving one hero ought not to serve another, and one serving such a demon should beware of serving another; otherwise he would offend the prior master of the demons, no differently than happens among men if someone takes another master besides the first. Now truly, if he thinks any detriment happens to heroes or demons from this, let him show it: for he will be forced either to fall into a sea of trifles and thus make his own words void; or, if he is loath to trifle, to openly confess that he knows neither the nature of heroes nor of demons. Now truly, as far as it pertains to men—that the first master is harmed if his servant wishes to serve another—Celsus must be asked in what matter he thinks the first is harmed by a servant taking to himself another master. For if he should answer like an unlearned man <term>idiotice: in the manner of a common person without philosophical training</term>, that the loss is not at all philosophical but a detriment of money (which is among external things and not properly our own), he will show himself to be ignorant of that noble saying of Socrates: *Anytus and Melitus can indeed kill me, but they cannot harm me: for [it is not permitted that] a better [man be harmed by a worse].* <margin>Plato's Apology</margin>

<column-break/>

->**Greek Text**<-

...to God alone (as a man seems to be harmed by one serving another along with him) by declining to serve any other than God through His Word and His truth; but rather so that we might not be harmed by separating ourselves from the portion of the God over all, as those living in a manner familiar to His blessedness by the special spirit of adoption. God is among the sons of the Father in heaven, to those crying out not with mere phrases, but with deeds in a loud voice according to what is hidden: "Abba, Father." <margin>Romans 8:15</margin> Thus, while the ambassadors of the Lacedaemonians did not prostrate before the King of the Persians, even though the bodyguards pressured them greatly, because they feared their one lord, the law of Lycurgus; those who serve a much greater and more divine embassy on behalf of Christ would prostrate to neither the ruler of the Persians, nor of the Greeks, nor of the Egyptians, nor of any nation whatsoever, even if the bodyguards of the rulers—demons and angels of the devil—should wish to compel them to do this, and persuade them to say a long farewell to the Law that is better than every law upon the earth. For Christ is the Lord of the ambassadors of Christ, on whose behalf they serve as ambassadors, being the Word who was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God. <margin>John 1:1</margin> Then, since Celsus thought fit to move a certain deeper argument (as it appeared to him) concerning heroes and certain demons, saying—not the argument about service to men—"that the first is harmed if someone wants to serve, if he should wish to serve a second also," and that the same would be the case "concerning both heroes and such demons"; we must inquire of him: what does he mean by "heroes"? And what kind of beings does he say these "demons" are? Such that one serving this hero must not serve another, and one serving such a demon must not serve another; as if the first demon were harmed in a manner analogous to men being harmed when someone takes a second. But if he thinks there is even some harm to the hero or to such a demon, let him only demonstrate it. For he will be forced either to fall into a sea of nonsense and take back his word, or to reject what has been said; or, not wishing to talk nonsense, to confess that he understands neither heroes nor the nature of demons. Regarding the argument about men, that the first is harmed if one serves a second, it must be asked: what kind of harm does he say happens to the first man, if the one serving him should wish to serve another also? For if he should speak as a common person, signifying a non-philosophical harm concerning external riches, he would be convicted of not even understanding what was well said by Socrates: "Anytus and Melitus can indeed kill me, but they cannot harm me." For [it is not possible for] the better [to be harmed by the worse]. <margin>Plato's Apology</margin>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

<margin>
* something, No one.

</margin>
...to be harmed by the inferior. But if by "harm" he means wickedness or a state of being according to it, it is clear that, since no harm comes to the wise, they could serve two wise men in different places. But if this is reasonable, then his citation of the quote, <quote>No one can serve two masters,</quote> <note>Matthew 6:24</note> was taken up by him in vain. Rather, the one who offers service to the God of all things alone would, for this reason, be held by God alone. Furthermore, we shall not worship God as if he were in need, or as if he would be grieved if we did not worship him; rather, we ourselves are benefited by the worship of God, becoming free from grief and passion through our service to the God over all, through his only-begotten Word and Wisdom. But see how he still speaks unclearly: <quote>For even if you should worship something else in the universe,</quote> in which he suggests that we might offer worship to something else besides Divine things without any harm to ourselves. But he immediately undermines himself, having spoken unsoundly, saying, "For even if you should worship something else in the universe," and then he repeats and offers a correction, <margin>* contains.</margin> *containing the statement: <quote>in this matter it is not even permitted for anyone to be honored to whom this has not been given by Him.</quote> And let us ask Celsus about those honored as gods, or demons, or heroes: from where or how is it demonstrated that they have been granted the right to be honored by God, and not rather from human ignorance and lack of learning by those who fashion and suppose them to be properly honored? For he asks—as you were saying a moment ago, O Celsus—about Hadrian’s favorite <note>Antinous, the youth loved by Emperor Hadrian, who was deified after his death.</note>; and surely you will not say that it was granted by the God of all things for Antinous to be honored as a God. We shall say the same about the others, demanding proof regarding the honor granted to them by the God over all. But if he should bring a similar objection against us concerning Jesus, we shall demonstrate that the right to be honored was given to him by God, so that <quote>all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father.</quote> <note>John 5:23</note> For the prophecies concerning his birth were the foundations of his honor. Moreover, the wonders performed by him were not by sorcery (as Celsus thinks) but by divinity witnessed by the prophets, so that those who honor the Son—who is the Word <note>Greek: Logos</note>—doing nothing irrational, may benefit from honoring him; and by honoring him who is Truth, they may become better by honoring the Truth. We decline to revere and worship these, whom other men worship as if they were servants (for we have been taught that they are servants of that [evil] one); and we say that the gods of the nations are demons. <margin>1 John 4:10</margin>

<margin>Hebrews 4:15</margin>
prayers, sacrifices, and intercessions to the God over all. Hence our faith rests in God, through his Son who confirms it in us; and Celsus cannot show any "sedition" <note>or "factionalism"</note> among us concerning the Son of God.

"How is it that there are many around the well, and no one in the well? Why, after completing such a journey, are you cowardly? It escapes you; for courage and a sword are at your side." <note>These cryptic lines appear to be Gnostic passwords or ritual formulas that Celsus is mocking.</note> Such is their stated purpose: positing another God * beyond the Father, a super-celestial one whom they worship in silence so that they may play the divine under a grand pretext; but they worship only the one presiding, the Son of Man, whom they declare to be stronger than and lord over the God who holds dominion. From this comes their commandment: not to serve two masters, so that this rebellion may be kept unshaken. And in these matters again—having taken these ideas from I know not what most obscure sect—he accuses all Christians based on them. I say "most obscure" because even to us, who have frequently practiced debating those from the sects, the opinion from which Celsus took these things is not clear; if indeed he took them at all, and did not invent them or add them as a supposed consequence.

But we clearly, who say that the Son created all things and the visible world, say that the Son is not stronger than the Father, but inferior. <note>Origen uses the term "inferior" (hypodeesteron) here in a functional or subordinatist sense common in early theology before the Council of Nicaea.</note> And we say this, obeying Him when He said: *The Father, who sent me, is greater than I.* <margin>John 14:28</margin> And none of us is so thunderstruck <note>original: ἐμβρόντητός (embrontētos) - literally "struck by thunder," meaning insane or senseless.</note> as to say that the Son of Man is Lord over God. We say the Savior has dominion especially when we understand Him as God the Word, and Wisdom, and Justice, and Truth, over all things subjected to Him in those capacities; but certainly not over the Father and God who holds dominion over Him.

Furthermore, since the Word rules over those who are not unwilling, and there are still some who are wicked—not only men, but also angels and all demons—we say He does not yet rule over these, since they do not yield to Him willingly. But according to another meaning of "ruling," He rules even them, just as we say man rules over irrational animals, not because he has subdued their governing faculty, but as he rules over certain lions and tamed beasts by taming them. Nevertheless, He does everything so that, by persuading even those who do not obey Him, He may rule over them as well. According to us, therefore, what is said by Celsus is a lie, as if reported by us: "Who else shall lord it over the God who holds dominion?"

Again, I think, mixing things up, he brings from another sect the saying: "Many around the well, and no one in the well"; and "Why, after completing such a journey, are you cowardly? It escapes you"; and "For courage and a sword are at your side." We, who belong to the Church named after Christ, say none of these things are true. These seem to be the words of characters he has invented to follow his own logic, which he claims are directed at us. For our purpose is not to worship some God based on a hypothesis, but the Creator of this universe, and not to [conceive of another...]

Whence comes that solemn precept of theirs, *One must not serve two Masters*; taking care lest anyone lose faith in this one. These things again, taken from I know not what most obscure heresy, he charges against all Christians: I call it most obscure, however, because it is not clear even to us, who have struggled much with heretics, from where Celsus received these things: if indeed he received them, and did not devise them, or add them as a sequel to the matter.

For we manifestly preach that the Son of the Creator, who fashioned this sensible world, is not stronger than the Father, but inferior. This we affirm from His own authority when He says, *The Father, who sent me, is greater than I*: nor is any of us so mad as to say, the Son of Man is the Lord of God. However, we ascribe dominion to Him, as the Word of God, wisdom, justice, and truth, over all who look up to Him by this name; but not over God the Father Almighty: and because the Word does not command the unwilling, and there are moreover certain evil ones, not only men, but also angels, and all demons, we say He does not yet have dominion over these, because they do not submit themselves of their own accord. Yet in another sense of dominion He also rules these, just as we say man rules over brute animals, although they are not so subject as tamed lions and broken beasts of burden: yet there is nothing He does not do to subject even those who now reject His dominion. It is false, therefore, what Celsus brought forward as if it were ours: *Who else shall lord it over the almighty God?* Then, as I think, again confusing matters, he mixes in from another heresy those words, *Many around the well, no one in the well?* and those, *Why, having measured out so much of a journey, are you fearful?* and those, *You are deceived, boldness and a sword are present with me*: all of which the Church of the Christian name regards as adulterated. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

...who enter upon another way or other paths, denying this one, and adopting for themselves a new fiction—God in name only—as if he were superior to the Creator of all things; and if there are any who affirm that the Son, as if he were stronger, is the Lord of the Almighty God. However, we have already given the reason why one must not serve two masters, when we also taught that no charge of sedition can be brought on account of the Lord Jesus, since all who confess him as superior rule over all, and that we ought to serve him alone as the Son of God. After this, Celsus says *that we flee from the dedication of altars, statues, and temples, so that we may confirm the faith of a hidden covenant by this as a token*; <note>original: "tessera" - a small tablet used as a token or password among members of a group.</note> not seeing that for us, each person's own mind serves as an altar, from which are sent up truly and intelligibly sweet-smelling incense—prayers from a pure conscience. Therefore it is said by John, in the Apocalypse, *The incense is the prayers of the Saints*; <margin>Revelation 5:8</margin> and in the Davidic hymns, *Let my prayer be set forth as incense in thy sight, O Lord*. <margin>Psalm 141:2 (Vulgate 140)</margin> Moreover, the statues to be dedicated to God are not the works of craftsmen, but are carved and formed in us by the word of God—namely, the virtues in imitation of the firstborn of all creation, in whom are the examples of justice, temperance, fortitude, wisdom, piety, and the rest of the virtues. These are the statues dedicated to God in the souls of those who practice justice according to the command of God, and fortitude, and piety, and the remaining virtues; by which we believe the first archetype of all such statues, the image of the invisible God, the only-begotten God, is fittingly honored. <margin>Colossians 1:15; John 1:18</margin> Indeed, those who have put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator, <margin>Colossians 3:9, 10</margin> having received this image, they make statues in themselves such as the best and greatest God delights in. And just as among the makers of statues the works of some excel even to the point of a miracle—as, for example, those of Phidias, or Polycletus, or among painters Zeuxis and Apelles—while those of others are less good, and again others even worse; in short, there is a vast difference between the preparation of statues and images. In the same way, there are those who make excellent statues of God, the Lord of all things, through the most perfect knowledge, to which the Olympian Jupiter of Phidias could be seen as of no value if compared to the beautifully represented image of God the Creator. But in all of creation, this has happened to no one more happily or excel-

<column-break/>

...or those walking another way or other paths, and denying this one, having introduced for themselves a new-fashioned fiction under the name of God alone, as if greater than the Creator, and if anyone says in succession that the Son is stronger than the Lord of those whom God rules. We have demonstrated the reasoning that appears to us regarding the fact that one must not serve two masters; at which time we also established that no sedition has arisen among those who acknowledge that the Lord of all has ascended, and that we must serve the Son of God as the only Lord. After these things Celsus says, "That we avoid setting up altars and statues and temples; since he thinks the faith of our hidden and secret society is a token." <note>original: "σύνθημα" (synthema) - a sign, signal, or secret password.</note> He fails to see that our altars are the mind <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) - the "ruling faculty" or inner spirit of a person.</note> of each of the righteous, from which are sent up truly and intelligibly sweet-smelling incense, prayers from a pure conscience. Therefore it is said by John in the Apocalypse, *The incense is the prayers of the saints*; and by the Psalmist, *Let my prayer be as incense before thee*. And the statues and offerings fitting for God are not prepared by mechanical craftsmen, but are fashioned and formed in us by the Word of God—the virtues, being imitations of the firstborn of all creation, in whom are the patterns of justice, and temperance, and courage, and wisdom, and piety, and the rest of the virtues. In all those, therefore (who have prepared for themselves temperance according to the divine Word, and justice, and courage, and wisdom, and piety, and the preparations of the rest of the virtues), there are statues; by which we are persuaded it is fitting to honor the archetype of all statues, the image of the invisible God, the only-begotten God. But also those who strip off the old man with his practices, and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him, taking up the things according to the image of his creator, they make statues in themselves such as the God over all desires. For just as among the statue-makers, some have wonderfully succeeded in the work, as we might say Phidias, or Polycletus, or the painters Zeuxis and Apelles; while others make a lesser statue, and others still lesser than these, and once and for all there is a great difference in the preparation of statues and images; in the same way there are some who make statues to the God over all better and according to perfect knowledge, so that there is no comparison between the Olympian Zeus prepared by Phidias and that prepared according to the image of the Creator God. Such men have not even considered what should be thought about God, or about the statues, temples, or altars that are fitting for Him. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.
## Page 393

Whoever can truly say, *We have risen together with Christ*, and that other saying, *He has raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ* <margin>Colossians 2:12; Ephesians 2:6</margin>, always keeps the days of Pentecost; especially when, ascending into the upper room as did the Apostles of Jesus, he devotes himself to prayers and supplications <margin>Acts 1:13, 14</margin>, so that he may become worthy of that rushing mighty heavenly wind which by its force drives out wickedness and its works from men, and likewise becomes worthy to receive from God some portion of the tongues of fire <margin>Acts 2:2, 3, 4</margin>. 

But the common crowd of those who seem to be believers more than they actually are—who either cannot or will not keep a feast every day—needs to be held together by such sensory reminders <note>i.e., specific calendar holidays</note>, lest they slip away entirely from their duty. Thinking of these things, I believe, Paul used the phrase "in part of a feast" <margin>Colossians 2:16</margin> to name a feast recurring on fixed days as compared to that other perpetual feast. He suggests by these words that eternal life consists not in a "part of a feast day," but in a continuous and complete festival, just as the holy Scripture teaches. 

Therefore, look again: when those things we have said about celebrated days are compared with the public feasts of Celsus and the heathens, are not our feasts far superior to those public ones? In those pagan feasts, the "wisdom of the flesh" <note>original Latin: *sapientia carnis*; Greek: *phronema tes sarkos*—referring to worldly or carnal thinking</note> takes a holiday and runs riot, petulantly indulging in drunkenness and lusts. It would be a long task at this time to explain why it was ordained in the feasts of the Divine Law to eat the "bread of affliction," or unleavened bread with bitter herbs <margin>Deuteronomy 16:3; Exodus 12:8</margin>; or that which is said, *Humble your souls* <margin>Leviticus 16:29, 31</margin>, or other similar things. For it is impossible for a man, since he is a composite being and *the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh* <margin>Galatians 5:17</margin>, to celebrate a feast in his entirety. For either someone keeping a feast in the spirit afflicts his body (which, because of the pride of the flesh, is not naturally suited to celebrate a feast with the spirit), or one taking a holiday according to the flesh is not capable of a spiritual feast. Let it suffice to have said these things about feasts for the present.

Now let us see with what words Celsus tries to persuade us not to abstain from things sacrificed to idols <term>idolothyta: food, usually meat, that had been offered to pagan gods before being sold or eaten</term>. *If idols*, he says, *are nothing, what harm is there in joining the public banquets? But if there are certain demons, without a doubt these too belong to God, and they should be believed in, and sacrificed to according to the laws; prayers should also be offered so that they might be favorable.* 

Here it will be worthwhile to take into one's hands that whole passage in the first Pauline epistle written to the Corinthians and to interpret it. There, meeting those who say an idol is nothing in the nature of things, he teaches those who are capable of understanding how this sin is more grievous

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

* We shall be satisfied with etc. by few proofs.
</margin>
For he who partakes of things sacrificed to idols destroys his brother, for whom Christ died. And by establishing that what is sacrificed is sacrificed to demons, he shows that those who partake of the table of demons become companions of demons; and he demonstrates that it is impossible for one to partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons. But since the explanation of these matters in the Epistle to the Corinthians requires a complete treatise, being demonstrated through many points, * we shall be satisfied even with what has been briefly rendered; in which the examination itself will show that, even if idols are nothing, it is nonetheless a terrible thing to share in the banquets of idols. For it has been stated by us in a moderate fashion that even if there are certain demons to whom the sacrifices are offered, we who understand the difference between the Lord’s table and the table of demons should partake of nothing belonging to them; and because of this understanding, we do everything so that we may always partake of the Lord’s table, and guard ourselves in every way so that we never become companions of the table of demons. Since Celsus says in these passages, “That surely demons belong to God, and for this reason they must be believed, and sacrifices must be offered to them according to the laws, and they must be prayed to so that they may be favorable;” those who wish to know must be taught regarding this, that the Word of God does not wish to proclaim any of the wicked to be a possession of God, judging such a thing unworthy of so great a title. For either all men are called men of God, or only those worthy of God. Such a one was Moses, and Elijah, and whoever else is recorded as a man of God, or is analogous to those so recorded. And let it be that all angels are called angels of God, yet only the blessed ones; but those who have fallen into wickedness are named angels of the devil; just as wicked men are called men of sin, and pests, or sons of unrighteousness. Since, therefore, among men some are upright and others are wicked—and some are said to be of God and others of the devil—so also among angels, some are of God, and others are the evil ones called demons; which was shown there, for all are demonstrated to be wicked. For this reason, we shall say that the statement of Celsus is false when he says, “If there are certain demons, it is clear that these also belong to God;” or let anyone who wishes show, by not accepting the logic regarding the division of men and angels, that a similar logic can be demonstrated to apply to demons. But if this is impossible, it is clear that demons do not “belong to God.” For God is not their ruler, but (as the divine words say) Beelzebub <note>original: "Beelzebul"</note>. Nor should demons be believed, even if Celsus exhorts us to do so; but—

Deuteronomy 33:1
2 Kings 1:10

Matthew 25:41
Hosea 10:9
2 Peter 1:21

—from things sacrificed to idols he loses a brother, for whom Christ died; where also, presupposing that those victims are sacrificed to demons, he teaches that participants in them communicate with demons, and that it is impossible for the same person to participate in the Lord’s table and the table of demons. But, because this matter needs an entire volume if this passage of the Epistle to the Corinthians were to be treated at greater length, we will be content with a few points: even if idols are nothing, yet it becomes a grave sin <term>piaculum: an act requiring expiation or a grave sin</term> to be present at their feast. Now certainly we have discussed in a moderate way that even if there are demons to whom victims are sacrificed, we ought not to become participants in those sacred rites, since we know the difference between the Lord’s table and the table of demons; and knowing this, let us do everything so that, always participating in the Lord’s table, we may by all means beware of communication with the table of demons. Moreover, since Celsus just said, *That even demons belong to God, and therefore they should be believed and sacrificed to according to law, and prayed to so that they may wish to be favorable;* let those who desire also learn about this, that it is the custom of the Sacred Scriptures that they call nothing of evil things the possession of God, as things which are by no means held worthy of so great a master. Wherefore not even all men are called men of God, but only those who are worthy of God; such as was Moses and Elijah, and if any other man is described, or is similar to these of whom it is written. Likewise, not all angels are called angels of God, but only the blessed: otherwise those who have turned to malice are named angels of the devil: just as evil men are called men of sin or sons, pests or sons of injustice. Since therefore men, while being partly good and partly evil, some are said to be of God, others of the devil; and some angels of God, others of that evil one; but demons are not so doubled, for it is demonstrated that all are evil: therefore we shall say that the speech of Celsus is false when he says, *that if there are certain demons, without a doubt these also are of God:* or let him who wishes demonstrate that our distinction concerning men and angels is not sound, or that in the same way a distinction can be found among demons. If that is impossible, it is clear that demons are not of God: for their prince is not God, but, as sacred Scripture testifies, Beelzebub. Nor must demons be believed, even if Celsus encourages us to this, but rather one should die sooner, and endure anything rather than believe a demon, nay even bravely—

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.

[Signature: Eee 2]

...bravely, by standing firm in the faith of God. Thus, one must not offer favorable sacrifices to demons; indeed, it is not even possible to sacrifice favorably to them, since they are evil and harmful to men. Now, according to what laws does Celsus wish us to sacrifice to demons? For if it is according to those laws accepted in the cities, let him show that these harmonize with the divine laws. If he cannot do this (since even the civil laws here do not agree among themselves), it is clear that they are not even properly laws, since they are evil, and consequently they are not to be obeyed. For one must obey God rather than men. <margin>Acts 5:29</margin> Away with this advice of Celsus ordering demons to be adored! He is not to be listened to even in the slightest degree; for God, the Best and Greatest, alone is to be adored, and prayers are to be offered to the only-begotten Word of God alone, the firstborn of all creation <note>original: "primogenito creaturæ totius"</note>, so that he, as High Priest, may carry them to his God and our God, and to his Father and the Father of all those living according to his word. And just as we would not desire for ourselves the favor of men who wish to draw us into evil habits, if they were benevolent to no one from the faction opposed to them (because their benevolence makes us enemies to God, who perhaps would not be benevolent to those having such "benevolent" friends); so those who know the nature, will, and malice of demons will never desire their benevolence for themselves. For even if the demons do not wish them well, they can inflict no evil upon those guarded because of their piety by their own God and the Lord of all, who appoints his angels to the protection of those who are worthy, lest they be harmed by demons. But whoever has the Lord God propitious because of his piety toward Him, and—having received Jesus the Lord, the Angel of Great Counsel <note>original: "consilii magni angelum," a traditional title for Christ in early theology</note>—is content with the favor of God through Jesus Christ, can say confidently, as one who will suffer nothing even from the entire army of demons: *The Lord is my light and my Savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid?* <margin>Psalm 27:1 (Vulgate 26:1)</margin> He will also say this: *If a whole camp should set its battle line against me, my heart shall not fear.* Thus far in response to the words of Celsus saying, *“That if there are certain demons, without a doubt these too are of God, whom one must both believe in and sacrifice to according to the laws; prayers must also be offered so that they might be propitious.”* Let us now approach what follows next and examine it according to our strength; it goes thus: *“Certainly, if some ancestral custom restrains these men from sacrifices, they ought to abstain entirely from the eating of living creatures, as seemed right to Pythagoras, who honored the soul and its instruments. But if the cause is...”*

-> [The Word forbids us to eat what has been strangled, because] <-

What has been said regarding the strangled animal sufficiently indicates the reason for abstaining from blood. Nor would it be out of place here to remember a beautiful sentiment found in Sextus <note>The "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of ethical aphorisms popular among early Christians.</note>, celebrated by many Christians: it goes like this, *The eating of living creatures is indeed a matter of indifference, yet to abstain is better and seems more agreeable to reason.* Therefore, it is not rashly or merely out of ancestral custom that we abstain from those things sacrificed to the commonly believed gods, or heroes, or demons; rather, we are moved by many reasons, part of which we have already set forth. But one must not abstain from the eating of all living creatures in the same way one must abstain from malice or its works. Indeed, we must abstain not only from the eating of animals, but from anything whatsoever if it is not permitted to eat without sin: (for we must not eat to indulge the throat, enticed by delicacies, but to care for the body for the sake of health,) although we are far from the opinion of the soul changing bodies <note>The doctrine of metempsychosis or reincarnation.</note> and falling even into brute cattle; lest we abstain from meat in the manner of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who avoided meat due to belief in the transmigration of souls.</note> to spare the animals. For we know how to honor only rational souls, and we deem their instruments <note>i.e., the human body.</note> worthy of the honor of solemn burial; for the dwelling-place of a rational soul deserves not to be cast aside rashly, like the carcasses of brutes; and especially because these [Christians] trust that the body is to be honored, which was the dwelling of the rational soul, and they esteem it for the sake of the one who received the soul that used such an instrument beautifully in its struggle. Furthermore, how the dead rise, and with what body they come, we have taught above in a few words, as the treatise required. Presently, Celsus brings forward that common response, shared by Christians and Jews, that they abstain from things sacrificed to idols <term>idolothytis: food offered to pagan deities</term> lest those consecrated to God feast with demons; which he attempts to refute. We certainly, as far as food and drink are concerned, know no other way of feasting with demons than if someone in a crowd eats the entrails of victims and drinks the wine poured out to demons: but Celsus thinks that even those who enjoy the fruits of the earth feast with demons, and whatever wine they drink, and the fruits of trees they taste; or if someone takes only water, he says this person also participates with demons by drinking: and he adds that even the air we breathe consists of demons.

One must abstain not only from the eating of animals, but also from every thought, if we should use food for malice and the things of malice; (for one must abstain from eating for gluttony, or insofar as we are led by pleasure, apart from receiving them for the care of the health of the body,) by no means, however, speaking of the reincarnation of the soul, and its descent as far as the irrational animals; for which reason those like Pythagoras might at some time abstain from animals, or we might use their flesh. Concerning how the dead are raised, and in what body they come, we have presented in the above in a few words (as the writing required). After these things, Celsus sets down the response admittedly spoken by Christians and Jews, defending the abstinence from things sacrificed to idols, and saying that those dedicated to the God over all must not feast with demons; he says what is set forth. <meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s claim that Christians are ungrateful to the local deities (demons) who control earthly resources. Origen argues that all physical sustenance comes from God via His angels, not from demons.</meta>

# Book 8. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...they fall into such impiety that they do away with providence <note>The Stoic and Platonic concept of *Providentia* or divine care for the world.</note>. Therefore, we do not receive the individual necessities of life from demons, especially those of us who have learned to use them properly; nor do those who enjoy the fruits of the earth, wine, the fruits of trees, water, and air feast with demons. Rather, we attribute these things to the angels of God, who are, in a sense, invited within the domestic walls of the pious man who holds to that precept: <margin>1 Cor. 10:31</margin> *Whether you eat or drink, do all to the glory of God*; and again elsewhere: <margin>Col. 3:17</margin> *Do all things in the name of God*. While, therefore, we eat, drink, breathe, and do all other things by the same principle for the glory of God, we do not feast with any demon, but with the angels of God. <margin>1 Tim. 4:4, 5</margin> *For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer*. It would not have been fitting, nor lawful, for these things to be consecrated if they had been committed to the care of demons. From this, the answer is now clear even to those things which follow in this manner: *Therefore, either one must not live anywhere at all, nor come into this life, or, since one has come into life on this condition, thanks must be given to the demons who have been allotted the governorships of earthly things, and prayers and first-fruits must be offered to them as long as we live, so that we may have them present and favorable.* On the contrary, we must live in such a way that life is established according to divine precepts, as far as it can be done and as far as it is granted to us; and it is granted if, in eating, drinking, and finally doing all things, we do them for the glory of God. Nor should we despise the gifts of the Creator, but use them with thanksgiving. For we come into life on this condition—not the one Celsus imagines—and we are not subject to demons, but to God the Lord of all, having been reconciled to Him through Jesus Christ. And by the law of God, no demon has been allotted the governorship of earthly things; but perhaps because of their own malice, certain places have been assigned to them where there is no knowledge of God and the pious life, or where all things are foreign to His worship; perhaps the Word, the moderator of all things, appointed them as suitable presiding officers and torturers of the wicked, so that they might rule over those who, despising God, prefer to serve their own vices. Wherefore, let Celsus also, being ignorant of God, pay his vows to demons; but we, who study to please the Creator of all things, eat the loaves offered with prayers and thanksgiving for the benefits received—loaves which, through prayer, have become a certain holy body that sanctifies those who use it with a sound purpose. Celsus...

<column-break/>

...desire, to increase the impious doctrines against providence. For we would not have the things taken for the needs of life from demons, especially those who have learned to use them properly; nor do those who partake of grain, wine, fruits, water, and air feast with demons; but rather with divine angels who are appointed over such things, who are, as it were, called upon by those who live holily and piously, and who listen to the Word teaching such things: <margin>1 Cor. 10:31</margin> *Whether you eat, or drink, or do anything, do all to the glory of God*; and again it is placed in another spot: <margin>Col. 3:17</margin> *Do all things in the name of God*. When, therefore, we eat and drink and breathe to the glory of God, and do all things according to the Word, we feast with no one of the demons, but with the divine angels. <margin>1 Tim. 4:4, 5</margin> *For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, being received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and intercession*. It would not be good, nor ordained to be sanctified, if (as Celsus thinks) these things had been entrusted to demons. From these things it is clear that we shall also meet his subsequent arguments which are as follows: *Either, then, one must not live anywhere in any way, nor come here [into life], or, having come into life on these terms, one must give thanks to the demons who have been allotted the things on earth, and render first-fruits and prayers as long as we live, so that we may find them to be lovers of mankind.* And we must live, among ourselves, and live according to the Word of God as much as is possible and as it is given to live according to it; and it is given also when, whether we eat or whether we drink, we do all to the glory of God. And we must not refuse the good things of thanksgiving to the Creator who fashioned them for our sake. And we have come into life by God on these terms rather than on those which Celsus thinks; and we are not subject to demons, but to the God over all through Jesus Christ who brought us to Him. And <margin>* law.</margin> by the law of God, no demon has been allotted the things on earth; but through their own wickedness, perhaps places were assigned to them where there is a desert of the knowledge of God and of the life according to Him, or where there is much that is foreign to the divine; and perhaps as being worthy of the wicked and their punishers, they were appointed by the Word who administers all things to rule over those who subjected themselves to vice and not to God. And because of such things, let Celsus, as one ignorant of God, render the thank-offerings to demons; but we, pleasing the Creator of the universe, also eat the loaves offered with thanksgiving and prayer over the things given, which become a body <note>original: "σῶμα" (soma). Origen is referring to the bread of the Eucharist.</note> through prayer, a certain holy thing and sanctifying those who use it with a healthy intent. But also first-fruits Celsus...

<summary>Origen argues that Christians do not owe gratitude to demons for the necessities of life, as all creation belongs to God and is sanctified through prayer. # ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

->**ORIGENES contra CELSUM. Lib. 8.**<-

<margin>Genesis 1:11</margin> Celsus wishes to attribute things to demons, but we attribute them to the One who said: *Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed according to its kind and likeness, and the fruit tree yielding fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth.* <note>Origen quotes the Septuagint version of the Creation story to emphasize God's sovereignty over nature.</note> To Him we also give the first-fruits, and to Him we send up our prayers, having a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God; and let us hold fast to this confession as long as we live, <margin>Hebrews 4:14</margin> <margin>* obtaining.</margin> by the * loving-kindness of God and of His only-begotten Son Jesus, who has been manifested among us. And if we also desire a multitude of those whose favor we wish to obtain, we learn that *thousand thousands stood before Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand <margin>Daniel 7:10</margin> ministered to Him.* These beings, seeing those who imitate their own piety toward God as kin and friends, cooperate in the salvation of those who call upon God and pray sincerely; appearing, and as it were, sensing the need to be present for the benefit and salvation of those praying to God, to whom they themselves also pray. For <margin>Hebrews 1:14</margin> *they are all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation.* Now, let the wise men of the Greeks say that "demons" <note>The Greek word *daimones* here refers to guardian spirits or lesser deities, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> have been allotted to the human soul from birth; but Jesus taught us not to despise even the little ones in the church, <margin>Matthew 18:10</margin> saying that *Their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.* <margin>Psalms 33:7</margin> And the prophet also says: *The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him, and will deliver them.* We do not, therefore, deny that there are many demons on earth, but we say that they exist and have power among the wicked because of their vice; but they have no power against those who <margin>Ephesians 6:11-12</margin> have put on the full armor of God and have taken up strength to stand against the wiles of the devil, and who always study their wrestling-moves, knowing that *our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly places.* Let us also consider another statement of Celsus: how they poured out, "Or if a satrap <note>A provincial governor in the ancient Persian Empire; used here as a metaphor for spiritual subordinates.</note> of the King of the Persians or Romans, or a prefect, or a general, or a procurator, or even those holding smaller offices or cares or services, could do great harm if neglected; then the satraps and ministers of God in the air and on earth would also do harm if insulted." See how humanly he creates satraps of the God over all, and prefects, and generals, and procurators, and the more specific offices and cares and services

<column-break/>

indeed he also wishes us to dedicate the first-fruits to demons: but we prefer to hold this honor for Him who said, *Let the earth sprout green herb bringing forth seed according to its kind & its likeness, & the fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind on the earth.* To Him, moreover, we offer the first-fruits, to the same we also direct our vows and prayers, having a great high priest, who has penetrated the heavens, *Jesus the son of God himself:* & we constantly retain this profession of faith, as long as we live by the kindness of God, and of his son, who was manifested among us. Because if the favor of many is also to be sought, we learn in our literature, that *thousands of thousands assisted him, & myriads of myriads ministered to him.* Which multitude, when it sees men imitating its own piety toward God, helps those striving for salvation & invoking God; sometimes by appearing to those praying, not deeming it an unworthy thing if it lends ears to them, and by agreement dwells on earth to gratify the invokers of the celestial divinity, to whom it also does not cease to offer prayers. *For all these are administrative spirits, sent into ministry on account of those, who will take the inheritance of salvation.* Although the wise of the Greeks affirm that to each of those being born his own demon falls by a certain lot: Jesus taught us that not even the least are to be despised in the Church, saying, *that their angels always behold his father, who is in the heavens;* The Prophet also says, *The angel of the Lord will encircle with a rampart those fearing him, & will rescue them.* Therefore not even we deny that there are many demons on earth, but we confess them to be, and to be able to do much against the evil on account of their malice: but to be able to do nothing against those, who have clothed themselves in the armor of God, and have received strength for resisting the devil trying to circumvent them, having meditated on contests of this kind; as those who know *that for us there is no struggle against flesh & blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of this world, against the wicked spirits of this air.* Let us see furthermore also another saying of Celsus such as, *Unless perhaps a satrap of the King of the Persians or Romans, or a governor, or a leader, or a procurator, or even someone bearing a lesser magistracy or custom or care and ministry, being neglected can hurt much: the aerial and terrestrial satraps and ministers can do little harm when injuries are received.* See in what manner after the fashion of men he makes satraps of the highest God, & governors, & leaders, & procurators, & lesser magistracies, and lesser ministries

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

introduces [beings] who cause great harm to those who insult them; not realizing that not even a wise man would wish to hurt anyone, being much more inclined to correct even the insolent—unless perhaps these "satraps" <note>A Persian term for a provincial governor, used here by Celsus to describe subordinate deities or spirits.</note>, governors, and generals of the Best and Greatest God, as Celsus calls them, are worse than Lycurgus the Spartan legislator and Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoic philosophy.</note>. Of these, Lycurgus, when the man who had struck out his eye was delivered into his power, was so far from avenging such a grave injury that he did not stop charming the man with wholesome warnings until he had induced him to take up philosophy. And Zeno, when an enemy said, *May I perish if I do not do you an evil*, replied, *And may I perish if I do not win you over to me*. I say nothing of those formed by the discipline of Jesus, to whom it was said, *Love your enemies, pray for those who curse you; that you may be children of your heavenly father, who commands his sun to rise upon the evil and the good, and rains upon the just and the unjust*. In the Prophetic oracles also, the just man speaks thus: *O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who repaid it to me: let me fall empty before my enemies, let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the earth*. 

But Celsus is mistaken; the true satraps, governors, generals, and stewards of God—the angels—do not harm insolent men. If any do harm, they are from the number of those evil ones whom Celsus also imagined, who have no satrapy or stewardship committed to them by God. They harm those who are subject to them, who have voluntarily submitted themselves to them as if to masters. This is, I believe, why in certain regions those who eat forbidden foods—if they are subjects of those demons—do not go unpunished; but if a stranger does the same, who does not subject himself to their dominion, he is free from the guilt, bidding those demons farewell. For while others, devoted to them through ignorance, may be subject to their injuries, certainly the Christian (who is truly a Christian, dedicated to the one God and His Word) cannot be harmed by demons, being superior to them. He is not harmed because the angel of the Lord will encamp round about those who fear Him and will deliver them; and his angel, perpetually beholding the face of the heavenly Father, always offers his prayers to heaven through the only high priest to the supreme God, himself also praying for the one committed to his charge. Therefore, let Celsus take away his "bogeymen" <note>original: "terriculamenta" / "μορμολυττέσθω" — referring to scary stories used to frighten children.</note>, threatening evil from demons whom we despise; for to us nothing—

<column-break/>

introduces [beings] having great power to harm those who insult them; not seeing that not even a wise man would wish to harm anyone, but (as much as is in his power) seeks to turn back and improve even the insolent. Unless perhaps the satraps, prefects, and generals of the God over all, according to Celsus, are worse than Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian legislator and Zeno of Citium. For Lycurgus, having received power over the one <margin>* Namely Alexander. Plutarch in Lycurgus.</margin> who knocked out his eye, not only did not take revenge, but did not stop soothing him with incantations until he persuaded him to practice philosophy. And Zeno, to one who said in anger, *May I perish if I do not <margin>Lacuna [gap] filled from the same Plutarch.</margin> punish you*, said, *[May I perish] if I do not make you a friend*. And I do not yet speak of those fashioned according to the teaching of Jesus, who heard the command, <margin>Matthew 5:44, 45.</margin> *Love your enemies and pray for those who spitefully use you; so that you may become sons of your Father who is in heaven*, who <margin>* "because", in the same place.</margin> makes His sun rise on the evil and the good, and rains on the just and the unjust. And in the prophetic words the just man says such things as: <margin>Psalm 7:3, 4, 5.</margin> *Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is unrighteousness in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me; then let me fall away empty from my enemies, let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground*. 

But now (as Celsus thinks) the true satraps, prefects, generals, and stewards of God—the angels—harm those who insult them. But if certain demons harm people, whom Celsus also imagined, they harm them as being wicked, having been entrusted with no satrapy, generalship, or stewardship by God; and they harm those who are subject to them and who have subordinated themselves to them as to masters. For perhaps this is why those in each place who observe the customary forbidden foods, if they are under those demons, are harmed by them; but if any are outside their influence, not having subordinated themselves to the local demon, they are free from suffering their effects, having bid a long farewell to such demons. Others, having subordinated themselves through ignorance, are able to suffer by them; but the Christian (the true Christian, who has subordinated himself to God alone and His Word) would not suffer anything from the demons, since he happens to be better than demons. He would not suffer, since *The angel of the Lord will encamp round about those who fear <margin>Psalm 33:7.</margin> Him, and will deliver them*, and his angel, always seeing the face of the Father in <margin>Matthew 18:10.</margin> heaven, always brings up his prayers through the only High Priest to the God of all, himself praying together with the one under his care. Therefore, let Celsus not try to scare us like children with "bogeymen," threatening harm from the demons who are neglected by us; for to us the demons [are] nothing—

For even some who completely do away with divinity and providence, and who have stirred up a company of supposed philosophers through certain impious dogmas, have themselves suffered none of those things which the common people consider evils, nor have those who embraced their opinions; rather, they enjoy health and wealth. Yet if anyone searches more diligently, they will appear as punished as anyone can be. For what heavier calamity is there than not to perceive the Creator from this order of the world? What greater misery than to have the eyes of the mind blinded, and not to see...

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

Since we have said much regarding this matter above, we will now intentionally pass over this place in silence, lest we seem to cause boredom by repeating the same things again and again. However, since he says, *Not even afterwards, through so many ages, has any of the torturers of Jesus paid the penalty*, we shall declare to him and to all who wish to learn, that that city (in which the Jewish people demanded Jesus for punishment, crying out *Crucify him, crucify him*; preferring that a robber thrown into prison for sedition and murder be released rather than Jesus, who was accused out of envy) was not much later attacked in war. It endured a long siege and was devastated to such an extent that it was utterly destroyed and laid waste: God Himself judging those who inhabited the place to be unworthy even of this common life. For, to say something incredible, although God had shown Himself more indulgent toward them, when He saw they were incorrigible and progressing daily toward the worse, He delivered them into the power of their enemies. And all these things were done on account of the blood of Jesus shed in that land by their treachery, which could no longer bear such a great crime perpetrated against Jesus by the impious. Therefore, great innovations followed his passion: one which happened to the city of the Jews, another which happened to the entire nation, and the numerous nation of Christians brought forth as if in a single birth. This also was new: that those who were strangers to the covenant of God and His promises, and far removed from the truth, received it through divine power. These were certainly not the works of a human sorcerer, but of God, who for the sake of His "statues" <note>original: "statuas" / "ἀγάλματα". Origen uses this term metaphorically for human souls or divine images within man.</note> had sent His word in Jesus: who, although subjected to punishment, endured it bravely and with unheard-of gentleness, so that he accused the cruelty of those who unjustly tortured him. His punishments did not corrupt the statues of God, but, if one may speak thus, brought them to the knowledge of man: just as Jesus himself testifies, saying, *Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone: but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit.* <note>John 12:24</note> Therefore, the grain of wheat having died, Jesus brought forth much fruit, and his Father provides for all in every age who come forth from the death of the fruitful grain. Therefore, the pious father is the father of Jesus, who *did not spare his own son, but delivered him up for us all, as his lamb; so that the lamb of God might take away the sin of the world, having died for the whole world*; wherefore, not by compulsion, but willingly and knowingly, he endured whatever the audacity of the wicked permitted themselves against him. After these things Celsus—

<meta>This page continues Origen’s systematic rebuttal of Celsus’s "True Word." Here, Origen addresses Celsus’s claim that the pagan gods avenge themselves upon those who insult their statues, transforming the argument into a spiritual battle between Christian martyrs and demonic forces.</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

Taking up the argument against those who blaspheme the statues, Celsus says: “I might say that these gods also—if you utter any blasphemy—allow it because they wish to, and for this reason they endure being blasphemed; for to return like for like is best. But since they also take great vengeance on the one who blasphemes, who either flees and hides because of this, or is caught and destroyed.” It is not those who blaspheme, however, but those who drive them out from the statues and from human bodies and souls <margin>* Christians.</margin> whom the demons think they are punishing when they attack Christians. Without realizing it, Celsus has said something true in this passage; for it is true that the souls of those who condemn Christians, and of those who betray them, and of those who take pleasure in warring against Christians, are filled with evil demons. But since the souls of those who die for the sake of Christianity depart from the body with glory because of their piety, they were destroying the power of the demons and making their plots against men weaker. For this reason, I believe, having learned by experience that they are defeated and crushed by the martyrs of the truth, the demons feared to come again to take revenge. And so, until they forget the labors they have suffered, it is likely that there will be peace in the world toward Christians; but when they have gathered their strength and are blinded by malice, and wish to take revenge again and persecute Christians, they will be destroyed again. And then again the souls of the pious, stripping off their bodies for the sake of piety, will destroy the camp of the evil one. I think that the demons, perceiving that those who conquer and die for piety destroy their dominion—while those who are defeated by the pains and deny their godliness become subject to them—sometimes incite the judges to harass Christians; they are tormented by the Christians' confession, but find rest in their denial. One can see traces of this even in the judges, who are tormented by the endurance of those undergoing outrages and tortures, but exult when a Christian is defeated. For they do not do these things out of any perceived humanity; they see clearly that while the tongue <margin>Euripides.</margin> <note>A reference to Euripides' *Hippolytus*: "My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn." Origen uses this to show that a forced denial of faith is not a true change of heart.</note> has sworn because it was overcome by pain, the mind is unsworn. And these things are in response to: “But since they also take great vengeance on the one who blasphemes, who either flees because of this and hides, or is caught and destroyed.” Even if a Christian flees, he does not flee out of cowardice; rather, he is observing the commands of his Teacher <note>Referring to Jesus' command in Matthew 10:23 to flee to the next town during persecution.</note> and keeping himself pure for the salvation of others who will be helped. Let us see also what follows: “What need is there to list all that has come from oracles, whether by prophets and prophetesses, or by others...”

<column-break/>

...turning his speech toward the revilers of images, he says, *I could say that these too, whom you provoke with insults, endure this because it pleases them; for to return like for like would be best: but they certainly take vengeance on the revilers, dragging those who flee and hide to punishment.* Therefore, they do not rage against revilers, but against Christian men who drive them out both from images and from human minds and bodies, so that they may avenge the injury received. For Celsus, being unwise, spoke the truth in this place. For it is true that the souls of those who either condemn Christians or differ from them, and of all those by whom the persecution of Christians is approved, are stuffed with evil demons. But since the souls of those killed on account of Christian piety, migrating gloriously from their bodies, were demolishing the power of the demons and breaking their snares—which they never cease to set for men—for this reason, I suppose, having been taught by experience that they were conquered and routed by the truth of the martyrs, they feared to attack them anew and to take vengeance on them for the loss sustained. And so, until they forget their past sufferings, it is likely they will not disturb the world against the professors of the Christian name; but when they have recovered their strength and, blinded by malice, wish to attack Christians again, they will be routed again, and the souls of the pious, stripped of their bodies for the sake of piety, will blot out the forces of the evil demon. Indeed, I think the demons—as those who feel that the victory of the pious is harmful to their power, while those who succumb in this contest and deny the faith become liable to them—sometimes favor Christians in judgment <note>The Latin "favere" here likely implies "focusing on" or "inciting," as the context describes the demons' agitation.</note>, because they are tortured by their confession and refreshed by their denial. A sign of this matter can be seen in the judges themselves, for whom it is very troublesome while they watch those bravely enduring tortures, but on the contrary, they leap with joy whenever a Christian is defeated. For they do not do this out of any humanity which they claim to possess; it is manifest that the mind is unsworn. Thus far regarding those words: *They certainly take vengeance on the revilers, while dragging those who flee and hide to punishment.* Yet a Christian does not flee out of fear, even if he flees, but observing the mandate of his teacher, and keeping himself pure for the utility of others. Now let us see what follows next in this manner: *What pertains to recounting how many things from oracles, partly by Prophets and Prophetesses, partly by others [inspired] by a spirit...*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

->Through ritual and inspiration, both men and women have foretold the future with a prophetic voice? How many wonders have they drawn from the very inner shrines of the Gods? How many things likewise were predicted from the entrails of victims to those consulting them? How many things were shown to others through portents? To some, even the manifest forms of the Gods offered themselves. All of life is full of examples: how many cities were established based on oracles, or escaped pestilence and famine; how many perished miserably because they were careless or unmindful of oracles; how many colonies were led out by their warning and increased with great fortune while they did not neglect the commands; how many leaders or private citizens fared well or ill by these accounts; how many, grieving that they had no children, obtained their wish; how many escaped the wrath of demons; how many, deprived of their limbs, received their former health; again, how many were punished on the spot for violating sacred things—some caught there and losing their minds, others voluntarily confessing their wicked deeds, some laying hands upon themselves, and others seized by incurable diseases; nor are examples lacking of those killed by a terrifying voice breaking out from the innermost shrines.<-

I do not know how it is that Celsus brings these things forward as if they were admitted facts, yet considers the miracles recorded in our own writings—whether Jewish or those produced concerning Jesus and his disciples—to be mere fables. Why are our accounts not rather the true ones, and those which Celsus brings forward the fictions? Especially since even the sects of Greek philosophers do not believe them—specifically those who follow Democritus, Epicurus, and Aristotle. Perhaps they would have been persuaded by our authors, due to their clarity, if they had encountered <note>original: *incidissent* / *ἐντετυχήκεσαν*</note> Moses, or any of the prophets who performed wonders, or Jesus himself. It is certainly reported in histories that the Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi who gave oracles.</note> sometimes gave corrupt oracles; but our prophets were held in great admiration not only in their own age, but also among posterity. For from their "oracles" cities were established, men were restored to health, and pestilences were stilled. A colony was also led out from Egypt into Palestine by the warning of an oracle—the entire people of the Jews—who flourished as long as they kept the precepts of God, but repented when they fell. Why should I mention how many princes or commoners <note>original: *idiotæ* / *ἰδιῶται* — meaning private citizens or unlearned men</note> are read of in sacred history as having fared well or ill, according as they either obeyed the Prophets or despised their warnings? And if we must speak of offspring sought through vows, we find that fathers and mothers were made so by invoking the power of the Creator of all things. Let the history of Abraham and Sarah be read, from whom Isaac was born when they were already decrepit—that father of all Jews—and of others besides. Let those things also be read which are produced concerning Hezekiah, who not only received deliverance from sickness...

Furthermore, the books of the Prophets, if anyone reads their predictions not carelessly, seem sufficient to persuade that those men were inspired by the Spirit of God. For these are men who are otherwise rustic, impure, without reason, and struggling with seditions. However, to those who hope they will have an eternal soul or mind (whether it should be called spiritual, or an intellectual spirit, holy and blessed, or a living soul, or the celestial and incorruptible offspring of a divine and incorporeal nature, or by whatever name one pleases to call it), I shall say this with God: that they think rightly that those who have lived well will be happy, but the unjust will be held by eternal evils—from which dogma neither these men, nor any of mortals, should ever shrink.
