<meta>This page continues Origen’s defense of Christian doctrine against the critiques of Celsus, specifically focusing on the nature of the soul versus the body and the rationality of the belief in resurrection.</meta>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

Regarding the rational nature, we say that it is more precious than any body. For the soul contains the image of the Creator; the body, however, in no way contains it. For according to our view, God is not a body; this is so that we do not fall into the errors of those who follow the philosophy of Zeno and Chrysippus <note>Zeno and Chrysippus were founders of Stoicism, a school of thought that believed God was a material substance or "pneuma" pervading the universe.</note>. Since Celsus reproaches us for a "longing for the body," let him know that if longing is a bad thing, we long for nothing; but if it is a neutral thing, we long for everything that God promises to the righteous. Thus, we both long for and hope for the resurrection of the righteous. 

Celsus thinks we are acting inconsistently with ourselves when we hope for the resurrection of the body as something worthy of honor from God, yet at other times throw it into punishments <note>Referring to Christian martyrs who willingly faced torture and death.</note> as if it were worthless. But nothing is worthless which suffers for the sake of piety, or which chooses hardships for the sake of virtue; rather, everything is worthless which is consumed by vice and pleasures. For the divine word also says: *What is the honorable seed? The seed of man. What is the dishonorable seed? The seed of man.* <margin>Sirach 10:19</margin>

Then Celsus thinks he should not even converse with those who hope for things concerning the body, as if they were wasting away irrationally for an impossible thing. He calls them "rustics" and "impure," <margin>* crowded together</margin> claiming they are crowded together in their assertions. But he ought, as a lover of humanity, to help even the more rustic. For social kindness is not written of as being limited to irrational animals, or even to the more rustic of men; rather, He who made us has made us social toward all men equally. It is worthy, therefore, to converse even with the rustic and (as much as is in our power) to lead them toward a more refined state; and to converse with the impure and persuade them, as far as possible, to live more purely; and to help those who lack reason to become sensible, and those with sick souls, so that they no longer act without reason or suffer in their souls.

After this, he accepts those who hope to have the soul—or the mind, or what is called among them the "spiritual" or "rational spirit," intellectual, holy, and blessed, or the "living soul"—as eternal, and that it will be with God. He considers the doctrine regarding those who have lived well, that they will be happy, to be very correct; and regarding the unjust, that they will be <margin>* eternally</margin> held in *eternal evils. And I have wondered at Celsus, that among all the things said by him, he concludes the preceding points by saying: "And this at least is right; may neither these people nor any other human ever depart from this doctrine." And he ought to have seen, writing against Christians (whose entire basis of faith is God, the promises to the righteous through Christ, and the teachings on punishment for the unrighteous), that anyone who turns a Christian away from accepting the [faith]...

<column-break/>

...rational, is better than any body: since the soul, not the body, receives the image of the creator. For we do not believe God to be corporeal, lest we fall into those absurdities into which certain philosopher followers of Zeno and Chrysippus fell. Moreover, since he reproaches us for the desire for the body: let him know, if desire is an evil thing, we desire nothing; but if it is indifferent, we desire whatever God promises to the just: and in this way we also desire and hope for the resurrection of the just. 

Celsus thinks we act inconsistently, while at one moment we hope God will deign to honor our bodies with resurrection, and at another we cast it into any kind of torture as a vile thing: yet nothing is vile which suffers on account of piety, and objects itself to adversities on account of virtue; but that which is consumed with vices in pleasures. Holy Scripture bears witness, saying, *Honorable seed is the seed of man, vile seed is the seed of man.* 

Then Celsus thinks one should not discuss with those having good hope concerning the body, as if they were wasting away with desire for a thing which it is impossible to attain, calling them rustics, brutes, and seditious, when he ought as a human to succor the unskillful: for kindness is not so narrowly circumscribed that it does not extend itself even to brutes, let alone to sub-rustic men; but our creator made us to be beneficial to all equally: therefore even the rustics are worthy with whom one may discuss, so that, as much as can be done, they may be rendered more refined; the impure also are to be made purer; and the brutes feeling anything rashly, and those languishing in soul, are to be cured, lest they do anything without reason hereafter or languish. 

After these things he approves of those who hope they will have an eternal soul—whether it should be called a spiritual mind, or an intellectual spirit, holy and blessed, or a living soul—and that it will live with God: he also praises the dogma concerning the eternal happiness of the just, and the eternal miseries of the unjust, nor do I wonder at any of all Celsus's sayings as much as that he now thus concludes the speech: *Neither others, nor anyone else [should depart] from this dogma.* And yet, when he was writing against the Christians (whose whole faith turns upon God, and the promises made to the just through Christ, and the threats aimed at the unjust) he ought to have noticed, that if anyone, on account of the speeches of Celsus against the Christians...

# Book 8. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

If he were to abandon the faith he has embraced, it is likely that, having rejected the doctrine, he would also despise this decree *which, he says, neither Christians nor any other human being has ever abandoned*. How much better did Chrysippus act in his book *On the Cure of the Passions* <note>original: "de curandis affectibus" / "περὶ παθῶν". Chrysippus was a major Stoic philosopher.</note>, who wishes to heal the passions—as things pressing upon and troubling the human soul—primarily by sound reasoning, but secondarily and thirdly even by doctrines he himself does not fully approve. *For he says: Even if there were three kinds of goods, the passions must be healed in this way, not by inquiring too curiously at the time of the inflammation of the passions into which doctrine the sufferer is already committed; lest perhaps, while we are untimely occupied in uprooting a doctrine from the soul, the opportunity for whatever healing might be admitted should perish. And he adds: Even if pleasure were the "good" in the opinion of the one affected, he must nonetheless be helped, and it must be shown that even those who place the highest good in pleasure admit that every passion is inconsistent with their own view.* Therefore, Celsus also (having once approved the doctrine of eternal rewards for the righteous and miseries for the unrighteous) ought to have confirmed this primary principle with arguments, and shown through many proofs that the persuasion is true regarding both those rewards and the punishments that never end. For we also, before all else, by those innumerable reasons by which we ourselves were led to Christian piety, attempt to lead all whom we can to the same; but where we find people preoccupied by the slanders with which we Christians are burdened—so that through their imagination of Christian "impiety" they cannot even bear to lend an ear to those who promise this divine teaching—there, out of a love for humanity <note>term: "humanitas" / "φιλανθρωπία" - a love for mankind or benevolence.</note>, we do our best, as far as possible, to make them fit to receive this teaching by persuading them at least of that doctrine concerning the eternal punishments of the impious, even those who do not wish to become Christians. We do the same by persuading them that what is said about the rewards of a rightly led life is true: since we see that even those estranged from the knowledge of our faith teach many things about ordering life well, and indeed things similar to our own decrees; for one will not find anyone who has totally lost the common notions of what is honorable and just, or unjust and shameful. Therefore all men, contemplating this world and the established motion of the heavens and the fixed stars, and also the order of the planets which are carried in a direction opposite to the motion of the world, and furthermore the temperament of the air for the use of living creatures, especially for men, and the rich abundance of things for the sake of men—

# Book 8. ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...they would defame Moses, the Prophets, and Jesus with his Apostles; nor would they reject the Jews alone out of all the nations of the whole world, saying that they are worse than the Egyptians—even down to the level of brute animals—whether through superstition or through whatever other error, as far as lies in them, they lower the honor of God. They affirm what they themselves do not know, neither with a **comprehensive perception** <note>original: "comprehensiva phantasia" / "καταληπτικῆς φαντασίας". It is written in the Gospel <margin>Luke 13:11</margin> that there was a certain woman who was bent over, not being able to raise herself up; when Jesus saw her, and noticed for what reason she was not permitted to lift her head, he said: *And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, lo, these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?* <margin>Luke 13:16</margin> How many even now, bound by Satan, rush toward the earth, as he does not permit them to look up at all, because he wishes us to look only at earthly things? Nor does anyone raise them up except the Word <note>original: "Verbum" / "Λόγος". Referring to Christ as the Divine Reason.</note> which arrived in Jesus, and which previously bore divinity. Truly, Jesus came to free all those oppressed by the devil, and of him he said with a certain fitting gravity: *Now the prince of this world is judged.* <margin>John 16:11</margin> Therefore, we do not merely revile the demons dwelling here, but we expose their machinations for the destruction of the human race, under the pretext of oracles and healings—

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

For we are armed with the **full armor of God**, standing as *athletes of piety* against the race of demons who lay snares for us. Therefore, even if Celsus, by his discourse, should drive us out from all life so that the earth were entirely desolate of our kind, we shall nevertheless persevere in the laws given by our Creator. We shall never serve the laws of sin. We shall take wives, if we wish, and we shall raise children who, God willing, will be sharers of the adversities of this life. We shall endure these as <term>trials of the soul</term> <note>Origen uses the concept of "trials" to explain why God allows suffering; it is a refinement process.</note> (for this is how the sacred Scripture is accustomed to name the accidents that befall men, in which, like gold examined by fire, the soul is either approved or rejected). Indeed, we are so prepared against those things which Celsus calls "evils" that we say: *Test me, O Lord, and prove me; burn my reins and my heart.* <note>original: "Tenta me, Domine, & proba me, ure renes meos & cor meum." quoting Psalm 26:2.</note> For no one is crowned unless he has striven lawfully here upon earth in this body of humility. Furthermore, we do not render the "due honors," as they suppose, to those to whom Celsus says earthly affairs have been committed. For we worship the Lord our God, and Him alone do we serve, desiring to become imitators of Christ; who, when the devil said to him, *All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me*, replied, *You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve.* This is why we do not render the honors supposedly due to those to whom Celsus says earthly matters are entrusted, because *no one can serve two masters*, nor can we serve God and <term>Mammon</term> <note>A term for wealth or worldly gain, often personified as a false god.</note> at the same time, whether this word signifies one thing or many. Moreover, if a legislator is insulted by the breaking of a law, it is clear to us that since there are two laws contrary to one another—the law of God and the law of Mammon—it is better for us to insult Mammon by breaking the law of Mammon, so that by observing the law of God we may honor God, rather than to insult God by breaking the law of God, so that by observing the law of Mammon we may honor Mammon. Celsus, however, thinks it belongs to the duties of life if men, until they are released from these bonds <note>Referring to the physical body as a "bond" or prison of the soul.</note>, render solemn sacred rites to those who are worshipped as Gods from town to town; he does not understand what duty truly is, nor does he measure it by true piety. But we say that he performs the duties of life who, mindful of the Creator and what things please Him, looks to the will of God in whatever he does. Celsus likewise wants us to be grateful toward the earthly demons, and thinks we owe sacrifices to them.

And they would accept us for being careful not to sacrifice to them or serve them; for they have no need of the vapors rising from the earth.” After this, Celsus says the following: “That authority has been given over even the smallest things in these matters, one might learn from what the Egyptians say: that the human body has been divided among thirty-six demons, or certain ethereal gods, partitioned into so many parts—though some say many more—and each is appointed to govern a different part of it. Indeed, they know the names of the demons in the local tongue, such as Chnumen, and Chnachumen, and Cnat, and Sicat, and Biu, and Eru, and Erebiu, and Romanor, and Rejanoor, and whatever other names they call them in their own language; and by invoking them, they heal the ailments of those parts. What then prevents someone from welcoming these and others, if one wishes to be healthy rather than sick, and to be fortunate rather than unfortunate, and to be delivered from torturers and punishers (as they are called)?” And through these words, Celsus tries from the beginning to turn our soul toward the demons, as if they had been allotted our bodies, and by declaring that each one cares for a part of our body, he wants us to believe in the demons he mentions and to serve them; so that we might be healthy rather than sick, and fortunate rather than unfortunate, and as much as possible, be delivered from those who are, as it were, torturers. He has so much contempt for the undivided and inseparable honor due to the God of all things, that he does not believe God alone is sufficient when worshipped and loudly honored—

...that we owe thanks to the same: but we, to speak more openly about gratitude, deny that we should be called ungrateful; because to the demons—who are not only not benefactors but are even adversaries—we neither sacrifice nor defer any honor. We only take care lest we be held ungrateful toward God, with whose benefits we are filled, since we are His creatures, and we owe this very fact, that we are whatever we are, to His providence, hoping also for better things from Him after this life. We also have a symbol of His thanksgiving, the bread, which is called the Eucharist. Nor do the demons have (as we taught above) any administration of the things created for our uses: therefore we do nothing iniquitous while we are participants in them, nor do we sacrifice to demons to whom these things do not belong. Nay, even if we know that not demons, but angels preside over the produce of crops and the offspring of animals, we proclaim them as blessed, to whom the utilities of men have been committed by God; yet we do not render to them the honor due to God alone: for neither does God want this, nor do they themselves to whom these things have been committed; and they love us equally for not sacrificing, as if we had offered to them: for they have no need of those smells of burnt offerings. Celsus proceeds in this manner: *“That even the smallest things do not lack their own presiding spirits, one may learn from the Egyptians, who say the human body is distributed into thirty-six parts, and each has its own power, whether it be a demon or some ethereal God. Some, however, say there are more, attributing different parts to different spirits, and they name those demons in their own language, such as Chnumen, Chnachumen, Cnat, Sicat, Biu, Eru, Erebiu, Romanor, Rejanoor, and other equally Egyptian names: and when invoked they heal the diseases of their respective parts. What therefore forbids seeking the favor of both these and others, if one prefers to be well rather than sick, and to be happy rather than unhappy, and to be freed from those who are thought to be torturers?”* By these words also Celsus endeavors to lead our souls to the demons, as if they had obtained our bodies by lot, asserting that to each is attributed his own part of our body, and wishing us to believe in the demons of which he tells, and to worship them, so that we may be well rather than sick, and happy rather than unhappy, and, as far as can be done, be freed from the torturers. # ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

->HHh<-

[Celsus claims that God] does not suffice to ward off the lurking demons from his holy worshippers: for he has not seen how the name of Jesus, when invoked by genuine believers, has freed many from sicknesses, fits of madness <note>Latin: *lymphationibus*; Greek: *δαιμονισμῶν* (demon-possessions)</note>, and other perils. It is possible that he who favors Celsus may laugh when we say that *At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.* <note>A citation of Philippians 2:10-11.</note> Though he may laugh, he will be able to hear clearer proofs of this truth than regarding the names just recited: Chnumen, Chnachumen, Cnat, Sicat, and the rest of the Egyptian names which are invoked to heal diseases in specific parts of the body. And see how, turning us away from believing in God through Jesus Christ, he calls us to faith through the healing of the body by thirty-six barbaric demons, whom only the Egyptian magicians invoke—I know not how—promising us better things. Therefore, according to Celsus, we shall be magicians and sorcerers rather than Christians, and we shall believe in an infinite number of demons rather than in the living and manifest God of all, through him who with great power sowed the purest word of piety throughout the whole world—not only for men, but also (which I say without falsehood) for other rational creatures, whoever have need of correction, healing, and a change from vice to virtue. Wherefore, having a suspicion of this slippery path, in which a fall into magic is easy, and sensing that the listener might be offended, he adds: *“One must take care, however, lest anyone melt away in the pleasure of such ceremonies, and being turned away from better things by love of the body, fall into oblivion of them. For it is necessary, I think, to have faith in wise men who say that most of the demons that hover about the earth, delighting themselves in procreation, blood, the smell of burnt offerings, melodies, and other things of that kind, being bound and fixed to them, are able to do nothing more than heal bodies, and predict what is to come to men and cities, and they know and are able to do whatever pertains to mortal affairs.”* Since therefore this place is so slippery, as the very enemy of divine truth testifies: how much better is it to be secure from that demonic pleasure, and the love of bodies, and the forgetting of better things, to entrust oneself to God the Lord of the universe through Jesus Christ the author of our doctrine, and to ask from him every help—

<column-break/>

—[every] blameless [help], providing to the one who honors Him the power to worship Him, which restrains the demons even from those who are holily pious. For he has [not] seen in what manner the name of Jesus, called upon by those who genuinely believe, has healed not a few from diseases and possessions and other circumstances. And it is likely that the one devoted to Celsus will laugh at us saying that *In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, and those on earth, and those under the earth; and every tongue is subject to the confession that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.* But having laughed, he shall receive more manifest proofs that these things are so, than concerning those names of which he relates: Chnoum, and Chnachoum, and Knat, and Sikat, and the rest of those from the Egyptian catalogue, as being called upon and healing the sufferings of the [body's] parts. And see indeed, in what manner he turns us away from believing in the God over all through Jesus the Christ, and calls us to faith, for the sake of the healing of our body, in thirty-six barbaric demons; whom only the magicians of the Egyptians call upon and, I know not how, promise us the better things. So that we, according to Celsus, should practice sorcery and be charlatans rather than live as Christians; and believe in some infinite number of demons rather than in the self-evident, living, and manifest God over all, through the word of true religion which has been sown with much power in the whole inhabited world of men; and I shall not be lying if I am persuaded to say, also among the other rational beings who need correction and healing and a change from wickedness. Celsus, at any rate, suspecting the slip into magic among those who have learned such things, and sensing somehow that harm would always come to the listeners, says, “That indeed must be guarded against, lest someone, by being devoted to the service of these things, should be consumed by them, becoming a lover of the body and forgetting better things, and be seized by oblivion. For it is perhaps necessary not to disbelieve wise men, who indeed say that the majority of <margin>demons.</margin> earthly demons are dissolved in procreations, and nailed to blood and the smell of fat and melodies and other such things, being bound; they can do nothing better than heal the body, and prophesy the future fortune to a man and a city, and they know and are able to do as much as concerns mortal actions.” Since the place is always on such a slippery slope, as even the enemy to the truth of God bears witness; how much better it is, without any suspicion of being consumed by such demons, or becoming a lover of the body and forgetting better things and being seized by the oblivion of better things, to trust oneself to the God over all, through Jesus Christ who suggested such teaching to us, and to ask from him all help—

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

Truth, and the protection afforded by holy angels and the righteous; which delivers us from the earth-bound demons <note>original: "περιγείων δαιμόνων" / "circumstantaneis dæmonibus"</note>, who are dissolved in the pleasure of generation, pinned to blood and the aroma of sacrifices, and led by strange melodies and other such attachments. It is admitted, even according to Celsus, that they are capable of nothing better than healing the body. But I would say that it is not even clear that these demons, however they are worshipped, are able to heal bodies. Rather, the healing of bodies, if one wishes to live more simply and commonly, should be sought through the medical art <note>term: medical art (iatrikē) — referring to rational, secular medicine as opposed to spiritual healing</note>; but if one seeks a better way, it should be through great piety toward the God over all, and through prayers to Him. And consider for yourself, which will the God over all more readily accept—He who is more powerful than any other for all things and for the benefit of men, whether regarding the soul, the body, or external matters? Is it the one who devotes himself entirely to Him, or the one who busies himself with the names of demons, their powers, their actions, their incantations, herbs peculiar to demons, stones, and the engravings upon them, and the forms of demons handed down to one another, whether symbolic or otherwise? But it is clear to anyone capable of following the argument even slightly, that the simple and uncurious character, devoted for this very reason to the God over all, will be acceptable to God and to all those who are His own.

<margin>p. 418</margin>
But as for the one who, for the sake of bodily health, love of the flesh, and success in worldly affairs, busies himself with the names of demons and seeks how to move them with certain incantations—as one who is wicked, impious, and more demonic than human—God and Jesus will leave him to be harassed by demons <insert>he chose to be disciplined</insert> by the thoughts suggested by each, or by other evils.

For it is likely that they, being base and (as Celsus admitted) pinned to blood, the aroma of sacrifices, melodies, and other such things, do not even keep faith or a "pledge of the right hand" <note>A metaphor for a binding oath or treaty</note> toward those who grant them these favors. For when others call upon them against those who previously served them, and purchase their slavery with more blood, aroma, and the service they require, they would plot against the one who served them yesterday and shared with them their favorite gift. Celsus, having said much in the preceding parts up to the point of the oracles, and having referred us to their divinations as if to certain gods, has now done something better by admitting that those who predict the future to men and cities, and those concerned with earthly affairs, are earth-bound demons, dissolved in generation, pinned to blood, aroma, and melodies, and bound to other such things, being capable of nothing better than these. But I might say that it is not even established that demons, in whatever way they are worshipped, can heal bodies: rather, health is to be sought in the common manner through the reason of Medicine, or beyond the common mode through piety toward God and prayers. Consider within yourself which character God, the Lord of the universe, would more likely approve—He who is more powerful than all others both in other matters and in doing good to men, whether you look at the body, the soul, or external things; that of him who commits all things to Him, or of him who is curious about the names of demons, their virtues, actions, incantations, peculiar herbs, and gems and carvings representing the forms of demons, whether symbolic or of any other kind. It is evident even to those considering it moderately, that simple and least curious ways please God for this very reason, and all His friends: but those who, for the sake of the body and its health, and happiness in indifferent matters, inquire too curiously into the names of demons and by what songs they are enticed, as evil and impious and more demonic than human, the Lord Jesus will leave to be driven by demons, both on account of other evils and because of the depraved thoughts which individuals have suggested: for it is probable, since they are evil, as Celsus himself confesses, and fixed to gore, smells, melodies, and the like; that they will not even keep faith with their own worshippers or the given right hand. For being invoked against their own worshippers by others, and corrupted by more gore, smells, and other services by which their labor is bought, they will plot against their worshipper of yesterday, although fed by his feast. But it is well that Celsus, who until now sent us to their oracles and mysteries as if to Gods, now confesses that those who predict the future to private men and cities, being occupied with mortal actions, are surrounding demons, delighting themselves in births, and fixed to gore, smells, melodies, and similar things, nor can they do anything better.

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

[...enduring] punishments and death: *for we read in our own letters <note>referring to the New Testament</note>, Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; for there is no power except from God: therefore he who resists the power, resists the ordinance of God.* <margin>Romans 13:1, 2.</margin> <margin>* those who resist.</margin> <margin>...shall receive [judgment].</margin> We have explained these words in our commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans in more than one way, as best we could; but now we have cited them simply according to the common understanding for the present matter, since Celsus denies that their dignity fell to them without the favor of demons. And, since much could be said about the state of kings and princes—because the matter is not without need of investigation due to the cruel tyranny of some princes, and others who, through the license of power, have fallen into luxury and wickedness—we therefore refrain from examining this topic for the time being. However, we do not swear by the **Fortune** of the king, just as we do not swear by other fictitious deities: for if (as some think) Fortune is merely the course of events, appearing to diverge equally, we do not swear by that which is nothing, as if by God or some thing possessing power, lest we abuse the oath; or if (as it seems to others) those who swear by the king's Fortune swear by the *genius* <note>the protective spirit or "daemon" associated with a person</note> of the Roman prince, so that we understand by that name one of the demons; even so, we must die rather than swear by an evil and faithless demon, who often sins along with the man he is allotted to, or indeed more often than the man. Then again Celsus, not unlike those possessed by demons—now collecting themselves, now falling back into their former evil—recovering his senses for a little while, speaks thus: *“But if someone should urge a worshiper of God either to act impiously or to say something shameful, he must not be obeyed; rather, all punishments are to be endured, and any deaths undergone, rather than that he should, I will not say utter, but even admit into his thoughts anything irreligious concerning God.”* Then again, as one ignorant of our doctrine, and therefore confusing everything, he adds this: *“But if someone commands you to speak well of the Sun or Minerva, a Paean <note>a song of praise or triumph</note> should be sung cheerfully: for in this way you will seem to venerate the great God more, if you also honor these with hymns and praises; for piety becomes more perfect if it passes through all things.”* We reply that we do not wait until we are commanded to speak well of the Sun, we who have learned not only that we must not speak ill of magistrates, but not even speak evil of our enemies. Therefore we speak well of the Sun, as a beautiful creature of God, keeping the laws prescribed for it by God, and obeying the voice of the Prophet inviting it: *Praise the Lord, Sun and Moon;*

And we see that by accepting Athena as the daughter of Zeus, one must also accept many myths and fictions; which a person who flees from myths for the sake of truth would not accept. Even if one were to speak allegorically, saying that Athena is "Wisdom" <term>phronesis: practical wisdom or prudence</term>, let them demonstrate her actual existence and essence, as if she truly existed according to this allegory. But if Athena was some ancient human woman who was honored * by those living under her power with mysteries and rites—because they wished her name to be celebrated among men as a Goddess—how much more is it wrong to sing hymns to her and glorify her as a God? For it is not even lawful for us to worship the great Sun, even if we speak well of it. Celsus says that we would seem to worship the Great God more if we also sang hymns to the Sun and Athena; but we know the opposite to be true. For we offer hymns only to the God who is over all, and to His only-begotten God the Word <term>Logos: the Divine Word or Reason, identified with Christ</term>. And we praise God and His only-begotten just as the sun, the moon, the stars, and all the heavenly host do. For all these, being a divine choir, praise the God over all and His only-begotten along with righteous men. 

Furthermore, regarding the fact that one ought not to swear by human kings or their so-called "Fortune" <note>The 'Tyche' or 'Genius' of the Emperor, a common Roman loyalty test.</note>, we have already spoken. Therefore, it is not necessary for us to defend ourselves again against the statement: "Even if someone commands you to swear by a king among men, this is not a terrible thing. For to him are given the things on earth; and whatever you receive in life, you receive from him." But we say that it is not the case that *all* things on earth are given to him; nor is it true that whatever we receive in life, we receive from him. For when we receive things justly and rightly, we receive them from God and His providence—such as the fruits of the season, and "bread that strengthens the heart of man." We also have the fruits of the olive from the providence of God, "to make the face shine with oil." Then Celsus says next, "that one must not distrust an ancient man, who long ago foretold that..."

<margin>

> —Let there be one prince,

yet it is not he to whom the son of "crooked-counseling" Saturn <note>original: "obliqua cogitantis," translating the Greek *ankylomētēs* (crooked-minded), a standard epithet for Saturn/Kronos</note> gave it; but he to whom He gave it, who establishes kings, and changes and restores them, raising up from the ground in His own time men useful to the Republic. It is not Jupiter—the son of Saturn who was driven from his kingdom (as the Greek fables tell) and cast into Tartarus—who distributes kingdoms and establishes princes region by region, even if you take that allegorically; but God, who rules all things, knows whom He ought to set as prince over which region. We judge that dogma about the distributor of kingdoms being the son of crooked-counseling Saturn to be vain, as we are persuaded that nothing crooked or winding is thought by God or the Father of God—saving, however, the dogma of providence, and those things which proceed from it either primarily or by consequence. Nor yet would we be deservedly punished by Caesar because we say the kingdom was given to him not by the son of Saturn, but by Him who both sets kings over kingdoms and removes them from government. And would that all, rejecting the sentiment of Homer, would rather approve the divine one and honor Caesar. There is no danger that, for this reason, he being deserted by his bodyguards and officials, the provinces would lie open to the incursions of the most savage barbarians: for if all should do the same as I, as Celsus says, without a doubt all the barbarians, having received the divine doctrine, would become most just and mild; and as other religions vanished, Christian piety alone would flourish—which is something that will happen one day, as the preaching spreads itself more widely through the souls of men. Afterward, Celsus, not noticing that he was saying things that did not agree with this statement, says: *If all should do the same as you. For you are not going to say that the Romans, persuaded by you, having abandoned their ancestral ceremonies and rites, are going to invoke your Most High, or whatever he is to be called, so that descending he might fight for them, and there be no need for other forces.* For the same God, having already before promised both this very thing and other greater things to his own (as you yourselves admit), you see how much he profited either them or you: since for them, instead of the hoped-for dominion of the whole earth, not even—

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

<margin>Matthew 10:29</margin>
(as the Scripture names it) are sold for a penny <note>original: "asse" / "ἀσσαρίου" - a small Roman coin of little value</note>, not one falls into a snare without the will of the heavenly Father: and so far does the providence of God embrace all things, that not even the number of our hairs escapes His knowledge.
<margin>Ibid. v. 30.</margin>
Then again Celsus, in his usual manner of mixing everything together, attributes to us things which have been written by no Christian, saying: *“Neither is that voice of yours to be endured, which says: If we draw the present Emperors over to our faith, others will be drawn over afterwards. And what if they should draw over others, and others still more, until all are drawn to your faith; at last some prince, acting more prudently, will foresee what is to happen, and will utterly extirpate your whole race before it goes on to destroy itself.”* To this there is no need to reply, since none of us speak in this way: "If we draw the present Emperors to our religion, all will be drawn over, one after another." How did it escape him that, even if princes were to come over to our religion one after another, why should one of them—sensing that this was happening because we, as enemies, were being spared—extirpate this whole race fundamentally? But he seems to have invented this from himself, since he connects nonsense to nonsense. Then, having prayed <note>The Greek text suggests "having spoken" or "having mentioned" rather than "prayed"</note> that the nations of *Asia, Europe, and Africa, both Greek and Barbarian, to the ends of the inhabited world*, might agree in the same laws, he considers this impossible and adds, *“that he who thinks this will happen knows nothing of affairs.”* Regarding this matter, the occasion demands that we speak even in a few words, although it ought to be treated more diligently, so that it may be clear that it is not only possible, but even true, that whatever is a participant in reason shall one day come under the same laws. The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught virtue and harmony with the divine reason (Logos)</note> say there will one day be a universal conflagration, with fire, as the stronger element, prevailing over the others: but we say that the preaching of the Word of God <note>original: "verbi Dei" / "λόγον" - referring to the Logos or Divine Reason</note> will one day prevail over every rational creature, and will change every soul into its own perfection, when each one, using his own power, shall choose what he wills, and shall do whatever he has chosen. For the condition of souls is not the same as that of bodies, where, just as there are certain diseases in the latter that are insuperable by the art of Medicine; so in souls there are no vices which it is impossible to be healed by the Word of God. Truly, there is no evil affection of the mind over which the Word of God is not more powerful: for He applies Medicine to each one according to the will of God, the effect of which is to take away vices. But whether this goes so far that the soul can never hereafter...

<column-break/>

...for a penny (as the Scripture named it), not one falls into a snare without the heavenly Father. And thus the divine providence has encompassed all things, so that not even the hairs of our head have escaped being known by it. Then again, as is Celsus's habit, he confuses things in what follows, saying things which none of us recorded, and he says these things: "Indeed, not even that is tolerable when you say, that if those who now rule are persuaded and captured, you will persuade those who rule hereafter. And if those others are captured, and others after others, until all who are persuaded are captured, some more prudent ruler, foreseeing what is happening, will destroy you all, root and branch, before he himself is destroyed." Since there will be no discourse about these things—for does any of us say that if those who now rule are persuaded and captured, and after them others are persuaded, and those being captured, again others in succession are persuaded? From where did he cast this out: that in succession, as we are always being persuaded and captured, because we do not defend ourselves against enemies, some one prudent authority, foreseeing what is happening, will destroy us root and branch? But he seems to join nonsense to these things in order, and he seems to have cast this out from himself. After these things, having said a certain prayer <note>or "wish"</note> again: "For if it were possible for those inhabiting Asia, and Europe, and Libya <note>Africa</note>, both Greeks and Barbarians, to agree into one law unto the ends of the earth," thinking this to be impossible he adds, "that he who thinks this knows nothing." But if it is necessary to speak on this, a few things shall be said on the point, which requires much examination and preparation, to show that what is said about all rational beings agreeing in one law is not only possible, but also true. Now those from the Stoa <note>The Stoics</note> say there will be a conflagration <note>original: "ἐκπύρωσιν" - a periodic destruction of the cosmos by fire</note> when the stronger of the elements prevails, [saying] that there will be a turning of all things into fire; but we say that the Word <note>Logos</note> will one day master the whole rational nature, and transform every soul into its own perfection; when each one, having used his own authority, chooses what he wishes, and exists in what he chose. And we say that it is not likely that, as with bodies where some diseases and wounds are stronger than all medical art; so also with souls, that there is any evil that is impossible to be healed by the Word and God who is over all. For the Word is more powerful than all the evils in the soul, and the healing within Him, to bring it to each one according to the will of God; and the end of affairs is the removal of evil. But whether [it is removed] so that it is never in any way left...

<margin>more prudent.</margin>
<margin>* there will be [a turning] of all.</margin>

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS. Book 8.

->**Page 426**<-

<margin>Zephaniah 3:8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14.</margin>
<margin>* "unto the day," according to the printed edition.</margin>
<margin>* "because in fire," according to the printed edition.</margin>

Whether I am able [to explain] this or not, it is the purpose of the present discourse to teach. Now, the prophets say many things in secret <note>original: *en aporrhētō* — referring to esoteric or mystical teachings intended for the initiated</note> concerning the total destruction of evils and the correction of every soul. However, it is sufficient for the present to set forth the passage from Zephaniah, which goes as follows: *Prepare yourself, wake early; all their gleanings are destroyed. Therefore wait for [me], says the Lord, until the day of my resurrection, for a testimony; because my judgment is for the gatherings of the nations, to receive kings, to pour out upon them all the anger of my wrath. For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed; for then I will change the tongue for the peoples unto its generation, that all may call upon the name of the Lord, to serve [him] under one yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring sacrifices to me; in that day, you shall not be put to shame for all your practices in which you acted impiously against me; for then I will take away from you the boastings of your insolence, and you shall no longer add to your pride upon my holy mountain. And I will leave in you a people meek and humble; and the remnants of Israel shall revere the name of the Lord, and they shall not do injustice, and they shall not speak vanities, and there shall not be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue; because they themselves shall feed and lie down, and there shall be no one to make them afraid.* 

Let him who is able, having considered all these things, present the clarity of the prophecy; but especially let him examine what it means that, after all the earth has been consumed, a tongue is changed for the peoples unto its generation—analogous to the state of affairs before the confusion <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel, suggesting a return to a single primordial language or spiritual unity.</note>. And let him consider what it means for all to call upon the name of the Lord and to serve him under one yoke, as the boastings of insolence are taken away, and there is no longer injustice, nor vain words, nor a deceitful tongue. It seemed right to set these things down briefly, without a very precise exposition, because of the statement of Celsus, who thinks it is impossible for those in Asia, Europe, and Libya <note>Africa</note>, both Greeks and barbarians, to agree in one mind. And perhaps it is truly impossible for those still in the body, but not impossible for those released from it.

Next, Celsus exhorts us "to help the King <note>The Emperor</note> with all our strength, and to labor with him in what is right, and to fight for him, and to serve in the army with him if he requires it, and to lead the troops with him." It must be said in response to this that we do help the kings at the proper time with a divine help (if I may put it so), putting on the whole armor of God. And we do this in obedience to the Apostolic voice which says: *I exhort you therefore, first [of all], that supplications, prayers, inter-*

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original 17th-century edition for scholars.</note>

—whether they fall back into the same evils, or the contrary; this is not the time for that dispute. Certainly, many more secret things are held among the Prophets concerning the total abolition of all vices from all souls at some time, with which words of Zephaniah we shall now be content: they are as follows: *Be prepared, watch in the morning: all their clusters are scattered. Therefore expect me, says the Lord, in the day of my resurrection in the future, because my judgment is that I may gather the nations, and collect the kingdoms, that I may pour out upon them all my indignation, the anger of my fury: for in the fire of my zeal all the earth shall be consumed; because then I will turn upon the peoples a language in its generation, so that all may invoke the name of the Lord, that they may serve him under one yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive my dispersed ones: they shall bring victims to me. In that day you shall not be confounded for all your inventions, in which you have acted impiously against me: because then I will take away from you the detraction of your contumely, and you shall not add further to be magnified through my holy mountain: and I will leave in you a people mild and humble; and they shall reverence the name of the Lord, who shall be the remnants of Israel, and they shall not do iniquity, and they shall not speak vain things, and there shall not be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue: for they themselves shall be fed and shall lie down, and there shall be no one who may terrify them.* 

Let everyone who can understand the interpretation of this Prophecy, especially examining that which he says: that after all the earth is consumed, it will come to pass that a language returns to the peoples in its generation, just as it was before that ancient confusion: and let him consider that the Prophet says all will invoke the name of the Lord, so that they may serve him under one yoke, and that contumelious detractions may be taken away; nor will there be hereafter iniquity and vain speeches, and a deceitful tongue. These things it seemed good to bring forward thus without a diligent narration, on account of the saying of Celsus, who thinks it impossible that the nations of Europe, Asia, and Africa, as much Greek as barbarian, should ever agree in one. And perhaps it is indeed impossible for those still living in the body, but not likewise for those released from the body. Finally, Celsus exhorts us to bring aid to the Emperor with all our strength, and to carry out just and pious wars under his auspices, nor to decline military service if the matter so demands. We respond, that we bring help to the Emperor in its own time, but a divine help (so to speak), relying on divine armor, not human: and this we do obeying the warnings of the Apostle, whose words are these: *I beseech you, first that you make deprecations, prayers, intercessions,*

<margin>1 Timothy 2:1, 2.</margin>

<summary>Origen uses the prophecy of Zephaniah to argue that a universal spiritual unity is possible through divine intervention, countering Celsus's skepticism. He also begins to explain that Christians support the Emperor through prayer and "divine armor" rather than physical warfare.</summary>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...intercessions, and thanksgivings, for all men, for kings, and all who are placed in authority <note>original: "pro omnibus hominibus, pro regibus, & cunctis in potestate collocatis" - a reference to 1 Timothy 2:1-2</note>. And the more distinguished a person is in piety, the greater aid he brings to the Emperor—more so than the soldiers standing in battle array, who kill as many of the enemy as they can. We can also respond in this way to those who are strangers to our faith and who urge us to take up arms for the Commonwealth and to kill men: behold, even the priests of your own idols and the guardians of your temples keep their right hands pure from blood for the sake of their sacred rites, so that they may offer the customary sacrifices to those you consider Gods with hands unstained and unpolluted by slaughter; nor do you ever draft priests into the ranks during any war. If there is a consistent reason for this custom of yours, how much more should the "military service" of our people not be despised while others are at war? For we keep our hands pure, yet we contend through poured-out prayers to God for the legitimate Emperor and for the soldier who carries out a pious and just war, so that whatever is an adversary to those acting justly may be destroyed. Therefore, by routing with our prayers all the demons who stir up wars and disturb peace and treaties, we confer more benefit upon Kings than those who carry arms for the Commonwealth. Moreover, we labor for the Roman Empire while living justly and making vows for it, training ourselves to despise pleasures and not allowing ourselves to be led astray by them. Thus, we fight for the Emperor more than others do: we do not serve in the military with him, even if he compels us; but for his sake, we organize our own camp of piety, conducting our campaign through prayers to the Divine. But if Celsus commands us also to hold military commands for our country: let him know that we do this as well, but not in the sight of men to catch empty glory; for in the secret of our minds, we pour out vows to God for our country just as priests do. Indeed, more benefits are conferred upon the country by Christians than by the rest of men; for they educate citizens in piety toward the God who is the guardian and protector of the country, and they pave the way for them to a certain heavenly city of God, provided they live rightly even in the smallest of cities. To these people that Gospel saying applies: *Because you have been faithful in a very small city, come also to the great one;* <note>original: "Quoniam in minima civitate fidus fuisti, veni & ad magnam" - a variation of the Parable of the Talents/Minas</note> where *God stands in the assembly of the Gods, and in their midst He judges them:* <note>original: "Deus stat in Deorum concilio" - Psalm 82:1</note> and He numbers you among them, provided *you do not die like a man, and fall like one of the princes.* Furthermore, Celsus exhorts us to hold magistracies in our country, if the preservation of the laws and of piety should require this.

<column-break/>

...intercessions, thanksgivings, for all men, for kings, and all those who are in high positions. And by as much as one is more pious, by so much is he more effective than the soldiers who go out in the ranks and kill as many of the enemy as they can. Then we might also say this to those who are strangers to the faith, and who demand that we serve in the military for the common good and kill men: that even the priests of certain images among you, and the temple-wardens of those you consider gods, keep their right hand undefiled for the sake of the sacrifices, so that with bloodless hands, and pure from murders, they may bring the customary sacrifices to those you call gods; and certainly you do not enlist the priests even in war. If, then, this is done with good reason, how much more, while others are serving in the army, do these also serve as priests of God and ministers? They keep their right hands pure, but they struggle through prayers to God on behalf of those who serve in a just war, and on behalf of the one reigning justly, so that all things contrary and hostile to those who act justly may be brought down. And we, by our prayers, bringing down all demons—those who stir up warlike things, and confuse oaths, and disturb the peace—help those who reign more than those who seem to serve in the army. We labor together in common affairs, we who offer up prayers with righteousness, along with disciplines and exercises that teach us to despise pleasures and not be led by them. We even more so fight for the king; and we do not serve in the army with him, even if he presses us; but we serve in the army on his behalf, organizing a private camp of piety through intercessions to the Divine. And if Celsus wishes us to lead the army of education: let him know that we do this also, not to be seen by men and to be vain-glorious about it. Doing these things in our secret place, in the governing part of our soul, there are prayers sent up as if from priests on behalf of those in our country. Christians benefit their countries more than the rest of men, educating the citizens and teaching them to be pious toward the God who protects the city, taking up into a certain divine and heavenly city those who have lived well in the smallest cities. To whom it might be said, *In a very small city you were faithful, come also to the great one;* where *God stands in the congregation of gods, and in the midst God judges;* and He numbers them together, if they no longer die as men, nor fall as one of the rulers. "Celsus also urges us to the governing of the country, if it should be necessary to do this for the sake of the safety of the laws and of piety; but we..."

He asserts that by educating citizens in piety, Christians provide a greater service to the state than those who hold traditional office or bear arms.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Origen’s eight-book defense of Christianity against the pagan philosopher Celsus. It follows the discussion on the civic duties of Christians and their role in the "commonwealth of God."</meta>

# ORIGEN against CELSUS. Book 8.

In every city, we recognize the existence of another sort of country <note>Greek: *systēma patridos*; Latin: *civitates*. Origen is contrasting the earthly city-state with the spiritual community of the Church.</note> established by the Word of God. We exhort those who are powerful in speech and who lead a wholesome life to rule over the churches. We do not accept those who are ambitious for power, but we compel those who, out of great modesty, are unwilling to readily take up the common care of the Church of God. Indeed, those who rule us well are those who have been constrained to do so, forced by the Great King, whom we believe to be the Son of God, the Divine Word <note>Greek: *Logos*. The creative and governing principle of the universe identified with Christ.</note>. And if those who rule well in the Church do so, it is because they are chosen by that country which is according to God—I mean the Church. They rule according to the commands of God, without defiling any of the laws. And if Christians avoid the more common public services of life <note>Greek: *leitourgia*. Public duties or offices often expected of wealthy citizens in the Roman Empire.</note>, it is because they are reserving themselves for a more divine and necessary service in the Church of God, for the salvation of men. They lead both necessarily and justly, caring for all: for those within, that they may live better every day; and for those who seem to be without, that they may become involved in the solemn words and deeds of piety. Thus, truly worshipping the One, and educating as many as possible (to the best of their power), they are blended with the Word of God and the Divine Law. In this way, they are united to the God who is over all, through the Son of God—the Word, Wisdom, Truth, and Righteousness—who unites them to Him, everyone who is determined to live according to God in all things.

You have here, holy Ambrose <note>Origen’s patron, who encouraged and financed the writing of this massive defense.</note>, the conclusion of the task you commanded of me, according to the strength currently present and given to us. We have described in eight books everything we thought appropriate to say in opposition to the work titled *The True Word* by Celsus. It remains for the seeker to judge, by comparing his writing and our counter-arguments against him, which of the two lies closer to the truth of God, and which leads toward piety toward Him, and which leads toward doctrines destructive to men. Know, however, that Celsus promised to produce another treatise after this one, in which he promised to teach how those who wish and are able to obey him ought to live. If, therefore, he did not write that second book despite his promise, these eight books we have written may suffice. But if he began and completed that work as well, seek it out and send the manuscript to me, so that we may respond to that also—whatever the Father of Truth may grant us—and overturn the false opinions within it. But if he should say anything true, we shall bear witness to it without contention, as being well said.

<column-break/>

Indeed, since we know that in every town other cities have been founded by the word of God, we urge those who are fit to preside by their life and sound doctrine to take up the leadership of the Churches. We do not approve the ambitious, but the modest; and we compel those who do not rashly thrust themselves into such arduous functions to take up these public cares. Even our magistrates who administer affairs well are compelled against their will, at the insistence of the Supreme King, whom we believe to be the Son of God and God the Word. While they preside well over these divinely constituted fatherlands—that is, the Churches—by which they were elected, they govern them according to the prescriptions of God, while also keeping the public laws safe. Nor do Christians do this because they shrink from those public duties of life; rather, they keep themselves for the more divine and necessary duties of the Church for the salvation of men. For they consider this both just and necessary, taking account of all people: of their own, that they may make progress daily; and of outsiders, that they may draw them toward the doctrine and works of piety and religion. Thus, by truly worshipping God and, as far as permitted, instructing as many as possible, they are joined to the Word of God and the divine law, and become one with God, the Lord of all things. This is achieved through the uniting of His Son, the Word of God, who is wisdom, justice, and truth, through whom anyone whose desire is to please God with their whole life is converted.

You have, holy Ambrose, the end of the work finished at your command, as best we could. Arranged into eight books, as we deemed fit, it is a response to Celsus’s work titled *The True Word*. It remains that we pray the reader, who deigns to know both his writings and ours, to judge which of the two more truly breathes of the true God and the manner of piety by which He is worshipped—a piety now received by men who, taught by Truth itself, order their lives well. Know, however, that Celsus promises he will publish another treatise, in which it is taught how those who wish and are able to obey his warnings ought to live. If he did not write it, despite the promise, we shall be content to have answered him in these eight volumes. But if that work was also completed by him: find it and send it to me, so that we may respond to it with whatever truth the Father suggests, and refute the lies; if, however, any truth should be mixed in, we shall confirm it with our testimony without contention.

->THE END.<-

->Glory to You, our God, glory to You.<-

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN,
# *ORIGEN’S Love of the Beautiful.* <note>original: "Philocalia" (Greek: Φιλοκαλία) literally means "love of the beautiful," referring here to the beauty of divine wisdom found in the scriptures.</note>

The present book contains a selection of scriptural questions and solutions, compiled or gathered from various books of Origen by those wise in divine matters, Gregory and Basil. It was sent in a small volume <note>original: "pyktio" (πυκτίῳ), a folded writing tablet or small codex.</note> by one of these two, Gregory the Theologian, to Theodore, who was at that time the Bishop of Tyana, as the letter written to him shows, which reads as follows.

<column-break/>

This book contains a selection of questions on Scripture and their solutions, composed from various commentaries of Origen by those most learned in divine matters, Gregory and Basil. One of these, Gregory the Theologian, sent it in a small volume to Theodore, the Bishop of Tyana at that time, as this Letter written to him declares.

---

->GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS<-

->*To THEODORE, Bishop of TYANA.*<-

->[ Nazianzus, Epistle 88. ]<-

Your letter is a feast, and what is even better is that you anticipate the season with your eagerness, granting us the joy of celebrating together. Such are the gifts from your Piety. As for us, what greater thing could we have to give in return than our prayers? But so that you may have some memorial from us and from Saint Basil, we have sent you a small volume of Origen’s *Philocalia*, containing selections useful to scholars <note>original: "philologois" (φιλολόγοις), meaning those who love learning, literature, or the study of words.</note>. Deign to accept this, and give us proof of its benefit, being aided both by diligence and by the Spirit.

<column-break/>

Your letter represents the joy of a feast day to us, and—what is far more excellent—you outrun time itself, and by your generous will and inclination, you provide the opportunity for an anticipated celebration. These are the things that proceed from your Piety; we, as much as we are able, respond with our prayers. And so that you yourself may have some monument from me and from Saint Basil, we have sent to you a little book of Selections from Origen, in which are contained excerpts useful to the studious; do not be burdened by receiving it. Then, signify what fruit you have gathered from it, aided both by study and by the spirit.

<margin>
*The divinely inspired Scripture. How it is to be read and understood. The reason for the obscurity found within it. Why some things in it, according to the letter, seem foreign to reason or impossible to have happened.*

Concerning the divine inspiration of the holy Scripture, and how it ought to be read and understood; and what is the reason for the lack of clarity in it, and for that which is impossible or irrational in certain literal passages.

### CHAPTER I.
*From the fourth book of "On First Principles," and various other treatises by Origen.* <note>original: "De Principiis" / "Περὶ ἀρχῶν". This is Origen's most famous work on systematic theology.</note>

Since, in examining such great matters, we are not satisfied with common sense and the understanding of things seen with the eyes, we take up testimonies for the demonstration of what we say from those Scriptures which we believe to be divine—both from the so-called Old Testament and the New—and we endeavor to strengthen our faith by reason. However, we have not yet discussed the Scriptures themselves as being divine; let us, therefore, discuss a few points concerning them in a brief summary, setting forth the reasons that lead us to regard them as divine writings. And first, before we bring forth testimonies from the writings themselves and the things declared in them, we must explain these matters concerning Moses, the lawgiver of the Hebrews, and Jesus Christ, the author of the saving teachings of Christian piety. For although there have been very many lawgivers and teachers among both the Greeks and the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, not necessarily "uncivilized" groups.</note> who professed the truth in the doctrines they put forward, we have no record of any lawgiver who was able to instill a zeal for adopting his laws in other nations, no matter how great an apparatus of persuasive demonstration he brought to bear. ### CHAPTER 1.
From the 4th book of *On First Principles*, and various other compositions of Origen.

Since, when examining such great matters, we are not satisfied with common notions and the evidence of things seen, we take up as evidence for the manifestation of our arguments the testimonies from the Scriptures believed by us to be divine—both the so-called Old Testament and the so-called New—and we attempt to confirm our faith by reason; and as we have not yet discoursed concerning the Scriptures as being divine, come then, let us also go through a few things concerning these, as if in a summary, presenting the things that move us to treat them as divine writings. And first, we must use the evidence from the writings themselves and the things manifested in them concerning Moses and Jesus Christ—the former the lawgiver of the Hebrews, and the latter the introducer of the saving doctrines according to Christianity. These things must be distinguished: for although there have been very many lawgivers among Greeks and Barbarians, and teachers announcing doctrines professing the truth, we have recorded no lawgiver who was able to produce a zeal in the rest of the nations for accepting his words, or who managed to make anyone do so even after bringing in a great deal of apparent logical demonstration. ...of those who promised truth, no one has been able to instill the truth they believed in into various nations, or even into a significant multitude of a single nation. And yet, even the legislators would have wished to relax <note>or "spread"</note> their laws for the better, if possible, among the entire race of men; and the teachers desired that the truth they imagined should be spread everywhere in the inhabited world. But because they were unable to call those of other languages and many nations to the observance of their laws and the acceptance of their teachings, they did not even attempt this from the beginning, not unwisely considering that such a thing was impossible for them. 

But all Greece, and the barbarian world throughout the inhabited earth, has countless zealots who have abandoned their ancestral laws and supposed gods for the observance of the laws of Moses and the discipleship of the words of Jesus Christ. And this is despite the fact that those who attach themselves to the law of Moses are hated by those who worship idols; and those who have accepted the word of Jesus Christ are not only hated but are in danger of death. 

And if we consider how, in a very few years—even though those professing Christianity were plotted against, and some were killed for this reason, while others lost their possessions—the word has been able to be preached throughout the whole world, even though teachers were not numerous, so that Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, have joined themselves to the piety through Jesus, we do not hesitate to say that the matter is greater than human, since the teachers of the word of Jesus taught with all authority and the persuasion of those who have prevailed from God. Therefore, one might reasonably consider his voices to be oracles, when he said:

But since they could not lead men of another language and of many nations to the observation of their laws and to the undertaking of their discipline, they did not attempt to do it from the beginning, not imprudently considering that they could in no way achieve it. 

But all Greece, as well as the Barbarian lands which open across the world, has innumerable devotees of the Mosaic law and the discipline of the words of Jesus Christ, having left behind their ancestral laws and received gods; although those who have applied themselves to the law of Moses are held in the deepest hatred by those who worship images; and besides hatred, those who have received the doctrine of Jesus Christ are engaged in danger to their lives. 

And truly, if we observe by what means, in so few years—although so many snares were created for those professing the Christian faith, not a few of these were killed, others were fined of their goods, and otherwise there was no great supply of teachers—that speech could be dispersed through the circle of the lands, so that Greeks and Barbarians, learned and unlearned, joined themselves to the pious faith of Jesus Christ, we will not hesitate to say the matter is greater than human powers, especially since Christ taught with the highest power and confidence concerning the force and stability of his doctrine. 

Therefore his voices ought rightly to be judged oracles, of which kind is this: *You shall be led before Kings and presidents because of me, for a testimony to them, and to the nations;* and, *Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name? and drink in your name? and cast out demons in your name? and I will say to them, Depart from me you who work iniquity, I never knew you.* It might perhaps have seemed credible that the Lord said these things in vain, so that they would not actually happen: but, since those things which had been spoken with such authority have occurred, it appears that God, having truly been made man, handed down a saving doctrine to men.

By demonstrating briefly the divinity of Jesus and using the prophetic words concerning him, we simultaneously demonstrate that the Scriptures which prophesy about him are divinely inspired <note>term: "θεοπνεύστους" (theopneustous) — literally "God-breathed," the standard term for the divine origin of the Bible.</note>. # Chapter I. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia* <note>original: "Philocalia" — a title meaning "Love of the Beautiful," referring to an anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>

### Lll <note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order for binding.</note>

It shows more clearly than any light that these books were composed by heavenly grace. Indeed, anyone who has applied themselves diligently and attentively to the reading of the Prophets will feel a trace of divine inspiration from that experience; from this, they will be most firmly persuaded that the words we believe to be divine utterances are not of human origin. Therefore, the light that resides in the Law of Moses, which was once covered by a veil, shone forth at the coming of Jesus Christ when that covering was rolled back; and the good things, of which the letter held only a shadow, immediately came into public knowledge. Now, it would be a great and worthwhile task to review the most ancient predictions of the Prophets concerning each event that was to come, so that anyone who doubts might be struck by them as being divine. Thus, setting aside all doubt and the hesitation of a wavering mind, they might devote themselves with their whole soul to the words of God. Furthermore, if to the less learned, thoughts greater than human understanding do not seem to occur in every single passage, it is no wonder. For in the works of that Providence which embraces the entire universe, some things appear most clearly as the works of Providence, while others are so hidden and concealed that they seem to provide a reason for doubting God’s governance—He who administers all things with unutterable skill and power. For the method of the divine Artist’s providence is not as obvious in things upon the earth as it is in the Sun, the Moon, and the stars; nor is it as manifest in human events and accidents as it is in the soul and body of living creatures. Those who apply diligence to investigating these things have clearly discovered why and for what reason these impulses exist, these forms in the mind, these natures of animals, and this condition and fabric of bodies. But just as among those who have once rightly accepted the concept of Providence, their faith in it is not diminished or destroyed because of things they do not comprehend; so too, nothing is taken away from the divinity of Scripture, which is diffused through its entirety, by the fact that our weakness cannot perceive the secret splendor of the doctrine in every single word—a splendor that lies hidden in thin and humble language. *For we have this treasure in earthen vessels* <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7.</note>: so that the excellence and loftiness of God's power may shine, and not be thought to come from us who are but men. For if the well-worn and common paths of demonstration used among men, when contained in the holy books, had been sufficient to conquer humanity, one might rightly think our faith was situated in human wisdom and not in the power of God. But now, it is clear to anyone lifting their eyes that the word of God and the preaching of the Gospel did not prevail among the people through the persuasive words of wisdom, but through the demonstration of the Spirit and the power of God. Wherefore, since a heavenly power—indeed, one superior to the heavens—compels us to worship Him alone who

<column-break/>

brought [these things] to light, as having been recorded by a well-tempered grace. He who encounters the prophetic words with care and attention, having felt from the very reading a trace of inspiration, will be persuaded by what he experiences that the words believed to be God's are not the compositions of men. The light inherent in the Law of Moses, hidden away by a veil, shone forth at the arrival of Jesus, the veil having been removed, and the good things—of which the letter held a shadow—gradually coming into knowledge. It would be a great task now to take courage and examine the most ancient prophecies concerning each future event, so that through them, the one who doubts might be struck as if by divine things, and putting away all double-mindedness and hesitation, might give himself over with his whole soul to the words of God. And if to the unlearned the meaning does not seem to manifest as superhuman in every single letter, it is no wonder; for even in the works of the providence that flows through the whole world, some things appear most clearly as works of providence, while others are so hidden as to seem to provide a place for unbelief regarding the God who manages the whole with unspeakable skill and power. For the technical logic of providence is not so clear in things on earth as it is in the sun, moon, and stars; and it is not so manifest in human accidents as it is in the souls and bodies of living things, where the "why" and "for what purpose" is greatly discovered by those who care for these things—concerning the impulses, the mental images, the natures of animals, and the structures of bodies. But just as providence is not bankrupt because of things not known (at least among those who have once rightly accepted it), so neither does the divinity of Scripture, which extends through it all, lose anything because our weakness cannot stand before the hidden brilliance of the doctrines stored in humble and contemptible language. For we have the treasure in earthen vessels; so that the excellence of the power of God may shine, and not be thought to be from us humans. For if the well-trodden paths of demonstrations common among men, being stored in the books, had overpowered men, our faith would reasonably be supposed to be in the wisdom of men, and not in the power of God. But now it is clear to the one who has lifted his eyes that the word and the preaching, as it says to the many, is not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and power.
