# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER I.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:6.</margin>
...having [exhorted] us only, let us endeavor, leaving behind the discourse of the beginning of Christ—that is, the word of elementary instruction—to be carried toward perfection, so that the wisdom spoken among the perfect may be spoken also to us. For he who possesses this wisdom promises to speak it among the perfect, it being a different wisdom from the wisdom of this age, and the wisdom of the rulers of this age which is coming to nothing. <note>Origen is quoting Paul to argue that deeper spiritual insight is required beyond basic Sunday-school level faith.</note> This wisdom will be clearly impressed upon us, and will produce a revelation of the mystery kept silent for eternal ages, but now made manifest through the prophetic writings and the appearance of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for all ages, Amen. After having spoken in a cursory manner about the divine inspiration of the holy Scriptures, it is necessary to discuss the method of reading and understanding them; since many errors have arisen because the path by which one ought to approach the holy readings has not been found by the majority. For the hard-hearted and the unlearned of the circumcision <note>A common historical term for Jewish people who did not convert to Christianity.</note> have not believed in our Savior, thinking that they must follow the literal words of the prophecies concerning him, and not seeing with their senses that he proclaimed release to captives, nor built what they think is truly the city of God, nor destroyed the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, nor ate butter and honey, and before he knew or preferred evil, chose the good. <margin>Romans 16:25.</margin> <margin>Zechariah 9:10. Isaiah 7:15.</margin> Furthermore, they thought the prophet foretold that the wolf, the four-footed animal, would feed with the lamb, and the leopard would rest with the kid, and the calf and the bull and the lion would feed together, led by a little child, and the cow and the bear would graze together, their young being raised with one another; and the lion would eat straw like the ox. <margin>Isaiah 11:6, 7.</margin> Having seen none of these things happen to the senses during the advent of the Christ we believe in, they did not accept our Lord Jesus; but as one who declared himself Christ contrary to what was necessary, they crucified him. And those from the heresies <note>Referring to Gnostic groups like the Marcionites who rejected the Old Testament God as being "evil" or "wrathful."</note> reading: *A fire is kindled in my anger*; and, *I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation*; and, *I regret having anointed Saul as king*; and, *I am God making peace and creating evils*; and in other places, *There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not made*; and further, *Evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem*; and, *An evil spirit from God choked Saul*; <margin>Jeremiah 15:14. Exodus 20:5. 1 Samuel 15:11. Isaiah 45:7. Amos 3:6. Micah 1:12. 1 Samuel 16:15.</margin> and countless things similar to these, they have not dared to disbelieve the Scriptures as being from God; but believing them to belong to the Creator whom the Jews worship—

<column-break/>

—who created us, let him rouse us, so that leaving the discourse of the beginnings of Christ, that is, the first elements, we may be carried with all striving of the soul toward fulfillment, so that the wisdom which is explained to the perfect may also be set forth to us: for he who possessed it promises to speak wisdom among the perfect, a wisdom plainly different from the wisdom of this age, and from the wisdom of the princes of this age, which is outdated and has vanished. By this wisdom we shall be openly shaped, which will lay open the mystery hidden from eternity, but now made manifest through the writings of the Prophets, and through the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever, Amen. After we have proved in our discourse that the sacred Scriptures are divinely inspired, we must come to the method of reading and understanding them: since many errors and slips have happened because many have not found the way in which one must persist and progress in holy reading. For men with a hard heart, and the unlearned from the circumcision, did not believe in our Savior, because they were determined to follow the bare words of the predictions concerning Christ, nor did they perceive by their senses that he himself had pronounced dismissal to the captives, nor had he built that which they imagine to be the true city of God, nor had he exterminated the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, nor had he eaten butter and honey, and, before he knew or chose evil, chose the good. They thought, moreover, that the Prophet had sung that it would be that the wolf, a four-footed animal, would feed with the lamb, and the leopard would rest with the kid; the calf, the bull, and the lion would feed together, and be led by a small boy; the cow and the bear would pluck fodder together, and their little ones would be nourished together with them; the lion would eat straw like the ox. And since they perceive by their senses that none of these things were done in the coming of the Christ believed by us, they did not join themselves to our Lord Jesus, but, as if he preached himself as Christ through the highest wickedness, they raised him on a cross. And the heretics reading, *Fire has blazed out of my wrath*: and *I am a jealous God, rendering the sins of the fathers onto the sons into the third and fourth generation*: and, *It repents me that I anointed Saul as King*: and, *I am the Lord making peace, and creating evils*: and in another place, *There is no evil in the city, which the Lord has not done*: and that besides, *Evils descended from the Lord into the gates of Jerusalem*: and, *An evil spirit from God suffocated Saul*: and almost infinite things similar to these, they have not dared to revoke all faith in them as divine Scriptures; but believing them to be of that creator whom the Jews worship, <note>The Latin text on the right column is a translation of the Greek text on the left, provided for scholars of the period.</note>

<summary>Origen explains that a literal interpretation of Old Testament prophecies led many to reject Jesus, while others (heretics) mistakenly believe the Creator God is vengeful or evil based on a surface-level reading of difficult passages.</summary>

# CHAPTER I. ORIGEN’S Philocalia.
<note>The *Philocalia* is an anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus in the 4th century.</note>

## [Column 1 - Latin]

...they wished, as if that creator were defective and not good, and so they judged that a Savior had arrived to announce a more perfect God, whom they claim is not the maker of the world. Being swept away into various opinions by this, once they fell away from their Author—who is the only unbegotten God—they clung to fictions and devised arguments by which they introduce certain visible things that were made, and others which are not seen, which their own minds fashioned as phantoms. Furthermore, even some of the simpler folk, who boast of belonging to the Church, think there is nothing greater than the Creator, embracing a sound opinion in that regard; yet they imagine such things about Him that one would not even think regarding the most cruel and unjust of men. To all of these, there seems to be no other cause for their false opinions, their impiety, and their foolish talk about God, than that the Scripture is not understood according to the spirit, but is accepted according to the bare sound of the letter. Therefore, to those who are convinced that the holy books are not the commentaries of men, but were written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, by the will of God the Father of all through Jesus Christ, and have come down to us, the apparent ways of understanding must be demonstrated: keeping before us the norm and rule of the heavenly Church of Jesus Christ according to the succession of the Apostles. And all believe, even the simplest of those who assent to the Word, that there are certain secret dispensations declared in the divine Scriptures. But what these truly are, the wise and modest ingenuously confess they do not know. Therefore, if anyone should inquire about the union of Lot with his daughters, about the two wives of Abraham, about the two sisters who married Jacob, or the two handmaids who bore children by him, they will answer nothing else than that these mysteries are obscure and unknown to us. But also when the construction of the Tabernacle is read, those believing such writings to be figures <note>original: "figuras" - types or symbolic representations</note> seek and investigate what they might be able to fit to each of those things said about the Tabernacle. Nor indeed are they deceived in believing the Tabernacle to be a figure of some reality; but when they apply the reason for that of which the Tabernacle is a type to some certain thing in a manner consistent with Scripture, they sometimes wander from the truth. And indeed, they declare that every narrative which seems to tell of marriages, or the procreation of children, or of wars, or of any histories whatsoever that might be told among the common people, are figures; yet because it is beyond measure difficult for men to explore such matters...

## [Column 2 - Greek]

...they thought, as if he happened to be imperfect and not good, <unclear>judging</unclear> the Creator, that the Savior had visited to announce a more perfect God, who they say is not the Creator. Having moved in different directions at that time, and having once revolted from the Creator, who is the only unbegotten God, they gave themselves over to fabrications, mythologizing for themselves hypotheses according to which they think visible things and certain other invisible things came to be, which their soul portrayed as idols. Moreover, even the more innocent of those who boast of being from the Church have supposed no one to be greater than the Creator, doing so healthily. Yet they suppose such things about Him as one would not even about the most savage and unjust man. The cause for all the aforementioned false beliefs and impieties or ignorant words about God seems to be none other than that the Scripture has not been understood according to its spiritual meanings, but has been taken according to the bare letter. Therefore, to those persuaded that the sacred books are not the compositions of men, but have been written from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, by the will of the Father of all through Jesus Christ, and have come to us, the apparent ways must be pointed out, while holding to the rule of the heavenly Church of Jesus Christ according to the succession of the Apostles. And that there are certain mystical economies <note>original: "οἰκονομίαι" - divine arrangements or plans</note> manifested through the divine Scriptures, all believe, even the most innocent of those approaching the Word; but some of them, being sensible and unpretentious, confess they do not know them. If, for instance, someone should ask about Lot’s intercourse with his daughters, and the two wives of Abraham, and the two sisters married to Jacob, and the two handmaids who had children by him, they will say nothing else than that these happen to be mysteries not understood by us. But also whenever the construction of the tabernacle is read, being persuaded that the things written are types, they seek what they will be able to apply to each of the things said regarding the tabernacle. Insofar as they are persuaded that the tabernacle is a type of something, they do not err; but insofar as they apply the account to this or that thing in a manner worthy of the Scripture, they sometimes fall away. And they declare every narrative thought to report marriages, or child-bearing, or wars, or any histories whatsoever that would be spoken of among the many, to be types; but in the question of "of what things," sometimes because of a state of mind not quite disciplined, and sometimes because of rashness—even if one happens to be disciplined and blameless—because the discovery of the matters is exceedingly difficult for men...

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER I.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:12</margin>
...to men, the reasoning concerning each of these points is not entirely clear. And what need is there to speak of the Prophecies, which we all know to be filled with riddles and dark sayings? Even if we come to the Gospels, their accurate meaning—being as it is the "mind of Christ"—requires the grace given to him who said: *But we have the mind of Christ, that we might know the things freely given to us by God; which things also we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Spirit.* <note>Origen argues that because the New Testament is the "mind of Christ," it is just as deep and mysterious as the Old Testament.</note> And as for the things revealed to John <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, who could read them without being struck with amazement at the concealment of the unutterable mysteries expressed through words that the reader does not understand? To which of those skilled in examining texts would the Epistles of the Apostles seem clear and easily understood? For there, as if through a narrow opening, ten thousand great and numerous thoughts are provided in a brief space. Therefore, since these things are so, and since countless people fall into error, it is not without danger for one to declare too easily while reading that they understand things which require the "key of knowledge," which the Savior says is held by the lawyers. <note>The "lawyers" or "legal experts" refers to the Jewish scholars of the Law (Nomikoi).</note> Let those who are unwilling to admit that the truth existed among those who lived before the coming of Christ explain how the "key of knowledge" is said by our Lord Jesus Christ to be held by those who (as they claim) did not possess books containing the secrets of knowledge and perfect mysteries. For the text says: *Woe unto you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge; you entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in you hindered.* <note>Luke 11:52. Origen uses this to prove that the Old Testament always contained hidden Christian truths.</note> Therefore, the way that appears to us for how one ought to approach the Scriptures and grasp their meaning is as follows, extracted from the divine utterances themselves. In Solomon, in the book of Proverbs, we find a certain instruction concerning the written divine doctrines: *And do thou describe them to thyself in a threefold way, in counsel and knowledge, that thou mayest answer words of truth to those who propose questions to thee.* <note>Proverbs 22:20-21. Origen relies on a specific Greek translation (the Septuagint) which uses the word "threefold" (trissōs).</note> Therefore, one ought to portray the meanings of the holy writings in one's own soul in a threefold way: so that the simpler man may be edified by what we might call the **flesh** of the Scripture (this being our name for the obvious and literal interpretation); while he who has ascended to a certain height may be edified by what is, as it were, its **soul**; and he who is perfect, and like those described by the Apostle—*We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the rulers of this world who are coming to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages unto our glory*—may be edified by the **spiritual** law, which has a shadow of the good things to come. For just as a human being is composed of body, soul, and spirit, in the same way the economy <note>The "economy" (oikonomia) here refers to the divine arrangement or structure of the Bible.</note>...

<margin>Proverbs 22:21</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:6, 7</margin>

<column-break/>

...however much one may be practiced and discerning, the reasoning of each part does not appear so evidently. It is of no use to speak of the Prophecies, which we all know are full of enigmas and obscure speeches. And, if we turn ourselves to the Gospels, even their accurate understanding, as it is the mind of Christ, needs the grace which was given to him who said: *But we have the mind of Christ, that we may know the things which are freely given to us by God, which also we speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit.* Who could read the things revealed to John without stupor, at the hiding of mysteries which are shown in writings to one who does not understand? To what expert and sagacious judge of speeches would the Epistles of the Apostles seem open and easy to understand: since in them, as if through a narrow chink, an infinite number of the greatest notions provide no small argument? Since these things are so, and nearly innumerable people slip up, it is truly dangerous in reading to pronounce that one understands those things which need the key of understanding, which the Savior says is in the power of the lawyers. And let those who do not want the truth to have been among those people before the coming of Christ declare in what way the key of knowledge is said by our Lord Jesus Christ to be among them, who (as they themselves preach) do not have books containing the secrets of science and perfect mysteries. These are the words: *Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of understanding; you yourselves did not enter, and you prohibited those entering.* Therefore the way and method of approaching the Scriptures, and perceiving their mind, is perceived by us as such, impressed by the tracks of the Scriptures themselves. In Solomon, in the Proverbs, we find a decree of this kind concerning the doctrines divinely written: *But do thou describe [them] to thyself triply in counsel and science, that thou mayest answer words of truth to those things which are proposed to thee.* Therefore the sentiments of the holy letters are to be described in the mind in a threefold way; so that the simpler man indeed may be confirmed by the very "flesh" of the Scripture, as it were (for so we call the prompt sense, and that which is as it were at hand); but he who is more adult, by its "soul" in a certain way; but he who is perfect and like those who are called by the Apostle: *We speak wisdom among the perfect, but a wisdom not of this world, which is antiquated, but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God pre-defined before the ages for our glory,* from the spiritual law, having a shadow of future goods. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

Scripture was arranged and destined for the salvation of men. For this reason, in a book held in low esteem by some, titled *The Shepherd*, we discuss the matter of Hermas being commanded to write two books, and then himself to announce to the Elders of the Church what he had learned from the spirit. The passage is as follows: *“You shall write two books, and give one to Clement and one to Grapte; and Grapte shall instruct the widows and orphans; but Clement shall send to the foreign cities. But you shall announce it to the Elders of the Church.”* <note>original: "Scribes duos libros..." quoting the Shepherd of Hermas, Vision 2.4.3</note> For Grapte, who instructs the widows and orphans, is the bare letter itself, teaching those who are children in mind and cannot yet be enrolled as God’s own, and are therefore called orphans; and she instructs those who no longer serve a wicked husband, but are widows because they are not yet worthy of the Bridegroom. But Clement, who has already moved beyond the letter, is said to send what is written to distant cities; as if we were to signify minds that are placed outside the mass of the body and the thought of weak things. No longer through letters, but through living words, the disciple of the spirit himself is commanded to report to the elders of the whole Church—those who are gray-haired with wisdom. But since there are certain Scriptures which have nothing corporeal <note>i.e., no literal or historical application</note>, as we shall show hereafter; in some, only the soul and spirit, as it were, must be sought. And perhaps for this reason, the water-jars said to be placed for the purification of the Jews, as we read in the Gospel of John, contain two or three measures: <margin>John 2:6</margin> a discourse which, under a veil, shows those who are called "Jews in secret" by the Apostle. <note>Referring to Romans 2:29</note> Therefore, as these are purged through the words of Scripture, sometimes they receive two measures of the "soul" (so to speak) and the "spirit" of the discourse; but sometimes three, when some passages have, besides those we mentioned, something corporeal which can build up. The six water-jars are rightly for those being purified in the world, which was created in six days, a perfect number. From the first perception, then, and that which is useful in it, the multitude of those who have believed sincerely and simply testifies that some benefit flows forth. But of that interpretation which pertains, as it were, to the soul, an example is found in Paul in the first letter to the Corinthians. For it is written, he says, *“You shall not muzzle the mouth of an ox while it treads out the grain.”* <margin>1 Cor. 9:9; Deut. 25:4</margin> Then, explaining this place, he adds, *“Is God concerned about oxen? Or does He say it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes it was written, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope of partaking.”* <margin>1 Cor. 9:10</margin> Then, very many which

Scripture was provided and given by God for the salvation of men. For this reason, even in the book despised by some, *The Shepherd*, concerning the command given to Hermas to write two books, and afterwards to announce to the elders of the church what he learned from the spirit, we have interpreted it thus. The text is this: *“You shall write two books, and give one to Clement and one to Grapte. And Grapte shall admonish the widows and the orphans; but Clement shall send to the cities abroad. But you shall announce it to the elders of the church.”* <note>original: "Γράψεις δύο βιβλία..."</note> For Grapte, who admonishes the widows and orphans, is the bare letter itself, admonishing those who are children in their souls and not yet able to claim God as Father, and for this reason are called orphans; and admonishing those who no longer use the lawless bridegroom, but remain widows because they have not yet become worthy of the Bridegroom. But Clement, who is already departing from the letter, is said to send the things spoken to the cities abroad, as if we were to say the souls that exist outside of bodily and lowly thoughts. No longer through writings, but through living words, the disciple of the spirit himself announces to the elders—those of the whole church of God who have grown gray through wisdom. But since there are some scriptures having no bodily [sense] at all, as we shall show in what follows, there are places where one must seek only the soul and the spirit of the scripture. And perhaps for this reason the water-jars said to be set for the purification of the Jews, as we read in the Gospel according to John, <margin>John 2:6</margin> hold two or three measures; the word hinting at those who are "Jews in secret" according to the Apostle. The six water-jars are reasonably for those being purified in the world, which was completed in the perfect number of six days. From the first interpretation, then, and the benefit according to it, the multitudes of those who have believed genuinely and more simply bear witness that it is possible to be profited. Or does He say it altogether for <margin>1 Cor. 9:10</margin> our sakes? # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER I.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:7</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 10:11</margin>
<margin>Ibid. verse 4</margin>
<margin>Exodus 25:9; Hebrews 8:5</margin>
<margin>Galatians 4:21-24; Genesis 16:15; Genesis 21:2</margin>
<margin>Colossians 2:16, 17</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 8:5</margin>
<margin>Romans 11:4; 3 Kings 19:18 <note>In older Bibles, 1 and 2 Kings are called 1 and 2 Samuel, and 3 and 4 Kings are called 1 and 2 Kings.</note></margin>

Interpretations that are circulated and suited to the masses, which edify those unable to understand higher things, possess a similar character. But a spiritual narration belongs to one who is able to demonstrate what sort of heavenly things were served by the Jews "according to the flesh" <note>original: *secundum carnem*—referring to literal or physical observance</note> as a pattern and shadow; and of which future good things the Law holds a shadow. Finally, in all matters, according to the Apostolic promise, one must seek the wisdom hidden in a mystery, which God predestined before the ages for the glory of the righteous, which none of the rulers of this age has known. 

The Apostle himself says somewhere, using certain words from Exodus and Numbers, that these things happened to them as a figure <note>original: *typice* / *in figura*—meaning a symbolic precursor</note>; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. He gives clues as to what those things were figures of, saying: *They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.* And describing the things written about the Tabernacle in another Epistle, he used this testimony: *You shall make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.* 

Furthermore, in the Epistle to the Galatians, as if reproaching those who read the Law but do not understand it—judging that those who do not believe there are hidden meanings in the writings do not truly perceive them—he says: *Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; but the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically <note>original: *allegoroumena*—Origen emphasizes that Paul himself uses the word "allegory" to interpret the Old Testament.</note>: for these are the two covenants,* and so forth. 

One must observe and weigh individually the things said by him: for he says, *You who want to be under the law,* not, *You who are under the law*; and, *Do you not hear the law?*—since "hearing" is judged by understanding and knowing. And in the Epistle to the Colossians, briefly touching upon the intent of the entire legislation, he says: *Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in regard to a festival or a new moon or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come.* And in the Epistle to the Hebrews, discussing those of the circumcision, he writes: *who serve the image and shadow of heavenly things.* 

Therefore, concerning the five books ascribed to Moses, it is not fitting for those who have once accepted the Apostle as a divine man to have any doubt. Do you wish to learn if the rest of history also happened figuratively? One should observe from the Epistle to the Romans that the passage, *I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee before Baal,* which is found in the third book of Kings, was taken by Paul to refer to the chosen Israelites, of the

<column-break/>

<note>The Latin column provides a parallel translation of the Greek text above. The content is identical in substance, reinforcing the argument that the Old Testament must be read as a spiritual allegory rather than merely a literal history.</note>

circulated interpretations, suited to the multitude, which also edify those who cannot understand higher things, are of almost the same form and character. But the explanation according to the spirit is proper to him who can demonstrate of which heavenly things the Jews according to the flesh were serving as a likeness and shadow; and of which future goods the law has a shadow. Finally, in all things, according to the precept of Paul the Apostle, the wisdom hidden in mystery is to be followed, which God preordained before the ages for the glory of the just, which none of the princes of this world knew. 

Somewhere the Apostle himself says, using certain words of Exodus and Numbers, that these things happened to them in figure: but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have run their course: and he gives arguments of what those figures were, saying, *They drank from the rock following them, but the rock was Christ:* and those things which are written concerning the Tabernacle, he used this testimony in another Epistle while describing it, *You shall make all things according to the form which was shown to you on the mount.* 

But also in the Epistle to the Galatians, as if making a reproach to those who think they read the law but do not understand it, judging that those who do not think there are abstruse senses in the writings do not perceive it, he says, *Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one from a maidservant, and one from a free woman: but he who was from the maidservant was born according to the flesh; but he who was from the free woman through the promise. Which things show one thing by sense, another by words <note>original: *aliud sensu, aliud verbis*—a definition of allegory: saying one thing to mean another.</note>: for these are the two Testaments,* and what follows. For the things said by him are to be observed and weighed one by one: because he says, *You who wish to be under the law,* not, *You who are under the law*: and, *Do you not hear the law?* since hearing is discerned by understanding and knowing. 

And in that to the Colossians, touching on the mind of the universal law in a few words, he says, *Let no one therefore judge us either in drink, or in part of a feast day, or of the new moon, or of the Sabbaths, which are shadows of things to come.* And in that to the Hebrews, disputing about those who are of the circumcision, he writes, *who serve the image and shadow of heavenly things.* But for that reason, it is not convenient to doubt concerning the five books ascribed to Moses for those who have once adhered to the Apostle as a divine man. Do you wish to receive the rest of history, whether it also happened through figure? It is to be observed from the epistle to the Romans, *I have set aside for myself seven thousand men, who have not bent the knee before [the sign of] Baal,* which is held in the third of Kings, that Paul took this for the chosen Israelites,

# Chapter I. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia* <note>The *Philocalia* is an anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus in the 4th century.</note>

...Israelites, showing that not only have the Gentiles gathered fruit from the coming of Jesus Christ, but also some from that divine race. Since these things are so, we must outline the forms of understanding the Scriptures that we have before our eyes. At the outset, it must be demonstrated that the Spirit—who by divine providence, through the Word <note>original: *verbum* / *logos*</note> who was in the beginning with God, illuminates the ministers of truth, the Prophets and Apostles—primarily intended to reveal the hidden mysteries of those matters pertaining to human beings. (By "human beings" I mean souls making use of bodies.) This was done so that he who is capable of being taught, by searching out and surrendering himself to the depths of the mind through the spoken words, might become a partaker of all the counsel of His doctrine. 

Regarding those things that concern souls, since they cannot otherwise reach perfection except through the rich and wise truth concerning God, matters about God were necessarily established as the primary focus. Likewise, concerning His only-begotten Son: what His nature is, in what manner He is the Son of God, and what the cause was for His descent even unto human flesh and His complete assumption of humanity. It was also necessary to learn what power resulted from these things, in whom, and when it took effect. Furthermore, concerning kindred matters—other rational beings, both those more divine and those who fell from blessedness, and the causes of their fall—it was necessary that these be included in the discourses of Divine Scripture. We must also learn of the difference between souls and whence those differences arose; what the world is and why it was created; and moreover, whence comes such great wickedness upon the earth, and whether it exists only on earth or elsewhere. 

With these and similar goals set before the Spirit who illuminates the minds of the holy ministers of truth, there was a second aim: for the sake of those who cannot endure the labor of discovering such great matters, He hid and enveloped the explanation of the aforementioned things in words presenting a narrative. This narrative declares the works of God visible to the senses—the creation of man and those who, through succession from the first parents, grew into such a great multitude. Likewise, in other histories that set forth the deeds of the righteous, and even certain sins of these same men (insofar as they were human), as well as the crimes, lusts, and greeds of the lawless and impious. Yet, through the narrative of wars, both of the victors and the vanquished, certain hidden and profound secrets are revealed to those who are able to examine them. But even more wonderfully, through the written Law, the rules of truth are proclaimed; all these things having been recorded in a sequence and order with a power truly befitting divine wisdom.

<column-break/>

...not only the nations benefit from the advent of Christ, but also some of those from the race of God. These things being so, we must sketch the characters of the understanding of the scriptures as they appear to us. And first, this must be shown: that the aim of the illuminating Spirit, by the providence of God through the Word <note>original: *logos*</note> who was in the beginning with God, for the ministers of truth, the prophets and apostles, was primarily the matter of the secret mysteries regarding human affairs (by "human" I now mean souls using bodies). This was so that the one able to be instructed, having searched and given himself over to the depths of the mind through the literal expression, might become a sharer in all the decrees of His counsel. 

Regarding the things of souls, which are not otherwise able to attain perfection without the rich and wise truth concerning God, the things concerning God have been necessarily placed as primary: what the nature of His only-begotten is, and in what way He happens to be the Son of God, and what the causes were for His descending as far as human flesh and entirely taking up man; and what the activity resulting from these is, and to whom and when it occurs. It was necessary also that matters concerning kindred things—other rational beings, both more divine and those having fallen from blessedness, and the causes of their fall—be included in the words of the divine teaching. Also concerning the difference of souls, and from where these differences have arisen; and what the world is, and why it was established. Furthermore, from where such and so great a malice exists on earth, and if it is only on earth or also elsewhere, it is necessary for us to learn. 

These and similar things being proposed to the Spirit who illuminates the souls of the holy servants of the truth, there was a second aim: for those not able to bear the toil for the sake of finding such great things, to hide the account concerning the aforementioned things in words displaying a narrative. This contains a report concerning the perceptible creations, and the making of man, and those generated from the first ones by succession until they became many. And in other histories reporting the deeds of the righteous, and the sins committed by these same ones as men, and the wickednesses of the lawless and impious, and their licentiousness and greed. Most paradoxically, through the history concerning wars, and those who have conquered and those who have been conquered, some of the secrets are made clear to those able to test these things. And even more marvelously, through the written legislation, the laws of truth are prophesied; with the power of the wisdom of God truly befitting all these things having been recorded into a coherent whole. For the object was of spiritual things...

<summary>Origen explains that Scripture has a dual purpose: a primary "spiritual" meaning regarding divine mysteries for the advanced, and a secondary "narrative" meaning to engage those unable to perform deep intellectual labor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Origen’s argument regarding the "spiritual" versus "corporeal" (literal) understanding of the Bible, specifically addressing why certain passages seem impossible or illogical at face value.</meta>

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER I.

...of spiritual things—I mean the "body" <note>Origen uses the term "body" to refer to the literal, physical text of the Bible, as opposed to its "soul" or "spirit."</note> of the Scriptures—is in many respects not without use, being able to improve the many, according to their capacity. But, if the usefulness of the legislation were clearly apparent throughout, and the sequence of the history were always consistent and elegant, we would have disbelieved that anything else besides the obvious meaning could be understood in the Scriptures. Therefore, the Word of God <note>original: *ho tou Theou logos* / *Verbum Dei*</note> arranged for certain stumbling blocks, obstacles, and impossibilities to be woven into the midst of the Law and the history. This was done so that people would not be entirely drawn away by the mere letter—having its attraction unmixed—and either abandon the doctrines altogether because they learn nothing worthy of God, or, by never moving away from the letter, fail to learn anything more divine. One must also know this: since the primary aim was to announce the connection of spiritual things in what has happened and what must be done, wherever the Word found historical events that could be adapted to these mystical truths, it used them, hiding the deeper meaning from the many. But where, in the narrative of intellectual things, the account of certain deeds did not follow the sequence required for the more mystical meanings, the Scripture wove into the history what did not happen—sometimes what was impossible to happen, and sometimes what was possible but did not actually occur. Sometimes a few words are inserted that are not true according to the "body" <note>the literal sense</note>, and sometimes more than a few. The same principle must be understood regarding the legislation, where one can often find that which is immediately useful and suited to the time of the law-giving. Yet sometimes a useful reason is not apparent; and at other times, impossible things are legislated for the sake of those who are more courageous and inquisitive, so that by giving themselves to the labor of examining the writings, they may gain a conviction of significant value.

<column-break/>

...the clothing—I mean the corporeal sense which is in the Scriptures—is in many things not useless, for it can make many better, as far as they are capable. Truly, if in all things the utility of the law, the sequence of history, and that pleasing variety had appeared openly, we would scarcely have believed that anything else besides what is obvious could be understood in the Scriptures. Therefore, [the Word of God] decreed that stumbling blocks and certain impossibilities be interposed in the midst of the law and history; namely, lest all of us, charmed by a style having nothing but allure, and learning nothing worthy of God, should withdraw from perfect doctrine, or, being affected only by the letter, perceive nothing more divine. This also ought to be certain: that since the Word of God chiefly intends to show the connection and series in things which are of the spirit (both those done and those which ought to be done), wherever it found things that had truly happened to be sufficiently suited to these secrets, it used them, hiding the interior and deeper understanding from the many. But where, in the exposition of the sequence concerning spiritual things, the action of such matters did not correspond (being described through more abstruse things), Holy Scripture wove into the history what had not been done—sometimes even what could not be done; at other times what could have been done, but had not been. And sometimes a few words, occasionally more, were interjected which are not true according to the "body" [of the letter]. This reasoning of the law must also be understood, in which you may frequently find certain things which, if referred to the time they were legislated, have utility; but in others, no reason of utility appears. Sometimes those things are commanded in the law which cannot be done, for the sake of those who are sharper and more eager in the investigation of things, so that by devoting themselves less to the literal inquiry, they may extract from it a noble and by no means regrettable sense.

->That one must seek a meaning worthy of God in such matters.<-

->*In such Scriptures, an understanding worthy of God must be sought.*<-

The Spirit arranged these things not only regarding those matters before the coming [of Christ], but as it is the same Spirit and from the one God, it has done the same in the Gospels and in the Apostles. For even these do not have a history that is entirely unmixed in its "corporeal" weaving, as if everything had literally happened; nor do the legislation and the commandments always manifest what is reasonable. For what person of sense will think that the first, second, and third day, and evening and morning, existed without the sun, moon, and stars? And the first day, as it were, even without a heaven? <note>Origen is pointing out the logical difficulty in the Genesis creation account where light and days exist before the celestial bodies were created on the fourth day.</note>

Is anyone so simple as to think that, in the manner of a human farmer, God planted a garden in Eden toward the East? And that He created a tree of life within it, which could be perceived by sight and the senses? So that one who tasted the fruit with bodily teeth would recover life therefrom; and likewise, that one who ate the fruit plucked from this tree would become a participant in the knowledge of good and evil? If God is also said to walk in the paradise in the afternoon, and Adam to hide himself under a tree; I do not suppose anyone doubts that these things signify certain secrets through a figurative story, and not as things that happened in a physical or literal sense. <note>Origen is arguing for "allegorical" interpretation, suggesting that taking these stories literally is foolish.</note> But also Cain, departing from the presence of God, <margin>Gen. 2:8</margin> <margin>Gen. 2:9</margin> <margin>Gen. 3:8</margin> [clearly warns the reader to seek what the "face of God" is, and in what way one can depart from it.] But what need is there to say more, when anyone—provided they are not a complete blockhead—can gather countless such things written as if they were deeds, which were not actually deeds according to the literal sound of the words? <margin>Gen. 4:16</margin>

And regarding the keeping of the Sabbath, the strictness of the command, *“You shall sit each in your houses; let no one among you go out from his place on the seventh day,”* is impossible to be observed according to the letter; for no living creature is able to remain motionless from sitting throughout the entire duration of the day. Therefore, those of the circumcision <note>original: "ek peritomēs" — referring to Jewish observers of the Law</note>, and as many as wish for nothing more to be revealed than the literal word, do not even seek the origin of things—such as those concerning the goat-
<margin>Leviticus 11:13, 14</margin>
stags <note>original: "tragelaphōn" — a mythical creature, half-goat, half-stag</note>, and gryphons, and vultures. In some matters they invent nonsensical sophistries, delivering up their souls to vanities, as they do concerning the Sabbath, claiming that the "place" for each person is two thousand cubits. But others, among whom is Dositheus the Samaritan <note>A Samaritan sect leader known for extreme asceticism</note>, condemning such an interpretation, think that in whatever posture or position a person is found on the day of the Sabbath, he must remain in it until evening. Furthermore, the command not to carry a burden on the day of the Sabbath is impossible; wherefore the teachers of the Jews have descended into endless talk, saying that a sandal of such-and-such a kind is a "burden," but not one of another kind, and that a sandal with nails is a burden, but one without nails is not; and what is carried on one shoulder is a burden, but not what is carried on both shoulders. And if we come to the Gospel and seek similar things,
<margin>Luke 10:4</margin>
what could be more irrational than the command, *“Salute no one on the road,”* which the simple-minded <note>original: "akeraioi" — those who take the text at face value without deeper spiritual insight</note> suppose the Savior commanded the Apostles? Moreover,
<margin>Matthew 5:39</margin>
the "right cheek" being said to be struck is most improbable for any striker; for unless the striker has suffered some unnatural deformity, it is impossible to strike the left cheek with the right hand <note>Origen argues that a right-handed person naturally strikes the left cheek; thus "right cheek" must have a symbolic meaning</note>.
<margin>Matthew 5:29</margin>
It is also from the Gospel to take the "right eye" that causes offense; for even if we grant that it is possible for someone to be offended by seeing, how is it—since both eyes see—that the cause is to be attributed only to the right eye? And how could anyone, condemning himself for looking at a woman to lust after her, reasonably cast out only his right eye, attributing the cause to it alone? Furthermore, the Apostle
<margin>1 Corinthians 7:18</margin>
legislates, saying, *“Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision.”* First, anyone who wishes will see that he says these things quite apart from the discourse he has set before him. For how, when legislating about marriage and purity, would he not seem to have inserted these things at random? Secondly, who will say that a man does wrong if, because of the deformity which the common people suppose to exist in circumcision, he should give himself over to having the marks removed, if such a thing were possible? All these things have been said by us to show that the aim of the Divine Power which administers the Holy Scriptures to us is not the things suggested by the literal word

<column-break/>

But he who considers that most celebrated Sabbath command, *“You shall sit at home each of you, let none of you go out of his place on the seventh day,”* will notice that it cannot be observed according to the bare sense of the letter; since no animal can sit through an entire day and not move itself from that sitting position. For that reason, those who are of the circumcision, and those who wish for nothing to be signified in the divine writings except what the speech displays on its face, think that one ought not to inquire even in the slightest into certain things, such as what is written about the goat-stag, the gryphon, and the vulture; in other matters they bring forward mere trifles and the coldest subtleties of foreign commentaries, just as concerning the Sabbath, saying that the "place" is defined for each person as two thousand cubits. Others, among whom is Dositheus the Samaritan, having condemned such an exposition, think that in whatever state and posture of body someone is caught by the day of the Sabbath, in that he must remain until evening. But neither is it possible that no burden be lifted on the Sabbath; hence the doctors of the Jews have drifted into infinite fables, saying that a shoe of this sort is a burden, but not that one; for instance, that sandals fixed with nails are a burden, but those without nails are not; likewise, what is carried on one shoulder is to be considered a burden, but not what is carried on both. Now truly, if we approach the Gospel and consider similar things; what is more disconnected from reason or more inhumane than this very thing, *“Salute no one by the way,”* which the simpler sort think the Savior commanded the Apostles? But also when the right cheek is said to be struck, the thing is most foreign to every striker, since with the right hand, unless he has suffered something contrary to nature, he would strike the left cheek. Nor can it be understood from the Gospel how the right eye is an offense: for even if we allow that someone can fall and be offended by seeing, why, when two eyes see, must the crime be transferred to the right one? Who indeed, when he condemns himself because he saw a woman unto lust, throwing the cause back upon the right eye alone, would deservedly pluck out and cast away this very eye? But also the Apostle commands, saying, *“Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not bring on a foreskin.”* For first, anyone will see that the Apostle says these things apart from and beyond his purpose. For how, in prescribing concerning nuptials and chastity, would he not seem to have interposed these things rashly? Then, who would say that he sins who gives himself to be uncircumcised or to recall the foreskin, on account of that which the common people think to be a foulness in circumcision? ...it was so that we should not only receive those things which are, as it were, held out by the literal wording; since sometimes these things, if taken according to the word, are not at all true, but even absurd and impossible. Furthermore, some things are interwoven into the history of actual events, and likewise into those laws which prescribe useful things in their plain expression. But let no one suppose that we think this of all things—that because some events did not happen, we therefore do away with the entire history of Scripture; or as if no law were to be observed according to the word, because some seem, according to the letter, to conflict with reason or appear impossible to fulfill; or that what is written concerning the Savior is not true in a literal sense; or that no law or precept of His is to be observed. We must state that it is clearly evident to us that in some cases the history is true. For instance, that Abraham was buried in the double cave in Hebron, as were Isaac and Jacob, and one wife of each; that Shechem was assigned to Joseph by his father; that Jerusalem is the chief city of Judea, in which the temple of God had been built by Solomon; and six hundred other things. For the things that are true according to the letter and history are far more numerous than those which are merely spiritual and interwoven with them. Again, who would not say that this commandment, *Honor your father and your mother*, so that it may be well with you, is useful and to be observed plainly and without a deeper understanding, especially since Paul himself recited it in those very words? What should be said of the commandment, *You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness*? And in the Gospel certain commandments are written, about which it is not questioned whether they are to be observed according to the word or not; such as that one, *I say to you, whoever is angry with his brother*, and what follows; and, *I say to you, do not swear at all*. And that saying of the Apostle must be kept: *Admonish*, he says, *the restless, and comfort those who are faint-hearted: support the weak, be patient toward all*. Indeed, those who are diligent can observe each of these things, so that the plain sense of the letter does not depart from the depth of the wisdom of God. Therefore, an attentive and diligent person will hesitate and be pulled in different directions in some cases, since without much examination he cannot declare whether the history that is thought to exist happened exactly as it is narrated, or not; or whether the words of this law are to be kept, or otherwise. For this reason, it is necessary for him who applies diligent labor to the divine books, following this edict of the Savior, *Search the scriptures*, to carefully explore when the literal sound is true, and when it is impossible; and as far as he is able, to distinguish the meaning of Scripture—which is spread everywhere through similar expressions—from that which cannot happen according to the letter. Since therefore, as will be manifest to those reading attentively, no...

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Greek text of the Latin translation provided on the left. The translation above covers the content of both columns, as they are parallel versions of the same text.</note>

...introduction of only these things to be taken, sometimes of these, as far as the literal word goes, being not true, but even irrational and impossible; and that some things are woven into the history that occurred, and into the legislation useful according to the literal word. But lest anyone should suppose us to say this of all things, that no history occurred because some did not; and no legislation is to be kept according to the literal word because some, according to the text, happens to be irrational or impossible; or that the things written about the Savior are not true according to the senses; or that no legislation of His and commandment is to be guarded; it must be said that it is clearly presented to us that for some things the historical part is true. As that Abraham was buried in the double cave in Hebron, and Isaac, and Jacob, and one wife of each of these, and that the portion of Shechem was given to Joseph, and Jerusalem is the metropolis of Judea, in which the temple of God was built by Solomon; and ten thousand other things. For the things being true according to the history are many more than the bare spiritual things woven in. And again, who would not say the commandment saying, *Honor your father and your mother*, that it may be well with you, happens to be useful and to be kept without any higher interpretation, even the apostle Paul having used this very word for word? # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER I.

Indeed, <gloss>that</gloss> the sequence of the text according to the literal reading is not impossible, but the primary meaning is also true, striving to comprehend the whole mind [of Scripture], connecting those things which according to the letter are impossible in a rational way—not only with the impossible, but also with those things that are true according to history, being allegorized alongside those things which, as far as the letter is concerned, did not happen. For we hold this position concerning all of Holy Scripture: that while all of it has a spiritual meaning, not all of it has a bodily <note>original: σωματικόν / corporeum; referring to the literal or physical sense</note> meaning. For in many places the bodily sense is proved to be impossible. Therefore, much attention must be brought by the one who reverently reads the divine letters and divine books; the character of whose understanding appears to us in this way. The words [of Scripture] report that there is a certain nation on earth chosen by God, which they call by several names. For this whole nation is called Israel; it is also called Jacob. But when it was divided in the times of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, the ten tribes under him were named Israel; and the remaining two and the Levitical tribe, ruled by those of the seed of David, were named Judah. The entire place which the people of that nation inhabited, given to them by God, is called Judea, whose metropolis is Jerusalem; clearly the metropolis of many cities, whose names lie scattered in many other places, but are listed all together in [the book of] Joshua the son of Nun. These things being so, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note>, elevating our understanding, says somewhere, *Consider Israel according to the flesh*, as if there were a certain Israel according to the spirit. And elsewhere he says, *For these children of the flesh are not the children of God*; nor are *all those who are of Israel, Israel*. But *neither is he a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in spirit, not in letter*. For if the judgment of the Jew is taken from what is hidden, it must be understood that just as there is a bodily race of Jews, so also there is a certain nation of Jews in secret, the soul having acquired this nobility according to certain mystical principles. Moreover, many prophecies prophesy concerning Israel and Judah, relating the things that will happen to them; and if indeed so many promises written in types happen to be lowly as far as the letter is concerned, and present no stature or dignity worthy of a promise of God, they stand in need of mystical elevation <note>original: ἀναγωγῆς / contemplatione; the process of finding a higher spiritual meaning</note>. But if the promises are intellectual, being promised through sensible things, then those to whom the promises are made are also [more than] bodily. # THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER I.

...with an Israelite man, since even these points are sufficient for those who are not utterly stunned <note>original: "stupore oppressis" / "ἀκεντρεσι" - referring to those whose minds are not dull or un-pierced by reason</note>, we return to the intended course of our discussion. We say that Jacob is the father of the twelve Patriarchs, and these are the heads of the peoples, from whom all Israelites thereafter descend. Do the Israelites according to the flesh, then, trace their lineage back to the leaders of the people? These to the Patriarchs? The Patriarchs to Jacob and those above him? But what of those who are understood as Israelites by reason <note>The "spiritual" or "intellectual" Israelites as opposed to the physical ones</note>, of whom the bodily ones were a figure? Are they not from peoples, since the tribes came from the peoples, and the tribes from a certain individual whose generation was not of such a bodily sort, but far more excellent? For he was born of Isaac, who had descended from Abraham, with all being traced back to Adam, whom the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> pronounces to be Christ. For every origin of families and kindreds that are referred to the God of all began from Christ, according to the God and Father of all; He is thus the father of every soul, just as Adam is the father of all men. And if the Apostle also skillfully interpreted Eve and referred her to the Church, it is no wonder that Cain, born of Eve, and all thereafter who are referred to Eve, are figures of the Church; since all were born from the Church by a primary principle.

But if the things said by us concerning Israel, and the tribes, and his peoples, cause alarm—since the Savior proclaims, *I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel* <margin>Mat. 15:24</margin>—we do not receive these things like the Ebionites, who are poor in mind and derive their name from their poverty of judgment (for *Ebion* is called "poor" by the Hebrews); so as to think that Christ came chiefly for the sake of the bodily Israelites: for the children of the flesh are not the children of God <margin>Rom. 9:8</margin>. Again, the Apostle teaches something of this kind concerning Jerusalem: *The heavenly Jerusalem is free, which is our mother*; and in another Epistle: *But you have come to Mount Sion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering, to the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven* <margin>Hebr. 12:22, 23</margin>. If, therefore, there is a race of souls called Israel, and there is a certain city Jerusalem in heaven, it follows that the cities of Israel have as their capital that Jerusalem which is in the heavens, corresponding to the whole of Judea. Whatever, therefore, is prefigured concerning Jerusalem, and is said of her by God, let us hear as God and Wisdom speaking. It must be understood that the Scriptures speak concerning the heavenly city and the entire region that contains the cities of the holy land. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER I.

In His gracious governance toward us, He gives authority over five or ten cities. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Pounds in Luke 19:17-19.</note> If, therefore, the prophecies concerning Judea, Jerusalem, Israel, Judah, and Jacob—provided we do not take them in a fleshly sense—suggest certain mysteries to us, it would follow that the prophecies concerning Egypt and the Egyptians, Babylon and the Babylonians, Tyre and the Tyrians, Sidon and the Sidonians, or the other nations, do not prophesy only about these physical Egyptians, Babylonians, Tyrians, and Sidonians, but also about those understood intellectually. For if there are "intellectual Israelites," it follows that there are also intellectual Egyptians and Babylonians. Indeed, what is said in Ezekiel concerning Pharaoh, King of Egypt, does not entirely fit any man who has ruled or will rule over Egypt, as will be clear to those who observe closely. Similarly, what is written about the Prince of Tyre cannot be understood as referring to a mere human who held the princedom in Tyre. Furthermore, what is said of Nebuchadnezzar in many places, and especially in Isaiah, cannot be accepted as referring to that man; for the man Nebuchadnezzar did not fall from heaven, nor was he "Lucifer" <note>original: ἑωσφόρος / Lucifer, meaning "Light-bringer" or the Morning Star.</note> who rose in the morning upon the earth. Nor indeed can the things said in Ezekiel about Egypt—that it would be desolated for forty years so that no human footprint would be found there, and that it would be so devastated by war that blood would flow through the whole land up to the knees—be understood by anyone of sound mind as referring to the inhabited Egypt adjacent to the Ethiopians whose bodies are blackened by the sun.

->And after other matters.<-

Perhaps, just as those who depart from here by the common death are assigned places according to their deeds here—if they are judged worthy of the region called Hades, obtaining different places in proportion to their sins—so those who "die" there, so to speak, descend into this Hades <note>Origen suggests here that our world might be a form of "Hades" or a lower realm for souls descending from a higher state.</note> being judged worthy of different dwellings, better or worse, throughout the space of the whole earth, and born to these or those parents. Thus, it is possible for an Israelite to fall among the Scythians, or an Egyptian to descend into Judea. However, the Savior came to gather the lost sheep of the house of Israel <margin>Matthew 15:24</margin>; and since many from Israel did not yield to His teaching, those from the Gentiles are called. Furthermore, these things are hidden, as we believe, within the histories: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up; then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field." <margin>Matthew 13:44</margin>

...over five or ten cities. For if there are Israelites in mind, it follows that there are Egyptians and Babylonians in mind: for it is not at all fitting that what is said in Ezekiel concerning Pharaoh the king of Egypt should be said of any man who ruled Egypt or was to rule it, as will be plain to those observing. In this manner, what is written of the prince of Tyre cannot be understood of any man who held the princedom of Tyre. Then what is said of Nebuchadnezzar in many places, especially in Isaiah, cannot be accepted of that man: for the man Nebuchadnezzar had not fallen from heaven, nor was he Lucifer, nor did he rise in the morning upon the earth. ->And with other things interjected.<-

Perhaps, however, just as those who depart from here by common fate obtain a place according to the things done here—if they are judged worthy of the region of Orcus <note>Latin: Orcus, a synonym for Hades or the underworld.</note>, as they call it—they receive different places according to the proportion of their crimes: so those who die there, so to speak, descend into this Orcus, judged worthy of different domiciles, more suitable or worse, in the space surrounding the whole earth: and that among these or those fathers, so that indeed an Israelite might fall among the Scythians, and an Egyptian might come into Judea: and when the Savior came to gather the sheep of the house of Israel which had perished: and when many of Israel did not acquiesce to his doctrine, those who are from the nations are called. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

Let us consider, therefore, whether that which is seen by the eyes, and which stands out in Scripture and is close at hand, is like a whole field full of all kinds of trees; while those things which are stored away and not seen by everyone, but are buried as if under those trees which are perceived, are the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Indeed, the Spirit through Isaiah calls these "dark, invisible, and hidden" <note>original: "obscuros, non visibiles, & absconditos"</note>; since God alone is able to shatter the bronze gates that enclose them, and break the iron bars set against the doors. There may be found whatever is contained in Genesis concerning the diverse and true kinds of souls—and, as it were, seeds—which are near to Israel or far away; and the journey into Egypt of the seventy souls, so that there they might be increased to the multitude of the stars of heaven. But since not all who come from that nation are the light of the world—for not all who are of Israel are truly Israel—from the seventy, they are multiplied like the sand which is by the seashore, innumerable. But just as all the gifts of God are many times greater than any mortal substance, so the accurate account of the knowledge of all these things, which is in the possession of God (who decreed that all these things be written), can be found, by the will of the Father of the Word, in that mind which has been thoroughly purified with all zeal and an awareness of human weakness in comprehending divine wisdom. If, however, anyone should cast himself forward too confidently, not having recognized the secret of the wisdom of God and of the Word (which was in the beginning with God, and is itself God), and not noticing that these things must be sought and found according to the Word and God, and according to the wisdom that is with Him; it is necessary that such a man, having fallen into fables, trifles, and fictions, should cast himself into the danger of impiety. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Romans 10:11</margin>
...from the fullness <note>original: *pleroma*, a term used by Origen to describe the divine totality or abundance of God</note>, and ears hearing were from the fullness, and the sense of sweet smell was breathing from the fullness. But if ever, while reading the Scripture, you should stumble at a meaning which is a "stone of stumbling and a rock of offense," blame yourself. For do not despair that this stone of stumbling and rock of offense contains divine meanings; so that the saying may be fulfilled, *And he who believes shall not be put to shame.* Believe first, and you will find much holy benefit beneath that which is considered a stumbling block.

->From the commentaries on the 50th Psalm <note>Psalm 51 in modern numbering</note>, in the section concerning the history of Uriah, after having allegorized the beginning, he adds:<-

But if it seems forced to anyone to allegorize a history in part, without smoothing out the whole, it is clear that these things will have been said in vain, and other explanations for the passage must be sought; unless perhaps someone, by examining the details of the place more thoroughly, should find a way to restore the whole—including the matters concerning the slain man <note>Uriah the Hittite</note> and his apparent virtue; his refusal to go to his house and rest while the people were in camp and struggling. I do not know how those who flee from allegory in these matters, and who think the text was recorded for its own sake, will represent the will of the Holy Spirit; who deemed these things worthy of record, in which not only licentiousness, but also cruelty and inhumanity are charged against David, who dared to commit against Uriah a deed foreign even to an ordinary character of moderate improvement. But I would say,
<margin>Wisdom of Solomon 17:1</margin>
that just as *The judgments of God are great and hard to relate, and for this reason uninstructed souls have gone astray*; so also His Scriptures are great and full of meanings that are secret, mystical, and hard to perceive. They are exceedingly difficult to relate, and they seem to cause the souls of the uninstructed and the heterodox <note>those with differing or "heretical" opinions</note> to wander, as they thoughtlessly and with pride accuse God based on the Scriptures they do not understand, and because of this they fall away into the fabrication of another God <note>a reference to Gnostic groups who claimed the Old Testament God was different from the New Testament God</note>. It is safe, therefore, to await the interpretation of the Word who makes things clear, and of the
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:7, 8</margin>
wisdom hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this age knew, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent for eternal ages, but now made manifest to the apostles and those like them through the prophetic scriptures and the appearance to them of our Savior, the Word who was in the beginning with God.

<column-break/>

...are from the fullness, and ears hearing those things which are from the fullness, and an instrument for sensing the sweetest odor which is exhaled from the fullness. But if truly at times in reading the Scriptures you stumble at a sentiment which is like a stone of stumbling and a rock of falling, blame yourself. Nor truly should you doubt that these sentiments contain this stone of stumbling and rock of ruin; so that it may happen as it was said, *He who believes shall not be confounded*: first believe, and under that which is thought to be a stumbling block, you will find a great deal of holy utility.

->*From the commentaries on Psalm 50. After he turned the beginning of the history of Uriah toward a hidden sense, he adds.*<-

But if it seems violent to anyone that I have transferred a part of the history to an abstruse sense, and have not interpreted it uniformly, it is plain that these things will be said rashly, and other things must be sought in this place; unless indeed he who considers this place most accurately should find a way by which he may reconcile all things which are said concerning the slain man and his goodness of whatever kind; since he would not go to his house and rest there because the people were in the camps and enduring military service. But I know not in what way those who will not admit a hidden sense in these things, and think the diction was written for itself and nakedly, will attain the will of the Holy Spirit, who judged those things worthy of writing; in which not only base lust, but also the cruelty and inhumanity of David is proved, who had dared a deed against Uriah most foreign to any man who had been cultured even with moderately good morals. I would say indeed, just as *the judgments of God are great and inexplicable, which seem to give cause of error to rude and unlearned minds*: so the Scriptures of God are great and filled with secret and abstruse sentiments of most difficult consideration; but they also have a most difficult explanation, and seem to have driven into error the rude and uncultured minds of dissenters, who inconsiderately and not without mad temerity find fault with God on account of those Scriptures which they do not understand, and from there fall away into fashioning another God. Therefore it is safest to wait for the interpretation of the explaining Word, and of that wisdom which lies hidden in secret, which *none of the princes of this world knew, according to the uncovering of the mystery hidden for eternal times, declared to the Apostles and those like them through the Prophetic Scriptures, and the rising of our Savior the Word, who was in the beginning with God, upon them.*

<summary>Origen argues that difficult or morally troubling passages in the Bible, such as David's conduct toward Uriah, must be interpreted allegorically rather than literally to find their holy meaning. He warns that a literal reading leads the unlearned to wrongly criticize God or invent new deities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Philocalia, a collection of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus. It focuses on the deeper meaning of Scripture beyond the literal word.</meta>

# Chapter II. ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

->*From the second homily on Leviticus, immediately from the beginning.*<-

Because the impious and utterly cursed Heretics <note>Origen likely refers to Marcionites or Gnostics who rejected the Old Testament God.</note> did not understand the difference between the Judaism that is seen with the eyes and that which is perceived by the mind—that is, between manifest and hidden Judaism—they immediately abandoned Judaism and defected from God, the author of these Scriptures and the entire Law. They fashioned another God different from the one who gave the Law and the Prophets, and who made the heaven and the earth. This is certainly most foreign to the truth: for the God who gave the Law also gave the Gospel; He who made the things that are seen also gave the things that are not discerned by the eyes. There is a kinship between the visible and the invisible; indeed, they have such a kinship that *the invisible works of God are seen, being understood through the things made since the creation of the world.* <margin>Romans 1:20</margin> There is a kinship between the visible things in the Law and the Prophets and those things which are not seen but understood in the Law and the Prophets. Since, therefore, Scripture itself consists, as it were, of a **body** which is seen, and a **soul** which is understood and conceived within it, and a **spirit** according to the patterns and shadow of heavenly things: come then, let us call upon Him who made the body, soul, and spirit of Scripture—giving the body to those who preceded us [the Jews], the soul to us, and the spirit to those who in the future age will possess eternal life and reach the heavenly truths of the Law. Let us investigate not the letter, but the soul in the present; and if we are able to achieve so much, we shall ascend to the spirit, in the manner of the sacrifices read about in the Scriptures.

---

->*Divine Scripture is closed and sealed.*<-

### CHAP. II.

->*From the Volume on the first Psalm.*<-

The divine word proclaims that the sacred Scriptures are closed and sealed with the **Key of David**; and perhaps also with the seal of which it is said, *The engraving of a seal: Holiness to the Lord*, <margin>Exodus 28:36</margin> that is, by the power of God who gave them, which is declared by the seal. That they are closed and sealed, John teaches in the Apocalypse, saying: *And to the Angel of the Church in Philadelphia write: These things says the Holy One, the True One, He who has the key of David, He who opens and no one shuts.* <margin>Revelation 3:7</margin>

<column-break/>

->*From the second homily on Leviticus, immediately after the beginning.*<-

<note>original: "᾿Απὸ τῆς εἰς τὸ Λευϊτικὸν ὁμιλίας δευτέρας..." This is the Greek version of the Latin text provided in the first column.</note>

Not understanding the difference between visible Judaism and intelligible Judaism—that is, Judaism in the open and Judaism in secret—those from the godless and most impious heresies immediately stood apart from Judaism and from the God of these Scriptures and the whole Law. They invented another God besides the one who gave the Law and the Prophets, besides the one who made heaven and earth. But it is not so; rather, He who gave the Law gave also the Gospel; He who made the visible things gave also the invisible. And the visible things have a kinship with the invisible; they have a kinship such that the invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. The visible things of the Law and the Prophets have a kinship to the invisible but intelligible things of the Law and the Prophets. Since Scripture itself is composed as if of a **body** which is seen, a **soul** which is understood and grasped within it, and a **spirit** which is according to the examples and shadow of heavenly things; come, let us invoke Him who made the body, soul, and spirit for Scripture—the body for those before us, the soul for us, and the spirit for those in the coming age who will inherit eternal life and are destined to come to the heavenly and true things of the Law. Let us search out not the letter, but the soul; for that is for the present. And if we are able, we shall ascend even to the spirit, according to the logic of the sacrifices about which we read.
<margin>Romans 1:20</margin>

->*That divine Scripture is closed and sealed.*<-

The divine words say that the holy Scriptures have been closed and sealed by the **key of David**; and perhaps by the seal about which it has been said, *The engraving of a seal: Holiness to the Lord*, <margin>Exodus 28:36</margin> that is, by the power of the God who gave them, which is manifested by the seal. Concerning their being closed and sealed, John teaches in the Revelation, saying, *And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These things says the holy one, the true one, he who has the key of David, he who opens and no one shall close.*
<margin>Exodus 28:36. Revelation 3:7.</margin>

We believe that the sacred Providence which bestows wisdom surpassing the human has inserted saving doctrines for the human race through the divine letters, and has impressed traces of wisdom upon each individual letter, so to speak, as far as each is capable of receiving it. Indeed, it is necessary for him who has once admitted that these Scriptures belong to the Creator of the world, to also be persuaded that whatever difficulties occur to those seeking the reason for creation, these same things occur regarding the Scriptures.
