->Why the divinely inspired books are twenty-two.<-

### CHAP. III.

->From the same author, from the volume on the 1st Psalm.<-

Since in the topic of numbers, each individual number possesses a certain power among existing things, which the Creator of all things employed for the constitution—sometimes of the whole, and sometimes of a particular species—one must pay attention and track down from the Scriptures the facts concerning them and each one of them. It should not be ignored, therefore, that the books of the Covenant <note>original: ἐνδιαθήκους βίβλους / *veteris Testamenti libros*. This refers to the Old Testament canon.</note>, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, which is the same as the number of their own letters <note>The Hebrew alphabet consists of 22 letters.</note>; this is not without reason. For just as the twenty-two letters seem to be an introduction to wisdom and to the divine teachings impressed upon men by these characters, so the twenty-two divinely inspired books are an elementary instruction in the wisdom of God and an introduction to the knowledge of all things.

->Concerning solecism and the humble style of the Scripture.<-

->From the 4th volume of the commentary on the Gospel according to John, three leaves from the beginning.<-

He who distinguishes in his own mind between the sound of the voice, the things signified, and the actual objects for which the 

<column-break/>

Thus, therefore, it must also be seen in the divine writings that many things are hidden in them, the explanation of which is very difficult for us. Those, therefore, who promise—after they have defected from the founder of the world and fled to him whom they fashioned as if to God—let them loosen the knots we have shown them, or let them persuade their own conscience to cease from impiety after such remarkable audacity, as fits their own institution, concerning the sought-after causes and those things which have been objected to. For if difficulties remain there nonetheless, after they have defected from the divinity, how much holier was it, clinging to the thought and sense of God, whom we contemplate as the parent and effector from his creatures, to affirm nothing impious or wicked about so great a God?

->*Why there are 22 divinely inspired books.*<-

### CAP. III.

->*From the same volume on the 1st Psalm.*<-

Since in the place of numbers each individual number has some force and power in things, which the maker of all has used, sometimes for the constitution of the universe, sometimes for establishing the appearance of individuals: those things which pertain to the numbers themselves individually must be observed from the Scriptures and thoroughly investigated. Nor should it be ignored that the books of the Old Testament, as the Hebrews hand down, are twenty-two, to which the number of Hebrew elements <note>The "elements" here refers to the letters of the alphabet.</note> is equal, which is not without purpose: for as the twenty-two letters seem to be an introduction to wisdom and divine doctrine impressed upon men in these forms: so the twenty-two books of Scripture are a foundation and introduction to the wisdom of God and the knowledge of things.

But the Apostles, who were not ignorant of the things in which they might stumble, and in which studies they had not been trained, profess themselves to be <term>idiots</term> <note>original: "idiotas"; here meaning "unskilled" or "laymen" in formal rhetoric, not the modern derogatory sense</note> in speech, but not in understanding: for it must be thought that this was said not by Paul alone, but by the rest of the Apostles, *But we, etc.* Likewise that other passage, *And we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be of God, and not from us,* we have received, as if the "treasure" refers to that which is taken from elsewhere—the treasure of hidden knowledge and wisdom; while the "earthen vessels" refers to the humble diction of the Scriptures, despised among the <term>Ethnics</term> <note>original: "Ethnicos"; the Pagans or Greeks</note>, wherein the excellence of divine power is truly declared. For the mysteries of truth and the virtue of the words were able, despite the thinness of the diction, to reach the ends of the earth, and to subject to the doctrine of Christ not only the foolish of the world, but sometimes even the wise. For we see the calling, not that there are no wise according to the flesh, but that there are not *many* wise according to the flesh. But Paul, in preaching the Gospel, is a debtor and bound to deliver his word not only to the barbarians, but also to the Greeks; and not only to the unlearned, who immediately assent, but also to the learned. For he had been made by God a fit minister of the new testament, using the demonstration of the spirit and of power, so that the assent of the believers might not be from human wisdom, but from the power of God. For if the divine writings had possessed elegance and an apparatus of diction like those writings which are an object of admiration to the Greeks, someone might have thought that it was not the truth that had conquered men, but that the apparent sequence and splendor of the diction had enticed the listeners, and circumvented them, having been soothed by such allurements.

For we see the calling, not that no one is wise according to the flesh, but that not many are wise according to the flesh. For he was made a sufficient minister of the new covenant by God, using the demonstration of the spirit and of power, so that the assent of those believing might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. For perhaps if the scripture had both beauty and a circuit of phrasing, like the things admired among the Greeks, someone would have suspected that the truth had not mastered men, but that the apparent consistency and the beauty of the phrasing had charmed the souls of the listeners, and had taken them in by deception.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER V.

->What constitutes "much speaking," and what are "many books"; and how all divinely inspired Scripture is but one book.<-

### CHAPTER 5.

->From the fifth volume of the commentary on the Gospel according to John, from the preface.<-

Since you are not satisfied with having undertaken the present work on our behalf, but meet me as a "taskmaster" <note>original: ἐργοδιώκτης / labor exactor. Origen is likely referring to his friend and patron Ambrose, who pressured him to write.</note> for the things of God, demanding that I devote myself to many tasks as a matter of duty; I, shrinking from the labor and fearing the danger that comes from God for those who have committed themselves to writing on divine matters, might plead my own cause using the Scripture, excusing myself from making many books. For Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, <margin>Ecclesiastes 12:12</margin> *My son, beware of making many books; there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.* For we—unless the passage before us has some hidden meaning that is currently unclear to us—have outright transgressed the commandment, having not guarded ourselves against making many books.

->Then, after saying that four volumes had been completed by him on only a few sayings of the Gospel, he adds:<-

"For as far as the literal wording goes, it signifies two things from the phrase, *My son, beware of making many books*: one, that one should not possess many books; the other, that one should not compose many books. If the first, then not necessarily the second; if the second, then not necessarily the first. Nevertheless, from either side we seem to be taught that we ought not to produce more books. I could have, sticking to the point we have fallen upon, sent this saying to you as a defense, and having established the case by the fact that even the Saints did not publish compositions of many books, I could have ceased for the future from dictating the things to be sent to you according to the agreements we made with one another. And perhaps, persuaded by the text, you would have made this concession to us for the future. But since one must examine the Scripture with a good conscience, and not rashly assume one has understood the matters at leisure simply by examining the literal wording, I will not withhold the defense that seems to favor me, which you might use against me if I should act disobediently toward our agreements. And first, since history seems to support the literal wording, as no one...

->*What constitutes "much speaking," and what are "many books": divine Scripture is one book.*<-

### CHAPTER V.

->*From the fifth volume on the Gospel of John. In the preface.*<-

Since you are not content to have taken up this work for my sake while I am absent, acting as a monitor and a driver of labor for me according to God's will, you even demand that I labor much more out of my duty to you. I, fleeing the labor and surrounded by that danger which hangs from God over those who have applied themselves to writing on the divine letters, could protect myself with the patronage of Scripture, refusing to write many books. For thus says Solomon in Ecclesiastes, *My son, beware that you compose many books: there is no end, and much meditation is a weariness of the flesh.* For we—unless that proposed sentence of Solomon's has a hidden sense, and one still obscure to us—have utterly broken that precept, we who did not take care lest we should fashion many books.

->*Then, after he [Origen] said that he had finished four volumes on a few words of the Gospel, he adds:*<-

For as much as can be gathered from the speech itself, two things are signified by these words, *My son, beware that you fashion many books*: first indeed, that many books are not to be owned; the other, that many are not to be composed. And if not the first, then clearly the second; if truly the second, then not the first at all: except that from both sides we seem to be taught that many books are not to be fashioned. I could have, adhering to that which comes under the edge of our discourse, sent the saying of Scripture to you in place of an excuse, and, the matter being confirmed by the fact that even the Holy ones did not study the composition of many books, I could have ceased henceforth to add commentaries to be transmitted to you according to the treaty entered into between us; and you, perhaps moved by that saying of Scripture, would have granted me that for the future. But since the Scriptures are to be shaken out <note>i.e., examined thoroughly</note> with a right mind and conscience, and one must not rejoice blindly as if you understood them because you perceived the bare wording, I do not bring forward the defense which seems to support me, which you could use against me if I did anything contrary to the pact. And first indeed, when history seems to agree with those words, since no one...

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER V.

If any of the Saints published many commentaries, and set forth their thoughts in many books, this must be discussed: for he who would reproach me, as I prepare myself to write more, will say that Moses, a man of such great character, left behind only five books.

*Then, having enumerated the Prophets and Apostles, each of whom wrote little, or rather not even a little, he [Origen] adds afterwards:*

I am then hesitant, and my eyes grow dim with a swirling dizziness, lest by obeying you <note>Origen is likely addressing his friend and patron, Ambrose of Alexandria, who encouraged his prolific writing.</note> I should fail to obey God, nor imitate the Saints—unless perhaps, out of the intensity of my love for you, and because I wish to cause you no distress, I am myself erring in this defense of my cause and am devising these excuses. Above all, we have set forth that saying from Ecclesiastes which teaches: *My son, beware of making many books.* Against this, I set this saying from the Proverbs of the same Solomon, which says: *In much speaking you shall not escape sin; but if you spare your lips, you shall be wise.* And I ask whether to speak much in any manner whatsoever is "loquacity" <term>loquacity: from the Latin 'multiloquium' or Greek 'polylogia', meaning excessive or empty talk</term>. For if this is the case, and he who discusses many useful things is "loquacious," then certainly Solomon himself did not escape sin, who poured out three thousand parables, five thousand songs, and spoke of trees, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and furthermore of four-footed beasts, of birds, of reptiles, and of fish. For how can anyone teach perfectly without that loquacity—understood in its simpler sense—when Wisdom herself says to the lost: *I stretched out my words, and you did not attend?* Moreover, it is clear that Paul taught assiduously from the rising of the sun until midnight, when Eutychus, overcome by sleep, fell down and troubled the listeners as if he were dead. If, therefore, it is true that *In much speaking you shall not escape sin*, and it is also true that Solomon did not sin when he discussed so many of the aforementioned things, nor did Paul, who extended his discourse until midnight: we must seek to understand what "loquacity" truly is, and from there we must move on to see what "many books" are. Now, the whole Word of God, which was in the beginning with God, is not "much speaking," nor is it "many words"; for the Word is one, composed of many theorems <note>original: "theorematon" / "sententiis". Origen argues that all divine truths form a single, unified Word.</note>, each part of which is a portion of the whole Word. But those who, outside of this, promise to provide any sort of digression or exposition—even if they are discourses about the truth—I will say something new and strange: none of theirs is a "Word," but each is "words"; for nowhere is there unity, nowhere is there harmony and oneness: but, because they are distracted and fight amongst themselves, the unity in them...

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER V.

...was lost from those [the unity], and they became numbers, and perhaps, infinite numbers. <note>Origen is discussing the philosophical idea that Truth is One, while error and sin lead to "multiplicity" or "many words."</note> Therefore, we may consistently say that whoever speaks anything foreign to divine piety is "talkative" <note>original Greek: *polyloyei*; Latin: *loquacem*. Origen redefines "talkativeness" not as speaking many words, but as speaking words outside of God.</note>, but he who speaks the things of truth, even if he says everything so as to leave nothing out, always speaks "One Word." The saints do not fall into the vice of talkativeness because they always have the goal of the one Word in view. If, therefore, "much speaking" is judged by the nature of the doctrines and not by the number of words announced, see if we are not able to say that all the [holy] writings are together **one book**, while the many books are those outside of these. 

But, since I need testimony from the Divine Scripture so that I may prove this most summarily, I will establish that concerning Christ, according to our view, it is not written in only one book—if we understand "books" in the common sense. For it is written in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, and it is spoken in each of the Prophets, and in the Psalms, and simply, as the Savior Himself says, in all the Scriptures. Referring us to these, He says: <margin>John 5:39</margin> *Search the scriptures, for in them you think you have eternal life; and these are they which bear witness of me.* If, then, He refers us to the Scriptures as bearing witness of Him, He does not send us to this one and not to that one, but to all that announce things concerning Him. Some of these He calls in the Psalms the "heading of the book," saying: <margin>Psalm 40:7</margin> *In the heading of the book it is written of me.* 

For let anyone who wishes to take this simply—*In the heading of the book it is written of me*—as referring to any single one of the volumes, explain by what reason he prefers that book over another. But lest anyone suppose that we refer that saying to the Book of Psalms itself, it must be said to him that it ought to have been said, "In *this* book it is written of me." But as it stands, He calls the whole a single "heading" <note>Greek: *kephalida*; Latin: *caput*. This implies a "summing up" or "recapitulation" of the Word.</note>, the summing up of the Word that has come to us concerning Him. 

Regarding this, before the book was seen, it was written by John as being "within and on the back" and "sealed," <margin>Revelation 5:1</margin> which no one was able to read or to loosen its <margin>Ibid. v. 5</margin> seals, except the Lion of the tribe <margin>Revelation 3:7</margin> of Judah, the Root of David, who has the Key of David, and who opens and no one shall shut, and shuts and no one shall open. For the **entire Scripture** is what is signified by that book: written on the "front" <note>The literal or historical meaning.</note> because of its obvious interpretation, but on the "back" because of its remote and spiritual sense. 

It should be observed further, if it can be demonstrated, that the holy writings are **one book**, while those of the contrary side are many. For the living, there is one "Book of the Living" from <margin>Psalm 69:28</margin> which those who have become unworthy of it are blotted out, as it is written: *Let them be blotted out of the book of the living.* But for those who are subject to judgment, there is not a "book," but...

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER VI.

Indeed, because of a lack of those who could maintain better arguments, and because you could not bear an irrational and unlearned faith—owing to your love for Jesus—you once gave yourself over to certain discourses. Later, however, using the understanding given to you as was fitting, you condemned those views and departed from them. I say these things as a defense, as it appears to me, for those who are capable of speaking and writing; but in defending my own case, lest I be found stumbling and lacking the quality required of one made a sufficient minister by God of the New Testament—not of the letter, but of the spirit <margin>2 Corinthians 3:6</margin>—I perhaps too boldly give myself over to dictating these words.

### CHAPTER VI.

-> From the second volume of the Commentary on Matthew, regarding the verse: "Blessed are the peacemakers." <-

And because nothing is crooked or perverse to such a man, he sees an abundance of peace in all the Scriptures, even in those that seem to disagree or to be in conflict and opposition with one another. There is also a third kind of peacemaker: the one who demonstrates that the conflict in the Scriptures, which appears so to others, is not actually a conflict. He presents their harmony and peace, whether it be of the Old with the New, the Legal <note>The books of the Law/Pentateuch.</note> with the Prophetic, the Evangelical with the Apostolic, or the Apostolic with other Apostolic writings. For according to Ecclesiastes, all the Scriptures <margin>Ecclesiastes 12:10, 11</margin> are "words of the wise like goads, and like nails firmly fixed," which were given by the masters of assemblies from one Shepherd, and there is nothing superfluous in them. Now, the Word <note>The *Logos*.</note> is the one Shepherd of rational beings; though the Scriptures seem to have a lack of harmony to those who do not have ears to hear,

### CHAPTER VI.

For just as the strings of a psaltery or a lyre—each of which produces its own distinct sound that does not seem similar to the sound of another—appear discordant to the unlearned and to one who is not skilled in the principles of musical harmony because of the dissimilarity of the sounds: so those who do not know how to hear the divine harmony in the sacred Scriptures think that the New Testament does not fit well with the Old, or the Law with the Prophets, or that the Gospels do not agree with one another, or the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> with the Gospel, or with himself, or with the other Apostles. From this music he learns to strike the strings at the right time: now the strings of the Law, now the Evangelical strings in harmony with them; sometimes the Prophetic strings, and when reason requires it, the Apostolic strings that sound in accord with them, and even the Apostolic in harmony with the Evangelical. For he knows that the whole of Scripture is the one perfect and tuned instrument of God, which produces from different sounds a single saving voice for those willing to learn—a voice that calms and restrains every influence of the evil spirit, just as David’s music calmed the evil spirit that had seized Saul and was choking him. <margin>1 Samuel 16:14</margin> You see, then, in a third way, the "peacemaker" <note>A reference to the Beatitude "Blessed are the peacemakers."</note> is the one who looks upon the Scripture and sees the peace and concord of the whole, and provides this peace to those who seek rightly and discuss with sincerity.

### CHAPTER VII.

*From the small volume on the Song of Songs, which he wrote as a young man.*

To one who has not understood the specific character of the persons <note>original: "personarum" / "προσώπων" (prosopon). In ancient literary analysis, this refers to identifying who is speaking in a dialogue.</note> in divine Scripture—both those who speak and those to whom the words are addressed—the things said will cause much confusion. Such a person will struggle to find who the speaking persona is, or who the one being addressed is, or where the persona who was speaking ceased. For often it is observed that while one is speaking, another is addressed; or the one to whom the speech was directed is no longer listening, but another has taken up the words, while the speaker remains the same. Sometimes both change: both the one who speaks and the one to whom it is said.

<column-break/>

to be heard, but in truth they are most harmonious. For just as the different strings of the psaltery or the lyre, each of which produces a certain unique sound and seems unlike that of the other, would be thought discordant by the unmusical man and one who does not understand the logic of musical harmony because of the unlikeness of the sounds; so those who do not know how to hear the harmony of God in the sacred scriptures think that the Old is inharmonious with the New, or the Prophets with the Law, or the Gospels with each other, or the Apostle with the Gospel, or with himself, or with the other apostles. But when he who is educated in the music of God comes—being wise in deeds and words, and because of this being called a "David," which is interpreted as "capable with the hand"—he will produce the sound of the music of God, having learned from this music to strike the strings in due season: now the legal strings, now the evangelical strings in harmony with them, and now the prophetic strings, and when reasonable necessity demands, the apostolic strings in the same key as them, and even the apostolic with the evangelical. For he knows that all the scripture is the one perfect and tuned instrument of God, producing from different sounds one saving voice to those who wish to learn, quieting and hindering every energy of the evil spirit, as the music of David quieted the evil spirit in Saul <margin>1 Samuel 16:14</margin> that was choking him. You see then, thirdly, that he is a peacemaker who looks upon the scripture and sees the peace of all of it, and creates this peace for those who seek rightly and love learning sincerely.

Indeed, there is a significant reason why the obscurity of what is said is not easily discerned. -> And again from the fourth homily on the Acts of the Apostles. <-

<margin>Acts 1:16.</margin>
"It was necessary that the Scripture be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas." Now, in the Psalm where the things concerning Judas are written, someone might say that it is not the Holy Spirit speaking; for the words are clearly those of the Savior
<margin>Psalm 108:1, 2. Ibid. v. 8. <note>Modern Psalm 109.</note></margin>
saying, "O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me," and so on until, "And let another take his office <term>Episcopatum: literally 'oversight' or 'bishopric'</term>." How then, if it is the Savior who says these things, does Peter say, "It was necessary that the Scripture be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David"? Is it not, then, that what we are taught here is something like this? The Holy Spirit employs <term>prosopopoeia: a rhetorical device where a speaker acts in the character of another</term> in the prophets; and if He assumes the person of God, it is not God who is speaking, but the Holy Spirit speaking from the person of God. And if He assumes the person of Christ, it is not Christ who is speaking, but the Holy Spirit speaking from the person of Christ. So also if He assumes the person of the prophet, or of that people, or of this people, or whatever person He assumes, it is the Holy Spirit who portrays all these persons.

---

-> Concerning the fact that one must not attempt to "correct" passages of Scripture that seem to be <term>solecisms: grammatical errors or non-standard usage</term> and do not preserve a literal sequence, provided they preserve the sequence of thought for those capable of understanding. <-

### CHAPTER 8.
### From the commentaries on Hosea.

Since things spoken in the manner of a solecism throughout Scripture—at least according to the literal word—confuse the reader, leading them to suspect that the words were not written correctly, nor consistently, nor as they truly are; so much so that some even dare, under the pretext of "correction," to alter them, changing the sense to fit what seems to be a more consistent reading; it is therefore very necessary—

<column-break/>

clearly signify that they remain. But what need is there to seek examples of each of these, when the writings of the Prophets are filled with an abundance of them? This is a cause of no small weight as to why the obscurity of the sayings is not distinguished. Moreover, it is the custom of Scripture to leap across immediately from one discourse to another; and the Prophets do this quite obscurely and confusedly.

-> *Now from the fourth homily on the Acts of the Apostles.* <-

"It was necessary to fulfill what the Holy Spirit had foretold through the mouth of David concerning *Judas*." In which Psalm it is written concerning Judas, someone might perhaps say that the Holy Spirit does not speak; for it is the speech of the Savior, *"O God, do not keep silence regarding my praise, because the mouth of the sinner, and the mouth of the deceitful, is opened against me,"* and so on until those words, *"And let another take his Bishopric."* How therefore, if it is the Savior who says these things, does Peter say, *"It was necessary that the Scripture be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David?"* Is it not, therefore, that what we are taught here is such as this? The Holy Spirit fashions characters <note>original: "personas fingit"</note> in the Prophecies; and if He brings in the person of God, it is not God who speaks, but the Holy Spirit speaks from the person of God: if He brings in Christ, it is not Christ who speaks, but the Holy Spirit speaks from the person of Christ. Thus also if He presents the person of a Prophet, or of this or that people, whatever person He introduces at last, it is the Holy Spirit who fashions all those characters.

-> *Nothing is to be corrected from those things which have the appearance of a Solecism in Scripture, and seem not to cohere according to the letter, since they preserve the sequence of meaning among those who are endowed with understanding.* <-

### Page 33

If something of this sort has necessarily occurred here, as far as one can gather from the phrasing in the proposed words, let us look at the hidden meaning within them. For when he spoke in the plural number, saying, *They wept and entreated me*, and again set forth what follows in the same number, *When I was at home, they found me*, he brings forth the rest in the singular number, saying, *And there he spoke to him*. <note>original Latin: "Et ibi locutus est ad ipsum." Referring to Hosea 12:4.</note> If someone looks only at the bare wording, thinking it was written by error, he will also write the latter part in the plural; or he will reduce the former parts to the singular. For he who reads, *They wept and entreated me*, and, *When I was at home, they found me*, will assert that what follows ought to be read thus: *There he spoke to them*, that is, to those who wept and prayed, and found God at home. 

And by observing similar words, we shall show that those things were also spoken coherently. In Genesis, God, giving a command to Adam, says: *Of every tree that is in paradise, eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you (plural) shall not eat of it; for on whatever day you (plural) eat of it, you shall die the death.* <note>original Latin: "morte moriemini." Origen notes the shift from the singular "thou shalt eat" to the plural "ye shall not eat."</note> For although he had begun there also from the singular by saying, *Of every tree that is in paradise, thou shalt eat*, he adds in the plural number, saying, *But of the tree of knowing good and evil, do not eat (plural) of it: for on whatever day you (plural) eat of it, you shall die the death.* 

For when he gives the command by which he wishes him to live as long as he observes it, he gives it in the singular number and says, *Of every tree that is in paradise, thou shalt eat.* For those who walk according to God and embrace his commandments, even if they are many, because they are of one mind and one sense, the many are one; therefore, when the command is given concerning the good, it is said in the singular, *thou shalt eat*; but when the command is divided concerning transgression, it is no longer in the singular, but in the plural number: *You (plural) shall not eat of it; for on the day you eat of it, you shall die the death.* 

So therefore, when those people weep and pray to God, it is said in the plural number, *They wept and prayed*; but when they find God, it is no longer said plurally, *There he spoke to them*, but *to him*. For now the many have become one because they have found God and hear his word. For the individual, when he sins, is "manifold," being cut off from God, divided into parts, and falling away from unity; but the many, who follow the commandments of God, are one; just as the Apostle also testifies, saying, *Because we, being many, are one bread and one body*; and then, *One God, one Christ, one faith, one baptism*; and elsewhere, *Because we are all one in Christ Jesus*; and again—

<column-break/>

<margin>Hosea 12:4</margin>
...and here, falling into a similar case, as far as the literal expression regarding the present words is concerned, let us see the mind lying within them. For having said in the plural, *They wept and entreated me*, and again having shown the following in the plural, *In the house where they found me*, he brings in the next part in the singular, saying, *And there it was spoken to him.* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτόν."</note> For someone looking at the bare wording and thinking it was written in error would either write the last part in the plural or change the preceding parts into the singular. For of necessity, one who reads *They wept and entreated me* and *In the house where they found me* would say that the next part ought to have been *There it was spoken to them*, that is, to those who wept and prayed and found God in the house. 

But not without observation shall we show that this was spoken consistently with a similar passage. In Genesis, God, giving the commandment to Adam, speaks thus: *From every tree in the paradise for food thou shalt eat, but from the tree of knowing good and evil, ye shall not eat of it; and in whatever day ye eat of it, ye shall die the death.* <note>Genesis 2:16-17. For when he commands concerning the commandment through which he wished him to live by keeping it, he commands in the singular and says, *From every tree in the paradise for food thou shalt eat.* For those who walk according to God and hold fast to his commandments, even if they are many, by being of one mind, the many are one. Because of this, when it is given concerning the good commandment, it is said to him in the singular, *Thou shalt eat*; but when he is already warned concerning the transgression, he says it no longer in the singular but now in the plural, *Ye shall not eat of it; and in whatever day ye eat, ye shall die the death.* 

Thus, therefore, here also, while they still weep and entreat God, it is said in the plural, *They wept and entreated*; but when they find God, he no longer says in the plural, *There it was spoken to them*, but *to him*. For the many have already become one by finding God and by hearing his word. For the one, when he sins, is a certain "many," being split off from God, and partitioned, and falling out of unity; but the many, following the commandments of God, are one; just as the Apostle also bears witness, saying, *That we the many are one bread and one body*; and again, *One God, and one Christ, and one faith, and one baptism*; and elsewhere, *That we are all one in Christ Jesus*; and again, *We—*

->What is the reason that Divine Scripture often uses the same name with different meanings, even in the same passage?<-

### CHAPTER 9.

<margin>Romans 7:7</margin>
->From the 9th volume of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: on the passage, "What then? Is the law sin?"<-

Just as "law" is a single name, the discourse concerning the law throughout Scripture is not always a single concept. Therefore, in every passage, one must carefully attend to and observe what is signified by the sound of the word "law," and what ought to be understood by it. This is also true for many other terms, for there are words in Scripture that are homonyms <note>original: ὁμώνυμοι; words that sound the same but have different meanings</note> for other things; these confuse people who think that wherever there is a single name, there is likewise a single meaning, whatever that name may be. Now, to show that the word "law" is not assigned to the same things, but to several, we shall—leaving aside many points that are difficult to approach and require complex solutions—set forth those things which may occur to anyone. For instance, the word "law" is placed upon several meanings, as when it is said in the Epistle to the Galatians:
<margin>Galatians 3:10</margin>
"For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law to do them.'" It is clear that here "law" refers to the literal law of Moses, which prescribes what must be done and forbids what must not be done for those subject to it. This same meaning is declared in the same Epistle, and in
<margin>Galatians 3:19</margin>
the passage: "For the law was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, being ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator"; and in
<margin>Galatians 3:24</margin>
the passage: "So that the law has become our tutor <term>paedagogus: a guardian or tutor who led children to school</term>" in

Referring to innate moral concepts.</note>, and as the Scripture says, "written on the heart," commanding what must be done and forbidding what must not be done: which <margin>Romans 2:14</margin> is declared in these words: *For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires: these, though they do not have the law, are a law unto themselves, who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness.* For the law written in hearts, even among the Gentiles who do by nature what the law commands, is no other than that which is naturally inscribed according to common sense in our "governing part" <note>original: *principi parti* / *ἡγεμονικῷ*. A Stoic term for the seat of reason in the soul.</note>, and which daily becomes more mature and solid as reason reaches its perfection and completion. This was the meaning of "Law" both in this place, *Sin is not imputed when there is no law;* and in this, <margin>Romans 5:13</margin> *I would not have known sin except through the law:* for before the law of Moses, sin was imputed <margin>Romans 7:7</margin> both to Cain, and to those who were swallowed by the flood, and to the Sodomites, and to countless others: and many knew sin before the law of Moses. Nor should you wonder that two meanings of this word "Law" are accepted in the same passage: for we find this custom in other Scriptures as well; such as, *Do you not say there are yet four months, and then comes the harvest? Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for <margin>John 4:35</margin> they are already white for harvest.* For "harvest" is named twice; the first refers to the physical harvest, the second to the harvest of the spirit. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>John 9:39</margin>
...and also in the case of the man blind from birth who was healed; to whom He <note>Jesus</note> addresses these words, using his physical condition as a metaphor: *For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind*, and so forth. And likewise: *But now, apart from*
<margin>Romans 3:21</margin>
*the law of nature, the righteousness of God has been revealed, being witnessed by the law [of Moses] and the prophets.* I would say to anyone who hesitates to accept that "the law" has a double meaning, that if the very same "law" is meant in the phrase, *But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been revealed*, and in the phrase, *Being witnessed by the law and the prophets*; then if it was revealed *apart* from the law, it is not witnessed *by* the law; but if it is witnessed by the law, it was not revealed apart from the law. Therefore, the law of nature in no way bears witness to the righteousness of God revealed by Jesus Christ, for it is lesser than that righteousness. However, the Law of Moses does bear witness—not according to the <term>letter</term><note>The literal or surface-level reading of the text</note>, but according to the <term>spirit</term><note>The deeper, spiritual, or allegorical meaning</note>; as do the prophets who correspond to the spirit of the law, and the spiritual word within them. Therefore, the one who reads the Divine Scripture must carefully observe that the Scriptures do not always use the same words for the same things. They do this sometimes because of <term>homonymy</term><note>When one word has multiple meanings</note>, sometimes through figurative language, and occasionally because the context requires the word to be used differently in certain intellectual concepts than it was used elsewhere. If we watch for this diligently, we shall be delivered from many errors and misunderstandings. It should be known, for instance, that the word *Saw* is not always used in the same sense; sometimes it refers to physical sight, and sometimes it is used instead of "to understand." For this must be understood as a general rule: because the Spirit in the prophets and the Word of Christ in the apostles intended to hide the meanings of the truth and not set them out plainly, the phrasing is often scrambled and does not follow a single sequence of speech. This was done so that those who are unworthy might not find, to the judgment of their own souls, things that are profitably hidden from them. This is frequently the reason why the whole of Scripture—and especially, as we said before, the Prophetic and Apostolic writings—seems to lack proper arrangement or sequence. This is particularly true of the Apostolic Epistle to the Romans, in which "the law" is referred to in various ways and applied to different things, so that it might seem as if Paul does not stick to his intended purpose in the writing of that Epistle.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text provided in the left column, which has been integrated into the English translation above for readability.</note>

...in the man blind from birth who was cured; to whom He speaks these things regarding his bodily blindness: *I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind.* So also: *Now, without the law of nature, the righteousness of God has appeared, foretold by the testimony of the law [of Moses] and the Prophets.* Truly, I would say to those who doubt that the law receives a double meaning: if the law itself is understood in this place, *without the law the righteousness of God has shone forth*, and in that place, *foretold by the Law and the Prophets*; if it appeared without the law, it is not foretold by the testimony of the law; but if it is proven by the testimony of the law, it was not declared without the law. Therefore, the law of nature by no means proves by its testimony the righteousness of God which was declared by Jesus Christ, for it is lesser than it: but the law of Moses, not the letter, but the spirit: and the Prophets responding to the spirit of the law, and the discourse of the spirit which is in them. Wherefore it is necessary for him who pours over the divine Scriptures to observe diligently that they do not always use the same words for the same things; which they do sometimes through shared names, sometimes through figurative reasoning, and sometimes because of the context of the elocution, which requires that a diction be used differently in some cases than it was placed in others: which if we observe attentively, we shall avoid many slips and sinister interpretations. It must be known, therefore, that *Saw* is not always placed with the same significance; but sometimes in the sight of the body; the same is sometimes to understand. For this must be known universally, that since it was decreed for the spirit, which is read in the Prophets, to hide, and not openly expose the senses of truth; just as by the word of Christ, in the Apostles, it is often mixed under the speech, nor is it woven as if under one series of oration; lest clearly the unworthy find to the judgment of their soul those things which are usefully hidden from them. Which is for the most part the cause why the Scriptures seem to not cohere with a sufficiently fit composition and succession, especially truly, as we said above, the Prophetic and Apostolic; and among the Apostolic, especially the Epistle to the Romans, in which those things said concerning the law are said in diverse ways, and imposed upon diverse things; so that it may seem that Paul does not follow the proposed matter in that Epistle.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

### CHAPTER X.

| | |
|---|---|
| *Concerning those things in holy Scripture which seem to contain some stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.* | <note>original Greek: Περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ δοκούντων ἔχειν τι λίθον προσκόμματος, ἢ πέτραν σκανδάλου.</note> |

### CHAPTER X. / CHAPTER 10.

| | |
|---|---|
| *From the 39th homily of the explanations on Jeremiah the Prophet: on the passage, "The Lord could no longer bear the face of your iniquities."* | <note>original Greek: Ἐκ τῆς λθ΄ ὁμιλίας τῶν εἰς τὸν Ἱερεμίαν ἐξηγητικῶν· εἰς τὸ, Οὐκ ἠδύνατο Κύριος φέρειν ἀπὸ προσώπου πονηρίας ὑμῶν.</note> |

<margin>Jeremiah 44:22</margin>

If ever, while reading the Scripture, you should strike upon a thought which is a <term>stone of stumbling and a rock of offense</term><note>A biblical metaphor for something that causes a person to trip or lose faith because it is difficult to understand or accept.</note>, blame yourself. For you must not lose hope that this stone of stumbling and rock of offense contains divine meanings, so that what was spoken might come to pass: *And he who believes shall not be put to shame*. First, believe, and you will find much holy benefit beneath that supposed obstacle. For if we have received a commandment not to speak an idle or useless word, as those who must give an account for it on the day of judgment; and if, as much as we are able, we strive so that every word coming out of our mouth might accomplish something both in us who speak and in those who hear: what then must be thought of the Prophets? Was not every word spoken through their mouths effective? It is not surprising if every word uttered by the Prophets performed a work fitting for that word. But I also believe that every wonderful letter written in the divine oracles performs a work; there is not one <term>iota</term><note>The smallest letter of the Greek alphabet.</note> nor one <term>apex</term><note>A tiny stroke or serif in writing; Origen is arguing that even the smallest grammatical marks in the Bible are divinely inspired.</note> written in the Scripture which does not perform its own work for those who know how to use the power of the letters. Just as each individual herb has its own power, whether for the healing of bodies or for some other purpose, yet not everyone knows what use each herb is for—only those who have received the knowledge, those who spend their time among herbs, so that they know when an herb should be taken, to which part of the body it should be applied, and how it should be prepared and mixed to help the user—so too, the holy and spiritual man is a kind of "herbalist." He gathers from the sacred Scriptures every iota and every ordinary element, finding the power of the letter and what use it may serve, and discovering that nothing in the writings is superfluous. If you wish to hear another example of this matter: every limb of our body was created for some work by God the Craftsman; but it is not for everyone to know what the power and use of each limb is, down to the most minute part. Those physicians who occupy themselves with the dissection of bodies can describe each thing individually, and for what use even the smallest part of the body was fashioned by <term>providence</term><note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Romans 9:33</margin>
If ever, while reading the Scripture, you should stumble at a thought which is a "fine" stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, blame yourself. For do not despair that this stone of stumbling and rock of offense has meanings, so that the saying may be fulfilled: *And he who believes in him shall not be put to shame*. Believe first, and you will find much holy benefit under the perceived offense. For if we received a commandment not to speak an idle word, as being about to give an account for it in the day of judgment; and if, with all our power, we take pride in making every word that goes out of our mouth work something both in us who speak and in those who hear; what must we think about the prophets? Or that every word spoken through their mouth was effective? And it is not a marvel if every word spoken by the prophets worked a work fitting to the word; but I think that also every wonderful letter written in the oracles of God works something; and there is one iota, or one tittle written in the Scripture, which does not work its own work for those who know how to use the power of the letters. Just as with herbs, each one has a power, whether for the health of bodies or for whatever else; but it is not for all to know for what each of the herbs is useful; but if some have received knowledge, these are the ones who spend time with herbs, so that they may see both when it is taken, and to which of the bodies it is applied, and in what manner it is prepared to benefit the user. In this way, the holy and spiritual man is like a certain herbalist, picking out from the holy Scriptures each iota, and each ordinary element, and finding the power of the letter, and for what it is useful, and that nothing of the things written is redundant. And if you wish to hear another example for this, each member of our body was made for some work by the craftsman God; but it is not for all to know what is the power and use of each of the members, even the ordinary ones. But those of the physicians who have busied themselves with anatomy can tell each thing, and for what use even the smallest part has been made by providence. Understand...

<margin>Matthew 12:36</margin>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia, CHAPTER XI.

Consider the Scriptures in this manner: either as a collection of all medicinal herbs, or as one perfect body of discourse. If you are neither a "botanist" of the Scriptures <note>original: "βοτανικὸς... γραφῶν" - Origen uses the metaphor of a herbalist who knows the specific power of every small plant to describe a careful reader of the Bible.</note>, nor an anatomist of the prophetic words, do not assume that any part of what is written is redundant. Instead, blame yourself or the sacred letters alone when you cannot find the meaning of what is written. This preface has been stated by me in a universal sense, as it can be useful for the entire Scripture; so that those who wish to devote themselves to reading may be encouraged not to pass over any letter without examination and diligent research.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for scholars. It mirrors the sentiment that every "jot and tittle" of the Bible has purpose.</note>
Consider therefore the Scriptures in this fashion, as if they were all herbs, or one perfect body of speech: if indeed you are neither a herbalist of the Scriptures, nor a dissector of the Prophetic sermons, do not for that reason think anything in the Scriptures is superfluous; but rather accuse yourself alone instead of the letters, when you do not find the reason for those things which are written. This preface was spoken by me in general, which can be applied to the whole of Scripture; so that they may be warned, who think to give themselves to this reading, to omit no letter that has not been discussed and diligently investigated.

# CHAPTER XII. ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

From the ancient Scriptures, some say that certain parts are from a more divine and supreme power, while others are from a weaker one. However, the Shepherd <note>Referring to Christ as the Good Shepherd</note> declares those to be his own sheep who do not despise what has been trampled under the feet of others, nor look down upon the water disturbed by the feet of the rejected sheep, the goats, and the kids. For they did not wish to be the sheep of the rams worthy of the right hand. We, therefore, who desire to be the sheep of the Shepherd, should never wish to refrain from being fed even by those things in the Scriptures which, as far as the literal word goes, seem discordant and are trampled upon because of the discrepancy of the language by those who neither wish nor are able to employ the full scope of the pasture. But, even if there be some water disturbed by the feet of those who have mixed dreadful doubts into the purest discourse of Scripture, let us not be turned away—on account of the disturbances they have brought into the divine words—from drinking even that which has been troubled by their feet. And observe diligently that it is said to those who troubled the water and trampled the pasture, concerning the better ones: *And my sheep fed upon what was trampled by your feet, and they drank the water disturbed by your feet.* <note>A reference to Ezekiel 34:19</note> But let us never trample the Prophetic pasture ourselves, nor disturb the Law’s water; and while some sin against the Evangelical pasture, so as to trample certain parts of the Gospels while feeding on others as good grass; and either cast out all of the Apostolic writings, or select some and reject others: let us feed upon all the Gospels, and trample nothing within them, and drinking all the Apostolic writings, let us preserve the water set before us as much as we can, and let us disturb nothing contained in them through the infidelity that agitates those who do not know how to perceive what is said.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XII.

->The names of the things spoken of, according to the difference of those who inherit the things said concerning various places.<-

Since it is difficult to find one who is so greatly benefited, we wish to encourage our listeners not to lose heart during the reading. We must state what the encouragement is for one not to lose heart when hearing such readings. Just as incantations <note>original: "ἐπῳδαὶ" / "carmina" - Origen uses the analogy of a physical or magical chant to explain the spiritual power of the sound of Scripture.</note> possess a certain natural power, so that the person being chanted over receives something from the incantation even without understanding it—according to the nature of the sounds of the incantation, whether for harm or for the healing of his body or soul—in the same way, I would have you consider the significance of the names in the Divine Scriptures to be more powerful than any incantation. For there are certain powers within us, the better of which are nourished by these (as if by incantations), being kindred to them; and though we do not understand them, those powers, understanding what is said, become more powerful within us to cooperate in our life. That there are certain invisible things within us, and many of them, is shown by the Psalm which says: <margin>Psalm 102:1 <note>Modern Psalm 103:1</note></margin> *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His holy name.* There is, therefore, a multitude of powers within us that have been allotted to our souls and bodies. If these are of a certain kind, they are benefited and become stronger when the Scripture is read. Even if our mind is unfruitful, as it is written concerning one who speaks in a tongue: <margin>1 Cor. 14:14</margin> *My tongue prays, but my mind is unfruitful.* Understand, therefore, that sometimes the powers within us—those which are salvific for the soul and the mind and all of us—are nourished by the rational food from the holy letters and the names within them, and being nourished, they become more powerful to assist us. And just as the better powers are nourished and benefited and become more powerful through such letters and names, so the opposing powers within us are, as it were, drawn down and conquered by the incantations of God, and being conquered, they are put to sleep. And if any of us has ever seen an asp put to sleep by incantations, or any other venomous creature, let him take that as an example for the Scripture. When it is read, do not think that the listener sometimes grows weary or loses heart [in vain]; let him know that the asps within him, and the opposing vipers, are made weak by the medicines of the healers—those found with the wise Moses, with the wise Joshua <note>original: "Ἰησοῦ" / "Jesu" - referring here to Joshua son of Nun, often called Jesus in Greek.</note>, and with the wise holy prophets. Let us not, therefore, lose heart when hearing Scriptures that we do not understand; but let it be done for us according to our faith, by which we also believe that all Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable. For one of two things—

<column-break/>

—must be admitted: either that the things spoken of are accommodated to the various persons who inherit what is mentioned concerning each place. But because it is difficult to find one who receives so much utility, we wish to exhort our listeners not to despond in spirit while reading. We must say, then, what the consolation is, so that he who attends to the reading does not succumb. Just as, therefore, songs have a certain inherent power, and as one who is enchanted receives something from the song without realizing it—such is the nature of the sounds of the song, whether for harm or for the health of his body or soul—so I would have you think the significance of the names of divine Scripture to be more powerful than any song. For there are certain faculties in us, the better of which are nourished by these, as if by songs, since they are kindred and allied to them; and while we do not perceive the faculties, they, understanding what is said, become more powerful in us for the support and help of our life. Indeed, that there are some things in us that are not seen, and many of them, the Psalm will indicate which says: *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His holy name.* There are, therefore, many faculties in us which, as if by lot, possess our souls and bodies; if these be holy, they are helped by the reading of Scripture and become stronger. Even if our mind does not perceive the fruit, just as it is written of him who speaks in a tongue: *Because my tongue prays, but my mind is without fruit.* Think, therefore, that when sometimes our mind does not perceive the fruit, the virtues which are a help to the soul and mind and to all of us are educated by this nourishment of reason, which is from the sacred letters and names; and being educated, they become more powerful to help us. Just as, therefore, the better virtues are, as it were, soothed and helped, and become more powerful through such letters and names; so those which are opposed to our faculties are led away, so to speak, by the divine songs, and are conquered, and being conquered, are put to sleep. And if any of us has ever seen an asp put to sleep by songs, or another of the venomous creatures, let him take that as an example for the Scripture: which, if it be read and not understood, sometimes the listener languishes and succumbs; yet let him believe that the asps within him, and the vipers within him, are made weaker by the medicines of those who cure, just as with the wise Moses, with the wise Joshua, and with the wise holy Prophets. Let us not, therefore, languish in spirit when we hear the Scriptures which we do not understand; but let it be done to us according to our faith, by which we also believe that all Scripture, being sent from God, is profitable. For one of two things—

He uses the analogy of charming serpents to describe how the words of Moses and the Prophets can pacify the "vipers" within the human heart.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*

...you must admit regarding these Scriptures: either they were not divinely given because they are not useful (as an unbeliever might suspect), or, as a believer, you must admit they were divinely given because they *are* useful. We must realize, then, that a benefit often comes to us without our even perceiving it. Just as we are often told to eat certain foods to sharpen the eyes, yet while eating we do not yet feel our vision being improved; but after a second or third day has passed, the distribution of the food that aids the eye makes us believe through experience that our sight has been enhanced. This can also be observed in other foods useful to specific parts of the body. So, be certain regarding the Divine Scripture: the soul is helped even if the mind does not immediately perceive the fruit of that utility which flows from the literal reading alone. For the powers within us are enchanted <note>original: *incantantur* / *ἐπάδεται*. Origen suggests the words of Scripture act like a holy incantation or charm upon the soul</note>, the better parts are nourished, and the worse parts are neutralized.

*When and for whom the disciplines of Philosophy are useful for the exposition of the Holy Scriptures, with testimony from the Scriptures.*

### CHAPTER XIII.

Rejoice in God, my most reverent lord and much-venerable son Gregory, from Origen. As you well know, natural ability <note>original: *ingenium* / *εὐφυΐα*</note> can contribute greatly to understanding when aided by practice, leading toward the appropriate goal of whatever subject one wishes to pursue. Your natural ability could make you a most accomplished Roman Lawyer <term>Jurisconsult: an expert in Roman law</term> or a Greek philosopher of those schools held in high esteem. But I have desired that you use the full force of your ability and mind toward Christianity as your ultimate goal, and as the means to achieve it. Therefore, I desired that you take from the philosophy of the Greeks those "circular" disciplines <term>Circular disciplines: the *enkyklia mathemata* or general education that formed the basis of classical learning</term> or introductory studies which can serve Christianity, and those parts of Geometry and Astronomy which will be useful for the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures. Just as the sons of the philosophers speak of Geometry, Music, Grammar, Rhetoric, and Astronomy as companions and assistants to Philosophy, so we may say the same of Philosophy itself in relation to Christianity. And perhaps something of this sort is hinted at in what is written in Exodus, where the children of Israel are commanded to ask 

<column-break/>

from their neighbors and roommates for vessels of silver and gold, and for clothing; so that by despoiling the Egyptians, they might find material for the things prepared for the service of God.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia, CHAPTER XIII.

...vessels of silver and gold, and also raiment; so that by despoiling the Egyptians they might find material for the preparation of those things intended for the service of God. For from the things of which the children of Israel despoiled the Egyptians, the contents of the Holy of Holies were constructed: the Ark and its cover, the Cherubim, the Mercy Seat, and the golden jar in which the Manna—the bread of angels—was stored. These things, then, were likely made from the finest Egyptian gold. From a second grade of gold, inferior to the first, was made the solid gold lampstand near the inner veil, the lamps upon it, the golden table upon which the Bread of Presence was placed, and between them both, the golden altar of incense. If there was a third or fourth grade of gold, from it the holy vessels were fashioned. And from the silver of the Egyptians other things were made; for by dwelling in Egypt, the children of Israel gained this from their stay: an abundance of such precious material for the useful service of God. From Egyptian raiment, it is likely that those things were made which required the work of what the Scripture calls "embroidery" <note>original: ῥαφιδευτοῦ / plumariis — referring to skilled needlework or weaving</note>, the wisdom of God weaving together such garments for such purposes, so that there might be curtains and veils, both inner and outer. But why should I make an untimely digression by listing how many things taken from Egypt were useful to the children of Israel—things which the Egyptians did not use as they ought, but which the Hebrews, through the wisdom of God, used for divine worship? For Holy Scripture knows that it is an evil thing for any to go down from the land of the children of Israel into Egypt; hinting that it is an evil for all to dwell with the Egyptians—that is, with the teachings of the world—after being enrolled in the law of God and the Israelite worship of Him. Hadad <note>The text refers to Hadad the Edomite (1 Kings 11), though Origen links the narrative to the later rebellion of Jeroboam and the golden calves.</note> the Edomite, as long as he was in the land of Israel and did not taste the bread of the Egyptians, did not fashion idols; but when he fled from the wise Solomon and went down into Egypt, as if fleeing from the wisdom of God, he became a kinsman of Pharaoh by marrying his wife’s sister, and fathering a son who was raised among the children of Pharaoh. Therefore, even though he returned to the land of Israel, he returned only to divide the people of God, and to make them say of the golden calf: *These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.* And I, having learned by experience, might say to you that rare is the man who takes the useful things of Egypt, departs from it, and fashions the things for the service of God;

But what does it profit me to explain in an untimely digression how many and how great were the uses provided to the Israelites by those things they had received from the Egyptians, which the Egyptians did not use well, but the Hebrews, instructed by the wisdom of God, used for divine worship? Furthermore, divine Scripture knows it to be an evil that some descended from the land of the children of Israel into Egypt; signifying that it is an evil for some to dwell with the Egyptians—that is, to be occupied in the disciplines of the world—after they have been inscribed in the law of God and the piety of the Israelites toward God. ...to have established: for many are the brothers of Hadad the Edomite <note>original: "Ader Idumæi." In the biblical context of 1 Kings, Hadad/Ader represents an adversary to Solomon; Origen uses him here as a symbol for those who use worldly wisdom to create heresy.</note>. These are the ones who, out of the quickness of their Greek intellect, have given birth to heretical opinions and have set up certain golden calves in Bethel, which means "the house of God." By this, the divine word seems to hint that they have attached their own inventions to the Scriptures—those places where the word of God dwells, which are called "Bethel" by way of a figure of speech <term>tropo: a figurative or metaphorical use of a word</term>. Therefore, some of those inventions which, as we have explained, the brothers of Hadad fashioned, are close to the borders of the Gentiles.

You therefore, my master and son <note>A respectful and affectionate address to his student, Gregory.</note>, apply yourself especially to the reading of the divine Scriptures. Apply yourself, I say, for we who read divine things have need of great attention, lest we should speak or think anything too rashly. And as you turn your mind to the reading of the divine books with a faithful and God-pleasing preconception, knock at those things which are closed within them, and they shall be opened to you by the gatekeeper, of whom Jesus said, *To him the gatekeeper opens.* <margin>John 10:3</margin> And as you attend to the divine reading, search rightly and with unshaken faith in God for the meaning of the divine letters, which is hidden from many. But do not merely knock and search: for prayer is especially necessary for understanding divine things. To this the Savior exhorted us, saying not only, *Knock, and it shall be opened to you; Seek, and you shall find,* but also, *Ask, and it shall be given to you.* <margin>Matthew 7:7</margin> I have ventured these things out of my fatherly love for you; whether I have ventured rightly or not, God and His Christ know, as does he who participates in the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. May you also participate in it, and may you always increase that participation, so that you may say not only, *We have become partakers of Christ,* but also, *Partakers of God.* <margin>Hebrews 3:14</margin>

<margin>1 Kings 12.</margin>
...service to God; but many are the brothers of Hadad the Edomite. These are they who, from Greek fluency, have generated heretical thoughts and fashioned golden calves in Bethel, which is interpreted as "the house of God." It seems to me that through these things the Word hints that they have dedicated their own fabrications to the Scriptures, in which the Word of God dwells, figuratively called Bethel. And the Word says the other fabrication was dedicated in Dan. Now the borders of Dan are the furthest limits, and near the borders of the Gentiles, as is clear from the records in the book of Joshua the son of Nun. Therefore, some of the fabrications which the brothers of Hadad fabricated, as we have explained, are near the borders of the Gentiles.

You therefore, my master and son, primarily attend to the reading of the divine Scriptures; but attend closely, for we who read the divine things need much attention, lest we say or think something rash about them. And attending to the divine reading, with a preconception of faith pleasing to God, knock at its closed doors, and it will be opened to you by the gatekeeper, about whom Jesus said, *To him the gatekeeper opens.* <margin>John 10:3</margin> And attending to the divine reading, seek rightly and with unwavering faith in God the mind of the divine writings which is hidden from the many. But do not be satisfied with knocking and seeking; for prayer is most necessary for the understanding of divine things. To this the Savior, encouraging us, said not only, *Knock, and it shall be opened to you,* and, *Seek and you shall find,* but also, <margin>Matthew 7:7</margin> *Ask, and it shall be given to you.* These things have been ventured from my fatherly love toward you; but whether these ventures are good or not, God would know, and His Christ, and he who partakes of the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ. May you also partake, and always increase the participation, so that you may say not only, *We have become partakers of Christ,* but also, *Partakers of God.* <margin>Hebrews 3:14</margin>

<summary>Origen concludes his letter to Gregory by warning that misusing Greek philosophy leads to heresy (symbolized by the golden calves of Bethel and Dan) and urges diligent, prayerful study of the Scriptures.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XIV.

> That for those who wish not to be deceived regarding the truth in the understanding of the divine Scriptures, it is most necessary to know the logical lessons—that is, the preparatory studies—which are fit for use; without an accurate understanding of these meanings, the truth cannot be presented in the proper manner.

<column-break/>

> *For those who wish not to stray from the truth in understanding the divine Scriptures, it is especially necessary that they grasp the liberal disciplines <note>original: "liberales disciplinas," referring to the classical arts of grammar, logic, and rhetoric</note> which are suited to this use, as primary instructions, without which we cannot attain an accurate understanding of the things signified.*

---

### CHAPTER 14.
### CHAPTER XIV.

-> From the third volume of the commentaries on Genesis. <-
-> *From the third volume of the commentaries on Genesis.* <-

<margin>Genesis 1:16, 17, 18.</margin>
And God made the two great lights: the greater light for the beginnings <note>original Greek: "eis archas"; Latin: "in principatum"</note> of the day, and the lesser light for the beginnings of the night, and the stars. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven, so as to shine upon the earth, and to rule over the day and over the night. It must be sought whether "For the beginnings of the day" is the same as "To rule over the day"; and whether "For the beginnings of the night" is the same as "To rule over the night." For Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek, known for his extreme literalism</note> maintained the proportion, using "For authority" <note>original: "eis exousian"</note> instead of "For beginnings," and "To exercise authority" instead of "To rule." Now, those who have cared to examine the meanings of words say that in places where there is a conjunction of "appellations" <term>appellation: a noun or name (prosēgoria)</term> and "predicates" <term>predicate: a verb or action attributed to a subject (katēgorēma)</term>, the appellations exist first, and the predicates follow from the appellations. They say an appellation is like "wisdom," while the predicate is "to be wise." Similarly, the appellation is "temperance," and the predicate is "to be temperate." And they say wisdom exists first, and then the predicate "to be wise" follows from wisdom. These things we have observed, even if we seem to some to be acting contrary to the intent of the Scripture; since God, in making the lights, makes the great one "for the beginnings of the day" and the lesser "for the beginnings of the night"; but He places them in the firmament of heaven no longer "for the beginnings" of day and night, but "to rule" over day and night. Because the appellations were placed first and the predicates were brought in afterwards—ordered and consistent with technical logic—it moved us to consider whether this matter was also handled thus by the Servant <note>Moses, traditionally regarded as the author of Genesis</note>; especially since Aquila, who aimed to translate most precisely, did nothing other than distinguish the appellation and the predicate. Furthermore, let the one who is reluctant to accept these things see if he can understand a problem of ethics, or natural philosophy, or theology, without accuracy of meanings and of those things according to the...

<column-break/>

*AND God made two great lights: the great light for the dominion of the day, and the lesser light for the dominion of the night, and the stars: and God placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine upon the earth and preside over the day and night. Now it must be asked whether "for the dominion of the day" is the same as "that they might preside over the day": and "for the dominion of the night" the same as "that they might preside over the night." For Aquila retained the corresponding expression, and for "in dominion," substituted "into power"; and for "that they might preside," "that they might have power." Furthermore, those who have more diligently pursued meanings say that in those places in which there is a joining of appellations and of those things which are said of something, those things which are appellations precede, and those things said of them follow: the appellation being that which is said of something, such as "intelligence," and that which is said of something being "to understand." Similarly, the appellation is "temperance," the predicate "to be temperate": and they say that intelligence precedes; and that which is said from intelligence, "to understand," succeeds it. These things, however, we have observed, even if we shall seem to some to act beyond the mind of the Scripture: since God who makes the lights makes the great one for the dominion of the day, and the lesser for the dominion of the night; but he places them in the firmament of heaven, not for the dominion of day and night, but that they might preside over day and night. For because the appellations were placed first in that passage, and then the predicates were joined, in an orderly way and congruent to the sentiment of one who teaches the art of Logic, it moved us, lest the matter be understood otherwise in the work of the servant <note>Moses</note>, especially since he who studied to interpret most aptly, Aquila, did nothing else besides the appellation and that which is said of another. Furthermore, let him who hardly admits these things see whether he can [understand] a proposition concerning morals, or the nature of things, or Theology, without an accurate [understanding] of meanings and of those...*

<summary>Origen argues that a proper understanding of the Bible requires training in logic and grammar, specifically distinguishing between nouns (appellations) and verbs (predicates). He uses the creation of the sun and moon in Genesis to demonstrate how the shift from "dominion" to "ruling" reflects a precise logical progression in the text.</summary>
