# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XIV.

->**Qqq**<-

How those things which are clarified by the study of <term>Dialectics</term><note>The art of logical discussion and the investigation of the meaning of words.</note> are to be understood correctly through knowledge. For what is so strange about listening to those who investigate the specific properties of words in individual languages and who diligently cling to the things signified? For sometimes, due to ignorance of that discipline which serves reason, we fall into grave error because we do not distinguish between <term>cognominations</term><note>Words shared by different things; synonyms or related titles.</note>, ambiguous terms, proper and improper expressions, and nuances of phrasing. 

For example, from ignorance of the word *World* <note>original Latin: "Mundus"; Greek: "Kosmos"</note>, and the similarity found in its diverse meanings, some have fallen into unspeakable opinions regarding the Maker of the world. They fail to discern what is meant by the passage: *The world is seated in wickedness* <margin>1 John 5:19</margin>; for in that place, John used the term to refer to the terrestrial globe and human affairs. But these people, thinking that the word "world" in that phrase signifies the entire sphere of heaven and earth and all they contain, pronounce most audaciously and—beyond what can be described—wickedly against God. For they cannot actually demonstrate how the Sun, the Moon, and the stars, which move in such a perfect order, could be "seated in wickedness." 

Furthermore, if we bring before them this passage: *Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world* <margin>John 1:29</margin>, because "World" is used in these phrases to mean the place where sin dwells (that is, the earthly regions), those who are sensible and sincere will admit what is said. But the contentious, returning to their views in a dull and foolish manner because of their ignorance of the similarity of words, will cling to the outrages they have once accepted and decreed. 

Moreover, if the opposite is presented: *God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself* <margin>2 Cor. 5:19</margin>, they will no longer be able to demonstrate what they had assumed about the "entire world"—that is, about everything in the whole universe—especially according to their own theories. For it is necessary to investigate the word itself as having multiple meanings. Indeed, anyone who studies this would find many examples of perverse interpretations arising from ambiguity, punctuation, and six hundred other such things. 

But we have said these things as a digression, to show that we also believe the knowledge of the <term>liberal arts</term><note>The traditional academic disciplines, including grammar and logic.</note> is absolutely necessary for those who wish to hold the truth in their understanding of the Divine Scriptures and not fall into error. We have had need of these arts to find the difference between those things which are written: *For the rule of the night*, and *That they might preside over the day and the night.*

<column-break/>

<note>The following column is the original Greek text of the Latin passage translated above.</note>

...of the logical place being clarified, in what manner one ought to be instructed. For what is strange about hearing of the proper literal meanings in various dialects, and attending diligently to the things signified? For there are times when, through ignorance of logic, we fall greatly, not clearing up <term>homonyms</term><note>Words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note>, ambiguities, <term>catachreses</term><note>The use of a word in a way that departs from its strict literal sense.</note>, literal meanings, and distinctions. 

For instance, through ignorance of the homonymous sound of the name *World* <note>original Greek: "Kosmos"</note>, those who have not cleared up what it refers to in the phrase *The world lies in the evil one* have fallen into the most impious thoughts about the Creator; for John spoke there of the earthly and human places. For thinking that "world" according to that very word signifies the system composed of heaven and earth and the things in them, they declare most boldly and unholily concerning God; being in no way able to show by the facts how the sun, and moon, and stars, which are ordered to move in such a way, "lie in the evil one." 

Then, if we set before them the passage: *This is the lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world*, showing that "World" is said in these words to be where sin abounds—that is, in the earthly places—those of good will will accept the things said, but the quarrelsome, behaving foolishly, will persist in the wicked things they were once persuaded of through ignorance of the homonymy. 

And again, if it is said: *God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself*, they will still have to explain their assumption about the whole world—that is, about the things in the whole world—especially to show it according to their own hypotheses. For it is necessary to examine the word itself as a homonym. And concerning the ambiguity of wicked interpretations, and because of the distinction of punctuation marks, and ten thousand other examples, one who is industrious could find not a few. 

We have digressed on these matters to show that even according to us, for those who wish not to be deceived concerning the truth in understanding the divine scriptures, it is most necessary to know the logical applications; which we even now needed in order to find the difference between the sayings: *For the beginnings of the night*, and *For the ruling of the day and of the night.*

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXI.

Concerning free will, and the resolution and interpretation of those passages of Scripture which seem to do away with it.

*Concerning the freedom of the will, and the solution and interpretation of the sayings of Scripture which seem to take it away.*

### CHAP. XXI.
### CAP. XXI.

->From the third book of *On First Principles*.<-
->*From the third volume of On First Principles.*<-

Since the teaching of the Church includes the doctrine of the righteous judgment of God—which, if believed to be true, summons its hearers to live a good life and to flee from sin by every means, clearly acknowledging that things worthy of praise or blame are within our own power—come, let us discuss a few points specifically regarding free will <note>original: *autexousion*, meaning "self-power" or "the power of self-determination"</note>, as it is a most necessary inquiry. In order to understand what free will is, we must unfold its definition, so that once this is accurately clarified, the subject of our investigation may be established. Of things that move, some have the cause of their motion within themselves, while others are moved only from without. Those things moved only from without are those that are carried along, such as wood, stones, and all matter held together by mere "habit" <note>term: *hexis* (habit) — a Stoic term for the lowest level of cohesion in inanimate objects</note>; let us set aside for now the argument that the very nature of bodies is a form of motion, as it is not needed for the present purpose. But animals, plants, and in short, everything held together by "nature" <note>term: *physis* — here referring to the vegetative power of growth</note> and "soul" <note>term: *psyche* — the animating principle</note> have the cause of motion within themselves; some say minerals also belong to this class. Furthermore, fire is self-moving, and perhaps also springs of water. Of those things having the cause of motion within themselves, some are said to move *out of* themselves, and others *by* themselves: inanimate things move *out of* themselves, while living beings move *by* themselves. Living beings move *by* themselves when an "impression" <note>term: *phantasia* — a mental image or stimulus</note> occurs which calls forth an "impulse" <note>term: *hormē* — a natural drive or inclination</note>. Again, in certain animals, impressions occur that call forth impulse, as their "imaginative nature" <note>the faculty that processes sensory images</note> moves the impulse in an orderly way. For instance, in a spider, the impression of weaving arises, and the impulse to weave follows, because its imaginative nature calls it to this in an orderly fashion; and the animal is believed to possess nothing else beyond its imaginative nature. So too with the bee in its making of wax cells. However, the rational animal <note>human beings</note> possesses reason in addition to the imaginative nature. Reason judges the impressions, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the living being may be led according to them. Therefore, since in the nature of reason there are resources for beholding the honorable and the shameful—by following which, and beholding the honorable and the shameful, we choose the honorable and avoid the shameful—we are worthy of praise when we devote ourselves to the honorable, and worthy of blame for the shameful.

<column-break/>

Since the preaching of the Church contains the discourse concerning the just judgment of God, which indeed, if it is believed to be true, exhorts the hearers to an honest life and to the fleeing of sin by all means of both mind and body; inasmuch as they confess that those things which are worthy of praise and reproach are situated within us: come, let us also dispute separately a few things concerning free will, a most necessary question. And, so that we may understand what free will is, its notion must be explained; so that, this being clearly declared, the question may be established. Of those things which are moved, some have the cause of motion in themselves, others are moved only from without. Therefore, those things which are carried are moved only from without, such as wood, and stones, and all matter which is contained under "habit" alone: and let that which is usually said—that motion is the flux of bodies—be placed outside the discourse now, because it contributes very little to the present matter. But animals and plants have the cause of motion in themselves, and finally all those things which consist of "nature" and "soul"; in which they also number metals, and perhaps also springs. Moreover, of those things which have the cause of motion in themselves, they say some are moved *out of* themselves, others *by* themselves: *out of* themselves indeed in the case of the soul-less, but *by* themselves in the case of the animated. For the animated are moved *by* themselves, an innate "appearance" <note>original: *specie*, translating the Greek *phantasia*</note> producing an appetite and an impulse: and again, in certain animals, appearances are present provoking an impulse, their "imaginative nature" moving the impulse in a certain order. Just as the appearance of weaving presents itself to the spider, and the appetite for weaving follows; the nature of the appearance being surely the effective cause in impelling it to that order; and the animal receiving the appearance of no other thing after its own imagining nature. The same is true of the bee for the shaping of honeycombs. But the animal endowed with reason has, besides the imagining nature, reason which judges the appearances, and indeed rejects some, but accepts others, by which the animal may be led. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are aids for contemplating the honorable and the base, using which in the despising of the honorable and the base we choose the honorable and avoid the base: we are certainly worthy of praise, while

<summary>Origen begins a philosophical defense of free will, distinguishing between the mechanical motion of inanimate objects and the self-determined motion of rational beings. He argues that because humans have reason to judge their impulses, they are morally responsible for their actions.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

->**On Free Will**<-

<note>The text is presented in two columns: Latin on the left and Greek on the right. Both convey the same philosophical argument regarding human agency.</note>

We have devoted ourselves to honor; to reproach, when we slip into the contrary. Nor should it be ignored that nature, which is distributed among all things, is occupied in living creatures in a certain way, more or less: so much so that the function of dogs in tracking wild beasts, and of horses in warring, approaches nearly, so to speak, the power of reason. Therefore, that something should happen from the outside, stirring this or that thought in us, is certainly not within our power; but to judge that we must use it in this or that way is the work of our reason alone. This reason either incites us to the impulses of the right and honorable without those external aids, or toward the contrary. 

But if someone says that the external movement is of such a kind that no one can resist its impulse, let him look into his own disturbances and motions, to see whether there is not a consent, and an inclination of the "ruling faculty" <note>original: *principis patris* / *hegemonikon*. This refers to the Stoic concept of the 'governing part' of the soul</note> toward that thing because of such persuasions. For a woman (for example) seen by a man who has embraced the purpose of continence and chastity, and who entices him to break that decree, is not in herself a sufficient cause for breaking his purpose. For altogether, he who did not wish to resist that tickling and the slipperiness of pleasure, nor to hold his holy purpose, slides into the disgrace of intemperance. 

Another man tends toward the contrary: to him, who is instructed and polished by many disciplines, ticklings and allurements occur; but his reason—because it has been strengthened, nourished in meditation, and conformed by doctrines to the study of the honorable, or brought very close to that firmness—shakes off the allurements and dissolves the lust. Since these things happen in us in this manner, to derive their cause from the outside, to free oneself from blame, and to declare oneself similar to wood and stones moved by an external force, is neither right nor consistent with the truth. Such a speech belongs to a man who desires to corrupt and adulterate the notion of free will <note>original: *liberi arbitrii* / *autexousion*</note>. 

If we were to ask him what free will is, he would answer that if nothing occurred from the outside, with me proposing and deciding something, that would be what impels me to the contrary. Again, he who transfers the cause to a weak constitution of the body fights against clear reason; for the teaching and instructing of reason takes hold of even the most lustful and savage men, if they obey its warnings, and so changes them that a conversion and a change for the better frequently occurs. And often, from those who previously did not seem to be such by nature,

<column-break/>

giving themselves over to the practice of the good; but they are blameworthy in the contrary case. However, it must not be ignored that the nature which is ordained for all things exists in some degree in animals, more or less. So that it is nearly, so to speak, close to the rational: the work in tracking dogs, and in war horses. Now, to fall under this or that external impression <note>original: *phantasia*</note> which moves us in such or such a way is admittedly not among the things in our power. But to judge to use the event in this way or another is the work of nothing else than the reason within us, either making us noble toward the starting-points that call us toward the good and toward duty, or turning us toward the contrary. 

If anyone says the external thing itself is of such a kind that it is impossible to look away from it when it becomes such, let him attend to his own passions and movements, to see if there is not an approval and a consent and a leaning of the ruling faculty <note>original: *hegemonikon*</note> toward this thing because of these persuasions. For example (let us say), a woman appearing to one who has decided to be continent and to restrain himself from sexual unions, and calling him forth to do something contrary to his purpose, does not become the self-sufficient cause of his setting aside his purpose. For having altogether approved of the tickling and the smoothness of the pleasure, and not having willed to look away from it, nor to ratify what was decided, he acts intemperately. 

But another man, conversely, meeting the same event—because he has taken up more lessons and has practiced—the ticklings and irritations occur, but his reason, inasmuch as it has been strengthened more, and nourished by study, and confirmed by dogmas toward the good, or having become near to being confirmed, beats back the irritations and weakens the desire. Since these things happen to us in this way, to blame external things and to release oneself from accusation, portraying oneself like wood and stones dragged by things moving them from the outside, is not true, nor is it the mark of a fair-minded man. Such a word is of one who wishes to counterfeit the concept of free will. 

For if we asked him what free will is, he would say that if nothing from the outside met me, when I had set forth this thing, it would be that which calls me to the contrary. And again, to blame the mere physical constitution is against the evidence of reason; for the teacher, taking the most intemperate and the most savage men, if they should follow the exhortation, changes them, so that the turning and the change for the better becomes very great; often the most intemperate become better than those who previously seemed to be such by nature; and the most savage

<note>The text ends mid-sentence, noting that even the most "incontinent" or "savage" individuals can become better through the application of reason and discipline.</note>

<summary>This page argues that while external stimuli (impressions) are beyond our control, our reaction to them is governed by reason and free will. Origen refutes the idea that humans are passive objects like "wood and stones," asserting that moral character can be transformed through discipline and rational consent.</summary>

But, because there are certain sayings in the Old and New Testaments which seem to lead to the opposite conclusion—namely, that it is not within our power to keep the commandments and be saved, or to break them and perish—come, let us set these forth one by one and look into their solutions. Thus, from the examples we provide, anyone may perceive the solution for all similar passages that seem to take away the freedom of the will. 

Truly, many are moved by what is said concerning Pharaoh, about whom God repeatedly declares, *I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.* For if he is hardened by God, and sins because of that hardening, he is not himself the cause of the sin; and if this is so, Pharaoh is not master of his own will. From this, someone might say that those who perish are not of their own volition, nor do they perish through themselves. 

And what is said in Ezekiel, *I will take away their stony hearts and put in hearts of flesh, so that they may walk in my precepts and keep my decrees,* might perhaps move someone to think that it is God who grants the walking in His commandments and the keeping of His decrees, by the very fact that He removed the impediment—the stony heart—and inserted something better, namely, a heart of flesh. 

But let us also see what the Savior answers in the Gospel to those asking why He speaks to the multitude in parables: He says, *That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand; lest at any time they should be converted, and their sins should be forgiven them.* Furthermore, in Paul, *It is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy;* and elsewhere, *Both the willing and the working are from God.* Does God, then, have mercy on whom He will, and whom He will He hardens? You will say to me then, "Why does He yet find fault? For who [resists] His will?"

## Rrr 2

...how he can be seen as good and just, or even just alone, when he hardens the heart of one who perishes because of that very hardening; and how the Just One can be the cause of destruction and rebellion for those whom he punishes because they were hardened and resisted him. Why indeed does he find fault with him, saying: *But you will not let my people go: behold, I will strike all the firstborn in Egypt, and your firstborn son:* <margin>Exodus 4:23</margin> and whatever else is attributed to God speaking to Pharaoh through Moses? For it is necessary that whoever believes the Scriptures to be true, and God to be just, must—if he is of good faith—strive to show clearly how God is just in those passages of Scripture. For if someone were to professedly, strenuously, and contentiously maintain that the Maker of the world is evil, one would have to deal with him by another method. But since these people <note>Likely referring to the Marcionites or Gnostics, who argued the Old Testament God was harsh or evil.</note> say they believe him to be just, and we are disputing about him as both good and just, how can the good and just one harden Pharaoh's heart?

See, therefore, if perhaps by that example which the Apostle used in the Epistle to the Hebrews, we might be able to show how by one and the same operation God has mercy on one and hardens another; yet he does not have the purpose to harden, but through a good purpose—from which, because some cling to the malice of their own vice, it follows that they are hardened—he is said to harden the one who is hardened. *The earth,* he says, *drinking in the rain falling upon it, and bringing forth a useful herb for those by whom it is tilled, receives a blessing from God; but bringing forth thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is to be burned.* <margin>Hebrews 6:7-8</margin> Is there not, therefore, one and the same action in the sending down of the rain? Yet from that same single rain, the cultivated earth produces fruit, while the waste and uncultivated earth produces thorns. And although it might seem harsh if the one who granted the rain should say, "I produced the fruit and the thorns in the earth," it is harsh, yet true: for if the rain had been absent, neither fruit nor thorns would have come forth; but when it flowed down seasonably and moderately, both fruit and thorns arose. Therefore, the earth which, after often drinking the rain sent upon it, brings forth thorns and thistles, is rejected and almost accursed. Did not the benefit of the rain also fall upon the inferior earth? But its neglected and uncultivated soil alone brought forth the thorns and thistles.

In that same manner, the wonders which God performed are like a certain rain; but the differing wills are like the cultivated and uncultivated earth, which is of one nature as soil. Just as if the Sun were to send forth a voice and say, "I liquefy and I dry up"—which are opposites—he would say nothing false regarding the subject matter, since by one and the same heat, wax...

<column-break/>

...good and just, or the just one alone appears just, hardening the heart of the one who perishes through being hardened; and how the just one becomes the cause of destruction and disobedience to those who are punished because of their hardening and disobedience to him. Who also blames him, saying, *But you do not wish to send away my people; behold, I will strike all the firstborn in Egypt, and your firstborn;* and whatever else is recorded as being said by God through Moses to Pharaoh? For it is necessary for the one who believes that the Scriptures are true, and that God is just, if he be fair-minded, to struggle with how in such words he may be clearly understood as just. For if you were to stand with your head held high <note>original: ὑποξαιρεῖσθαι ὑμᾶς τῇ κεφαλῇ, an idiom for being stubborn or arrogant</note> toward the Creator being evil, we would want another [argument] against him. But since they say they are disposed toward him as toward a just one, let us also consider him as both good and just: how could the good and just one harden the heart of Pharaoh?

Look then, if through the image spoken by the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews, we might be able to present how by one operation God has mercy on one, and hardens another; not purposing to harden, but through a kind purpose, which is followed—on account of the underlying malice of the evil in themselves—by the hardening, he is said to harden the one being hardened. *The earth,* he says, *which has drunk the rain coming upon it, and brings forth a plant fit for those for whom it is also farmed, partakes of a blessing from God; but bringing forth thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near a curse, the end of which is for burning.* Is there then one operation regarding the rain? And while there is one operation regarding the rain, does the farmed earth bear fruit, while the neglected and dry earth bears thorns? And we might seem to think it right for the one who rains to say, "I made the fruits, and the thorns in the earth," and even if it is ill-omened to say, yet it is true; for if the rain had not happened, neither fruits nor thorns would have occurred, but when it flowed opportunely and in measure, both occurred. Therefore, all the earth that has often drunk the rain coming upon it and brings forth thorns and thistles becomes rejected and near a curse. Did not the benefit of the rain also come upon the worse earth? But the neglected underlying [soil], being unfarmed, sprouted thorns and thistles. Thus, therefore, the wonders performed by God are, as it were, rain; but the different choices of will are, as it were, the farmed earth and the neglected earth, being one in nature as earth. Just as if the sun also said, emitting a voice, that "I melt and I dry up"; though melting and drying are opposites, he would not be speaking a lie because of the underlying matter, since by the one heat, [wax] is melted...

<summary>Origen explains the theological difficulty of God hardening Pharaoh's heart by using the metaphors of rain and sun, arguing that God's "rain" (miracles/grace) is uniform, but the result depends on the "soil" (the individual's will).</summary>

He uses Paul, Isaiah, and Jeremiah to argue that human free will, not divine whim, is responsible for stubbornness.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

->**Chapter 21: On Free Will**<-

<note>The Philocalia is an anthology of Origen's writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus. This section deals with why God appears to "abandon" or delay the punishment of sinners.</note>

...until our sins have reached their peak? He leaves many unpunished for a time, so that the character of each individual may be examined through our own free will, and so that the better men may be made manifest through that trial. As for the rest—who are not hidden from God, for He knows all things before they happen—they may later find the way of salvation for themselves and for other rational creatures. They would not have acknowledged the benefit of God's grace unless they had first condemned themselves. Indeed, it is beneficial for everyone to perceive their own condition and the grace of God. For he who does not feel his own weakness and the grace of God, even if he is helped, will think that the achievement was his own doing—granted to him by divine gift though it was—unless he has first experienced his own lack of strength and learned to commend himself to God. This opinion, through the swelling of a proud mind and spirit, leads to a fall; which is exactly what we believe happened to the Devil, who, while he was still blameless, claimed that excellence and those privileges for himself. <margin>Luke 14:11</margin> *For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, just as whoever humbles himself will be exalted.* For this reason, He understands that divine things are hidden from the wise and the prudent; so that, as the <margin>Matthew 11:25; 1 Corinthians 1:29</margin> Apostle says, *no flesh should glory in the sight of God*; and that they are revealed to "infants"—those who, after their infancy, have grown toward better things and remember that they reached such happiness not so much by their own efforts as by the inexplicable and singular benefit of God. Therefore, he who is "abandoned" is reserved for divine judgment, and God is patient toward certain sinners. This is not without cause, but for their own advantage and fruit, so that in view of the immortality of the soul and the eternal age, they are not immediately rushed into salvation; rather, they are brought to it more slowly, after they have experienced many evils. For just as physicians, though they could cure a patient more quickly, might do the opposite if they suspect a hidden poison is in the body—because they wish to cure the patient more surely—they judge it better to keep the patient in the heat of inflammation and labor for a longer time to ensure a more lasting health, rather than appearing to heal them quickly only for them to suffer a relapse later, making the quick cure merely temporary. In this same way, God, who knows the secrets of the heart and foresees the future, in His kindness draws out the hidden evil through external circumstances. He does this to purge the one who, through negligence, contains and nourishes the seeds of sin within himself; so that, when they have come to the surface,

...but even that our failings should remain hidden until they reach their full magnitude? The rest—not that they were hidden from God, for He knows all things before their birth, but from themselves and other rational beings—may later obtain the path of healing. They would not have recognized the benefit if they had not first condemned themselves. This is profitable for each person: to perceive his own particular nature and the grace of God. He who does not perceive his own weakness and divine grace, even if he receives a benefit, will—if he has not examined himself or condemned himself—suppose that the gift supplied to him by heavenly grace is his own brave achievement. This conceit, producing a "puffing up" <note>original: "τύφωσιν" (typhōsin) – a state of delusion or pride</note>, will be the cause of a downfall; which is what we believe happened to the Devil, when he credited to himself the advantages he possessed while he was still blameless. *For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, just as everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted.* And He says that for this reason divine things are hidden from the wise and the prudent; so that, as the Apostle says, *no flesh should boast before God*; and they are revealed to infants—those who, after their infancy, have advanced to better things and remember that they have arrived at such a great height of blessedness not so much because of their own cause as because of an unspeakable benefit. Therefore, the one who is abandoned is abandoned by divine judgment, and God is long-suffering toward some of those who sin; not without reason, but because it will be profitable for them, in view of the immortality of the soul and the infinite age, not to be quickly brought to salvation, but to be led to it more slowly after experiencing many evils. For just as some physicians, though able to heal more quickly, work in a way contrary to healing when they suspect a hidden virus <note>original: "ἰὸν" (ion) – can mean poison, venom, or rust</note> exists in the body—doing this for the sake of a safer cure, thinking it better to keep someone for a long time in inflammation and pain so they may recover health more firmly, rather than seeming to strengthen them quickly only for the illness to return—in the same way God, knowing the secrets of the heart and foreknowing the future, perhaps permits the hidden evil to be drawn out through long-suffering and external events, for the sake of cleansing the one who through neglect has harbored the seeds of sin; so that, when they have come to the surface, he may vomit them up, even if...

...having been immersed longer in evils, it might later be able, after obtaining purification, to be rebuilt from its foundation <note>original: ἀναστοιχειωθῆναι (anastoicheiōthēnai) - to be restructured or re-educated in its basic elements</note> away from vice. For God manages souls, not merely for the sake of—let us say—the fifty years of life here, but with a view toward the boundless eternity. For He has made the intellectual nature incorruptible and akin to Himself; and the rational soul is not excluded from healing as it is from this present life. But come, let us also use such an image from the Gospel:

<margin>Matthew 13:5, 6.</margin>

There is a certain rock, having a little and superficial soil, into which if seeds fall, they quickly bloom; but having bloomed, because they have no root, when the sun rises, they are scorched and withered. And this rock is the human soul, hardened through negligence and turned to stone through vice; for God created a stony heart for no one, but it becomes such through wickedness. Just as, therefore, if someone were to blame a farmer for not casting seeds more quickly upon the stony ground, seeing someone else’s stony ground which had received seeds and bloomed, the farmer might answer that he would treat this ground later by applying what is beneficial for the things to be produced, and that the slower and surer growth in the soil would be better than that which received it more quickly and superficially. One would be persuaded that the farmer spoke reasonably and acted skillfully. So also the great Creator of all nature delays the legislation <note>The "legislation" here refers to the internal moral law or divine intervention</note> so as not to produce it too quickly, lest it become superficial. But it is likely someone might raise an objection to this: Why then does some of the seed fall upon the superficial soil, that is, the soul that is like a rock? It must be said to this, that it was better for one who desired better things too impulsively <note>original: φρονιμώτερον (phronimōteron) - here used ironically for one who thinks they are wise but acts without depth</note> and did not travel toward them by the proper path, to obtain what they desired; so that, condemning themselves for this inferior cultivation, they might later endure to receive it over a long period of time. For our souls are, as one might say, infinite, and their characters are infinite, and their movements, purposes, designs, and impulses are very many; of which God alone is the manager <note>term: οἰκονόμος (oikonomos) - a household manager or steward; Origen uses this to describe God's providential care</note>, knowing both the seasons and the fitting helps, and the trainings, and the ways—the God and Father of all. He knows how He leads even Pharaoh through so many things and the drowning, in which the management of Pharaoh will conclude. For he was not destroyed because he was drowned; for both we and our words are in the hand of God, as is all wisdom and knowledge of works. Just as therefore, if anyone should rebuke a farmer, who did not sooner send seeds into the stony ground, because he sees another's stony ground conceive seeds and flourish, the farmer would answer, that he would perform the sowing in this ground later, when he has brought together those things which can sustain the sowing, since this earth is safer than that which conceives more quickly and only on the topmost surface; he will believe the farmer, as one who has both spoken truly and acted skillfully and knowingly: so the great Maker of all nature, first delays the good work that appears immediately, as if throwing it on top, lest it be only on the topmost surface; but it is also fitting for us to add to these things. Why indeed does part of the seeds fall into that light and outermost soil, a soul plainly like a rock? <meta>This page continues Origen’s discussion on free will, specifically addressing the theological challenge posed by God’s promise to replace "hearts of stone" with "hearts of flesh."</meta>

# CHAPTER XXI. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

...I will put in hearts of flesh, *so that they may walk in my statutes and keep my commands*. <note>A reference to Ezekiel 11:19-20.</note> For if, when God wills, He takes away stony hearts and puts in fleshy ones so that His commands may be kept, it is not within our power to cast away wickedness. For to have stony hearts removed is nothing else than for wickedness—by which one is hardened—to be taken away from whomsoever God wills. And to have a fleshy heart put in, so that one walks in God’s commands and guards His edicts, what else is this but to yield and not resist the truth, but rather to pursue the virtues? But if God promises that He will do these things, and we do not lay aside stony hearts until He Himself takes them away, it appears clearly enough from this that it is not situated within us to lay aside wickedness. If, truly, we effect nothing toward having a fleshy heart within us, but it is the work of God, then it will not be our own work if we live according to the prescription of virtue, but plainly a divine benefit. 

Thus will he argue who, from those bare words, would take away our freedom and our powers. But we shall respond that these things are understood by us in this way: just as if someone, ignorant and unlearned and conscious of his own evils, is driven either by the exhortation of a teacher or from elsewhere and gives himself up of his own free will to the one he thinks will lead him by the hand toward erudition and virtue. To him, when he gives himself up, the teacher promises that he will remove ignorance from him and instill learning—not because he who committed himself to be cared for contributes nothing toward erudition and fleeing ignorance, but because the teacher promises that he will provide the cure when he [the student] so wills it. 

In this way, the divine word promises to drive out the wickedness (which it calls a stony heart) of those who approach it—not of those who are reluctant or refusing, but only of those who have given themselves over to the Physician of the sick. Just as we read in the Gospels that the sick, approaching the Savior and praying that they might receive health, are cured; and indeed, that work by which the blind receive sight, insofar as they asked for it, is the work of those who believed they could be cured; but in the restoring of the sight, it is the work of our Savior. So, therefore, the word of God promises that it will instill knowledge in those who approach, taking away the hard and stony heart (that is, wickedness), so that one may walk in the divine commands and keep God’s edicts. 

There followed that point from the Gospel, when the Savior says that He speaks to those outside in parables for this reason: *That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest at any time they should be converted, and it should be forgiven them.* <note>Mark 4:12.</note> Having seized upon this, the adversary will suggest: "If some would plainly have converted upon hearing clearer things, so as to become worthy of the pardon of sins..."

<column-break/>

...I will put in [hearts] of flesh, so that they may walk in my justifications and guard my ordinances. <note>original Greek: "βαλῶ σαρκίνας, ὅπως ἐν τοῖς δικαιώμασί μου πορεύωνται..."</note> For if, when God wills, He removes the stony hearts and puts in fleshy ones so that His ordinances are guarded, it is not because of us that wickedness is put away. For the removal of stony hearts is nothing else than the removal of the wickedness by which one is hardened, from whom God wills. And the putting in of a fleshy heart, so that one walks in the ordinances of God and guards His commandments, what else is it but to become yielding and not to be resistant toward the truth, and to follow after the virtues? But if God promises to do these things, and before He removes the stony hearts we do not put them away, it is clear that it is not in our power to put away wickedness. And if we do not do something so that the fleshy heart may be produced in us, but it is God’s work, it will not be our work to live according to virtue, but entirely divine grace. 

These things, then, will be said by the one who, from the bare words, does away with what is in our power [free will]. But we shall answer, saying that these things ought to be heard thus: that just as one being in ignorance and lack of education, perceiving his own evils, either from the encouragement of a teacher or otherwise by himself, gives himself up to the one he thinks is able to lead him by the hand to education and virtue; and the teacher promises this: to take out the lack of education and to put in education—not as if the one presenting himself to be healed contributes nothing toward being educated and fleeing ignorance, but as promising to improve the one who has applied. 

In this way the divine word promises to remove the wickedness of those who approach, which it named a "stony heart," not of those who are unwilling, but of those who have presented themselves to the Physician of the suffering. Just as in the Gospels the suffering are found approaching the Savior and requesting to obtain healing, and being cured. And it is possible to say, on the one hand, that the blind seeing again was their work according to their having requested it (of those who rightly believed they would be healed), but on the other hand, according to the restoration of sight, it was the work of our Savior. So in [this way] the word of God promises to instill knowledge in those who approach, having removed the stony and hard heart, which is wickedness, for the sake of one walking in the divine commandments and guarding the divine ordinances. After which things [comes] this from the Gospel, when the Savior said that for this reason He spoke to those outside in parables, <margin>Mark 4:12.</margin> "That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest at any time they should turn back and it should be forgiven them." And the one from the opposite side will say: "If they would have turned back entirely upon hearing clearer things, so as to become worthy of the forgiveness of sins..."

<summary>Origen argues against a fatalistic reading of Scripture, explaining that God's promise to change "hearts of stone" requires human cooperation, much like a patient seeking a physician. He uses the analogy of a student and teacher to reconcile divine grace with human free will.</summary>

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXI.

It is not within their power to hear the clearer teachings, but within the teacher’s; and for this reason he does not announce things to them more clearly, lest they should perhaps see and understand, and it be within their power to be saved. If this is so, salvation and destruction do not rest upon one's own conscience <note>Greek: *syneidesis*; here implying moral awareness or agency</note>. Now, a plausible defense against these points would be possible, were it not for the addition of the phrase, *Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven*. The Savior says more mystically that he did not wish those who were not earnest to understand in a "good and beautiful" <note>Greek: *kalos kai agathos*; a classical Greek ideal of nobility/virtue</note> way, and for this reason he spoke to them in parables. But as the text stands—*Lest they should ever turn back and be forgiven*—the defense is more difficult. 

First, then, it must be noted that this passage is used against the heterodox <note>referring here to Gnostic groups like the Marcionites who rejected the Old Testament</note>, who, seeing such expressions in the Old Testament, claim there is evidence of what they dare to call the "cruelty of the Creator," or a "vengeful and retaliatory disposition toward the worse," or whatever else they wish to name it, simply so they may separate "goodness" from the Creator. And likewise, they either disingenuously forget the New Testament, or they pass over things similar to what they think is blameworthy in the Old. For the Savior is shown even more clearly in the Gospel, as they themselves say, not speaking plainly for this reason: so that men might not turn back, and by turning back, be deemed worthy of the forgiveness of sins. This point, in itself, is no less a charge than all those brought against the Old Testament. 

If they always seek a defense for the Gospels, we must ask them whether they act blamelessly when they take different stands on similar charges; they do not attack the New Testament, but seek a defense for it. For they ought to defend the Old Testament regarding similar matters, just as they do for the charges brought from the New. By these similarities, we shall bring them to agree that everything depends on the one Word of God. 

Come then, let us make a defense of the matter at hand as best we can. We stated when examining the case of Pharaoh <note>referring to the "hardening of Pharaoh's heart" in Exodus</note> that sometimes it is not for the good of those being healed to be cured too quickly; especially if, having fallen into severe troubles, they were easily rid of what they had fallen into. Despising the evil as if it were nothing, they would fall into it a second time. Therefore, in such cases, the eternal God, the Knower of secrets, who knows all things before they come to be, in His kindness postpones the faster help for them. He—if I may put it this way—helps them by not helping them, for that is what is then profitable for them. It is likely, then, that those "outside" <note>non-believers or those not yet ready for deep truth</note>, about whom the discourse is concerned, are held in this state by the Savior according to the plan set before us.

<column-break/>

...lest they be, and it is not placed in them to hear plainer speeches, but in the teacher: and therefore if he does not declare it to them more plainly, lest perhaps they see and understand, it is not in them to be saved: which if it is so, we are not free to be saved or to perish. And certainly if there had not been added, *Lest at any time they should be converted and be forgiven*, it would be easily and probably answered, that the Savior did not wish those who were not good and holy to understand the more hidden things, and for that reason spoke to them in parables: but, since it is added, *Lest at any time they should be converted and be forgiven*, the defense of this place is more difficult. 

Therefore, first the place against the heretics must be noted, who are accustomed to hunt for certain sayings from the Old Testament, from which, as they themselves dare to say, a certain cruelty of the Craftsman <note>Latin: *opifices*; referring to the Demiurge</note> in his plan of avenging and punishing, or by whatever other name they prefer to call it, seems to be proved, only so that they may show that goodness is not in the Creator. But they do not deal with the reading of the New Testament in one way nor candidly, but they reject those things similar to what they think should be blamed in the Old; for clearly the Savior in the Gospel, as they say, is shown by those former words not to speak openly, lest men be converted and, being converted, become worthy of the remission of sins. Which itself is in no way better than those things which are blamed in the Old Testament as being against humanity. 

If they seek a defense of the Gospel, we answer: are they not worthy of blame who deal differently with similar questions? Since they find no stumbling block in the New Testament, but seek its defense; yet in the Old they blame similar things, for which likewise an explanation should have been sought. Whence we shall lead them by similarity to this point: that they believe both Testaments to be of one and the same God. But let us bring as clear an explanation as we can of the proposed question. We were saying, while discussing Pharaoh, that it is not always good for the sick to be cured immediately, if as soon as they have fallen into a difficult disease they are very easily relieved of it; for despising the evil as if it were easy to cure, and not at all taking care lest they fall back into it, they will lie in it longer. Wherefore for such sick people the eternal God and Knower of secrets, because He knows all things before they are, according to His goodness defers the swifter cure; and, so to speak, He cures them while He does not cure them. It is necessary that those whom, as it is stated, the Savior in conversion...

He argues that God sometimes delays healing (spiritual salvation) to ensure it is deep and lasting, rather than superficial, using the hardening of Pharaoh's heart as a parallel.</summary>

# Chapter XXI. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

seeing that they would not be stable in their conversion if they heard his words more clearly, they were so dealt with by the Lord that they might not openly understand deeper things. This was lest, by turning and being healed too quickly through obtaining forgiveness, they might despise the wounds of their vices as if they were very easy to cure, and so fall back into them again even more swiftly. For perhaps the time for the punishments of those things they committed by forsaking virtue had not yet been fulfilled; during which time, being left by divine care and satisfied with the very evils they had perpetrated, they might later be called to a more firm repentance. This prevented them from falling back immediately into their former sins, by which they had corrupted the dignity of honesty and given themselves over to wickedness. Therefore, those who are called "outsiders," when compared with those who are "inside," are not placed very far from them; though they hear obscurely while the others hear openly, because the Lord speaks to them in parables. But others, distinct from those who are outside, are the Tyrians <note>The inhabitants of Tyre, referenced in Matthew 11:21</note>; although it was foreknown of these that they would have repented long ago sitting in sackcloth and ashes had the Savior approached their borders, they do not even hear the things the "outsiders" hear. This is more fitting, as they are far removed from the dignity of the outsiders; so that at another time—after it has been more tolerable for them than for those who did not receive the word (among whom he mentions the Tyrians)—hearing at a more opportune time, they may repent more strongly and lastingly. But see whether we do not strive, beyond the zeal of investigation, to preserve piety in all things when we contend to prove in every way concerning God and his Christ, that the immortal God provides for the soul in such great and various works of providence. If anyone, therefore, should ask concerning those who are rebuked—that seeing wonders and hearing the divine word they profited nothing, whereas the Tyrians would have repented if such things had been said and done among them—and should ask with words of this sort: "Why did the Savior preach to them to their own destruction, so that a heavier sin might be imputed to them?" we shall answer: God, who knows how all are disposed, refutes those who find fault with His providence (as if they did not believe because He did not grant them to see what He offered to others to behold, nor disposed them to hear what profited others to hear). To show that their excuse is not just, He provides the very evidence that those fault-finders of the divine administration had sought; so that having received these things and nonetheless being convicted of the utmost impiety—because they perceived no utility even when supported by these aids—they might desist from that audacity and temerity of theirs. And being liberated by that very fact, they might learn that God, in dispensing benefits, sometimes hesitates and lingers,

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>Romans 9:16</margin>
...and to confirm that He does not grant the privilege of seeing and hearing such things to those for whom, having seen and heard them, their sin would be proven weightier and more severe than the sin of those who had not believed in such great things. But let us also look at the passage: *“So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”* For those who seize upon this say: if it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, then being saved is not up to us, but comes from our constitution—either from the way the created being was fashioned, or from the choice of Him who shows mercy when He wishes. We must then ask them: is willing what is good a good thing or a bad thing? And is running with the desire to reach the goal while hastening toward good things praiseworthy or blameworthy? For if they say it is blameworthy, they will be answering contrary to the obvious truth; for they would be making the worth of those who will and run a matter of blame. But if they say that willing good things and running toward good things is good, let us ask how a "lost nature" <note>Origen is likely arguing against Gnostic groups like the Valentinians, who believed some people were created with a "lost nature" and could never be saved.</note> can will the better things? For it would be as if a bad tree bore good fruit, if indeed willing the better things is good. Thirdly, they might say that willing good things and running toward good things is a "middle" thing <note>A technical term in Stoic philosophy (adiaphora) referring to actions that are neither inherently virtuous nor vicious.</note>, being neither noble nor base. To this it must be said: if willing good things and running toward good things is a middle thing, then its opposite is also a middle thing—that is, willing evil things and running toward evil things. But willing evil things and running toward evil things is certainly not a middle thing; therefore, willing good things and running toward good things is not a middle thing. I believe we can make the following defense regarding the verse: *“So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”* Solomon says in the book of Psalms—for the Song of Ascents is his, from which we shall set forth the words: <margin>Psalm 127:1</margin> *“Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it; unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.”* He is not discouraging us from building, nor teaching us not to stay awake to guard the city within our soul; rather, he is persuading us that things built without God, and those that do not obtain His protection, are built in vain and kept to no purpose. For the Lord of all is rightly inscribed as the Master of the building and the Ruler of the city’s guard. Just as if we were to say, "This building is the work not of the builder, but of God," and "It is the gift not of the guard, but of God over all, that this city suffered nothing from enemies," we would not be speaking wrongly. While it is understood that something was indeed done by the men, the successful achievements are gratefully attributed to God.

<column-break/>

...nor to provide those things to be seen and heard, by which, once seen and heard, the fault of those who were not led to faith by such great things would be proven more heavy and difficult. Therefore, let us inspect this: *“It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”* For they take it this way: If it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, it does not follow from what is within us that we are saved, but from the duty and equipment of Him who fashioned and equipped us such as we are, or from the nod and will of Him who shows mercy when He wishes. From them I first ask this: is willing honorable things a good thing or otherwise? Then, is it worthy of praise or reproach for one who wills to run to attain the end when he hastens toward honorable things? If they answer the latter, it is surely contrary to what is clear and transparent, since the saints will and run, and it is certain they do nothing worthy of reproach. If they say it is honorable to will good things and to run toward honorable things, we will ask how a ruined nature wills good things; which is just as if a bad tree were to bear good fruit, if indeed it is good to will better things. If they answer a third way, that willing good things and running toward good things is a certain "intermediate" thing, and neither upright nor wicked, we will counter: if willing good things and running toward good things is a middle, then its contrary is also a middle, namely willing evil things and running toward evil things. But willing evil things and running toward evil things is not a middle; therefore, neither will willing good things and running toward good things be a middle. Therefore, I think it can be asserted in defense of this passage, *“Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy,”* what Solomon said in the book of Psalms—for the Song of Degrees is his, from which we produce these things: *“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build labor in vain: unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards watches in vain.”* Not that he discourages us from building, or teaches that we should not watch for the defense and custody of the city that is in our soul: but showing that whatever things are built without God, and which are not hedged in by His custody, are built in vain and guarded for nothing, since by right God must be prescribed as the Lord of the building, and the Lord of all as the prefect of the defense and custody of the city. Just as if we were to say, "The building is the work not of the builder, but of God"; "It is the benefit not of the guard, but of the highest God, that this city suffered nothing from enemies"; we would not be in error, since it is understood that something was done by the man, but the head of the work is attributed to God as a sign of a grateful mind.

<summary>Origen argues that human salvation requires both human effort (willing and running) and divine grace, using the metaphor of a house that cannot be built without both a builder and God's blessing. He refutes the idea that human nature is fixed or that free will is irrelevant to the process of salvation.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXI. ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

...be referred to God, the perfecter. Thus, because it is not enough for a man merely to wish in order to reach the goal, nor is it enough for athletes to run in order to carry off the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus (for these things are accomplished through God’s cooperation and help), it is truly said: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* <note>original: "Non volentis, neque currentis, sed Dei est miserantis" — quoting Romans 9:16.</note> Just as in agriculture, it might be said as it is written in Paul: *I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.* <note>original: "Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit, Deus autem dedit incrementum" — 1 Corinthians 3:6.</note> Thus, neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but *God* who gives the increase. We could not piously say that rich and mature fruits are the work of either the farmer or the one who watered, but rather the work of God. In the same way, our perfection does not happen while we do nothing, yet nothing is completed by us alone; rather, God effects that which is greatest. 

To make this more manifest and clear, we shall take an example from the art of navigation. Besides the blowing of the winds, the mildness of the air, and the brightness of the stars—each of which contributes something to the safety of those sailing—what rank and place should the art of steering hold in reaching the desired harbor? Even if, out of modesty, pilots often do not dare to claim they saved the ship themselves, but attribute everything to God as the author, it is not because they did nothing, but because that which is done by Providence is far greater than what is done by art. And in our salvation, how much greater is that which comes from God than that which is in our own power? For this reason, I think the Apostle said: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* 

For if this passage of Paul were to be understood as those people <note>Likely referring to Gnostics or fatalists who denied free will.</note> think, there would be no need for commandments. In vain would Paul himself blame some for having fallen away, or approve others for having conducted themselves well; in vain would he give laws to the Churches; in vain would we embrace better things, and in vain would we run. But Paul does not command these things in vain, nor does he blame or approve in vain; nor do we embrace good things and strive for better things in vain. Therefore, those people interpret this passage incorrectly. Furthermore, if "to will" and "to effect" are from God—and it is on many people's lips that willing and acting are from God—then if we will evilly and act evilly, these things would have happened to us from God. If that were so, we would not be free agents. And again, when we will good things and perform better ones, if both the willing and the doing are from God, we did not do the better things ourselves; rather, we only seemed to, while God gave them. <unclear>Where-</unclear>

...referred to God the perfecter. Thus, since human willing is not sufficient to attain the goal, nor is running like athletes sufficient to receive the prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus (for these things are fulfilled with God assisting), it is well said: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* Just as if it were said regarding agriculture, as it is written: *I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.* So that neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth. And we would not piously say that the fruits becoming full was the work of the farmer, or the work of the one who watered, but the work of God. So also our perfection does not happen without us doing anything, nor is it completed [entirely] by us; but God works the greater part of it. 

And so that you may be more clearly convinced of this, we shall take an example from the art of steering a ship. For with favorable winds, the tempering of the air, and the brightness of the stars all cooperating for the safety of those on board, what degree of credit for the restoration to the harbor should be said to belong to the steering art? Which the pilots themselves, out of piety, often do not dare to admit to having saved the ship, but refer the whole to God—not because they themselves worked nothing, but because that which comes from Providence is many times greater than that from art. And indeed, regarding our salvation, that which is from God is many times greater than that which is from us. Therefore, I think it is said: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* 

For if one must take the meaning as those people assume, the commandments are superfluous, and Paul himself in vain blames some as having fallen away, and accepts some as having succeeded, and gives laws to the churches. And in vain do we give ourselves over to willing the better things and to running. But Paul does not advise these things in vain, nor does he blame some and accept others in vain; nor do we give ourselves over to willing the better things and to hastening toward the things that matter in vain. Therefore, those people have not well understood the passage. Moreover, if the willing and the working are from God, and some say the willing is from God and the working is from God, even if we will evilly and even if we work evilly, these things would belong to us from God. But if this is so, we are not masters of our own will. And again, when willing better things and working at things that matter, since the willing and the working are from God, we have not done the things that matter. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAP. XXI.

And in this we would not be masters of our own will <note>original: *autexousioi* (αὐτεξούσιοι), a technical term for free will or self-determination</note>; and to this it must be said that the Apostle’s wording does not say that willing evil is from God, or that willing good is from God, or likewise that performing better or worse actions is from Him; but rather the general capacity to will, and the general capacity to run. For just as we have from God the fact that we are living creatures and that we are humans, so also we have the general capacity to will, and, as I might say, the general capacity to move. For just as we have the capacity to be living creatures and to move—for instance, to move these members, the hands or the feet—we could not reasonably say that we have from God this specific movement, namely moving to strike or to kill, or to take away what belongs to others; rather, we received the general capacity for movement from God, but we ourselves use that movement for worse or for better things. Thus, the power to act, by which we are living creatures, we have received from God, and the capacity to will we received from the Creator; but we use that will for the most beautiful things or their opposites, and likewise with the power to act. Furthermore, the Apostolic saying will seem to stand against our being masters of our own will, in which he says, bringing an objection against himself: <margin>Rom. 9:18, 19, 20, 21.</margin> *Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. You will say to me then, Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will? But indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why did you make me thus? Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?* For someone will say, if the potter makes from the same lump some vessels for honor and some for dishonor, so God makes some for salvation and others for perdition; and it is not up to us whether we are saved or perish, nor are we masters of our own will. But it must be said to the one who uses these arguments: is it possible to think that the Apostle himself says things that conflict with one another? I do not think anyone would dare to say this. If, therefore, the Apostle does not speak things contrary to himself, how can he, according to such an interpretation, reasonably blame the one who committed fornication in Corinth, or those who fell away and did not repent of the licentiousness and lack of self-control they practiced? And how does he bless as having done well those whom he praises, such as the <margin>2 Tim. 1:16, 17, 18.</margin> household of Onesiphorus, saying: *May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains; but when he was in Rome, he searched for me diligently and found me; may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day.* It is not right for the same Apostle to rebuke the sinner as worthy of blame and to accept the one who has done well as worthy of praise, and then again, as if nothing were in our power, to say—

<column-break/>

—and in this matter we are not of our own accord. Furthermore, the Apostle does not say that willing evil or willing good is from God, nor likewise doing better or worse things, but both to will in a universal sense, and to run in a universal sense. For as we have from God that we are animals and men, so also to will in a universal sense, and to be moved in a universal sense, so to speak. Just as, therefore, although we have from God that we are animals, that we are moved, that we move these or those members, hands or feet, we would not rightly say that we have from God this specific kind of motion, such as being moved to strike or kill, or to snatch the property of others: but we received motion in general from God, yet we use motion for better or for worse things. So also the power of acting, by which we are animals, and the power to will we received from the Maker; but we, as men, use the will for honest things or for the opposite, just as we use the virtue of acting. Then, the word of the Apostle seems to oppose the freedom of our judgment, in which he objects by way of a speech-exception: *Therefore does he have mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens? You will say to me then, Why then does he get angry? For who has resisted his will? Indeed, O man, who are you who responds from the opposite side to God? Does the thing formed say to the potter, Why did you make me thus? Does the potter of the clay not have the power to make from the same clay one vessel for honor, another for ignominy?* For someone will say, if as from the same clay the potter makes some vessels for honor, others for ignominy; so also God makes some for salvation, others for perdition: it is not in us that we are saved or perish, nor are we free. To the one acting thus with us we shall respond: Would he dare to think the Apostle says things fighting against himself? But I think no one would be of such audacity as to say this. If therefore the Apostle does not say things contrary to himself, how in the sense of those people does he justly accuse him who had committed whoredom at Corinth, or those who had sinned, and who had not repented of their lust and intemperance? In what way also does he bless those whom he praises as if they acted rightly, such as the house of Onesiphorus, in these words? *May the Lord give mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chains; but, when he was in Rome, he sought me most diligently and found me: may the Lord give to him, that he may find mercy from the Lord in that day.* Is it not therefore the case that the same Apostle is accustomed to censure the one who sinned as worthy of rebuke, and to approve the one who acted rightly as worthy of praise? And again, as if nothing were in our power, to say—

...to say that the Creator is the cause of one vessel being made for honor and another for dishonor? How would that statement of the Apostle stand: *For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil*? <note>original: "Nos omnes adsistere oportet..."</note> For if those who did evil reached that point because they were created as vessels of dishonor, and those who lived according to the rule of virtue did so because they were prepared for it from the beginning and made into vessels of honor, [judgment would be meaningless]. Furthermore, how does it not conflict—as some think—with the passages we have cited to say the cause of a vessel being honorable or dishonorable does not lie with the Creator, as is said elsewhere: *In a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, and some for dishonor. If anyone, therefore, purifies himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, prepared for every good work.* <note>original: "In magna domo..." quoting 2 Timothy 2:20-21</note> If, therefore, he who purifies himself becomes a vessel for honor, while he who neglects himself in impurity becomes a vessel for dishonor, as far as can be gathered from these words, the Creator is not the cause of it. For the Creator makes vessels of honor and vessels of dishonor, not from the start and origin through foreknowledge <note>The term "foreknowledge" (praenotionem) here refers to God knowing the future without necessarily forcing it to happen.</note>—since He does not prejudge either side because of it—but He makes those who have purified themselves honorable vessels, and conversely, those who have left themselves impure and unclean, vessels of dishonor. Thus, it is not from the primary causes of creation that one becomes for honor and another for dishonor. But if we once admit that there are certain causes older than the vessels of honor and dishonor, what is the absurdity if we move to the topic of the soul? Namely, that the older causes for the loving of Jacob and the hating of Esau existed in Jacob before he was created, and in Esau before he was in Rebecca’s womb? At the same time, it is clearly shown that, as far as the underlying nature is concerned—just as there is one clay for the potter, from which mass vessels for honor and dishonor are made—so, since there is one "matter" of the whole soul before God, and one "lump" (so to speak) of rational substances, He made certain older causes so that some might be for honor and others for dishonor. But if the Apostle’s saying interrupts, *But indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God?* <note>original: "Enimvero, homo, tu quis es..." quoting Romans 9:20</note> it teaches that to him who deals freely with God, who is faithful to Him and lives well, it is not said, *Who are you to answer back to God?* Such a man was Moses; for he spoke, and God answered him with a voice. And just as God answers Moses, so the holy man answers God.

<column-break/>

->**[Right Column: Greek Original]**<-
<margin>2 Corinthians 5:10</margin>
...the cause of the Creator, that one vessel is for honor and the other for dishonor? How [shall it be that] *we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad*? For those who have done bad things would have come to this because they were created as vessels of dishonor; and those who lived according to virtue, because they were prepared for this from the beginning and became vessels of honor, having done what is good. Furthermore, how does it not conflict with what some suppose from the words we set forth, that the vessel is honorable or dishonorable [not] because of the Creator, as is said elsewhere: *In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some for honor, and some for dishonor. If then anyone purifies himself, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and useful to the master, prepared for every good work.* <margin>2 Timothy 2:20, 21</margin> For if he who purifies himself becomes a vessel for honor, and he who overlooks his own lack of purification becomes a vessel for dishonor, as far as these words go, the Creator is in no way the cause. For the Creator makes vessels of honor and vessels of dishonor, not from the beginning according to foreknowledge; since He does not pre-condemn or pre-justify according to it, but [makes] vessels of honor those who purified themselves, and vessels of dishonor those who overlooked themselves in their unpurified state. So that from older causes <note>Origen suggests that the "older causes" are the choices made by souls in a pre-existent state, explaining why God "chooses" some over others.</note> the construction of the vessels for honor and dishonor occurs. And if we once accept that there are certain causes older than the vessel of honor and the vessel of dishonor, what is the absurdity in ascending to the topic of the soul, and saying that older causes for Jacob being loved and Esau being hated existed in Jacob before his embodiment, and in Esau before his conception in the womb of Rebecca? At the same time it is clearly shown that, as far as the underlying nature is concerned, just as one clay lies before the potter, from which lump come the vessels for honor and dishonor; so with one nature of every soul lying before God—one lump, so to speak, of rational existences—He has made certain older causes [the reason] some are for honor and some for dishonor. And if the word of the Apostle takes hold, saying, *But indeed, O man, who are you who answers back to God?* <margin>Romans 9:20</margin> it teaches that he who has boldness toward God, and is faithful and lives well, will not hear, "Who are you who answers back to God?" Such a one was Moses; for Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice; and as God answers Moses, so also the holy man answers God.

Both must be brought together, and one perfect rationale must be rendered from both. Neither is that which is in our power independent of the knowledge of God, nor does the knowledge of God compel us to progress unless we also contribute something toward the good.
