# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXIII.

->Concerning Fate<-

Those who stumble regarding the topic of fate <note>original: "de fato"</note> due to the conjunction of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> with those in the Zodiac, believe that everything happens to those on earth and to every individual human—and perhaps even to irrational animals—according to these movements. Indeed, many who are considered believers have been led astray, wondering whether human affairs are not perhaps driven by necessity, such that they cannot happen otherwise than as the stars effect through their various configurations. For it follows for those who hold these dogmas that they must utterly destroy our free will <note>literally "that which is in our power"</note>. Consequently, praise and blame, and actions that are either acceptable or reprehensible, are also done away with. If this were the case, the established judgment of God vanishes, as do the threats against sinners as those who will be punished, and the honors toward those who have devoted themselves to better things as those who will be blessed; for none of these things would any longer be happening with any reason. 

And if one were to look at the consequences of these dogmas, faith itself will be in vain, and the coming of Christ achieves nothing, as does the entire dispensation of the Law and the Prophets, and the labor of the Apostles to establish the Churches of God through Christ. Unless, of course, according to those who dare such things, Christ himself was subject to the necessity of the movement of the stars when he was born before his ascension, and did and suffered all things not because God and his Father granted him miraculous powers over all things, but because of the stars—a claim which follows from these impious words. It would even follow that those who believe are said to believe in God only because they are led to it by the stars. 

But we would ask them: What was God’s purpose in making such a world? Was it so that men within it should suffer the passions of women, having in no way been the cause of their own licentiousness? Or that others, having taken on the disposition of wild beasts because the motion of the universe made them so—since God so ordered the whole—should give themselves over to the most cruel and utterly inhuman acts, to murders and piracy? And why need we speak of the myriad other things that happen among men and the sins committed by them? Certain people, desiring these "feminine" <note>a derogatory philosophical term for weak or illogical arguments</note> doctrines, release these men from every accusation and attribute the causes of all evil and blameworthy deeds to God. 

If some of them, as if defending God, say that the "Good One" is someone else who is not the source of any of these things, and instead blame the Creator <note>the Demiurge</note> for all such causes, first of all, they will not even then be able to piously demonstrate that he is just. For how could the father of so many evils, according to them, be reasonably dogmatized as just? Secondly, we must examine what they will say: are those who have been alienated <note>likely referring to Gnostic "aliens" to the material world</note> and who are in this life subject to the motion of the stars, or do they experience nothing 

<column-break/>

this topic of fate from the conjunction of the wandering stars with the signs of the Zodiac, they have come to think that everything on earth and to individual men—and perhaps even in brute animals—happens by necessity. But many of those who are considered faithful, distracted by this same error, doubt whether human affairs are contracted into the narrow straits of necessity, unable to happen otherwise than as the diverse positions and figures of the stars perform. By these views, they must fundamentally remove the freedom of the will, praise and blame, and upright or wicked actions. Thus, that terrible judgment of God celebrated in preaching, the threats of punishment intended for the wicked, and the rewards promised to the good with eternal blessedness all vanish; for which of these things could then be done justly? 

And if these people would attend to what follows from that doctrine of theirs, they would notice that faith is vain, the coming of Christ is useless, the administration of the law and the prophets is superfluous, and the labors of the Apostles in establishing the Churches of God through Christ were empty and void. Why should those who dare such things not also say that Christ was born under that necessity of the motion of the stars, and did and suffered all things as if the stars, rather than God—his Father and the Father of all—had given him those wonderful and stupendous virtues? From this nefarious and impious rashness of words, it also follows that the faithful believe only by the force and inducement of the stars. 

But I ask of them: to what end did God make such a world? Was it so that those men who inhabit it should suffer womanly things, yet fall into such a depth of disgrace and obscenity through no fault of their own? Or that others, changed into the habit and character of wild beasts because the fear and rotation of the universe so instituted by God made them such, should devote themselves to the most cruel crimes, furthest removed from humanity, such as slaughter and robbery? Why should I commemorate more concerning the remaining affairs of men and their innumerable sins? The assertors of that "excellent" doctrine free these people from every crime and ascribe the cause of all malfeasance to God. 

If any of them, as if to act as patrons for God, say that there is another who is "Good," who is the principle or author of none of these things, and refer the causes of all evils to the Craftsman <note>the Creator of the physical world</note>, first they will not be able to prove what they wish—that he is just. For how can the author of so many evils, as they think, be rightly considered just? Then, it must be investigated what these people are going to say about themselves: are they subject to the rotation of the stars, or are they free from its command? And do they experience nothing in life—

For if they say they are subject to the stars, it is certainly from the stars that they learned this, and the Creator, through the revolution and order of the universe, would have subjected them to the knowledge of that higher God whom they imagine—which is something they themselves do not want. If they say they are placed outside the laws inscribed and entrusted to the stars by the Creator, then, lest they seem to have denied this without reason, let them more powerfully compel us by showing the distinction between a mind subject to birth and fate, and another mind immune from these. For it is clear to those who know such people that if they are asked for a reason, they can in no way provide one. Furthermore, vows are undertaken and prayers are made in vain. But what need is there for a longer discourse, since we have shown the impiety of this opinion on fate—an opinion worn out by many and rashly trampled upon—and since these things suffice for a rough and sketched explanation of the matter? But how we fell into this while explaining that passage, *Let them be for signs*, must now be recalled: those who have learned the truth about any matter, or were present at the carrying out of the deeds themselves, are accustomed to report them truly and in detail; for they have observed the outcome of those who suffered or the action of those who acted, or they have knowledge of them from the reliability of those who did not cause those things. Nor should it be suggested in this discourse that those who acted or suffered, by telling what they suffered or did, can lead someone who was not present into a knowledge of what was done. If, therefore, he who learns from one who gave no cause to the events that certain things happened or will happen to these or those people, does not see that the one from whom he learned what was done or will happen is in no way the cause of that thing—if he should think that the one who explains these or those past or future deeds has done or will do what he narrates—it is clear that he who judges thus is in error. For the things said are sufficient for a sketch. But let there be excluded from the discourse itself the ability of those who have done or suffered, by relating what they have practiced or suffered, to lead into knowledge of the past one who was not present. Thus, if one were to go deeply into the argument that God foreknows all things, and were to consider the reasons for the impressions of His foreknowledge, he would understand that neither is the one who foreknows entirely the cause of the things foreknown, nor are the things which receive the forms of foreknowledge the cause of the one who foreknows. For God knew each thing that was to happen long before it occurred; and even without the testimony of Scripture, this is clear from the very concept of God, as it honors the dignity of God’s power. But if it is necessary to establish this from the Scriptures as well, the prophecies are full of such examples, such as the story of Susanna; where she speaks thus to God, who knows all things before they come to be: <margin>Susanna verses 42, 43.</margin> *O eternal God, Knower of secrets, who knows all things before they come to be, you know that they have borne false witness against me.* <note>original: "ὁ τῶν κρυπτῶν γνώστης" — Knower of hidden things.</note> And most clearly in the third book of Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings.</note>, both the name of a king, and the name of his reign and his deeds were recorded more than three hundred years before the things prophesied, <margin>1 Kings 12:32.</margin> as follows: *And Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like unto the feast that is in Judah, and he offered upon the altar which was in Bethel, which he had made for the calves which he had made.* Then, after a little: *And, behold, there came a man of God out of Judah by the word of the Lord unto Bethel: and Jeroboam stood by the altar to burn incense. And he cried against the altar* <margin>Ibid. 13:1, 2, 3.</margin> *in the word of the Lord, and said, O altar, altar, thus saith the Lord; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men's bones shall be burnt upon thee. And he gave a sign the same day, saying, This is the sign which the Lord hath spoken; Behold, the altar shall be rent, and the ashes that are upon it shall be poured out.* And a little later it is shown that the altar was indeed rent, <margin>Ibid. verse 5.</margin> and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by the word of the Lord. And in Isaiah, long before the captivity in Babylon (after which captivity Cyrus the King of the Persians later arose, who established the building of the temple that took place in the times of Ezra), <margin>Isaiah 45:1, 2, 3, 4.</margin> these things are prophesied of Cyrus by name: *Thus saith the Lord God to my anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut; I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron: And I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I, the Lord God, which call thee by thy name...*

<column-break/>

...they show that He foreknew what would proceed from that man's malice. Thus, if anyone contemplates and searches more deeply and profoundly into the reasons of divine providence, and into those things in which He has impressed them, he will observe that in no way is the one who foreknew the cause of the events, nor are those things which have received the forms and characters of His foreknowledge [the cause of His knowledge]. Therefore, that God foreknew all future things long before they happen—even if the testimony of Scripture were lacking—is sufficiently seen from the sense and thought of God by anyone who understands the power and majesty of the divine mind. But if this must also be sanctioned by the testimony of the Scriptures, the oracles of the Prophets are full of such examples, such as those words of Susanna, which testify that God knows all things before they happen: *O eternal God, Knower of secrets, who has known all things before they happen, you know that they have spoken false things against me.* And most clearly in the third book of Kings, both the name of the kingdoms, and the name of the king and his deeds were described many years before they happened, which are thus predicted: *And Jeroboam made a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, according to the feast day in the land of Judah, and he went up to the altar which was in Bethel, which he made for the calves, which he had made.* And a few things being interposed: *And, behold, a man of God from Judah was present in the word of the Lord in Bethel, and Jeroboam was standing at his altar to sacrifice: and he cried out at the altar in the word of the Lord, and said, Altar, altar, thus says the Lord, Behold, a son is procreated for the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places, who now sacrifice upon you, and he shall burn the bones of men upon you. And he gave a sign in that day, saying, This is the sign that the Lord has spoken, saying, Behold, the altar is broken, and the fat which is upon it shall be poured out.* And a little after it is signified that the altar was broken and the fat poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God gave in the speech of the Lord. And in Isaiah, who lived long before the Babylonian captivity (to which time Cyrus king of the Persians is posterior, who took care that the temple be restored in the times of Ezra); these things are prophesied of Cyrus by name: *Thus says the Lord God to my anointed Cyrus; whose right hand I have held, that nations may obey him, and I will break the strengths of kings: I will open gates before him, and cities shall not be closed. I will go before you, and I will level mountains; I will shatter bronze gates, and I will break iron bars; and I will give you dark treasures, I will open hidden, unseen things to you; that you may know that I am the Lord God, who calls you by name.*

<summary>Origen argues that God's foreknowledge of future events, such as the reigns of Josiah and Cyrus, does not cause those events to happen, but rather demonstrates His divine majesty. He uses biblical examples of specific names and deeds prophesied centuries in advance to prove that God knows all things before they occur.</summary>

*...the God of Israel. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I will call you by my name and I will embrace you.* <note>Original Latin: "Deus Israel... amplectar te." # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXIII.

...men indeed (for it is far beyond human capacity to be able to truly perceive from the motion of the stars what each person will do or experience), but rather the <term>Powers</term><note>Refers to spiritual beings or angelic forces, often called "Virtues" in the Latin tradition.</note> who must necessarily know these things for many reasons, as we shall show to the best of our ability in what follows. For men, having put together observations, or even from the teaching of the angels who transgressed their own order <margin>The fallen angels</margin> and taught our race on earth certain things about these matters to gain a foothold over us, have come to think that those things from which they believe they receive signs are actually the *causes* of the things which the Word says they only *signify*. Regarding these very matters, we shall immediately discuss them more carefully in summary, as far as we are able.

The following problems are therefore proposed:
1. How, since God has foreknowledge from eternity concerning the actions thought to be performed by each individual, is our **free will** preserved?
2. In what manner are the stars not *productive* of human affairs, but only *signifying* them?
3. That men cannot have an exact knowledge of these things; rather, the signs were set for Powers greater than men.
4. What is the reason for God having made the signs for the knowledge of the Powers? This will be examined fourth.

And so, let us look at the first point, which some of the Greeks <note>Refers to pagan philosophers, likely Epicureans or certain Stoics</note> feared; thinking that things are driven by necessity and that our free will is in no way preserved if God foreknows the future, they dared to adopt an impious doctrine rather than admit a Foreknower—which, as they say, is glorious for God but destroys our free will, and through this, destroys praise and blame, the acceptance of what is pleasing, and the reproach of vice.

For they say: "If God knew from eternity that a certain person would be unjust and commit these specific injustices, and if the knowledge of God is unfailing, then that person will certainly be unjust and commit these injustices. If He foresaw it, it is impossible for him not to act unjustly; and if it is impossible for him not to act unjustly, he is driven by necessity to act unjustly, and it is impossible for him to do anything other than what God knew." If it is impossible for him to do anything else, and since no one is blamed for not doing the impossible, we would be wrong to blame the unjust. From the unjust man and his injustices, they move on to other sins, and then conversely to what are considered right actions; and they say it follows from God having foreknown the future that our free will cannot be preserved.

To these it must be said: that God, applying Himself to the beginning of the creation of the world—since nothing happens without a cause—traverses in His mind each of the things that will be, seeing that: "since this has happened, this follows; if this following thing happens, this other thing follows; and when this exists, that will be"; and so

<column-break/>

...men indeed (for it is beyond human strength to be able to truly perceive from the motion of the stars what each one may do or suffer); but the Powers, whom it is necessary to know these things for many reasons, as we shall show hereafter, as far as possible. But men, concluding from some observations, or from the teaching of the Angels who transgressed their order and taught some of these things for the occupation of the human race, have thought that those things from which they think they receive signs are the causes of those things which the Word of God affirms they signify, but do not effect. Concerning these we shall immediately dispute accurately by way of a summary of the discourse.

These things are therefore proposed to be discussed:
**First**, How, since God has foreknown from eternity what each person would do, the freedom of the will remains.
**Second**, How the stars do not effect human affairs, but only signify them.
**Third**, That men cannot attain an exact knowledge of these things, but these signs were proposed to Virtues superior to man.
**Fourth**, What the cause is why God made signs for the notice of the Powers; this will be the fourth question.

Let us therefore first look at that which some of the Greeks, fearing to admit that human affairs are driven into necessity and that the freedom of the will can by no means stand if God foreknows the future, thought it better to rashly take up an impious doctrine than to cast this aside—which is, as they say, glorious to God, but which takes away free will from man; and thus takes away praise and blame, the approval of virtues, and the disgrace of vices.

They also say: "If from eternity God knew this man would be unjust, and would commit this or that against right and law, and the divine knowledge can neither fail nor err; clearly he will be unjust who is to commit these things against the law, since God foresaw him to be such, nor can it happen that he does not act unjustly. But if he cannot do otherwise than act unjustly, it is necessary that he be unjust, nor can he do otherwise than God foresaw." Wherefore, since no one is blamed if he omits what he cannot do, we rashly rebuke the unjust. But from the unjust and injuries they come to other sins, then conversely to those which are held to be duties of justice: and they say from that divine prescience of the future it follows that the will of man is not free.

To whom it must be answered thus: That God from the beginning of the creation of the world, since nothing happens without a cause, proceeds through individual things in His mind and foresees all future things: if this happens, that will follow; if this which follows occurs, that also will follow; which when it has been, that will then follow; and so to

<summary>Origen addresses the conflict between divine foreknowledge and human free will, arguing that while God foresees all future events as a chain of causes, this does not impose necessity on human actions. He also refutes the idea that stars cause human behavior, suggesting they are merely signs intended for higher spiritual powers.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXIII. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

...to the very end of the progress of things, He knows what is to come: yet for no thing is He the cause of why it so happens. For just as if someone, seeing a person who is reckless through ignorance, and because of that recklessness walking thoughtlessly, should enter upon a slippery path and fall foully, he is by no means the cause of that fall; so it must be understood that God, who foresaw what sort of person each would be, and the causes why he would be such, sees if indeed he will sin, and knows these things if he will act rightly. Yet the foreknowledge <note>Latin: *praenotio*; Greek: *prognosis*</note> of those things which have happened is not the cause; for God does not embrace or take up a man because He foreknew he would sin. Indeed, I shall say something further removed from common human opinion, yet most true: that the future event is the cause of such foreknowledge about itself. For it does not happen because it was foreknown, but because it was going to happen, it was foreknown. But a distinction is needed: for if someone interprets the phrase, *It will altogether be*, in such a way that it is necessary for what was foreknown to happen, we do not grant it. For we shall not say that because it was foreknown that Judas would be a traitor, it was absolutely necessary for Judas to be a traitor. For this reason, in the prophecies concerning Judas, reproaches and censures against him are contained, by which his wicked crime and shame are shown. However, he would nowhere be sprinkled with censure if he had been a traitor by necessity, nor could he have been like the other Apostles. See, then, whether this can be established from the words we shall bring forward: <margin>Psalm 108:12, 16, 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 109.</note></margin> *Let there be none to pity his fatherless children, because he remembered not to show mercy: but persecuted the poor and needy man, and the broken in heart, that he might slay him. He loved cursing, and it shall come unto him; and he delighted not in blessing, and it shall be far from him.* But if someone understands that phrase, *It will altogether be*, and interprets it thus: "These or those things will happen, but they could also have happened otherwise," we admit that as true. For it is impossible for God to lie; but it is possible for Him to understand concerning non-necessary things—things which can both happen and not happen—that they happen or do not happen. But we explain the matter more clearly: if it is possible for Judas to be an Apostle just like Peter, it is also a contingent possibility that God understands concerning Judas that he remain an Apostle just like Peter; or, if it is possible for Judas to be a traitor, it is also possible for God to think concerning him that he will be a traitor. If Judas will be a traitor, God, by His foreknowledge—since two things were predicted which could happen otherwise—when the truth of one of them coincides with him, He will foreknow that Judas will be a traitor. Yet that of which there is foreknowledge could also happen otherwise; and the knowledge of God would say that it is possible for this man to do such a thing, but

<column-break/>

...to the end of things, having traveled through them, He knows what will be; it is not at all the case that for each of the things known, the fact of its being known is the cause of it happening. For just as if someone, seeing a person who is headstrong through ignorance, and because of that headstrongness walking unreflectively on a slippery road, should say that he will slip and fall, he has not become the cause of the slip for that man; so must we conceive of God, who has foreseen what sort of person each will be, and beholds the causes of his being such, and that he will sin, He knows these things, or if he will do right, He knows those. And if one must speak of foreknowledge as the cause of things happening: for God does not [force] those things foreknown to be sinned further. But we shall say something rather paradoxical, yet true: that the future event is the cause of the foreknowledge being of such a kind about it. For it does not happen because it has been known; but because it was going to happen, it has been known. But this requires a distinction: for if someone interprets the "It will altogether be" as meaning that the thing foreknown happens by necessity, we do not yield to him. For we shall not say, since it was foreknown that Judas would become a traitor, that there was every necessity for Judas to be a traitor. For in the prophecies concerning Judas, there are rebukes and accusations of Judas recorded, which make him blameworthy to every believer. But blame would not be attached to him if he were a traitor by necessity, and if it were not possible for him to become like the rest of the apostles. See if these things are not made clear through the sayings we shall set forth, which are as follows: <margin>Psalm 108:12, 16, 17</margin> *Let there be no one to be compassionate to his orphans, because he did not remember to perform mercy; and he persecuted the poor and needy man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death. And he loved a curse, and it shall come to him; and he did not wish for a blessing, and it shall be far from him.* But if someone will explain the "It will altogether be" by saying it signifies this: that these certain things will be, but it was also possible for them to happen otherwise, we agree with this as true. For it is not possible for God to be false; but it is possible for Him to perceive, concerning things that are possible to happen and not to happen, their happening and their not happening. We shall state this more clearly thus: if it is possible for Judas to be an apostle like Peter, it is possible for God to conceive concerning Judas that he remains an apostle like Peter; or, if it is possible for Judas to become a traitor, it is possible for God to think concerning him that he will be a traitor. And if Judas will be a traitor, God, by His foreknowledge of the two aforementioned possibilities, the truth of the matter having converged upon one, He will foreknow by foreknowledge that Judas will be a traitor. But that about which the knowledge is, can also happen otherwise; and the knowledge of God would say that it is possible for this man to do this, but...

<summary>Origen argues that God's foreknowledge of future events, such as Judas's betrayal, does not cause those events to happen nor impose necessity upon them. He asserts that human free will remains intact because the event itself is the cause of the foreknowledge, not the other way around.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXIII.

...and the opposite. Since both options are possible, I know that he will do this specific thing. For it is not as if God said, "it is impossible for this particular man to stumble"—as if he were giving an oracle—or as if he were to say of someone that "it is impossible for this man to be self-controlled." For the power to fly is simply not in a human being at all; but the power to be self-controlled and the power to be licentious both exist within him. Since both powers are present, the man who does not pay attention to words of conversion and instruction gives himself over to the worse path; but the man who seeks the truth and wishes to live according to it gives himself to the better path. One man does not seek the truth because he leans toward pleasure; another examines these things because he is led by common notions <note>The Stoic concept of "prolepsis" or innate ideas shared by all humans</note> and encouraging arguments. Again, one man chooses pleasure—not because he is unable to look it in the face and resist, but because he does not struggle against it; while another man despises it, seeing the ugliness that is often found within it.

That God’s foreknowledge <term>prescience; Greek: prognosis</term> does not impose necessity on the things He has perceived beforehand will be shown by the following, in addition to what has already been said: in many places in Scripture, God commands the prophets to preach repentance <term>Greek: metanoia; a change of mind or heart</term>, without pretending that He does not already know whether those who hear will turn back or remain in their sins. As He says in Jeremiah:

<margin>Jeremiah 26:3</margin>

**Perhaps they will hear and repent.** For God does not say, "Perhaps they will hear and repent" because He is ignorant of whether they will repent or not; rather, He is, as it were, showing the equal balance of their powers through these words. This is so that His foreknowledge, if announced in advance, might not cause the listeners to act in a certain way by introducing the idea of necessity—as if it were not in their power to turn back—and thus the foreknowledge itself would become a cause of their sins. Or again, for those who do not know the good that has been foreknown about them, but who are able to live pleasingly by struggling and resisting wickedness, the foreknowledge might become a cause of relaxation <note>A loss of moral tension or effort</note>. They might not stand firmly against sin if they believed that what was predicted would happen regardless; thus, the foreknowledge of a future good might actually become an obstacle. Therefore, God, who administers all things in the world for our benefit, has reasonably blinded us to the future. For the foreknowledge of it would have drawn us away from the struggle against wickedness; it would have discouraged us—thinking the outcome was already seized—from wrestling against sin, making us fall under its power more quickly. At the same time, if someone were to know through foreknowledge that they would certainly be good, they might become less intense in their struggle for virtue; for there is a need for great vehemence and tension <note>Greek: tonos; a Stoic term for the "tension" of the soul</note> to become honorable and good. But the anticipated knowledge that one will certainly be good...

<column-break/>

...and the contrary. But since he can do either, I know he will do that; for it is not, as if God had said, possible for this man to fly, so an oracle (for example) sent concerning someone will say it is impossible for this man to be temperate: for there is no faculty of flying in man, but the faculty for both temperance and intemperance is in him. Since both faculties are in man, he who does not apply his soul to the words of discipline follows the worse things; but he follows the better who seeks the truth and wishes to live by its rule. But that man does not seek the truth because he inclines toward pleasure: another searches out the truth, led by common notions and exhortation: another obeys pleasure, not because he could not resist it, but because he does not strive: another rejects pleasure when he sees its foulness and disgrace. Wherefore God’s foreknowledge imposes no necessity on those things which He foresaw: which, besides the previous points, shall also be shown by these. God in the Scriptures often commands the Prophets to preach repentance; not that He hides that He foreknew whether those who heard would return, or whether they would remain in their sins; as it is said in Jeremiah, *Perhaps they will hear and they will repent.* For God, not being ignorant whether they would betake themselves to a better fruit or not, says, *Perhaps they will hear and they will repent:* but as if by these words He demonstrates that the faculty for both is equal: and lest His foreknowledge, being made public and announced, should bring ruin to the hearers, and they should think themselves constrained by necessity, as if it were not in themselves to be converted; and that opinion should be, as it were, a cause of sins: nor again to those who are ignorant of the good foreknown of them, though they are able by striving and resisting vices to live with virtue, should the foreknowledge be a cause of remission and negligence, so that they no longer rise up bravely against vices, because that which was predicted would plainly come to pass; and thus foreknowledge would in a way hinder the future good. God therefore, who usefully administers the world, rightly willed us to be blind to future things, the foreknowledge of which would have led us away from the fight and struggle against vices, and would have brought it about that, thinking we had grasped the result, we would not resist sin, and would more quickly be subjected to it: likewise, if someone knew he would be entirely good, he would be made more remiss and languid in that struggle of his toward virtue: for we have need of vehement and sharp study beyond our innate powers, that we may be upright and honest: but the anticipated knowledge of future honesty [would weaken] our exercise...

<summary>Origen argues that God's foreknowledge of the future does not force human actions or destroy free will. He explains that God uses "perhaps" in Scripture to encourage human effort and prevent people from becoming lazy or fatalistic.</summary>
<keywords>free will, foreknowledge, Origen, Philocalia, Jeremiah, repentance, moral struggle, necessity, providence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine providence and human free will, specifically addressing why God keeps the future hidden from us and beginning a critique of astrological determinism.</meta>

# CHAPTER XXIII. Origen’s *Philocalia*. <note>The *Philocalia* is a 4th-century anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>

<margin>Exodus 4:11</margin>
...our [nature] and broke our impulse toward virtue. For this reason, it is useful that we are ignorant of whether we shall be good or evil in the future. And since we have said that God has rendered us blind to future events, see whether we can apply that difficult passage of Exodus to this sentiment: *Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?* <note>original: "Quis fecit surdastrum & surdum, videntem & cæcum? nunquid ego Dominus Deus?"</note> so that He has made the blind and the seeing—seeing as to present things, but blind to the future. As for the part concerning the mute and the deaf, this is not the time to explain it. Truly, we do not doubt that many things which are not within our power provide the cause for many things that are within us; if those things which are not in our power had not existed, I say that those things which are within us would never have come to pass. However, certain things within our power happen as a consequence of those things which preceded them (which were not in our power), though it remains possible that those preceding events could have produced different results from the ones we chose. If anyone desires our free will <term>arbitrium nostrum: the capacity for choice</term> to be entirely disconnected from the universe, so that we choose this or that regardless of what happens to us, he forgets that he is a part of the world, contained within human society and the compass of the universe. Briefly then, as if in a summary of the argument, I believe I have demonstrated that divine providence imposes no necessity upon the things it foreknows.

<margin>N. page 74. line 38.</margin>

But come, let us endeavor to show that the stars in no way cause human affairs, but only signify them. For it is certain that if any configuration of the stars is thought to cause the things that happen to a person (let us allow this for the sake of argument), a configuration occurring today, for instance, cannot be understood to have caused things that happened to another person, or even to others in the past; for every cause is older than its effect. Yet, according to the discipline of those who profess these arts <note>referring to astrologers</note>, human affairs are judged to be predicted by configurations or aspects that are older than the events themselves. For they claim to grasp a certain location, having taken the hour of a person's birth, and they affirm how each of the wandering stars <term>planets</term> corresponds to the position of this part of a sign, or to its specific degrees; and which star of the Zodiac was at the Eastern horizon; which at the West; which at the mid-heaven; and which was at the region opposite to it. <column-break/>

...and weakens the practice of goodness. Therefore, it is for our benefit that we do not know whether we shall be good or evil. Since we said that God blinded us toward the future, we must seek whether we can clarify the literal text of Exodus in this way: *Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?* <note>original Greek: "Τίς ἐποίησε δύσκωφον καὶ κωφὸν, βλέποντα καὶ τυφλόν; οὐκ ἐγὼ Κύριος ὁ Θεός;"</note> so that the "blind and seeing" refers to one who sees present things but is blind to the future. To explain the part about the mute and the deaf is not for the present moment. However, we will also admit that many things within our power have their causes in things not within our power; if those things not within our power had not happened, these specific things within our power would not have been practiced. But these things within our power are practiced as a consequence of those preceding events not within our power, even though it was possible for those same preceding events to result in different actions than those we performed. If anyone seeks for that which is within our power to be released from the whole, so that we do not choose things because of what has happened to us, he has forgotten he is a part of the world, enclosed in the fellowship of men and the surrounding universe. Moderately then, as in an epitome, I think it has been demonstrated that the foreknowledge of God is not a compelling force over all that is foreknown.

Come then, let us also contend regarding the fact that the stars are in no way the makers of human affairs, but are only signs. For it is clear that if a certain configuration of stars were thought to be the maker of what happens to a man (for let this be the question for the present discussion), the configuration occurring today, for example, cannot be thought to have made the things that have already passed for another, or for others; for everything that makes is older than that which is made. But as far as the teachings of those who profess such things go, human affairs are thought to be predicted as being older than the configuration. # ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXIII.

...to have shaped the moment of a certain person's birth; having completed these observations at such a time, they [the astrologers] are accustomed to examine not only future events, but also the past, and the circumstances surrounding the birth itself: details concerning the child who has been born; concerning the father, what sort of man he happens to be, whether rich or poor, whole in body or <term>maimed</term><note>original: σεσινωμένος / læso; referring to physical disability or injury</note>, of better or worse character, possessing nothing or possessing much, and whether his business is grand or meager. Furthermore, they inquire into the details concerning the mother, and concerning older brothers, if there happen to be any. 

Let us, for the present, allow them to assume they can grasp the truth in these matters—though we shall later demonstrate that this is not the case. Let it then be asked of those who suppose that human affairs are <term>necessitated</term><note>original: κατηναγκάσθαι / cogi; the idea that stars force or compel human action, denying free will</note> by the stars: In what way can today’s configuration, being such as it is, have caused things that are older than itself? If this is impossible—inasmuch as the findings regarding older events are not found to be false in time—it is clear that the stars, by their movements in heaven, did not *cause* the past events, even if they are found to be in such a position. 

If this is so, perhaps one who claims they speak the truth, having considered what is said about the future, will say they speak truly not because the stars *cause* events, but only because they *signify* them. But if someone should claim that the stars do not cause the past, but rather that other configurations were the causes of those earlier births, while the current configuration has only *signified* them—revealing the future from the present configuration of a certain person's birth—let him explain the difference in the power of the stars. Let him show why some things are true as if from *causes*, and others only as if from *signs*. 

Failing to show a difference, they might honorably concede that nothing that happens to men is caused by the stars, but as we said before, if anything is signified, it is as if one received the past and future not from the stars, but from the mind of God through a certain prophetic word. Just as we previously demonstrated that God’s foreknowledge of what each person will do does not harm the argument for <term>free will</term><note>original: τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν / liberi arbitrii; literally "that which is up to us"</note>, so too the signs which God appointed for signifying do not impede our free will. Rather, like a book containing the prophecies of the future, the whole heaven, being as it were the **Book of God**, can contain the things to come. 

Therefore, in the *Prayer of Joseph*, what is said by Jacob can be understood in this way: *For I have read in the tablets of heaven whatever shall happen to you and your sons.* And perhaps also the saying, *The heaven shall be rolled up like a book*, declares that the words contained therein, which signify the things to come, are to be fulfilled.

They inquire the same regarding the mother, and regarding the older brothers, if there are any. 

But let it be; for the present let us admit that they have found the logic of that place; which, however, we shall later demonstrate to be otherwise. Let us therefore ask of those who think human affairs are compelled by the stars: How can today's position, being such as it is, have effected older things? Because if that cannot happen, since what was predicted concerning the past is found to be true, it is evident that the stars moved in the heaven in such a way did not *cause* those things which had happened before that positioning of the stars existed. 

If this is so, perhaps he who thinks the truth is predicted by them, weighing those things which are said of the future, will answer that the truth is told by them not because the stars *cause* it, but because they only *signify* it. But if anyone should affirm that the stars do not cause the past, but that other positions were the causes of those births, while the position or aspect which exists now has only *signified* them, and that certain future things are designated by the present position of someone's birth, let him bring forth the distinction: why he can maintain from the stars that these things are understood as if from *causes*, but those others only as if from *signifiers*. 

Where they cannot show this distinction, they will nobly acknowledge that nothing of human affairs is caused by the stars, but in the manner we said before. If, therefore, anyone should accept that the past and future are signified, not as if by the stars, but as if by the divine mind through prophetic speech; just as we demonstrated before, it does nothing against the logic of free will that God knows what each person is going to do: so neither do the signs, which God established for signifying, hinder our freedom, but, like a book which contains the prophecies of the future, the entire heaven, as the book of God, can contain the future. Wherefore in the *Prayer of Joseph* it can be understood in this way what is said by Jacob: *For I have read in the tablets of heaven, whatever things will happen to you and your children:* and perhaps that [verse], *The heaven shall be folded up, like a book,* declares that the words contained in it signifying the future are to be completed.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. [CHAPTER XXIII.

...be known, and if what happens arises from the source where the knowledge is obtained, why should future events be signaled by the stars rather than by the flight of birds? <note>original: "οἰωνῶν" / "avibus" - referring to augury, the practice of interpreting the will of gods from the flight of birds.</note> And why by birds rather than by the entrails of sacrificial victims? Why by these rather than by the flashing paths of shooting stars? For the present, these points shall suffice to refute the idea that the stars are the *active causes* of human affairs. As for the point we previously conceded—for it did not undermine our argument—namely, that men are capable of understanding the celestial formations, the signs, and the things of which they are signs: come now, let us examine if this is actually true.

Those who are experts in these matters <note>The "Genethliaci" or casting of birth charts.</note> claim to know the future by accurately grasping the moment of birth, knowing not only in which twelfth-part <note><term>twelfth-part: the Zodiac signs, which divide the 360-degree celestial circle into twelve 30-degree segments.</term></note> a wandering star <note>A planet.</note> is located, but also in which degree of that twelfth-part, and in which sixtieth <note>Minutes of a degree.</note>; and the more diligent among them even look for the sixtieth of the sixtieth <note>Seconds of a degree.</note>. They say this must be examined for each wandering star in its relation to the fixed stars. Furthermore, they say one must look at the eastern horizon to see not only which sign is upon it, but also the degree, and the sixtieth of the degree, or the second sixtieth.

How then, since an hour contains half of a twelfth-part in general terms, can anyone grasp the sixtieth part without having a technical division of the hours? For example, how could one know that someone was born at the fourth hour, and a half, and a quarter, and an eighth, and a sixteenth, and a thirty-second part of an hour? For they say the meaning changes entirely not just through ignorance of a whole hour, but even of a tiny fraction of it. In the case of twins, who are often born with only the smallest particle of an hour between them, many variations in their life events and circumstances occur. This happens, as the astrologers say, because of the specific positioning of the stars and the specific portion of the sign on the horizon—details which cannot be grasped even by those who believe they have observed the hour. No one can truly say that a thirtieth of an hour intervened between the birth of one twin and the other.

But let it be granted to them that the hour can be grasped. Yet they have also devised a theorem demonstrating that the Zodiac circle, like the wandering stars, moves from west to east one degree every hundred years, and that over a long time this changes the position of the signs. They claim there is one "conceptual" sign <note>The mathematical/astrological sign.</note> and another "physical" constellation <note>The actual stars in the sky.</note>; they say the effects are found not from the physical constellations, but from the conceptual sign—which is hardly possible to comprehend. Nevertheless, let even this be granted: that the conceptual sign can be grasped.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXIII.

Those who investigate these topics more diligently will press you on the question: what is the reason God created these signs in the heaven? To them, we must first reply that we believe in the majesty of God, who has embraced within Himself all knowledge of every single thing that exists; so that not even the most trivial or seemingly minute detail escapes His divinity. This glory encompasses what is, in number, effectively infinite, held within Himself—not by a visible demonstration, but by a faith that is fitting for the unbegotten Mind <note>original: "ἀγεννήτῳ νῷ" / "ingenitæ menti" — referring to God as the uncaused source of all intellect</note> which transcends all nature. 

So that this might be understood through experience by those beings greater than man, and by holy souls who have been loosed and freed from the bonds of the body, God created in the heaven—as if they were letters and characters formed by the revolution of the celestial spheres—signs for those who are taught and those to be taught to read the signs of God. Nor is it a wonder that God has done certain things to clearly demonstrate His power to the blessed, since the 

<margin>Exodus 9:16</margin>
Scripture says to Pharaoh: *For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.* For if Pharaoh was preserved to declare the power of God and so that His name might be preached in all the earth, consider how great a declaration of God’s power the celestial signs contain, since all things from the first age until the consummation of the world are impressed and inscribed in the heaven, which is a book worthy of God. 

Secondly, I conjecture that certain signs are arranged for those Powers <note>term: "Virtutibus" / "δυνάμεσιν" — referring to angelic or spiritual hierarchies that govern the world</note> by which human affairs are managed, so that they may know some things only, and perform others. Just as in our own sacred books, some things are written so that we may know them—such as the creation of the world and other mysteries—while others are written so that, knowing them, we may act, such as the commandments and mandates of God. Therefore, it is possible that the celestial letters, which angels and divine powers know well how to read, contain some things to be read by the angels and ministers of God so that they may rejoice in the knowledge; and other things so that they may receive them as commands and carry them out. 

We shall not be in error if we say that the heaven and the stars contain something analogous to the Law. If, however, worse powers <note>note: Origen refers here to fallen angels or demons</note> and other agencies distinct from man perform certain things from among those foreknown and signified in heaven, it is not necessary that they are prompted by the divine letters to do what they strive to do. Rather, just as men who commit an injustice do not do so because they have learned that God foreknew this person would be wronged by them, but rush into the injustice out of their own wickedness; so too the Powers opposed to God, having foreknown the malice of men who intend evil, fulfill that purpose by their own choice. The holy angels, however, the ministers...

<column-break/>

...will press you, those who investigate the passages of Scripture more accurately, as to what the cause is for which God made these signs in heaven. To whom it must first be answered, that we believe the greatness of the divine mind comprehends in itself all knowledge of individual things; so that not even the smallest things, and those which are weighed as nothing, can be hidden from His divinity: which shows exceedingly that He comprehends in Himself things almost infinite in number, not by a clear demonstration, but by faith, which is appropriate to the unbegotten mind that precedes all nature. 

So that this might be understood by experience by those who are greater than man, and by holy minds released and free from the bond of the body, God made in heaven, as it were, letters and characters through the conversion of the celestial orbs, where both the learned and those to be taught might read the signs of God. Nor truly is it to be wondered at, that God has done certain things to show Himself to the blessed, when the Scripture says to Pharaoh: *For this reason I have raised you up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name may be spread abroad in all the earth.* For if Pharaoh was preserved so that the power of God might be declared, and His name preached in all the earth, notice how great a declaration of God the celestial signs comprehend, since from the first age to the consummation of the century all things are impressed and inscribed in the heaven, the worthy book of God. 

Next, I conjecture that in those Powers by which human affairs are ruled, certain signs are inherent, so that they may know some things only, and effect others: just as in our sacred books certain things are written that we may know, such as the workmanship of the world and other mysteries; some that we may keep and do, such as the precepts and mandates of God. Therefore, it can happen that the celestial letters, which angels and divine powers can easily read, contain some things to be read by angels and ministers of God, so that they may rejoice in the knowledge of them; others so that they may receive mandates and carry them out. 

Nor have we spoken beside the point in saying the heaven and stars contain something similar to the law: but if worse powers, and others different from man, should do certain things from those foreknown and expressed and designated in heaven, there is no necessity that they, being warned by the divine letters, do what they labor at: but just as men doing an injury, not knowing that God foreknew this person would be affected by an injury from them, do the injury through their own wickedness; so the Powers opposed to God, who have foreknown the malice of men thinking of crimes, perfect it by their own and most foul will. But the holy angels, the ministers...

# CHAPTER XXIII. Origen’s *Philocalia*.

the ministers of the spirit, and those sent out for ministry <note>original: "ministri spiritus, & in ministerium emissi"</note>, certainly as if receiving commands from the law of God, perform better things rightly and in order, when and how and as much as is necessary. For it would be absurd for those who are divine to come to something by mere chance and not by a definite purpose—for example, to minister to Abraham and Isaac, to deliver Jacob from danger, or to be present with the spirit of this or that Prophet. Therefore, so that they do not do this by lot or by accident, they read the book of God; and thus they perform what is in the commands. But we, as we said before, do what we do by our own counsel and will, and likewise the opposing powers <note>demonic forces</note> who act against us; we act with a depraved and corrupt will when we sin, but with an educated and intelligent one—though not without the help of Angels and divine writings and the ministers of deeds—when we do things pleasing and acceptable to God. # THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXIV.

...of men, that the stars do not hold a good position for some and a bad one for others at every hour. For that circle <note>The zodiac or celestial sphere.</note> is composed of equal parts and is multifaceted, possessing infinite pretexts for interpretation, from which anyone can say whatever they wish. For just as with obscure dreams, we sometimes understand nothing, but once the events have occurred, we seem to bring forth a most fitting interpretation; so too the mathematical discipline <note>original: "μαθήμα" / "Mathematicorum disciplina" — here referring specifically to astrology, often called 'the mathematics' in antiquity.</note> can declare nothing clearly to us regarding the outcomes beforehand. But after the result, the cause appears manifest. Indeed, those who predict often stumble, and after the outcome they blame themselves, saying, "This was the factor that caused it, and we did not see it." 

Now, the fact that even the most skillful stumble happens because they do not know—as I said yesterday—which things are absolutely the causes of a birth <note>original: "γενέσεως" / "ortûs" — referring to the 'genesis' or horoscope of an individual.</note> and which are not, and which things will certainly produce joy, or which will certainly produce variety. But the reason is clear to us who have learned the mystery: because we possess free reason, and sometimes when we hasten to restrain a particular impulse, we triumph. But the astrologers, being ignorant of this very mystery, pronounce judgment on every choice as if it were a fixed starting point; when they stumble, they invent "climacterics" <note>term: climacterics — critical periods or 'turning points' in a life, used by astrologers to explain away failed predictions.</note> to cast our free choice into obscurity, as we demonstrated yesterday. Now, if you have anything to say in response to these things, speak. And having sworn an oath, he replied: "Nothing is truer than the things you have said."

### Concerning matter: that it is not uncreated, nor the cause of evils.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

### From the seventh book of the Gospel Preparation by Eusebius.

That it is impossible for two uncreated things to exist at the same time, I do not think you are ignorant. But if you especially think to grasp this, add this to the argument: that one of two things must necessarily be said—either that God is separate from matter, or conversely, that He is entirely inseparable from it. If, then, someone wishes to say He is united with it, he will be speaking of a single uncreated thing; for each of these will be a part of the other. But things that are parts of one another will not be two uncreated things, just as different parts divided into many pieces are not many uncreated things. Rather, as reason demands, we say that man is a single living being of many parts created by God; so it is necessary, if God is not separate from matter, to speak of one uncreated thing. But if He is separate by nature, it is necessary that there be...

<column-break/>

...of men, not in every hour do these stars have a good position and those a bad one: for that circle is equal in its parts and varied, and has infinite handles for lying; whence anyone can feign whatever he wishes. For just as we understand nothing of tangled and doubtful dreams, but, when they have happened, we are accustomed to bring an most apt exposition: so the discipline of the Mathematicians, before anything has happened, can declare nothing clearly to us: but when the thing has happened, then the cause of the event appears manifest: and so frequently, those who predict err and slip, and after the event they themselves rebuke themselves, and say, "That thing had effected the matter, and we did not know it." Therefore that slip and error of the most expert is from this, that they are ignorant, as I said yesterday, which things are altogether the causes of origin and birth, and which are not altogether, and which things we altogether desire to do, but do not altogether do: because this cause is clear to us who have learned the mystery: because since we have the free faculty of reason, when we have sometimes decided to restrain it, we have conquered. But the Astrologers, to whom that mystery is unknown, pronouncing immediately concerning every counsel, have often, having slipped, devised "steps" <note>original: "gradus" — referring again to the climacteric degrees or stages in astrology.</note>, leading the free will of man into ignorance, as we demonstrated yesterday. But, if you have anything which you may respond to these things, come. And having sworn he responded, "Nothing is truer than those things which you have said."

# CHAPTER XXIV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.
## <note>The *Philocalia* is a 4th-century anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>

->Between two things, there must be something intermediate; this demonstrates their separation. For nothing can be understood as separate from another unless a third thing intervenes to cause that separation. This holds true not only for two things, but for many. For the same logic we apply to two <term>uncreated beings</term> <note>original: *ingenitis* / ἀγεννήτων; referring to things that have no beginning or cause, like God</note> must necessarily be accepted if three uncreated beings were proposed. I would ask of these: are they placed apart from one another, or are they joined together? Whoever answers the latter will hear the same rebuttal we gave before; but if they are separate, they cannot deny the existence of a third thing that separates them.<-

->If someone takes another path to speak consistently and appropriately about uncreated things—affirming that God is not separate from matter, nor again that both are joined like parts, but rather that God is in matter as if in a place, or likewise that matter is in God—let him hear what follows. For if we say matter is the "place" of God, we must necessarily say he is circumscribed <note>limited or enclosed within a boundary</note> and existed even before matter. But he would be carried along inordinately and by chance just like matter; he would neither stand firm nor remain within himself, since that in which he exists is carried here and there, in one way and then another. Furthermore, one would have to admit that God existed in inferior things. If matter was once raw and unformed, and he adorned it when he wished to change it for the better, then certainly God was in the midst of uncomposed things before the world began.<-

->But from those who hold these views, I would rightfully ask: did God fill all of matter, or was he in some specific part of it? For if someone says God was in some part of matter, he says God is much smaller than matter, if a mere part of it contained the whole of God. But if he says God was in all of matter, let him explain how he fashioned it: for they must devise either a certain "contraction" of God so that he might create that from which he had withdrawn, or say that he created himself along with matter, since he had no place to which he could withdraw.<-

->But if someone should say that matter was in God, it must likewise be asked: was it in him as if he were divided within himself—just as the genera of living creatures are in the air, while the air is divided and distributed to receive those things within it—or was it as if in a place, the way water is in the earth? For if it is as in the air, it necessarily follows that God is divisible. But if it is as water in the earth, and matter was inordinate, uncomposed, and also evil, it follows that God is the "place" of uncomposed and evil things. This seems to me a dreadful and ominous statement, and no less dangerous. For you wish matter to exist so that you do not have to call God the "maker of evils";<-

<column-break/>

->...there must be something intermediate between both; which shows their separation. For it is impossible to seek the distance of one thing from another unless there is a third thing by which the distance of each occurs. This remains equal not only for two, but even if there are more. For the argument we spoke of regarding two uncreated beings must of necessity proceed similarly if three uncreated beings were granted. For we shall ask concerning these whether they are separated from one another, or if again each is united to its neighbor. For if one wishes to say they are united, he will hear the same as the first argument; but if again they are separated, he must say by necessity that the things separating them have a substance. But if someone should speak a third argument, speaking fittingly about uncreated things, saying that God is not separated from matter, nor again united as parts; but either God is in matter as in a place, or matter is in God, let him hear the consequence: that if we [place] God in matter, it is necessary to say he is both contained and circumscribed by matter. Furthermore, it is necessary that he is carried about inordinately just like matter, and does not stand, nor remain by himself, because that in which he is is carried now one way, now another. In addition to these, it is necessary to say that God has been in worse things. For if matter was once unadorned, and he adorned it, choosing to turn it toward the better, there was a time when God was also in unadorned things.<-

->Rightly would I also ask this argument: did God fill the matter, or was he in some part of the matter? For if one wishes to say God was in some part of the matter, he says God is much smaller than the matter, if a part of it contained him whole. But if he says [God was] in all the matter, let him tell how he fashioned this; for it is necessary to say either that God contracted himself to fashion that from which he withdrew, or that he fashioned himself together with the matter, having no place of withdrawal. But if someone says that matter is in God, it must be examined similarly: whether it is as if he were divided in himself, and just as living things are in the air, it is necessary for him to be divided and partitioned for the reception of the things becoming in him; or as in a place, like water in the earth? For if we say as in the air, it is necessary to say God is divisible; but if like water in the earth, and matter was inordinate and unadorned, and in addition to these, evils are present; it is necessary to say God is the place of unadorned things and of evils; which does not seem to me to be of good omen, and is rather dangerous. For you want matter to exist so that you do not call God the maker of evils; and choosing to flee this, you [make] him the receiver of evils...<-

->...and while you avoid that, [you make him] the seat and conception of evils.<-

If you had said that you supposed matter to be an uncreated thing among existing beings, I would have needed to use many arguments to demonstrate the impossibility of it existing in such a way. But since you stated that the origin of evil was the cause of such a suspicion, I think it best to proceed to this specific examination. For when the argument becomes clear to me—the manner in which you say God is not the cause of evil by assuming He created from matter—understand that such a suspicion is being dismantled. 

Do you say, then, that matter without quality <note>Greek: *apoios hyle*; matter lacking any defining characteristics or properties</note> co-existed with God, and from this He fashioned the creation of this world? 

"So it seems to me." 

If matter happened to be without quality, and the world was made by God, and qualities exist in the world, then has God become the creator of these qualities? 

"That is so." 

But since I heard you say earlier that it is impossible for something to come into being from things that do not exist, answer my question: Does it seem to you that the qualities of the world are made from pre-existing qualities? And are they something different from the substances <note>Greek: *ousiai*; the underlying "stuff" or essence of a thing</note> themselves? 

"That is so." 

If, therefore, God fashioned qualities neither from pre-existing qualities nor from the substances (since they are not substances themselves), it is necessary to say that they were made by God from things that did not exist. This is why you seemed to me to be speaking in vain when you said it was impossible to think that anything was made by God from nothing. 

But the argument against you holds thus: for even among ourselves, we observe men making certain qualities from things that do not exist, even if they seem most especially to be making them in something. Let us take an example from architecture: for they do not make cities out of cities, nor a temple likewise out of temples. If you think that because substances are underlying, they do not make these things out of nothing, you are mistaken in your reasoning. For it is not the substance that makes the city or the temple, but the art <note>Greek: *techne*; craft, skill, or applied knowledge</note> related to the substance. And this art does not come from some pre-existing art within the substances; rather, it comes into being from that which was not in them. 

You will likely answer my argument by saying that the craftsman makes the art in the substance out of the art which he possesses. To this I say that he does not seem to "possess" it in that way, because even in the man, it does not come from some pre-existing art. For it is not possible for the art to give anything of itself while existing on its own; for it is one of the accidents <note>term: *accidents* (Greek: *symbebekota*); properties that can change without destroying the essence of the subject, like a man learning a skill</note>, and of those things which only receive existence when they come to be in a substance. For a man can exist without the art of building, but the art will not exist unless there is first a man. Hence, it is necessary to say that arts are naturally born among men from things that did not exist. 

If, therefore, we have shown this to be the case among men, why was it not also fitting to affirm that God...

<column-break/>

...the world itself you call. If, therefore, you had said that you considered matter to be unbegotten from existing things, I would have demonstrated with more words that it could not exist so; but because you said the birth of evils was the cause of this opinion, for that reason I descend into this dispute. For when it has been perceived by me in what way evils exist, and that it is impossible for God not to be called the cause of evils if He is subject to matter itself, this suspicion seems to me must be removed. 

Do you say, therefore, that matter void of quality existed with God, from which the Architect fashioned the workmanship of this world? 

"I judge it so." 

If, therefore, matter was void of quality, and the world was made by God, and there are qualities in the world; did God make the qualities? 

"It is so." 

But since I heard from you that nothing can exist from things which are not; respond to those things which I propose. Does it also seem to you that the qualities of the world are not made from underlying qualities; and that they are something other than the substances? 

"I think so." 

If the Creator did not fabricate qualities from underlying qualities, nor from substances (because they themselves are not substances), it is necessary to say they were made by God from those things which are not. Wherefore you seemed to me to speak in vain, that no one could think anything was effected by God from those things which were not. 

And let these things be so disputed: for we ourselves daily see men making some things from those which are not; even if they seem to make something in some thing most especially. Let us repeat the example from architects: for these make cities, but not from cities; also temples, but not from temples. If truly from this, that substances are subject to them, you think they make these things from things which are not, you are surely in error; for it is not the substance which makes the city, or the temples, but the art which is in the substance. Moreover, art does not come from some underlying art in the substances; but from that which is not in them. 

But you seem likely to meet my reason thus: that the craftsman, from that art which he has, makes that art which is in the substance. To that, however, I seem to be able to respond thus: that even in man it does not come from any underlying art. For it cannot happen that the art, subsisting in itself, gives art: for that is of the accidents, and of those things which then, when they have been in a substance, receive that they may be: for a man will be without architecture, but likewise this will not be unless there was first a man: whence it is necessary to say that arts were born among men from things which were not. 

If therefore we have demonstrated that this is so in men, why was it not also fitting to affirm that God...

# CHAPTER XXIV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

->Xxx<-
<note>This is a signature mark for the bookbinder.</note>

Could God not only make qualities out of things that did not exist, but also substances? For when it appears possible for something to be made from what is not, the same is clearly demonstrated regarding substances. But since your mind impels you to inquire about the origin of evil, I shall enter upon this discussion; and I will ask you a few questions: do you think evils are substances, or qualities of substances? 

**I think they are qualities.** 

But was matter void of qualities and formless? 

**So I previously established.** 

If, therefore, evils are qualities of substances, and matter was devoid of qualities, yet you said God was the author of qualities, then God will also be the author of evils. Since, therefore, we cannot maintain that God is not the author of evils even in this way—if we join matter to Him as a co-cause—come, begin, if you have anything to oppose to these points. For if our dispute were merely contentious, I would not think we should define evil anew; but since we investigate these things for the sake of friendship and helping our neighbor, I determine that the matter must be defined from the very beginning. And indeed, I think my own mind, my zeal for learning, and my method of disputing have long been known to you: that I do not wish to seek victory from a plausible lie, but have it as my purpose that the truth may shine forth from accurate inquiry. I have clearly perceived that you have the same mind; therefore, use whatever method you confidently hope can attain the truth. For by using a more excellent and better way, you will not only help yourself, but also me in those things which I do not know. 

**You seem to have clearly demonstrated to me that evils are certain substances, for I do not see them existing outside of substances.** 

But, look here! Since you say evils are substances, let us indeed investigate the definition of "substance" <term>substantia: the underlying essence or "stuff" of a thing</term>. Does a substance seem to you to be a certain bodily composition? 

**It seems so.** 

And does a bodily substance exist in itself, needing nothing else by whose addition it has its being? 

**That is so.** 

Do evils seem to you to be the result of some action? 

**They seem so.** 

But actions exist only when the one who acts is present? 

**Clearly.** 

If, therefore, the one who acts is absent, that which he does will never exist? 

**Never.** 

Therefore, if a substance is a certain bodily composition, and it does not need anything in which to exist to receive its being, but evils are the actions of someone, and actions need something in which to exist to receive their being, then evils will not be substances. But if evils are substances, and murder is an evil, then murder will be a substance. Yet murder is the action of someone; therefore, murder will not be a substance. If, however, you wish the *agents* to be the substances, I certainly agree with you—as the man who commits the murder is the author; for by what rea—

Could one say God is able to make not only qualities out of non-beings, but also substances? For the possibility of showing that something comes from non-beings demonstrates that substances are also thus. But since you have a desire to seek concerning the generation of evils, we shall come to this argument; and I wish to ask you briefly, do evils seem to you to be substances, or qualities of substances? 

**It seems to me I should say qualities of substances.** 

And was matter without quality and without form? 

**That is how you stated the argument when you received it.** 

Therefore, if evils are qualities of substances, and matter is without quality, and you said God was the maker of qualities, God will also be the creator of evils. Since, then, it is not even thus possible to say God is blameless for evils if one is persuaded to attach matter to Him, it seems to me: if you have anything to say against these things, begin the argument. For if our inquiry were happening out of rivalry, I would not ask to define evil a second time; but since we make the examination of arguments for the sake of friendship rather, and for the benefit of our neighbor, I ask to define these things from the beginning. I think my own purpose and my diligence in arguments has often been made manifest to you, that I do not wish to win by speaking persuasively; but I wish the truth to be cross-examined and accurately investigated. And I know clearly that you are so disposed; wherefore, use whatever way you think you can find the truth, being in no way put out of countenance; for you will not only benefit yourself by using the better way, but certainly also me concerning the things I am ignorant of. 

**You seem to me to clearly present that evils are also certain substances, for I see them existing within substances.** 

Since then, my friend, you say that evils are also substances, it is necessary to examine the definition of substance. Does substance seem to you to be a certain bodily composition? 

**It seems so.** 

And does the bodily composition exist itself by itself, or needing something in which to come to be to receive its being? 

**That is how it is.** 

And do evils seem to you to be of a certain energy <term>energeia: action or operation</term>? 

**So it appears to me.** 

And do energies receive their being then, whenever the one energizing is present? 

**That is how it is.** 

And if the one energizing is not there, will there ever be an energy at all? 

**There will not.** 

Therefore, if substance is a certain bodily composition, and the bodily composition does not need something in which to come to be to receive its being, but evils are energies of someone, and energies need something in which to come to be to receive their being, evils will not be substances. But if evils are substances, and murder is an evil, murder will be a substance; but murder is the energy of someone; therefore murder will not be a substance.
