# ORIGEN’S PHILOCALIA. CHAPTER XXIV.

<column-break/>

...insofar as he is a man, he is a **substance** <note>original: *ousia* / *substantia*; the underlying reality of a thing</note>; but the murder which he commits is not a substance, but rather an action of a substance. We call a man "evil" at one time because of a murder, and at another time "good" because of a good deed. These names are attached to the substance from its **accidents** <note>original: *symbebekota* / *accidentia*; non-essential properties that can change without destroying the thing itself</note>, which are not the substance itself. For murder is not a substance, nor is adultery, nor any similar evil. But just as a "Grammarian" is named from the art of Grammar, a "Rhetorician" from Rhetoric, and a "Physician" from Medicine—though the substance of the person is neither Medicine, nor Rhetoric, nor Grammar, but receives its title from the things that happen to it—so it seems to me that the substance receives its name from those things thought to be evil, though it is none of them.

And consider likewise if you imagine in your mind some other author of evils for men: even he, insofar as he acts in these matters and undertakes to do evil, is himself "evil" based on what he does. For he is called evil because he is the author of evils; but the things a person does are not the person himself, but are his actions, from which he receives the name of being "evil." For if we were to say that he *is* the things he does—and he commits murders, adulteries, thefts, and similar outrages—then he himself would be those things. If he is those things, and those things have a form and state only when they are being done, and cease to exist when they are not being done, and are done by men: then men would be the authors or causes of why they exist or do not exist. But if you call these his actions, he is evil because of what he does, not because of the things that make up his substance.

We have said that "evil" is spoken of from the accidents of a substance, which are not the substance itself, just as a Physician is named from Medicine. If he begins to be evil from the things he does, then he began to be evil, and these evils also began to be. If this is true, then evils are not without a beginning, nor are they uncreated, since you say they have arisen from him.

You seem to me, my friend, to have completed one part of the argument sufficiently; for from the premises you assumed, you appeared to conclude clearly. For in truth, if **matter** <note>original: *hyle* / *materia*</note> was devoid of quality, and God is the maker of qualities, and evils are qualities, then God would be the author of evils. This was rightly said in response to that person. But to me, it does not seem true to say that matter is devoid of quality; for no substance can be said to be devoid of quality. By the very fact that it is called "devoid of quality," its quality is declared, and the nature of the matter is described, which is itself a type of quality. Therefore, if it is not a trouble, weave the speech again: for to me, qualities...

# CHAPTER XXIV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

## [Page 87]

...matter seems to possess qualities without a beginning; likewise, I say that evil things flow from that flux, so that God is not the author of evils, but matter is the cause of all these things. I approve of that eagerness of your mind, my friend, and I praise your zeal in disputing: and indeed it befits anyone desirous of learning not to assent immediately, lightly and rashly, to those things which are said, but to weigh them diligently and accurately. For even if the one who inquires defines a matter otherwise than is right, and thereby provides a handle for the other to conclude whatever he wishes, he will not therefore persuade the listener; but, if something seems able to be said correctly, the one present will say it. For it will be one of two things: either, when he has fully heard that toward which he seems to incline, he will gather fruit, or he will prove that the one arguing with him has spoken falsely. 

But it does not seem to me that you have correctly said that matter primarily and without a beginning possesses qualities: for if it is so, of what thing, pray, is God the author? For if we say he is the author of the substance, we were saying this existed before; but if of the qualities, we maintain those also existed. Therefore, if substance and qualities are already granted, what is the point of calling God the author? But, lest I seem to assume this without reason, come, tell me: In what way do you say God is the "Artisan" <note>Latin: *opificem*; Greek: *δημιουργὸν* (demiurge). A term for God as a master-craftsman who shapes pre-existing material.</note>? Is it because he reduced the substances which were there so that they were no longer what they were, but rather became others? Or because he preserved those substances which had been there before, but changed their qualities? 

I do not think any change of substances was made, for that seems to me an absurd thing to say; but I say a certain conversion of qualities was made, and according to that, I judge God to be the Artisan. Just as a house is commonly said to be made from stones—though no one would say the stones no longer remain stones in their substance when they have become a house; for I say the house was made by the quality of the composition, the prior quality of the stones having been changed—so I think that God, while the substance remained, made a certain conversion of its qualities, and according to that, I say the origin of this world is from God. 

Since, therefore, you say a certain conversion of qualities was made by God, answer these few things which I ask. Tell me also: Do evil qualities seem to you to be of the substances? 
—Entirely. 
—Did these qualities exist in matter previously, or did they have a beginning of existence? 
—I say these qualities were always with matter without a beginning. 
—Do you not say that God made a certain conversion of the qualities? 
—I do. 
—Was it then for the better or for the worse? 
—For the better, certainly. 
—Therefore, if the qualities of matter...

<column-break/>

...seems to have qualities without beginning; for in this way I say that evil things are from its very confluence, so that God may be blameless of evils, and matter may be the cause of all these things. I accept your readiness, O friend, and I praise the diligence in your words; for it truly befits each of those fond of learning not to agree simply, nor as it happens, to the things being said, but to make an accurate examination of the arguments. For even if the questioner, having defined something contrary to reason, provides a starting point for the one conversing to conclude as he wishes, he will not by this persuade the listener; but, if something seems possible to be said well, he will say this while present. For it will be one of two things: either, having moved what he seems to move and having heard it fully, he will be benefited, or he will refute the one conversing as saying something not true. 

But you do not seem to me to have spoken as is necessary in saying that matter has qualities from above <note>original: *ἄνωθεν* (anothen), meaning from the beginning or from a higher source.</note>. For if this is so, of what will God be the creator? For if of the essence <note>original: *οὐσίας* (ousias), the fundamental "being" or substance of a thing.</note>, we would say that we already mentioned this; or if again of the qualities, we say these also exist. Therefore, since essence exists and qualities exist, it seems to me superfluous to call God the Creator. But so that I do not seem to construct an argument for myself, answer me as I ask: In what way do you call God the Creator? Is it because he turned the essences so that they no longer exist as they once were, but others came to be in their place? Or that he guarded those essences which they were even before, but turned their qualities? 

It seems to me that a change [of essence] has not occurred, for indeed it appears absurd to say this; but I say a certain turning of the qualities has occurred, according to which I call God the Creator. Just as if someone says to you that a house has been made of stones, of which it is possible to say that they are no longer stones in their essence—for we can no longer [call them] stones—but we say the house has come to be by the quality of the arrangement, the former quality of the stones clearly having been turned. So it seems to me that God also, while the essence existed, made a certain turning of its qualities, according to which we say this world has come to be by nature from God. 

Since then you say a certain turning of the qualities has been made by God, listen to me as I wish to inquire briefly. Tell me likewise, if it also seems to you that evil things are qualities of the essences? 
—It seems so. 
—And were these qualities in matter from the beginning, or did they have a beginning of being? 
—I say these qualities were with matter without beginning. 
—And do you not say that God made a certain turning of the qualities? 
—This indeed I say. 
—Was it then toward the better, or toward the worse? 
—It seems to me [right] to say toward the better. 
—[Then consider] that: if the qualities of matter are evil, and he turned its qualities toward the better...

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXIV.

If God turned <note>original: Ἔστρεψεν / convertit. This refers to the act of shaping or transforming primordial matter.</note> [matter], it is necessary to ask from where evils come. If the qualities remained exactly as they were by nature, or if there were no evil qualities previously, but you say that because the primary qualities were changed by God, such qualities came to exist in relation to matter, then God will be the cause of evils, having turned qualities that were not evil into being evil. Or does it not seem to you that God turned the evil qualities toward the better? Do you say that he turned only the remaining and indifferent qualities for the sake of order? This is how I held it from the beginning. How then do you say he left the qualities of the wicked as they were? Was it because he was able to remove them but did not wish to, or because he did not have the power? For if you say he was able but did not wish to, it is necessary to say he is the cause of these things; because, though able to make them not be evil, he permitted them to remain as they were—especially when he began to fashion the matter. For if he had no care for matter at all, he would not be the cause of those things he allowed to remain; but since he fashions part of it and leaves part of it as it is, though able to turn that also toward the better, he seems to me to deserve to be blamed for leaving a part of the matter wicked, to the destruction of the part he did fashion. Furthermore, it seems to me that the greatest injustice has been done in this part; I mean in that part of matter which he constructed, which now perceives evils. For if one examines the facts accurately, he will find the wicked matter in a worse state now than in its previous disorder. For before it was ordered, it had the benefit of not even perceiving evils; but now every one of its parts receives a perception of evils. Take the example of a human being: before he is formed and becomes a living creature by the art of the Creator, he had it from nature to perceive nothing of evils; but from the moment he is made a man by God, he also receives the perception of approaching evil. And this, which you say happened to matter by God for its benefit, is found rather to have resulted in its detriment. But if you say that evils have not ceased because God was not able to remove them, you say that God is by nature powerless. This powerlessness would be either because he is weak by nature, or because he is overcome and enslaved by fear of someone more powerful. # CHAPTER XXIV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

...which are able to overcome God, as you were just saying? <note>The speaker is challenging the idea that matter could have a power independent of or equal to God.</note> Especially since we define "God" as that which holds power over all things. But I would like to ask you a few questions about matter itself. Come now, answer me: was matter **simple** or **composite**? <note>In ancient philosophy, "simple" means made of one single substance, while "composite" means made of multiple parts mixed together.</note> For the diversity of things that have been made leads me to this inquiry. If matter was simple and of one single form, but the world is composite and constituted of diverse substances and mixtures—for the name "composite" indicates a certain mixing of simple things—then you must admit that if you call matter composite, it was composed of certain simple elements. If it is composed of simple elements, those simple elements must have existed at some point by themselves and alone, from which matter was then composed; thus, matter is shown to be *created* or *generated*. For if matter is composite, and composite things consist of simple ones, there was once a time when matter did not exist—that is, before the simple elements came together. If there was a time when matter did not exist, and yet there was never a time when that which is **uncreated** <note>original Latin: *ingenitum*; Greek: *ἀγέννητον*. This refers to something that has no beginning and was not made by another.</note> did not exist, then matter cannot be uncreated. Furthermore, from this logic, many things would be "uncreated." For if God was uncreated, and the simple elements from which matter was composed were also uncreated, then there would not be only two uncreated things. 

Now, I suppose you believe that nothing among existing things is contrary to itself? 
*It seems so.* 
And is water contrary to fire? 
*It appears to be contrary.* 
Likewise darkness to light? Cold to heat? And moist to dry? 
*I believe so.* 
If, therefore, nothing among existing things is contrary to itself, these things cannot be one single matter, nor can they be derived from one single matter. But I wish to ask something related to this: Does it seem to you that parts of a whole do not destroy one another? 
*It seems so.* 
And do fire and water, and the rest, seem to be parts of matter? 
*Entirely so.* 
What then? Does it not seem to you that water destroys and eliminates fire, and darkness destroys light, and other such things? 
*It seems so.* 
If, therefore, parts do not destroy one another, but the "parts" of matter do destroy one another, then they cannot be parts of one another. If they are not parts of one another, they cannot belong to one single matter; indeed, they cannot even *be* matter, because no thing, according to the logic and nature of contraries, destroys itself. For nothing is contrary to itself; contraries are contrary to *other* things, not to themselves. Just as "white" is not contrary to itself, but is called contrary to "black"; and light is not opposed to itself, but to darkness; and many such examples. If, therefore, matter were one, it would not be contrary to itself. Since, however, that is the nature of contraries, it is demonstrated that matter <note>as a single, eternal substance</note> does not exist.

<column-break/>

...of God, being able, according to your argument, to overcome God? <note>This column provides the original Greek text of the dialogue translated in the first column.</note> If indeed we call that "God" which has authority over all things. I wish to ask you briefly about matter itself. Tell me, was matter something simple or composite? For the difference between things that have come into being has brought me to this examination of the argument. For if matter happened to be something simple and uniform, <margin>* See G.S. in the notes on this passage.</margin> *but the world is composite, and has its constitution from different substances and mixtures—for "composite" signifies a mixing of certain simple things—if, on the other hand, you wish to say that matter is composite, you will certainly say it has been composed of certain simple things. But if matter was composed of simple things, those simple things (from which matter was composed) existed by themselves. For if matter is composite, and composite things have their constitution from simple things, there was once a time when matter was not—that is, before the simple things came together. If there was a time when matter was not, and there was never a time when the **uncreated** was not, then matter will not be uncreated. From this, it follows that there will be many uncreated things. For if God was uncreated, and the simple things from which matter was composed were also uncreated, there will not be only two uncreated things. 

Does it seem to you that nothing that exists is opposed to itself? 
*It seems so.* 
Is water opposed to fire? 
*It appears to me to be opposed.* 
Similarly darkness to light, and cold to heat? And in addition to these, the moist to the dry? 
*It seems to me to be so.* 
Therefore, if nothing that exists is opposed to itself, they will not be one matter, nor indeed from one matter. I wish to ask something similar to this again. Does it seem to you that parts are not destructive of one another? 
*It seems so.* 
And are fire and water parts of matter, and likewise the rest? 
*I hold it to be so.* 
What then? Does it not seem to you that fire is destructive to water, and darkness to light, and the other things similar to these? 
*It seems so.* 
Therefore, if the parts shall not be destructive of one another, but the parts of matter are destructive of one another, they will not be parts of one another. And if they are not parts of one another, they will not be of one matter; but neither will they themselves be matter, because nothing that exists is destructive of itself, according to the logic of the contrary; for nothing is contrary to itself. For contraries are by nature contrary to *others*; as white is not contrary to itself, but is said to be contrary to black; and light similarly is shown not to be contrary to itself, but to darkness. It appears to be so; and likewise for very many other things. If, therefore, matter was also some one thing, it would not be contrary to itself; but according to the logic of contraries, it is shown that matter <note>as a single eternal principle</note> does not exist.

The speaker uses logic to show that if matter is composite, it must have been created, and if its elements are contrary to each other, they cannot originate from a single, eternal substance.</summary>

### CHAP. XXV.

*From the 1st book of the commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans; regarding those words: Set apart for the Gospel of God.*

---

<margin>Rom. 1:1</margin>
<margin>Gal. 1:15, 16</margin>
The third point to examine is the phrase, *Set apart for the gospel of God*; and in the Epistle to the Galatians, the Apostle says of himself: *But when it pleased Him, who set me apart from my mother’s womb, to reveal His Son in me.* For those who do not understand that God’s setting apart based on foreknowledge is not the cause of the events foreknown, seize upon such words; for they imagine through these that a person is saved not by their own choice, but by their constitution and nature. Against such people, who use these sayings to destroy our free will, we must grant a defense.
<margin>Psalm 58:3</margin>
*The sinners were alienated from the womb*; this is stated in the Psalms. To those whom we must answer on this point, we should ask about the
<margin>Ibid. v. 3, 4</margin>
following words; for it is written: *The sinners were alienated from the womb, they went astray from the belly, they spoke lies, their venom is like the likeness of a serpent.* And we shall ask those who treat these words as if they were literal: if the sinners were alienated from the womb, did they go astray and fall into speaking lies the very moment they came out of the belly or their mother? How could they? How could those alienated from the womb have gone astray and spoken lies from the belly? Show us that at the moment of birth they ever uttered an articulate voice to speak a lie! But if we pay attention to what is said regarding the "setting apart" in the Epistle we are examining, we will be able to refute the most ungodly claims of the many who accuse God of injustice, and by tearing down that "knowledge falsely so-called" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:20, often used against Gnostic "knowledge"</note>, we can offer a defense for the one set apart from his mother's womb—Paul, the servant of Jesus Christ, a called Apostle, set apart for the gospel of God.
<margin>Rom. 8:28, 29, 30</margin>
Let the words be these: *And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are [called] according to his purpose...*

<column-break/>

*In the third place, we must examine that phrase: Set apart for the Gospel of God; and in the letter to the Galatians the Apostle proclaims this of himself: But when it pleased him, who set me apart from my mother’s womb, that his Son might be declared in me. Those who do not understand foreknowledge interpret these words as if predestination were the cause of why foreknown things happen; and for that reason, they introduce the idea that some are saved by their very nature and condition. Some of them use these words to take away our freedom of will; to which they add from the Psalms: The sinners were alienated from their mother’s womb. One may meet this with a question; for it is written: The sinners were alienated from the womb, they wandered from the belly, they spoke false things, their spirit is according to the likeness of a serpent. And we shall ask of those who take those words as if they were plain: whether those who were alienated as sinners from the womb, as soon as they emerged from the maternal womb, wandered and were led away from the path of salvation by some act of their own. How indeed could those alienated from the womb have wandered from the mother's belly and spoken false things? For it is certain that as soon as they were born, they did not emit a true and full voice, uttering anything false. But if we look at those things which are said concerning predestination in this epistle which we are explaining, we will be able—once those things are destroyed which the simpler people pervert into an opinion that accuses divine doctrine of injustice—to respond concerning him who designates from the mother's womb, and who separates the servant of Jesus Christ, the called Apostle Paul, for the Gospel of God. These are the words: We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who [are called] according to his purpose...*

# CHAPTER XXV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

*called according to his purpose*: for those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified. <note>original: Romans 8:28-30</note> Let us attend to the sequence of these words. God justifies those whom he previously called, but he has not justified those whom he did not call: he calls those predestined before the calling, whom he would not have called unless he had predestined them. Nor is predestination itself the very beginning of justification and calling; (For if this were the beginning of those things which follow, those who devise the absurd theory of "natures" <note>A reference to Gnostic groups like the Valentinians, who believed people were born with fixed "natures" (spiritual or material) that determined their salvation regardless of choice.</note> would undoubtedly prevail:) but before predestination is foreknowledge <note>original: *praenotio* / πρόγνωσις (prognosis)</note>; for *those whom*, he says, *he foreknew, these he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son*. Therefore God, who looked upon the sequence of future events, and knew the inclination of our liberty <note>The "inclination of our liberty" refers to the exercise of free will.</note>, and the impulse and affection of some toward piety—following this inclination, and that they would give themselves entirely to virtue—he foreknew them, knowing indeed present things, but foreknowing future things: and those whom he thus foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Therefore, the Son of God is the image of the invisible God, and the image of this [Son] is that which is called the "image of the image of the Son of God," which we judge to be that human soul which the Son of God assumed, which was made an image through the virtue of the image of God. <note>Origen suggests a hierarchy: God -> The Word (Son) -> The Human Soul of Jesus -> The Believer.</note> God predestined those whom he foreknew to become conformed to this [soul], which we consider to be the image of the image of the Son of God. Therefore, foreknowledge is not to be thought of as the *cause* of future events: but because an event was going to happen according to the specific impulses and affections of the one acting, for that reason he foreknew it, who knows all things before they come into being; he foreknew some and predestined them to be conformed to the image of his Son, while others he saw would be alienated. But if anyone should object to this, asking: Is it possible that those things which God foreknew would be such, might not happen? we shall respond that it is impossible for them not to happen, but not for that reason—because it is impossible for them not to happen—is it *necessary* for them to happen or not happen. For they happen by no means out of necessity, but it is also possible for them not to happen. But this topic concerning "possibilities" requires a sharpness of reason and understanding, so that he who has wiped clean the eye of his mind, having attained the subtlety of these demonstrations, may be able to understand how, even in the smallest things, it is not prevented that something which could result in many ways remains one thing out of many possibilities, which is the thing that will be: and thus it is foreknown that it will indeed be, but not that it will *necessarily* be. But since it is possible for it not to be,

...called according to his purpose, because those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified. Let us look at the order of what is said. God justifies, having first called, and would not justify those he did not call; and he calls those predestined before the calling, and would not call those he did not predestine; and the beginning of their calling and justification is predestination; (for if this were the beginning of what follows, then those introducing the absurd arguments about "natures" would have most persuasively prevailed;) but higher than predestination is foreknowledge; for *those whom he foreknew*, he says, *he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son*. Therefore, God, having looked from afar at the sequence of future things, and having understood the inclination of our free will <note>original: τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν (to eph' hēmin) - "that which is up to us."</note> toward piety in some, and the impulse toward this following that inclination, and how they would give themselves entirely to living according to virtue, he foreknew them, knowing present things and foreknowing future things; and those whom he thus foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. The Son of God, then, is the image of the invisible God, and the image of this is the so-called "image of the Son of God"; which we think is the human soul which the Son of God took up, which became an image of the image of God through virtue. God predestined those whom he foreknew to become conformed to this seen image of the Son of God. Therefore, foreknowledge must not be considered the cause of future events; but because it was going to happen according to the individual impulses of the one acting, for this reason he foreknew it, knowing all things before their birth; some he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, while others he saw would be alienated. But if someone should counter this, saying: "Is it then possible for those things not to happen which God foreknew would be so?" we shall say that it is impossible for them not to happen, yet it is not because it is impossible for them not to happen that there is a necessity for them to happen; or that they happen entirely out of necessity, for it was also possible for these very things not to happen; this topic of "possibilities" possesses a logical dexterity and contemplation, so that he who has cleansed the eye of his soul may be able to follow the subtlety of the proofs and understand how, even in chance events, the fact that something is possible in many ways is not hindered, even though the thing that will happen is one of many. And let no one think that we have kept silent regarding that phrase *According to his purpose* <note>original: "Κατὰ πρόθεσιν" / "Secundùm propositum"</note> as if it oppressed our argument; for Paul says, *And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.* But let him observe that the Apostle immediately gave the reason for that calling *according to his purpose*, saying, *For whom he foreknew, he also predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son.* And whom else was it fitting to be called into the righteous calling by the purpose of God, other than those who love Him? The cause of this purpose and foreknowledge is provided by what is in our own power <note>The Greek term "τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν" (to eph' hēmin) refers to human agency or free will—literally "that which is up to us."</note>, as is shown by: *We know that all things work together for good to them that love God.* For he almost said that all things which work together for good do so for this reason: because those who love God are worthy of that cooperation. At the same time, let us question those who say the opposite, and let them answer us regarding these things: let it be assumed for the sake of argument that something is in our power, and let this be granted to those who would take away our free will, until their argument is proven unsound by the hypothesis itself. Let there be, then, something in our power; will God, looking into the chain of future events, foreknow what will be done by each of those who possess free will, or will He not foreknow it? To say He will not foreknow it is the mark of one ignorant of the mind and majesty of God. But if they grant that He will foreknow, let us ask them again: Is His knowledge the cause of the things that are to happen (given that something is in our power), or did He foreknow them because they were going to happen? In no way is His foreknowledge the cause of those things which happen to each of us from our free choice; for it was possible for the one created with free will <note>term: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion) — a technical term for being "master of oneself" or having self-determining power.</note> not to do this, but to do that, before the events occurred. If these and similar things are said, then that saying is preserved: *Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord*; and all praise is preserved; and the reasonableness of: *Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou oughtest to have put my money to the exchangers.* Only in this way will those things be preserved which are justly said to those on the right hand: *Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat*, and so on; and to those on the left: *Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat*, and so on. That the cause of this purpose and foreknowledge is in our liberty is sufficiently declared by this: *We know that to those who love God all things lead to good.* Just as if he had said, all things which lead to good do so for this reason, because they who love God are worthy of help. Let there be therefore in us a free will: will God then, having beheld the series of future things, foreknow those things which each of us, being possessed of liberty, is about to do from liberty, or will He not foreknow? He who would answer that He will not foreknow, let him be ignorant of the infinite mind and greatness of God. If they acknowledge that He will foreknow, we will ask of them again, whether His knowledge is the cause why future things are to happen, since it is granted that something is in our power, or did He foreknow because it is to be; and is foreknowledge in no way the cause of those things which are to happen to each of us from the liberty of judgment? ### CHAPTER XXV. ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

<margin>Romans 1:1. Galatians 1:15.</margin>
If those words, *Set apart for the Gospel of God* <note>original Latin: "Destinatus in Evangelium Dei"</note> and, *He who set me apart from my mother’s womb*, implied a kind of necessity, how could Paul rightly say, *I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway* <note>or "disqualified"</note>; and also, *Woe is unto me if I preach not the Gospel*? For by these words he clearly declares that unless he punished his body and brought it into subjection, it was possible for him—after preaching to others—to become a castaway; and that "woe" could indeed befall him if he did not proclaim the Gospel. Was it not, therefore, that God set him apart from his mother’s womb and separated him for the Gospel of God because He saw the cause for a just separation? Namely, that Paul was the kind of man who would discipline his body and bring it into subjection, fearing lest after preaching to others he might be disqualified; and that, knowing "woe" would be his lot unless he preached, and fearing that this "woe" from God might come upon him, he did not remain silent but preached the Gospel? And He who set him apart for His Gospel saw these things: that he would be in labors more abundantly; in prisons beyond measure; in stripes above reach; in deaths often; that from the Jews five times he would receive forty lashes minus one; three times he would be beaten with rods; once he would be stoned; and that he would suffer other things of this kind. Boasting in his distresses, and knowing that tribulation produces patience, and enduring those things which God had foreknown would happen, he was set apart from his mother’s womb and separated for the Gospel of God. He was worthy to be separated for the Gospel of God, not because of some superior nature <note>Origen is arguing against Gnostic ideas that some people are born with a "divine nature" while others are not</note> that was so constituted as to far surpass those who are not like him, but because of his actions—which were foreknown before they were later performed—arising from a certain Apostolic resolve. It was not the right time to interpret the saying from the Psalm here, as it was outside the current purpose; therefore, God willing, it will be explained in its proper place when we expound upon that Psalm. But let these points, discussed at length regarding the phrase *Set apart* and the rest, suffice.

If the phrase, *Set apart for the gospel of God* <note>original Greek: "Ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον Θεοῦ"</note> and, *He who set me apart from my mother’s womb*, contained a necessity, how could he reasonably say, *I beat my body and lead it as a slave, lest perhaps having preached to others I myself should become disqualified*; and, *For woe is to me if I do not preach the gospel*. For he clearly shows by these things that if he did not beat his body and lead it as a slave, it was possible for him, having preached to others, to become disqualified; and that it was possible for this to happen to him if he did not preach the gospel. Did God then, seeing these things, set him apart from his mother’s womb, and set him apart for the gospel of God because He had seen the cause of the just separation? Namely, that he would beat his body and lead it as a slave, being careful lest perhaps having preached to others he himself should become disqualified; and that, knowing what would happen to him if he did not preach the gospel, through fear toward God he took care that it should not happen, and did not keep silent, but preached the gospel? And He who set him apart for His own gospel saw these things: that he would be in labors more abundantly; in prisons more abundantly; in stripes exceedingly; in deaths often; by the Jews five times he would receive forty less one; thrice he would be beaten with rods; once he would be stoned; and he would suffer such things; boasting in tribulations, and knowing that tribulation works endurance; and enduring what was foreknown to happen, and being set apart from his mother’s womb, he was set apart for the gospel of God. Because of these things he was worthy to be set apart for the gospel of God, not because of a nature having something excellent, as far as its constitution, above the natures of those who are not such; but because of the foreknown deeds, which later happened from his choice and his apostolic resolve. But now to give the explanation for the same passage of the Psalm was not opportune, for it would be a digression; therefore, in its proper order, God granting, it will be given when we explain the Psalm. And these things said at length regarding the *Set apart* will suffice.

Since there is always much inquiry among men concerning what things are good and what are evil—some saying that good and evil are outside of our choice <note>original: ἀπροαίρετα (aproaireta) - things we cannot control, like health or wealth</note>, as those who declare pleasure to be a good and pain an evil; others confining good and evil to matters of choice alone, saying that virtues and the actions according to them are the only goods, while vices and the activities according to vice are evils; and there being a third group who mix these, saying that good and evil exist both in things within our choice and outside of it—it is natural that the many, being drawn away by the persuasiveness of those who teach, and desiring to learn about the topic of "the goods," would say: *Who will show us good things?* That the nature of good things exists in matters of choice, anyone who seriously considers the argument of judgment would acknowledge without being taught. They will even touch upon the Gospels, saying that the Savior came and took away bodily blindness, deafness, and the paralysis of limbs as if they were "evils," and that He healed every disease and every infirmity; granting "goods" in place of the previous evils, such as bodily sight, hearing, and other health. And they will press you and put you to shame, saying: "Must we not also confess that it is an evil to be possessed by a demon or to be an epileptic <note>original: σεληνιάζεσθαι / lunaticum; literally 'moon-struck'</note>; just as, conversely, it is a good to be delivered from these?" Furthermore, the Apostles, by performing gifts of healing and works of power, did good to men through their piety and delivered them from evils. Those who say these things also point to the age to come, claiming that "evil" is the pain to which He delivers sinners in eternal fire. But if pain is an evil, then pleasure must necessarily be a good. Now, from what has been said, it is clear what things are most able to confound those who are unable to solve the arguments brought forward concerning the three kinds of goods and three kinds of evils according to the logic of the Scriptures. Therefore, not only those among the believers who are admittedly simple-minded <note>original: ἀκέραιοι / simplices; literally 'unmixed' or 'innocent'</note> have succumbed to this reasoning, but even some of those who profess the wisdom of Christ, thinking that the promises of the Creator <note>term: Creator (demiurge); Origen is likely addressing Gnostic views that distinguished the God of the Old Testament from the Father of Christ</note> are of this sort, and that nothing else is signified beyond the literal threats. Against all those who take such things from the Scriptures—

<column-break/>

the vintage, and the vintage shall overtake the sowing, and you shall eat your bread to fullness, and you shall dwell securely upon your land; and so forth. From Deuteronomy they will bring these forward: *It shall be, when you have crossed the Jordan into the land which the Lord God gives to you, and you shall take care to fulfill all His commandments which I prescribe to you today: and the Lord your God will grant you to be above all, and all these blessings shall come upon you, and shall find you, if you hear the voice of the Lord your God. Blessed are you in the city, and blessed are you in the field; blessed the fruit of your womb, and the buds of your earth, and the herds of your oxen, and the flocks of your cattle; blessed your storehouse, and your remains, etc.* just as on the contrary it is said to the impious, *Accursed are you in the city, and accursed are you in the field; accursed your barns, and your remains; accursed the sons of your womb, and the buds of your earth; accursed the herds of your oxen, and the flocks of your cattle:* and those who want goods and evils to exist in bodily and external things can bring forth innumerable other things. They will also touch upon the Gospel, and say that the Savior, when He came, took away from men bodily blindness, deafness, and the loosening of limbs as if they were evils, and healed every disease and every infirmity; giving goods for the prior evils, both keenness of the body, and hearing, and other health and strength: and you will be ashamed when they ask of you, whether we do not also think it an evil to be vexed by a demon and to be a lunatic; as on the contrary to be freed from these is a good? But also the Apostles, who performed gifts of healing and works of virtues, in that very act bestowed goods upon men, and delivered them from evils. Finally, those who feel this way will pass over to the future age, and say that pain is an evil, or that sinners are adjudged to eternal fire. But if pain is an evil, it is necessary that pleasure be a good. From these things are manifest those points by which they can most greatly move those who cannot dissolve those arguments which show, according to the opinion of the Scriptures, that there are three kinds of goods and evils. Therefore, not only those who have a bare and simple faith are circumvented by this error; but also some of those who profess wisdom in Christ, opining that such are the promises of the Creator and that nothing more is signified by them beyond the sound of the words. By all those, therefore, who think these things are established from the Scriptures—

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXVI.

For those who hold such opinions, we must ask whether the Prophets—against whom no sins are charged—kept the Law. For instance, Elias <note>Elijah</note>, who was so utterly destitute that he did not even have bread of his own to eat, and was therefore sent to a woman in Sarepta of Sidonia; and Elisæus <note>Elisha</note>, who received from the Shunammite woman only the most cramped lodging, a bench, and a cheap lamp, and who eventually died of a disease; and Esaias <note>Isaiah</note>, who walked naked and barefoot for three years; and Hieremias <note>Jeremiah</note>, who was cast into a pit of filth and was constantly mocked, so much so that he even prayed for a desert to dwell in; and Joannes <note>John the Baptist</note>, who lived in the wilderness and ate nothing but locusts and wild honey, girded with a leather skin about his loins and clothed in camel’s hair. For they will surely admit that these men kept the Law. We shall ask them, then, whether these things they consider "good" were present for those who kept the Law. Since they cannot demonstrate this, they will be forced to say either that the promises said to be given to the godly and religious are false; or, if they are true, that they must be interpreted in a higher, spiritual sense. If they are compelled to turn to a hidden meaning <note>original: "reconditum sensum" / "ἀλληγορίαν" (allegory)</note>, their own opinion will be destroyed—namely, the idea that the Law threatens the ungodly with bodily disease and what are thought to be external evils, or promises bodily health and riches to those who cling to God. Indeed, how would it not be foolish to boast in evils, and for the saints to rejoice while held by them? For if afflictions are "evils," and the Apostle says he boasts in his "evils" <note>referring to Paul in Romans 5:3</note>, that would be foolish; but the Apostle is not foolish. Certainly, then, those things by which a holy man is exercised are not "evils." Such a man, though afflicted in every way, is not crushed; though impoverished, he is not forsaken; though tested unto death, he is not brought down. And while he is thought to be a beggar, he enriches many; while believed to possess nothing, he possesses all things. For to the faithful man, the whole world of riches belongs; but to the unfaithful, not even a penny <note>original: "obolus," a small Greek coin</note>. Furthermore, according to the opinion of those who claim that three kinds of goods and as many kinds of evils can be found in the Scriptures, it follows that the righteous are always in the midst of many "evils," since this Prophecy is true which says, *Many are the afflictions of the righteous*. Nor would it be untimely to remind those who think such things are "evils" of what happened to Job: after he had most bravely endured the struggles that surrounded him, the Book says of him, *Do you think I have spoken with you for any other reason than that you might appear righteous?* For if Job only appears righteous because these various calamities surrounded him, how can we now call "evils" the very causes that allowed his justice to shine forth? From these things we may also gather that not even the devil is an "evil" to a holy man. To Job, therefore, the devil was not an evil; because for those who love...

<margin>Deuteronomy 15:6</margin>
...to all, God works all things together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. <note>original: "πᾶσι τὸν Θεὸν πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθὸν..." / "tibus Deum omnia in bonum..." quoting Romans 8:28</note> Furthermore, we say it is evident that the righteous man is not feasted with blessings according to the literal sense of the "goods" supposedly laid down in the Scriptures; for much of the history examined concerning holy men contradicts such interpretations. For who would think that being a "holy man" consists in being a money-lender, opening banks in every city for many nations, being preoccupied with giving and receiving <note>i.e., commercial transactions</note>, and doing forbidden things? *For he did not give his money at interest, and did not take bribes against the innocent;* <margin>Psalm 15:5</margin> and he who does these things shall never be moved. And according to Ezekiel, the holy man did not give his money for interest or increase. <margin>Ezekiel 18:8</margin> To think that even a fever happens because of sins is the doctrine of an exceedingly uneducated person; for the causes of such diseases are often manifest: either due to the surrounding air, or such waters, or such foods. If health and wealth were the prizes for the righteous, then none of the impious ought to be healthy or wealthy. Rather, one must seek health as a certain stable condition of the soul; and wealth according to Solomon, which happens to be the ransom of the soul, saying: *A man’s own wealth is the ransom of his soul.* <margin>Proverbs 13:8</margin> But poverty is to be fled, concerning which it is written: *The poor man does not withstand a threat.* <margin>Proverbs 13:8</margin> Furthermore, wounds, bruises, and diseases must be understood as those things occurring through vice in souls that have fallen away; concerning which the Prophet also blames those found in such states, saying: *From feet to head there is neither wound, nor bruise, nor inflamed stripe; there is no ointment to apply, nor oil, nor bandages.* <margin>Isaiah 1:6</margin> These things are sufficient for those who are not entirely negligent, so that by collecting the most divine sayings of the Scriptures for themselves, they may flourish with an understanding worthy of the working of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, to silence those who think that these [material] goods are given to the holy and these [physical] evils to the sinners, this must be added: everything that exists for the sake of something else is lesser than that for which it exists. For example, incisions, cauterizations, and plasters, which are employed for the sake of health, are lesser than health itself. Even if these are called "goods" as medical aids, one must understand that they are not the *final* <term>final good: the ultimate goal or "telos" of an action</term> goods of medicine, but the *productive* <term>productive good: a means to an end</term> goods. The final good in medicine is the health of the body. Therefore, if these commandments are to be kept by those seeking to obtain "goods," and the prizes are merely bodily and external, then good actions will not be good as final ends, but only as producers of goods; and wealth would be superior...

<column-break/>

...to God, God administers all things for good to those who are called according to his purpose. Moreover, we shall say it does not sufficiently appear that the just man will be a participant in those blessings which are considered "goods" as placed in the Scriptures: for many histories of that holy man, if they are weighed, refute that interpretation. For who would deem it right for a holy man to be a usurer, who opens tables <note>original: "mensas" / "τραπέζας" - referring to money-changing or banking tables</note> in the city for many nations, and is occupied in giving and receiving, and does forbidden things? *For he gave not his money to usury, and took no rewards against the innocent; and he who does these things shall not be moved forever;* and in Ezekiel, *The holy man did not occupy his money for usury and gain.* But also, let no one, unless he be altogether raw and ignorant, think that a fever happens on account of sins; since the causes of this disease are often manifest: either on account of the encompassing air, or on account of such waters, or on account of such nourishments. And, if health and riches are proposed as rewards to the just, it would be necessary that no wicked man be healthy or rich. But health must be sought as the right constitution of the mind: and riches truly, which, in the opinion of Solomon, are the price of a man's soul: *The riches of a man,* he says, *are the price of his soul: but poverty is to be fled, of which it is written, But the poor man undergoes not threats:* wounds moreover, and welts, and diseases are to be understood as those which happen on account of vice to dissolved minds; whence also the Prophet rebukes those who are in them: *From the feet,* he says, *even unto the head there is neither wound, nor welt, nor inflamed plague: there is no medicine that may be put to it, nor oil, nor binding.* These things therefore suffice even for those who are not plainly negligent, so that having collected for themselves the sayings of Scripture which seem to conflict, they may study to attain an understanding worthy of the action of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, that the mouth may be shut of those who judge that these "goods" are to be given to the holy, and "evils" to the wicked, these things seem necessary to be added. Everything which is for the sake of something, is less than that for the sake of which it is: just as sections, burnings, and plasters, which are taken for the sake of health, are less than health. Even if these, as in the aids of medicine, be called goods, it is so to be understood that they are not the goods of the end or the ultimate things of medicine, but the efficient things. But the good of the end in medicine is the health of the body. So therefore, if these mandates are to be kept so that we may follow these goods; and the rewards are bodily and external goods, then good actions will not be good as ultimate and perfecting, but as efficient of goods; and wealth will excel...

<meta>This page continues Origen’s discussion on the nature of "good" things, specifically distinguishing between what lies within our own will and what is granted by God. The catchword from the previous page, "ferens" (bearing/bringing), leads into the discussion of worldly rewards.</meta>

# ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*

...riches, which some believe the Scripture promises, and bodily health as a reward for justice, and from holiness itself, and piety, and religion—those great and noble achievements. To accept such things <note>i.e., to believe that material wealth is the primary reward for spiritual virtue</note> is the mark of men who are ignorant of the dignity of virtue, and who prefer coarse and humble things instead. For it is the most absurd thing of all to say that riches and bodily health are superior to noble deeds. Some have even believed in this wicked doctrine to the extent of thinking that when our bodies are raised and brought back to life, according to those first promises, we shall eat such and such foods and drink; some even think we shall beget children. These ideas, if they reach the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos," referring to non-Christians or Gentiles</note>, will attach a great reproach of stupidity and folly to Christianity, since those outside the faith often hold better views than these. We, however, will now set forth what we have been able to perceive from a careful reading of the sacred books. For we were saying that it pleases us to hold that there are "goods" and "evals" both in things within our will <term>arbitraria: things subject to our free choice or "proairetic"</term> and things outside our will. Truly, among the goods outside our will, we did not enumerate health, soundness, beauty, glory, or riches; and as much as we were able, we have tried to briefly resolve every doubt. What those goods are, then, which are not freely undertaken <note>meaning they are not achieved by human effort alone</note>, must now be stated; since it is true that, <margin>Psalm 127:1</margin> *Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it;* <margin>Ibid. same verse</margin> and, *Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it.* Whoever makes progress builds a house; whoever is perfect guards a city. But the work of the builder is vain, and the watch of the guard is vain, unless the Lord builds and the Lord guards. Therefore, there is a good outside our free will: the power of the Lord, which assists the building of the one who builds, and helps him, and builds together with him who cannot complete the building by himself. The same must be understood regarding the guarding of the city. And just as if I were to say that the "good" of agriculture, which produces fruit, is a mixture of the freedom found in the farmer’s skill and the factor outside his will which comes from Providence—namely, the temperament of the air and a sufficient supply of rain—so the "good" of a rational being is a mixture of his own will and the conspiring divine power in him who undertakes the most honorable things. Therefore, not only is our will and the conspiring divine help (which, as far as we are concerned, is outside our will) necessary for someone to become honorable and good, but it is also necessary so that he who has emerged as honorable and good may persevere in virtue. For undoubtedly even a perfect man will fall into ruin if he becomes puffed up in his honorableness and arrogates the cause of it to himself, not giving the due glory

<column-break/>

...wealth, which they think the Scripture promises, and the health of the body resulting from righteousness, and from holiness itself, and piety, and godliness—those great manly virtues. To accept these <note>material rewards</note> belongs to men who do not know the worth of virtue, but prefer its material results. For it is the most absurd of all things to say that being rich and being physically healthy are superior to manly virtues. Because of these wretched doctrines, some have consequently thought that even after the resurrection, in the first promises, we are destined to have such foods and to drink; and some even to beget children. These things, reaching even those from the nations <note>original: "ethnon," the Gentiles/Pagans</note>, will create a reputation for great silliness and lack of refinement in Christianity, since some who are strangers to the faith hold much better doctrines. We, however, will now present what appears to us from the examination of the sacred oracles. For we were saying that it pleases me in this argument that "goods" and "evils" exist both in things within our choice and things outside our choice. Among the goods that are not within our choice, we did not include health, beauty, eloquence, good reputation, or wealth; and, as far as possible, we attempted to resolve the persuasive arguments against this in summary. What, then, are the goods outside our choice? This must now be told; since it is indeed true: *Unless the Lord builds the house, they who build it have labored in vain;* and, *Unless the Lord guards the city, the guard has kept watch in vain.* Everyone who is making progress builds a house; and everyone who is perfect guards a city. But the work of the builder is vain, and the guard’s watch is vain, unless the Lord builds and the Lord guards. There would be a good outside our choice: the assisting power of the Lord for the building of the one who builds, building together with the one who is not able to finish the building by himself. We must understand the same things regarding the guarding of the city. And just as if I were to say that the "good" of farming, which produces fruit, is a mixture of the choice involved in the farmer’s craft and the factor outside his choice which comes from Providence through the fair temperature of the air and the bringing of sufficient rain; so the "good" of the rational being is a mixture of his own choice and the breathing-together <note>original: "sympneuseos," a divine cooperation or "conspiration"</note> of divine power with the one who has chosen the most beautiful things. Therefore, not only is there a need for our choice and the divine cooperation (which, as far as we are concerned, is outside our choice) in order to become beautiful and good; but also to remain in virtue once one has become beautiful and good. For even the one who has been perfected will fall away if he is overly uplifted by his beauty <note>i.e., his moral excellence</note> and credits himself as the cause of it, not referring the due glory <note>to God</note>.

<summary>Origen argues that true virtue is a partnership between human free will and divine assistance, refuting the "absurd" idea that material wealth or physical health are the primary rewards of a religious life. He uses the analogy of a farmer needing both skill and rain to explain how human effort and God's providence must work together.</summary>

Perhaps therefore the most holy Apostle, who knew that our will contributes much less to the obtaining of good things than does divine virtue, finally says: *It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.* Not as if God does not help those who will or run, but as if willing and running were nothing compared to the mercy of God; and therefore it is right that the good be ascribed to the mercy of God rather than to human will or effort. # CHAPTER XXVII. ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

He gave health, and sight, and hearing to men: yet a higher sense <note>anagogical or spiritual interpretation</note> in these things must be sought above all, since the Word <note>the Logos/Christ</note> signifies the healing of the soul's disturbances through these histories. Nor would it be absurd to understand that those things promised in the history were indeed done, for the sake of the wonder and amazement of the men of that time; so that those who would not believe the discourses of demonstration and doctrine might adhere to the teacher, having been struck with awe by the powers of the miracles.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

**T**he Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he would not let them go. Those words so often repeated in Exodus, *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*, and *I will harden the heart of Pharaoh*, disturb almost all readers—both those who do not believe the Scripture, and those who profess that they do believe. For to the unbelievers, this seems to be a cause for not believing (among many other things), because things are said of God that are unworthy of God. For it is unworthy of God to effect hardness in the heart of anyone, and to effect that hardness so that one resists the will of Him who does the hardening. And how, they say, is it not absurd for God to do certain things so that one does not obey His will; namely, because He does not wish to have Pharaoh obedient to His commands? 

To those, however, who are thought to believe, no small controversy arises from these words, *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*. For those who believe that God is none other than the Maker of the world <note>The Demiurge; Origen is likely addressing Gnostic views here</note> feel that God, by His own authority, has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills; though there be no cause why this one should be pitied and another hardened by Him. Others, who follow a better opinion, say that many other meanings of Scripture are hidden from them, and they are not turned away from the right faith on that account; but that the right and true reasoning of the Scripture itself is one of those hidden things. A third group, saying that God is someone other than the Maker, wish Him to be just but not good <note>A reference to Marcionite theology which separated the "Just God" of the Old Testament from the "Good God" of the New</note>. This they do foolishly and impiously, since they separate justice from goodness, and goodness from justice; yet even while saying this, they admit things contrary to their own opinion regarding a just God—namely, that He Himself hardens the heart of Pharaoh and makes him disobedient to Himself. For if He is just who renders to each according to his merit, and gives to those who have become better or worse by their own doing that which each deserves; He knows...

<column-break/>

...He bestowed health, and sight, and hearing upon men; but a higher spiritual interpretation <note>original: "ἀναγωγὴν" (anagoge) - the lifting of the mind from the literal to the spiritual</note> must certainly be sought, as the Word indicates the healing of the passions of the soul through these histories. It is not out of place that such results also occurred according to the literal history for the sake of startling the men of that time; so that those who were not persuaded by demonstrative and instructional arguments, being put to shame by the miraculous powers, might agree with the teacher.

->Regarding the passage: The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh.<-

### CHAPTER 27.

**T**he Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he was not willing to send them away. The phrase found many times in Exodus, *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*, and *I will harden the heart of Pharaoh*, disturbs nearly all who encounter it—both those who distrust it and those who claim to believe. To the unbelievers, along with many other things, this seems to be a cause for unbelief, as things are said about God that are unworthy of God. For they suppose it is unworthy of God to instill hardness in a heart, and to work hardness for the purpose of disobeying the will of the one hardening the person being hardened. And how, they say, is it not absurd for God to work something for the purpose of disobeying His own will? For it is clear that He did not wish to have Pharaoh obedient to what He commanded. 

To those who are considered to believe, no ordinary disagreement has arisen because of the phrase, *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*. For some, being persuaded that there is no other God besides the Creator, think that God, as if by lot, has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills; with no cause existing for this one to be pitied and that one to be hardened by Him. Others, faring better than these, say that many other meanings are hidden in the Scripture from them; and they are not turned from sound faith because of this; but that the sound reasoning concerning the Scripture itself is one of the hidden things. Certain others, claiming there is another God besides the Creator, want Him to be just, but not good; behaving quite ignorantly and impiously at once by separating justice from goodness, and goodness apart from justice. Nevertheless, even in saying this, they are carried away into things contrary to their own assumption about a just God—namely, that He hardens the heart of Pharaoh and prepares him to be disobedient to Himself. For if He who assigns to each according to merit is just, and renders to those who have become better or worse by their own causes that which each is fit to...

But how are you just, if you are the cause of a worse sin for us in the case of Pharaoh? And I do not mean simply, but insofar as you cooperated in those things which they received, so that he became most unjust. For those who attribute the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart to a just God, without referring it to anything worthy of His choice, I do not know how they will preserve God as just—even if they wish to explain it as you do—while He is the one capable of hardening Pharaoh’s heart. Therefore, they must be pressed on the points concerning the present passage, so that they may either explain how a just being hardens, or dare to say that because He hardens, the Creator <term>Demiurge; the Gnostic term for the creator of the material world, often viewed by them as inferior or evil</term> is evil. Now, let these questions about God be set aside in the present problem. But since those who suppose that some are created for destruction by their very nature also bring up these points—saying that the Teacher <note>Likely referring to Paul or a specific Gnostic authority</note> is right because the heart of Pharaoh was hardened by the Lord—come, let us question them on these matters. If one created for destruction could ever do anything better, while his very inherent nature fights against him regarding good things, what need was there for Pharaoh (who, as you say, was already a "son of destruction") to be hardened by God so that he would not send the people away? For if he had not been hardened, he would have sent them. Let them be pressed with this: What would Pharaoh have done if he had not been hardened? For if he would have released them without being hardened, he was not of a "destroyed nature." But if he would not have released them even then, his heart was already stubborn without being hardened; for he would equally have refused to release them even if not hardened. By what action, then, did God harden him through his <term>hegemonikon; the "ruling faculty" or inner mind that directs a person's choices</term>? And how does He accuse him, saying: *Because you disobey me, behold, I will kill your firstborn, and all the Egyptians shall know,* He says, *that I am the Lord*? This implies that these perceived hardships are brought upon them so that they might know God.

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXVII.

...of bodily things and those considered pleasant, before leaving them to themselves until, being sated with what they long for and desire, they might as it were even wish to vomit them up. Thus, having been burdened by them to the greatest extent and having been so tormented by them, they will not quickly fall back into the same things. For those who have looked down upon secondary things <note>Likely referring to lesser or worldly concerns</note> are led more slowly to healing if they were to fall into the same things again, because they were freed from their evils too quickly. Since God the Craftsman alone is able to scientifically apply healings to the dispositions of each person—knowing how He instills them, what must be done, and when to do it for each individual. 

Just as in the case of certain bodily ailments, when the evil has moved into the depths (so to speak), the physician draws the matter to the surface by means of certain drugs and rouses it, causing painful inflammations, swellings, and more pains than the person had before they set out to be healed—as they are accustomed to do for those bitten by mad dogs <note>Rabies</note> and others suffering from similar conditions—so I believe God also manages the hidden wickedness that has moved into the depths of the soul. 

And just as the physician says regarding such a suffering: "I will produce inflammations around the area of relief, and I will force these certain parts to swell so as to create a painful abscess"; when the physician says these things, the one who hears him with more scientific knowledge will not blame him, but will even praise the one who, as it were, threatens to perform these acts. But the one who claims that causing pain is foreign to the physician’s profession—saying that he ought to heal rather than lead the patient toward inflammations and abscesses—[would be mistaken]. 

In this same way, I believe God said: *I will harden the heart of Pharaoh.* <note>Exodus 4:21</note> When these things are written, the one who hears them as a divine oracle accepts the entire authority of the Speaker and seeks how he may find, even in these words, a demonstration of the goodness of God. This is seen more clearly in the salvation of the people, who were brought to faith through many wonders; and secondly, regarding those Egyptians who, being struck with awe by what was happening, were to follow the Hebrews. For it says: *A large mixed multitude from the Egyptians went out with them.* <note>Exodus 12:38</note> 

But perhaps there is a more secret and deeper meaning regarding the benefit to Pharaoh himself: that he should no longer hide the poison nor restrain his habitual state, but rather, by being drawn into the open, he might perhaps dissolve it through the very act of doing it. Thus, having completed all the eruptions of the wickedness dwelling within him—which the tree that bears evils later produced—it might perhaps be dried up at the end when he is submerged [in the sea]. This happened not, as one might think, for his total destruction, but so that by washing away his sins he might be lightened; and perhaps in peace from such a great war of the soul, he might [descend] to...

...he leaves behind things that are thought to be corporeal and pleasant; until by satiety, they cast away the things they most greatly desire, as if they wished to vomit them up, and—having been sated and exercised by the heaviest punishments—they are not likely to return to them immediately. Moreover, those who did not fear that they might fall back into those same things are cured more slowly, because they had been freed from evils immediately. 

But God the Creator knows the affections of each person, and, as is fitting for Him, He alone can scientifically and skillfully practice medicine, applying what is suitable for each, and when. And just as in certain diseases of the body, if the evil has penetrated to the innermost parts (so to speak), the physician attracts the matter to the outermost surface with certain medications, bringing on most troublesome inflammations, tumors, and more pains than the patient sustained before he was treated; as is customary to do in those who have been bitten by a rabid dog, and certain others who are afflicted by evils of this kind: so I think God treats the hidden malice which has penetrated to the innermost soul. 

And just as a physician says of such a sick man: "I will create inflammations in the place of the wound, and I will cause these or those parts to swell, so that they may create a more serious abscess"; if any skilled person should hear the physician saying these things, he will not find fault, but rather will praise him who threatens that he will do these things. But another, ignorant of medicine, will say it is foreign to the profession of physicians, who, since they ought to heal, bring the matter to inflammations and abscesses: so also I think God said, *I will harden the heart of Pharaoh.* 

He who receives these written words as the oracles of God, having revered the authority of the Speaker, approves them; and everyone *who seeks finds* how in these things also he may show the goodness of God: more clearly indeed for the salvation of the people, who are brought to faith by many miracles; secondly in the Egyptians, whoever, being stunned by the miracles, were going to follow the Hebrews; *A large promiscuous multitude,* it says, *of Egyptians went out together with them.* 

But more secretly and more deeply perhaps, it was even for the benefit of Pharaoh himself, who would no longer hide the poison, nor restrain his desire, but would draw it forth and bring it into the open, and perhaps by acting would dissolve it; so that, by the feigned boiling over and ejection of the inherent malice, he might afterwards have a weak tree which bears evil; and perhaps finally dried up, when Pharaoh is submerged: not so much, as anyone might have thought, that he should utterly perish, but that with his sins cast out he might be relieved; and perhaps in peace from so great a war of the soul [he might go] to the lower world.

...to descend to the fierce <note>The text here picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, likely discussing the soul's descent or the depths of judgment.</note>. But it is not without reason that readers will bear it heavily, thinking it violent and strange, what we were saying: that it was useful for Pharaoh that his heart be hardened, and that for his sake all those things were done which are written, even up to his drowning. But see if we can prove those sayings from this point, removing all doubt and opposition; *Many*, says David, *are the scourges of the sinner*: <margin>Psalm 32:10</margin> and his son <note>Referring to Solomon, traditionally the author of Proverbs.</note> teaches this, that God rebukes with scourges every son whom He loves and approves. <margin>Proverbs 3:11; Hebrews 12:6</margin> Furthermore, David himself, prophesying the promise concerning Christ and those believing in him, says, *If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments, if they violate my justifications, and keep not my commandments; I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their crimes with scourges: but my mercy I will not take away from them.* <margin>Psalm 89:30-33</margin> It is therefore the grace of God when the lawless man is visited with a rod, and the sinner with scourges. But it is likely that those who encounter this will find it difficult to bear, supposing that what is said is forced—namely, that it was actually beneficial for Pharaoh to have his heart hardened, and that for this reason all the recorded events took place, even up to the drowning.
