<meta>This page continues Origen’s defense of the unity of God, specifically addressing the difficult scriptural passages where God is said to "harden" hearts. He argues against Gnostic dualists who claimed the "Good God" of the New Testament was different from the "Severe God" of the Old Testament.</meta>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia. CHAPTER XXVII.

<column-break/>

...the one who hardens and the one who shows mercy? For it is not the work of one to show mercy and another to harden, according to the Apostle’s voice <note>Referring to Romans 9:18: "Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth."</note>, but the work of one and the same. Either, then, those who receive mercy from God belong to the same one who hardens Pharaoh’s heart—and they [the heretics] vainly imagine another God for themselves—or the "Good God," according to them, is not only merciful but also the one who hardens; in which case He would no longer be "good" in the way they suppose. 

We have pursued these points at greater length on purpose against those who, without careful examination, arrogantly claim understanding for themselves and insult our simplicity. They strive with all their might to show that our discourse does not support their views on God or their doctrines on nature. We, however, having been led to this conviction by many reasons, believe that the pain, trouble, labor, and punishment brought by God are never directed *against* those who suffer them, but are always for their benefit. 

Even the harshest terms thought to be attributed to God—"fury" and "wrath"—are said to "rebuke" and "instruct," as it says here: *O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor instruct me in thy wrath* <margin>Psalm 6:1</margin>. When one prays this, he asks that he might not have need of the correction that comes through fury or the instruction that comes through wrath; as if it were certain that some are indeed rebuked by God’s fury and instructed by His wrath. 

And so that we may agree more and more with these statements, we must seek similar testimonies from the New Testament. The Savior says: *I came to cast fire upon the earth; and how I wish it were already kindled!* <margin>Luke 12:49</margin>. Unless the fire He came to cast upon the earth was a saving fire, and saving for mankind, the Son of the Good God would never have said these things. 

Indeed, Peter—who by his word killed Ananias and Sapphira because they had sinned by lying to God and not to men <margin>Acts 5:1-2</margin>—was not only caring for the edification of those who, seeing this, would become more religious and pious in the faith of Christ, but he was also caring for those who were dying. He wished to free them from the body unexpectedly, having been purified by a sudden death. They even had some grounds for justification, since they had given at least half of their goods for the use of the needy. 

And Paul, blinding by his word the man who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus <note>The sorcerer Elymas/Bar-Jesus</note>, converted him to piety through pain and trouble, saying to him: *O man full of all deceit and fallacy, son of the Devil, enemy of all justice, will you not cease perverting the right ways of the Lord? And now you shall be blind, not seeing the sun for a time.* <margin>Acts 13:10-11</margin> What "time"? Surely until the moment when, having been corrected for his sins and moved by repentance, he should be worthy...

<column-break/>

<meta>The catchword "dignus" (worthy) indicates the sentence continues on the next page, likely describing the restoration of the sorcerer's sight upon his repentance.</meta>

<summary>Origen argues that God's "severity," such as hardening hearts or inflicting punishment, is actually a form of divine medicine intended for the salvation of the individual, citing examples from both the Old and New Testaments.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S *Philocalia*.

would he be worthy to see the Sun both in soul and in body, so that the divine power might be proclaimed in the restoration of his sight; in the soul as well, because by receiving faith he was to attain the worship of God? But even Demas and Hermogenes, whom he <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note> delivered to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme, suffered something similar to those mentioned before: and he who at Corinth had possessed his father’s wife is himself delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord. It is not surprising, therefore, if everything concerning the hardened Pharaoh, surrounded at last by so many punishments, is administered by divine kindness. Let these things be said for the present, as they have occurred to us, concerning the passage: *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*. Furthermore, if anyone, while preserving piety toward God, should find better explanations than these—and those furthest removed from impiety—supported by the testimonies of divine Scripture, those are to be preferred to ours.

<margin>1 Timothy 1:20</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 5:5</margin>

->*And elsewhere.*<-

Moreover, I reflect upon that passage in this way: whether, just as physicians of those who have been bitten by a rabid dog draw the poison out into the open—lest by consuming the man within it should kill him—and thereby cause a more severe sensation of pain and inflammations: so God, by His own medicine, draws out the wickedness hidden and shut up, as it were, in the very marrow of the soul, so that it may become open and evident, and that He may then apply a suitable cure. To this point I believe these words written in Deuteronomy pertain: *And you shall remember the whole way through which your God led you, now the fortieth year in the wilderness, that He might afflict you, and test you, and that the things in your heart might be known, whether you keep His commandments or not: and He afflicted you, and exhausted you with hunger, and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, so that it might be declared to you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God shall man live*. Observe in these words that God pressures and tests so that the things in each person's heart may be discerned—things which were indeed there, but hidden in the depths, and which break out into the open through anguishes and troubles. Of such a kind is that which is promised to Job by the Lord through the whirlwind and the clouds: *Do you think I have spoken with you for any other reason than that you might appear righteous?* For He did not say, "*That you might become righteous*," but "*That you might appear*"; since you were such even before the temptations, but you appeared so in the things that had happened.

<margin>Deuteronomy 8:2, 3</margin>
<margin>Job 40:8</margin>

<column-break/>

would he be worthy to see the sun in both ways, both in soul and in body, so that the divine power might be proclaimed upon the restoration of his sight—and in the soul’s sight, because he was about to receive the worship of God through faith? But Demas and Hermogenes also, whom he delivered to Satan so that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme, have suffered something similar to those previously mentioned. And the man in Corinth who had his father’s wife is delivered by him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord. It is not a wonder, then, if the matters concerning the hardened Pharaoh, who was surrounded by such great punishments, are also managed by the goodness of God. Let these things be said by us for the present, as they occurred to us, concerning the phrase: *The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh*. But if anyone, maintaining a sense of piety toward God, finds better things, and things in no way touching upon impiety, with testimonies from the divine scriptures, those should rather be used.

->And in other writings concerning the same subject.<-

I also turn my attention to the matters in this passage: whether, just as the physicians of those bitten by rabid dogs draw the venom to the surface, so that it does not spread within and destroy the man, they produce more difficult conditions and inflammations; in this way God, through His own medical art, draws out the wickedness hidden and nesting in the depths of the soul to the outside, so that it becomes manifest by being exposed, in order that after this it may subsequently receive healing. I consider the words in Deuteronomy to be of this sort, being in this manner: *And you shall remember the whole way which the Lord your God led you, this fortieth year in the wilderness, so that He might afflict you, and test you, and that the things in your heart might be discerned, whether you would keep His commandments or not; and He afflicted you, and pinched you with hunger, and fed you the manna, which you did not know, and your fathers did not know; so that He might announce to you that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding through the mouth of God shall man live*. Observe in these things that God afflicts and tests so that the things in each person's heart may be discerned, as they were indeed present, but stored up in the depths, and coming into the open through the afflictions. Such is also that which was declared to Job by the Lord through the whirlwind and clouds: *Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might appear righteous?* For He did not say, "*So that you might become righteous*," but "*So that you might appear*"; that is, being such a person before the temptations, you might appear so in the things that happened.

<summary>Origen argues that God's "hardening" of Pharaoh's heart was a form of divine medicine intended to bring hidden wickedness to the surface for eventual healing, comparing it to how a doctor draws out venom. He uses examples from Deuteronomy and the story of Job to show that trials are meant to reveal a person's true character rather than change it.</summary>

# THE PHILOCALIA OF ORIGEN. CHAPTER XXVII.

### And again in another volume, in the same notes on Exodus.

<margin>Romans 2:4, 5, 6.</margin>
One of our predecessors <note>literally "one of those before us," likely referring to a previous Christian teacher or commentator</note> used to say, in order to soothe the difficulty of the question at hand, that kind masters, when showing great patience toward their sinning servants, are often accustomed to say: "I have ruined you," or "I have made you wicked." By saying this, they mean that their own kindness and patience became the excuse for the servant's increased wickedness. Just as someone might maliciously twist these words to say the master admitted to making the servant wicked, so too the things proceeding from God’s goodness—which became the excuse for Pharaoh’s hardness—are recorded as having "hardened the heart of Pharaoh." This person would further soothe the difficulty by using the Apostle’s words: *Or do you despise the riches of His kindness, and forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But in accordance with your hardness and your impenitent heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation and righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his deeds.*

<margin>Romans 9:22.</margin>
For the same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: *What if God, wanting to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction?* It is as if His longsuffering "bore" the vessels of wrath and, so to speak, gave birth to them. For if, because He was patient and did not punish the sinners but showed mercy, they increased in their outpouring of sin, then He in a sense "bore" the vessels of wrath through His own patience and—if I may put it this way—He Himself made them all vessels of wrath; and in this sense, He hardened his heart. For when Pharaoh is not persuaded despite so many signs and wonders, but resists after such great events, how is his hardness and unbelief not exposed? This hardness and unbelief seems to have arisen from the very power of the miracles.

<margin>John 9:39.</margin>
A similar point was made in the Gospel: *For judgment I have come into this world.* For the Savior did not set out with the purpose of coming for judgment, but the judgment followed as a result of His coming, for those who did not believe in Him after the miracles, and so He came for their fall.

### And after other matters, he continues thus:

The miracles that were performed were a mercy to those who received them and believed, such as the mixed multitude of Egyptians who went out with the people <note>referring to the "mixed multitude" mentioned in Exodus 12:38 who left Egypt with the Israelites</note>; but to the unbelieving, they brought hardness to their hearts. And from the Gospel, one can set forth similar points to those already mentioned, regarding how the Savior seems to some to have been the cause of evils.

<column-break/>

### Again in another volume in the same commentaries on Exodus.

<note>This column is the Latin translation of the Greek text provided on the left. The meaning remains consistent with the first column.</note>

Someone among our associates used to say, softening the problem currently under inquiry, that good masters, being patient with the faults of their servants, are often accustomed to say: "I have destroyed you," and "I have made you a rogue." In this way, with a certain affection, they show that their goodness and patience appeared to provide the cause for why the servants' wickedness increased. Therefore, just as someone can quibble when these things are said, claiming the master confessed that he made the servant a rogue; so the things which proceeded from the benevolence of God, as if they were the cause of Pharaoh's hardening, are said to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh. But they shall be softened by the words of the Apostle in this manner: *Do you despise the riches of His goodness, and sustenance, and patience, being ignorant that the kindness of God leads to repentance? But because of your hardness, and a heart that knows not how to repent, you heap up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, and of the declaration, and of the justice of God; who will render to each according to his works.* The same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: *But if God, willing to show His wrath, and to make His power known, bore with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction:* as if His patience bore the vessels of wrath, and as it were, procreated them. For if, because He was gentle and patient, not punishing the sinners but having pity, those vessels abounded, He Himself made all the vessels of wrath; and thus He Himself hardened their heart. For when Pharaoh does not comply after so many signs and wonders performed, but fights back after so many and such great portents, how is he not proven more hard and unfaithful? Since the hardness and incredulity seem to have been able to arise from the wonders. That in the Gospel is similar: *I came into this world for judgment:* for it was not the Savior's purpose to come for judgment, but from the fact that He came, it was brought about that He came for the judgment of those who did not believe Him after the miracles, but rather He came for their ruin.

### And after other things in this manner.

The wonders performed were a mercy to those receiving and believing them, such as those promiscuous Egyptians <note>original: "promiscuis illis Aegyptiis," referring to the mixed crowd</note> who departed with the people; but to those not believing, they bring on hardness of heart. Then, furthermore, certain similar things can be brought forward from the Gospel, which seem to speak of the Savior to some as the author of evils.

<summary>Origen explains that God "hardens" Pharaoh's heart only in the sense that His divine patience and miracles provide the occasion for a stubborn person to become more defiant, much as a kind master's leniency might be exploited by a wicked servant.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXVII Origen’s *Philocalia*.
<note>The *Philocalia* is a 4th-century anthology of Origen’s writings compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>

<margin>Matthew 11:21, 22.</margin>
*Woe to you, region of Zin <note>original: "Zin", likely a variant or error for Chorazin</note>, woe to you, Bethsaida: for if the signs that were done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for you*, etc. For did God—who foreknew the hardness and unbelief of the inhabitants of the region of Zin, and Bethsaida, and Capernaum, and knew it would be more tolerable for the people of Sodom on the day of judgment than for those for whom he performed miracles in the region of Zin and Bethsaida—see that because of these things it would be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the Tyrians and Sidonians than for these?

->And after other things.<-

<margin>Exodus 4:22, 23.</margin>
*But you shall say to Pharaoh, Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. And I said to you, Let my people go, that they may serve me; but if you will not let them go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.* It must be said, therefore, to those who think these are the words of a just God, yet from the bare literal wording <note>original: "nuda dictione" / "κατὰ τὸ πρόχειρον τῆς λέξεως"</note> believe the heart of King Pharaoh was hardened so that he would not let His people go: How is He just, who hardened the heart and yet threatens that unless he lets them go, He will kill his firstborn son? For if they are pressed, they will be forced to admit He is evil. Then again, they will be overturned by other passages and led to the point where they do not cling to the bare wording, which in their opinion cannot defend the justice of the Creator <term>Opifex: a term for God as the 'Maker' or 'Demiurge'</term>. Finally, if they are now compelled to weigh these things, they reach the point where they no longer find fault, but affirm that He is good. Therefore, those who think they understand the phrase, *The Lord God hardened the heart of Pharaoh*, must be asked: Do they think these things were truly spoken by God through Moses, inspired by the divine spirit, or falsely? For if falsely, God will be neither just in their opinion, nor true; nor indeed will He be God. But if truly, let them consider whether He does not rebuke him as one possessed of free will <term>arbitrii liberum: the capacity to choose between different courses of action</term>, saying: *But if you will not let him go*. And elsewhere, <margin>Exodus 10:3.</margin> *How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?* This is said to Pharaoh to put him to shame for not showing reverence—not because he was unable, but because he was unwilling. And what is said by Moses to Pharaoh, <margin>Exodus 9:29, 30.</margin> *That you may know that the earth is the Lord’s; but as for you and your servants, I know that you have never feared the Lord*, signifies that they will eventually fear Him. This indeed has force against those who wander from the right opinion concerning the goodness of God, and who introduce the idea of a "perishing nature" <note>A reference to Gnostic views that some people are created with a nature that is inherently incapable of salvation.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Matthew 11:21, 22.</margin>
Woe to you, region of Zin, and to you, Bethsaida; for if the miracles that happened in you had happened in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for you, and so forth. For since God is the foreknower of the unbelief of those in the region of Zin, and those in Bethsaida, and those in Capernaum, and that it becomes more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for them, why did he perform the wonders in the region of Zin and in Bethsaida, seeing that because of these things it becomes more tolerable in the day of judgment for the Tyrians and Sidonians than for these?

->And after other things.<-

<margin>Exodus 4:22, 23.</margin>
But you shall say to Pharaoh, Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. And I said to you, Let my people go, that they may serve me; but if you do not wish to let him go, see then, I will kill your firstborn son. It must be said then to those who claim these are the words of a just God, and who suppose according to the plain sense of the wording that the heart of Pharaoh the king was hardened so that he would not let His people go: How is He just who hardens the heart and threatens, if he does not release them, to kill his firstborn son? For being distressed, they will confess Him to be evil. Then again they will be overturned by other things, and will be led back to not being enslaved to the plain wording, which according to them is able to save the justice of the Creator. Once they are now forced to examine these things under pressure, they will ascend to no longer accusing the Creator, but claiming Him to be good. Those who think they have understood the phrase, *The Lord God hardened the heart of Pharaoh*, must be asked: Do they believe these things are said truly by God, through Moses being divinely inspired, or falsely? For if falsely, according to them God is neither just nor true; and as far as this goes, not even God. But if truly, let them observe if He does not blame him as having free will, saying, <margin>Exodus 10:3.</margin> *But if you do not wish to let him go.* And elsewhere, *How long do you not wish to respect me?* It is said to Pharaoh to make him feel ashamed as one not respecting, not because of being unable, but because of not wishing. And that which is said by <margin>Exodus 9:29, 30.</margin> Moses to Pharaoh, *That you may know that the earth is the Lord’s, and you and your servants, I know that you have never yet feared the Lord*, shows that they will fear; which is fitting against the heterodox <note>original: "ἑτεροδόξους", those holding different/wrong opinions, likely referring to Marcionites or Gnostics</note> concerning the goodness of God, and the idea that there is no such thing as a "perishing nature."

<summary>This page presents Origen's argument for human free will, reconciling God's "hardening" of Pharaoh's heart with divine justice by suggesting the biblical language implies Pharaoh's own stubbornness rather than a lack of choice. It also addresses the problem of why Jesus performed miracles in cities he knew would not repent, contrasting them with Tyre and Sidon.</summary>

# ORIGEN’S Philocalia, CHAPTER XXVII.

### From the second volume of the Commentary on the Song of Songs.

Pay attention also to this: that the sun, though it is bright and shining, appears to be the cause of darkening <note>original: "μελανεῖν" / "denigrandi" — to turn black or tan</note>, not because of itself, but because of the one who, as we have explained, is darkened. In the same way, the Lord never hardens the heart of Pharaoh without the cause being present in Pharaoh himself—he who wore down the life of the Hebrews with harsh labors, with mud, and with brick-making, and with all those works, not only those in the mountains and hills, but also those in the plains. For being made "material" <note>term: "material" (hylikos) — in Origen's thought, this refers to a person focused entirely on physical matter rather than spiritual reality</note> by his own vice, and living entirely according to the flesh, being a friend to the mud, he wished to make the Hebrews work the mud as well, since he did not keep the governing part of his soul <note>term: "governing part" (hegemonikon) — the highest part of the mind or soul that makes decisions</note> pure from the mud. Therefore, just as mud is hardened by the sun, so was he hardened by the rays of God as He looked upon Israel.

<column-break/>

*Again, from the second volume of the Commentaries on the Song of Songs.*

Observe this as well: that the Sun, while it is clear and bright, seems to have the cause of blackening, not through itself, but on account of him who, as we said, is blackened. Thus the Lord never hardens the heart of Pharaoh [arbitrarily], since the cause of this hardening is in the man himself, who exhausted the life of the Hebrews with hard works, with mud, with the baking of bricks, and with all works—not only those in the mountains and hills, but also those in the fields. For having become in a certain way "material" by his own fault, and living in every way according to the flesh, a friend to the mud, he wished also to make the Hebrews soak the mud, for he did not have the principal part of his soul pure from the mud. Indeed, just as mud is hardened by the Sun, so was he hardened by the rays of God as He watched over Israel. That these things are specific to that passage, and that a bare history is not merely being proposed there, will be plain if anyone notices that when the children of Israel were distressed and groaned, they groaned neither because of the brick-factory, nor because of the mud, nor because of the straw, but because of the *works* <note>Origen distinguishes between the physical "mud" and the spiritual "works" or "labors" that represent a state of soul</note>; and their cry ascended to God, not from the mud, but again from the works. Therefore the Lord heard their groaning, though He does not hear the groaning of those who cry out to Him not from their works, but from the mud and earthly actions.

->THE END.<-

<summary>Origen uses the analogy of the sun hardening mud to explain that God's "hardening" of Pharaoh's heart was a result of Pharaoh's own materialistic and cruel nature rather than a change in God's character. He argues for an allegorical rather than a purely literal reading of the Exodus narrative regarding the labors of the Israelites.</summary>

### Annotations on the first book of Origen against Celsus.

Page 1. line 17. **Beloved of God, Ambrose** <note>original: Φιλόθεε Ἀμβρόσιε</note>] We have learned from Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* book 6, chapter 22) that this man flourished around the times of Caracalla, Macrinus, Elagabalus, and Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperors of the early 3rd century AD</note>. As far as I can gather from conjectures, he was a native of Alexandria. He was also a Marcionite <note>A follower of Marcion, who held that the God of the Old Testament was different from the God of the New</note>, as Jerome testifies in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the entry for *Ambrose*: **Ambrose was first a Marcionite**; and he had also imbibed the depravity of the Valentinian error <note>A form of Gnosticism</note>; **In this also Ambrose [followed] the things of the heresy of the mind of Valentinus**; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* book 6, chapter 18. Suidas says he was addicted to both heresies; but being convicted and illuminated by the truth, the side of which Origen had taken in disputation, he laid aside the former opinion he had entered into concerning matters of faith, and embraced the most certain Ecclesiastical rule of believing and living: **Who, having striven to come to the knowledge of him, departed from the heresy of Valentinus and Marcion**; Suidas in the entry for *Origen*. **Being refuted by the truth preached by Origen, and having his mind illuminated as if by light, he drew near to the word of Ecclesiastical orthodoxy**; Eusebius, ibid. **Later he was corrected by Origen**; Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* in *Ambrose*. And this happened perhaps at that time when Origen the Orthodox, and the heretics Megethius, Marcus, Drosorius, Valens, and Marinus, were disputing among themselves concerning the dogmas of the Christian Religion, with the Philosopher Eutropius having been chosen as the judge of the discourse: to which dialogue you will find the title *On the Right Faith in God* attached. But whether it is truly Origen’s or not—since Rivetus has said, "It is not easy to judge"—we shall discuss in another place. At any rate, an uncertain author added a preface to the same work, quite appropriate to the matter we have at hand. "Sometimes," he says, "heretics came to him to dispute, and when a frequent disputation had been instituted, he so prepared many gentiles (whom he had persuaded to detest the insane worship of Idols) that they obtained the crown of Martyrdom: among these also was Ambrose, who, having become a rival <note>in the sense of a zealous follower or emulator</note> of Origen, and having been instructed by him in our decrees, separated and removed himself from the heresy of Valentinus and Marcion." As far as I know, only Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* in *Ambrose*) has related the nobility of his family in express words: **But he himself was a most noble man.** Indeed, he and many others have supplied us with no small proofs of both his dignity and his wealth—

<column-break/>

**By his zeal, and expenses, and urging, Origen composed very many Treatises for him**; Jerome, ibid. **But he died before Origen; and in this he is blamed by many, because, being wealthy, he did not remember his own friend, who was old and poor, when he was dying**; Jerome, ibid. **Ambrose, whom he [Origen] caused to turn from the error of Marcion to the true faith, urged Origen to write commentaries on the divine scriptures, having provided him with seven and more shorthand writers, and their expenses, and an equal number of calligraphers; because of which, he was always demanding the work from him with a greater and unbearable zeal; wherefore in one letter Origen calls him his "taskmaster,"** Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* in the entry for *Hippolytus*. **From that time also the beginning of the commentaries on the divine scriptures was made for Origen, with Ambrose urging him on to the greatest extent, not only with countless encouragements and through words and exhortations, but also with the most abundant supply of necessities. For more than seven shorthand writers were present for him as he dictated, succeeding one another at appointed times; and no fewer book-writers, together with girls who had been trained in calligraphy, for all of whom Ambrose provided a necessary and abundant supply of provisions.** Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* book 6, chapter 22.

Photius disagrees concerning the truth of this matter, in *volume* 121, speaking of Hippolytus. **It is said that he also used to address the people in imitation of Origen, with whom he was especially familiar and a lover of his words; so that he even urged him to write commentaries on the divine scriptures, and provided him with shorthand writers to take notes, and as many others writing for beauty, for whom he himself was the provider of the expense; and serving him in these things, he demanded the work from him without excuse; whence he was called "taskmaster" by Origen in one of his letters.** It is credible that either Photius, or those on whose authority he reports these things, fell into this error from a poorly understood passage of Jerome in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* in the entry for *Hippolytus*. If you read it, I have no doubt that you will agree with me.

Suidas in the entry for *Origen*, and Nicephorus Callistus (book 5, chapter 15), have also mentioned the same munificence along with many others. But how much he profited in good literature, and how successfully secular and Christian learning [met] in him—

# Annotations on Book I.

Jerome and Origen have taught us where he lived. For the former passed judgment on his writings as being not unworthy of a learned man. <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἀκομψῶς ἐν τῇ εὐφυΐᾳ ἐγένετο, καθὰ αἱ πρὸς Ὠριγένην τότε δηλοῦσιν ἐπιστολαί.</note> **"He was not without elegance in his natural talent, as the letters written to Origen at that time reveal."** Jerome in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* under the entry for "Ambrose." Origen also, relying on a man of such exceptional erudition, granted him permission to correct what he had written as he saw fit; for at the end of the letter which he had sent to Africanus concerning *Susanna*, he has these words: *"He greets you who was the assistant in dictating the letter, and was present for it all, correcting what he wished—my lord and holy brother, Ambrose."* In another letter concerning the same man, Origen wrote these things, from which you may understand that he was a student of all branches of learning: <note>original Greek: Ὁ ἱερὸς Θεῷ, καὶ γνησίως ἀνακείμενος Ἀμβρόσιος...</note> **"The man sacred to God and sincerely devoted, Ambrose, having urged many things—who, thinking me a friend and very thirsty for divine things, challenged me by his own industry and love for studies. Whence he has so far surpassed me that I am in danger of failing to meet his demands. For it is not possible to dine without comparing texts, nor after dining is it permitted to walk and rest the little body; but even in those times we are forced to study literature and refine the copies. Nor is it permitted for us to sleep at night for the sake of bodily care, extending our literary labors far into the night."** Suidas under the entry for **Origen**. The aforementioned authors have committed to memory the singular piety of the man: the former in his preface to the *Gospel of John* says: *"And yet, what do all these things mean? You will say, coming upon these writings, O Ambrose, truly a man of God, and a man in Christ, and one who strives with all his might to be spiritual, and no longer merely a man."* The latter [Jerome] in a letter to Marcella says: *"Ambrose—by whose provision of paper, expenses, and secretaries our 'Man of Adamant' and 'Brazen-Guts' <note>The Greek nicknames Adamantius and Chalcenterus refer to Origen's unbreakable endurance and tireless work ethic.</note> explained so many innumerable books—relates in a certain letter which he had written to the same man from Athens, that he never took food in Origen's presence, nor ever went to sleep, unless one of the brothers made the sacred scriptures resound; he did this by day and by night, so that reading followed prayer, and prayer followed reading."* What have we, creatures of the belly, ever done like this? We, whom if the second hour <note>About 8:00 AM.</note> finds reading, we yawn, rubbing our faces with our hands, holding our stomachs, and as if after great labor, we occupy ourselves again with worldly business. Truly, he advanced so far in faith and constancy that he did not fear to confess Christ and suffer the punishments that would follow, <note>original Greek: καὶ θείας ἐξομολογήσεως ἐπίσημος ἐγένετο·</note> **"and he became distinguished for his divine confession of faith."** Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* under "Ambrose." <note>original Greek: Τὸν γε μὴν Ῥωμαίων αὐτοκράτορα Ἀλέξανδρον...</note> **"When the Roman Emperor Alexander [Severus] had completed thirteen years of rule, Maximinus Caesar succeeded him. He, out of hatred toward the household of Alexander, which consisted of many believers, raised a persecution and ordered that the leaders of the churches alone, as those responsible for the teaching according to the Gospel, be put to death. At that time Origen also composed a work 'On Martyrdom,' dedicating the book to Ambrose and Protoctetus, a presbyter of the parish in Caesarea, because a no ordinary trial had overtaken them both in the persecution. In which trial, the story holds that the men distinguished themselves in their confession of faith."** Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, Chapter 27.

<column-break/>

There remains another eulogy for so great a man; if I were silent about it, the very stones with which the temple of God is built would cry out, and its inner chambers, more than the lashes of the Furies, would pierce my ears with an angry voice. My pen has acted and hastens to commit the purpose of such a pious mind to letters once and again, and to commend it to the most noble youth.

->**AMBROSE LIVED DURING THE REIGN OF SEVERUS; HE WAS WEALTHY, BORN OF A NOBLE LINEAGE, HOLY, LEARNED, A PATRON, AND LIKEWISE A DEACON OF THE CHURCH.** Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* under "Ambrose."<-

However, it will be my concern—whom nature seems to have fashioned too harshly to be amazed by others or to flatter them—to also uncover his blemishes, and to more sorrowfully deplore his slips. For Origen himself, in the letter he wrote to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, performs penance for why he wrote such things, and refers the causes of his rashness to Ambrose: because he brought into public view things that had been produced in secret. Jerome to Pammachius and Oceanus, *On the Errors of Origen*. I would certainly wish that what Naso <note>The poet Ovid.</note> boasts regarding the body, I could promise regarding the characters of men:

> There shall be no blemish in an excellent body:

but to both their own deformity and baseness adhere; and a characteristic of certain souls is an excessive love and admiration.

It escapes no one even moderately studious of history that several men of the same name lived under the Emperors Trajan and Hadrian. Spartianus mentions Celsus the Jurist, whom the Emperor had as an assessor among others, in his life of Hadrian. *"When he gave judgment,"* he says, *"he had in his council not only his friends or companions, but also legal experts, and especially Julius Celsus."* Another Celsus...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

The aforementioned author has reported to us that Celsus, a man of Consular rank, lived at that time; *Palma* and *Celsus*, who were always his enemies, came into the pledge of adoption. The same author says in the same place and elsewhere: *Wherefore Palma at Terracina, Celsus at Baiae, Nigrinus at Faventia, and Lusius on a journey, were killed by order of the Senate, against the will of Hadrian, as he himself says in his own biography.* <note>Referring to the "Augustan History," a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note> We have received the memory of a third and fourth Celsus from Origen, who in the first book against Celsus provided us with some knowledge of both, on page 8: <note>original Greek: Δύω δ' παρειλήφαμεν Κέλσους γεγονέναι Ἐπικούρειους...</note> *We have understood that there were two Celsuses who were Epicureans, the first during the time of Nero, and this one during the time of Hadrian,* and further down. The most illustrious Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and ecclesiastical historian.</note> is of the opinion that Lucian, a man most devoted to the Epicurean sect if ever there was one, dedicated his *Alexander*, or *The False Prophet*, to this man (for he wrote it at his encouragement). No one has doubted this matter who has either read that book carefully or looked upon it with clear eyes; for in it, Lucian briefly encompassed the life, crimes, absurdities, and deceptions of Alexander of *Abonoteichos*, a most notorious impostor. I believe Celsus was greatly delighted by this discourse, since all Epicureans are accustomed to dispel and scatter the frauds and impositions of such scoundrels with laughter and hisses. 

You will perhaps object: How can these things be? For Celsus mentions *Marcellina* (book 5, p. 272), who was a female follower of the Gnostic sect; having found an opportunity for "the highest perfection" under *Anicetus* (that is, if I am not mistaken, a little before the times of Antoninus the Philosopher <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note>), she went to Rome and destroyed many of the Orthodox, as witnessed by *Irenaeus* (book 1, ch. 24) and *Epiphanius* (Heresy 27). But Lucian flourished during the reign of Trajan; <note>original Greek: λέγει δ' ἤκμαζε...</note> *it is said he was at his peak under Caesar Trajan and beyond.* Many authors by no means to be despised are of this opinion. The most celebrated *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> responds (book 2, ch. 15, *On Greek Historians*): *It seems otherwise to me, and not for a slight reason: for Lucian mentions Marcus Caesar and the Marcomannic war waged by him. The passage is in Alexander, or the False Prophet:* <note>original Greek: Διαπέμπεται ἐν Γερμανίᾳ...</note> *A message was sent into Germany, while the war was at its height, when the Divine Marcus was already engaged with the Marcomanni and Quadi.* You see that he not only mentions the war waged with the Marcomanni and Quadi, but calls Marcus "Divine," that is, *Divus*; this proves he had departed from nature and had already been placed in heaven. Therefore, it ought to be placed beyond controversy that Lucian lived during the age of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, since he relates conversations which he himself had both with Alexander the False Prophet and under Commodus, the son of Antoninus the Philosopher, seeing as he calls Marcus "Divine." I judge that the same must be determined regarding the age of Celsus. Even the most illustrious Baronius, when he had cited this very 

<column-break/>

passage of Lucian concerning the war waged with the Marcomanni and Quadi (in the year of Christ 171), says: *As for what pertains to Lucian, who wrote these things, although everyone affirms he was famous in the times of the Emperor Trajan; nevertheless, from these same writings it is clearly established that he reached as far as these times, and even surpassed them.* You are quite right, *Baronius*; but I am less pleased with what you hold regarding the year 145. Furthermore, that the origin of these people (that is, the Ophites <note>A Gnostic sect that revered the serpent.</note>) was so ancient that they were not later than Valentinus, can easily be known from the fact that Celsus—who lived in the times of Hadrian (as the same Origen testifies) and undoubtedly those of Antoninus—being well-versed in their dogmas, was accustomed to throw the same at the Catholics as an insult, as if they were common to all Christians. For it is not at all credible that either Celsus or Lucian flourished in the times of Hadrian; since the latter mentions the war undertaken with the Marcomanni and dedicated the aforementioned book to Celsus. Between these times—namely, the Empire of Hadrian and the Marcomannic war—I think a space of about fifty years intervened; therefore Origen cautiously added, *And further down.* 

But you will say, how is it clear to you that such a friendship was contracted with this Celsus? I answer: First, the most celebrated men agree with me, *Caesar Baronius* (in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year of Christ 132) and *Gerardus Vossius* (in the book *On the Sects of Philosophers*). Second, it is evident from Origen and Lucian that a certain man so named wrote *Against Magic*. Third, in both authors, he is known as an Epicurean. Fourth, they agree in time. And so much for his age.

As for his writings, since they seem to reek equally of impiety and erudition, if I were to judge them worthy of both blame and praise, who (excepting perhaps Lucian, his closest friend) would take it badly? And we have the testimony of this matter at hand in *The True Word* <note>original Greek: Ἀληθῆ λόγον (Alethe Logos), the title of Celsus's lost work against Christianity.</note>, a book divided into two volumes and most pleasant to read: whether you desire to know the disputes of the philosophers and the most ancient Christians; or to test your own strengths; or if you wish to honor Origen with your praise as he strenuously refutes him. Besides this book of Celsus which I have already mentioned, titled *The True Word*, he wrote another most learned work *Against the celebrated arts of the Magi*; concerning which, hear Lucian in *The False Prophet*: <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ...</note> *There are also many other things devised against this, all of which it is not necessary to mention, lest we seem tasteless, and especially those things which you wrote in two books "Against the Magi"—writings at once most beautiful and most useful, and capable of bringing wisdom to those who encounter them.*

# Annotations on Book I.

...those who are knowledgeable, having set forth sufficient evidence and much more than this. <note>original Greek: νουντας, ἱκανὰ παραθεμένους καὶ πολλῷ τούτων πλείονα</note> Our Origen agrees with this, who (in Book 1, page 53), relying greatly on his own conjectures, does not hesitate to attribute to him a certain book written *Against Magic*: *You see how through these things he as it were admits magic, which I do not know if he is the same one who happened to write several books Against Magic.* <note>original Greek: Ὁρᾷς ὡς διὰ τούτων οἱονεὶ παραδέχεται μαγείαν...</note> In Book 4, page 186, he doubts whether he was also the author of two books which he says were composed against the Christians: *But he who is better able to judge Plato than Celsus the Epicurean (if indeed this is the same man who also composed the two books Against the Christians) perhaps out of a desire to contend with us, inserted things he did not believe, and named them divinely inspired.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ κρίνειν μᾶλλον Πλάτωνος δυναμένους...</note> Besides those already mentioned, he promised to give another work *On the Precepts of Living Well*: whether he finished it himself, or if once finished it perished, I simply do not know. At the end of this work you have Origen attesting to it, in Book 8, page 428: *Regarding Celsus promising to make another composition after this one, in which he promised to teach how those who wish and are able to obey him ought to live.* <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τῷ τοι ἐπαγγελλομένῳ τὸν Κέλσον...</note> To which Sect he truly adhered, we understand more certainly and fully from Origen and Lucian; the former of whom everywhere charges him with the dogmas and errors of Epicurus <note>Epicurus was a Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure/absence of pain was the highest good and that gods do not intervene in human affairs—views often seen as atheistic by early Christians.</note>, in Book 1, pages 8, 10, 16; Book 2, page 97; Book 3, pages 131, 141, 159; Book 4, pages 200, 213; Book 5, page 232. The latter [Lucian] professes that he wrote the *Pseudomantis* <note>The "False Prophet," a satirical work by Lucian of Samosata.</note> for this reason: so that he might leave his gratitude toward Celsus testified, and vindicate Epicurus who was most dear to him: *I have thought it worthy to write these few examples out of many, my dear friend, both to gratify you, a companion and friend, and one whom I have admired most of all for your wisdom, your love for truth, the gentleness of your character, your fairness, your calm life, and your dexterity toward those you associate with; but more so, which is also more pleasing to you, to avenge Epicurus, a man truly sacred and divine in his nature.* <note>original Greek: Ταῦτα, ὦ φιλότης, ὀλίγα ἐκ πολλῶν δείγματα...</note> For indeed Alexander <note>Alexander of Abonoteichus, the "False Prophet" attacked by Lucian.</note> was so hostile to Epicurus and his followers that to someone asking what Epicurus was doing in the Underworld, he said, *he sits in the mud wearing leaden shackles.* He burned his books in the Forum; he even warned the people of Pontus, Christians, and Epicureans to *drive them out with stones*; and he never gave an oracle to an Amastrian because many Epicureans lived in that city: and no wonder; *For against whom else would a man who was a grace-less charlatan and a friend of trickery, but an enemy of truth, more justly wage war than against Epicurus, a man who looked into the nature of things and alone knew the truth within them? For he was a friend to those around Plato, Chrysippus, and Pythagoras, and there was deep peace toward them. But the harsh Epicurus (for so he named him)*

<column-break/>

*was an enemy, and rightly so, setting all these things at naught with laughter and jest.* Lucian, in the same place. *And in this time also, concerning the things written against us by Celsus the Epicurean, he composed the "True Word" in eight books in number.* Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 36. I have cited all these things for this reason: so that I might rouse *Hornius* <note>Georg Horn (1620–1670), a historian who mistakenly categorized Celsus as a Stoic.</note> from the very deep sleep in which he is held, who, disregarding the reliability of Histories, reckoned Celsus among the Stoics. For he says thus (Book 5, chapter 4, *History of Philosophy*): *But Origen, who wrote against that sacred head, Celsus the Stoic, was a most learned philosopher who accurately searched out all the Sects.*

You see, Reader, what kind of and how great an adversary of the Christian religion the fire of glory and the malevolence of demons has raised up—an adversary endowed with genius, cultivated in the disciplines, equipped with philosophy, adorned with eloquence, most well-versed in the Historians, and enriched with every kind of literary abundance; to all of which was added a malice that sharpened his tongue and infected the whole strength of his wit with poison, as if he had drunk the flowing blood of *Nessus* <note>In mythology, the blood of the centaur Nessus was a deadly poison that killed Hercules.</note>: but God, providing for His own, animated Origen—an equal to the stronger, superior to that man—to join the battle; who, taught to brandish the spear and hurl back the darts, threw down the attacking enemy with one hand almost faster than he stripped and carried off the spoils of the fallen with the other. Hence that saying of Jerome (in the *Letter to Magnus, a Roman orator*): *Celsus and Porphyry wrote against us: Origen responded most bravely to the former; Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinarius to the latter; of whom Origen wrote eight books; Methodius proceeded up to ten thousand lines; Eusebius and Apollinarius composed twenty-five and thirty volumes. Read them, and you will find us most unskilled in comparison to them, and, after the leisure of so much time, we can scarcely remember, as if through a dream, what we learned as boys.*

Page 4, line 51. **The Love of Christians**] Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, page 4. *They charge us with three crimes: atheism, Thyestean feasts <note>Accusations of cannibalism, named after the myth of Thyestes.</note>, and Oedipean mixtures <note>Accusations of incest.</note>.* Origen mentions a fourth in this place, namely, sedition. Celsus noted everything, saying *that Christians do and teach the things pleasing to themselves in secret*, page 5. To this, and to the remaining crimes by which Christian piety seemed to be crushed, the Fathers respond: and

First, they repel the accusation brought by the infidels: *Justin*, in the *Second Apology*, and elsewhere; *Athenagoras*, *Embassy for the Christians*, page 5; *Tertullian* very often in the *Apologeticus*.

Second, *Justin*, in the *First Apology*, page 50. *For I myself,* he says, *rejoicing in the teachings of Plato...*

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

<margin>Athenagoras, *Embassy*, near the end. Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book 3. Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*: "Among us there is no devouring of human flesh; you who hope for such things have become false witnesses." <note>original: Παρ' ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνθρωποφαγία...</note> Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 9.</margin>

...rejoicing in these teachings, when I heard the Christians being slandered but saw them fearless in the face of death and all other things considered terrifying, I reflected that it was impossible for them to exist in vice and a love of pleasure. For what lover of pleasure, or person lacking self-control, who considers the devouring of human flesh to be a good thing, could embrace death so as to be deprived of his own goods? Would he not rather attempt by every means to live the life here forever and escape the notice of the rulers, rather than denounce himself to be put to death? <note>This is a quote from Justin Martyr's *Second Apology*, explaining his conversion.</note> **Let your error blush before the Christians, who do not even include the blood of animals in our edible feasts, and who for that reason also abstain from things strangled or that die of themselves, lest we be contaminated by blood in any way, even if buried within our entrails. Finally, among the trials of Christians, you even offer them sausages distended with blood, being perfectly certain, of course, that it is unlawful among them, and by this means you wish to make them deviate. Furthermore, what kind of thing is it, that you believe those whom you are confident shrink from the blood of a beast to be gasping for human blood? Unless perhaps you have found it to be sweeter.** <note>Quoted from Tertullian's *Apology*, c. 9.</note> The same author, chapter 7: **We are called the most wicked of men, regarding the sacrament of infanticide, and the fodder therefrom, and incest after the banquet; which the dogs that overturn the lamps—the pimps of darkness, forsooth—procure for the shamelessness of impious lusts. Yet we are always called so, and you do not take care to unearth what we have been called for so long: therefore, either unearth it, if you believe it, or do not believe it, since you have not unearthed it. From your own dissimulation it is prescribed that it does not exist, because you yourselves do not dare to unearth it.** And Minutius Felix in *Octavius*: **For us, it is not lawful to see nor to hear of homicide; and we guard against human blood so much that we do not even know the blood of edible beasts in our food.**

Regarding the third point, Minutius Felix likewise says: **And concerning the incestuous banquet, a great fable has been lied about against us by a gathering of demons, so that it might stain the glory of our modesty with the aversion of a hideous infamy.** Likewise Justin, who in his *Second Apology* rejects the aforementioned outrages onto the disciples of Simon, Menander, and Marcion; and he thinks they gave the cause of suspicion to the Gentiles: "But whether they also perform those infamous deeds of myth—the overturning of the lamp, the unrestrained mixtures <note>referring to sexual promiscuity</note>, and the devouring of human flesh—we do not know; but we do know that they are not persecuted nor put to death by you, even on account of their doctrines. We also have a treatise composed against all the heresies that have existed, which, if you wish to read it, we will provide." <note>original: εἰ δὲ καὶ τὰ δύσφημα ἐκεῖνα...</note> Eusebius follows the same in book 5, chapter 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. See also Epiphanius, *Heresy 48*, at the end. But—

<column-break/>

—what if the servants of Christians, faithful neither to Christ nor to their masters, in order to avoid death and punishments, babbled many things at the whim of the executioners, such as the Christians by no means committed? I have learned that this certainly happened once from Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 1): "Some ethnic <note>pagan</note> servants of our people were also seized (since the governor publicly ordered all of us to be sought out), who, through a snare of Satan, fearing the tortures which they saw the saints suffering, and with the soldiers urging them to this, falsely accused us of **Thyestean feasts** <note>A mythological reference to eating children</note> and **Oedipodean intercourse** <note>A reference to incest</note>, and things which it is lawful for us neither to speak of nor to think of; nor even to believe that any such thing ever happened among men. When these things were rumored, everyone was driven to a beastly rage against us, so that even if some had previously been moderate due to kinship, they then became greatly incensed and were gnashing their teeth against us." <note>original: Συνελαμβάνοντο δὲ καὶ ἐθνικοί...</note> But the Christians gave kisses <note>the "Holy Kiss" or Kiss of Peace</note>: (*Justin, Apology 2, page 97*) indeed they called each other brothers and sisters: (*Tertullian, Apology c. 39; Athenagoras, Embassy; Clement, Stromata 5*) and from this, perhaps, the Pagans snatched an opportunity for slandering. Do you wonder? I will tell you. If any Christians sinned gravely, the leaders of the Church used to cast them out; they, moved by grief, would entreat for pardon, and roll themselves before the knees of the brothers and the feet of the priests; hence phrases of this sort occur everywhere among Ecclesiastical authors: **To be rolled before the Presbyters, and to wipe the boots of the brothers by wallowing.** Such was the discipline of the ancient Christians; which, however, Caecilius in Minutius, having snatched an opportunity from this gesture of the body, thus slandered: **Others, he says, report that they worship the genitals of the prelate and priest himself.** See Rigaltius on the passage in Minutius.

Regarding the fourth point, Tertullian, *Apology* chapter 39: **This gathering of Christians is rightly indeed unlawful, if it is like unlawful ones; rightly to be condemned, if anyone complains of it on the same grounds that a complaint is made against factions. For whose destruction have we ever met? We are the same when gathered as when dispersed; the same as a whole as we are as individuals; harming no one, saddening no one. When the honest, when the good meet, when the pious, when the chaste are gathered: it is not to be called a faction, but a Senate.** The same author, chapter 30: **Looking up thither, Christians, with hands spread out, because they are innocent, with head bare, because we do not blush, finally without a monitor, because we pray from the heart, are always praying for all Emperors; for a long life for them, a secure empire, a safe house, brave armies, a faithful Senate, an honest people, a quiet world, and whatever are the prayers of a man and of a Caesar.** Likewise Justin, *Apology 2*, page 64.

In the following centuries, I find the use of miracles of this kind to be rarer. And no wonder: for

That those Heretical impostors were most skilled in **Magic**, one may see by consulting either Epiphanius or Irenaeus: the former in Book 1, Heresy 22, concerning Menander; the latter in Book 1, Chapter 21, regarding the same man. Likewise, the former in Book 1, Heresy 23, concerning Saturnilus; and Irenaeus in Book 1, Chapter 23, on the same. *They use, he says, both images, and incantations, and invocations, and all other forms of <term>periergia</term> <note>original: "periergia" — a Greek term for "superfluous arts" or "curiosity," often used to denote sorcery or meddling in the occult.</note>.* For the deceptions of Marcus and his arts of seduction, see Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapters 8 and 9, and Epiphanius, Heresy 34. Hear also how much the Carpocratians <note>A Gnostic sect from the 2nd century known for their radical views on social and religious laws.</note>, by practicing wicked arts, harmed the name of Christian: Epiphanius teaches in Heresy 27: <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τούτῳ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἐπίκειται...</note> *For this reason it is imposed upon them to be called Christians, so that they might be a scandal to the nations and turn away the benefit of the holy Church of God and the true preaching through their unlawful deeds and unimaginable wickedness; so that the nations, observing their repeated acts of lawlessness, might think that those of the holy Church of God are also such as they, and might turn away their hearing (as I said before) from the truth of God's teaching, or seeing some of them, might blaspheme against all alike. And for this reason most of the Gentiles, wherever they see such people, because they present themselves to us in a fellowship of nonsense, or opinion, or hearing of the divine word, have a certain impression imprinted on their hearing, a confusion arising from these unlawful and unholy deeds.* Irenaeus also teaches this in Book 1, Chapter 24.

Secondly, very many called the truthfulness of Christ and the Apostles into doubt, and believed them to be most skilled in the **Magical arts**; to refute whom, a long series of miracles seemed entirely necessary. Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity.</note> slanders Christ more than once, claiming he learned the Magic art from the Egyptians. The Jews and Simon the Samaritan (the father and teacher of all Heretics, if you believe Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 30) suspected the same. The leaders of Heresies and the defenders of pagan worship also asserted this with all their might. *But if they say the Lord performed such things through phantasms <note>i.e., illusions or mere appearances rather than physical reality.</note>; leading them back to the Prophetic writings, we shall demonstrate from them, etc.* Irenaeus, Book 2, Chapter 57. For which reason [they claim] he did not suffer, but that a certain Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry his cross for him, and this man, through ignorance and error, was transfigured by him so that he was thought to be Jesus himself, while Jesus himself took the form of Simon and stood by mocking them. Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 23; also Epiphanius, Heresy 24. Regarding the other enemies of the Christian religion, you may make a conjecture from Julian alone <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note>, whom you may hear in his usual manner in the sixth book of Cyril of Alexandria,

<column-break/>

disparaging the miracles of Christ: <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς, ἀναπείσας...</note> *But Jesus, having persuaded the worst part of you, has been celebrated for little more than three hundred years, having performed during his lifetime no work worthy of hearing, unless one thinks that healing the lame and the blind, and exorcising those possessed by demons in the villages of Bethsaida and Bethany, are among the greatest works.* What he thought of Paul you have in the third book: *But even Paul, who surpassed all the sorcerers and deceivers of all time everywhere;* likewise regarding Peter in the ninth book; and regarding all of them in the tenth book: *Whence it is likely that your apostles, not having handed down to you from the beginning—the first who believed—everything revealed by divine power, themselves more technically contrived these sorceries for you, to show how those after them might publicly display the workshops of this sorcery and loathsomeness.* Arnobius, in Book 1 of *Against the Heathen*, page 15: *Perhaps another will encounter us with many other such calumnious and childish words: "He was a Magician; he performed all those things with secret arts; he stole the names of powerful Angels and remote disciplines from the inner shrines of the Egyptians."*

Thirdly, how else could one refute the persistence of the most foolish scoundrels—especially those who boasted that they were now equal, now superior to Christ—except through the demonstration of divine powers and an abundance of miracles? Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 24, says of the Carpocratians: *These men, he says, are in no way inferior to Jesus. For their souls, coming from the same cycle and therefore similarly despising the creators of the world, were deemed worthy of the same power, and return again to the same place. But if anyone should despise the things that are here more than he did, he can be better than him.* Epiphanius, Book 1, Heresy 27; and Irenaeus likewise, Book 2, Chapter 57: *But saying that they have souls from the same cycle as Jesus and are similar to them, and sometimes even better, when brought to the works which he performed for the benefit and strengthening of men, they are found to perform nothing such, nor similar, nor anything that could come into comparison in any respect.*

Fourthly, perhaps some received these benefits of God with an ungrateful mind and abused the singular kindness of the deity, either by demanding payment, or by denying help at their whim, or by doing good only to the wealthy, or by claiming the glory of such great power for themselves: moved by all these things, God unwillingly withdraws what he freely communicated. Page 5, line 53. **As to Socrates**] Understand those dangers into which he threw himself, such as when he defended Theramenes from the fury of Critias and his soldiers (*Diodorus, Book 14*); or when he alone forbade the votes to be carried against the law, which all the other Prytanes <note>Executive officers in ancient Athens</note> attempted with great effort out of hatred stirred up against the Generals (*Xenophon, Greek History, Book 1*); or when he showed himself unyielding to the Thirty Tyrants and did not lead Leon out from Salamis to suffer the death penalty as they had ordered (*Plato, Apology of Socrates*); or when he strenuously protected Alcibiades at the siege of *Potidaea* (*Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades; Plato, Charmides*); or when he took Xenophon upon his shoulders after he fell from his horse in the battle at Delium and carried him for many furlongs to save him (*Diogenes Laertius, Life of Socrates; Strabo, Book 9*); or when Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon stirred up the people with false accusations and took the life of an innocent man (*Plato and Xenophon, Apology*).

Others record that he died in the Metapontine faction: as Porphyry does in the *Life of Pythagoras*. Others report that after the house in which they frequently met was consumed by fire, he escaped, having been saved by a bridge made of his disciples' bodies; but when he felt himself bereaved of them, he was overcome with grief and took his own life. *Laertius, citing Hermippus*, reports that he brought aid to the Agrigentines: but that he, while the others turned to flight, was slaughtered in a field of beans which he was trying to go around (*Laertius, Life of Pythagoras*). And the people of Heraclea banished Anytus on the very day he arrived." *Tertullian, Apology, ch. 14.* "But Socrates was condemned for the reason that he was destroying the Gods. Plainly, of old—that is, always—truth is an object of hatred. Nevertheless, the Athenians later punished the accusers of Socrates in repentance for their sentence, and placed his image in a bronze temple; the rescinded condemnation is the proof."

Indeed, the citizens so hated those who falsely accused Socrates—viewing them as having reached the peak of villainy—and so turned away from them, that they would neither provide them with fire to light a flame, nor answer their questions, nor share the water of the baths with them. Consequently, the bath-attendants were forced to pour out that water as if it were defiled; until at last, unable to bear the hatred, the accusers hanged themselves.* See also *Diodorus*, book 14. And read, if you have the time, Socrates himself warning his enemies of future miseries in *Plato’s* *Apology of Socrates*, pages 38, 39. All these things the Athenians suffered through God’s vengeance, because they branded Socrates with the mark of Impiety and Atheism <note>original: "Atheismi"</note>, and delivered to death a man conscious of no crime. Truly, holy and learned men, led by discernment rather than rashness, have judged far differently: *Justin*, Apology 2, page 55; also in his *Exhortation*, page 48; *Arnobius*, book 1, *Against the Heathen*, page 14; *Clement of Alexandria*, *Exhortation to the Heathen*, page 15; *Numenius*, in his book *On the Secrets of Plato* as cited by *Eusebius*, book 13, chapter 5 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*; and *Lactantius*, book 5, chapter 15. I would not wish you to wonder, Reader, or be struck by more than usual horror, if even in these days some—whose minds are clouded by mist and darkness, and to whom the more upright way of worshipping God the Best and Greatest is not so clearly known—are driven as if by a gadfly <note>original: "παροιστρεῖ"</note> and agitated by furies against modest men. Because they know these men are little pleased by their own blindness and obstinacy, they hurl charges of Scepticism and atheism <note>original: "ἀθεότητα"</note> at them; though from this you may be certain that even in ancient times it was a settled custom to envy the glory of the learned and to condemn men of the highest integrity and innocence. Nor do we dwell on the fact that certain people might appear irreligious, or even Atheists. *In reality they are not Atheists; but, when they perceived that false and horrendous attributes were being attached to God by some, they preferred to believe in no such deity rather than one like that: if He were honored with true attributes, they would be so far from not believing that, if no such deity existed, they would pray for one.* Thus says the most illustrious Hero, Baron Herbert, in his book *On Truth*.

Page 6, line 1. **Nor against Pythagoras** <note>original: "Ὁυδ' ἐπὶ Πυθαγόρᾳ"</note>] *Strabo* in book 9 and *Polybius* in book 2 of his *Histories* mention this sedition that arose between the Pythagoreans and the Italians. That they truly repented is clear from *Iamblichus*, chapter 35, *On the Life of Pythagoras*: *After many years had passed, and those around Dinarchus had died in another danger, and Litagus—who had been the chief leader of the insurgents—had also died, a certain pity and repentance fell upon them, and those who remained wished to—*

<column-break/>

*—bring back the exiles. Having sent for elders from Achaia, they negotiated through them with those who had been cast out, and deposited their oaths at Delphi. There were about sixty of the Pythagoreans who returned under the guidance of the elders; among them were some who, having been brought back, practiced medicine and healed the sick through diet, becoming leaders of the aforementioned method. It also happened that those who were saved were exceptionally well-regarded by the masses at that time, when laws were being discussed against transgressors.* I have cited these things chiefly so that those most wicked scoundrels, whose entire effort is spent in insults and hatred of the learned, might restrain their madness. May they extinguish the torches lit everywhere for the burning of good literature with the power of the tears poured out from a contrite heart. For after reading these instances of those who repented too late, the sting of conscience pricks more sharply, the fear of the deity strikes the mind, and infernal dread agitates them; they spend restless days and nights, and finally, distrusting their own deceits, they may spare the innocent to favor themselves. By changing their counsels, they shall appease the common father and avenger of the just, before vengeance breaks forth like lightning from a cloud, or changes His former leniency into fury. Surely anyone would endure such miseries with a more level mind if he were wretched by his own fault rather than the rage of others; or if the author of such great evil had brought a doctrine equal to that impiety. But the facts speak for themselves: *Cylon of Croton (whom I, on account of his harsh manners and unbridled license, would judge a hard man, or rather scarcely a man at all),* having amassed great wealth, thought himself far most worthy of the *Pythagorean* brotherhood. But *Pythagoras*, having examined the man’s nature, immediately dismissed him; lest Cylon, through his lust for power, should tear apart the peace he cherished and the harmony of the disciples, and contaminate the most holy discipline with his crimes. Hence the house of Milo was set on fire, in which they had gathered for the sake of piety and exercise; hence the ranks of the associates were scattered; hence those who wish to defile the symbols and obliterate them foam at the mouth; hence the insane greed of Cylon meditated stealing the "Golden Verses"; hence the cries and wailing, whereby the venerable sacrament of the five-year silence was broken—which the old man commanded for no light reason, nor did the youth profess it lightly. Do you wonder? I speak of things not unknown: that foam, which internal discords and the rising storms have stirred up, delights to mock and insult the waters. *The Dwarf laughed, looking down at Hercules from the edge of the well.*

"Ivory," says Plato, "is not a pure gift to God." *What then? Are those things and precious fabrics also impure? Nay, rather, whatever can be corrupted or stolen is not a pure gift to God; but just as he saw this—that one ought not to bring anything to a living being that comes from a dead body—why did he not see that one ought not to bring a bodily gift to the incorporeal?* More correctly, if I am not mistaken, Theodoret interpreted it in the aforementioned Discourse: "That the lawgiver of the Athenians <note>Referring to Plato's ideal laws.</note> almost entirely forbade the making of statues is easy to learn from the facts. First, he forbade anyone from privately preparing images of the Gods; then he cast out gold and silver as enviable materials that provoke sacrilege; he called ivory troublesome, and said bronze and iron belong to war, not to the sculpting of Gods. He commanded that idols be carved only from wood and stone, materials that are easily carried away and sufficient to persuade those who see them not to think them divine, nor to worship things that are cheap and common." I could confirm this conjecture of a most learned man with innumerable arguments which a diligent reading of Plato will supply, if it were my task; but the most elegant poem of Xenophanes of Colophon calls me elsewhere:

> But mortals think that Gods are born,
> And have their own senses, voice, and body.
> *At mortales homines gigni putant Deos*
> *Sensibus æquales, & voce, & corpore nobis.* <note>The Latin translation of the Greek verse above.</note>

There follows from the same author:

> But if oxen or elephants had hands,
> Or could draw with their hands, or accomplish works like men,
> Horses would draw the forms of gods like horses, and oxen like oxen,
> And they would make such bodies
> As they themselves possessed.
> *Si manibus possent uti tauri, atq; elephantes,*
> *Pingere vel manibus, vel, quæ nos, facta referre,*
> *Jam similes se equis divos bobusq; videres*
> *Cornipedes pinxisse, & equos taurosque bicornes,*
> *Haud alio factos, quàm quo ipsi corpore nunc sunt.* <note>The Latin translation of the Greek verse above.</note>

Numa, imitating Moses, passed a similar law: as Clement of Alexandria relates in *Stromata* Book 1. Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch agree with this, giving the same reason for the introduced law

It is said there are eighty punishments, which the one to be initiated must pass through by degrees: for example, first, to swim through much water for many days; then to throw himself into fire; then to live in a desert and fast, and other such things, until, as we said, he passes through the eighty punishments, and then finally they initiate him into the more perfect rites, if he survives. *Which last words indicate that some rare individuals, and very few indeed, passed through all those kinds of punishments and trials without danger to their lives.* See also *Casaubon in his notes on the passage of Lampridius, Suidas under the entry "Mithras."* The *Cave* in which they were accustomed to be initiated is mentioned by *Justin, Dialogue with Trypho, and the Apology.*

Who is so rude and unskilled in syllogisms that he would say *Scaliger's* opinion is confirmed by this passage? Who would attempt to prove the aforementioned censure by this kind of reasoning? How, I ask, can anyone by art, even if greater than the great *Scaliger*, gather certainties from doubts and manifest things from the obscure? Would not children, who have tasted Logic with only the tips of their lips, be stunned upon hearing these things? Was it in *Origen's* interest to introduce a *spurious* writer in defense of the *Jewish* nation? Did he not for that very reason allege *Philo's* judgment on *Hecataeus*, so that the truth of the matter might stand more firmly, inasmuch as a wavering opinion would shake it less than stabilize it? In truth, if anyone were to weigh this very passage of *Origen*, or the opinion of *Herennius*, he would judge this censure of the most illustrious man to be rash. When you have leisure, read *Eusebius, Book 1, Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 9*, where *Philo* embraces the theology of the *Phoenicians* and the fabulous narrations about the Gods with both arms; he rejects with nausea the allegories of the *Greeks*. Meanwhile, "he worships gods who are base and the very vice of all wickedness" (Eusebius, ibid.) and he professes that he was led by the disagreements of the *Greeks* to place faith in the writings of *Sanchuniathon* <note>A Phoenician author whose works are lost</note> concerning the Phoenician Gods, and that he wrote three books on the disputes of the Greeks. Forgetting the *Jews*, he calls the *Phoenicians* and *Egyptians* the most ancient of the Barbarians. He agrees with their dogma on the origin of the world in the same place: "such is their cosmogony, introducing outright atheism" <note>original: τοιαύτη δὲ αὐτῶν ἡ κοσμογονία ἄντικρυς ἀθεότητα εἰσάγουσα</note>, which plainly exterminates all divinity. If you consider these things, you would say it is least to be hoped that he would have brought forth the praises and encomiums of the *Jews* with a fair mind—he who had so stubbornly adhered to the trifles of the *Phoenicians* and had rejected all allegories about the *Greek* deities, from which they sought to win some favor for their religion. Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, an ancient Physician who wrote medical precepts in Heroic verse <note>original: "carmine Heroico," referring to dactylic hexameter</note>, took care to prepare an amulet for curing the semitertian fever <note>original: "morbum Hemitritæum," a form of malarial fever</note> using these characters.
