Against the throbbing of the heart, <term>Kardiagkon</term> <note>Greek: "heart-strangler" or "heart-pain"</note> is effective, but I do not understand how that name would procure the grace of God for itself. Marcellus, in *On Empirical Medicines*, chapter 21: Against the throbbing or pain of the heart, a wonderful remedy, which you shall write on a leaden <gloss>read: tin</gloss> plate, <term>"Kardiagkon chariagkon, kariagkon"</term>, and you shall fumigate the amulet with storax resin, and hang it from the neck by a string: it will be so beneficial that you will be amazed. Against heart pain, he orders the following "song," as he calls it, to be recited: *Corce, corcedo, stagne, shepherds found you, gathered you without hands, cooked you without a hearth, ate you without teeth; three virgins in the middle of the sea had a marble table placed, two were twisting, and one was untwisting: just as this was never done, so may Gaioseia never know the pain of the heart.* But how much do the names of God, such as *Adonai, Sabaoth*, etc., differ from *Corce, corcedo, stagne*, and similar trifles? Yet words of both kinds have had their results. The same can be said of the amulet mentioned by Alexander Trallianus, book 9, chapter 29. <term>Taking a piece of iron, make the ring itself octagonal, and write thus on the octagon: "Flee, flee, behold the bile, the lark seeks you." On the character placed below, write then on the head of the ring. Having had much experience with this, I thought it a failure not to pass on such a power having an antipathy toward the disease.</term>

<image-desc>A rectangular diagram containing a large stylized letter 'Z' with three small circles or dots arranged horizontally at the top and three at the bottom.</image-desc>

Regarding such incantations, Cardano decided nothing, not knowing whether the words or the faith were beneficial; book 18, *On Wonders*. It so happened to me that once, while I was writing these things, blood from a cut lip could be restrained by no art, especially since I was eating; I had applied salt, I had bound it; nothing worked. I used that incantation

<column-break/>

which is taken from the Passion of the Lord; and immediately, to my wonder, it ceased; neither while speaking nor eating did blood appear, even though the place then pained me greatly and the wound was visible. You will wonder—I myself do not know whether the words or the faith were beneficial. I will not disdain to include the words; they are these:

> "Blood, stay in you, as Christ did in himself,
> "Blood, stay in your vein, as Christ in his pain,
> "Blood, stay fixed, as Christ when he was crucified.

Grotius, however, and Hammond (in the Annotations on Matthew, chapter 12) ascribe this to God, not to the words. Therefore, exorcisms of this kind have often had their result, not because any power was situated in the pronunciation of the syllables, but because the true God wished to be known and called upon by those names especially, and therefore exerted his power only when it was established by the clearest speech that He, and not any of the pagan gods, was being invoked.

Page 17, line 43. <term>To the Unknown</term> <note>Greek: "Agnostois"</note>.] The books from which we could draw knowledge of this matter have perished; yet you might not ineptly refer here to what Iamblichus has in the book *On the Mysteries*, in the chapter *On Divine Names*. Lay aside, therefore, suspicions falling away from the truth, by which you suspect that the Egyptian language is applied there only where the one invoked is Egyptian, or used the Egyptian tongue. Rather, consider that since the Egyptians were the first of all to obtain the presence and participation of the Gods, he who invokes the Gods prefers to do so by the Egyptian rite, when they are called by the Egyptian rite. Nor should it be said that these "barbarous" and obscure names of the gods are certain devices of jugglers and charmers; for in what way would things that are most closely joined to the Gods also join us to them, and have powers almost equal to the celestial beings, if they were fantastic fictions without which no work is accomplished in sacred matters? Arnobius, book 1, *Against the Heathen*.

"A name is therefore a significant sound by convention, without reference to time, of which no part is significant when separated." and a little later, "By convention, because none of the names exist by nature, but only when it becomes a symbol." Arnobius, book 1. *Against the Heathen*. *Although, if you look at the truth, no speech is perfect by nature, and similarly none is defective: for what natural reason is there, or what law written in the constitutions of the world, that this should be called a wall, and this a chair, since they have no sexes distinguished by feminine and masculine genders? Nor could any most learned man teach me what "THIS" [masculine] and "THIS" [feminine] actually are? Or why one of these designates the male sex, while the following applies to feminine types? These are human agreements, and certainly not necessary for everyone for the purpose of making speech:* and a little later, *Do you not say "THESE LEATHER BOTTLES" in one way [feminine], and "THESE LEATHER BOTTLES" in another [masculine], and "SKY" [masculine] and "SKY" [neuter], etc.* In Plato, a name is *a kind of teaching instrument, and a means of distinguishing essence,* an instrument adapted for teaching things, and by which the nature of things themselves is discerned. Plato in the *Cratylus*, page 388. Would this be the strongest of arguments for us, or rather that one: that we received them from certain barbarians (and the barbarians are more ancient than us), or that because of their antiquity it is impossible to examine them, just as with barbarian words." And not far from the end of that work he determines, *that there is some power greater than human which established the first names for things;* and on page 438. he professes that he is utterly ignorant of the reason for assigning a name, especially if it regards the Gods: *What would anyone think it a solemn thing to know, why it is correct to call that river Xanthus rather than Scamander; or if you wish, concerning the bird which he says,*

*Is the knowledge trivial or low, as to whether it is more correct for the same bird to be called Chalcis rather than Cymindis? These things are perhaps too great for me and you to find out.* (Plato in *Cratylus*, pages 391, 392.) and pages 400, 401. Finally he was doubtful; he proves nothing of those things he spoke, nor does he stick to his own discourse, even if it is supported by some probability, pages 428, 440. He ascribed to the supreme wisdom of Pythagoras the task of having imposed names on all things. Cicero, book 1. *Tusculan Disputations*. Theodotus, *Epitome from the Theophanies*. Nigidius taught most subtly (as Gellius says) that names are not conventional, but natural. See Gellius, book 10. chapter 4. *Attic Nights*. Origen thinks that the angels fashioned various dialects, and assigned a different language to each of the provinces over which they ruled. See the Annotations to page 19. When we heard or read these and other such "stings of clever and delightful idleness" (as Gellius once said), and saw in these scruples neither any solid benefit pertaining to the conduct of life, nor any end to the searching, we approved of Ennius's Neoptolemus, who indeed says:

> "One must philosophize only a little, for it does not please me at all."

Saturn, because he "saturates" himself with years; Mars [Mavors], because he "turns great things" [magna vertit]; Minerva, because she "diminishes" [minuit], or because she "threatens" [minatur]; Venus, because she "comes" [venit] to all things; Ceres from "bearing" [gerendo]; how dangerous is this habit? For you get stuck on many names. What will you do with Vejovis? What with Vulcan? **Page 19, line 26.** *Truly it shall be found* <note>original: "Ὅντως εὑρεθήσετ'"</note>] Origen in *Homilies on Numbers*, 11. So that, for example, there was one who then impressed the Babylonian language upon one man, another who gave the Egyptian to another, and another the Greek; and thus those very leaders were perhaps the princes of the different nations, who also appeared to be the authors of the languages and speech. However, the language originally given through Adam—which we believe to be Hebrew—remained in that portion of men which did not become the part of any angel or prince, but which remained the portion of God.

It is given to our race to be sacrificial offerings to expiate public dangers; now I will give the legions of the enemy with myself to be slaughtered for Mother Earth and the gods of the Underworld.* Having been devoted therefore with the same prayer and in the same habit in which his father had ordered himself to be devoted, he said: *He drove before him dread and flight, slaughter and blood, the wrath of the celestial and infernal gods, and he would touch the standards, weapons, and arms of the enemy with funeral curses, and the same place would be the ruin of himself and the Gauls.*

I would be excessive if I were to speak of the Phoenicians, Tyrians, Cyprians, Egyptians, Scythians, Indians, Massagetae, Tauri, Thracians, Germans, Ionians, Massilians, Persians, Spartans, and Athenians, or if I were to recount—using the testimonies of geographers, historians, and poets—the men who were customarily sacrificed in Crete, Sicily, Salamis, Britain, Tenedos, Rhodes, and Rome. Nor is it possible that I would delight the minds of readers by explaining the Roman *Februa* <note>purification rites</note>, lustrations, expiations, substitutes, and the formulas of devotion in which they invoked the Gods as *Averrunci* <note>Averters</note> and *Dispellentes* <note>Drivellers-away</note>. Rather, I think I shall achieve more if I recite the words of the most illustrious Herbert <note>Lord Herbert of Cherbury, a 17th-century philosopher</note> concerning the sacred rites which the nations devised to expiate crimes: *But the East Indians, above all others, show themselves strenuous in performing this duty: for at a certain solemn time of the year they betake themselves to the woods, and using a sharp rock or flint, they draw blood in great quantity, almost to the point of fainting, crying out meanwhile that the fuel and causes of their evils lurked in that blood; which they therefore testify they pour out for the expiation of their sins, and thereafter*

<column-break/>

*striving to be reconciled with God.* But to what purpose do you tell these Greek fables and the savage sacrifices of barbarians? Why do you boast of a plague among the people driven away by a heavier pestilence? Why do you thrust into my ears and hammer home the image of sterile fields watered by the blood of their own masters, or the roaring of the sea made peaceful by the sobs of the slaughtered? As if a fever could settle a plague, or a storm could calm a tempest. Now a stronger hand has wrenched away the knife;

Or are the mysteries of the Christian faith so shrouded in darkness that we find it necessary to borrow light from the Gentiles and Pagans? Who, once the Sun has risen, has need of

to see things far off?

Truly, if it should please you to look upon this discourse which we are about to have concerning these dogmas with attentive eyes and mind, you will at least gain this benefit: that you may laugh at and firmly despise the youth who babbles in vain. If it was a custom among all peoples, scattered everywhere on earth, to appease the Gods they worshipped with the blood of men, and by the same means to avert punishments and expiate committed crimes; where in the world will you find a man of such hardened forehead <note>i.e., such audacity</note> who will deny *Jesus* Christ, the sacrificial victim for the human race, the driver-away of evil, and the origin of salvation? For any dictate of nature binds most strongly and demands the obedience of the whole mind: nor is it in anyone's power—except perhaps for one or two of the most wicked of all mortals—to shake off its yoke. If you do not give credit to this dictate, you will seem to despise all others in comparison to yourself, and to claim for yourself alone a knowledge such as God has neither impressed generally upon the mind nor promulgated through his heralds. You will also seem to accuse the Best and Greatest God of both fraud and <term>respecter of persons</term> <note>original: προσωποληψίας - partiality</note>: as if He had either freed you alone from a most grave error while scorning the inhabitants of the whole world, or, unmindful of you, had implanted a common knowledge of Himself in the rest. You will also seem to hold in low esteem the most beautiful idea of divine benevolence, illustrated and adorned by the testimonies of all nations. For where would anyone flee when the sting of conscience pricks sharply, natural fear invades, and the vengeance of an angry deity pursues? Nowhere, except to the solemn rites of expiation; the use of which—whether we wish to appease God or remove guilt—was taught not by some dark and <term>faint</term> <note>original: ἀμυδρά</note> notion, but by a universal and clear one, and not by a charlatan, but by the heralds of the Word. # Annotations on Book I.

Having heard these things, they raise their crests <note>a metaphor for becoming arrogant or prideful</note>; and not without irritation do they rush to attack the sacrifices of the Gentiles: for it does not escape them that anyone [provided it is granted that the Gods they worshiped could be appeased by such victims] would, by the same reasoning, accept Christ as both a <term>lytron</term> <note>original: λύτρον; a ransom or price paid for freedom</note> for sins and a propitiation for all the wrath of God. Among these critics, the most acute, *Crellius* <note>Johannes Crellius (1590–1633), a prominent Socinian theologian who argued against the traditional view of Christ's satisfaction</note>, holds the first rank; hear him in his *Response to Grotius, chapter 10*: "*Plutarch, when in his book 'On Superstition' he had severely censured the sacrifices of the Gentiles as partly ridiculous and partly impious and cruel—such as human victims—adds: 'There is no disease of the soul so full of many errors and disturbances, and so filled with opinions disagreeing and fighting among themselves, as superstition.' What wonder, indeed, if the Demons—to whom, as we have noted elsewhere, the Gentiles sacrificed, and who in that darkness held a kind of empire in the world—brought it about that both the rest of divine worship and the system of sacrifices were perverted, and more was attributed to those external things than God willed to be attributed to them, either before the Law or under the Law. Furthermore, those victims of the Gentiles were not usually supplied to men by the Deity himself, nor were they believed to proceed from his singular love toward men; but they were usually offered by men themselves to an angry Deity to appease his wrath and earn his favor. But this victim of ours, of whom we treat, was supplied by God himself for the eternal happiness of men—while they were thinking of no such thing—and proceeded from his immense love toward us, and was accomplished by the sole will, so to speak, of Christ himself.*"

Do you rejoice, *Crellius*, that *Plutarch* so seriously laments and so sharply accuses the inhumanity of *Cytherus*, *Amestris*, and the *Carthaginians*? Consider this with yourself: they slaughtered infants, boys, and men at fixed times, or rather at any time at all; even when no plague pressed upon them, nor any atonements were commanded by the Gods, nor public calamity demanded it. He places the blame on the unbridled license and cruelty of one or two nations; he does not refute the victims of the rest, which were commanded by God for the public good. I should like to add that *Plutarch* elsewhere praised the purpose of those who, to consult the common good and repel public calamities, were ready to bring death upon themselves or offered themselves to be slain by others. For so he says, in *Precepts of Statecraft*:

> — <term>You could see no greater thing, nor anything truly more striking for a statesman, nor more useful in another way, than a man exposing himself in the midst of terrors, but also taking thought, and sailing, and speaking first, and alone (among many)</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ ὀκ ἂν μείζοντα... This passage emphasizes the self-sacrifice of a leader for the state.</note>
> <term>I heard that by killing, you drove away the plague—but even if he shares in the dullness of the many.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἤκουσα δὲ κτείναντες...</note>

<column-break/>

<term>undertaking dangers on their behalf. For this is noble, and in addition to being noble, often the virtue and wonderful spirit within a man has darkened the anger against everyone, and scattered the fearful and bitter nature of the threat. Such things the Persian seems to have experienced toward Bulis and Sperchis, the Spartans.</term> <note>original Greek: τοὺς κινδύνους ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν... referring to the Spartan envoys who offered their lives to Xerxes to atone for the murder of Persian heralds.</note> 

But truly, if *Plutarch* calls into question the sacrifices of the nations, or the milder rites of expiation, I have an answer ready. One man censures what everyone else praises, and a wise man mocks those wiser than himself. Then [you say], "those victims of the Gentiles were not from the Deity," etc. Fine words, *Crellius*: did not *Diana* command *Iphigenia* to be sacrificed? Did not the Soothsayer (whom they believed to be God's minister) command *Metella*? Did not *Gortynian Apollo* command *Menippa and Metiocha*? Did not the *Pythian* command the father of *Cyanes*? Did not the oracle command the daughter of *Ambarus*, and *Praxithea*, *Theope*, *Eubule*—the dear pledges of *Leos*—and the son of *Lophri Parthenomenis* to be slaughtered and sacrificed? And these were believed to proceed from the singular love of the Gods toward men, even though *Crellius* denies it a thousand times over. 

For the Gods provided these and similar remedies for all troubles to the people who consulted them: the Gentiles, mindful of their own safety and more obedient to the Gods, made use of these. By this art they repelled plagues, famines, and storms; and if by chance they fell into the same calamities again, they went to the Temples, entreated the Priests, consulted the Oracles, and wearied the Gods with prayers until they broke them; so that the hand which had inflicted miseries in anger might, being more benign, remove them. 

Indeed, as far as can be understood from the histories of the ancients, they supposed that sometimes neglect of worship, sometimes slaughter and injustice, and any other very grave sins provoked the full wrath of the Gods. Therefore, the unhappy crowd of men, languishing under a double sense of guilt and calamity, and ignorant of the remedies by which they might appease the Gods, turn away evils, and procure internal peace, asked the Gods that they—who had thrown darts because of violated laws—might spare the unhurt and apply a remedy to the wounded. Hence the Gods, pitying the human race, announced things pleasing to the people: now they command beasts to be slaughtered, now the wicked to be sacrificed, and sometimes they say they will repel calamities on the condition that someone offers himself voluntarily to be sacrificed, and by his own death atones for the crimes and punishments of the rest. Finally, I would gladly ask: Why did the Gods devise these remedies? Why did they make their intentions known? Why are evils stilled once the sacrifice is made? Unless it had pleased the Gods to reconcile men to themselves by these means. For the examples of ancestors, and even license and impunity, encouraged the mind of every individual prone to evil to commit any sins. Hence men first dared to defile themselves...

What should be thought concerning Epiphanius and Damascenus <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian</note>, I confess I am utterly uncertain, partly because they themselves do not declare from where they drew these things, or by whose authority they committed them to writing; and partly because *Africanus* <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, an early Christian traveler and historian</note>, who flourished in the two hundred and twentieth year after Christ, and deserved very well of the Church for his learning, and who wrote letters to Aristides *Concerning the harmony of the genealogies in the Gospels* <note>original Greek: Περὶ συμφωνίας τῶν ἐν Εὐαγγελίοις γενεαλογίας</note> (*Eusebius, book 1, chapter 6, Ecclesiastical History*) and spoke with those who proclaimed themselves "the Lord's own" (that is, the kinsmen and fellow-tribesmen of Christ), mentions neither Panther nor Barpanther, although he refutes the opinions of others concerning Christ's genealogy which seemed to stray from the truth, and explains what he had received from the elders: (*Eusebius, book 1, chapter 8, Ecclesiastical History; Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 11*) and partly because Herod burned the genealogies of the Hebrews, which had been recorded in tables, so that he might procure honor for his own lineage. (*Eusebius and Nicephorus, ibid.*) Indeed, the Jews relate monstrous things concerning Stada and the son of Pandeira: (see *Buxtorf under the words* **Pandera** and **Stada**; likewise *Schickard in the Preface to Tarich, from page 84 to page 97*) whom they say was killed on the eve of Passover because of magic and evil deeds: namely, so that by this fiction they might burn a mark of infamy upon our Jesus. From these sources the most illustrious *Vossius* thinks Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note> learned to slander the Savior (*Dissertation on the Genealogy of Jesus Christ, chapter 5*). But it becomes more credible from the Talmud that this opinion was drawn from the Jews: for (in the twelfth chapter of the Sabbath) the son of Mary is called **ben Pandera** <note>Hebrew: בן פנדירא, "Son of Pandera"</note> and the reason is given that Pandera had lain with Miriam: where there is no doubt that Pandera is Joseph, surnamed Panther or Pantherus, which he had received from his parent Jacob. For what wonder is it if he called Jesus the son of Pandera, or Panthera—that is, of Joseph—when the same Jesus is called the son of Joseph in the Gospel itself, as we have seen before? It follows from the same, page 39: But here, as I think, he had not drawn this from Apocryphal writings, but rather had received it from the Jews, whose assistance he seems to have used in attacking the Christian religion.

With all due respect to such a great man, I would say that I was led by the reading of Origen and Epiphanius to feel otherwise.

For this reason, they say, the priest was commanded by the lawgiver himself to have bells, so that whenever he enters to minister, the one striking and hearing the bells might hide this <unclear>frightful thing</unclear>, so that his phantom-like face might not be detected." It is credible that from these, or similar books of the Gnostics, Celsus, Epiphanius, and Damascenus drew what they hand down concerning the Savior's birth and genealogy: the former sought out whatever was profane, spurious, and fabricated to bespatter the worshippers of the Christian religion with stains; the latter, whatever [seemed to support] the truth...

Page 29, line 31. **On Vultures** <note>original: "Περὶ γυπῶν"</note>] *Ambrose, Book 5 of the Hexameron, chapter 20.* We have spoken of the widowhood of birds, and how that virtue first arose from them. Now let us speak of integrity <note>chastity/virginity</note>, which is asserted to be such in many creatures that it can even be detected in vultures. For it is denied that vultures indulge in copulation, or are mixed by any conjugal use or the lot of nuptial joining; and thus they conceive without any seed of males, and give birth without union. Those born from these proceed into a great age of long life, so that the series of their lives is extended up to a hundred years; nor does the end of a narrow lifespan easily overtake them. What do they say, those who are accustomed to mock our mysteries when they hear that a virgin gave birth? Do they think a birth impossible for an unwed woman whose modesty no intimacy with a man had violated? Is that thought impossible in the Mother of God which is not denied to be possible in vultures? A bird gives birth without a male, and no one refutes it; yet because Mary, betrothed to a man, gave birth, they make a question of her modesty. Do we not notice that the Lord first sent forth many examples from nature itself, by which He might prove the beauty of the assumed Incarnation and establish its truth? *Tertullian in his book against the Valentinians; Basil, Hexameron, homily 8; Aelian, Book 2, chapter 46, On Animals. Vives, Commentary on Book 8, chapter 4 of Augustine's City of God.* In my opinion, whoever does not think Plato was somewhat more than a man, or certainly of that best and rarest mark of men, is mistaken.

...they agree, it is not so clear, as Cicero says in Book 1 *On Divination*. In many places, the weighty authority Democritus would approve of the foreknowledge of future events. Those things which Diodorus reports concerning specters seen in Africa will explain his opinion not unsuitably: "A marvelous thing happens concerning this region, both the mainland and the Libya beyond Syrtis. For at certain times, and especially during calms, they see compositions in the air displaying the forms of all kinds of animals; some of these remain still, others take on motion, and sometimes they flee, sometimes they pursue. All of them, having an immense size, produce a wonderful astonishment and disturbance in those who are inexperienced. For those pursuing the men, when they catch them, pour around their bodies, cold and shivering, so that the strangers, being unaccustomed to it, are struck with fear." Diodorus, Book 3 *Historical Library*, page 184. Mela on Mauritania. Kircher, in the book *On the Spectacles of the Rhegians*. Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* and *On the Images of Epicurus*. Apuleius in his *Apology*, and Lucretius throughout: for he asserted that the images of things, wandering here and there, invade and run into the sleeper with such subtlety and vigor that they touch and strike his mind, from which he was able to conjecture about the future.

Page 32, line 44. **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note>] Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 2, *Preparation for the Gospel*: "All the Peripatetics refuted the famous oracles and the divinations wondered at by all as bringing nothing true, and they declared them to be useless," etc. Cicero seems to feel otherwise in Book 1 *On Divination*: "Dicaearchus the Peripatetic took away the other kinds of divination, but left those of dreams and frenzy." Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book 5, chapter 1. Cicero, Book 2 *On Divination*. Tertullian, in the book *On the Soul*, chapter 46: "Aristotle, reciting with a greater opinion of falsehood, also acknowledges the truth": that is, according to the interpreter Pamelius. Although he thinks the greater part of dreams are a lie, yet he also acknowledges the truth in them from time to time. Aristotle, Book 1 *On Divination through Sleep*: "Concerning the divination occurring in sleep and said to happen from dreams, it is neither easy to despise it, nor to be persuaded by it." For it is established that some have had insomnia <note>here used in the sense of 'dream-visions'</note>, whence they are not to be spurned: "but to see no reasonable cause by

<column-break/>

which this might happen, makes one distrustful; for that God is the sender is absurd, in addition to other irrationality, and that He sends them not to the best and wisest, but to random people. Tertullian, in the book *On the Soul*, chapter 49: "For if even Aristotle notes a certain Hero of Sardinia depriving the 'incubators' <note>those who sleep in a temple to receive a vision</note> of his shrine of visions: it will also be in the lusts of Demons to take away dreams as much as to bring them; so that the fame of Nero as a dreamer, and the distinction of Thrasymedes, proceeded from there: but we also derive dreams from God. What then? Would the Atlantes not dream even from God? Either because no nation is now a stranger to God, with the Gospel shining into all the earth and to the ends of the world. Has fame then either lied to Aristotle, or is there still a reason for Demons: so long as no nature is believed to be immune to dreams?"

When a certain oath was demanded of him by his fellow soldiers for some reason, he affirmed that it was absolutely not permitted for him to swear, for he was a Christian; and he confessed this plainly. At first, he was thought to be joking: but when he persisted in his affirmation, he was led to the Judge; and, since he had confessed the same thing there consistently, he was handed over to chains. However, when the brothers in the Lord came to him and inquired about the cause of this sudden and wonderful change, he is said to have told them how Potamiæna <note>A famous martyr of Alexandria, known for her purity and courage under the persecution of Septimius Severus.</note>, three days after her martyrdom, stood by him at night and placed a crown upon his head, saying that she had interceded for him with the Lord himself and had obtained what she asked, and that it would not be long before he was taken up. Having said these things, and having received the seal of the Lord <note>A common early Christian term for Baptism.</note> from the brothers, he underwent martyrdom for the Lord the following day by being beheaded. Moreover, they write that many other Alexandrians at that time came in crowds to the doctrine of Christ because Potamiæna had appeared to them in dreams and called them to the faith. The most illustrious Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio, a 16th-century Cardinal and ecclesiastical historian.</note> at the Year 205, number 10. The same, Epistle 8, 34, and 54 to Cornelius of the African Synod, concerning giving peace to the lapsed <note>The "lapsed" were Christians who had renounced their faith under persecution and sought readmission to the Church.</note>. Page 35, line 41. **Unbelievable**] Flavius Josephus, book 18, chapter 4, page 621. <note>This is the famous "Testimonium Flavianum."</note> "Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man. I will endeavor to establish what I have said from the fact that Josephus interpreted the prophecy concerning the Messiah, whose coming the Jews were expecting at that time, not as referring to Jesus Christ: but most foolishly applied it to Vespasian, after he saw all the affairs of the Jews going backward. Hear him in book 3, chapter 14, *Of the Jewish War*, page 854: "Vespasian, however, ordered him to be guarded with great security, as if he were about to send him immediately to Nero. Having heard this, Josephus said that he wished to speak with him alone. When all the others had been removed except for his son Titus and two friends, he said: 'You, Vespasian, think you have taken Josephus as a captive deserter; but I come to you as a messenger of greater things. For if I had not been sent by God, would I not have known the law of the Jews, and how it is fitting for generals to die? Do you send me to Nero? Why? Will those after Nero succeed until you? You, Vespasian, are Caesar and emperor, you and this son of yours. Bind me now more securely, and keep me for yourself. For you, Caesar, are master not only of me, but of the land and the sea, and the whole race of men; and I ask for a greater guard for my punishment if I am lying against God.'" Suetonius in *Vespasian*, chapter 5: "In Judea, when he consulted the oracle of the God of Carmel, the lots confirmed him so; that whatever he thought or revolved in his mind, however great it might be, that would be..."

But others among them, sharing the same name, escaped the strange absurdity of those mentioned, not denying that the Lord was born of a Virgin and the Holy Spirit. Yet these, likewise not confessing that he pre-existed as God the Word and Wisdom, were turned back into the impiety of the former group, especially when they were equally eager to observe the physical worship regarding the Law.* Theodoret, book 2 of *Compendium of Heretical Fables*. Damascene, *On Heresies*. But of the first kind of Ebionites, if you believe Grotius, Irenaeus makes no mention. Take the book and read: *Those who are called Ebionites agree indeed that the world was made by God; but regarding the things that concern the Lord, they do not think similarly to Cerinthus and Carpocrates.* Irenaeus, book 1. chapter 26. # ORIGEN against CELSUS.

I said these things, caring for no nation other than to speak the truth; I would speak without being intimidated by anyone, even if I were to be punished by you immediately. For I do not speak on behalf of my own race, nor out of concern for the Samaritans. When I was formerly speaking with Caesar, I said they were deceived by following the Magician Simon <note>Simon Magus, a figure from the New Testament (Acts 8) often cited by early Church fathers as the first heretic</note> from their own race, whom they claim is a God above every principality, authority, and power. I do not know, however, whether Flavius *Josephus* refers to this same Simon and his Samaritan followers in Book 18, Chapter 15 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*. See the *Justinian Code*, Book 1, Title 5, *ON HERETICS, MANICHAEANS, AND SAMARITANS*; the *Justinian Novels* <note>New laws issued after the initial Code</note> *ON THE SAMARITANS*; and the *Theodosian Novels*, Title 2, *ON JEWS, SAMARITAN HERETICS, AND PAGANS*.

Page 68, line 15. **Sicarii** <note>original: Σικαρίοι; literally "dagger-men," a term for Jewish zealots or assassins</note>] *Modestinus*, in Book 6 of the *Rules, ON THE CORNELIAN LAW CONCERNING ASSASSINS*: "By a decree of the Divine Pius <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius</note>, only *Jews* are permitted to circumcise their own sons; if anyone not of that religion does this, the penalty for castration is imposed." *Julius Paulus*, in the *Received Opinions*, Book 5, Title 22, *ON SEDITIOUS PERSONS*: "Roman citizens who allow themselves or their slaves to be circumcised according to the Jewish rite shall have their property confiscated and be permanently relegated to an island. Doctors who perform it are punished by death. *Jews*, if they circumcise slaves purchased from a foreign nation, are either deported or punished by death." Likewise, *Novel* 146. *Pius* therefore granted to the *Jews* what *Hadrian* had denied; for at that time the *Jews* also started a war because they were forbidden from mutilating their genitals, as *Aelius Spartianus* says in his life of *Hadrian*. Unless, perhaps, *Isaac Casaubon* <note>A famous 16th-century classical scholar</note> interpreted this passage of Spartianus more correctly; he believes that by the laws of Domitian, Nerva, and Hadrian, which forbade the emasculation of males, the restriction on circumcision was also included. But what if the *Jews* intended, after the collapse of their Republic, to restore it to its former happiness and renew their ancestral rites? And they hoped they would achieve this better if they were allowed to attract foreigners, whom they would possess as the most faithful defenders of their religion once circumcision was applied; and the farsighted Emperor forbade the mutilation of the genitals of foreigners for this reason? Certainly, many favor this conjecture: some believe the war was undertaken by the *Jews* to build the Temple; others to restore the ancient administration of their Republic. Nor do the constitutions of later Emperors conflict with this, as they repeatedly denied permission to circumcise foreigners. *Justinian Code, Book 1, Title 9, ON JEWS; Title 10, NOT A CHRISTIAN.* *Theodosian Code, Book 16, Title 4. Novels of Leo*, 55.

Page 69, line 21. **Jason** <note>original: Ἰάσωνα</note>] See the Annotations to page thirty-five.

Page 69, line 36. **Phlegon** <note>original: Φλέγων</note>] See Origen, pages 80 and 96. He was a freedman of Hadrian and wrote a Chronicle consisting of sixteen books, containing the events of 229 Olympiads <note>Four-year periods used by Greeks to track time</note>; the last of which ended in the fourth year of Antoninus Pius. *Scaliger*, in his *Observations on Eusebius* at the year 2044. *Vossius*, Book 2, Chapter 11, *On Greek Historians*. *Suidas* under the entry *Phlegon*. *Salmasius* on *Spartianus*. *Photius*, Section 97. From *Stephanus*, under the entry *Tarsus*, it is clear what the main subject of his Chronicles was: "On those things which the seers predict as destruction"; for under each Olympiad he recounted all the prodigies <note>unnatural events or omens</note> that occurred, for which reason he is criticized by *Photius*. But I cannot entirely approve of what the same critic finds fault with—that anxious care in recounting the Olympiads and noting what happened during each. Indeed, I wish the entire Chronicle survived; for much light would undoubtedly be shed on the times of the early Church. And we think this all the more justified because, among other proofs of his diligence, he also mentioned that Eclipse which occurred at the time of the Lord's Passion, as *Vossius* says in the same place. But he says that Christ foreknew future things: was it because He predicted the destruction of Jerusalem or other calamities of that kind? Since those books are lost, this would be mere guessing. Regarding the eclipse of the sun, which happened at the time when the *Jews* nailed Jesus to the cross, his testimony exists most fully in the *Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the Year 2040: *"Jesus Christ, according to the prophecies spoken about him, came to his passion in the 18th year of Tiberius. At which time we also find these things written word-for-word in other commentaries of the Pagans: 'A failure of the sun occurred; Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake, and many buildings collapsed in the city of Nicaea. All these things agree with what happened during the passion of the Savior.' Indeed, Phlegon, who is an excellent calculator of Olympiads, also writes about these things in his thirteenth book, saying: 'In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and excellent failure of the sun occurred, beyond all that had happened before. At the sixth hour, the day turned into such dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and an earthquake in Nicaea in Bithynia overturned many houses.'"* *Origen, Treatise 35 on Matthew.* And *Phlegon* indeed wrote in his Chronicles that this happened in the reign of Tiberius Caesar, but he did not indicate that it happened during a full moon. *Tertullian, Apology, ch. 21*: "At that same moment, while the sun was marking the middle of the world, the day was withdrawn..."

For he says that woman became breathless and pulseless, differing in no way from the dead, except for having a slight warmth in the middle parts of the body. At any rate, the book is titled *The Breathless Woman* by Heraclides; and he said a search was made by the physicians present as to whether she was not yet dead. Later, some followers of Heraclides, wishing to preserve some sign of breathing even if it did not appear, say they called for a clear vessel of water to be placed near the nostrils for an accurate diagnosis, to see if any breath was carried inward and out again. Others command a bowl full of water to be placed on the mouth or belly, for the liquid would be kept perfectly still if no breath were preserved at all. If all women in such a state died, the inquiry would be simple; but since some are saved, our inquiry into the distinction becomes twofold."

# ORIGEN OF ALEXANDRIA against CELSUS.
## Ffff
-> catchword: tarch. <-

...of these things, by which the function of breathing is destroyed, and even more so how those who do not breathe at all still live. For it is believed that living is inseparable from breathing, and breathing from living. Thus, one who lives must certainly breathe, and one who breathes must certainly live; or if this is more difficult, it is not truly so in reality. But the one is easier to manifest. For even those animals that appear like corpses in their pulses seem to draw in no breath from the outside <note>The Greek text discusses the physiological paradox of "breathless" life, likely referring to states of coma or suspended animation</note>. For once this was known and clearly demonstrated by those who investigated the soul of animals, it was also proven that the greatest use of breathing is for the preservation of the innate heat, occurring through cooling and fanning. It is not difficult to conceive of a way for the small amount of heat remaining in them to be preserved through the action of the arteries and the heart—called by some physicians "perspiration" <term>diapnoe: the subtle release of vapors through the skin</term>, just as that through the chest and lungs is called "respiration." It is possible, therefore, that in "uterine breathlessness" <note>original: *hysterikēs apnoias*; a historical medical term for a condition where a woman appeared dead due to "hysteria"</note>, since the whole body is sleeping—as is clearly evident—breathing through the mouth does not occur at all, but it does occur through the arteries. It is also possible that, while occurring, it is so minimal as to escape the senses.

Hence one must wonder: why, among others, **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> and **Origen** <note>The early Christian Church Father</note>, men of the highest erudition, used these and similar instances of no weight? By these they could neither confirm the mystery of the resurrection, nor move the Pagans from the opinion they had conceived concerning matters of faith, nor refute the Heretics, nor stabilize the doubtful and wavering. Even those from whose writings we have drawn these examples of "living again" <term>palimbiois: those who return to life</term> never dreamed of any special influence of the Divine, or a power more than human, which might now call forth the spirit serving the body, or now restore it to its seat when weary of exile. *Hear Pliny in Book 7 of his Natural History, chapter 52: A boy, exhausted by heat and travel, slept in a cave for fifty-seven years; marvelling at the face and change of things, he woke as if on the following day. From this, in an equal number of days, old age came upon him, yet he lasted until his one hundred and fifty-seventh year of life. The female sex seems most susceptible to this evil, through a displacement of the womb; if this is corrected, the breath is restored.* To this belongs that noble story, etc. *Galen*, in the place cited. *Suidas* under the entry "Breathless." *Heraclides* in his book *On Diseases*, *Laertius* in his life of *Empedocles*. Whether, therefore, it was effected by Magical operation or by skill in preparing medicines, so that a body "breathless and pulseless" <term>apnoun kai asphykton</term> was preserved for the space of thirty days: on either count, you will argue most foolishly. For anyone who has happened to read the

<column-break/>

books of either Physicians or Historians would admit that the soul, sometimes forced into straits by an imbalance of the body, recalls its powers within; sometimes by the power of Magic it migrates from the body to serve the deceits of Demons. But no one would attempt to prove the mystery of the resurrection—which presupposes a separation of body and soul made either by force or by the laws of nature—from this common operation of diseases and Mages. Even those who reported to us concerning these types of faints and unusual incarcerations of souls believed that those souls were still enclosed in the body, confined to the arteries and the heart; and the warming members of the body produced that belief: for heat escaping moderately here and there through the pores proved that the same heat was gathered together within.

You will agree with me if you run through *Philostratus*, book four, chapter sixteen, *On the Life of Apollonius*: "And there was this wonder of Apollonius. A girl in the flower of her marriage-age seemed to have died, and the bridegroom followed the bier, crying out as much as one would for an unfulfilled marriage; and all Rome mourned with him. And it happened to be raining while the girl was being carried out. Apollonius, happening upon the scene of suffering, said, 'Set down the bier; for I will make you cease from your tears for the girl.' At the same time, he asked what her name was. Most people thought he was going to deliver a speech, such as funeral orations that stir up lamentations; but he did nothing other than touch her, and having whispered something secretly, he woke the girl from her apparent death. And the girl let out a sound and returned to her father’s house, like Alcestis brought back to life by Hercules. When the girl’s relatives offered him one hundred and fifty thousand pieces of gold, he said, 'Give them to the girl as a dowry.'" And whether he found a spark of the soul in her, which had escaped the notice of those tending her (for it is said that while Zeus was drizzling rain, she was steaming from her face), or whether he rekindled and recovered the soul that had been extinguished—the understanding of this has remained unutterable <note>original: *arrhētos*; secret or inexpressible</note> not only to me, but also to those who were present.

*Philostratus*, as you see, seems to ascribe the return to life of the new bride to the falling rain, which cherished and excited the exhausted and almost lost powers of heat, rather than to that man's Magic. Nor is this foolish: since *Galen*, in that place I cited, says it was a custom among Physicians to place a glass full of water on the bellies of women suffering from this disease; from its movement or stillness, they judged them to be either alive or dead. See *Eusebius against Hierocles*, in the refutation of the fourth book.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

...human and divine, when they are present, they are not seen unless they themselves wish it; and it is within their will to be seen or not to be seen. It was the grace of God that allowed him to appear to Abraham, or to the other Prophets: not because the eye of Abraham's heart alone was the cause of his seeing God, but because the grace of God voluntarily offered itself to be seen by the righteous man. You should understand this not only regarding God the Father, but also regarding the Lord the Savior, and regarding the Holy Spirit: and, to come to lesser things, regarding the Cherubim and Seraphim. For it is possible that even now, as we are speaking, an Angel may be present with us, and yet, because we do not deserve it, we are unable to see him. For although the eye, whether of our body or our soul, may strive to contemplate, unless the Angel appears spontaneously and offers himself to be seen, he who truly desires it will not see. Therefore, wherever it is written, *God appeared to him*, or to that person, as also now, *An Angel of the Lord appeared to him standing at the right of the Altar of incense*; understand it in this way, as I have said. Whether God or an Angel appeared to Abraham or Zechariah, when he willed or did not will it, he would either not be seen or be seen. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> explains Origen's opinion thus (in the Annotations to chapter 24, verse 32 of the Gospel according to Luke): The opinion of Origen seems to have been different from these, who in his accurate dispute against Celsus says that the body of Christ during those forty days was *Visible, when he willed, and to whom he willed* <note>original Greek: Ὁρατὸν, ὅτ’ ἐβούλετο, καὶ οἷς ἐβούλετο</note>. For he thinks that very most sacred body was at that time *in the borderland* <note>original Greek: ἐν μεθορίῳ</note>, between that—as he himself calls it—*thickness* <note>original Greek: παχύτητα</note> which decaying bodies have, and those natures free from this mortal concretion. But Epiphanius <note>Bishop of Salamis, known for his fierce attacks on Origenism.</note> is indignant at Origen, as if he had believed that Christ rose again clothed in a body far different from that which was fixed to the Cross; whereas he only supposes a body (as he says on page 99) *being transformed* <note>original Greek: μεταμορφούμενον</note>, purified, to be sure, from dregs and mortal thickness. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 64, which is against the Origenists: *And you see, that this very psychic body is itself spiritual; just as our Lord rose from the dead, not raising another body, but the very one that was; and not another besides that which was, but instead of that which was, changing it into a spiritual fineness, and uniting it as a whole spiritual thing; entering through closed doors, which is not possible for our bodies to do, being here because of their thickness; and how, being united into spiritual fineness, is that which entered through closed doors anything other than the crucified one? Or is it the crucified one itself? Surely, Origen, you will not be able to avoid confessing it is the crucified one itself.* <note>This Greek passage argues that the spiritual body is the same physical body, just refined, rather than a different substance.</note> See Origen’s dogma on the resurrection of the body as explained by Saint Jerome in the *Letter to Pammachius, against the errors of John of Jerusalem*.

# Annotations on Book III.

From the time your judgment arises, let there be free opportunity for you until the Sabbath, so that you may be able to settle that controversy and reconcile peace between those who are litigating. Let the Deacons and Presbyters be present at the judgment, intending to judge with integrity, as Men of God, with justice. When both persons have come, as the law commands, let both who are litigating be placed in the middle of the tribunal; and having heard them, pronounce judgment holily, striving to reconcile them before the Bishop's sentence; lest a judgment against a sinner go out upon the earth, since you have Christ the Son of God as a partner and sharer of the case in the tribunal. See *Augustine, On the Works of Monks.* <note>original: "De operibus Monachorum"</note>

Page 132. line 38. **Antinous**] <note>Antinous was the young favorite of the Emperor Hadrian; after his death, he was deified.</note> Aelius Spartianus in *Hadrian*. He lost his Antinous while sailing through the Nile, for whom he wept like a woman. Regarding him there is various talk; some asserting he was a sacrifice for Hadrian; others asserting what both his beauty and the excessive pleasure of Hadrian suggest. And the Greeks indeed, at Hadrian's wish, consecrated him, asserting that oracles were given through him; which Hadrian himself is rumored to have composed. Innumerable writers have mentioned this *catamite* <term>catamytus: a term for a younger partner in a pederastic relationship</term>. Truly, to save time, read Scaliger in *Observations on Eusebius*, and Salmasius, and Casaubon, in the notes on Aelius Spartianus.

Page 132. line 50. **Others**] <note>original: "Ἔτεροί"</note> Furthermore, regarding the Prophets of Antinous, there is an elegant passage of Origen *Against Celsus*, which learned men have already produced, but less than fully: I read it thus: *Others, however, being deceived by the deceptive demon established there, and being convicted by a weak conscience, seem to produce a sort of breath from Antinous.* <note>original Greek: "Ἔτεροί δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκεῖ ἱδρυμένου δαίμονος ἀπατεῶνος..."</note> Salmasius in the notes to Aelius Spartianus. Page 133. line 28. **The sacrifices**] <note>original: "Τὰς θυσίας"</note> Origen *Against Celsus*, book 7, p. 334. *Such a thing shows that he himself happens to be nourished, either from the vapors of sacrifices, or from the odors of blood and burnt offerings, their bodies being fond of pleasure.* Origen in the *Preface* to book 1, *On First Principles*. In this booklet he called a Demon "incorporeal," for the reason that the very habit, or the boundary of the Demonic body, is not similar to this thicker one of ours, as a visible body; but it must be understood according to the sense of him who composed that Scripture: that is, it is not such a body as Demons have, which is naturally subtle and thin like a breeze, and because of this is either considered by many or called "incorporeal"—but that it has a solid or palpable body. From the opinion of Origen and others, Demons are corporeal: which being granted, it will also be held among the *accepted opinions* <term>endoza: likely a typo for 'endoxa', meaning reputable or accepted scholarly opinions</term> that Demons gape after the smell of burnt fat.

Page 133. line 31. **Of another nature**] <note>original: "Ἄλλης φύσεως"</note> In this place, by "nature" understand disposition and character: otherwise how will Origen agree with himself? Volume 23 on *John*. "But in this," says Heracleon, "those to whom the speech is directed were of the substance of the Devil." Just as if the substance of the Devil were different from the essence of the holy Angels, possessing reason. And it seems to me that he suffered something similar in this as he who says there is a different essence of a healthy eye and an eye seeing wrongly; and that there is one essence of impaired hearing, and another of healthy hearing. For as in these it is not a divine essence, but a certain cause happened so that the hearing or the eye were impaired: so the essence of anyone naturally fit for attaining reason is the same, whether they admit reason or refuse it.

Page 141. line 3. **Monogamous**] <note>original: "Μονόγαμον"</note> *Apostolic Canons*, chapter 17. *He who has been involved in two marriages after baptism, or has kept a concubine, cannot be a bishop, or a presbyter, or a deacon, or at all in the list of the priestly order.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δυσὶ γάμοις συμπλακεὶς..."</note> Ambrose, *Letter 82*, To the Church of Vercelli, etc. Therefore the Apostle laid down the law, saying, "If anyone is without crime, the husband of one wife." Therefore, because the husband of one wife is without crime, let him be bound to the law of undertaking the Priesthood; but he who has repeated marriage does not indeed have the fault of being defiled, but is stripped of the prerogative of a Priest. We have said what is of the law, let us also say what is of reason: but first let us recognize that not only did the Apostle establish this concerning the Bishop and Presbyter, but also the Fathers in the Council of Nicaea added treatises that no one ought to be a Cleric who has obtained second marriages. For how can he console a widower, honor him, and exhort him to guard his widowhood and keep faith with his husband, which he himself did not keep for his prior marriage? Or, what would be the difference between the People and the Priest, if they were bound by the same laws? The life of the Priest ought to outweigh, just as grace outweighs. Tertullian, book 1, chapter 7, *To his Wife*. How much second marriages detract from faith, how much they hinder holiness, the discipline of the Church and the prescription of the Apostle declare: since he does not allow those twice-married <term>Digamos: from the Greek for twice-married</term> to preside. The same in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 7. Thence therefore among us it is prescribed more fully and strictly, that those who may be chosen into the Priestly order ought to be of one marriage; to such an extent that I remember certain twice-married men being cast down from their place. See the book *On Monogamy*, chapters 11 and 12. Basil (first *Canonical Letter to Amphilochius*).

For the horse of wickedness is heavy, leaning and weighing down toward the earth, if he has not been well-trained by his charioteers; there the ultimate toil and struggle is set before the soul. For those called immortal, when they reach the summit, go outside and stand upon the back of the heavens. As they stand, the revolution carries them around, and they behold the things outside the heavens. But the region above the heavens no poet here has ever yet sung of, nor will ever sing of worthily.** And page 250. **Beauty was then bright to see, when with a happy choir we followed a blessed vision and sight, we following with Zeus, and others with other Gods, and we saw and were initiated into the mystery which it is lawful to call most blessed; which we celebrated being ourselves whole and untouched by the evils that awaited us in later time; being initiated into and beholding whole and simple and calm and happy apparitions in pure light, being ourselves pure and unmarked by this which we now carry about and call a body, bound to it like an oyster to its shell.** <note>original Greek: "Πολλαὶ μὲν οὖν καὶ μακάριαι θέαι τε..."</note>

Page 159. line 38. **Concerning the intellect from without**] Aristotle, book 2, chapter 3, *On the Generation of Animals*. **Following this, we must clearly speak about the sensitive soul and the intellectual soul. For it is necessary to have all powers potentially before they are in actuality. It is necessary that either they all come to be without having existed before, or all pre-exist, or some do and some do not; and that they come to be either in the matter without having entered in the semen of the male, or having come from there. And in the male, they either all come from without, or none do, or some do and some do not. That it is not possible for all to pre-exist is clear from such things. For of those principles whose activity is bodily, it is clear that these cannot exist without a body; for example, walking without feet; so that it is also impossible for them to enter from without. For they can neither enter by themselves, being inseparable, nor enter in a body; for the semen is a residue of changing nourishment... it remains then that only the intellect enters from without, and that it alone is divine; for bodily activity has no communion with its activity.** <note>original Greek: "Ἐπομένως δὲ δηλονότι καὶ περὶ τῆς αἰσθητικῆς λεκτέον ψυχῆς..."</note>

# Annotations on Book IV.

Just as there are various differences in bodily ailments, some of which are easily cured while others are more difficult—requiring surgery, cauterization, and the drinking of bitter medicines to remove the disease troubling the body—so too does the judgment following these things promise a healing for the sicknesses of the soul. <note>original Greek: "περ εἰσί τινες κατὰ τὸ σῶμα..." from Gregory of Nyssa</note> To those who are more careless, it is a threat and the rising of a grim countenance, so that through fear of painful consequences, the soul might be disciplined against its vice. But to those who are more sensible, it is a medical treatment and a healing from God, who leads His own creature back to the grace and instruction held from the beginning. See what we have cited from the same Nyssen in the Annotations to page 158. Just as Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for the controversial view that all beings, including the damned, might eventually be saved.</note> says the punishments of all will end, so Justin says those of certain people will end, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 223: "But indeed, I do not say that all souls die; for that would truly be a stroke of luck for the wicked. But what then? That the pious remain in a better place, while the unjust and wicked are in a worse place, awaiting the time of judgment. Then some, having appeared worthy of God, never die again; but others are punished as long as God wills them both to exist and to be punished." What Theophilus of Antioch, Tatian, Arnobius, and Irenaeus thought on this matter, let the more skilled judge. Theophilus of Antioch, Book 2 *To Autolycus*, page 96: "In the same way that it happened regarding man, who was the master and yet sinned, the things that served him sinned with him. Whenever man returns again to his natural state, no longer doing evil, those things shall also be restored to their original gentleness." See pages 101, 103 in the same. Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, page 152: "The soul is not immortal in itself, O Greeks, but mortal; yet it is possible for the same soul not to die. For it dies and is dissolved with the body if it does not know the truth; but it rises again later at the end of the world with the body, receiving death through punishment in immortality." See pages 150, 151, 152, 153 in the same. Irenaeus, Book 2, chapter 64: "For just as the heaven, which is the firmament above us, and the Sun, Moon, and the rest of the stars and all their ornaments, were made when they did not exist before, and they endure for a long time according to the will of God: so also regarding souls and spirits, and generally all things that were made, one would not err in thinking that all things which were made have a beginning of their creation, but endure as long as God wills them to exist and endure." The Prophetic spirit also bears witness to these views, saying, "For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created: he established them forever and

<column-break/>

ever." <note>Psalm 148:5-6</note> And again, concerning the saving of man, he says: "He asked life of thee, and thou gavest him length of days for ever and ever" <note>Psalm 21:4</note>—as if the Father of all were granting it, even perseverance forever and ever to those who are saved. For life is not from ourselves, nor from our nature, but is given according to the grace of God. And therefore, he who preserves the gift of life and gives thanks to Him who provided it, shall receive length of days forever and ever; but he who casts it away and proves ungrateful to his Maker for the fact that he was made, and does not recognize Him who provides, deprives himself of perseverance forever and ever. And a little after this he has: "Since God grants both life and perpetual perseverance, it follows that souls, which at first did not exist, thereafter endure as long as God wills them to exist and subsist." The same author, Book 5, chapter 4. Arnobius, Book 2, page 31: "Do you dare to laugh at us when we speak of Gehennas <note>A term for Hell or a place of fiery torment.</note> and certain unquenchable fires, into which we have learned that souls are cast by their enemies? What of your own Plato in that volume he composed *On the Immortality of the Soul*? Does he not name the rivers Acheron, Styx, Cocytus, and Pyriphlegethon, in which he asserts souls are tossed, submerged, and burned? And he, a man of no small prudence and of weighed judgment, undertakes an inexplicable thing: that while he says souls are immortal, perpetual, and deprived of bodily solidity, he nevertheless says they are punished and afflicted with the pains of the senses. But who among men has not seen that what is immortal and simple cannot admit any pain? Whereas that which feels pain cannot possess immortality? Yet his authority does not decline very far from the truth. For although he, being a mild man of benevolent will, believed it inhuman for souls to be condemned by a capital sentence, he nevertheless not unreasonably suspected that they are cast into rivers rushing with globes of flames and foul, dark abysses. For they are made; and they vanish, reduced to nothing by the frustration of perpetual destruction. For they are of a middle quality (as has been discovered on the authority of Christ), such as can perish if they ignore the God of life, and be freed from exile if they apply themselves to His seeds and indulgences. And so that what is unknown may be revealed, this is the true death of man, this which leaves nothing remaining: for that death which is seen before our eyes is the separation of souls from bodies, not the final end of abolition. This, I say, is the true death of man: when souls, not knowing God, are consumed by a fierce fire through the torment of a very long time, into which certain cruelly savage beings cast them—beings unknown before Christ, and detected only by Him who knows." See pages 40, 47 in the same, and the Annotations to page 168 and page 419.

Page 168, line 11. **Rule**] Origen, *Homilies*.

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Homily 24 on Luke: Just as John waited by the river Jordan for those coming to Baptism, and drove others away, saying, "You generation of vipers," and so forth; yet he received those who confessed their vices and sins: so shall the Lord Jesus stand in a river of fire next to the flaming Sword <note>original: "Romphæam," referring to the flaming sword of the cherubim guarding Paradise</note>; so that whosoever desires to pass into Paradise after the end of this life, yet stands in need of cleansing, He may baptize him in this river and send him through to the things he desires. But he who does not have the sign of the earlier Baptisms, He shall not baptize in the bath of fire. For it is necessary for one to first be baptized with water and the spirit, so that when he comes to the river of fire, he may show that he has kept the washings of water and spirit, and then deserve to also receive the Baptism of fire in Christ Jesus.

The same author, Homily 6 on Exodus: All must therefore come to the fire, all must come to the furnace: for the Lord sits and refines and purifies the sons of Judah. But even when one arrives there, if a man brings many good works and only a small amount of iniquity, that small amount is dissolved by the fire like lead, and purified, and the whole remains as pure gold; and if someone brings more lead there, he is burned more, so that he may be further refined, so that even if there be but a little gold, it may remain cleansed. But if someone comes there entirely made of lead, let that which is written happen to him: "He shall be submerged in the depths, like lead in the mightiest waters." But it would be a long task if we wished to explain these things in order; let it suffice to touch upon a few.

And Homily 3 on Psalm 36: If indeed in this life we despise the words of warning in the divine Scripture, and refuse to be cured or corrected by its rebukes, it is certain that that fire awaits us which is prepared for sinners; and we shall come to that fire in which the fire shall prove what sort of work each man has done: and (as I judge) it is necessary for us all to come to that fire, even if one be a Paul or a Peter, he nonetheless comes to that fire. But such as they hear the words: "Even if you pass through the fire, the flame shall not burn you." If, however, someone be a sinner like me, he will indeed come to that fire like Peter and Paul, but he shall not pass through it as Peter and Paul did. See Homily 25 on Numbers; Homily 27 in the same; Homily 12 on Jeremiah; and Book 8 of the Explanation of the Epistle to the Romans. See also Book 4, page 206, *Against Celsus*, and Book 5, pages 240, 241, 242; and Book 6, pages 292, 324, 325.

Clement, *Stromata* 4, page 536: <note>original Greek: Ἰστέον γὰρ τοι...</note> For you must know that all the painful things that befall those who fall into sins are types of discipline. For earlier sins are cleared away by a discerning discipline. And *Stromata* 5, page 549: And indeed, justice shall overtake the craftsmen and witnesses of all things, as the Ephesian <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus</note> says.

<column-break/>

For he himself also knew, having learned from barbarian philosophy <note>Clement often refers to Hebrew/Jewish wisdom as "barbarian philosophy"</note>, the purification by fire of those who have lived evilly.

Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 35 and chapter 58: Whether you wish it or not, there are already both punishments and refreshments there <note>in the afterlife</note>; you have the poor man and the rich man <note>referring to Lazarus and Dives</note>. And because I deferred something on this part, I will now opportunely return it in the conclusion. And this is nothing else, according to my reasoning, than to be in God Himself. See the same, pages 654, 657, 658, 659, 660, 691, 692. And since it is agreed that the Gods are most blessed, and no one can be blessed without virtue, nor can virtue exist without reason, nor reason exist anywhere except in the human figure, it must be confessed that the Gods are of human appearance. For it was the ancient custom among the Jews for the prophets to foretell from above the evils and goods that were going to overtake them."** And a little later: **"And that this is true, and that God foretold all things that were going to happen to them, I will provide proof not only from here, but also from the very events that happened to them, both bad and good. Consider with me how, even if the man who wrote these things was a Jew, he nevertheless did not endure to follow your stubbornness; for having said that Jerusalem would be taken, he did not dare to go further and say that it would rise again, nor that a specific time had been set."** It follows immediately: **"But while he wrote that Jerusalem and the temple would be made desolate, he did not add that the desolation would ever stand [end]; since he did not see any prophet foretelling this."** But *Josephus* (says the most celebrated *Grotius*) <note>Hugo Grotius, a major 17th-century legal scholar and theologian.</note> **just as he dared not promise anything certain to his people, so he did not cast away all hope, as appears even from this passage; where, deploring the crimes of the city and the punishment due to them, he addresses it thus: 'You might become better again, if ever you appease the God who destroyed you.'** Another argument is taken from the event...

By the outcome: <note>original: "Καὶ ὅτι ἐψευδσθ’..."</note> "And to show that what was said was false, let us bring forward some evidence from the events themselves. If they had not even attempted to rebuild the Temple, one might say that even if they had tried, the success of the building would be a matter of dispute. But now I show that they attempted it not once, nor twice, but three times, and were shattered, just as in the Olympic games, so that the crown of the Church remains undisputed." See the rest, which is most worthy of reading, by all of which he endeavors to prove that the *Jews* are never to be restored to their homeland. *Justin* feels differently, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 306. "Tell me truly," says Trypho, "do you acknowledge that this place, Jerusalem, will be rebuilt, and that your people will be gathered together and rejoice with Christ, along with the patriarchs and the prophets and those of our race, or those who became proselytes before your Christ came? Do you expect this, or have you conceded these points in our discussion just to appear to prevail over us?" To whom Justin replied: "I am not so miserable, O Trypho, as to say things other than what I think. I acknowledged to you before that I and many others hold these views, as you certainly know this will happen; but I also indicated to you that many who are of the pure and pious Christian mind do not recognize this. For I showed you that those who are called Christians, but are actually godless and impious heretics, teach things that are in every way blasphemous, godless, and foolish. But so you may know I do not say this only to you, I will make a compilation of all our conversations to the best of my ability, in which I will record myself acknowledging this very thing which I acknowledge to you. For I choose to follow not human teachings, but God and the teachings from Him." See the same work, pages 245, 249, 259, and *Apology 2*, page 87. Besides *Justin*, other authors of great name defended this opinion, a catalog of whom you will find in Jerome, in the Preface to the 18th book of his *Commentaries on Isaiah*. Nor am I ignorant of how great a diversity of opinions exists among men: I do not speak of the mystery of the Trinity, the right confession of which is the "ignorance of knowledge" <note>A mystical concept suggesting God is best known by acknowledging His unknowability.</note>; but of other Ecclesiastical dogmas, namely concerning the resurrection, and the state of souls and human flesh, and the promises of future things—how they ought to be received, and by what reason the *Apocalypse of John* is to be understood. If we take it according to the letter, we must "Judaize" <note>To follow Jewish literalism or customs.</note>; if we discuss it spiritually, as it was written, we will seem to contradict the opinions of many ancients: of the Latins, *Tertullian, Victorinus, Lactantius*; of the Greeks, to pass over the others,

<column-break/>

I shall make mention only of *Irenaeus*, Bishop of *Lyons*, against whom the most eloquent man *Dionysius, Bishop of the Alexandrian Church*, wrote an elegant book, mocking the "fable of a thousand years" <note>The Millenarian belief in a literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth.</note>, and a golden and jeweled Jerusalem on earth, the restoration of the Temple with the blood of sacrifices, the rest of the Sabbath, the "injury" of circumcision, marriages, births, the education of children, the delicacies of banquets, and the servitude of all Nations, and again wars, armies, triumphs, the slaughter of the defeated, and the death of the hundred-year-old sinner. To him *Apollinarius* responds in two volumes, whom not only men of his own sect follow, but also a great multitude of our own people in this part at least. So that I already perceive with a foreboding mind how much madness is to be stirred up against me. See the same in the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 36, and in the *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* under Papias. *Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 22, etc. Tertullian, in the book On the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 25, and book 3 Against Marcion, chapter 24.* But concerning the restoration of *Judea*, which the *Jews* themselves hope for exactly as it is described, being led by the names of places and regions—how the Allegorical interpretation applies spiritually to *Christ* and the *Church*, and its condition and fruit, is both a long matter to pursue and is digested in another work which we entitle *ON THE HOPE OF THE FAITHFUL*. In the present work it is perhaps idle, because the question is not about an earthly promise, but a heavenly one. For we also confess that a kingdom is promised to us on earth, but before heaven, though in another state, namely after the resurrection for a thousand years, in the city of divine workmanship, Jerusalem, brought down from heaven, which the Apostle also designates as our mother above, and pronouncing our <term>politeuma</term> <note>Greek: citizenship or commonwealth.</note>, that is, our citizenship, to be in the heavens, he surely assigns it to some heavenly city. Ezekiel knew this, and the Apostle John saw it. *Lactantius, book 7, chapter 24. Augustine, book 20, chapter 29, Of the City of God.* Through this Elijah, the great and wonderful Prophet, having explained the law to them, it is a most celebrated belief in the talk and hearts of the faithful that in the last time before the judgment, the *Jews* will believe in the true *Christ* (that is, in our Christ).

But perceive what the truth holds. Can the name of this God be known, who rules by a mere nod and contains all things, whose will all things serve, whose world can neither be estimated nor enclosed by boundaries? But when the Magi wished to grasp the individual titles of his power, as they thought, they designated them in an abusive manner through the powers of nature, and attempted to call him God as if by the nobility of many Divinities; as if the names were drawn from the effect of each thing, just as Orpheus did, and Moses the highest Priest of God, and Isaiah, and those like them. The Etruscans confirm that a Nymph, who remained unmarried, proclaimed that it is not lawful for a human to hear the name of the highest God because of the fragility and pollution of nature; to assert this with evidence, she spoke the name of the God into the ear of a bull in the sight of others, which immediately died as if seized by madness and driven by an excessive whirlwind. There are those who, although they say they know it in secret, know what is false; since an ineffable thing cannot be grasped.

“...and in sins did my mother conceive me.” <note>Psalm 51:5</note> The same author <note>Origen</note> says in Homily 14 on Luke: *Little children are baptized for the remission of sins.
