Or, how can any reason for the font exist in little children, unless according to that sense of which we spoke a little earlier:* “No one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been but one day upon the earth”? <note>Job 14:4-5, Septuagint version</note> *And because through the sacrament of Baptism the filth of birth is laid aside, for that reason even little children are baptized.* In Homily 8 on Leviticus: *But even he himself who is born, whether of the male or female sex, the Scripture pronounces concerning him that he is not clean from filth, even if his life is but one day. And, so that you may know there is something great in this, I know not what, and of such a kind that it did not occur to any of the saints to celebrate: no one from all the saints is found to have kept a feast day or a great banquet on the day of his birth; no one is found to have had joy on the day of the birth of his son or daughter.* And a little later: *But if it pleases you to hear what other Saints have felt concerning this birth, hear David saying,* “In iniquities,” he says, “was I conceived, and in sins did my mother bring me forth”; *showing that every soul born in the flesh is polluted by the filth of iniquity and sin: and for that reason was that said which we have already mentioned above,* “Because no one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been but one day.” See Homily 12 on Leviticus. Justin, *Exposition of the Faith*: <note>original Greek: Ἐπειδήπερ ἁμαρτιῶν ὁ Ἀδάμ...</note> “Since Adam subjected the race to death through sins, and made the whole of nature liable for the debt.” And in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, page 315: <note>original Greek: Καὶ οὐχ ὡς ἐνδεᾶ αὐτὸν...</note> “And we know that he did not come to the river as if he were in need of being baptized, or of the Spirit coming upon him in the form of a dove; just as he did not endure being born and crucified as if he were in need of these things, but for the sake of the human race, which from Adam had fallen under death and the deception of the serpent, by the individual fault of each of them who acted wickedly.” Irenaeus, Book 5, chapter 14: *Through which things he clearly shows him to be God: whom indeed we offended in the first Adam, by not performing his commandment; but in the second Adam we are reconciled, having been made obedient even unto death.* See Book 3, chapter 20, not far from the beginning; Book 4, chapter 5; and Book 5, chapters 14, 16, 17; and elsewhere. Tertullian, in the book *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 1: *So that she might not act more in filth and rather affect squalor, carrying herself about as Eve herself, mourning and repenting, so that she might more fully expiate that which she draws from Eve (I mean the ignominy of the first offense, and the odium of human perdition) by every habit of satisfaction. It remains for them, as it seems, to say consequently that birth is evil; not only that of the body, but also that of the soul, because of which the body also exists. And when David says, ‘In sins was I conceived, and in iniquities did my mother long for me,’ he says prophetically that Eve was his mother; but Eve became the mother of the living; and if he was conceived in sins, yet he himself was not in sin, nor indeed was he himself sin.” But this and other passages which we have already cited, everyone is accustomed to twist according to how it seems fit to them. Similar, not to say more abundant, testimonies occur among other Fathers, both Greek and Latin; which for the sake of brevity we pass over, intending to speak more copiously of these elsewhere. See the Annotations to page 365.

Page 191, line 17. **Growing wings** ] Read **shedding wings**. I confess, “growing wings” <note>original: πτεροφυεῖν</note> occurs more than once in Plato, as on pages 251, 255; and “to grow feathers,” page 251. But the passage to which Origen looked warned me to correct it thus, page 246: “Every soul takes care of all that is soulless; it patrols the whole heaven, appearing at different times in different forms. When it is perfect and winged, it soars on high and governs the whole world; but that soul which has **shed its wings** is carried along until it takes hold of something solid; where having settled, and taking an earthly body, which seems to move itself because of the soul's power, the whole was called a living being, soul and body joined together, and received the name 'mortal'.” And page 248: “But when, being unable to follow, it does not see, and meeting with some misfortune, is weighed down by being filled with forgetfulness and vice, and being weighed down, **sheds its wings** and falls to the earth,” etc.

Page 191, line 37. **Having all things** ] See Origen, in the second Homily on Genesis.

Page 193, line 21. **In Ascalon** ] Perhaps Origen saw those wells when he traveled to Palestine, where he was graced with the honor of the Priesthood: Nicephorus, Book 5, chapter 10, *Ecclesiastical History*. Thirty volumes on Isaiah, twenty on Ezekiel...

<column-break/>

But I doubt whether Clement and Eusebius are as much partners in fault as Scaliger himself is in suspicion. The words are as follows (2 Maccabees chapter 1, verse 10): "In the year one hundred and eighty-eight, those in Jerusalem and in Judea, and the senate, and Judas, to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the race of the anointed priests, and to the Jews in Egypt, greeting and health." To King Ptolemy: that is, of Ptolemy Lathyrus, son of Euergetes, according to Junius. Nor have I found anything so far that would move me from this interpretation. See his allegories in Eusebius, book 7 chapter 14, book 8 chapter 10, and book 13 chapter 12 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.

For Jannes and Mambres were brothers, Magicians and sorcerers of the Egyptians, who by their magical art thought they could resist the power of God acting through Moses with a counterfeit rivalry; but when the power of Moses grew in its works, they were humbled and confessed with the pain of their wounds that God was working in the deeds of Moses.* The passage from Numenius <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher</note>, to which Origen refers us, you will find in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 9, chapter 8: <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ βίβλῳ...</note> *And in the third book, the same author [Numenius] mentions Moses, saying the following: Next in order were Jannes and Jambres, Egyptian Sacred Scribes, men judged second to none in the practice of magic at the time when the Jews were being driven out of Egypt. At any rate, they were the ones chosen by the Egyptian multitude to stand against Musaeus <note>A name used by some pagan authors for Moses</note>, the leader of the Jews, a man who had become most powerful in praying to God; and they were seen to be able to undo the most violent of the calamities which Moses brought upon Egypt.* Artapanus mentions the same men in his book *On the Jews*, though he did not express their names: Eusebius, book 9, chapter 27. Whether Apuleius <note>Author of 'The Golden Ass'</note> obtained knowledge of these men from these and similar Apocryphal books, or from the Holy Scriptures and that familiarity he had with Christians, I simply do not know. Certainly, Augustine speaks thus of Apuleius being called to trial (*City of God, book 8, chapter 19*): *Finally, was Apuleius himself ever accused of magical arts before Christian judges?* Apuleius says in his *Apology*: *If you can prove even the slightest profit; let me be that Charinondas, or Damigeron, or that Moses, or Jannes, or Apollonius, or Dardanus himself, or whoever else has been celebrated among Magicians since Zoroaster and Hostanes.* But these are trivial matters, hardly worth remembering. Only Macarius <note>Saint Macarius of Alexandria, a 4th-century desert father</note> saw the monument which the Magicians had constructed; he entered the garden, found much gold deposited there, struck seventy Demons with horror, saw the well, the bronze jar, and the iron chain—which, alas! time had so consumed that it seems equally impossible for us to draw the truth from this narrative as it was for Macarius to draw water from that well. Hence one must wonder how it could happen that most learned men would give credit to these and similar fables of the Monks, which are partly openly fabricated and partly rashly babbled. Indeed, the Jews—fairer judges in this cause—reported that they were overwhelmed by the waters <note>i.e., drowned in the Red Sea</note>. But those Teachers [the Monks] instilled a far different belief in the more ignorant, while they transcribed this skillfully devised fable piece by piece. But if I were to recite the whole thing, those who have hitherto

<column-break/>

been held by stupor and admiration would laugh with wide-open lips and shake their lungs with mirth. Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 20, *Concerning Macarius of Alexandria*: <note>original Greek: Ἐπεθύμησέ ποτε καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς...</note> *The same man also desired, as he himself related to us, to enter the garden-tomb of Jannes and Jambres, the magicians; for the sake of history, or perhaps to encounter the demons there. For it was said that many and difficult demons had been assigned by those very men to that place, due to the excess of their dishonorable art. For this garden-tomb was made by the brothers Jannes and Jambres themselves, who possessed unspeakable power in the magical art at that time under Pharaoh. Having acquired a certain sovereignty in Egypt over a long time, they built that work out of four-sided stones during their lifetime, making a tomb in it and depositing much gold. They also planted all kinds of trees and dug a very large well of water, for the place was like a marsh. They did all these things hoping that after their death they would arrive there to luxuriate in this paradise. Finally, then, the servant of Christ, Macarius, not knowing the way to this unknown place, followed the stars by guesswork alone, just as sailors crossing the seas. Thus the saint traversed the entire desert, and taking a bundle of reeds, he placed one at every mile as a sign, so that he might find his way back by it. Having traversed that whole desert within nine days and coming near that garden, he slept a little as night overtook him. But the ancient demon, who always opposes the athletes of Christ, gathered all those reeds of Macarius and placed them at his head while he slept, as if they were a single sign. Rising, he found the reeds tied together, just as he had fixed them for a sign. Perhaps God permitted this for a greater exercise of his faith, so that he would not hope in reeds for guidance, but in the grace of God which guided Israel by a pillar of cloud for forty years in that fearful desert. The saint said that as I barely approached the garden-tomb, seventy demons of every shape came out to meet me; some shouting, some leaping, some gnashing their teeth loudly against me; others fluttering like crows dared to fly at my face saying, "What do you want, Macarius?" etc.* And a little later: *Entering, he says, I beheld everything, in which I also found a bronze jar hanging by an iron chain over the well, which had been consumed by time.* You see how it pleases Macarius...

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.

Page 199. line 13. *Jason*] Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> mentions this book and charges it with one error. For in his *Questions on Genesis* he has these words: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth. Most people think, just as it is written in the dispute of Jason and Papiscus, and as Tertullian argues in his book against Praxeas, and as Hilary also affirms in his Exposition of a certain Psalm, that the Hebrew has: '**In the Son, God made heaven and earth**.'" The truth of the matter itself proves this to be false. From which passage it is clear that this book existed at that time. This Jason was a Hebrew and a Christian. He is said to have been from Thessalonica, of whom mention is made in Romans 16 and Acts 17, and whom Dorotheus of Tyre later writes in his Synopsis was the first Bishop of Troas. See Pamelius in his Annotations to the book *On the Unbelieving Jews* among the works of Cyprian: and Sixtus of Siena in his Library. I would gladly ask: by whom is he called a Thessalonican? If they can produce even a single testimony from ancient writers, I will confess that I am most grievously hallucinating. Papiscus was a Jew, and an Alexandrian by birth, who by this "altercation" (as Jerome calls it), or "admonition and gentle rebuke" (as Celsus calls it in the book *On the Unbelieving Jews* at the end of Cyprian's works)—that is, by this debate—was softened and overcome, and believed in Jesus Christ the Son of God; and, praying to receive the sign <note>The "signaculum" or seal, referring to Baptism.</note>, he requested Jason to perform it. Who this Celsus was, and who Bishop Vigilius was to whom he dedicated the aforementioned book, I confess I am entirely ignorant, and I do not wish to guess. Vigilius was learned, according to Celsus: *The proof of this labor I commit to you, dearest friend, who are established in the instruction of both languages, at your earnest request.* If you read the book, you will find Celsus foretelling martyrdom for him, and earnestly entreating that he remember him when he is placed in heaven. At the end of the work he added: *Keep now in mind your servant Celsus, most holy one.* From this it is clear, says Pamelius, that the author of this translation is not Cyprian, but a certain Celsus. I believe this book was rendered into Latin before Origen composed his volumes against Celsus the Epicurean; or else Celsus, the author of this book, had not read Origen’s works: otherwise he would have quite appropriately rebuked the malice of Celsus the Epicurean, and in his preface wiped away the slanders and insults with which he defiled this book. Hear the aforementioned Celsus in his book *On the Unbelieving Jews to Bishop Vigilius*: "For, so that you may support the minds of the hard-hearted and impious people of that time, converted to the fear of the Lord by the Lord’s own Gospel preaching; and so that I may pass over in silence the people of believers multiplied throughout the whole world and returned by the preaching of his Apostles: there occurs that noble, memorable, and glorious dispute of Jason the Hebrew Christian and Papiscus the Alexandrian Jew. The obstinate hardness of the Jewish heart was softened by Hebrew admonition and gentle rebuke, and Jason’s teaching on the infusion of the Holy Spirit was victorious in Papiscus’s heart. By this, Papiscus was admitted to the understanding of the truth, and formed to the fear of the Lord by the Lord’s own mercy; he believed in Jesus Christ the Son of God, and, praying to receive the seal, he requested Jason. The writing of their debate proves this, which—concerning the collision between Papiscus opposing the truth and Jason asserting and defending the arrangement and fullness of Christ—was recorded in a work of the Greek language. To the translation of this into the Latin understanding, encouraged by God’s help and the firmness of a living faith, preserving the proper meaning of the words, I have approached fearlessly; and for those who are strangers to the understanding of Greek learning, having interpreted the full significance of the words and revealed the manifestation of all understanding and truth, I have discussed it by the method of the Roman speech. The proof of this labor I commit to you, dearest friend, who are established in the instruction of both languages, at your earnest request; so that you, who are reverent in your veneration of the Holy Spirit, may explore with the boldness of a modest daring, by comparing the reading of both works, and by the examination of your judgment, may approve and amend those things which were perhaps digested by us less well or improperly, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, which has flowed into your breast by an inundation of heavenly grace." Let him who can, bring forth more certain facts.

<column-break/>

Page 200. line 21. *From the Timaeus*] Plato in the *Timaeus*, page 41. <note>original: "Ἀπὸ τῶ Τιμαίε"</note> "Since therefore all those gods, both those who revolve openly and those who appear as far as they wish, have had a beginning; he who generated this universe says these things to them: 'Gods of gods,' etc." And a little later: "Now therefore, learn what I say to you by way of indication. There remain three mortal races yet ungenerated. If these are not brought into being, the heaven will be incomplete; for it will not contain within itself all the races of living beings. But it must, if it is to be sufficiently perfect; yet if these were brought into being by me and participated in life, they would be made equal to the gods. Therefore, so that they may be mortal, and that the universe may truly be a whole, turn yourselves according to nature to the craftsmanship of living beings, imitating my power regarding your own generation." And on page 69: "And indeed he himself became the craftsman of divine things, but he assigned the task of crafting the generation of mortals to his own offspring. And they, imitating him, having received—" <note>The text cuts off here, matching the catchword "λαβον-" (having received) from the original.</note>

# Annotations on Book IV.

...having received the immortal principle of the soul, they then fashioned around it a mortal body, and gave the whole body to be its vehicle. Within it, they built another form of soul, the mortal one, which contains within itself terrible and necessary passions: first, pleasure, the greatest lure of evils, etc. <note>original: "λαβόντες ἀρχὴν ψυχῆς ἀθάνατον..." This is a quote from Plato's *Timaeus* describing the creation of man.</note>

Page 200 line 36. **Animals**] Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in Book 1 of *On Duties*. "But since (as was famously written by Plato) we are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, our parents a part, and our friends a part: and (as the Stoics please) all things produced on earth are created for the use of men, but men were generated for the sake of men; so that they might be able to benefit one another: in this we ought to follow nature as our guide." See the same author in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, Seneca in Book 2, chapter 23 of *On Benefits*, and Lactantius, chapter 13 of *On the Wrath of God*.

Page 202. line 21. **The Mixing Bowl**] See page 204. Plato in the *Timaeus*, page 41. "And insofar as it is fitting for them to share the name of the immortals, being called divine and ruling among those who are always willing to follow justice and you, I will deliver the seeds and beginnings. For the rest, you, weaving the mortal to the immortal, fashion living beings and bring them forth; give them food to make them grow, and receive them again when they perish." He said these things; and again into the former mixing bowl <note>Greek: *krater*, the vessel where the Creator mixed the soul of the universe</note>, in which he had blended and mixed the soul of the universe, he poured the remains of the previous elements, mixing them in somewhat the same way, yet no longer pure in the same manner, but of a second and third degree of purity. And a little later: "It would be necessary, when he had sown them into the instruments of time proper to each, that the most god-fearing of living beings should be produced. Since human nature is twofold, the better kind would be such as would thereafter be called man."

Page 203. line 8. **I do not know**] You know many things, Origen: but you believe more. Why do you doubt *concerning the body*? You hope for a new world to come: for indeed Methodius, Bishop of Tyre, wrote a book *On the Resurrection* against Origen, in which he introduces himself and Auxentius as speakers; also Proclus and Aglaophon, who speak on behalf of Origen. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 64, number 40 and number 38, addresses Theophilus. *Which, however, I think is an appellative name, not a proper one*, says Petavius in his *Observations on Epiphanius' Heresy* 64, number 17. *But if that disputation is by Proclus, which is woven together from Number 17 to this point; I do not see how it defends Origen's cause, since it most strongly refutes his dogma and affirms the resurrection of bodies: but neither does the subsequent refutation by Methodius pertain to the preceding speech of Proclus; and he convicts Aglaophon by a speech which does not appear here.*

<column-break/>

Here, therefore, I am stuck, and it is likely that many things there have been either transposed or omitted; which, if Methodius's book were extant, could be discerned and corrected. Petavius, in the same place; see his *Observations* at numbers 12 and 17. At any rate, in that disputation of Proclus these words occur, which seemed to me to greatly favor Origen's opinion. "For truly, God did not create destruction for nothing, nor in vain, according to those who think vain things—God is the All—but for the sake of being, and being inhabited, and remaining. # Annotations on Book V.

<meta>catchword: Page.</meta>

They claim that souls both remain forever and frequently pass into other new bodies. To these ideas, they add further distortions of the truth: that human souls return into cattle, birds, and wild beasts. Jerome in his *Apology against Rufinus* <note>original: "Apolog. adversus Ruffinum"</note> says: "Hear what Pythagoras first discovered among the Greeks: that souls are immortal and pass from some bodies into others." Indeed, Virgil also speaks of this, following the same path in the sixth volume of the *Aeneid*:

> "All these, when they have rolled the wheel for a thousand years,
> "God summons in a great column to the river Lethe:
> "That is, so that being forgetful, they may revisit the vaulted sky above,

"During those months in which Vespasian was waiting at Alexandria for the seasonal summer winds and a calm sea, many miracles occurred, by which the favor of heaven and a certain leaning of the Divine Powers toward Vespasian were shown. One of the common people of Alexandria, known for a wasting disease of the eyes, fell at his knees, begging with groans for a remedy for his blindness, by the advice of the god Serapis, whom that nation, devoted to superstitions, worships above all others. He prayed the Prince that he might deign to moisten his cheeks and eyeballs with the spittle from his mouth. Another with a diseased hand, at the prompting of the same god, prayed that he might be stepped upon by the foot and tread of Caesar. Vespasian at first laughed and rejected them; but as they pressed him, he feared the reputation of vanity on one hand, and on the other was led into hope by their entreaties and the voices of flatterers. Finally, he ordered the Physicians to estimate whether such blindness and infirmity could be overcome by human aid. The Physicians discussed it in various ways: for the one, the power of sight was not entirely eaten away and would return if the obstacles were driven out; for the other, the limbs had slipped out of place but could be restored if a healing force were applied. Perhaps this was pleasing to the Gods, and the Prince had been chosen for divine service. Ultimately, the glory of the performed remedy would belong to Caesar, while the ridicule of a failure would fall upon the poor wretches. Therefore, Vespasian, thinking all things lay open to his fortune and that nothing was any longer incredible, with a joyful expression—the multitude standing by in suspense—executed the orders. Immediately the hand was restored to use, and the day shone again for the blind man. Both events are still remembered by those who were present, even now when there is no reward for lying. From this, a deeper desire came upon Vespasian to visit the sacred seat, to consult about the affairs of the Empire. He ordered everyone to be kept away from the temple; and having entered, intent upon the Deity, he looked behind his back and saw one of the Egyptian nobles named Basilides, whom he knew was being held

far from Alexandria by a journey of several days and a sick body. At the same time, the same youth was seen to be carried up into heaven in a great fire. Ptolemy, excited by the omen and the miracle, revealed the nocturnal vision to the Priests of the Egyptians, whose custom it is to understand such things. But since they knew little of Pontus and foreign matters, he questioned Timotheus the Athenian, of the family of the Eumolpidae, whom he had summoned from Eleusis as a high priest of ceremonies, as to what that superstition or deity might be. Then he ordered ambassadors and gifts to be prepared for King Scydrothemis (who then ruled the people of Sinope), and instructed those about to sail to visit the Pythian Apollo. For them, the sea was favorable; the lot of the oracle was not ambiguous: they were to go and bring back the image of his father, but leave that of his sister behind. When they came to Sinope, they delivered the gifts, prayers, and mandates of their King to Scydrothemis. He was of a divided mind, now fearing the deity, now terrified by the threats of the opposing people; often he was swayed by the gifts and promises of the Ambassadors. And in the meantime, three years having passed, Ptolemy did not omit his zeal nor his prayers. He increased the dignity of the Ambassadors, the number of the ships, and the weight of the gold. # Annotations on Book V.

" the vision is presented to Scydrothemis, so that the one destined for the God should delay no longer. As he hesitated, various destructions, diseases, and the manifest anger of the heavenly beings—growing heavier by the day—exhausted him. Having called an assembly by order of the divinity, he explains his own visions and those of Ptolemy, and the encroaching evils. The common people opposed the King, envying Egypt, fearing for themselves, and they surrounded the Temple. From here, a greater rumor passed down that the God himself spontaneously boarded the ships pushed to the shore: a marvel to tell, on the third day, having traversed such a vast sea, they are driven to Alexandria. A Temple was built according to the greatness of the city, in the place named Rhacotis: there had been a small shrine there consecrated to Sarapis and Isis since ancient times. These are the most celebrated accounts of the origin and arrival of the God. Nor am I unaware that there are some who say he was summoned from Seleucia, a city of Syria, during the reign of Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes</note>, whom the third generation produced: others say the author was the same Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy I Soter</note>: but the seat from which he passed over was Memphis, once famous and the pillar of ancient Egypt. Many consider the God himself to be Aesculapius <note>The god of healing</note>, because he heals sick bodies: some say Osiris, the most ancient deity to those nations: most say Jupiter, as the ruler of all things: very many say Father Dis <note>Pluto/Hades</note>, based on the insignias which are manifest in him, or by conjecturing through ambiguities." *Clement in the Protrepticus:* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἡ περὶ ταῦτα διατριβὴ...</note> "And the study concerning these things would show you who this god or great demon is. This image was a statue of Pluto; which, having received the statue, he established on the promontory which they now call Rhacotis; where also the temple of Sarapis is honored." Indeed, the very quality of the sound and the power of the Egyptian names possess within themselves the energy of the things spoken; but when distorted, they become both obscure and ineffective."

Finally, carry yourself around: consider man within and without. Even this work of our God will please you, whom that 'better' God of yours loved; for whose sake he labored to descend from the third heaven into these poor elements; for whose cause he was even crucified in this little cell of the Creator. But that God, even until now, has not rejected the Creator’s water, with which he washes his own; nor the oil, with which he anoints his own; nor the fellowship of honey and milk, with which he feeds his own as infants; nor the bread, by which he represents his own very body: even in his own Sacraments needing the 'beggarly' things of creation.”* But you, a disciple above the Master, and a servant above the Lord, are more sublimely wise than He, destroying the things He desires to sustain. Justin Martyr, *Apology 2*, page 70: <note>original Greek: "Μαρκίωνά δέ τινα Ποντικόν..."</note> *“And a certain Marcion of Pontus, who even now is still teaching those who believe him to think there is some other God greater than the Creator; who, throughout every race of men, through the aid of demons, has caused many to speak blasphemies and to deny the God who is the Maker of this universe, and to confess some other who, being greater, has done greater things than this one.”* Theodoret, Book 1, *On Heretical Fables*, regarding Marcion: *“This Marcion raved furiously against the Creator, and indeed twice as much: for I have passed over the greater blasphemies in silence. When those present asked, 'How then do you eat? How do you drink? Therefore, without doubt, Noah could have succeeded in the delegation of the preaching; or because he would not have been silent otherwise, both concerning the disposition of God his preserver and the glory of his own house. If he did not have this so readily at hand, this too would protect the assertion of that Scripture: likewise, he could have restored it in the Spirit when it had been destroyed by the violence of the flood, just as it is well known that after Jerusalem was destroyed by the Babylonian conquest, every instrument of Jewish literature was restored through Ezra. But since the same Scripture of Enoch also preached concerning the Lord, nothing at all is to be rejected by us which pertains to us. And we read that 'Every Scripture [is useful] for edification'...”*

He claims she issued from the Father with this purpose in mind, but leaped down into the lower regions; and there, anticipating the Father’s design, she gave birth to the Angelic powers who were ignorant of the Father, the artisan of this world. By these powers she was thereafter held captive out of envy, lest if she departed, they should seem to be the offspring of another. And for that reason, she was subjected to every insult, so that she could never depart as a free woman; she even fell into human form, to be restrained as if by the chains of the flesh. Thus, through many ages, she passed through various female bodies; she was even that Helen who was so ruinous to Priam, and later to the eyes of Stesichorus <note>A Greek poet said to have been blinded for insulting Helen in verse.</note>, whom she blinded because of his insulting poem, and then restored his sight as a reward for his praise. Consequently, migrating from body to body, in her final disgrace she was a prostitute under the name of Helen. This, then, is the "lost sheep" to whom the Supreme Father—namely Simon—descended; and having first recovered her and revealed her (I know not whether on his shoulders or his thighs), he then looked toward the salvation of men, as if to avenge their liberation from those Angelic powers, to deceive whom he transformed himself into the likeness of men and feigned being a man; acting as the Son in Judea, but as the Father in Samaria. See Pope Clement, Justin, Irenaeus, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Theodoret in the cited places.*

# Annotations on Book V.

...to God through auspicious self-control, and those things are said which were spoken to Salome, which I mentioned previously. These are found, I believe, in the *Gospel according to the Egyptians*; for they say that the Savior himself said, <note>original: "Ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὰ ἔργα τῆς θηλείας..."</note> "I came to destroy the works of the female." By "female," he means desire; and by "works," he means birth and decay. See Theodoret’s *Epitome* at the end of Clement’s works, page 799. I confess that the Encratites <note>A sect practicing strict abstinence</note> and the Carpocratians were utterly unlike and embraced doctrines diametrically opposed; nevertheless, it could happen that some of the Carpocratians might cite things in that Gospel which seemed to favor their opinion in any way. If Celsus read this anywhere, it would give him an occasion to assert that the Carpocratians originated from Salome.

Page 272. line 38. ***Mariamne***] I believe certain heretics invented prophets and prophetesses for themselves and assigned names to them at their own discretion. Regarding Basilides, we have the testimony of Agrippa Castor, a very famous writer of his time, in Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 7 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and Jerome, in the *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* under "Agrippa." He composed a <note>original: "κατὰ Βασιλείδου ἔλεγχον"</note> *Refutation against Basilides*, in which he refuted twenty-four commentaries that the heretic had written on the Gospel; he also exposed his deceptions and arts of seduction. <note>original: "Ἐκφαίνειν γὰρ τὰ ἀπόῤῥητά φησιν..."</note> For he says that he [Basilides] revealed secrets, having composed twenty-four books on the Gospel; and that he named prophets for himself, Barcabbas and Barcoph, and others non-existent whom he set up for himself, giving them foreign names to strike terror into those who are astonished by such things. Eusebius, ibid. Jerome reads *Barcaban* and *Barcob*. Epiphanius, Heresy 26, has *Barchabbas*. Elsewhere I have found written *Barthoban* and *Barchobeth*; and perhaps Mariamne and Martha were names of the same origin and served a similar use. And what if Marthana and Marthus, sisters descended from the line of Elxai, followed in their footsteps with some slight change of names? Epiphanius, Heresy 19, which is that of the *Ossenes*; <note>original: "Ἕως μὲν γὰρ Κανσανίτις..."</note> For as long as Kausanitis, of his own race, lived, a certain Marthas and Marthana, two sisters in the same region, were worshipped as goddesses because they were supposedly of the seed of the aforementioned Elxai. Marthas died a short time ago, but Marthana remained until now; the deluded heretics in that region used to carry away their spittle and other bodily fluids, supposedly for the warding off of diseases.

Page 272. line 45. ***Marcionists***] Justin, *Apology* 2, pages 70, 92. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapters 30, 51. The same wrote five books against Marcion. Origen, *On the Right Faith in One God against the Marcionists*, whom he criticizes throughout his works. Clement, *Stromata* 3, 4, 7, and elsewhere. Eusebius, Book 4, chapters 11, 24. Epiphanius, Heresy 42. Theodoret, Book 1, *On Heretical Fables*. Augustine, *On Heresies*. Damascene, *On Heresies*. The rest of the Fathers mentioned them and refuted their doctrines.

Page 272. line 56. ***In the things before these***] See the Annotations to page 132.

Page 273. line 36. ***Branding irons***] Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 24, concerning the Carpocratians: *But others of them mark their own disciples, cauterizing them on the back parts of the lobe of the right ear.* Epiphanius, Heresy 27, concerning the same, page 106: <note>original: "Σφραγίδα δὲ ἐν καυτῆρι..."</note> They apply a seal with a branding iron, or by means of a surgical scraping, or a needle, those following Carpocrates; they mark the right lobe of the ear of those deceived by them.

Page 273. line 38 ***Enigmas***] These and the previous things which Celsus had said about the Carpocratians seem to be expressed confusedly and less distinctly than the matter required; for the Carpocratians were not called "branding irons of hearing," but they were accustomed to imprint a certain mark or character with a glowing iron, a razor, or another instrument more suitable for this purpose, on the ears of the disciples whom they received into their fellowship. Nor were there lacking other heretics who used symbols, who secretly and obscurely—that is, <note>original: "δι᾽ αἰνιγμάτων"</note> through enigmas which they fashioned for themselves—signified the foolish concepts of their minds; thus they established the *lost sheep* [Luke 15] as a symbol of the celebrated Helen, mystically and enigmatically. Epiphanius, Heresy 21, page 58. Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 20: *And that this is the lost sheep.* Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 34. See Annotations to page 272. Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 13: *The generation of the Aeons <term>Aeons: divine emanations in Gnostic thought</term>, and the error of the sheep, and the discovery of the one who unites into one, these men who have reduced all things to numbers dare to announce mystically.* That woman whose blood had flowed for twelve years [Matthew 9:20], they believed signified the passion of the twelfth Aeon. Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 1: *They say that this passion, which occurred around the twelfth Aeon, is signified by the apostasy of Judas, who was the twelfth of the Apostles, and because he suffered in the twelfth month; for they want him to have preached for one year after his Baptism. Furthermore, they say this is most clearly signified in her who suffered a flow of blood: for having suffered for twelve years, she was healed by the Lord's coming when she touched the hem of his garment; and because of this the Savior said, "Who touched me?" teaching the Disciples the mystery that occurred among the Aeons.*

# ORIGEN’S Against Celsus.

<margin>☞</margin> ...the healing of the Aeon <note>Aeons are divine emanations in Gnostic cosmology</note> who suffered. They believe the wandering sheep denotes the wanderings of *Achamoth* <note>A figure in Gnostic myth representing fallen wisdom</note> outside the *Pleroma* <note>The "Fullness" or divine realm</note>. And since *Achamoth* wandered outside the *Pleroma*, and was formed by Christ, and sought by the Savior, they clearly say this regarding his statement, *that he himself came for her who had wandered, the sheep*. For they claim the wandering sheep refers to their mother, from whom they want the Church here to have been seeded. They want the woman who sweeps the house and finds the coin to be held as a symbol of the higher Sophia <note>Wisdom</note>. Irenaeus, ibid. For they do not speak according to the Church, but otherwise, contrary to the preaching of the truth. They primarily use the scriptures called the Acts of Andrew and John, and Thomas, and certain Apocrypha, and whatever words of the Old Testament they wish.

And the same man, even when he tasted something of the truth by denying the Gods, nevertheless ordered a Cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius at the very end. I believe this was in honor of his father; because Apollo declared Socrates the wisest of all."* And in book 1 *On the Soul*, chapter 1. Lactantius, book 3, chapter 20:
> "Was it not indeed a sign of the greatest vanity that,
> "before his death, he asked his friends to sacrifice
> "a cock for him to Aesculapius, which he had vowed?
> "He feared, evidently, lest before Rhadamanthus <note>A judge of the underworld</note>
> "the recoverer [*receiver] of the vow,
> "he might be held liable by Aesculapius. I would
> "think the man most insane if he had perished
> "afflicted by disease; but since he did this while sane,
> "he is himself insane who thinks him to be wise."
But I, O Lactantius, would not indeed call you insane; since you have written not a few things both prudently and learnedly: but I would contend that Socrates was a man of good heart for those times; whose life is praised by the most learned as a certain image of Christian holiness. But that you have by no means grasped Plato's meaning is proven by this: that those things which are delivered in veiled figures, and are never to be understood except by **Allegorical** explanations, you have accepted as if spoken simply; forgetting (as it seems) that maxim: *He will never be a Platonist who does not think Plato must be understood Allegorically:* as Caelius Rhodiginus says, book 16, chapter 12 of *Ancient Readings*. These words of the dying Socrates have been interpreted more kindly by Caelius Rhodiginus in the place cited, and also by Theodoret and [Pico della] Mirandula. The latter, in his *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, says: "Finally, he will admonish us to nourish the cock; that is, to feed the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things, as if with solid food and heavenly Ambrosia. This is the cock at whose sight the lion (that is, all earthly power) feels dread and reverence: this is that cock to whom we read in Job that understanding was given: when this cock crows, erring man returns to his senses: this cock in the morning twilight, with the morning stars,

<column-break/>

praises God, and may he harmonize with us daily: this cock the dying Socrates—when he hoped he would join the divinity of his soul to the divinity of the greater world—said he owed to Aesculapius (that is, the Physician of souls), being now placed beyond all danger of disease." The former <note>Theodoret</note> in his seventh discourse *To the Greeks, On Sacrifices* says: "And I think that Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus, when he ordered the cock to be sacrificed, did so to refute the indictment brought against him. For Anytus and Meletus accused him of not recognizing the Gods; yet he clearly showed in other places that he understood the divinity to be without need. For these very things—if indeed Plato recorded his doctrines—show that God did not make the world for the sake of need, so that he might reap honors from men, and from other Gods and spirits, and that we might receive something standing by from the sacrifice: from us, smoke; but from Gods and spirits, their own proper service."

## Page 77
->Llll<-

...material for praise! Exercise your pen, bring forth more certain evidence, and you will extort thanks which a man envious of such great honor would scarcely give of his own accord. For our part, that saying of Scaliger has pleased us thus far, and will continue to please: "Finally, nothing is so common as to see these *relief-images* <note>original: ἐκτυπα (ektypa)</note> enclosed in gems, even very ancient ones. No one understands them except the one who saw to their making, and labor is spent in vain trying to interpret them. For how many likely things can be said, none of which might open their true meaning?" The ancient Heretics, especially the Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher</note> and the Marcosians, left many things of this sort behind; these are preserved today in the cabinets of Antiquarians, along with their God ABRAXAS. I think I still have one. Joseph Scaliger, Letter 119, to Isaac Casaubon.

Page 292, line 2. **Places** <note>original: Τόπες (Topes)</note>] Namely Rome (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 13), Arabia, Egypt, and Palestine (ibid, book 6, chapter 19). See the Annotations for page 193.

Page 292, line 8. **Leviathan** <note>original: Λεβιαθάν</note>] This Leviathan and Behemoth <note>original: Beemon</note>, as far as I know, do not occur in Tertullian, Irenaeus, Epiphanius, or other authors who wrote about Heresies. I believe the Ophites <note>A Gnostic sect that revered the serpent (ophis)</note> used these names to denote the Devil, and, so that the fable might be even more fabulous, they added these words of their own to the Heresy of the Valentinians, whom they followed in most things. In Rhenanus’s diagram, which is placed before Tertullian’s book *Against the Valentinians* in the Pamelian edition, the individual powers of the Aeons and the Genealogies are placed in the order in which Valentinus arranged them, and the Devil has his seat almost at the lowest part of it; this favors our conjecture to some extent. For Origen says: *He also thought of the one named Behemoth within it, as if stationed by the lowest circle.* Irenaeus (book 1, chapter 1) concerning the Valentinians, and Tertullian in his book against the same (chapter 22), make mention of the Devil. "Infamy," he says, "is more tolerable among them regarding the Devil, perhaps because he takes a filthier origin. For he is assigned from the wickedness of that sorrow, from which they mark the births of Angels, Demons, and all spiritual malices." And yet they also affirm the Devil to be the work of the Demiurge <note>The "craftsman" or lesser deity who created the physical world in Gnostic thought</note>, and they call him the "World-holder," and maintain he is more knowledgeable of higher things as being spiritual by nature, than the Demiurge who is merely "soulish" <note>original: animalem</note>. He deserves preference from those by whom all Heresies are managed. The Greek of Irenaeus is found thus in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 31, page 187: *From the rest of the spiritual things of wickedness, they teach that things were made; from whence the Devil had his origin, whom they also call the World-ruler, and the demons, and the Angels, and the whole spiritual substance of wickedness.*

Page 292, line 28. **Gehenna** <note>original: Γεένναν - Hell or a place of fiery torment</note>] It is not clear from the Heretical writers whether the Ophites or Valentinians thought about Gehenna or Tartarus. Yet hear what the Valentinians dreamed regarding the three kinds of men. Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 1: "They say there are three kinds of men: Spiritual, Soulish, and Earthly <note>original: Spiritalem, Psychicum, Choicum</note>, just as there were Cain, Abel, and Seth: to show from these three natures, not according to the individual, but according to the genus. And the Earthly indeed goes into corruption; but the Soulish, if it chooses better things, will find refreshment in a middle place; but if worse things, it too passes to its like. But Achamoth <note>A personification of Wisdom in Gnosticism</note> sows spiritual things from that time until now, because of which souls are indeed educated here; and the seeds, having been nourished because they were sent out small, are afterwards rendered as brides of the Savior, having been held worthy of perfection. They correspond as Angels to their souls, who of necessity will find refreshment forever in the middle place with the Demiurge." Tertullian, in his book against the Valentinians, chapter 32: "The human race will go to these ends: the Earthly and material mark into total destruction, because all flesh is grass. And the soul is mortal among them, unless it finds salvation through faith. The souls of the righteous—that is, ours—are sent to the Demiurge in the receptacles of the middle place." Why then would these Heretics think of Gehenna, Tartarus, and infernal punishments, when they believed the souls of the good are received into a middle place, but those of the wicked go into total destruction?

Page 292, line 45. **Purification** <note>original: Κάθαρσιν (Katharsin)</note>] See the Annotations for page 168.

Page 292, line 55. **Nor to all** <note>original: Οὔτε πᾶσιν</note>] Origen, at the end of the eighth book of his *Explanations on the Epistle to the Romans*: *But he who despises the purifications of the word of God and Evangelical doctrine, reserves himself for sad and penal purifications; so that the fire of Gehenna may purge in torments him whom neither Apostolic doctrine nor the Evangelical word purged, according to that which is written: "And I will purify you with fire unto purification." Truly, how long this very purification, which is applied through the punishment of fire, exacts torments from sinners, and for how many ages, he alone can know to whom the Father has handed over all judgment; because He so loves His creature that for its sake He emptied Himself of the form of God and took the form of a servant, so that men might be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Nevertheless, we must always remember that the Apostle wished the present passage to be held as a mystery; so that the faithful and perfect might cover such a sense within themselves in silence like a mystery of God, and not bring it forth everywhere to the imperfect and those less capable. "It is good," says the Scripture, "to conceal the mystery of the King."*

Page 294. line 22. **Ophites**] <note>original: Ὀφιανοὶ</note> Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 37: *“For the Ophites, as heretics, took their pretexts from the Nicolaitans and Gnostics, and the heresies surrounding them. Clement, *Miscellanies* <note>Stromata</note> book 7: *“Some are named from the theories they have sent forth, such as those called Cainites and Ophites.”* Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 47: *“To these were added those heretics also who are called Ophites. For they magnify the serpent to such an extent that they even prefer him to Christ himself. For he, they say, gave us the origin of the knowledge of good and evil. Moses, they say, perceiving his power and majesty, set up the bronze serpent; and whoever looked upon it obtained health. Furthermore, they say, Christ himself in his Gospel imitates the sacred power of that very serpent, saying: 'And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.' They introduce the serpent to bless their Eucharists.”* Damascene, *On Heresies*: "The Ophites worship a snake and think it is Christ; they even keep a real serpent in a cave." Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 37, which concerns the Ophites: *“For they keep a natural serpent in a certain chest, which they bring out from its hole at the hour of their Mysteries; and casting loaves of bread upon a table, they summon the serpent. When the hole is opened, it comes forth. And so the serpent, having climbed onto the table and knowing the folly of these people through its craftiness, goes up onto the table and coils itself among the loaves; and this they say is the perfect sacrifice. Whence also, as I have heard from someone, they not only break the loaves in which the serpent has coiled and distribute them to those receiving, but each person also kisses the serpent on its mouth—the serpent having been either charmed into tameness by some sorcery, or the animal acting through some other operation of the devil to deceive them—and they worship such a thing; and they call this the Thanksgiving <note>Eucharist</note> which has been brought about through its coiling.”* Theodoret, book 1, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* on the Ophites: "But some of them say that Christ, having changed into a lower form, entered the womb of the virgin, and thus the wretched men understand the saying of the Apostle: 'Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery, etc.'"

Page 294. line 43. **Euphrates**] Origen alone records that Euphrates was the author of this heresy. Whether he is the same as the one mentioned by Theodoret, book 1, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* on the Peratics, let the studious decide. "Ademes," he says, "the Carystian, and Euphrates the Peratic, from whom they are called Peratics, who were of that opinion, say one, etc." Certainly, Clement testifies that the heresy of the Peratics or Peraticans was very ancient, *Miscellanies* 7: *“Of the heresies, some are called by a name, such as that from Valentinus, Marcion, and Basilides, even if they boast of following the opinion of Matthias; for as the teaching of all the Apostles was one, so also was the tradition. Page 297, line 29. **Iaoia** <note>original: *Ἰαωΐα*</note> ] Grotius in his *Annotations on chapter 22 of the Gospel according to Matthew*: I do not doubt that what is found in Origen as *Iaoia*, called so among the Hebrews, should be read as *Iao* or *Ia*, so that there are two names: Yahweh and Yah <note>original: יהוה & יה</note>. Jerome also thinks this name should be read no differently than *Iao*. Clement of Alexandria says: *Iaou* <note>original: *Ἰαοὺ*</note> is a mistake, unless it is in the Scripture. Others pronounce it differently; I have found it written in some places as *Iau*. Among the Samaritans it is *Iabe*. Theodoret, *Question 15 on Exodus*. Epiphanius, *Heresy 40, page 296*. Photius, *Epistle 162*: "I am He who is" <note>original: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν</note>. This is called *Aia* among the Hebrews, but *Iabe* among the Samaritans. It is also written with these letters: *yod, aleph, vau, he* <note>original: ἰῶδ. ἄλφ. ὐαῦθ. ἢθ.</note>, through which the beginningless and endless nature of God is shown. Diodorus in book 2 of the *Historical Library*, Macrobius in book 1, chapter 18 of the *Saturnalia*, and others, read it as *Iao*. Philo, quoting Sanchuniathon, uses *Ieuo* <note>original: *Ἰευώ*</note>, found in Eusebius, book 10, chapter 9 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.

Page 299, line 50. **Nowhere** <note>original: *Οὐδαμοῦ*</note> ] Grotius in his *Annotations on Matthew, chapter 13, verse 55*: Either memory failed Origen, or the copies of Mark [chapter 6, verse 3] at that time had a different text; for he explicitly says, "Nowhere," etc. What do you mean, Origen? Do we not call him who makes yokes and plows a Carpenter? Hear Justin in his *Dialogue with Trypho, page 316*: "And when Jesus came to the Jordan, and was thought to be the son of Joseph the carpenter, and appeared without beauty, as the scriptures proclaimed, and was thought to be a carpenter (for he worked at these carpentry jobs while among men, making plows and yokes; through these he taught the symbols of righteousness and an active life)." Even the most ancient pictures show us Joseph together with Jesus handling wooden boards and tools proper to this art. In everyone's mouth, he is heard of as either the Carpenter or the son of the Carpenter. Only Bede and Hilary separately suggest he practiced the craft of a Blacksmith. The latter, in his *Commentary on Matthew 13*, says: "Clearly he was the son of a Smith, conquering iron with fire, refining all the power of the age by judgment, and forming the mass into every work for human utility"; the former, in his book on the Gospel according to Mark, chapter 2: "For even if human things are not to be compared to divine, the type is nonetheless complete; because the Father of Christ works by fire and Spirit: whence his precursor says of him as if of the son of a Smith; 'He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire'; because he changes the vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy by working them with the fire of his spirit."

Yet they did not cultivate that friendship with such loyalty or great service that it could be said of Euphrates that "certain not unskillful philosophers were captured by the magic within Apollonius." Page 303, line 1. **Angels**] Origen, *Tractate 5 on Matthew*: "Likewise you may ask, concerning the Angels of these little ones who are set over them, when they begin to have care of them; whether it is from the moment they are born in Christ through the washing of regeneration <note>Baptism</note>, like infants then being born and no longer subject to a certain opposing power; or from the time of their fleshly birth, according to the foreknowledge of God and His pre-ordination," *Whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the glory of Christ.* You see that he who carefully examines both sides must determine which of them is true, and bring forth Scripture as testimony agreeing with one of the two. For much can be said on either side, yet let us bring forth a little from the much. For those who wish that an Angel be assigned to them as soon as they are born—those who are foreknown by God—use the voice of the Apostle saying: *Who separated me from my mother's womb, that he might reveal his son in me:* as if it were necessary from that point for him to have an Angel ruling him, since he was separated according to the foreknowledge of God. Likewise, in the Epistle of Jude it is written thus: *To those beloved in God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called:* by whom are they preserved, if not by the Angels to whom they had been delivered, so that they might be preserved and rescued from every evil, they who were held as foreknown and pre-ordained? Likewise, one might bring forth that which is said in the Psalms;

<column-break/>

" *From my mother's womb you are my protector:* so that God is the protector of the foreknown, having deputed Angels for this very ministry. Thus also he will accept that phrase, *You took me from my mother's womb:* likewise; *I was cast upon you from the womb;* and a thousand other such things having this sense. But he who wishes that a helping Angel be given to men from the moment they are made newborn infants in Christ through the washing of regeneration, will say that it is not credible that a holy Angel should preside over the senseless, the unbelieving, the erring, and those serving various and foul desires, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another, fornicators and adulterers, and sometimes even those who lie with males, thieves, drunkards, and the greedy; lest he be defiled in such acts of the man to whom he was given as a guardian. Rather, a man is indeed, in the time of his infidelity and of his sins born from infidelity, under the Angels of Satan and malignant spirits and foul demons: but when he has received the faith, then Christ, who is the redeemer, who redeems him with the price of his own blood from malignant Masters when he believes in God, delivers him to a holy Angel, who because of his purity always sees the face of the Father." Clement, *Stromata* 5, page 592: <note>original Greek: Τῶν μικρῶν ὧ...</note> "Of the little ones, according to the Scripture, and the least, he says the Angels who see God; and he shows that an overseer is sent to us through the Angels stationed there, as Plato ventured to write. Since all souls and our lives, as if by lot, are carried in order toward Lachesis <note>one of the Fates</note>, to each of them is sent as a guardian for life the spirit (daemon) which he chose, to fulfill the things chosen. Perhaps also the 'divine sign' (daemonion) of Socrates hinted at something of this sort." Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 18: *Because the face of the Father is always seen by the Angels in heaven.* Great is the dignity of souls, that each one has from the beginning of birth an Angel designated for its custody. Whence we read in the Apocalypse of John, " *To the Angel of Ephesus, of Thyatira, and to the Angel of Philadelphia, and to the Angel of the four remaining Churches, write these things.*" The Apostle also commands that the heads of women in the Churches be veiled because of the Angels. Behold a great thing: to have the weakness of a man, and the security of a God.*"

### To the Most Illustrious and Learned Man, CLAUDE SARRAU, Henri Valois sends greetings.

> "I remember, (most illustrious and learned *Sarrau*,) when you were at my house yesterday, opening to you my conjecture regarding a certain most faulty passage in Origen; when I had pointed out its correction to you, having brought out the manuscript, you immediately seemed to me, in your kindness, to modestly approve it. But since the arguments and testimonies upon which this correction rests were not then at hand, let that passage of Origen—a passage truly intricate and difficult—become clearer by my explanation; nor let any room for doubting our correction be left to anyone.
> "Origen responds, therefore, in that place (that is, in the seventh book of *Against Celsus*, page 315) to a certain significant argument which Celsus had used to tear down the faith and belief of Christians concerning Jesus Christ: which seemed to rest chiefly on this foundation, that the Prophets had predicted of him long before whatever happened afterward.
> "But what, Celsus said, if the Prophets predicted that the supreme God of all would serve, or be sick, or even die; will it therefore be necessary for him both to serve, and be sick, and die, so that a dead God might be believed in? But surely, he says, the Prophets never predicted these things: for they are impious and entirely foreign to reason. Hence, it is not what the Prophets predicted,

<column-break/>

> "or what they did not predict, that must be investigated; but whether that which they predicted is fitting for the divine Majesty. For if it is unseemly and base, even if all men, seized by madness, predicted it, it will never deserve belief.
> "Origen responds that in this argumentation of Celsus, two connected premises are detected, the consequences of which are mutually opposed and repugnant to each other in this way: If, he says, the true Prophets of the supreme God predicted that he would serve and die, these things will necessarily happen, since they are true Prophets of God. Again, if those same Prophets pronounced these things about God, they will not happen, since they are contrary to the divine nature. These are two connected premises whose consequences are mutually repugnant; namely, they will happen, and they will not happen. Whenever, however, Origen says, in two connected premises the antecedent is the same, but the consequences are mutually repugnant, then the antecedent, which is common in the two connected premises, is usually refuted by that argumentation which the Stoics call <term>through two tropes</term> <note>original: "διὰ δύο τροπικῶν" — a technical term in Stoic logic for a specific type of syllogism.</note>. In the common copies of Origen today, it is read as <term>by the so-called theorem through two prophetic [arguments]</term> <note>original: "τῷ καλουμένῳ διὰ δύο προφητικῶν θεωρήματι"</note>; but I truly do not doubt that it should be read, as I said, <term>tropes</term> <note>original: "τροπικῶν"</note>. For thus *Sextus Empiricus* in the second book of *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*, at the beginning, calls that kind of argumentation: '<term>For just as he who does not know what the indivisible is, or the theorem through two tropes, is not even able to say anything about them</term>.' And *Galen* in the second book of *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*, page 254, at the end: '<term>But now,</term>' he says, '<term>how syllogisms are resolved by the [theorem] through two tropes</term> (delete <term>three</term>) <term>and how those which conclude indifferently, or some others of such a kind... employing the first and second theme, to many who have been accurately trained in continuities, just as indeed in others which are resolved into a syllogism through the third or fourth theme. And most of these it is possible to resolve otherwise more briefly, as Antipater wrote</term>.' And these things indeed concern the name of the syllogism. But why it was so called is difficult to say, and much more by what reasoning it was constructed. A <term>trope</term> <note>original: "Τροπικὸν"</note> indeed is the same as a proposition, or <term>lemma</term>, just as *Sextus Empiricus* teaches, *Against the Mathematicians*, pages 300 and 301. Nevertheless, Origen adds certain things in the same place, from which (though obscurely) it can be perceived what was the reason and method of that argumentation of the Stoics. For after he said, whenever in two connected premises..."

# ORIGEN against CELSUS.
## Mmmm 2

Claude Sarrau to Henri Valois, at Paris.

I acknowledge that I owe you a great deal, and I most gladly profess it, my dearest Valois <note>original: "suavissime Valesi"</note>, for that letter of yours which our most dear and learned friend Ménage delivered to me. Indeed, not content with merely pointing out a remarkable observation—and one not obvious to everyone—concerning a most difficult passage in Origen, you also wished to strengthen and illuminate it with new testimonies. And yet, your authority certainly carries such weight with me that even standing alone it would have immediately won my approval. Nevertheless, that care of yours was not unwelcome, by which you wished to place in the open light an exceptional emendation of immense value, drawn from the decrees of other most excellent Masters. Few, truly very few, read the ancients in such a way, and search into them so deeply, as to extract such hidden meanings from them. O blessed hours! those which I happened to spend three days ago with you and with your brother Hadrian—truly your brother as much by nature as by sublime learning—with Ménage and the younger Heinsius also present. As often as I revolve these things in my mind, the sum of my prayers is that:

> "Many such days may often come to me." <note>A quote from Ovid's Tristia.</note>

Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> enumerates various types of argumentation by Chrysippus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher known for his logic.</note> in his life of Zeno, which I will not be loath to transcribe here, since I have no doubt they will bring a little light and provide a fuller understanding of this passage to a curious investigator of such subtleties. *There are five types of arguments with Chrysippus through which every discourse is woven; these are employed in analytical matters, in syllogisms, and in tropes <term>tropes: here referring to logical modes or figures of speech</term>. The first is the indemonstrable, in which every discourse is composed of a conditional and its antecedent, from which the conditional begins, and it brings in the consequent; for example: If A, then B. But A is the case. Therefore B is the case. The second indemonstrable is that which proceeds through a conditional and the opposite of the consequent, having the opposite of the antecedent as its conclusion; for example: If it is day, it is light. But it is night <insert>i.e., it is not light</insert>. Therefore it is not day. For the minor premise arises from the opposite of the consequent, and the conclusion from the opposite of the antecedent. The third indemonstrable is that which proceeds through a negative conjunction, and from one of the parts in the conjunction brings in the opposite of the rest; for example: It is not the case that Plato is dead and Plato is alive. But Plato is dead. Therefore Plato is not alive. The fourth indemonstrable is that which proceeds through a disjunctive and one of the parts in the disjunctive, having the opposite of the rest as its conclusion; for example: Either the first or the second. But the first. Therefore not the second, etc.* <note>original Greek: Παρὰ τῷ Χρυσίππῳ πέντε... This passage outlines the foundations of Stoic propositional logic.</note> Laertius mentions "tropes" in this place, and in the Catalog of books which Chrysippus composed, you will find several whose titles display Chrysippean subtlety in de-

<column-break/>

vising theorems of this kind. For example: *On tropical ambiguities, book 1. On ambiguities of conditional tropes, book 2.* Laertius in his life of Chrysippus: *A comparison of tropical axioms, book 1.* Ibid: *Tropical inquiries addressed to Zeno and Philomathes, book 1. Logical arrangements then concerning arguments and tropes. The first art of arguments and tropes, addressed to Dioscurides. On the arrangement of tropes. To the work on friendly tropes and to Timocrates. On the matters concerning arguments and tropes, book 1.* Ibid. He also treated "Connectives" more extensively in his commentaries: *On probable conditionals, addressed to Dioscurides, book 4,* etc. To this belongs the twisted argumentation of Chrysippus in Cicero, book 4 of the *Academic Questions*: *How then do you judge this conclusion: if you say it is now light, and you speak the truth, it is light. But you say it is light, and you speak the truth; therefore it is light. You certainly approve the type, and say it is most rightly concluded. And so, in teaching, you hand this down as the first mode of concluding. Either, therefore, you will approve whatever is concluded in the same way, or that art of yours is nothing.* See then whether he is likely to approve this conclusion: *If you say that you are lying, and you speak the truth: you are lying. But you say that you are lying, and you speak the truth: therefore you are lying. How can you not approve this, when you have approved the former one of the same kind?* <note>This refers to the famous "Liar's Paradox."</note> These are Chrysippean matters, and were not even resolved by him. I shall pray that the most learned Valois pardons my talkativeness if I briefly remind the Reader, concerning the testimony of Galen, that the word "three" <note>original: τριῶν</note> should hardly be deleted rashly or with a hurried pen, since in Laertius a book of Chrysippus occurs which is titled: *On things through three, again addressed to Gorgippides, book 1.* Laertius in his life of Chrysippus.

At Lindus, which is a town of Rhodes, there are sacred rites of Hercules, the ritual of which is far different from others; for they are celebrated not with *pious silence* <note>original: "εὐφημίᾳ" (euphemia) - literally "good speech," often meaning ritual silence to avoid ill omens.</note> (as the Greeks call it) but with insults and cursing; and they consider the rites violated if ever a "good word" should escape even an impudent person during the solemnities. The reason given for this—if indeed there can be any reason in such vain things—is this: Hercules, when he had landed there and was suffering from hunger, saw a certain plowman at work. He began to ask him to sell him one ox. But the man said it could not be done, because all his hope of tilling the earth rested on those two beasts. Hercules, using his accustomed violence, because he could not receive one, took both. But that unhappy man, when he saw his oxen being slaughtered, avenged his injury with curses; which was most pleasing to that elegant and refined man [Hercules]. For while he prepared a feast for his companions and devoured the oxen of another, he listened with laughter and cackling to the man most bitterly reviling him. But after it was decided that divine honors should be deferred to Hercules out of admiration for his valor, an altar was placed for him by the citizens, which he named from the event *Bouzygon*, that is, the Yoke of the Ox; at which two joined oxen should be sacrificed, just like those he had taken from the plowman. And he appointed that very man as his Priest, and commanded that he should always use those same curses in celebrating the sacrifices: for he claimed he had never feasted more pleasantly. Philostratus, book 2 of the *Images*, regarding Thiodamas, from whom Hercules snatched away the oxen along with his associates: *Whence a plowing ox is sacrificed to Hercules, and they begin the rites with cursing—the very ones, I imagine, the farmer used then. And Hercules rejoices, and grants good things to the Lindians who perform these purifications.*

# ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.
## Nnnn
<meta>catchword: law</meta>

They assigned [the body parts] and attributed individual Decans <note>Decans are 36 deities or stars in ancient Egyptian astrology, each ruling ten degrees of the zodiac and specific parts of the human body.</note> to each, and the diseases of those parts, of which they were also the specific "Climacterics" <note>Critical points or periods of life/health influenced by the stars.</note>. There is a notable passage on this matter by Celsus in Origen’s work against him, in these words from Book VIII: "That to these, etc." <note>original: "Ὅτι δὲ τοῖς δὲ, &c."</note>. That he is speaking of the Decans is indicated by the number itself, and those whom he calls "Fixed Ethereal Gods" <note>original: "Θεὸς αἰθερίους"</note>. But even more so by what follows regarding their Egyptian names: "And of the demons, etc." <note>original: "Καὶ τ̃ δαιμόνων, &c."</note>. It is clear that these are the names of the Decans from the catalog we set forth above. However, some names here are corrupted or named differently than among those Mathematicians <note>In this context, "Mathematicians" refers to astrologers.</note> from whom I drew them. *Chnoumis* is the third Decan of Cancer there, and *Charchoumis* is the first of Leo, who is here wrongly called *Chnachoumis*. *Siket* is the name there, which in Origen is *Sikat*. In the common editions of Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrologer.</note>, it is read as *ASICATH*, which seems to confirm the writing in Origen’s book. For *Kyat Smat*, it is written in Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, an astrologer.</note> as the first Decan of Capricorn. Celsus’s *Ere* is Hephaestion’s *Ero*, the second Decan of Taurus. *Erebiu* is not in our catalog, but in its place is either *Ppeiu* or *Rheiu*, the first Decan of Sagittarius. For *Biu*, there is *Asiu* in ours, the first Decan of Pisces; what is called *Pamanor* in Origen, I believe to be what Hephaestion calls *Roumanes*. *Ranur* is also clearly corrupted for *Chontare* or *Eure*, or for *Sro Isro*. But these are of little importance. We only wished to show here that Celsus spoke of the Decans, to whom individual parts of the body are attributed as presiding Gods, and the diseases of those parts as if they were the ones causing or rather repelling the disease-bearing Climacterics.

Page 419, line 32. *Of every rational being* <note>original: "Παντὸς λογικοῦ"</note>] Origen, Book 1, Chapter 6, *On First Principles*: "Of those, indeed, who remained in that beginning which we described as similar to the future end, some, by the arrangement and dispensation of the world, obtained the rank of Angels, others of Virtues, others of Principalities, others of Powers—namely, that they might exercise power over those who need to have power over their heads—others the rank of Thrones, that is, having the office of judging or ruling those who need it. "And of everyone, whence both from common conception and from the tradition of the Scriptures, there is a certain nature outside of the bodily births, disposed contrary to the good and harmful to human life, which voluntarily fell away from the better conception, and by its apostasy from the good, established within itself that which is understood as the opposite. All say the Apostle numbers these among the 'under-earthly' <note>original: "καταχθονίοις"</note>, signifying in that discourse that when wickedness is eventually abolished through long periods of ages, nothing will be left outside of the good. One may read several things leading to this in Jerome’s *Commentary on Psalm 23*: *"Lift up your gates, O ye Princes."* <note>original: "Tollite portas, Principes, vestras."</note> This is the voice of the good Angels to the bad Angels, whose Prince is the Devil. And in Ambrose’s *Commentary on Chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Ephesians*: "That the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the Principalities and Powers in the heavenly places through the Church." God thought so well of this [the Church] that He gave it as a teacher not only to the nations, but also so that through it the truth of Christ might become known to the spirits in the heavenly places, who are the Principalities and Powers. They are "Powers" because they are more powerful among the other spirits; "Principalities" because they rule over the powers, so that recognizing through the Church—which has been drawn to life in Christ in many ways—that the mystery of the one God remains, they may cease from error. For the aim is that the preaching of the Church may benefit even these, and they may desert the assent of the Devil’s Tyranny, with which they armed themselves in impious presumption against the faith of the one God. This sense is prescribed in Psalm 23, where God is shown as the Lord of the universe, the Spirit of God saying through David: "The earth is the Lord's, etc." It is said, therefore, to these princes who are in error in the heavenly places, or to his ministers on earth, that they should remove the gates of their Prince—that is, the Devil—from their minds, through which the error of asserting many gods entered. One remedy, as you see—namely, the discipline of the good Angels to assist in the salvation of Demons—was devised by Origen. Behold another described in this manner by Jerome in his *Letter to Avitus*, regarding what to beware of in the books *On First Principles*: "At the end he introduced (which is sacrilegious even to think) that for the salvation of Demons, Christ would also suffer in the air and in the higher places; and although he did not say it, it is understood as a consequence: just as he became a man for men to liberate men, so also for the salvation of Demons, God would become what they are, to liberate those to whom he is to come." Lest we be thought to assert this from our own opinion, his own words must be placed: "For just as through the shadow of the Gospel he fulfilled the shadow of the Law; so because every..."

# Annotations on Book VIII.

The law is an example and a shadow of heavenly ceremonies <note>A reference to Hebrews 8:5</note>; it must be more diligently investigated whether we rightly understand that the heavenly law and the ceremonies of the supernal worship also do not possess fullness, but require the truth of the Gospel. We read of this as the "Eternal Gospel" in the Apocalypse of John <note>Revelation 14:6</note>, in comparison, evidently, to this Gospel of ours, which is temporal and preached in a passing world and age. Indeed, even if we wished to inquire into this up until the passion of the Lord Savior—though it may be bold and rash to seek His passion in heaven—nevertheless, if the "spiritual forces of wickedness are in the heavenly places" <note>Ephesians 6:12</note>, and we do not blush to confess the cross of the Lord for the destruction of those things which He destroyed by His passion: why should we fear to suspect something even in the higher places at the consummation of the ages, so that the Nations of all places might be saved by His passion? See the same author in the *Letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem*, in the *Commentary on Jonah*, ch. 3; *Commentary on Proverbs*, ch. 2; and *Commentary on Isaiah*, ch. 66. See also Augustine, *The City of God*, book 21, ch. 17, and the book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus.

But Polycarp, looking with a severe countenance upon the whole crowd in the stadium, waving his hand at them, groaning and looking up to heaven, said, 'Away with the atheists!' When the governor pressed him and said, 'Swear, and I will release you; revile Christ,' Polycarp replied, 'Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He has done me no wrong; how then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' When the governor persisted again, saying, 'Swear by the Fortune of Caesar,' Polycarp said, 'If you vainly imagine that I should swear by the Fortune of Caesar, as you say, pretending to be ignorant of who I am, hear plainly: I am a Christian.'" To swear by "Fortune" and by the "Geniuses of the Caesars" <note>The *Genius* was the divine spirit believed to protect an individual</note> amounts to the same thing. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 32: "But we also swear, just as not by the Geniuses of the Caesars, so by their safety, which is more august than all Geniuses."
