At the end of the fifth book of his *Explanations of the Epistle to the Romans*, he tears down this opinion: "Wherefore I wonder that some, against this evident opinion of Paul, wish to assert that in future ages it is necessary for Christ to suffer again the same or similar things, so that even those might be liberated whom the medicine of His dispensation in the present life could not heal. For they say: 'Can there be any age in the future where neither anything good nor anything evil is done; but things are numbed and remain according to their substance?' They assert this seems absurd. 'We shall grant, therefore, that something is done; and where something is done, it is necessary,' they say, 'that something be done rightly, and something also less rightly; and in the act itself some progress, and become better, others worse. For **freedom of will** <note>original: *liberum arbitrium*</note> will always remain for a rational nature, and just as it is possible,' etc. Proposing these and similar things, they think that the same dispensations must be repeated by Christ in future ages. But to these we shall respond briefly as we are able: we do not deny that free will always remains for a rational nature, but we assert that the power of the **Cross of Christ** and of this death, which He undertook at the end of the ages, is so great that it suffices for the health and remedy not only of the present and future, but also of past ages; and not only for this our human order, but also for the heavenly powers and orders," etc. Nevertheless, it is probable that Origen believed in the alternations of punishments and rewards: both because he asserted the world must be inhabited anew (See Annotations for page 203) and because he devised a heavenly war, which the opposing powers would undertake against the people of God. Jerome describes his opinion in this manner, in the *Letter to Avitus* regarding *What to beware of in the books "On First Principles"*: "Not content with this discussion, he says that at the end of all things, when we are to return to the heavenly Jerusalem, wars of opposing powers will rise up against the people of God: let their virtue not be idle, but..."

Page 427, line 33. **We do not serve in the army** <note>original Greek: Ὁυ συστρατευόμεθα</note>] Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 37: "We are but of yesterday, and yet we have filled all the places you have—cities, islands, forts, towns, marketplaces, the very camps, tribes, companies, the Palace, the Senate, the Forum: we have left you only the temples." And chapter 42: "We sail with you, and we serve in the army, and we farm, and we trade, accordingly we mix our arts and publish our works for your use." But in the books *On Idolatry*, chapter 19, and *On the Military Crown*, chapter 11, he hesitates, disputes, and finally seems to favor most that opinion which is opposed to military service. The things which that incomparable man Hugo Grotius discussed on this question are most worthy of reading, Book 1, chapter 2, section 9, *On the Law of War and Peace*: where he makes a very heavy judgment regarding the "fickleness" of Tertullian and Origen. "It is customary," he says, "for those who attack war to bring forward certain sayings of the ancient Christians, to which I have three things to say. First, that nothing more can be gathered from those sayings than the private opinion of certain individuals, not the public opinion of the Churches: add to this, that almost all those whose sayings these are, love to go a separate way from others and teach something more 'magnificent'; such as Origen and Tertullian, who are not even consistent with themselves: for the same Origen says that examples were given by God **so that just and ordered wars might be waged among men, if ever necessity should require it** <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ δικαίως κῂ τεταγμένως πολέμους εἴποτε δέοι γίγνεσθαι ἐν ἀνθρώποις</note> [Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book 4, page 217]: and that same Tertullian, who elsewhere seems to approve less of capital punishment, said, 'No one denies that it is good when the guilty are punished'; and he hesitates regarding military service. For in the book *On Idolatry*, he says, 'The question is asked whether the faithful can be converted to military service, and whether military service can be admitted to the faith.'" See Origen, *Against Celsus*, pages 217, 253, 349.

# Annotations on ORIGEN

...they stole away, not the sacrifices, but among the Romans it seems to be unknown. <note>original: "φέων ὑπέκλεψαν μὴ θυσίας, ἀλλὰ παρὰ τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἄγνωστος εἶναι δοκεῖ."</note> See Origen, *Homily 8 on Numbers; Homily 13 on Ezekiel; Homily 35 on Luke; Book 1 On First Principles, chapter 3; On the Holy Spirit; Book 3, chapter 2; On Contrary Powers.* Clement, *Miscellanies <note>original: "Stromata"</note> 1, pages 311, 356; Miscellanies 2, pages 360, 384; Miscellanies 4, page 503; Miscellanies 6, page 638.* Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of Christ; Second Apology for the Decrees of the Nicene Synod.* Eusebius, *Book 3, chapter 3; Book 5, chapter 8 of the Ecclesiastical History.* Tertullian, *On Prayer, chapter 12; and On Modesty, chapter 10.* Rufinus’s *Creed*, at the end of the works of Cyprian, and the book itself which Johann Schott printed at Strasbourg in the year 1522. Truly, we shall dispute concerning the authority of this book at another time with more words, where we shall discuss the testimonies and individual opinions of the ancients more accurately.

Page 13, line 51. *But if even impossible things* <note>original: "Ἐι δὲ καὶ ἀδύνατα"</note>] *Vossius, Book 3, chapter 99, On the Progress of Idolatry.* "But Griffins <note>original: "Gryphes"</note> are, if they are understood as Golden Eagles, or another genus of Eagle: as in Leviticus 11:13, where Moses, among the unclean birds, refers in the first place to the Eagle, the Griffin <note>The translator notes this refers to the ossifrage or bearded vulture</note>, the Sea-eagle, the Kite, and the Vulture. Surely the Mosaic order itself shows it to be a genus of Eagle differing from the common Eagle and the Sea-eagle. But Origen understood the Griffin of the poets: for in Book 4 *On First Principles* <note>original: "Περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>, reviewing various laws which ought to be understood not according to the letter, but Allegorically and spiritually; among other things he writes, in the translation of Rufinus: 'For if concerning impossible things,' etc. He would not have written thus if he had determined the Hebrew **פרס** (*peres*) to be a genus of Eagle, and not a fabulous bird; for if it truly existed, there was no reason why Moses should forbid the eating of it," etc.

Page 14, line 14. *Of song* <note>original: "Ἀοιδῆς"</note>] See *Baronius in the Apparatus, number 13; Casaubon, Exercise 1 on the Apparatus; and the fourth Epistle of Synesius to Euoptius.*

Page 14, line 48. *If possible* <note>original: "Ἐι δυνατόν"</note>] But it cannot be done, if you believe Jerome in his *Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 52.* For it is not in our power to bring back the foreskin after circumcision, according to those who are said in the book of Maccabees to have made foreskins for themselves: which is said of the sons being born, and not of the fathers. Epiphanius feels otherwise, and says it was a custom among the Jews and Samaritans "to cover the circumcision of the private parts," <note>original: "τὴν αἰδοίων περιτομὴν ἐπικαλύπτειν"</note> as *Josephus* expresses it. And they mention that this artifice was discovered by Esau. *Epiphanius, in the book On Weights and Measures:* "In the times of Sadechus, a certain Symmachus, a Samaritan among them, a wise man <unclear>***</unclear> by his own nation, sensing a love of power and being indignant against his own tribe, fled to the Jews, became a proselyte, and was circumcised with a second circumcision. And do not wonder about this, as if it were impossible; for it happens. For as many as flee from the Jews to the Samaritans are re-circumcised; likewise those coming from the Samaritans to the Jews. But what is even more difficult than these, is that even from circumcision they become uncircumcised, by a certain medical art through the so-called 'spatula-tool,' having the skin under the members loosened by the spatula, they produce a foreskin for themselves again." <note>This refers to the ancient medical procedure of *epispasm* to reverse circumcision.</note> See *Cornelius Celsus, Book 7, chapter 25.*

<column-break/>

Page 17, line 32. *Ebionites* <note>original: "Ἐβιωναῖοι"</note>] See *Annotations to Book 2 Against Celsus, page 56; Book 5, pages 272, 274.*

Page 18, line 35. *Perhaps* <note>original: "Τάχας"</note>] See *Annotations to Book 1 Against Celsus, page 26.*

Page 21, line 5. *Those from the* <note>original: "Οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς"</note>] *Marcionists.* See *Annotations to Book 5 Against Celsus, page 267.*

Page 22, line 39. *From the Hebrew* <note>original: "Ἀπὸ τὰ Ἑβραία"</note>] Origen very often had conversations with the wise men of the Jews. *Book 1 Against Celsus, pages 34, 42, 43; Book 2, page 79; Philocalia, page 103.*

Page 24, line 6. *The Creator* <note>original: "Κτίσαντα"</note>] *Marcionists.* See *Annotations to Book 5 Against Celsus, page 267.*

Page 25, line 8. *Taskmaster* <note>original: "Ἐργοδιώκτης"</note>] Signifies Ambrose. See *Annotations to Book 1 Against Celsus, page 1.*

Page 28, line 27. *Volume/Scroll-head* <note>original: "Κεφαλίδα"</note>] Both in this place, and on page 37 of the first book, and page 278 of the sixth book of Origen’s *Against Celsus*, it ought to be rendered *volume*. "The head of a book, which some call a roll. In the head of the book it is written of me." <note>original: "Κεφαλὶς βιβλίου ὅπερ τινὲς εἴλημα φασίν. ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γέγραπται περὶ ἐμοῦ."</note> *Suidas, under 'Kephalis'.* For the paper of the Hebrews was not usually distinguished into pages, but rolled into a small circle, as may be seen in *Jeremiah chapter 36, verse 27*, says *Grotius in his Annotations on the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 7*; whence they named the paper thus rolled up a *Kephalis* <note>literally "little head"</note> from the round shape of a head. See *Grotius*, in the place already cited, and *Nicholas Fuller, Book 2, chapter 10 of the Sacred Miscellanies.*

Page 29, line 30. *Of Marcion* <note>original: "Μαρκίωνος"</note>] *Epiphanius, Heresy 42*, which is that of the Marcionists. "But I shall come to the things written by him, or rather, his forgeries. For he has only the Gospel according to Luke." And a little after: "He uses only the character of the Gospel according to Luke."

Page 30, line 12. *He himself at least* <note>original: "Αὐτὸς γοῦν"</note>] It was Ambrose, when he was a Marcionist. See *Annotations to Book 1 Against Celsus, page 1.*

Page 34, line 9. *To the Shepherd* <note>original: "Τῷ ποιμένι"</note>] See *Annotations to the Philocalia, page 9.*

**Page 38, line 46. "But the ancient"]** The Marcionites <note>A dualist Christian sect following Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and its God.</note>. See the Annotations to Book 5 of *Against Celsus*, page 267.

"Gregory"]** Jerome, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* regarding Theodore: "Theodore, who was later called Gregory <note>Known as Gregory Thaumaturgus, or the 'Wonderworker.'</note>, Bishop of Neocaesarea, while still quite young, on account of his education in Greek and Roman letters, traveled from Cappadocia to Beirut, and from there to Caesarea in Palestine, together with his brother Athenodorus. When Origen discovered their exceptional natural talent, he urged them toward philosophy, and by introducing them bit by bit to the faith of Christ, he made them his own followers. Having been educated by him for five years, they were sent back to their mother; upon departing, Theodore wrote a panegyric <note>A formal speech of praise.</note> of gratitude to Origen. Having called everyone from the region together, and with Origen himself present, he read this; it is a discourse which exists to this day." This *Panegyric* and all the extant works of Gregory were published in the year 1604, with the most illustrious Vossius as translator and commentator. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 30; Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of Gregory Thaumaturgus*; and Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, chapter 22.

**Page 45, line 14. "Arming themselves"]** The Marcionites. See the Annotations to Book 5 of *Against Celsus*, page 267.

**Page 47. "To the mountain"]** See Book 2 of *Against Celsus*, page 99.

**Page 47, line 26. "Transfiguration"]** See the Annotations to Book 2 of *Against Celsus*, page 99.

**Page 65, line 33. "Holy elder women"]** Origen, Volume 5 on John. For it is probable that, while these things were truly said by Jacob and written for this reason, even that phrase, "he supplanted his brother in the womb," was prudently false. But look and see whether the very famous question concerning Jacob and Esau has a solution; for while the boys were not yet born, and had done neither good nor evil—so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, not of works but of Him who calls—it was said to her: "The elder shall serve the younger, as it is written: Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Far from it. Therefore, if we do not look back to works preceding this life, how will it be true that there is no injustice with God, if the elder serves the younger and is hated before he does anything worthy of either servitude or hatred? See the Annotations to Book 1 of *Against Celsus*, page 26.

**Page 73, line 23. "Concerning Judas"]** See the Annotations to Book 2 of *Against Celsus*, page 73.

<column-break/>

**Page 76, line 52. "Of Joseph"]** Origen, Volume 5 on John. But if anyone accepts the *Prayer of Joseph* inscribed in those books which are called "Apocrypha" among the Hebrews, he will soon find this doctrine openly stated there: namely, that those who from the beginning possessed something extraordinary above other men, being far better than other souls, descended to human nature although they were Angels. Jacob says, therefore: "I who speak to you, I am Jacob and Israel, I am an Angel of God and a primary spirit; and Abraham and Isaac were created before every work. But I, Jacob, am called Jacob by men, but my name is Israel; I who am called Israel by God: a man seeing God, because I am the first-born of every living thing animated by God." And he adds: "But when I had come from Mesopotamia of Syria, Uriel the Angel of God came out and said that he had descended to earth and dwelt among men, and that he had been called by the name of Jacob; and he was envious and fought with me and wrestled with me, telling me that his name had primacy over my name and before every Angel. And I asked him his name and what rank he held among the sons of God. Are you not Uriel, the eighth from me, and I Israel the Archangel, the power of the Lord and the Chief Captain of the Host among the sons of God? Am I not Israel, the first minister in the presence of God? And I called upon my God by the unquenchable name."

**Page 77, line 55. "By star-gazing"]** Vigerus in his notes on Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 6, chapter 11. There is a manifest transposition. It should therefore be read: "no longer by star-gazing and by natural science." For here "star-gazing" and "natural science" are the same thing.

**Page 79, line 18. "Of those being tripped up"]** It is read in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 6, chapter 11: "Which is indicative of things supposed." And the most learned Vigerus renders it into Latin in this manner: *But he who has tested these very things by his own experience will surely recognize that this class of men, in those premonitions which they conceive either by voice or in writing, wanders far more often than they touch upon the truth which they imagine for themselves.*

**Page 77, line 44. "But the spirits"]** Salmasius in his book *On Climacteric Years*. Apocryphal tradition holds that from Adam until the one hundred and sixtieth year of Enoch—which was the year 1,286 of the world—the computation of time was not accustomed to proceed by years, but by weeks. For the Archangel Uriel first indicated to Enoch "the name of the four years." For this was kept written in the book of Enoch himself: "And that the year has 52 weeks, and that in 1,286 years there are [a certain number] of days—"

**Page 82, line 22. In the Circuits]** Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, Book 30, "On the Ebionites," page 139: "They also use certain other books, supposedly called the *Circuits of Peter*, written by the hand of Clement, though they have corrupted the contents while leaving a few true things; just as Clement himself convicts them in every way through the encyclical letters of his which are read in the Holy Churches, showing that his own faith and discourse have a different character than the things corrupted by them in his name in the *Circuits*. For he himself teaches virginity, which they do not accept; he praises Elijah, David, Samuel, and all the Prophets, whom these people detest. In these *Circuits*, they have adapted everything to suit their own whims."

**Page 87, line 10. Illogical]** Read *paralogon* <note>meaning "unreasonable" or "fallacious"</note>. "Here I think *aphormē* <note>starting point or occasion</note> is taken for that which Logicians commonly call the 'middle term,' and its placement in both the major and minor premises," says *Vigerus* <note>François Viger, a 17th-century French Jesuit scholar</note> in his notes to Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 7, Chapter 22. "However, a *paralogon aphormē* is a sophisticated and deceptive method of arguing, which someone misuses as a kind of 'starting point' to more easily lead another into error. The Socratics seemed to catch at such starting points. The same Vigerus, as it seems to me, better grasped Origen's mind when he interpreted it in this manner: 'For if someone disputing with another thrusts forward some deceptive and catchy type of argument fabricated by himself, concluding it from his own mind and sense, he will not necessarily persuade the listener of what he wishes by this art; but he will only achieve something if he brings into the open that which is seen to be said with reason. For then one of two things follows: either the listener will finally rest with great profit in that direction where he feels himself driven and carried, or he will himself convict his adversary of error and falsehood.'"

<column-break/>

**Page 89, line 8. Composite]** These parts are mutilated, says *Vigerus* in the same place. You may conveniently fill the gap thus: "how indeed the world is composite, and..." etc.

**Page 90, line 3. "It is not yet sufficiently defined," says *Vigerus* in his notes on the passage, "who that Maximus was. There was indeed a Maximus, Bishop of Jerusalem, a contemporary of Eusebius; but I fear that a great Arian <note>A follower of the Arian heresy, which Eusebius was often accused of favoring</note> would hardly recognize this Maximus—a true enemy of the Arian impiety—as 'great,' even though he might call this Maximus, whoever he was, 'Dionysius of Alexandria' rather coldly as above. But Jerome defines him in his *Catalogue of Church Writers* under 'Maximus': 'Maximus, under the same emperors (namely Commodus and Severus), composed a wonderful inquiry in a notable volume, that is, *On the Origin of Evil*, and *That Matter was Created by God*.'"

<meta>This page contains the scholarly annotations of David Hoeschel on Origen’s "Against Celsus." Hoeschel was a 16th-century humanist who edited the first Greek edition of this work. These notes provide philological corrections and cross-references to other ancient authors.</meta>

-># NOTES OF DAVID HOESCHEL ON THE VIII BOOKS OF ORIGEN AGAINST CELSUS.<-

# DAVID HOESCHEL’S
### TO
# ORIGEN’S
### VIII Books against CELSUS.

<margin>Homily 13 on Exodus; Diogenes Laertius.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius, Book 6 of Church History, chapter 14.</margin>
<margin>Photius, Library, Page 159.</margin>
<margin>* Compiler. Epiphanius Page 126. Suidas.</margin>
Page 1. line 1. **Origen**] Enough has been said about him in the Prolegomena <note>The introductory preface</note>. However, he seems to have been the first so named (for a Grammarian named Origen is also mentioned by the Etymologist), as if "mountain-born" <note>original: ὄρρος τὸ γένος, Ὀριγενὴς, ἐν ὄρει γεννηθείς</note>, born on a mountain; or as certain Ascetics are called "those in the mountains" by John Chrysostom, and as Heraclitus of Ephesus is described as "living in the mountains." In the same dialect, poets use "mountain-bred" <note>original: ὠρεσίτροφος</note>, which in common language is *oresitrophos*, and "mountain-nurtured" in an Oracle found in Lucian. Our author also began to be called **Adamantius**, because "his soul was like adamant <note>unbreakable stone</note>, neither breaking nor yielding to any labors whatsoever"; or, as Photius says, "because the arguments he would give were like adamantine bonds." Indeed, a third name was bestowed upon him, **Syntacticus** <note>The Arranger/Compiler</note>, or *Syntaktikos*, because of his having produced many books; see Suidas under "Origen" and "S."

<margin>Suidas.</margin>
L. 3. **Celsus**] An Epicurean. Eusebius, Book 6 of Church History, chapter 36, line 17. **God-loving Ambrose**] Origen called this Ambrose "a holy man of God and sincerely devoted" in a certain Epistle.

I shall be more sparing in noting these things: for since almost everything is clear enough, and the margin displays many things besides the Interpretation: there is almost nothing for me to advise, except for some Typographical errors which must be corrected, [however, we do not express all the things noted by Hoeschel; since we have corrected most of them in passing during the care of printing, as we did many other things:] and concerning the variant readings from the *Philocalia* of Origen. Since the authors of that *Philocalia*, Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, transcribed entire pages from these books *Against Celsus*: we may judge the dignity and utility of this work from that fact.

Page 2. line 14. For *diasyras* <note>tearing apart/mocking</note>, read with R. and the most distinguished Anton Welser *distasas* <note>doubting</note>: whose conjecture (being a man of the highest learning, both in other matters and in Greek, and not a late learner of Greek affairs, but self-taught) the Palatine Codex confirms. Macarius, Homily IX: "he was patient, doubting in nothing."

<column-break/>

P. 6. line 43. Read *legesthai*, *Homoia*, etc. *poiein*, that is, "likewise." Ibid. *domois lescheneuoito* <note>original: δέμοις λεχλωσθεᾶσι</note>, the same as "talking to a wall" among the Proverb-writers. Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*: "But you, if you will not listen to a prophetess, at least listen to your own philosopher, Heraclitus of Ephesus, who reproaches the statues for their lack of sensation. 'And they pray to these statues, just as if someone were to chatter to houses.'" line 46. Read *to allo eth’*. A. Welser, Bavarian Codex. line 51. **Herodotus**] book 1. page 18. Basel edition. line 54. **for nothing is sacred**] These things are read a little differently in Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* V. p. 249. "One should not consider a temple of great value, nor anything holy, nor anything of great value and holy that is the work of builders and artisans."

P. 7. line 56. Read *epha’ alle d’ en*.

P. 8. line 39. **After these things**] *Philocalia* of Origen, chapter xvii. "After this." line 44. **transfusion** <note>original: μετεγχύσεως - likely referring to the migration of souls</note>] Concerning these, see Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*. same line. **making portents**] Deuteronomy 18. Zechariah 3. same line. **mitres** <note>original: μίθραις - also referring to the mysteries of Mithras</note>] Concerning the Rites of Mithras, consult Justin Martyr, *Apology II* for the Christians, and *Dialogue with Trypho*, and Niketas in the Greek Homilies of Nazianzen "on the holy lights," and the well-known verse of the Theologian <note>Gregory Nazianzen</note> on those Mithraic matters:

> Mithraic evil deeds and rites and not to be spoken of.

# Notes of David Hoeschel on Origen
<meta>catchword: P. 26.</meta>

...but they rot in a most wicked life before men. If there were any other thing prepared <note>original: "κατασκευαστὸν"</note> for God, even to the smallest degree <note>original: "μέχρι ἐλαχίστου"</note> (Philocalia, verse 43 and the last verse). <margin>* drink.</margin> Or by having provided such teaching, or well (Philocalia, incorrectly for "otherwise").

Page 10, verse 9. *He comes* (Philocalia, v. 11). Or *the Plato* (Philocalia, v. 12). *More humanly* (Philocalia, v. 13). *Heresy humanly agreed upon* (Philocalia, v. 17). *Of those becoming* (Philocalia, v. 21). *Upon someone* (Philocalia, v. 34). *Better to be persuaded, because of which also the opposites* (Philocalia, v. 42). *How would this more reasonably be* (Philocalia, v. 47). *Surpassing in care and...* (Philocalia, v. 53). *By the risking*, (Philocalia, omitting "of all" in this place as well as previously in v. 30).

Page 14, verse 5. *In Zeus*] Against Apion, <margin>* Tatian, Book 1, Against the Greeks.</margin> of whom there then existed *five books of Egyptian History. Verse 8: *In a word to the Greeks*] because none of the practices with which the Greeks adorn themselves is Greek, but had its discovery from the barbarians. Published in Greek and Latin among the *Orthodoxographa*. Verse 26: *In which he named*] *In the names* (Codex B). Verse 48: *Cutting off his private parts*] For Kronos, during whose time they say a harmonious life occurred, emasculated his father and swallowed his children. (Sextus Empiricus).

Page 15, verse 32. Read, *ethical*.

Page 16, verse 23. *About to be prepared* (A. Velser).

Page 17, verse 10. *They escaped him*] Because Epicurus removed all divine providence, and Aristotle (as it seems to some) limited it to the sphere of the Moon. Verse 19: *If he has* (A. Velser). Verse 28: *To be circumcised*] Theodoret proves in *Question 3 on Exodus* that the Egyptians began to be circumcised later than the Jews. In Philo (who writes that other nations, and especially the Egyptian, used circumcision), the passage near the end of *On Circumcision* should be corrected thus: *if the associations of those growing old in childlessness are incomplete*. For what does "the sesquialteral of those who accused" mean? Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata I* is the authority that Pythagoras also allowed himself to be circumcised so that the entrance to the mysteries of the Egyptians might be open to him.

Page 18, verse 7. *Having exercised Memory, the Muses from Zeus*] (Hesiod, *Theogony*). Verse 8: *The Hours from Themis*] (Hesiod, ibid., v. 901). Verse 16: *Eurynome, one of the Graces*] It should be read *Eurynome, mother of the Graces* (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 907). In the *Orphic Hymn* she is called Eurynome; <margin>* Plutarch, *On Having Many Friends*; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata IV*.</margin> Coronis in Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* book 48. By Phurnutus also called Evanthe, and synonymously with her daughter, Aglaia. To the same author, unless it is a scribal error, she is Eurysyne (*an epithet for a bastard daughter), who to others is Euphrosyne. Verse 37: *Celsus says that...* (Philocalia of Origen).

<column-break/>

Chapter XVII, verse 39. *Whether Adonaios*, (Philocalia), which is a variation of reading also below. Verse 40: *Rejoicing they name* (Philocalia). Verse 41: *And in the following he says*, (Philocalia). Verses 44 & 45: *To so-and-so* (Philocalia). Verse 49: *By position*] *according to convention* (Aristotle, *On Interpretation*, chapters 2 & 4). Verse 52: *The true meaning* (Philocalia). Verse 53: *Or as*] clearly the same sentiment as in verse 49, with the words varied only synonymously; so that A. Velser thinks it can be deleted without harm.

Page 19, verse 11. *Unheard of*] *unstable* (Philocalia). Verse 15: *Adonai, and whatever other things... we are handed over* (Philocalia). Verse 31: *In the things, lest he ever suffer something similar* (Philocalia). Verse 34: *The appellation of God* (Philocalia). Verse 45: *They rubbed together. Kronos...* (Philocalia).

Page 20, verse 6. *Inhabitants* (Philocalia). Verse 7: *Of the calling* (Philocalia). Verse 9: *Named after the things*] (Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, ch. 4). Verse 10: *According to the will* (Philocalia). Verse 20: *Whichever it may be* (Philocalia). Verse 30: *The name God* (Philocalia). Verse 32: *The nature of men... certain wise ones* (Philocalia). Verse 34: *The [word] God* (Philocalia). Verse 41: *Since Philip [called] God* (Philocalia). Verse 45: *Commanding* (Philocalia).

Page 22, verse 14. The sense requires *many times more* (A. Velser). Verse 52: Read, *from these, but*.

Page 23, verse 43. *I would not*] Plutarch in the *Apophthegms*, more briefly: "I would not have become famous being a Seriphian, nor you being an Athenian." Verse 50: *A woman who works with her hands* <note>original: "χερνῆτις"</note>] *useful, or spinning with her hands, perhaps divine* (Eustathius on *Iliad* book 12). Oenomaus in Eusebius <margin>Book 6, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 7.</margin> *decided to sell walls, and not to take a rich wife, but a certain hand-worker or a retail-dealer.*

Page 25, verse 14. *That some were placed by the community*] Valerius Maximus (Book 5, ch. 6) and Lactantius (Book 3, *On False Wisdom*, ch. 12) record examples of these. Verse 26: *A certain poetic virgin*] such as Pallas [Athena], about whom Homer says:

> For the works of golden Aphrodite <margin>Hymn to Aphrodite, v. 9.</margin> did not please her.

Verse 29: The marginal reading is truer, for those words are taken from the beginning of *Iliad* book 5:

> Then Pallas Athena gave to Diomedes, son of Tydeus,
> strength and courage, so that he might become conspicuous among all
> the Argives, and might win noble glory.

# BOOKS AGAINST CELSUS.

->Catchword: *Bacchomuthon* <note>original: Βακχόμυθον - likely a reference to "Bacchic speech" or a specific textual marker</note><-

It must be laid down as well, Philocalia <note>The *Philocalia* is an anthology of Origen's texts compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen.</note> vol. v. 45. As Celsus says, Ph. v. 46. But toward the whole examination by reasoning, Ph.

P. 230. v. 5. To attribute to God even those things belonging to herself. Ph. v. 12. The sacred [writings] say they discourse on divine matters concerning these things, Ph.

P. 233. v. 25. to worship] Those who advocate for the Law also introduced the worship of angels <margin>Galatians 3:19.</margin> because the Law was given through them. This practice remained even among certain Christians; so much so that the Council of Laodicea prohibited by law the cult of angels and being devoted to them; from which also there are many temples among them dedicated to the Chief Captain Michael. Oecumenius on chapter 2 of Colossians, which is missing in the printed edition of the book.

P. 234. v. 5. *atheists* <note>original: ἀθέοι</note> are to our author (as also frequently to Philo) the same as those whom Aristotle calls "uneducated," those who possess virtue [only in potential].

P. 236. v. 44. *undertaking* <note>original: ἐγχείρησιν</note> Codex B. but above *undertaking* in the same hand, both.

P. 267. v. 49. **the sons of God**] Not angels, as certain Greeks and Latins thought; but the sons of Seth (Augustine, book 15, ch. 23. *On the City of God*) and of Enos (Caesarius, brother of Nazianzen, *Dialogue I*) and of Enoch (Suidas in *Unlawful Marriages*): those, called by another name **the Watchers**, were called sons of God for this reason, if we trust the Anonymous Chronicler in manuscript; "Seth, having been snatched up by an angel, was initiated into the things that were to happen to his race regarding the transgression (namely of the Watchers, who were also called sons of God) and the things regarding the flood, and the coming of the Savior. Having been invisible for 40 days, he came and explained to the first-created humans as much as he was initiated into by the angel. For then it was 40 days. And Seth was pious and very well-formed, both himself and the Watchers descended from him; who were called sons of God because of the brightness and distinction of Seth, and they inhabited the higher land of Eden, except for Paradise, living like angels until the first cosmic year. The Author of Evil, not enduring their virtuous way of life, wounded them so that they looked upon the beauty of the daughters of men, that is, of Cain."

# BOOKS AGAINST CELSUS.
## Page 211

**v. 52. Dositheans]** Dositheos, according to *Epiphanius*. Dosit hianos, according to *Theodoret*. <note>Dositheus was a Samaritan sect leader often associated with early Gnostic movements.</note>

**P. 286. v. 33. camel]** regarding the nature of the animal] Some say the "camel" is the animal, but others say it refers to the thick rope used by sailors for casting anchors. *Theophylact.* In this latter sense, the Grammarians say "kamilos" <note>original: κάμιλον</note> is written with an iota. <margin>Suidas & Scholiast on Aristophanes' *Wasps*.</margin> *Artemidorus* derives the etymology of "Camel" from *Evenus* in Book 1 of his *Interpretation of Dreams*, chapter 5. As I correctly conjectured in *Hesychius*, Book 2, chapter 100, it should read: "Because a camel is, as it were, a 'bent-thigh' <note>original: κάμμηρος</note> word." *Diodorus Siculus* (Book 2) lists the types of camels, some of which are double-humped. Regarding the "gluttony" of this animal, there is a proverb: "But the camel, they say, even when treading through sand, takes up the burdens of many donkeys." *Synesius, Epistle 113.* Those who ride camels were called "camel-riders" by the Arabs, according to *Clement of Alexandria* (*The Instructor*, Book 3, ch. 3), just as the wealthy of the Chalcidians were called "horse-riders," according to *Herodotus* (*Terpsichore*).

**P. 287. v. 42. by participation]** *Gelenius's edition.* [Which we follow; the Hoeschel edition reads "the participation."]

**P. 289. v. 51. a ladder reaching to heaven]** a high-ladder, according to *Philo*.

**P. 292. v. 15. dragon]** the devil, who is "shaken off like rain" by the saints. *Manuscript Paraphrase.* **v. 16. instead of calling the dragon Leviathan in Hebrew]** For so it is in *Job* 40:20 and *Isaiah* 27:1.

**P. 294. v. 22. Ophians]** Ophiani, *Clement of Alexandria* (*Miscellanies* VII); the same as the Ophites. "They are called Ophites because of the serpent <note>Greek: ophis</note> whom they glorify." *Epiphanius*, p. 102; where in the same place it should read "to glorify as God and to worship" instead of "to provide for and knowing God from the nature of Christ by law." <note>The Ophites were a Gnostic sect that revered the serpent of Genesis as a bringer of knowledge.</note>

**P. 296. v. 21. Ialdabaoth]** *Epiphanius*, p. 121, where it should read "not having allowed one to go to the things above." **v. 32. Iao]** Iae, *Clement of Alexandria* (*Miscellanies* V). Iao, *Epiphanius*, p. 83. That "four-letter name" <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>, which is unpronounceable to the Hebrews, according to *Isidore of Pelusium* (Book 1, Ep. 453) and *Photius* (Ep. 163). More on this in the *Notes* to *Philo’s* "On the Change of Names."

**P. 298. v. 48. Prounikos]** *Epiphanius* mentions "Prounikos above" in his section on the Ophite Heresy. <note>Prounikos is a feminine personification in Gnostic cosmology, often identified with Sophia.</note>

**P. 300. v. 15. To lull to sleep]** to put to sleep with a song, "to soothe by singing." Hence the compound "I will lull to sleep" below in Book VI, p. 327, v. 1. An example of this "lulling" is found in *Theocritus*, *Idyll 15*.

**P. 305. v. 10. Beliar]** Beliar in the Hebrew tongue signifies an "apostate," according to *Suidas*. Belial in *Judges* 20:13 and 2 *Corinthians* 6:15, as in the Hebrew. *Gregory of Nazianzus* in his *Poems*: "the opposing Belias."

<column-break/>

And, "To those of Beliar, envious things by disease." And, "If bitter Belias steals you," <margin>* read Belias or Belies in the Ionic dialect.</margin> "For Belie is a wretched disease to me."

**P. 305. v. 27. dragon]** *Chrysostom* thinks the demon is so called because he is both "venomous" and "venom-casting" (*Homily 6 on Ephesians 2*). *Theophilus* (Book II *Against Autolycus*) says it is because he "ran away" <note>Greek: apodedrakenai</note> from God. What if it is also because of his "gazing intently" <note>Greek: derkein</note> upon our sins?

**P. 306. v. 4. Satan]** *Theophilus, ibid.* *Justin Martyr*, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, makes "Satanas" a compound word; see his entry. **v. 6. the adversary]** because he "stands against" <note>Greek: antikeisthai</note> the good, according to *Basil the Great* in the book "That God is not the cause of evils." **v. 38. just as faces are not alike]** *Proverbs* 27:19.

**P. 312. v. 7. that the great one having given]** *Gelenius* reads "having given" following the ancient interpreter.

**P. 314. v. 23. evils]** All ambiguity is removed by the distinction between the "evil of fault" <note>sin</note> and the "evil of punishment" <note>suffering</note>. *Tertullian*, Book 2, ch. 14, *Against Marcion*.

**P. 316. v. 9. repentance]** for the wills of God are "without repentance" <note>unchangeable</note>. **v. 20. already as if from words of human passion]** [or] "condescendingly" in relation to the things spoken of in Divine Scripture, according to *Theodoret*, Book 4, *Against the Audians*.

**P. 326. v. 10. the rays of the sun are defiled in the filth]** *Diogenes* said to one reproaching him for entering unclean places: "For even the sun enters the privies, but it is not defiled." Similar things regarding the Sun and the Virgin Birth were written by *Athanasius* (*On the Incarnation of the Word*), *Basil the Great* (*On the Nativity of Christ*), and *Macarius* (*Homilies 7, 11, 16*).

**P. 327. v. 14. following these things]** *Philo* chapter 15. **same verse: divine spirit]** *Philo*. **v. 15. to shine forth already]** *Philo*. **v. 16. or even until]** *Philo*. **v. 18. for the divine]** *Philo*. **v. 19. to differ, but this nothing]** *Philo*. **v. 20. which indeed]** *Philo*. **v. 22. he wishes Jesus as believing... it seemed to him... leading the way... opportunities]** *Philo*. **v. 39. he might persuade]** *Philo*. **v. 36. as a child]** *Philo*. **v. 39. and failing]** *Philo*. **v. 40. he heard, since he thought it useful to him]** *Philo*. **v. 51. upon the high place]** *Philo*. **v. 52. when Moses]** *Philo*. **v. 56. the following and]** *Philo*.

**P. 328. v. 2. great in the preparation that the... Jesus]** *Philo*. **v. 8. into Jesus]** *Philo*. **v. 10. infinite, failing]** *Philo*. **v. 12. and the aforementioned things, but also according to the Gospel]** *Philo*. **v. 16. to receive]** *Philo*. **v. 18. concerning Jesus]** *Philo*. **v. 20. certainly to change something in the]** *Philo*. **v. 22. or even amazement]** *Philo*. **v. 28. which the master... better]** *Philo*.

**Page 333, line 35. "The Cassalian"** <note>Referring to the Castalian spring or the Pythia</note>] Lucian, in *The Tripod and the Delphic*, and also **Chrysostom**. The words of the latter, which are not unrelated to this passage, are as follows: <note>original: "Λέγεται ἡ Πυθία..."</note> "It is said that the Pythia, being a woman, once sat upon the tripod of Apollo with her legs spread; then an evil spirit, rising from below and penetrating through her female parts, filled the woman with madness. She then let down her hair and began to rave in a Bacchic frenzy, foaming at the mouth, and in such a state of intoxication uttered the words of her madness." **Same line. "To receive the spirit"**] "To fall into," according to Lucian.

**Page 338, line 52. "Why is it that the epileptic came to you?"**] Biblical words, 4 Kings 9:11 <note>Modern 2 Kings 9:11</note>. "Why did this madman come to you?" That is, "seized in the mind," according to Suidas. "Mind-struck," according to Nazianzen's *Poems*; "deprived of mind." 1 Kings 21:14 <note>Modern 1 Samuel 21:14</note>. "Look, you see a man who is epileptic <note>original: ἐπίληπτον</note>;" whence in the same place the verb "to act like an epileptic," for which in the *Lexicon* "to be epileptic" is incorrectly read.

Which Maximus the Martyr affirms in general regarding all Sacred Scripture when he says: "The divinely inspired Scriptures now have a bodily form, hidden in thickness, escaping the notice of the many. For the things written are types and images of certain more divine and mystical things." From a manuscript in the Augsburg Library.

**Page 346, line 50. "Daughter of Babylon"**] "The wretched soul, which is as it were a daughter of confusion, just as of sin; for Babylon is interpreted as *confusion*." <note>original: σύγχυσις</note> From a manuscript paraphrase.

Same Paraphrase.

# Books against CELSUS.

Page 373. verse 7. but hardly the <note>Philo</note>. verse 13. they might corrupt.

Page 377. verse 15. read: "and yet another."

Page 378. verse 30. there are appointed wicked demons] <note>original: "μοχθηροὶ δαίμονες"</note> God did not make instruments of calamities; but he readily used those who were appointed to this by themselves. Synesius, Letter 57. In the same place he calls those demons "evil" and "mischievous powers." verse 44. indeed from a fall. <note>printed books</note>.

Page 380. verse 38. serving someone not proportionately and to another. <note>Palatine Manuscript</note>.

Page 383. verse 51. unphilosophical] <note>original: "ἀφιλόσοφος"</note> so Gelenius seems to have read.

Page 387. verse 47. printed books: "the father is greater than me because"] <note>original: "ὁ πατὴρ με μείζων"</note> the "greater" refers to a person, or to God in time; but the birth is through the Father himself. Athanasius, Oration 2 against the Arians; and, "as God to God, not as Father or Son when he became man." The same author, Dialogue 1 on the Holy Trinity.

Page 389. verse 19. the seals.

Page 394. verse 40. sons of pestilence] 1 Kings 2:14. <note>Note: In some older bibles, 1 Samuel is listed as 1 Kings.</note>

Page 398. verse 49. for great are the judgments, etc. and hard to describe] Wisdom of Solomon 17:1.

Page 400. verse 15. who (thousands and myriads, namely of angels) seeing] A "solecism-like" phrasing, for the participle refers back to the angels. Whoever wishes for examples of this locution may seek them from the Notes to the Library of Photius, page 920. To which, from Plato’s *Greater Hippias*, this could be added: "which of the two ways I should answer, he did not select the one that was fitting and <margin>* book *On Tranquility*.</margin> beautiful," etc. verse 25. of the Greeks, indeed, the wise] Menander, quoted in Plutarch and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* Book 5:
> To every man a guardian spirit stands by
> As soon as he is born, a guide to the mysteries of life.
The same was the opinion of the Messalians, or Euchites. Theodoret, Book 4, *On Heretics*.

<column-break/>

Page 401. verse 11. I shall live] Euclides the Socratic said the same to his angry brother. Moreover, just as we have supplied a gap here from elsewhere, so in Plutarch’s book *On the Control of Anger* there is a gap to be filled from his book *On Brotherly Love*; and there it should read: "But I (he said) would perish, if I did not persuade you to cease from your anger, and to love us as you loved us before."

Page 403. verse 31. Late] Elsewhere this proverbial verse is read in full:
> Late do the mills of the Gods grind, but they grind fine.
That is, as Philo says, "justice is accustomed to move hardly at all; but once moved, it arrives suddenly, overtaking those who flee." For divine wrath proceeds with a slow step to its vengeance, and compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its weight. Valerius Maximus, Book 1, chapter 2.

verse 49. their teeth were set on edge] Jeremiah 31:29.

Page 404. verse 8. already of images. <note>Manuscript B</note>. already * images to the <note>Manuscript P</note>. verse 10. images <note>Manuscript B</note>. images <note>Manuscript P</note> and the old Translator who, thinking it meant the same as "herds," translated it as "flock and sheep," both here and on the following page. But it seems "of images" and "statues" should be read. Proclus: "For God made man, in the image of God he made him. Wherefore he also implanted in him something of his own statues: <margin>* of statues/images.</margin> permanence, so that he might not be easily overcome by corruptions," in Epiphanius, Book 2, *Against Heresies*, pages 234, 235.

Page 405. verse 34, and 37. the marginal reading is a conjecture; where Manuscript B and Gelenius have "herds" and "statues," as before: and Manuscript P again has "herds" and "statues." [Hoeschelius had conjectured "herds" and "statues"; since this reading easily proved itself to us, we have moved it from the margin into the text.] verse 44. the grain] Athanasius, Homily *On the Sower*.

Page 412. verse 22. and Empedocles] These verses are his:
> There is an oracle of Necessity, etc.

Page 414. verse 5. who will deliver me from the body of this death] Methodius understands by "body" the "law of sin, which lurks in our members through transgression, and always presents the soul with the death of unrighteousness"; in Photius’s *Library*, page 485. See also Macarius, Homily 1. verse 12. to try to release] "they killed the great James with a club, and Herod beheaded the other James." Theodoret, Question 42 on Deuteronomy.

### Various readings in the Books against CELSUS

<margin>
* such as the forty martyrs, regarding whom Encomiums <note>Laudatory speeches</note> by Gregory of Nyssa and Basil the Great are extant.
</margin>

"to be racked"] <note>original: στρεβλοῦσθαι</note> on the wheel, according to Lucian. On the wood <note>the rack</note>, according to Basil the Great in his *Homily on Gordius the Martyr*, who in his *Oration on the Giving of Thanks* also recites other kinds of tortures <note>original: βασάνων</note>, such as being scraped by a wheel, having eyes gouged out, and he mentions the reward * for "shameful blows," * to be frozen by cold, or to be wasted away by hunger. To the same category belongs "to be fallen upon by claws" or "to be scraped by spears," according to Hermias Sozomen, Book V, chapter 19; Gregory Nazianzen, pages 166 and 311; and whatever other instruments of torture the authors of Ecclesiastical History describe.
Page 415, line 21. read in the margin 2 Timothy 2:5.

Page 418, line 3. "at once both creator"] <note>original: ἅμα τε καὶ κτίστην</note> Lucian, in *Icaromenippus*, verse 12. "by a medical approach"] <note>original: ἐφόδῳ ἰατρικῇ</note> according to the precept of Sirach, chapter 38:2. Line 14. "by piety toward the God over all, and by prayers to Him"] <note>original: εὐσεβεία τῇ εἰς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι Θεὸν, καὶ ταῖς πρὸς ἐκεῖνον εὐχαῖς</note> following the admirable example of Gorgonia, the sister of Gregory Nazianzen, who, having been thrown from a carriage with her bones and limbs broken and crushed, is read to have been restored to health by God—to whom she had consecrated herself—without any physician.
Page 424, line 41. "something strong"] <note>original: ἰσχυρόν τι</note> the edition reads "it is implanted."
Page 427, line 37. it seems it should be read "it must be noted for the sake of instruction."

<margin>
Gregory Nazianzen, page 55. Funeral Oration for his sister Gorgonia.
</margin>

### Various readings in several places of the Books against CELSUS, noted from a collation of the PHILOCALIA.

The reader should be advised that, since Jean Tarin observed in his *Notes on the Philocalia* a reading that varied from the one frequently presented in Hoeschel’s edition of the books *Against Celsus*, we in turn—led by your convenience rather than our own, and having noted the page and line of our edition for each place where the authors of the *Philocalia* transcribed the books *Against Celsus* into it—send you there, from where those excerpts were first taken. Lest we deprive you of that variety of reading which Tarin once provided, we have noted the variants of the Paris edition and the readings differing from Hoeschel’s, and have given them to be printed separately (marked by the page and line of that edition) after Hoeschel’s Notes; we shall subsequently present the remaining notes of Tarin after these.

> [* Philocalia notes in the first Annotation a variant reading of the Philocalia published by Tarin in Paris, 1618, which is indeed understood in the others as well.]

->### *Notes on the Philocalia of ORIGEN*<-
->### **By JOANNES TARINUS.**<-

**IN** these notes which we have marked below the text, Gentle Reader <note>Latin: L.B. for Lector Benevole</note>, brevity itself will sufficiently excuse itself; for besides the variety of readings, and some few errors which are here corrected, there seemed to be no reason at all why I should interpose myself in your studies, especially with the presses hurrying, and in the daily persistence of a laborious duty, demanding from me their daily task. If in any place I shall seem to have held to this limit less strictly, I would wish you to be persuaded that it is a matter of necessity rather than of will. For that which I had chiefly taken upon myself was to compare the Royal Manuscript—the use of which was granted by that most learned man, Nicolaus Rigaltius, who guards that most exquisite treasury of books with equal fidelity and authority—with the published books *Against Celsus*, and likewise with two other manuscripts which P. Puteanus brought forth from the most choice library of that greatest hero, *Jacobus Augustus Thuanus*, of blessed memory, with singular human kindness and elegance of learning. I have done this as accurately as I could, and I have made that selection which I would prefer to be judged by you, once these things are known. Effort also had to be given at times to the places of Scripture, so that they might be compared among themselves. The interpretation of Ruffinus...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly notes by Joannes Tarinus on Origen’s Philocalia. Tarinus is comparing various Greek manuscripts (notably the "Thuanian" codices) with the Latin translation by Ruffinus, often criticizing Ruffinus for his loose paraphrasing.</meta>

# NOTES OF JO. TARINUS ON THE *PHILOCALIA* OF ORIGEN.
->## Qqqq ##<-

<margin>catchword: builds</margin>

interpretation, if indeed he is an interpreter and not an <term>independent writer</term> <note>original: αὐτόνομος Scriptor</note>, I have been afraid to touch upon the <unclear>sharpness</unclear> of others even when it occurred to me: why should I constantly advise how far he deflects from Origen, since I have always thought that a limit should be set on writing rather than seeking out an abundance of words? Certainly, it must not be allowed that these notes, however small they are, should grow through the disparagement of another’s industry.

***Of Origen***. In both Thuanian codices <note>The library of Jacques Auguste de Thou</note>, it is constantly written *Of Origen* <note>Greek: Ὠριγένους</note>. And immediately after the index of chapters, there is prefixed: *The Introduction of Origen. A Selection, etc.* Perhaps it will be said that "Of Origen" is used as if "Concerning Origen" or "The Origin of Origen." Jerome gives him a fourth name, ***Chalcenterus*** <note>meaning "Brazen-gut," a nickname for the tireless scholar Didymus of Alexandria</note>: more justly, I think, than his own age gave it to Didymus, who had written three thousand five hundred books; whereas six thousand are commonly attributed to Origen; and Epiphanius does not disagree.

***Philocalia***. And Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> in his letters speaks of Origen as "a lover of beauty" <note>original: φιλοκάλων</note>. Phot. Indeed, I would say this work belongs no more to Origen than to Basil and Gregory, who were "lovers of beauty" <note>original: φιλοκαλώντων</note>. You see the use of this word among the Latins in the age of Augustine, in the 2nd book *Against the Academics* and chapter 1 of the *Retractations*. What this *Philocalia* is, the 86th letter of Gregory demonstrates. In it, one should read "and the useful things" <note>original: ἐ. κὶ τὰ χρ.</note> where, instead of our "we give back the greater of what we have," those words are entangled: "of what we have the greater, we give back." And where it is read here, "may you have this yourself," there it is "may you have. this same thing." Here "usefully," there "it is necessary for useful things."

**Chap. I. p. 1. v. 28. *Of a Philosopher*.** Both Thuanian Codices rightly have "to practice philosophy" <note>original: φιλοσοφεῖν</note>. Furthermore, Ruffinus twisted this entire proem and, as is his custom, went off into something else entirely. Origen got these things from his master, Clement, at the end of the 6th book of the *Stromata*. **P. 2. v. 2. *to implant*.** Ruffinus: *to grow in*. So also Gellius in 12. n. 16. *those considered*. Ruffinus: *the Gods, whom they thought*. Clearly enough: but that word sounds like something even greater. **v. 21. *towards the*.** perhaps "at the." **v. 22. *of the words*,** restore "to the word." **v. 32.** I read "let us join the company" <note>original: θιασώμεθα</note>. **v. 35. *to whom that*,** both Thuanian Codices have "something like" <note>original: διόν τι</note>; erroneously. Common edition: *you shall be brought before governors or even kings*. **v. 43. *to have said*,** Ruffinus substituted his own words here. **v. 51.** Common edition: *the things stored up for him may come*. Both the Greek and Latin Fathers use this. **P. 3. v. 1. *earth*** is redundant. **v. 10. *in the*, etc.** Ruffinus did not touch this. **same verse. *under*** perhaps "from." **v. 12. *Of the rulers*.** The Jews call such people <note>Hebrew: ראשים הפלת</note> "heads or princes of the exiles." To these, Ruffinus added not a few things, being eager for explanation, as he himself says. **v. 14.** "and" <note>original: κὶ</note> is missing in the common edition. **P. 4. v. 11. *virgin*.** Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion had corrupted "virgin" into "young woman" <note>original: νεᾶνις</note>. **v. 17. *having given*.** Ruffinus adds from his own, I believe, "as if we exist as certain spoils of his victory." **v. 28. *to the most unjust*.** Ruffinus: *Nothing by him for harming*; which phrasing was familiar to that century. **v. 50. *to confirm*.** read *to have finished*. **v. 51. *clear*.** Ruffinus cut out many things. **P. 5. v. 4.** Ruffinus runs on at great length in his own spaces, I think, not Origen's; lest I always stick to the rocks, I shall hereafter sail past them. **v. 25.** I would read "if the," if it were permitted, *the method of the craftsmanship of a providing God*. I could not do it more correctly. Ruffinus: *Since the reason is hidden from them, through which in a certain ineffable*

<column-break/>

*art all things are dispensed*. **v. 40. *a treasure in*.** both Thuanian Codices: *this treasure*. **P. 6. v. 9. *of the things*.** Common edition: *to the steel-workers*, and below p. 8. but Origen referred it to wisdom. **v. 15. *in the*.** This is the beginning of chapter 2 in Ruffinus. **v. 33.** read "he shall rest together with." **v. 42. *from the age*.** These are Marcionites. See Origen everywhere, Tertullian, Epiphanius, Augustine, etc. **P. 7. v. 6. *uncreated*** <note>original: ἀγένητον</note>. Ruffinus: *who is the God of all, or by the will of God the Father of all things, were described through Jesus Christ*. **v. 36. *mysteries*.** *sacraments* in Ruffinus, and everyone in that age. **P. 8. v. 6.** these are held separately. **v. 16, 12, & 13. v. 12. *of mysteries*.** *of sacraments*. Hence Jerome to Paulinus: *The Apocalypse of John has as many sacraments as words, etc.* **v. 24. *to the*,** I would read "types" or "faiths." **v. 35. *praying out*,** read, if you prefer, "discovered." **v. 28. *Of the elements*.** Common edition: "her own," and "into depth [and thought] and knowledge." **v. 40. *to you*.** Common edition: "si." **v. 49.** insert, if you please, "nor at their beginning," etc. **v. 53. *for just as*.** See Irenaeus book 5, chap. 9. Clement in the 6th book of the *Stromata* calls "the body of the scriptures the diction and the names." **P. 9. v. 3. *of those being brought down*** and not without injury, if it was the one we have. **v. 7. *behind*.** Origen had written commentaries on *The Shepherd* <note>The Shepherd of Hermas</note>, see book 1, chap. 2. **v. 14. *of the...*** Ruffinus: *childish souls, which he also calls orphans*; namely **v. 19. *bridegroom*.** Ruffinus reads *heavenly*. Perhaps "heavenly" <note>original: ὑρανίῳ</note> should be added. **v. 21. *he might say*.** Ruffinus: "if he should say." He read "he ought to say" <note>original: λέγοι ὤφ.</note>; he changed this meaning. **v. 32. *that of gifts*,** Common edition: "grace or...?" which custom, above others, Synesius Letter 121 designates: "in the boundaries, the cleansing water of the city." I omit the profane rite. **v. 50. *the luminary*,** *you shall not bridle*. Ruffinus: rightly. **P. 10. v. 18. *of the*.** Common edition: "in the...?" and for "to be placed," "to have been bound." **v. 22. v. 31. *he has been stripped*.** Common edition: "stripped." **v. 32.** Thuanian Codex: "which things it is necessary... for they are two covenants to be allegorized" incorrectly. **v. 38.** "to which" is missing in both. **v. 41. *us, you*.** and after "let him move" both have "or in food." **v. 45. *by examples*.** Ruffinus and Common edition: "by an example." Hebrews 8. **v. 50. *and that one*.** Thuanian: "and to those." "and those things." **P. 11. v. 13. *the spiritual things*,** you may understand, of the senses. **v. 27. *into the words, etc.*** that is, to be recalled to the reason of divine doctrine. **v. 51. *of the digging*,** both Thuanian: "of the scripture," nor is it foreign; and Ruffinus: *by legal scripture*. **P. 12. v. 9. *to be hidden in*.** both Thuanian: "to happen upon good things." **v. 25. *not*.** Thuanian: "if" and **v. 29.** with the help of both I restored "more" from "perfectly." **v. 29. *the analogous*.** It will be rendered more clearly: "the same is to be understood also concerning the law." **v. 38. *concerning the necessity, etc.*** Ruffinus continues these; if correctly, this will be the meaning: "persuasion, etc." since they persuade themselves with reason that in such scriptures a meaning worthy of God must be sought. **v. 40. *concerning the*** Ruffinus read "until the advent," namely "at the presence." Either is correct. **v. 44. *of these, etc.*** Here and in the following I implore the faith of the Codices. **P. 13. v. 2. *Origenist...*** yet the greatest Theologians have chosen these. **v. 10.** the other Thuanian: "under the wood." **v. 16. *to seek a person*.** read "what person." and presently "and the." read "and what." **v. 28. *to the one composing heights*.** try it. **v. 35. *to weave together*** perhaps a particle is missing. **v. 47. *to take away*.** see if it is to your taste, what he builds

# NOTES OF JEAN TARIN ON ORIGEN’S *PHILOCALIA*.

<margin>Page 14</margin>
Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, the 4th-century translator who brought Origen's works into Latin</note> relates that it was ordered that parents be punished who did not circumcise their sons, as well as those who raise small children. *Who could bear this?* verse 48. The Common Edition <note>The standard printed Greek text of the time</note> has it thus: *and the uncircumcised male, who shall not be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be destroyed from its kin.* v. 54. *to bring forward*. Rufinus: *to worship*. I say: *to offer*. v. 55. *of men*. Both Theologians' Codices: *to a man*. Page 14. v. 1. *to cut through*. Rufinus observes a most esteemed point. v. 2. *to be established*. Common edition: *to be established by himself*. v. 10. *gold*. Rufinus: *griffin*. Concerning Dositheus the Samaritan, who falsely claimed to be the Christ, see Origen, Commentary 27 on Matthew; Irenaeus, book 1; and Epiphanius; Jerome against Lucifer; Philastrius's Catalogue. v. 20. *saying*. Theologians' Codex: *claiming*. v. 26. Rufinus interjects: *Concerning the two tunics, as also in the following, Concerning the struck cheek*. v. 37. *in the...* Rufinus adds: *or who shall be held beyond the greatest crime, laying hands upon himself;* he skips the rest. v. 50. *the... of the...* The other Theologians' Codex: *by which they are made like*. Rufinus thinks that is indeed impossible in every respect, as does Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian and on Isaiah chapter 52. But not so for one who knows the word and custom of "re-skinning" <note>The practice of surgically reversing circumcision (epispasm)</note> from Cornelius Celsus, book 7, chapter 25; 1 Maccabees 1; Josephus, book 12, chapter 6. Concerning the Jews: *and they covered the circumcision of their private parts so that they might be Greeks even when undressed.* Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, where he names the *spathiftherem* as the instrument for recalling the foreskin. Theoph. Page 15. v. 36. *of the impossible*. Common edition: *of the weak*. Page 16. v. 31. *and elsewhere*. These are missing in Rufinus at those points. Page 17. v. 27. *but if how great*, which are also read in a distorted way. Page 17. v. 21. *to have been commanded*. The other Theologians' Codex: *to have been commanded*. v. 42. *assembly... from*. Common edition: *and from*. Page 18. v. 15. *to fit*. Both Theologians' Codices: *it fits*. v. 20. *by power*. Both: *of power*. v. 34. A few things were passed over here by the "Philocalian" Theologians. v. 42. *into the...* Treat Origen humanely and cautiously here. Page 19. v. 17. *of the multitude*. Both Theologians' Codices: *the multitudes*. v. 29. *of weakness*. Both: *of the weakness of the mind*. v. 38. The other Theologians' Codex: *to cast away*. The other: *to suggest*. The Royal Codex: *to remove*, but the matter does not proceed well in either place. v. 13. *From the Inquiries*. These are missing. v. 7. *that*. Read: *when*. Page 21. v. 1. *From the...* etc. You will not find these in the commonly circulated Homilies on Leviticus; from which it appears how many torn fragments we retain from such a great shipwreck <note>A metaphor for the loss of Origen's original Greek library</note>. v. 3. *let us understand*. Both Theologians' Codices: *thinking*. v. 5. *those from...*] these are the *Antitactae* <note>A Gnostic sect</note>, so named for their "opposition" to the Creator: among whom the Giant Thermaches and Marcion are leaders. *Stromata*, book 3.

**Chapter II.** page 21. v. 37. *From the...* etc. This book does not exist either: but Epiphanius reports these things up to page 22, line 39, *And lest ever*, in Heresy 64. v. 45. *and to the angel*. This and the following passage are read variously in the Complutensian, Royal, and Common editions. Page 22. v. 11. *to see it*. Both Theologians' Codices: *to befit him*. v. 25. *they will say*. Common edition: *he will say*. v. 29. *confessedly*. Both Theologians' Codices: *to the things confessed*. v. 30. *not captured*, read: *scarcely perceived*. v. 41. *From the Exodus*. See Hilary in the prologue of his Explanation of the Psalms, who either received it from some Hebrew or translated it from this passage of Origen. v. 45. *security*. The Royal Codex had *security*. v. 47. *excludes*. Both Theologians' Codices: *will shut out*.

<column-break/>

Page 23. v. 19. *I have already said* from both Theologians' Codices. v. 29. we made *some peculiarities* out of *peculiarity*. Both Theologians' Codices: *some peculiarities*. v. 47. *of the whole*. Both: *of the saints, so to speak*. Page 24. v. 6. *which*. Both: *whom*.

**Chapter III.** page 24. v. 21. *From the...* etc. Suidas: *Indeed, he first made an exposition of the explanation of the Psalms, having already grasped the matters of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, saying how and in what word. And it must not be ignored that the books of the Testament, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, which is the number of the letters among them.* "they say" instead of "of the Testament" v. 28. Both Theologians' Codices: *in the Testament*. v. 31. *they are*. Read: *which is*.

**Chapter IV.** page 24. v. 41. We require these. page 25. v. 8. these were read continuously. *in the gospel*. Theologians' Codices: *by the evangelist*. v. 14. *of the word*. Both: *of the word...* v. 16. *the* is missing in both. v. 35. *to God*. Both: *to the*.

**Chapter V.** page 26. v. 5. this preface has fallen out. v. 7. *Since not*. In the Royal Codex it was written in the margin: *He hints at Ambrose, to whom almost all his explanatory writings were made.* See Epiphanius; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*; Suidas. But Photius attributes it to Hippolytus. See Jerome on Hippolytus; Eusebius, book 6; Nicephorus Callistus, book 4. v. 8. *taskmaster*, a brilliant epithet for Origen declares it. v. 16. *blame*. They later twisted this weapon against Origen. v. 20. *the word the*. Both Theologians' Codices: *the surrounding word*. v. 32. *through impulses*. Both Theologians' Codices: *through upright things*. v. 39. *they think upon*. Both Theologians' Codices: *they forbid*. Incorrectly. v. 41. *the scripture* both Theologians' Codices: *to the scripture*. Page 27. v. 22. *needing to speak much*. It was missing in the Royal, I restored it from the Theologians' Codices; whence there should also be substituted: *even if one speaks saving things many times.* v. 28. *to the wall*. Both Theologians' Codices: *to the wall*. See 3 Kings 4. v. 33. *I stretched out words*. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion: *my hand* from the Hebrew. So the Latin Vulgate; but he was expressing the custom of orators commanding silence with the right hand. So Paul, *Acts* 13: *beckoning with his hand, he said...* 19 and 21; and Persius, *Satire* 4:
> *The mind brings me to have made silence for the hot crowd,*
> *By the majesty of the hand.* — and Caesar in Lucan,
> — — — — — — — — — — — — *the tumult*
> *He settled with his face and commanded silence with his right hand.*
v. 44. *indeed*. Both: *may be*. In the same place *the word which*, etc. was noted in the margin: *Understand "Word" here not as God, the holy intellect, for that God is impartible; but the word that is always the same, composed of various contemplations, which itself is called "in the beginning with God" synonymously with the first.* Which caution is surely our own caution. Page 28. v. 54. *becoming*. Both Theologians' Codices: *having been made*. Page 30. v. 15. *Jesus*. Both Theologians' Codices: *the Lord*.

**Chapter VI.** page 30. v. 26. *the divine*. Both Theologians' Codices: *all the divine*. v. 29. *From the...* And this one we also miss. v. 45. *to see*. Common edition: *the things to see*. v. cod. *set on fire*. So Aquila from the Hebrew. Common edition: *set on fire*. Others: *for the ones set on fire*. For things set on fire are more easily fixed in, as Nazianzen observes. Theodotion: *fixed*. v. 46. *of bonds*. Common edition: *of signs*. Others: *of arrangements*. Gregory explains the matter in Oration 55: *I know how you urge souls and prick like the sun the commands of the wise, or pierce bodies labored upon by a goad or a nail.* Page 31. v. 14. *to the...* both. v. 15. *David*. *Beloved, desirable, strong or fit in hand.* Jerome on Psalm 33. Elias of Crete in the Oration of Nazianzen. v. 16. *of music*. Both Theologians' Codices: *of musicians*.

# NOTES OF JO. TARINUS ON THE *PHILOCALIA* OF ORIGEN.

->Qqqq 2<-

**Chapter VII. p. 31. v. 35.** *From the* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν"</note> is missing. **v. 45.** where, read *why*. **v. 46.** let it be observed, read *let it be reserved*, and other things as she herself speaks, etc. **P. 32. v. 10.** *And again* <note>original: "Καὶ πάλιν"</note>, nor are the rest found. **v. 16.** *are the words* <note>original: "εἰσὶν οἱ λόγοι"</note> in both Thuanian manuscripts; <note>original: "δεῖν ὁ λόγος"</note> *the word must*. **v. 22.** *the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "τὸ πν. ἅγ."</note> in both Thuanian manuscripts; *the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα"</note>.

**Chapter VIII. p. 32. v. 37.** *the divine* <note>original: "ἡ θεία"</note> in both Thuanian manuscripts; *of the divine having become* <note>original: "ἡ θείας γεγ."</note>. **v. 41.** *From the* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν"</note>. These have fallen out. **P. 33. v. 6.** *they nodded* <note>original: "ἐνεῦρ."</note> more examples have *they beckoned* <note>original: "ἔνευσαν"</note>. Those who distorted these things wrote: *he wept and entreated him, and in Bethel he found him.* **v. 8.** *him* <note>original: "αὐτόν"</note>. Common edition: *of him* <note>original: "αὐτοῦ"</note>. But Origen should be heard. **v. 22.** *you may eat* <note>original: "φάγητε"</note>. Symmachus used to corrupt these into: *eat from the wood, you shall be mortal.* **P. 34. v. 9.** *To the Shepherds* <note>original: "Ποιμέσι"</note>. Book 3, similitude 9.

**Chapter IX. p. 34. v. 19.** *From the* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν"</note>. A good many of Origen's fifteen volumes on this Epistle of Paul were already missing from everyone's libraries in the time of Jerome: see Jerome's preface. **v. 46.** *the* <note>original: "ὁ"</note>. Common edition: *to whom* <note>original: "ᾧ"</note>. **P. 35. v. 18.** Aquila transferred Paul's words into his own interpretation: for in Isaiah v. 11: *through the mocking of lips, through another tongue.* **v. 27.** *having been inscribed* <note>original: "ἐγγεγραμμένος"</note>. presently *written in the heart* <note>original: "γραπτὸν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ"</note>. *From Plato, or rather from the truth, Cicero says: reason is implanted by nature, which commands those things which ought to be done, and forbids the contrary: what one must do, and what one must avoid.* <note>original: "ἅτε δεῖ ποιεῖν, ἀπεμή"</note> Xenophon. **P. 36. v. 18.** *itself*, read *the same*. **v. 21.** *and the* <note>original: "καὶ ὁ"</note>. The other Thuanian manuscript: *and those* <note>original: "καὶ οἱ"</note>, etc. in the plural number.

**Chapter V.** <note>Note: Likely a misprint for Chapter X in the original text</note> **p. 37. v. 5.** *from the* <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν"</note>. Only fourteen have escaped to us. **v. 9.** *to the good* <note>original: "καλῷ"</note>, I distrust this writing. **v. 10.** *of stumbling blocks* <note>original: "σκανδάλ."</note> *Stumbling block* <note>original: "σκάνδαλον"</note> is well defined by the Etymologist as *that which causes a limp regarding the truth*. *Stumbling-stone* <note>original: "πρόσκομμα"</note>, in the old lexicons: *a hindrance*. **v. 31.** *of herbs* <note>original: "βοτανῶν"</note>. There is nothing that is not effected by the power of herbs, but the powers of most are unknown. And Herophilus says, *perhaps some even when trodden upon are beneficial.* Fl. 24. **v. 39.** *botanist* <note>original: "βοτανικός"</note>, Dioscorides 1.

**Chapter XI. p. 38. v. 21.** *From the 20th* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν κ'."</note> only these remain. **v. 23.** *I set up in the midst* <note>original: "ἀνακείνω ἀναμέσον"</note>. Common edition: *I dispose in the midst* <note>original: "διακείνω ἀνὰ μέσον"</note>. **v. 26.** *trample* <note>original: "καταπ."</note>. Common edition: *you trample down* <note>original: "καταπατεῖτε"</note>, you were treading underfoot. **P. 39. v. 7.** *to the blameworthy* <note>original: "ψεκτῷ"</note>. You might translate *rejected* from Cato and Varro. Origen notes the Marcionites. But as for what the demanding kids trampled underfoot, see in Epiphanius, Heresy 42.

**Chapter XII. p. 39. v. 44.** *from the 20th* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν κ'."</note>. The elderly Adamantius <note>note: A nickname for Origen meaning "Man of Steel"</note> delivered these 26 short orations extemporaneously in the Church. **v. 8.** *and to the* <note>original: "καὶ τῷ"</note> Jerome makes this the beginning of the 12th chapter, who not only interprets these things most abundantly, but also, as was the custom of that age, explains them. **P. 40. v. 17.** *of those understanding* <note>original: "νούντων"</note>. Another manuscript: *of those understanding so that* <note>original: "νούντων ὥστε"</note>. **v. 37.** *by* <note>original: "ὑπὸ"</note> both Thuanian manuscripts: *from* <note>original: "ἀπὸ"</note>. **v. 39.** *to give back* <note>original: "ἀποδῶν"</note>. Jerome: *incantations*. **P. 41. v. 8.** *the* <note>original: "ὁ"</note> is missing in both.

**Chapter XIII. p. 41. v. 27.** *the [way] into* <note>original: "ἡ εἰς"</note>. Do you want the meaning just as the words themselves demand? *The natural disposition which is prepared for understanding, as you yourself know, if practice is added, can produce a work, which, etc.* And when Origen had seen the excellent natural disposition of our Theodore (or Gregory) and his brother Athenodorus, *he exhorted them,* says Jerome, *to Philosophy.* Nyssen commends his *love of learning and industry* <note>original: "φιλομαθὲς καὶ φιλόπονον"</note>: but he, having accepted *the education of external wisdom* <note>original: "παιδείαν τὴν ἔξω σοφίας"</note>, nowhere else than at Alexandria, with a certain Firmilian, *frequented Origen, who at that time was the teacher of Christian philosophy.* **v. 31.** *lawyers* <note>original: "νομικοί"</note>. See Gregory’s Panegyric on Origen. **v. 35.** *finally* <note>original: "τελικῶς"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *of final things* <note>original: "τελικῶν"</note>. As also for *poetically* <note>original: "ποιητικῶς"</note>, *of poetic things* <note>original: "ποιητικῶν"</note>. Both are wrong: but let it be read correctly without punctuation, *poetically or through the...* etc. **v. 38.** *general studies* <note>original: "ἐγκύκλια"</note>. This is from the Master (Stromata, Book 1): *But just as general studies contribute to philosophy, their mistress; so also philosophy itself works together for the acquisition of wisdom. For philosophy is a pursuit, but wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human and their causes.* Aristotle, Ethics 3; Quintilian, Book 1. **v. 39.** *preparatory studies* <note>original: "προπαιδεύματα"</note>.] *And very many of the outside philosophers, frequenting him, gathered the greatest benefit. For he was considered great even among them, handing down geometry and arithmetic and other preparatory studies.* **P. 42. v. 24.** *flow together* <note>original: "συρρ."</note>. read *and flow together*. Exodus 27. **v. 27.** *courts* <note>original: "αὐλαὶ"</note>, read *curtains* <note>original: "αὐλαῖαι"</note>; Exodus 26. Hesychius: *tents*. see manuscript *within* <note>original: "ἔσω"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *inner and outer*. **v. 50.** *to say of him* <note>original: "αὐτοῦ εἰπεῖν"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *you might say to him*. **P. 43. v. 3.** *having understood* <note>original: "νοήσαντες"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *having understood*. **v. 5.** *Bethel* *house of God,* Genesis 28. **v. 24.** *to use* <note>original: "χρᾶσ'"</note> both Thuanian manuscripts: *to use*. **v. 31.** *on which* <note>original: "ἐφ' ᾗ"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *on which*. **v. 39.** *and not* <note>original: "καὶ οὐ"</note>, etc. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *and always and you might increase*.

**Chapter XIV. p. 44. v. 3.** *most necessary* <note>original: "ἀναγκαιότατον"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *most necessary things are* <note>original: "ἀναγκαιότατα ἔστ'"</note> not badly. **v. 9.** *From the* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν"</note>. Besides the homilies on Genesis, he had dictated thirteen tomes or volumes of continuous explanation on the first four chapters of Genesis. **v. 12.** *the* <note>original: "τὰς"</note> is redundant, see manuscript *the lesser*. **v. 16.** *indeed* <note>original: "δή"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *but* <note>original: "δέ"</note>. **v. 22.** *they say* <note>original: "φασί"</note>. See Diogenes Laertius, book seven: *a predicate is that which is predicated of someone,* etc. whence Suidas: *accusation and predicate*. **v. 46.** *pe.* read *pu.* **P. 45. v. 19.** *orderly* <note>original: "τεταγμένως"</note>. Both Thuanian manuscripts: *orderly*. **v. 29.** *to reconcile* <note>original: "καταλλάσσειν"</note>. Royal Manuscript: *condition* <note>original: "κατάστασιν"</note>. Here the Thuanian manuscripts fail, in whose place the books *Against Celsum* edited by the illustrious David Hoeschelius conveniently succeed.

**Chapter XV. p. 275. l. 6.** *Against Celsum*. **v. 7.** *the things of truth* <note>original: "τὰ τῆς ἀληθείας"</note>.] Hoeschelius reads *the truth*. But this is the true reading, which the manuscripts of his *Philocalia* also provide. **v. 19.** *to her* <note>original: "αὐτῇ"</note> is missing in the Philocalia of Hoeschelius. **v. 22.** *to contain us* <note>original: "ἡμῖν περιέχειν"</note>, which Gelenius also has, though obscurely; but I am not yet dissatisfied with it. **v. 24.** *and* <note>original: "καὶ"</note> is missing in the published editions of *Against Celsum*, but is held in the *Philocalia*; you will better judge this *disagreement* <note>original: "διαλογίαν"</note> of the manuscripts yourself, having inspected Hoeschelius's notes. **v. 30.** others: *of those returning*; badly. **v. 41.** in the same place: *let them take up* <note>original: "ἀναλάβωσιν"</note>. Gelenius: *let them perceive*; but the *Philocalia* of Hoeschelius acts with us. **P. 276. v. 2.** *of those feeling shame* <note>original: "αἰδουμένων"</note>. Philocalia of Hoeschelius: *of those perceiving*. **v. 7.** *with persuasion* <note>original: "πειθοῖς"</note> is the true reading before those others: another: *with persuasive words of wisdom*. another: *with the persuasive word of human wisdom*. **P. 5. l. 1.** *Against Celsum*. **v. 42.** *upon the* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῇ"</note>. Philocalia of Hoeschelius: *to those happening upon*. **v. 46.** *upon the body* <note>original: "ἐπὶ σῶ."</note> Philocalia of Hoeschelius: *whatsoever*. **P. 276. l. 6.** *Against Celsum*. **v. 28.** *many* <note>original: "πολλοί"</note>. in the same place: *by much* <note>original: "πολλῷ"</note>. read *many*, or *much better*. **v. 30.** *he commands* <note>original: "ἐπιτάσσει"</note>. in the same place: *he might command*. another: *he would command*—both wrongly. **v. 34.** *the... having become*.
