Another Ogygian flood in Attica, a third in Thessaly called the Deucalionean. These are very well known. However, the Alexandrian Presbyter <note>Clement of Alexandria</note> calls this last one "due to another care" <note>original: *δι’ ἑτέραν ἐπιμέλειαν*</note>; as to the time of the "conflagration" <note>original: *ἐκπύρωσις*</note> of Phaethon, see Book 1 of the *Stromata*. Hence the "appearance" <note>original: *ἐμφανισμός*</note> of Ida. v. 24. These things which the theologians passed over, because they are few, will be easily supplied, "to have more," etc. v. 46. "the following things" <note>original: *τὰ ἑξῆς*</note>. This is to be interpreted kindly both in Origen and in others. P. 11. v. 23. "for truth is dear" <note>original: *φίλη γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια*</note>. He looked toward that saying of Aristotle: "for while both are dear, it is a sacred duty to prefer the truth." <note>original: *ἀμφοῖν γὰρ ὄντοιν φίλοιν, ὅσιον προτιμᾷν τὴν ἀλήθειαν*</note> *Ethics*, Book 1, ch. 4. v. 43. "The secrets of the Vigils" <note>original: *Ἀγρυπνίων ἀπόῤῥητα*</note>. Those, namely, "concerning the immortality of souls," etc. "and the initiation into all kinds of lots in Hades according to virtue and vice" <gloss>from one side</gloss> <insert>or "from which things"</insert> all of which the Pythagoreans transferred to the Greeks. Suidas under the word "hieroglyphics" <note>original: *ἱερογλυφικά*</note>. v. 45. "to see" <note>original: *ἰδεῖν*</note>] others read "to say." v. 50. "matters" <note>original: *πράγματα*</note>] read "letters" <note>original: *γράμματα*</note>. Not without reason: they are both fables and letters. P. 12. v. 20. "chirpings" <note>original: *τερετίσματα*</note>] "To chirp" <note>original: *τερετίζειν*</note> belongs to crickets. "Chirpings and warblings" belong to flutes and the cithara. Here I had read "monstrous things." Read, *Who everywhere deride the subtleties of Plato*. For Timon in the *Silli* had satirized him with this mockery:

> The sweet-voiced cricket, a writer of equal rank, who from the 
> trees of Hecademus sends forth a lily-like voice.

P. 51. v. 5. the things following are abrupt up to "it may be similar." v. 5. P. 51. v. 6. read "by which he has made." others "or he has made." v. 11. "as against the impious," read "impiously" either by Eurymedon the Hierophant, or as Phavorinus says, by Demophilus. See more than one cause for the false accusation against him in Laertius, Book 5. # NOTES BY TARIN ON ORIGEN’S *PHILOCALIA* 70.

**v. 35.** Codex Thuanus <note>original: "Cod. Th." - a famous 17th-century manuscript collection</note> reads *of the speech*. **v. 51.** Codex Thuanus reads *give to me*. **P. 53. v. 9.** *of anger*] Ruffinus <note>Tyrannius Ruffinus, the 4th-century Latin translator of Origen</note> reads *of judgment*. **v. 14.** *in wickedness*.] Codex Thuanus reads *in injustice*. **v. 17.** with others, *glory*. **v. 20.** Codex Thuanus reads *standing by*. **v. 48.** commonly edited books read, *so that seeing they may see, and not perceive.* Codex Thuanus reads *they may not hear*. Ruffinus: *so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear, and understand.* Corrupted. **v. 54.** *is*] Supply from Codex Thuanus and Ruffinus *and in others*. Ruffinus: *and again in another place*. **P. 54. v. 25.** *we began*] The Thuanus Codex prefixed: *why God hardened the heart of Pharaoh*. **v. 16.** Codex Thuanus reads *he will be persuaded*. Ruffinus: *by these*. **v. 27.** It should altogether be read *he is disobedient, what need is there of the heart*. If however he resists, what need is there for his heart to be hardened, and that not just once? etc. **v. 22.** *him*] Ruffinus adds: *Except that it was certainly possible for him to be persuaded; nor would he be said to be hardened by another, unless he who was not previously hard. But if he was not hard of himself, it follows that he was not of an earthly nature, but such a one who could yield, being struck by signs and wonders.* **v. 47.** Codex Thuanus reads *to expect*. **v. 49.** *those*. The followers of Basilides <note>An early Gnostic teacher</note>. **v. 50.** *the*. The Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament God</note>. **P. 55. v. 7.** *firstborn*. Ruffinus: *primitive*. **v. 14.** *with a bare head* <note>meaning "openly" or "shamelessly"</note>. So often Chrysostom; so Gregory in *Apology 1*: *with a bare head, as the saying goes, rushing toward all lawlessness.* **v. 37.** *the raining one*] I would read *the rain*. Or if you refer *raining* to the one who waters. **v. 40.** read *they produced*. **v. 42.** *for*] Codex Thuanus: *for*. **v. 44.** *it becomes*. **v. 51.** *it is*. **v. 53.** *reproof*. The codex reads *still*. **P. 56. v. 2.** King's Codex: *being hardened*. **v. 7.** *heart*] Ruffinus reads *house*. **v. 19.** Codex Thuanus: *those who will fail*. **P. 282. v. 34.** *altogether*] Codex Thuanus: *again*. Ruffinus: *also*. **v. 41.** Codex Thuanus: *unaffected*. **v. 45.** *having sinned* Ruffinus adds, with whom the Prophet, making himself one, says: Isaiah 63. **P. 57. v. 8.** Codex Thuanus: *themselves*. **v. 34.** *immortality of the soul*. Understand that of which Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 15. Another Ruffinus. **P. 58. v. 4.** *fifty years*. Ruffinus: *sixty years*. **v. 43.** Codex Thuanus: *here*. **v. 16.** *by*] Codex Thuanus: *from*. and **v. 29.** *creator*] *farmer*. Ruffinus: *husbandman*. **v. 43.** Codex Thuanus: *desires*. **P. 59. v. 18.** in the Codex: *if*. **v. 22.** *the*] Codex Thuanus. **v. 24.** Ruffinus seems to have read *one ought not to hear, but as* etc. *this ought not to be understood in such a way*. **v. 37.** *not*] Codex reads. **v. 56.** read with the Codex and Ruffinus *to turn upward, they might be converted, and so be healed*. **P. 60. v. 31.** Codex: *they seek someone for someone*. **v. 30.** *better*] read: *less*. **v. 14.** *if indeed himself*] Codex: *if among themselves*. **P. 61. v. 1.** Codex: *firmly*. **v. 15.** Codex: *they had fallen*. **v. 17.** *they show*] perhaps *it is clear that*. **v. 26.** Codex: *in them*. **v. 44.** Codex: *of those*. **v. 44.** *having granted*. **v. 50.** *nothing*. **v. 51.** *already*. **P. 62. v. 17.** Codex reads *the*. **v. 23.** *in the middle*] thus Herillus said *the things between virtue and vice are indifferent*. As Miltiades of Chios called it *indifference*, Zeno *relaxations*, who also wanted *something to be predicated in the middle things*. **v. 35.** Codex: *for he says*. Psalm 126. **v. 54.** in the Codex: *and*. **P. 63. v. 27.** read with Codex Thuanus *by*. **v. 36.** *to a free man*] Codex: *honorably*. **v. 37.** *forever*. Codex: *the treaties having persuaded*. Aristotle, *Magna Moralia*, book 1, ch. 6. From this all human li-

# Notes of JOANNES TARINUS on ORIGEN’S Philocalia.

**Pamphilus. v. 39. unbegotten]** *unbegotten & begotten* <note>original: "ἀγένητα & γενητά"</note> God. Royal Manuscript. Damascenus, among others, explains the difference between these in his book *On the Orthodox Faith*. Zeno and Chrysippus <note>Famous Stoic philosophers</note> were the first to invent this distinction regarding matter. **P. 83. v. 16. the not]** correction: *that is, not*. **v. 28.** error in the printed book. **v. 32. for.** correction: *in*. **v. 34. if for.** printed book: *if for*. **v. 36. being carried.** book: *of those carrying*. **v. 45. in him** book: *himself*. **P. 84. v. 8.** in book: *to me*. **v. 12. he thinks.** book: *it seems to me*. **v. 19. I was hearing.** **v. 21. and to you.** book and correction: *and you seem to me*. & **22. it seems to you.** same verse, printed book: *to have happened & certain other things*. & **23. if not.** **v. 28. to say.** printed book: *having reasoned*. **v. 32. if not these.** the writing of the Royal Codex was this: *if not these things seem to be done*. marginal note: *it is necessary that these things do not seem to be done*. **v. 39. ships.** printed book: *ship*. **v. 50. let it become.** printed book: *let it be*. & **v. 51. or from that.** **v. 53. it becomes.** read with Codex Th.: *to become*. **P. 85. v. 17. to speak.** manuscripts: *to say*. same: manuscripts & correction: *beginning*. **v. 23. God.]** *Lord*. **v. 2.** correction: *wherever*. same verse: manuscripts: *by nature*. **v. 12.** manuscripts: *having*. & **v. 17. word.** **v. 42.** manuscript: *come now*, & **24. and those things.** **v. 39.** correction: *and spirit*. & **v. 42. which is.** **v. 47. impossible]** another Th.: *to exist weak among them*. same verse: correction: *it. was.* **P. 89. v. 1.** manuscripts: *being able*. **v. 15. let it be silenced.** **v. 27.** correction: *the heat to the cold*. **v. 36.** printed manuscripts: *it has*. & **36. destructive]** *overturning*. **v. 39. it is.** as also **41. v. 45. underlying.** **P. 90. v. 3. as he says.** who also at the end says, *so many things also the aforementioned author*. **v. 4. not obscure]** Who nevertheless was unknown to Jerome, and almost unknown to most writers. **v. 5. he might find]** *or these. having been said]* *lying*. **v. 6. in the.** in the third dialogue *concerning cause and knowledge of evils*. In which Eutropius maintains the persona of the judge. Nor indeed can there be any doubt but that the greatest Theologians excerpted from there; that this is one of theirs, not from the observation of some writer, is sufficiently proved to me both by its form and because it is found in three codices, I know not if in all. Wherefore Origen will not yield his property to these recoverers.

### Chapter XXV. Page 90. Philocalia.
**v. 9. he from.** **v. 4. from the.** These are different in the interpretation of Saint Jerome. **v. 13. of the commentaries]** That was a body of fifteen volumes, which *the Greek speech produced to nearly forty thousand lines or more* according to Jerome. **v. 17.** correction: *to himself*. **v. 18. he was well pleased.** printed Commentary: *God was well pleased*. **v. 21. the.** correction: *to the*, & *to the foreordained*. & **v. 33. in the unclear.** **v. 44. of the receptions.** **P. 91. v. 10. to him was.** **v. 13.** another Th.: *of absurdities*. **v. 16. having met beforehand.** **v. 23. and about.** **v. 24. in the same.** **v. 27. in the one being thought.** **v. 33. foreknowledge of God.** **v. 34. but since it was going to be]** This is the wise commentary of Justin Martyr: *Answer: and foreknowledge is not the cause of that which is going to be, but that which is going to be is the cause of the foreknowledge; for the future does not follow the foreknowledge, but the foreknowledge follows the future, and in no way is the one who foreknows the cause of the betrayal, but the betrayal is the cause of the Lord's foreknowledge.* Concerning the devil and the first man the reasoning is the same, says Origen both here and in Genesis, which was then at hand for all who followed after: Athanasius in the Oration *From the passions*: *and not because they say it, for this reason do the things that happen come to be, but because they are going to happen, for this reason they also foretell them, etc.* just as *as they happen we see them, and it is not because they are seen that they happen.* To Chrysostom in *On the obscurity of prophecies*, where he speaks of Judas: *Not because Christ foretold it did that man become a traitor, but because he was going to become a traitor, for this reason Christ foretold it.* And in Homily 60 on Matthew; also in Jerome, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, and others. same verse: *to become*. **v. 45. of logic.** And one may understand Logical contemplation, which is found in Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics*. **P. 92. v. 7. you were approaching.** **v. 20. they might be moved away.** **v. 23. upon the]** *from the being given*. **P. 93. v. 36. you might tear down.** **v. 41.** read with the codex: *it might suffice*.

### Chapter XXVI. P. 94. Philocalia.
**v. 2. but not, etc.** are missing in the Th. codex. **v. 6. earth]** correction: *to the*. does not exist. **v. 20. by]** *by*. correctly. **v. 21. fond of learning.** correction: *loving*. **v. 25. word]** *place*. **v. 35. good.** **v. 38.** correction: *and not these*. **46. those]** He understands Plato and Aristotle, whose partition this is: *of goods, some are in the soul, some in the body, and some external.* These indeed are Plato's peculiar things, three kinds again: *some external, some shared, some inherent.* To which those four kinds are recalled which the same man established: first *having virtue*, second *virtue*, third *body*, etc. fourth *competitive, underlying*, and such like. Then these are bipartite, in the book *On Laws*: *goods are double, some human, some divine.* which Theodoret examines in book 6 *On Providence*. Finally, *of goods some are for their own sake, others for the sake of other things*, which Aristotle took from his Master: *of all of which we say those concerning the soul are most sovereign.* Aristotle, chapter 8, book 1 of the *Nicomachean Ethics*. Otherwise Zeno and the Stoics. Basil in Epistle 42: *the only thing to be greatly desired and praised is this lasting good, and this is the honor toward God.* To which his brother <note>Gregory of Nyssa</note> is kin, in the Oration on the dead: *only from all things is it necessary to be added as beautiful; that which is always and to all similarly beheld in the nature of the beautiful, being always such, and for which there is no change toward external circumstances.* The same in Philo, *Concerning that he begat Noah*. Which is the mind of Origen. **P. 95. v. 9. about.** correction: *of the most difficult*. **v. 42. you]** *to you*. **v. 25. they might seek]** *they might bring*.
